Ohm's law connects three things you can measure on a resistor: the voltage across it, the current through it, and its resistance.
It says voltage equals current times resistance, V equals IR . Know any two and you can find the third.
Engineers use it to predict how much current a given voltage will push through a part.
Think of water flowing through a pipe. Pressure is the voltage, the flow rate is the current, and a narrow section of pipe is the resistance. More pressure gives more flow.
A narrower pipe gives less flow for the same pressure.
The picture breaks down for some parts, such as diodes (one-way valves for current), where doubling the pressure does not simply double the flow.
Current flows out of the source's + terminal, through R, and back.
Measured with the passive sign convention (current entering R's + end), V R = +IR and the resistor absorbs P = VI = 25 milliwatts.
Voltage (V): the electrical "push" between two points, measured in volts.
Current (I): how much electric charge (the "stuff" of electricity, carried by tiny particles called electrons) flows past a point each second, measured in amps (A).
Resistance (R): how strongly a part resists current, measured in ohms (Ω). Resistor: a part made to have a known, steady resistance.
kΩ and mA: kilo-ohm is 1,000 ohms, and milliamp is one thousandth of an amp.
Put 5 volts across a 1 kilohms resistor. Current is voltage divided by resistance: I equals 5 over 1000 equals 0. 005 amps, which is 5 milliamps .
Double the voltage to 10 volts and the current doubles to 10 milliamps. Keep 10 volts but double the resistance to 2 kilohms and the current falls back to 5 milliamps.
That is the whole idea.
"Ohm's law is V equals IR : the voltage across a resistor is the current through it times its resistance, so I equals V over R and R equals V over I as well.
5 volts across 1 kilohms is 5 milliamps. It means current is proportional to voltage, a straight-line I–V curve.
The caveat is that it only applies to ohmic, linear elements at a steady temperature. Diodes and LEDs aren't ohmic, and a bulb's resistance changes as it heats."

Ohm's law, conceptually. The question: Conceptually explain ohm's law.
A metal wire is full of free electrons that can move. A voltage pushes them along, but they keep bumping into the atoms of the metal, so they never speed up forever.
They settle at a steady average drift speed. A bigger push means a faster drift and more current, and resistance is how much the material gets in the way.
Picture a marble rolling down a tilted board covered in pegs. It bounces off pegs all the way down, so it travels at a steady average speed instead of accelerating.
Tilt the board twice as steeply and it moves about twice as fast. The tilt is the voltage, the pegs are the atoms, and the marble flow is the current.
Real electrons are far more numerous and the drift is very slow, but the logic is the same.
An electron (accent path) zig-zags between collisions with lattice ions (grey).
Each free flight bends slightly with the field, so although the motion is mostly random, there's a slow net drift.
That drift, times the enormous number of electrons, is the current.
Free electron: an electron in a metal that is not stuck to one atom and can carry current. Electric field: the push on each charge, caused by the voltage across the material.
Collision: a bump between an electron and an atom or impurity that wastes some of its energy. Drift speed: the slow average speed at which electrons move along the wire.
Resistance: how hard the material makes it for electrons to move.
Put 1 volts across a wire and 1 milliamps flows. Put 2 volts across it. The push is twice as big, so the drift speed is twice as big, and 2 milliamps flows.
The extra energy lost in the collisions becomes heat, which is why resistors get warm.
If the wire heats up, its atoms jiggle harder, collisions become more frequent, and the resistance rises. That is the whole idea.
"Voltage is the push, current is the flow, and resistance is how much the material fights it.
A voltage creates an electric field that pushes electrons, but they keep colliding with the atoms in the lattice, so they settle at an average drift speed proportional to the field.
Double the voltage, double the drift speed, double the current. That's why V equals IR is linear.
The collisions are also where the I to the 2R heat comes from, and why a hotter metal has higher resistance."

Basic circuit analysis laws. The question: What are some basic circuit analysis laws?
Circuit analysis rests on a small set of rules that let you find every voltage and current in a circuit. Ohm's law covers each single part.
Kirchhoff's two laws cover how parts connect. Shortcuts and theorems built on those three save time on bigger circuits.
Think of a network of roads. Cars do not vanish at an intersection, so the cars arriving equal the cars leaving. That is Kirchhoff's current law.
If you hike around a loop of trails and return to your start, your net change in height is zero. That is Kirchhoff's voltage law, with height standing in for voltage.
With those two bookkeeping rules plus a rule for each part, you can account for everything.
The analogy fails for fast signals, where loops can pick up extra voltage from changing magnetic fields.
Everything rests on KCL, KVL and the element laws.
The shortcuts and theorems are consequences you use for speed and intuition; nodal/mesh analysis is the brute-force method that always works.
Node: a point where two or more parts connect. KCL: (Kirchhoff's current law): the current flowing into a node equals the current flowing out.
KVL: (Kirchhoff's voltage law): going around any closed loop, the voltage rises and drops add up to zero.
Series / parallel: parts in one chain share a current; parts side by side share a voltage.
Thevenin equivalent: a whole network replaced by one battery-like source and one resistor.
Connect 12 volts across two 1 kilohms resistors in series. The total is 2 kilohms, so the current is 12 over 2000 equals 6 milliamps through both.
Each resistor uses up 6 volts of the push (its "voltage drop"). Check with KVL: 12 minus 6 minus 6 equals 0 . That is the whole idea.
"The core three are Ohm's law, KCL and KVL. KCL says currents into a node sum to zero, conservation of charge; KVL says voltages around a loop sum to zero, conservation of energy.
From those you get series and parallel rules and the voltage and current dividers.
For linear circuits you also have superposition and Thevenin/Norton equivalents, plus maximum power transfer.
For anything bigger I'd use nodal analysis, which is what SPICE does."

KCL and KVL explained. The question: What are KCL/KVL?
Kirchhoff's laws are two bookkeeping rules for circuits. The current law (KCL) says that at any junction, the current going in equals the current coming out.
The voltage law (KVL) says that if you go around any closed loop, the voltage rises and drops add up to zero. Together with Ohm's law, they let you solve circuits.
For the current law, picture water pipes meeting at a junction. Pipes can't store water there, so whatever flows in must flow out.
For the voltage law, picture a hiking loop that ends where it began. You climb some and descend some, but your total height change is zero.
Voltage works like height (the same idea as water pressure on the Ohm's law page), and the battery is the climb.
I₁ enters node B and splits into I₂ and I₃ (KCL). Loop L1 goes through the source, R₁ and R₂; loop L2 goes through R₂ and R₃. Each gives one KVL equation.
Node: a junction where wires or parts meet. Loop: any path through the circuit that returns to its starting point.
KCL: the currents into a node sum to zero, counting current that leaves as negative. In other words, in equals out. KVL: the voltages around a loop sum to zero.
Voltage drop: the voltage lost across a part as current passes through it.
KCL: 5 milliamps flows into a node, and one branch takes 2 milliamps. The other branches must carry the remaining 3 milliamps.
KVL: a 9 volts battery drives two resistors in series, and the resistors drop 3 volts and 6 volts. Going around the loop, 9 minus 3 minus 6 equals 0 . That is the whole idea.
"KCL says the currents into any node sum to zero, so what flows in must flow out. That's conservation of charge.
KVL says the voltages around any closed loop sum to zero, so the source voltage equals the sum of the drops. That's conservation of energy, because voltage is a potential.
With Ohm's law, those two let you solve any circuit. They assume a lumped circuit; if a loop links a changing magnetic field, you get an induced voltage that has to be modelled."

Solving KCL/KVL circuit problems. The question: Basic KCL/KVL circuit problems.
Solving a circuit problem is mostly following a routine. Label the nodes, pick one as ground (0 volts), and write KCL at each unknown node, using Ohm's law for each current.
That gives equations you solve for the node voltages. Then check that your answers make sense.
Imagine connected water tanks joined by pipes. The water level in each tank is its node voltage. Flow through a pipe depends on the level difference across it.
Once the levels settle, each tank has as much water flowing in as out. Writing that balance for each tank gives you the equations.
The analogy hides one thing: electrical current can run in either direction, and a negative answer just means it flows the other way.
The habit that prevents mistakes: set up, choose the cheapest method, then check. Interviewers notice the checking step more than the algebra.
Node voltage: the voltage at a node measured from ground. Ground: the node you choose to call 0 volts.
Nodal analysis: writing KCL at each unknown node and solving for the node voltages. Mesh analysis: writing KVL around loops and solving for the loop currents.
Series / parallel reduction: replacing resistors with one equivalent resistor to simplify first.
A 12 volts source feeds a 1 kilohms resistor to node A, and 2 kilohms runs from A to ground.
By Ohm's law, the current through each resistor is the voltage across it divided by its resistance.
KCL at A says current in equals current out: (12 minus V A) over 1000 equals V A over 2000 . Solving gives V A equals 8 volts. Check: the current is 4 milliamps on both sides.
That is the whole idea.
"I label nodes, pick a ground and assign current directions first. If the circuit reduces with series and parallel rules, I collapse it and use dividers.
Otherwise I use nodal analysis: KCL at each unknown node with each current written as voltage difference over resistance, then solve the equations.
Mesh analysis is the KVL alternative when there are many voltage sources. Finally I check that currents balance at every node and that source power equals resistor power."

Power equations: P = VI. The question: What is the equation to find power?
Power is how fast energy is being used or turned into heat. In an electrical part, it equals voltage times current, P equals VI , measured in watts.
Knowing the power tells you how hot a part gets and how fast a battery drains.
Think of a waterfall driving a water wheel. The power depends on how far the water falls (voltage) and how much water flows each second (current).
A tall waterfall with a trickle and a short one with a huge flow can deliver the same power.
Add Ohm's law and the same power can be written using only current and resistance, or only voltage and resistance.
Power pulses at twice the source frequency. For a resistor it never goes negative and averages V pI p/2 = 10 watts.
With a 60° phase shift it dips negative (energy flows back to the source) and averages half as much. A pure reactance swings symmetrically and averages zero.
Drag φ toward 90°: the negative lobes grow until the average (red line) reaches zero, and the red curve becomes the dashed reactance case.
Power (P): energy used per second, measured in watts (W). Energy: the capacity to do work or make heat, measured in joules (J). One watt is one joule per second.
Dissipation: power turned into heat in a part. Power rating: the most power a part can safely dissipate. Ohm's law: V equals IR .
Put 12 volts across a 1 kilohms resistor. The current is 12 over 1000 equals 12 milliamps. The power is 12 times 0. 012 equals 0. 144 watts, or 144 milliwatts .
Using the resistor form gives the same answer: V squared over R equals 144 over 1000 equals 0. 144 watts.
Many small resistors are rated well below that, so this one would overheat. That is the whole idea.
"Power is P equals VI , voltage times current, which is energy per second.
For a resistor you can substitute Ohm's law to get I to the 2R or V squared over R , whichever uses what you know.
For AC, average power is V rmsI rms cosine , so a pure capacitor or inductor averages zero.
I use it all the time to check resistor wattage, regulator heat like (V in minus V out) times I for an LDO, and battery life."
Quick check. A 5 volts, 50% duty square wave drives a 10 ohms resistor. What is the average power?
Why losses scale with current. The question: Why is power loss often due to current, not voltage?
Any wire, circuit-board trace (a flat copper track), or connector has a little resistance, and the power it wastes as heat is I to the 2R .
The resistance is fixed, so the loss depends on the current, and it grows with the square of the current.
For a given power delivered, a higher voltage needs less current, so the loss drops.
Imagine moving a fixed amount of cargo along a rough road. Bigger trucks mean fewer trips, so there is less wear on the road.
Sending power at higher voltage is like using bigger trucks: the same power moves with less current. The analogy understates it, though.
Wear grows with the number of trips, but electrical loss grows with the square of the current.
The same current I flows through the load and through both halves of the wiring (KCL). The load gets V·I.
The wires, with total resistance R w, burn I²R w no matter what the voltage is.
Conduction loss: power wasted as heat because current flows through resistance. I to the 2R loss: the power lost in a resistance R carrying current I .
Power ( P equals VI ): voltage times current. Voltage drop: the small voltage lost along the wire, equal to IR .
Switching loss: energy lost each time a switch turns on or off, which depends on voltage too.
Deliver 100 watts through wires with 0. 5 ohms total. At 10 volts the current is 10 amps, so the loss is 10 squared times 0. 5 equals 50 watts.
At 20 volts the current is 5 amps, so the loss is 5 squared times 0. 5 equals 12. 5 watts. Doubling the voltage cut the loss to one quarter. That is the whole idea.
"Losses in wires, traces and switches are I to the 2R , and the resistance is fixed by the conductor, so current is what you control.
For a given power, P equals VI , so raising voltage cuts current proportionally and cuts conduction loss with the square.
That's why the grid uses high voltage and USB-PD goes to 20 volts. The V squared over R form doesn't contradict it, because that V is the drop across the wire.
Switching and dielectric losses do scale with voltage, so it's a trade-off."

Voltage divider: draw, equation, derivation. The question: Draw a voltage divider circuit. What is the voltage divider equation? Derive it.
A voltage divider is two resistors in a row that turn a bigger voltage into a smaller one.
You connect the big voltage across both resistors and take your output from the point between them.
The output is a fixed fraction of the input, and the two resistor values set that fraction.
Think of a staircase that drops 9 meters from top to bottom. If you stop at a landing partway down, you have only dropped part of the height.
Two equal flights put the landing at half height. A short flight on top and a long flight below put the landing high up.
Voltage "drops" across resistors the same way height drops across flights of stairs: the bigger resistor takes the bigger share of the drop.
The output is the voltage across R₂ , measured from the middle node to ground. With nothing attached at V out, the same current I flows through both resistors.
Voltage (V): the electrical "push", measured between two points. Like height difference on the staircase. Current (I): how much charge flows per second, measured in amps.
Like how many people walk down the stairs per second. Resistance (R): how hard a part makes it for current to flow, measured in ohms (Ω). Ohm's law: V equals I times R .
The voltage across a resistor equals the current through it times its resistance. In series: connected end to end, so the same current must pass through both.
Ground: the point we call 0 volts and measure everything else from.
Put 10 volts across two equal 1 kilohms resistors in series. The same current flows through both, and they are identical, so each one drops the same voltage: 5 volts each.
The point between them sits at 5 volts , half the input. Now make the bottom resistor 3 kilohms and keep the top one at 1 kilohms.
The bottom resistor is 3 parts out of 4 total, so it gets 3/4 of the voltage: the middle point sits at 7. 5 volts .
That is the whole idea: the output is the input multiplied by "bottom resistor over total resistance".
"A voltage divider is two resistors in series across V in , with the output taken across the bottom one: V out equals V in R 2 over (R 1 plus R 2) .
It comes straight from series current: I equals V in over (R 1 plus R 2) , and V out equals IR 2 . The key caveat is that it assumes no load current.
A load appears in parallel with R 2 and pulls the output down, so dividers are for setting references and scaling signals, not for powering things."

RLC circuit analysis basics. The question: Basic RLC circuit analysis.
An RLC circuit combines a resistor (R), an inductor (L) and a capacitor (C).
The capacitor and the inductor both store energy, and their opposition to current changes with frequency in opposite ways.
In a series RLC circuit, at one special frequency, the resonant frequency, their effects cancel and only the resistor limits the current.
The resistor also decides whether the circuit rings after a sudden change or settles smoothly.
Picture a child on a swing. The swing wants to go back and forth at its own natural rate. That is resonance.
Friction is the resistor: with a lot of friction the swing creeps to rest, and with very little it keeps swinging for many cycles. Pushing at the natural rate builds a big swing.
The capacitor is like the swing at the top of its arc, holding energy as height. The inductor is like the swing at the bottom, holding energy as speed.
Energy trades between them every cycle.
One current flows through all three elements.
The resistor dissipates, the inductor stores energy in its magnetic field (½Li²), and the capacitor stores it in its electric field (½Cv²).
Capacitor / inductor: a capacitor stores charge; an inductor is a coil of wire that resists changes in current. and "What is inductance?"
Frequency: how many times per second a back-and-forth (AC) signal repeats, in hertz (Hz).
Reactance / impedance: a capacitor's or inductor's opposition to AC, in ohms; impedance is the total, including resistance. and "Inductor impedance equation".
Damping: how quickly the ringing dies out. Q (quality factor): how sharp the resonance is. High Q means little damping.
Take a series circuit with 20 ohms, 1 millihenries and 1 microfarads. It resonates at f 0 equals 1 over (2 pi square root of LC ) , about 5 kilohertz.
There both reactances are about 31. 6 ohms, so they cancel and the impedance is just 20 ohms. A 1 volts source then drives 50 milliamps. That is the whole idea.
"Treat R, L and C as impedances: R , j omega L and 1 over j omega C .
In series, the reactances cancel at omega 0 equals 1 over square root of LC , so impedance drops to R and current peaks.
In the time domain you get a second-order equation, and the damping ratio equals R over 2 square root of C over L decides the response: overdamped above 1, critically damped at 1, ringing below 1.
Q equals 1 over (2 ) tells you how sharp the resonance is and how much it rings."

LPF, HPF and BPF analysis basics. The question: Basic LPF/BPF/HPF filter analysis.
A filter lets some frequencies through and blocks others. A low-pass filter (LPF) passes slow signals and blocks fast ones. A high-pass filter (HPF) does the opposite.
A band-pass filter (BPF) passes only a middle range. A resistor and capacitor can build the simplest ones, because a capacitor's behavior changes with frequency.
Think of a car's suspension driving down a road. It smooths out quick, small bumps but follows the slow rise and fall of the hills. That is a low-pass filter.
A high-pass filter would be the reverse: it would ignore the hills and react only to the quick bumps.
Both are really just a voltage divider ("Voltage divider: draw, equation, derivation") whose bottom or top part changes with frequency.
Same two parts, swapped positions. In the LPF, the output is across the capacitor, which shorts high frequencies to ground.
In the HPF, the capacitor sits in the signal path and blocks DC, so only changes get through.
Frequency: how many cycles per second a signal repeats, in hertz (Hz). Corner (cutoff) frequency: the point where the output has fallen to 0. 707 of the input.
For an RC filter, f c equals 1 over (2 pi RC) . Capacitor: a part that stores charge. It blocks steady, one-direction (DC) current but passes fast changes.
and "Capacitor impedance equation". dB (decibel): a way to say how much a signal shrinks. minus 3 decibels is about 0. 707 of the input, and minus 20 decibels is one tenth.
Roll-off: how steeply the output falls past the corner, here 20 decibels (ten times smaller) per tenfold rise in frequency.
Build a low-pass with a 1 kilohms resistor in series and a 159 nanofarads capacitor to ground.
Then f c equals 1 over (2 pi times 1000 times 159 times 10 to the -9) , about 1 kilohertz. At 100 hertz almost everything passes. At 1 kilohertz the output is 0. 707 of the input.
At 10 kilohertz it is only about 10%. That is the whole idea.
"I treat a filter as an impedance divider.
An RC low-pass, R in series and C to ground, gives H equals 1 over (1 plus j omega RC) : unity at DC, minus 3 decibels and minus 45° at f c equals 1 over 2 pi RC , then minus 20 decibels per decade.
Swap R and C for a high-pass with the same corner.

For a bandpass, cascade a high-pass and a low-pass with enough impedance separation or a buffer, or use a series RLC with output across R, centred at 1 over 2 pi square root of LC with bandwidth R over 2 pi L ."

Passive components' parasitics. The question: Passive components' parasitics.
A real resistor, capacitor (a part that stores charge) or inductor (a coil that resists changes in current) is never purely that one thing.
Each also contains small amounts of the other two, caused by its shape, wire legs (leads) and materials. These unwanted extras are called parasitics.
They are small at low frequency, but at high frequency they take over and make the part behave differently from its label.
Think of a spring from a hardware store. In theory it only stretches and pushes back. In reality, the metal also has weight, and it rubs a little as it moves.
Move it slowly and you only notice the springiness. Shake it very fast and the weight dominates.
A capacitor is the same: at high enough frequency, its hidden inductance matters more than its capacitance.
At low frequency the capacitor is an open circuit and the inductor a short, so you see R.
At high frequency C p shunts the resistor and the part becomes capacitive; for a large R the C p effect arrives first.
Parasitic: an unwanted extra property, like stray inductance in a capacitor. ESR: equivalent series resistance, the small resistance hidden inside a capacitor.
ESL: equivalent series inductance, the small inductance of a capacitor's leads and plates. DCR: the resistance of an inductor's copper wire to steady (DC) current.
Self-resonant frequency: where a part's hidden inductance and capacitance cancel and it stops acting like itself.
A 100 nanofarads capacitor has about 0. 5 nanohenries of ESL. Its capacitance and ESL cancel each other (resonate) at 1 over (2 pi square root of LC ) , about 22 megahertz.
Below that, it acts as a capacitor and works as you drew it. Above 22 megahertz it acts as an inductor, so it no longer soaks up fast noise the way the schematic suggests.
That is the whole idea.
"Every real passive has the other two elements in it. A resistor has a little series inductance and a little shunt capacitance.
A capacitor has ESR and ESL, so above its self-resonant frequency, around 20 megahertz for a small 100 nanofarads part, it acts like an inductor.
An inductor has winding resistance and winding capacitance, so above its self-resonance it acts like a capacitor.
They come from geometry: lead length, plate loops, and turn-to-turn spacing. So I always check the impedance curve, not just the nominal value."

Basic op-amp circuit analysis. The question: Basic opamp circuit analysis.
An op-amp (operational amplifier) is a chip that amplifies the voltage difference between its two inputs, plus (+) and minus (minus ), by a huge amount.
When you feed part of its output back to the minus, or inverting, input (negative feedback), it adjusts its output until the two inputs are at nearly the same voltage.
The inputs draw almost no current. That lets two resistors set the gain precisely, without depending on the op-amp's own huge gain.
Think of a thermostat. It compares the room temperature to your setting and keeps heating until the difference is zero.
An op-amp does the same with voltage: it keeps changing its output until the difference between its two inputs is almost zero. Whatever output that takes is your answer.
The analogy fails if the target is out of reach. The op-amp's output can't go beyond its supply rails.
The inverting node sits at 0 volts (virtual ground), so I in = V in/R 1 and it must all flow through R f. Gain = -R f/R 1 = -10; input resistance is R 1 = 1 kilohms.
Negative feedback: sending the output back to the inverting input so errors get corrected. Virtual ground: an input held at 0 volts by feedback without being connected to ground.
Gain: output voltage divided by input voltage. Rails: the supply voltages, which are the limits of the output. KCL: the currents into a node sum to zero.
Build an inverting amplifier with R1 = 1 kilohms in and Rf = 10 kilohms in feedback, with the plus input grounded. Apply 0. 5 volts.
Feedback holds the minus input at 0 volts (a virtual ground), so 0. 5 milliamps flows through R1. None enters the op-amp, so all of it goes through Rf and drops 0.
5 milliamps times 10 kilohms equals 5 volts. The output is minus 5 volts , a gain of minus 10. That is the whole idea.
"First check for negative feedback. If it's there, the op-amp holds both inputs at the same voltage and they draw no current, so I just do KCL at the inverting node.
For an inverting amp the input current Vin over R1 flows through Rf, so gain is minus Rf over R1.
For a non-inverting amp the feedback divider sets the inverting node equal to Vin, so gain is one plus Rf over R1. Same method for summing amps and integrators.
Then I'd check real limits: rails, gain-bandwidth, and slew rate."

Resistor symbol (US vs IEC). The question: Draw the symbol for a resistor.
A schematic symbol is a quick drawing that stands for a real part. The resistor has two common styles.
In US-style drawings it is a zigzag line, and in IEC (international, common in Europe) drawings it is a plain rectangle. They mean exactly the same thing.
A resistor has no polarity, so it works the same either way around.
Think of road signs, which look a little different from country to country but carry the same message. The zigzag and the rectangle are two dialects for one idea.
Small changes to the picture, like an arrow added through or into the body, tell you the resistor is a special type.
The analogy is loose, since the symbol also carries labels like R1 and 10 k that make it unambiguous.
Same part, two drawing conventions. Neither has polarity, so you can rotate or mirror it freely. CAD libraries let you choose which one the schematic uses.
Schematic symbol: the standard drawing used in place of a real part. Reference designator: the label like R1 or R2 that names one specific part.
Polarity: having a required direction, like a battery. Resistors have none. Potentiometer: a variable resistor with three terminals, including a movable wiper.
Thermistor: a resistor whose value changes with temperature.
Draw a short zigzag with a wire at each end. Write R1 next to it and 10 k beneath it. That is a complete resistor on a schematic.
If you flip it around, nothing changes, because it has no polarity. Now add an arrow pointing at the middle of the zigzag. It becomes a potentiometer with three terminals.
That is the whole idea.
"A resistor is a zigzag line in US-style schematics, or a plain rectangle in IEC drawings. It's a two-terminal part with no polarity.
I label it with a reference designator like R1 and a value like 10 k. A potentiometer adds an arrow to the middle for the wiper, giving three terminals.
A thermistor adds a diagonal line and a little t. I'd also mark junction dots so the connections are clear."
Quick check. Which statement is true about a fixed resistor's schematic symbol?
What resistance is. The question: What is resistance?
Resistance is how strongly a material opposes the flow of current. We measure it as the voltage across a part divided by the current through it, R equals V over I , in ohms.
One ohm means one volt for each amp. The opposition comes from the electrons bumping into atoms, which also turns some of their energy into heat.
Picture people walking down a corridor. A longer corridor means more chances to bump into things, so it is harder going.
A wider corridor lets more people through, so it is easier. Rough, crowded flooring makes it harder still.
Resistance behaves the same way: it grows with length, shrinks as the conductor gets thicker (a bigger cross-section area), and depends on the material.
The analogy only captures the idea; real electrons are not individual walkers.
The resistor's I–V is a straight line, so V/I equals dV/dI everywhere.
The diode curve is nonlinear: V/I (the line from the origin to the point) is very different from the slope dV/dI = V T/I, which sets its small-signal resistance.
Ohm (Ω): the unit of resistance. One volt per amp. Resistivity ( ): how strongly a material resists current, regardless of its shape.
Conductor / insulator: a material with low resistivity, like copper, or very high resistivity, like glass. Joule heating: the heat produced when current flows through resistance.
Ohm's law: V equals IR .
Put 2 volts across a part and measure 4 milliamps. Then R equals 2 over 0. 004 equals 500 ohms. For shape, imagine a 1 m wire with 10 ohms.
A 2 m piece of the same wire is 20 ohms, because it is twice as long. A 2 m piece with twice the cross-section area is back to 10 ohms. That is the whole idea.
"Resistance is the opposition to current: R equals V over I, measured in ohms.

What resistance depends on. The question: What does resistance depend on?
A part's resistance depends mainly on its shape and its material: R equals L over A . Longer wire means more resistance. A thicker wire means less. The material sets .
Beyond that, resistance also changes with temperature, frequency, light, stretching (strain) and age, and which one matters depends on the application.
Imagine a highway. A longer road takes longer to get through, so it resists traffic more. More lanes let more cars through, so it resists less.
A rough surface slows everyone, like a different material. In hot weather the road could get worse, like metals whose resistance rises when heated.
The analogy is loose: real resistance is about electron collisions, not lanes.

Realistic resistor model and parasitics. The question: Draw a realistic circuit model for a resistor. What are the parasitics and where do they come from?
An ideal resistor has only resistance.
A real one also has a little inductance (a tendency to resist quick changes in current), because current through its leads and body makes a magnetic field.
It also has a little capacitance between its two ends, which lets fast signals leak across.
The standard model is the resistance R in series with a small inductance, with a small capacitance across the whole thing. At low frequency only R matters.
At high frequency the extras take over.
Imagine a toll booth on a road. The booth is the resistance. A heavy revolving door at the booth resists quick changes in traffic, like the inductance.
A side road runs around the booth, like the capacitance. At slow speeds, traffic uses the booth. At high speeds, cars take the side road and never meet the booth.
The analogy is loose, but it shows the idea of a path that only fast signals take.
R and L s carry the DC and low-frequency current; C p sits across both and provides the high-frequency bypass. The dashed box is the physical package, whose terminals are 1 and 2.
Series inductance ( L s ): the small inductance of the leads and body. It matters most for low-value resistors.
Parallel capacitance ( C p ): the small capacitance across the two terminals. It matters most for high-value resistors.
Corner frequency: the frequency where the extra part starts to change the impedance noticeably.
Impedance: the total opposition to an AC (back-and-forth) signal, in ohms, including these extras. Parasitic: an unwanted hidden property.

Now take a 10 ohms resistor with 1 nanohenries in series. Its inductive corner is R over (2 pi L s) , about 1. 6 gigahertz. That is the whole idea.

High-value resistors go capacitive first: 10 k with 0. 1 picofarads has a corner near 160 megahertz. Low values go inductive.
The best behaved is near the square root of L over C, roughly 80 ohms for a chip. Wirewound parts are the worst because they're coils."

Common resistor values (E-series). The question: What are some common resistor values?
You cannot buy a resistor of every possible value. Manufacturers make a limited set of standard values called the E-series.
Each value is a fixed percentage bigger than the last (about 21% in the E12 series), so the steps grow as the values grow.
The spacing is set by the part's tolerance, so any value you want is close to a standard one.
Think of shoe sizes. Shops do not stock every possible foot length. They stock sizes spaced so that each one fits a range of feet well enough.
A finer series, like half sizes, fits more closely but means more sizes to stock. Resistor series work the same way.
More values per decade means a closer fit and a tighter-tolerance part.
The more values per decade, the closer you can get to any target. E12/E24/E96 are the points where the grid error matches the usual 10 %, 5 %, 1 % tolerances.
E-series: the standard set of preferred values, such as E12, E24 and E96. The number is how many values per decade.
Decade: a tenfold range, such as 10 to 100 ohms or 1 kilohms to 10 kilohms. Tolerance: how far a real resistor may be from its labeled value, such as 5% or 1%.
Preferred value: a value in a standard series, which is cheap and easy to buy. Voltage divider: two resistors that set a ratio.
E12 has 12 values per decade: 10, 12, 15, 18, 22, 27, 33, 39, 47, 56, 68, 82. Say you need 13 kilohms. E12 has no 13, but a 12 kilohms part at 10% may really be anywhere from 10.
8 kilohms to 13. 2 kilohms, so if your design can live with that, it will do. E24 has 13 exactly, with a 5% tolerance. That is the whole idea.
"Resistor values come from the E-series: preferred numbers spaced logarithmically in each decade.
E12 has 12 values and goes with 10 percent parts, E24 has 24 for 5 percent, and E96 has 96 for 1 percent. The spacing makes neighbors overlap within tolerance.
The ones I use constantly are 10, 100, 1k, 4. 7k, 10k, 100k, 1 meg, plus 22 or 33 ohms for series termination.
For dividers I use E96 and then compute the real output with the actual values."

Common resistor packages and sizes. The question: What are some common resistor packages and sizes?
Surface-mount (SMD) resistors come in standard sizes. Each size has a four-digit code that gives its length and width.
A bigger resistor can shed more heat, so it can handle more power and a higher voltage. A smaller one takes less board space but handles less power.
Think of pots and pans on a stove. A large pan has more surface to spread and shed heat, so it copes with a bigger flame. A tiny pan on a big flame scorches fast.
Resistors are the same: the larger body can dissipate more power before it overheats.
The analogy leaves out voltage, which also limits small parts because the gap between their ends is short.
Body sizes grow from 0402 to 2512; the darker ends are the metal terminations.
Larger bodies carry heat to bigger pads, which is what raises the power rating (a 2512 has about 40 times the body area of a 0402 and roughly 10 to 20 times the typical power rating).
SMD: surface-mount device, a part soldered flat onto the board surface. Package code (0603): the size in hundredths of an inch, so 0603 is 0. 06 by 0. 03 inch, about 1. 6 by 0.
8 mm. Power rating: the most heat the part can dissipate continuously. Derating: using the part well below its rating, often at half, for a safety margin.
Through-hole: a part with leads that go through holes in the board.

A 0603 is about 0. 1 watts, and a 1206 is about 0. 25 watts, so both are too small. A 2512 at about 1 watts works. That is the whole idea.

Power rating scales with size, roughly 1/16 to 1/10 watt for 0402 and 0603, 1/4 watt for 1206, 1 watt for 2512, and voltage rating scales too.

Resistor failure modes. The question: What are some common failure modes of a resistor?
Resistors are simple parts, and most failures are simple too.
The most common is an open circuit: the resistor gets too hot or takes a surge, and the element burns through like a broken wire.
Less often, the value slowly drifts over time, or the part cracks mechanically from board flex.
Think of a rope holding a weight. Overload it and it frays and snaps, which is the burnout. A sudden jerk can snap it even if the average load is small, which is a surge.
Over years, it slowly stretches, which is drift. Bend it back and forth and it fails at the bend, like a crack from board flex.
The analogy is incomplete: a resistor is overloaded by heat, not by pulling.
Above 70 degrees Celsius the allowed power falls linearly to zero at the maximum film temperature (155 degrees Celsius in this example; many parts use 125 degrees Celsius).
An enclosure at 100 degrees Celsius allows only about 65 % of the rating before any additional derating.
Open circuit: a break in the path, so no current flows. It is the usual way a resistor fails. Drift: a slow change in value over time because of heat, humidity or aging.
Derating: running a part well below its power rating, often at 50%. Surge / pulse rating: how much short, high-energy burst the part can take.
Thermal overstress: heat damage from dissipating more than the part's rating.
Put 5 volts across a 100 ohms resistor in a 0603 package rated at about 0. 1 watts. It dissipates 5 squared over 100 equals 0. 25 watts, which is 2. 5 times the rating.
It runs hot, browns, and eventually burns open. Then the circuit behaves as if the resistor were removed.
The fix is a larger package, such as 2512, so the part runs well within its rating. That is the whole idea.
"The dominant failure for a resistor is open circuit from overheating or a pulse.
Others are drift from heat, humidity or aging, mechanical cracking from board flex or thermal cycling, sulfur corrosion of silver terminations, and rarely a short from arcing or contamination.
I prevent them by derating power to about half, checking voltage and pulse ratings, picking anti-surge or anti-sulfur parts when needed, and keeping them away from flex areas."

Pull-up and pull-down resistors. The question: What are pullup/pulldown resistors? How do you spec them?
A pull-up or pull-down resistor ties a signal line to the supply voltage or to ground through a resistor.
That gives the line a known default state when nothing else is driving it. A pull-up gives a default high. A pull-down gives a default low.
When something actually drives the line, it overrides the resistor, because the resistor is deliberately weak.
Imagine a flag on a light spring. With no one touching it, the spring holds the flag up. That is the pull-up.
If you push the flag down, it goes down easily, and it pops back when you let go.
The analogy breaks in one place: while you hold the flag down, the spring keeps pulling, which is like the wasted current through the resistor.
With the switch open, no current flows (apart from the input's leakage) and R PU holds the node at V DD.
Closing the switch pulls it to 0 volts and draws V DD/R PU, here 330 microamps at 3. 3 volts.
Floating: not connected to anything, so the line picks up noise and has no reliable value.
Logic high / low: the two states of a digital line, near the supply voltage or near ground. Pull-up / pull-down: a resistor to the supply or to ground that sets the default state.
Open-drain: an output that can only pull the line low. It needs a pull-up to get high again. Weak: a high enough resistance that any real driver can overpower it.
Connect a button between a microcontroller input (a pin on a small computer chip) and ground, with a 10 kilohms pull-up to 3. 3 volts.
With the button open, no current flows, so the pin reads 3. 3 volts (high). Press the button and the pin is tied to ground, so it reads 0 volts (low).
The current through the resistor is 3. 3 over 10 000 equals 0. 33 milliamps. That is the whole idea.

I size it between two limits: small enough for rise time (RC) and to beat leakage, big enough that the current when pulled low is acceptable, V over R, and within the driver's sink rating.
Typical values are 10 k for control lines, 4. 7 k for I2C, and 100 k for low-power or gate pull-downs."

Capacitor schematic symbols. The question: Draw the symbol for a capacitor.
A capacitor is a part that stores electric charge. Its symbol is two short parallel lines with a gap between them and a wire to each line.
It is a cartoon of the real part: two metal plates separated by an insulator.
Some capacitors have a required direction, and their symbol adds a mark to show which side is positive.
Picture two sheets of metal facing each other, with a thin layer of insulating material between them, like a sandwich with a gap in the middle.
The two lines are the two slices of bread seen from the side. The wires connect each slice to the rest of the circuit.
For a part that must be hooked up one way, picture a sandwich with a labeled top. The picture shows the structure only, not the size or the technology.
The two straight plates mean "either terminal can be positive".
In the polarized symbol, the "+" sits beside the straight plate and the curved plate is the negative (cathode) side.
Plate: one of the two conductors in a capacitor. Dielectric: the insulating layer between the plates.
Polarized: having a required direction, like most electrolytic and tantalum capacitors. Electrolytic: a capacitor type with high capacitance that is usually polarized.
Reference designator: the label such as C1 that names one part.
Draw two equal parallel lines with a gap between them. Add a wire to the middle of each line. Label it C1 and 100 nanofarads.
That is a ceramic capacitor (a common small type), and it works either way around.
For a 10 microfarads electrolytic, mark a plus sign next to one plate, or draw one plate curved, and connect the plus side to the more positive voltage. That is the whole idea.

You label it C 1 with a value like 100 nanofarads.
For electrolytic or tantalum parts there's a polarized symbol: one plate is curved, or drawn as a box in IEC style, and there's a plus sign on the positive side.
That matters because those parts are damaged if you reverse-bias them."

What capacitance is. The question: What is capacitance?
Capacitance tells you how much charge a device stores for each volt across it: C equals Q over V . It is measured in farads.
A capacitor is two conductors separated by an insulator. Put a voltage across it and charge collects on the two sides.
Capacitors are used to store energy briefly and to smooth out voltage changes.
Think of a bucket. The water level is the voltage, the amount of water is the charge, and the width of the bucket is the capacitance.
A wide bucket takes a lot of water to raise the level by one centimeter. A narrow one takes little. Likewise, a large capacitance takes a lot of charge to change its voltage.
The ideal bucket never overflows, but a real capacitor has a maximum voltage rating.
For an ideal capacitor, Q vs V is a straight line through the origin and the slope is C. A bigger capacitor stores more charge for the same voltage.
The area under each line (½QV) is the stored energy.
Charge (Q): the amount of electric charge stored, measured in coulombs. One coulomb is the charge of about 6 times 10 to the 18 electrons. Farad (F): the unit of capacitance.
One farad is one coulomb per volt. Real parts are pF to mF. Plates: the two conductors that hold the opposite charges. Dielectric: the insulator between the plates.
It sets how much capacitance you get. Current into a capacitor: i equals C dv over dt , where dv over dt means how many volts per second the voltage changes.
Changing the voltage takes current and time.
Charge a 1 microfarads capacitor to 5 volts. It holds Q equals CV equals 1 micro F times 5 volts equals 5 micro C . To charge it, push 1 milliamps into it.
That raises the voltage by 1 volts every millisecond, so it takes 5 milliseconds to reach 5 volts. The voltage cannot jump, because charge takes time to arrive.
That is the whole idea.
"Capacitance is how much charge something stores per volt: C equals Q over V , measured in farads.
It's set by geometry and material, so for parallel plates it's A over d : bigger area, thinner gap or a higher-permittivity dielectric all increase it.
The energy lives in the electric field, 1 over 2 CV squared .
And because i equals C dv over dt , you need current to change a capacitor's voltage, which is why capacitors hold rails steady and why stray capacitance slows down edges."

Dielectrics and permittivity. The question: What is a dielectric?
A dielectric is an insulator that does not conduct, but its atoms can shift slightly when an electric field is applied.
That small shift partly cancels the field from the charges on the plates. So for the same voltage, the plates can hold more charge, which means more capacitance.
The number that says how much more is called the relative permittivity.
Picture rows of tiny compass needles between two plates. With no field, they point every which way. Apply a field and they all turn to line up.
Their alignment creates a small field of their own that works against the main field.
With part of the push canceled, you can pile more charge onto the plates before the voltage reaches the same value.
Real materials also shift electron clouds and ions, not just needles.
Each molecule's charge shifts so its negative end faces the positive plate.
Inside the bulk the dipoles' charges cancel, but at each surface an uncancelled layer of bound charge remains, opposite in sign to the nearby plate.
That bound layer cancels part of the plate's field.
Insulator: a material with almost no free charges, so it does not carry current. Polarization: the slight shifting or turning of charges inside an insulator in a field.
Relative permittivity ( r ): the factor by which a dielectric multiplies capacitance compared with vacuum. Air is about 1.
Breakdown strength: the field at which the insulator fails and conducts. It sets the voltage rating. Capacitance: charge held per volt.
Take two 1 cm by 1 cm plates with a 0. 1 mm air gap.
The capacitance is C equals 0 r A over d ( 0 is a fixed constant of nature, A the plate area, d the gap), which works out to about 8. 85 picofarads.
Fill the gap with FR-4 circuit board material, where r is about 4. 3, and the same plates give about 38 picofarads. Nothing else changed, only the material.
That is the whole idea.
"A dielectric is an insulator that polarizes in an electric field: no free charges flow, but bound charges shift and molecular dipoles line up.
In a capacitor that polarization partly cancels the field, so the plates hold more charge per volt. That's the relative permittivity r , multiplying capacitance in 0 r A over d .
The dielectric also sets the voltage rating through its breakdown strength, plus losses and stability. So it's why C0G is stable and X7R is dense but drifts."

Capacitor impedance equation. The question: What is the equation for impedance of a capacitor?
Impedance is how much a part opposes AC (alternating current, which keeps reversing direction, like a wave). For a capacitor, the opposition gets smaller as the frequency goes up.
At DC (steady current in one direction) it is infinite, so it blocks current. At very high frequency it is nearly zero, so it passes current easily.
Its size is 1 over (2 pi f C) , where f is the frequency and C the capacitance.
Imagine a rubber sheet stretched across a water pipe. A steady push stretches the sheet and then no more water flows, so DC is blocked.
If you push back and forth quickly, the sheet flexes with each push and water moves on both sides. The faster you push, the more easily it passes.
A bigger sheet, meaning more capacitance, also passes more easily. The analogy ignores the 90 degree phase shift that real capacitors add.
At 1 kilohertz, the current peaks a quarter period (0. 25 milliseconds) before the voltage.
Current is largest when the voltage is crossing zero (steepest slope) and zero when the voltage is at its peak (flat slope), which is exactly i = C dv/dt.
Impedance (Z): the AC opposition to current, measured in ohms. Reactance: the part of impedance from a capacitor or inductor. It depends on frequency.
Frequency ( f ): cycles per second. The symbol omega is 2 pi f . Phase: the timing offset between voltage and current.
For a capacitor, current peaks a quarter cycle (90°) before voltage. Open / short: no current at all, or no voltage drop at all.
Take a 100 nanofarads capacitor. At 1 kilohertz, Z equals 1 over (2 pi times 1000 times 100 times 10 to the -9) , about 1. 6 kilohms.
Raise the frequency by 1,000 times to 1 megahertz and the impedance falls by 1,000 times, to about 1. 6 ohms. That is the whole idea.
"A capacitor's impedance is 1 over (j omega C) , or -j over ( omega C) , with omega equals 2 pi f .
It comes from i equals C dv over dt : for a sinusoid, the derivative is multiplication by j omega .
The magnitude 1 over (2 pi fC) drops with frequency, so it's open at DC and approaches a short at high frequency, and the phase is minus 90°, meaning current leads voltage.
For example, 100 nanofarads at 1 megahertz is about 1. 6 ohms."

Capacitor differential equation. The question: What is the differential equation for a capacitor?
The defining equation of a capacitor is i equals C dv over dt . The current through it equals its capacitance times how fast the voltage across it is changing.
If the voltage is steady, no current flows. If the voltage changes quickly, a lot of current flows. This one equation explains most of what capacitors do.
Go back to the bucket from "What capacitance is". The water level is the voltage and the flow from the hose is the current.
The level rises only while water flows in, and a wide bucket (a large capacitance) needs more flow to raise its level at the same speed. Shut the hose and the level stays put.
The level can never jump instantly, because that would take an infinitely strong flow. A real capacitor leaks a little, like a bucket with a pinhole; the ideal one does not.
While +1 milliamps flows, v rises at 1 volts/ms; when the current flips to minus 1 milliamps, v falls at the same rate.
The capacitor integrates the current: flat segments of i become straight slopes of v. Here both traces are normalized to ±1 so the shapes line up; the triangle actually swings ±0.
5 volts.
Rate of change ( dv over dt ): how many volts per second the voltage is rising or falling. Capacitance (C): how much current you need per volt per second.
Time constant ( RC ): the natural time scale of a resistor charging a capacitor. Open circuit: no current flows. A charged capacitor at steady DC looks like this.
Continuity: a capacitor's voltage cannot jump instantly.
Push a constant 1 milliamps into a 1 microfarads capacitor. Then dv over dt equals i over C equals 0. 001 over 10 to the -6 equals 1000 volts/s, which is 1 volts per millisecond.
After 5 milliseconds the voltage is 5 volts. Stop the current and the voltage stays at 5 volts, because no current means no change. That is the whole idea.

The integral form is v equals v(0) plus 1 over C the integral of i dt , so the capacitor integrates current and remembers its initial voltage.
Consequences: constant voltage means zero current, so it's open at DC; constant current makes a linear ramp; and voltage can't jump instantly.
With a resistor it gives RC dv over dt plus v equals V s , the exponential RC response."

Sign of capacitive reactance. The question: Does a capacitor have positive of negative reactance?
Reactance is the part of a capacitor's or inductor's opposition to AC that comes from storing and returning energy, not from making heat.
A capacitor's reactance is negative: X C equals -1 over ( omega C) , where omega equals 2 pi f . The sign is not just bookkeeping.
It records timing: the capacitor's current peaks a quarter cycle before its voltage.
An inductor (a coil, the capacitor's opposite partner) has a positive reactance and the opposite timing.
Picture the ocean tide. Water flows in fastest around mid-tide, when the level is rising most quickly. High tide comes a quarter cycle later, when the flow has dropped to zero.
The flow, like the capacitor current, peaks first. The level, like the voltage, follows.
The picture only works for a back-and-forth signal such as a sine wave, which is what reactance describes.
The impedance plane. Inductors point straight up (+90°), capacitors straight down (minus 90°). A series RC lands in the fourth quadrant: positive resistance, negative reactance.
On a Smith chart this is the lower half.

j : a math marker for the part of impedance that is shifted a quarter cycle in time. Since 1 over j equals -j , the capacitor's sign comes out negative.
Lead / lag: which of voltage or current peaks first. Capacitor current leads. Inductor reactance: plus omega L , the positive counterpart.

Their reactances subtract, so the net is about minus 96 ohms. A negative net reactance means the circuit looks capacitive at this frequency. That is the whole idea.
"Negative. Z C equals 1 over (j omega C) equals -j over ( omega C) , so the reactance is -1 over ( omega C) .
That negative sign means current leads voltage by 90°, the opposite of an inductor's plus j omega L .
Many books write X C as a positive magnitude and put the minus in Z equals R minus jX C , which is equivalent.
The practical point is that inductive and capacitive reactances cancel in series, which is what resonance is."

Continuity condition and inductors. The question: What is the continuity condition? What do inductors resist change to?
An inductor is a coil of wire that stores energy in a magnetic field while current flows through it.
The continuity condition says that an energy-storing part like this cannot change its state instantly. For an inductor the state is its current.
So an inductor resists sudden changes in current. If you try to force a sudden change, the inductor produces a large voltage to oppose it.
Think of a heavy freight train. Its speed is like the inductor's current. You cannot stop it instantly. If you somehow tried, the force would have to be enormous.
In a circuit, the "force" is voltage, and so trying to stop the current suddenly makes a huge voltage spike.
A capacitor has the matching rule for voltage: like the water level in a bucket, it cannot jump. The analogy hides the energy: both store energy that must go somewhere.
The diode's cathode faces the +12 volts side, so it's reverse-biased (off) while the switch is closed.
When the switch opens, the coil's current, which cannot stop instantly, swings over into the diode and circulates around the green loop.
Continuity: a stored quantity, like inductor current, cannot jump. v equals L di over dt : the inductor's rule. Voltage equals inductance ( L ) times how fast the current changes.
Inductive kick: the voltage spike when current through an inductor is suddenly interrupted.
Flyback diode: a diode (a one-way valve for current) across a coil that gives the current a safe path. Lenz's law: the induced voltage always opposes the change in current.
A relay coil (an electromagnet switch) of 10 millihenries carries 120 milliamps, and the transistor switch driving it turns off in 1 microseconds.
The coil tries to keep its current going. The voltage is v equals L di over dt equals 0. 01 times 0. 12 over 10 to the -6 equals 1200 volts. That would destroy the transistor.
A flyback diode across the coil lets the current circulate harmlessly. That is the whole idea.
"The continuity condition says inductor current and capacitor voltage can't change instantaneously.
Inductors resist changes in current: since v equals L di over dt , an instant change in current would need infinite voltage, and the stored energy 1 over 2 Li squared can't change in zero time.
That's why interrupting a coil's current produces a huge voltage spike, and why we put flyback diodes across relays and motors.
Capacitors are the dual: they resist changes in voltage."

Capacitor initial vs DC steady state. The question: How does a capacitor behave when initially excited and at DC steady-state?
An uncharged capacitor acts like a short circuit at the very first instant after a voltage is applied. After a long time with a steady DC voltage, it acts like an open circuit.
In between, the current fades away and the voltage rises toward its final value, quickly at first and then more and more slowly (an exponential curve).
Knowing these two end points lets you solve many problems quickly.
Think of a dry sponge dropped into water. At first it soaks up water very fast, as if nothing were in the way. That is the short circuit. As it fills, it takes up less and less.

Capacitor failure modes. The question: What are some common failure modes of a capacitor?
Capacitors do not all fail the same way. The type decides the failure. Ceramic ones are brittle and crack, usually shorting.
Aluminum electrolytics slowly dry out, losing capacitance and gaining resistance. Tantalum ones can fail short suddenly under a surge and may burn.
Film capacitors are the gentlest. Knowing the type tells you what to prevent.
Think of three household items. A ceramic capacitor is a dinner plate: strong until it is bent, and then it cracks.
An electrolytic is a wet sponge: it dries out slowly, faster when hot. A tantalum is like a fuse that can flare when overloaded: fine most of the time, then sudden when pushed.
The comparison is rough, but it matches how each type tends to fail.
Every 10 degrees Celsius cooler doubles the life, so a capacitor running at 65 degrees Celsius core temperature lasts about 16 times as long as at 105 degrees Celsius.
The core temperature includes the ripple self-heating, so a low-ESR part or a larger part at the same ripple lasts longer.
MLCC: multilayer ceramic capacitor, the small ceramic chip type. Dry-out: the electrolyte in an electrolytic evaporating, which raises ESR and lowers capacitance.
Derating: using a part well below its voltage or ripple rating for margin. Inrush current: a surge into an uncharged capacitor when power is applied.
Thermal runaway: a part heating, conducting more, and heating even more until it fails.
A board flexes during assembly and a 100 nanofarads ceramic on the 5 volts rail cracks. The crack lets the inner plates touch, so the rail shorts to ground and the part heats up.
For an electrolytic, a rule of thumb is that life roughly doubles for every 10 degrees Celsius cooler, so a part run 20 degrees Celsius cooler lasts about four times as long.

Inductor current continuity condition. The question: What is the continuity condition? What do inductors resist change to?
The continuity condition says the current through an inductor cannot change instantly. The current just after a switching event equals the current just before it.
The voltage across an inductor can jump, but the current cannot. This is how an inductor resists changes in current.
Picture a heavy merry-go-round. Its rotation speed is like the inductor current. You cannot stop it in zero time, however hard you try, since that would take an infinite force.
Its speed carries over from just before to just after. The force you apply, like the voltage, can change suddenly and be as large as needed.
The analogy fits well, but a merry-go-round has friction and an ideal inductor does not.
Before t = 0 the inductor shorts R d and carries 12 volts / 12 ohms = 1 amps downward. When the switch opens, the only remaining path for that 1 amps is up through R d.
Continuity condition: the inductor current is the same just before and just after a switch changes. State variable: the stored quantity that cannot jump, current for an inductor.
Inductive kick: the large voltage that appears when you try to interrupt the current suddenly. Flyback diode: a diode across a coil that gives the current a safe path.
Inductor equation: v equals L di over dt .
An inductor carries 2 amps. A switch then moves so that the only path for the current is through a 5 ohms resistor.
The inductor current cannot jump, so 2 amps flows through the resistor. The resistor voltage is 2 times 5 equals 10 volts, and it appears instantly.
The current stayed the same, but the voltage jumped. If there were no path at all, the voltage would rise until something conducts. That is the whole idea.
"The continuity condition says inductor current can't change instantaneously: i L(0^ plus ) equals i L(0^-) .
That comes from v equals L di over dt : a jump in current would need infinite voltage, and it would change the stored energy 1 over 2 LI squared in zero time.
So inductors resist changes in current, while their voltage can jump.
Practically, if you interrupt an inductor's current, its voltage spikes as high as needed to keep current flowing, which is why relay coils need flyback diodes."

Inductor at t = 0⁺ and DC steady state. The question: How does an inductor behave when initially excited and at DC steady-state?
An inductor is a coil of wire that resists changes in the current through it.
Right after you switch a voltage on, the current in the coil is still zero and cannot jump, so the coil acts like a gap in the wire.
After a long time the current is steady, and an ideal coil acts like a plain piece of wire.
Picture a heavy merry-go-round. At the first push it barely moves. Once it spins steadily, it needs almost no push to keep going.
The coil's current is the spin speed, and the voltage across it is the push.
The analogy breaks in one place: a real coil's wire has a little resistance, like a bit of friction, so it never drops exactly zero volts.
The switch closes at t = 0 with the inductor de-energized. The node voltage v x is also the inductor voltage.
Inductor: a coil of wire that stores energy in a magnetic field. Open circuit: a break in the path. No current flows, but voltage can appear across it.
Short circuit: a plain wire. Current flows freely and there is zero voltage across it.
DC steady state: the condition after all the switching is over and nothing is changing anymore.
Current cannot jump: an inductor's current is the same just after a switch as just before it.
Time constant ( tau ): the time the current takes to make most (about 63%) of its change, equal to L over R .
Connect a 10 volts source through a 10 ohms resistor to an inductor, and close the switch.
At that instant the inductor current is 0 amps, so the inductor is open and has the full 10 volts across it. Much later, the current stops changing and the inductor drops 0 volts.
All 10 volts is across the resistor, so the current is 10 volts / 10 ohms = 1 amps. That is the whole idea.
"When first excited from zero current, an inductor acts like an open circuit: its current can't jump, so it's still zero right after the step and the full voltage appears across it.
At DC steady state it's a short, because constant current means L di over dt equals 0 ; a real one shows just its DC resistance.
In between, the current rises exponentially with tau equals L over R . If it was already carrying current, at the switch instant it acts as a current source.
It's the dual of a capacitor."

Inductor impedance from DC to ∞. The question: What is an inductors impedance at DC vs infinitely high frequency? Plot this behavior.
Impedance is how strongly a part opposes alternating current at a given frequency. For an inductor, that opposition grows as the frequency goes up.
At DC the inductor opposes nothing and acts like a wire. At very high frequency it opposes almost everything and acts like a gap.
This page asks you to describe and sketch that rise.
Think of pushing a heavy swing. Push slowly and it follows along easily, so it feels no resistance.
Push back and forth faster and faster, and the heavy swing fights every reversal harder and harder.
The coil works the same way: more current reversals per second means more pushback.
The analogy only covers the ideal coil: a real one has small extra effects that matter at both ends of the frequency range.
A straight line through the origin with slope 2πL about 62. 8 ohms per MHz. Zero at DC, growing without limit as frequency rises.
Impedance ( Z ): the opposition to AC current, in ohms. It is the AC version of resistance. Reactance: the part of impedance that comes from storing energy.
For an inductor it is omega L . Frequency ( f ): how many cycles per second the signal makes. Here omega equals 2 pi f . Inductor impedance: Z L equals j omega L .
Its size is omega L ; the j just marks that the voltage peaks a quarter cycle ahead of the current.
Self-resonant frequency: the frequency where the tiny capacitance between a real coil's turns takes over from the inductance.
Take a 1 millihenries inductor. At 0 hertz its impedance is 0 ohms, a short. At 1 kilohertz, omega L equals 2 pi times 1000 times 0. 001 about 6. 3 ohms.
At 10 kilohertz it is ten times more, about 63 ohms. At 100 kilohertz it is about 630 ohms.
Each ten-fold step in frequency gives a ten-fold step in impedance, which is a straight line going up on a log-log plot. That is the whole idea.

Plotted, Z is a straight line through the origin, or on log–log axes a line rising at 20 decibels per decade with a constant +90° phase.
A real inductor bottoms out at its DCR at low frequency, peaks at its self-resonant frequency because of winding capacitance, and turns capacitive above it."

Inductor saturation. The question: What happens when an inductor saturates?
Saturation is when an inductor's magnetic core is full and cannot hold any more magnetic flux. Up to that point, the core multiplies the inductance.
Past it, the inductance collapses, and the coil behaves like a much smaller inductor. The current then shoots up fast, which can damage other parts in the circuit.
Think of a sponge soaking up water. A dry sponge soaks up a lot, so it does its job well. Once it is completely soaked, more water just runs off.
A core is the sponge, and the magnetic flux is the water. Past the point of fullness, extra current gets almost no help from the core.
The analogy is loose about one thing: some cores fill up gradually, and others hit their limit suddenly.
The steep initial slope is high permeability: lots of flux for little current. Past a few hundred A/m the curve flattens at B sat, and adding more H only adds flux at air's slope.
The inductor's L is proportional to this slope.
Magnetic flux: the amount of magnetic field passing through the coil and core. Core: the magnetic material, such as ferrite, that the wire wraps around.
Saturation current ( I sat ): the current at which the inductance has dropped by a set amount.
Peak current: the highest current the inductor sees, which is what you must compare to I sat .
Slope of current: di over dt equals V over L , so a smaller L means a faster current rise.
Apply 10 volts across a 10 microhenries inductor. The current rises at V over L equals 10 over 0. 00001 equals 1 amps per µs.
Now suppose the core saturates and the inductance falls to 2 microhenries. The same 10 volts now makes the current rise at 5 amps per µs, five times faster.
In a buck converter (a circuit that switches a coil on and off to step a voltage down), the switch would see a sharp current spike. That is the whole idea.
"Saturation is when the core's flux density hits its material limit: the magnetic domains are all aligned, permeability collapses toward that of air, and inductance drops sharply.
Since di over dt equals V over L , the current then ramps much faster and spikes.
That overstresses switches, trips current limits and adds heat, which in ferrite lowers the saturation current further.
So you size an inductor's I sat above the worst-case peak current, DC plus half the ripple, with margin and at temperature."

Realistic inductor model and parasitics. The question: Draw a realistic circuit model for an inductor. What are the parasitics and where do they come from?
A real inductor is not just an ideal coil. The wire has resistance. The turns sit close together and act like a small capacitor. The core wastes some energy as heat.
A realistic model adds those extras to the ideal inductor, so you can predict where the part stops acting like an inductor.
Think of a garden hose that is supposed to be a perfect pipe. In real life the hose is slightly narrow, so it has some friction. It also bulges a little, so it stores some water.
A real inductor is the same: the ideal coil is the pipe, and the extras are the friction and the bulge.
The model is a simplification, since the extras are spread through the part, not sitting in separate lumps.
R s is the copper (DC resistance rising to AC resistance with frequency).
C w is in parallel with the whole winding, so at high frequency it provides a bypass path around the inductance. R p represents the core loss across the inductance proper.
DCR: the DC resistance of the wire, in series with the ideal inductor. Winding capacitance ( C w ): tiny capacitance between the turns, drawn in parallel with the coil.
Core loss: energy wasted in the magnetic core as heat, drawn as a resistor.
Self-resonant frequency (SRF): where L and C w resonate, f 0 equals 1 over (2 pi square root of LC w ) . Quality factor ( Q ): how good the inductor is, omega L over R .
High Q means low loss.
Take a 10 microhenries inductor with 5 picofarads of winding capacitance. Below about 22 megahertz it acts like an inductor.
At about 22 megahertz the inductance and capacitance resonate (pass energy back and forth between them), and the impedance peaks. Above that, the part acts like a capacitor.
That is the whole idea.

"The real inductor is the ideal L in series with winding resistance, DCR going up to ACR with frequency, with a parallel capacitance across the whole winding from turn-to-turn coupling, and a parallel resistor for core loss.
That gives a self-resonant frequency one over two pi root L C. Below it, it's an inductor; at it, the impedance peaks; above it, it's a capacitor.
A 10 microhenry coil with 5 picofarads resonates near 22 megahertz. It also saturates, so L drops at high current."

What inductor cores do. The question: What do cores do on inductors?
A core is a chunk of magnetic material, like ferrite, that the coil's wire is wrapped around. It guides the magnetic field and concentrates it.
That lets the same number of turns give far more inductance, so inductors can be smaller. The price is that cores can fill up (saturate) and waste some energy as heat.
Think of a river and a concrete channel. Spilled water spreads out in all directions. Put it in a channel and all of it follows one path.
A core is the channel for the magnetic field: air lets the field spread out weakly, while the core guides it along a strong path. A channel can only carry so much, though.
That limit is saturation.

In an air-core coil (left, orange turns) the flux returns through the surrounding space (long, wide path, high reluctance), while a closed high-permeability core confines nearly all of it to a short, well-defined path (dashed line inside the blue ring).
The orange bars across the toroid are the winding turns.
Magnetic flux: the amount of magnetic field the coil and core carry. Permeability ( micro ): how well a material carries magnetic flux. Higher means a stronger guide.
Reluctance: how much a flux path resists carrying flux. Inductance equals the number of turns squared ( N squared ) divided by the reluctance.
Saturation: the core cannot carry any more flux. Air gap: a deliberate cut in the core that lowers inductance but lets it carry more current.
Wind the same coil twice. In air, you get some inductance, call it L 0 . Now put it on a ferrite core with a relative permeability of 2000.
The inductance rises by about a factor of 2000, so L is roughly 2000 times L 0 . You can get a target inductance with far fewer turns. That is the whole idea.
"A core is magnetic material, ferrite or powdered iron, that concentrates the flux.

Inductance goes as turns squared over reluctance, and a high-permeability core has far lower reluctance than air, so you get hundreds or thousands of times more inductance from the same turns, in less space.
The costs are saturation, where inductance collapses at high current, and core loss. An air gap lowers the inductance but raises the saturation current and stores the energy."

Typical inductor core materials. The question: What are typical core materials?
Inductor cores come in several materials, and each one is good at a different job. The main ones are ferrite, powdered iron, silicon steel, and nanocrystalline alloys.
The answer is a short match-up: which material fits which frequency and current. You choose by how much magnetic flux it can hold, how much energy it wastes, and its cost.
Think of choosing a vehicle. A sports car is fast but carries little. A truck carries a lot but is slow. A van sits in between.
Core materials are the same: ferrite is the sports car (fast at high frequency, small load capacity), silicon steel is the truck (high capacity, only low frequency), and powder cores are the van.
The comparison simplifies one thing: every material also has a cost and temperature behavior.
Approximate regions (illustrative; grades vary).
Metals (powder, steel, nanocrystalline) reach high B sat (energy per volume), ferrites trade low B sat for high resistivity and low high-frequency loss.
Powder cores sit at low micro because their distributed gaps dilute the permeability.
Permeability: how strongly the material concentrates magnetic flux. Saturation flux density ( B sat ): the most flux the material can carry.
Core loss: energy wasted as heat in the core, which rises with frequency. Ferrite: a ceramic of iron oxide. It is an insulator, so it has low loss at high frequency.
Powder core: metal particles in a binder, which saturate gradually.
You need an inductor for a buck converter (a power supply that switches on and off 500,000 times a second to step a voltage down). It carries a large steady (DC) current.
A ferrite core has low loss at 500 kilohertz but saturates hard, so you add an air gap. A powdered-iron core saturates softly and handles DC well.
You pick the powder core, or a gapped ferrite. That is the whole idea.

Ferrite is low loss for tens of kHz to a few MHz but saturates hard around 0. 3 to 0. 5 tesla.
Powder cores have distributed gaps, so low permeability, around 1 tesla, and soft saturation, which suits DC-biased power inductors. Silicon steel is for line frequency.
Nanocrystalline is for common-mode chokes."

Inductor loss mechanisms. The question: What are the main loss mechanisms of an inductor? Where do they arise from?
An inductor wastes some power as heat, and this page asks where that waste comes from. There are two main sources.
Winding loss is the heat from current pushing through the copper wire. Core loss is the heat from the magnetic material being pushed back and forth every cycle.
Knowing both tells you why a real inductor runs warm.
Think of rubbing your hands together. Two things make them warm. Your skin drags against itself, which is like current dragging through the wire's resistance.
And if you flex a stiff rubber band back and forth, it warms up too, which is like the core being magnetized one way and then the other. Faster rubbing or flexing makes more heat.
The analogy is rough, because real core loss has several separate causes.
With inductance held fixed, a higher switching frequency reduces ripple current and flux, so both core loss and ripple-copper loss fall quickly while the DC copper loss stays the same.
The catch (not plotted) is that switching losses in the FETs rise with frequency, and the inductor's AC resistance factor grows; real optimizations balance them. Exponents α = 1.
4, β = 2. 5 are illustrative.
Winding loss: heat in the copper wire, equal to current squared times the wire's resistance ( I to the 2R ). The wire's resistance to steady current is its DCR.
Core loss: heat in the magnetic core from hysteresis and eddy currents. Hysteresis: energy lost each time the core's magnetism is flipped to point the other way.
Eddy currents: small circulating currents induced in the core by the changing flux.
Skin and proximity effects: at high frequency, current crowds toward the wire's surface and away from neighboring turns, so less copper carries it and resistance rises.
Run 3 amps of DC through a winding with 20 milliohms of resistance. The loss is I to the 2R equals 3 times 3 times 0. 02 equals 0. 18 watts. That is copper loss alone.
Now add ripple current at a high switching frequency. Skin and proximity effects raise the wire's AC resistance, and the core also loses energy each cycle. That is the whole idea.
"Two buckets: winding loss and core loss. Winding loss is I squared R, where the AC resistance is higher than DC because of skin and proximity effects.

Core loss is hysteresis, proportional to the B-H loop area times frequency, plus eddy currents in the core, roughly f squared B squared, summarized by the Steinmetz equation k f to the alpha B to the beta.
There's also fringing loss near a gap and capacitive loss at high frequency."
