AC resistance (ACR) of inductors. The question: What is ACR? Where does it arise from and how is it impacted by frequency?
AC resistance, or ACR, is the resistance an inductor's winding shows at its working frequency. It is higher than the DC resistance you measure with a basic meter.
At AC, the current does not use the whole cross-section of the wire. It crowds toward the surface, so less of the wire carries current, and resistance goes up.
Picture a wide highway at rush hour where every driver crowds into the outer lanes and the middle lanes sit empty.
The road is just as wide, but it carries less traffic than it could.
A wire at high frequency is that highway: the middle copper carries little current, so the usable area shrinks and the wire acts like a thinner one.
The analogy is loose, since the current falls off smoothly toward the center.
Current density in a round wire.

At low frequency the whole cross-section conducts; as δ shrinks below the radius, the current is confined to a thin skin at the surface, so the effective area, and thus the resistance, change by r over 2 delta .
DC resistance (DCR): the resistance with steady current, using the whole wire. Skin effect: AC current crowds toward the wire surface.
Skin depth ( delta ): how deep the current reaches. For copper it is about 66 µm at 1 megahertz.
Proximity effect: neighboring turns' magnetic fields push current into crowded patches. Litz wire: many thin insulated strands that give the current more surface to use.

Pass 3 amps of 500 kilohertz current through it, measured as rms (the effective value of a back-and-forth current). The loss is 3 squared times 0. 01 equals 0.
09 watts if you wrongly use DCR, but 3 squared times 0. 03 equals 0. 27 watts with the real ACR. That is the whole idea.
"ACR is the effective series resistance of an inductor's winding at the operating frequency, and it's higher than DCR.
Skin effect pushes current to the surface within a depth of delta, 66 micrometers in copper at 1 megahertz, so resistance rises as the square root of frequency for thick wire.
Proximity effect from neighboring turns' fields adds more, especially with many layers. Litz wire, foil, fewer layers and interleaving reduce it."

Signals inductors pass and block. The question: What sort of signals can inductors pass through and block? What sort of filter behavior is this?
An inductor lets slow signals through and holds back fast ones. At DC, which never changes, it acts like a plain wire. As the signal changes faster, the inductor fights it more.
That is why inductors are used to smooth out power and to filter out noise. It is the opposite of a capacitor, which blocks DC and passes fast signals.
Picture a heavy door. If you push it slowly and steadily, it moves along with you and hardly resists.
If you try to shake it back and forth quickly, its weight fights every change of direction, and it barely moves. A slowly changing current is like the slow push, so it passes.
A quickly changing signal is like the shaking, and the inductor blocks it.

Build an LPF or HPF with one inductor. The question: Build a LPF/HPF using a single inductor.
A filter needs a way to split a signal, and an inductor alone cannot do that. You pair it with one resistor.
The two form a divider: they share the input voltage, and the output is the share across one of them.
Put the inductor in series with the signal and you get a low-pass filter: slow signals pass, fast ones are blocked.
Put the inductor from the output to ground and you get a high-pass filter. Either way, one number sets the corner frequency.
Think of a water pipe with a heavy paddle wheel (the inductor) and a side drain. Slow, steady flow turns the wheel with little effort and gets through.
Rapid pulsing meets the wheel's resistance and gets stopped.
If you place the wheel in the side drain instead, steady flow slips out the side, and only rapid pulses are left going straight ahead.
The analogy is loose in one way: a real inductor also has wire resistance and stops working at very high frequency.

Inductor failure modes. The question: What are some common failure modes of an inductor?
Inductors fail in a few typical ways, and it helps to know them as a checklist. The most important is saturation, where the core fills up and the current spikes.
Next is overheating, from copper and core loss. Last are physical problems, like a cracked core or a broken wire.
Most failures happen not at normal load but during start-up, a load step or a short.
Think of a bridge with a posted weight limit. Normal traffic is fine. One day a very heavy truck crosses, and the bridge fails, even though it carried ordinary loads for years.
Inductors are the same. They run fine at the rated current, and break down only when the rare peak goes past the limit.
Heat is more like slow wear on the bridge: it builds up over time and weakens it.
With a 20 milliohms winding and 40 K/W, 7. 1 amps gives the rated 40 K rise (ignoring TCR).
The positive feedback of copper's resistance makes the rise grow faster than I² and diverges near 18 amps.
Real parts rarely get there because other things fail first (insulation, solder, core), but it shows why derating matters at high ambient temperature.
Saturation current ( I sat ): the current where the core fills up and inductance drops.
Heating current ( I rms ): the current (measured as rms, a kind of effective average) that warms the part by a rated amount, often 40 degrees Celsius.
Peak current: the highest current at any instant, including ripple (the small up-and-down wobble) and brief surges.
Derating: using a part well below its rating, for safety margin. Inrush: the large current surge at start-up.
Take some round example numbers. Say an inductor has I sat equals 4 amps. In normal operation the load is 3 amps with 1 amps of ripple from bottom to top, so the peak is 3 + 0.
5 = 3. 5 amps. That is fine. During a load step, the peak briefly hits 5 amps.
The core saturates, the inductance collapses, and the current climbs even faster, which can destroy the switch. That is the whole idea.

Then thermal overstress from copper and core loss, which breaks down the insulation and causes shorted turns or an open winding.
Mechanical failures such as cracked ferrite and broken terminations, and aging of iron powder cores. I specify with both Isat and Irms and derate."

Conductors, insulators, semiconductors. The question: What is a conductor/insulator/semiconductor?
Materials differ in how easily electric current flows through them. A conductor, such as copper, lets current flow very easily. An insulator, such as glass, almost never does.
A semiconductor, such as silicon, sits in between, and you can control how well it conducts. That control is what makes transistors and diodes possible.
Picture a parking lot with a fence. Electrons are cars. In a conductor, there is no fence, and the cars roll freely. In an insulator, the fence is very tall, and no car gets over.
In a semiconductor, the fence is low enough that a few cars hop over when they get a boost from heat or light.
The analogy breaks down in one way: electrons really sit in energy levels, not in a lot.
The three classes differ in where the highest occupied states sit. A metal's band is only partly full, so empty states are right next to filled ones.
A semiconductor has a small gap that heat can bridge for a few electrons (each leaving a hole). An insulator's gap is too wide for anything to cross at room temperature.
Free electron: an electron that can move through the material and carry current. Valence band: the energy levels of electrons stuck in bonds between atoms.
Conduction band: the energy levels where electrons move freely. Band gap: the energy needed to jump from the valence band to the conduction band.
Doping: adding a tiny amount of impurity to change how well a semiconductor conducts.
Compare band gaps. Copper has no gap, so electrons move freely. Silicon has a gap of about 1.

Skin effect. The question: What is the skin effect?
Skin effect is the habit of alternating current to flow near the surface of a wire, not through the whole thickness.
The higher the frequency, the thinner the layer that carries current. Because less of the wire is used, the wire's resistance goes up at high frequency.
It matters in inductors, transformers and fast circuit-board traces.
Picture a crowded concert hall with doors on the outside wall. People rush toward the outer edges and the middle stays empty. The hall is big, but only the outer ring is used.
In a wire carrying fast AC, the current plays the part of the crowd, crowding to the surface.
The analogy is loose: the crowd thins out smoothly into the middle, rather than stopping at a sharp edge.
At DC the whole cross-section carries current. Once the skin depth is comparable to the radius, density is visibly higher at the rim.
At high frequency almost all the current sits within a few δ of the surface and the center is nearly idle copper.
Alternating current (AC): current that reverses direction over and over.
Skin depth ( delta ): the depth at which the current has dropped to about a third (37%) of its value at the surface.
Eddy currents: small circulating currents made by a changing magnetic field. Resistance: how hard a wire makes it for current to flow.
Litz wire: many thin insulated strands, which use more surface.
For copper at 1 megahertz, the skin depth is about 65 µm, which is 0. 065 mm. Take a wire 1 mm across, with a 0. 5 mm radius. Its full cross-section is about 0. 79 mm².
The ring that carries current is about 0. 2 mm², roughly a quarter. So its resistance is roughly four times the DC value. That is the whole idea.
"Skin effect is AC current crowding toward a conductor's surface.
The changing magnetic field inside the wire induces eddy currents that cancel current in the center and reinforce it at the edges.
Current density falls off exponentially with skin depth delta equals square root of over ( pi f micro) : for copper about 65 µm at 1 megahertz and 2 µm at 1 gigahertz.
So effective area shrinks and resistance rises like square root of f .
That's why inductors and transformers have AC resistance above DC resistance, and why we use litz wire, foil and smooth copper at high frequency."

Photoelectric effect. The question: What is the photoelectric effect?
The photoelectric effect is when light hitting a material knocks electrons out of it. Light arrives in tiny packets called photons. One photon gives its energy to one electron.
If a photon carries enough energy, the electron escapes. If it does not, nothing happens, no matter how bright the light is. Solar cells and camera sensors use a version of this.
Picture a coconut shy at a fair. Each ball is a photon, and each coconut is an electron held on its stand. A fast ball knocks a coconut off.
A slow ball just bounces off, and throwing a hundred slow balls does not help, because each hits on its own. Brighter light is more balls per second, not faster balls.
The analogy is loose: a photon's "speed" is really its energy, set by its frequency.
Light ejects electrons from the emitter. With the source polarity shown, the collector is negative, so it repels them; only electrons with kinetic energy above eV ret reach it.
Raising V ret until the current just reaches zero measures KE max directly as the stopping voltage.
Photon: one packet of light. Its energy is hf , where f is the frequency and h is a fixed number of nature (Planck's constant). Frequency: how many wave cycles per second.
Blue light has a higher frequency than red. Work function ( ): the energy needed to free an electron from a metal's surface.
Band gap: in a semiconductor, the energy needed to free an electron. Electron-hole pair: a freed electron and the empty spot it left behind.
Energies here are in eV (electron-volts, a tiny unit of energy). Take a metal with a work function of 2 eV.
A photon of 3 eV frees an electron and leaves 3 - 2 = 1 eV as energy of motion (kinetic energy). A photon of 1. 5 eV frees nothing, even if you shine a million of them.
A brighter 3 eV beam gives more electrons, each still with 1 eV. That is the whole idea.
"It's light knocking electrons out of a material.
The key facts are that there's a threshold frequency, below which nothing happens however bright the light, and that the electrons' maximum energy depends on frequency, not intensity.
Einstein explained it with photons: each photon has energy hf , gives it all to one electron, and KE max equals hf minus , where is the work function.
In semiconductors the same idea, with the band gap instead of , is how photodiodes, solar cells and image sensors work."

Dielectric losses and their mechanisms. The question: Explain any dielectric losses and how they occur.
A dielectric is an insulator that sits between the plates of a capacitor, or inside a circuit-board laminate. An ideal one stores energy and gives it all back.
A real one wastes a little as heat. That waste is dielectric loss.
It comes from small leakage current, and mostly from charges inside the material that cannot keep up when the field flips back and forth.
Picture pushing a child on a swing through thick mud. A bit of the effort is stored in the swing's motion, but some is lost to friction in the mud every cycle.
A dielectric is similar: the field twists molecules back and forth, and they rub against their neighbors, producing heat. Faster flipping means more twists per second.
The analogy breaks down at very high frequency, where molecules cannot follow at all.

The small in-phase component times the voltage is the dissipated power. For C0G, δ is under 0. 06°; for standard FR-4 at GHz, about 1°.
Dielectric: an insulating material that stores energy in an electric field. Polarization: charges in the material shifting or turning in response to a field.
Leakage current: a tiny current that flows through a nonperfect insulator. Loss tangent ( delta ): the power turned into heat as a fraction of the power sloshing in and out.
Smaller is better. Capacitor: two conductors separated by a dielectric, which store charge.
Put 10 volts at 1 kilohertz across a 1 microfarads capacitor. Energy sloshes into and out of the capacitor every cycle.
That flow, called reactive power, is V squared omega C , where omega equals 2 pi f : here 100 times 6. 28 times 10 to the -3 about 0.
63 VA (volt-amperes, watt-like units for power that is not used up). If the loss tangent is 0. 01, the heat is 1% of that, about 6 milliwatts. With a poorer dielectric at 0.
1, it is about 63 milliwatts. That is the whole idea.
"Real dielectrics turn some AC field energy into heat.

Mechanisms: leakage conduction, mainly at low frequency; polarization lag, where dipoles and ions can't reorient fast enough and lose energy to the lattice, peaking near the relaxation frequency; interfacial charge in composites; hysteresis in ferroelectric ceramics like X7R; and partial discharge at high voltage.
We quantify it with the loss tangent: P equals V squared omega C delta . That's why C0G and film caps are used in resonant circuits and low-Df laminates for high-speed boards."

How electricity works. The question: How does electricity work?
Electricity is the movement of electric charge, and the energy it carries. A battery sets up a voltage, which is an electrical push.
When you connect a closed loop of wire through a lamp or other load, that push moves charge around the loop. That flow is current.
The load turns the energy into light, heat or motion.
Picture a closed loop of water pipe, already full of water, with a pump in it. The pump does not make the water. It only pushes the water that is already in the pipe.
Where the pipe is narrow, the water pushes harder against it and the pipe heats up a bit.
In a wire the battery is the pump, the electrons are the water, and a narrow spot is resistance.
The analogy breaks in one place: the energy really travels in the electric and magnetic fields around the wire, at nearly the speed of light, while the electrons themselves only creep along.
The battery supplies energy, not electrons: the electrons were already in the copper.
Closing the switch establishes the field around the whole loop in nanoseconds, so current starts everywhere at once. 9 volts across 30 ohms drives 0. 3 amps, delivering 2.
7 watts to the lamp. Conventional current is drawn from + to minus .
Voltage (V): the electrical push between two points, in volts. Current (I): how much charge flows past a point each second, in amps.
Resistance (R): how hard a part makes it for current to flow, in ohms. Ohm's law: V equals IR . Power (P): energy used per second, P equals VI , in watts.
Connect a 1. 5 volts battery across a 3 ohms resistor. The current is I equals V over R equals 1. 5 over 3 equals 0. 5 amps. The power is P equals VI equals 1. 5 times 0.
5 equals 0. 75 watts, which the resistor turns into heat. That is the whole idea.
"Electricity is charge moving and the energy it carries. A source like a battery creates a voltage, which is energy per unit charge.
Connect a closed circuit and that voltage sets up a field in the wire, which pushes the free electrons that are already there, and that's current.
Collisions with the metal's atoms are resistance, so V equals IR , and energy gets delivered at P equals VI .
The electrons drift really slowly, fractions of a millimetre per second, but the field and energy move near the speed of light."

How lightning works. The question: How does lightning work?
Lightning is a giant spark of static electricity. Inside a thundercloud, charge separates, leaving one region strongly negative and the ground below positive.
When the electric field grows strong enough, air, normally an insulator, breaks down and conducts. A huge current flows for a moment.
For electronics, the lesson is that lightning creates large, fast surges.
Picture shuffling across a carpet in socks and then touching a doorknob. Your body builds up charge, and nothing happens until you get close.
Then the air gap breaks down, and a spark jumps. A thundercloud is the same thing on an enormous scale. The cloud is your charged body and the ground is the doorknob.
The difference is size: the spark is kilometers long and carries vastly more current.
Lightning is a chain: charging by microphysics, separation by convection, breakdown when the field is high enough, and a discharge that's limited by how fast the channel can carry current.
Each box is a different physics problem.
Charge separation: positive and negative charge ending up in different places. Electric field: the push on charge, which grows as charge builds up.
Dielectric breakdown: an insulator, such as air, suddenly conducting once the field is strong enough.
Stepped leader: a thin channel of air made conductive (ionized: electrons torn off its atoms) that works its way down in jumps before the main flash.
Surge: a brief, large voltage or current spike.
In the story of a single strike, ice and hail collide in the storm, and a big region in the middle of the cloud builds up negative charge. The ground below turns positive.
The field grows until a conducting channel forms. Then charge rushes along it in a huge return stroke, which makes the flash and the thunder. That is the whole idea.
"Lightning is a huge electrostatic discharge.
In a thunderstorm, collisions between ice crystals and graupel separate charge: the cloud's middle ends up negative, and that induces positive charge on the ground.
When the field gets high enough the air breaks down.
A stepped leader of ionized air works its way down, an upward streamer meets it, and a return stroke of tens of kiloamps flows in microseconds, heating the channel to ~30,000 K.
That's the flash, and the explosive expansion is the thunder. For electronics, the big di over dt induces surges, so we need surge protection."

Energy bands where electrons move. The question: Which atom bands do electrons move in?
In a solid, electrons can only have certain energies, and those allowed energies form wide groups called bands.
Current flows when electrons have empty energy levels nearby to move into. A band that is completely full cannot carry current.
A semiconductor has a full lower band, an empty upper band, and a gap between them.
Picture a parking garage with two floors and a ramp gap between. The lower floor is completely full of cars, so none of them can move.
The upper floor is empty, so any car that gets up there can drive freely.
When a car does leave the lower floor, it leaves an empty space, and the cars next to it can shuffle into it. That moving empty space is a hole.
The analogy is rough, since electrons are not really cars on floors.
Schematic of band formation (not to scale). Far apart, atoms have sharp 3 seconds and 3p levels. As they approach, the levels broaden and mix (sp³ hybridization).

At silicon's actual lattice spacing (red line) they've reorganized into a lower bonding band, which the four valence electrons per atom exactly fill, and an upper antibonding band, separated by the 1.
12 eV gap.
Valence band: the lower band, holding the electrons that form the bonds between atoms. Conduction band: the upper band, where electrons can move freely.
Band gap: the range of energies between the two bands where no electron is allowed to sit.
Hole: an empty spot in the valence band that moves around and acts like a positive charge. Carrier: anything that moves and carries current, an electron or a hole.
Take pure silicon at absolute zero. The valence band is full and the conduction band is empty, so no current flows.
At room temperature, heat kicks a tiny number of electrons across the 1. 12 eV gap (eV, the electron-volt, is a tiny unit of energy).
That is about 10 to the 10 electrons in each cubic centimeter, which holds 5 times 10 to the 22 atoms. Each leaves a hole behind, so both electrons and holes carry current.
That is the whole idea.
"In a solid, atomic levels merge into bands.
Current-carrying electrons move in the conduction band, the band above the band gap, where there are plenty of empty states to move into.
In a semiconductor the valence band below the gap also carries current, via holes: missing electrons that act as positive carriers.
A completely full band can't conduct and an empty one has no carriers, so you need electrons in the conduction band or holes in the valence band.
In metals the top band is only partly full, so it conducts directly."

P-type vs N-type semiconductors. The question: What is the difference between P-type semiconductors vs N-type semiconductors?
N-type and P-type are two flavors of silicon, made by adding a tiny amount of a different element on purpose. N-type has extra free electrons.
P-type has a shortage of electrons, which creates holes that act like moving positive charges. Neither flavor is charged overall.
The difference is only which carrier is plentiful.
Picture a theater where every seat is taken. For N-type, a few extra people stand in the aisles, and they can move around freely. For P-type, a few seats are empty.
People next to an empty seat slide over, and the empty seat appears to move the other way. The standing people are electrons, and the empty seats are holes.
The analogy fails in one way: holes are not real objects, only the absence of an electron.
In the N-type lattice the phosphorus atom has one valence electron that no bond needs, so it wanders off as a free electron and leaves a fixed P⁺ ion.
In the P-type lattice the boron atom is one electron short; an incomplete bond (the open red circle) can be filled by a neighbour, so the hole moves while the B⁻ ion stays put.
Dopant: the impurity atom added on purpose to change the silicon. Majority carrier: the carrier type that is plentiful. Minority carrier: the carrier type that is scarce.
Hole: an empty electron spot that moves like a positive charge. Valence electrons: the outer electrons that form bonds. Silicon has four.
Add phosphorus, which has five valence electrons, to silicon. Four bond with neighbors and the fifth is free. That is N-type.
Add boron, which has three, and one bond is missing an electron. That is P-type.
With 10 to the 16 phosphorus atoms in each cubic centimeter, there are about 10 to the 16 free electrons there and only about 10 to the 4 holes. That is the whole idea.
"N-type and P-type are silicon doped on purpose so one carrier dominates.
N-type uses a donor like phosphorus with five valence electrons, so the extra electron is free and electrons are the majority carrier.
P-type uses an acceptor like boron with three valence electrons, which leaves a missing electron, a hole, that behaves like a mobile positive charge.
Both are electrically neutral. The minority carrier is set by np equals n i squared . Joining a P and an N region makes a PN junction, the basis of diodes and transistors."

Depletion region and how it forms. The question: What is a depletion region and how does it form?
When you join P-type and N-type silicon, a thin layer near the join empties of free carriers. That layer is the depletion region.
It forms because electrons and holes spread toward each other, and then are held back by the fixed charge they leave behind.
It is the heart of the diode, since it is the barrier that current must cross.
Picture two crowded rooms with a door in between. When the door opens, people wander at random, and more of them drift into the other room than come back.
But the people who left are missing from their original spots, and that leaves a lopsided imbalance near the door that pushes the crowd back.
The flow stops when the push-back equals the spreading.
In a real junction the push-back is electric: the charged atoms left behind near the join repel any more carriers trying to cross.
Top: the depletion region sits on both sides of the junction, with negative acceptor ions on the P side and positive donor ions on the N side; it is wider on the lighter-doped side.
Middle: space-charge density is a step function; the P side is taller but thinner (heavier doping), the N side shorter but wider, so the two areas (total charge) match.
Bottom: the field is the integral of charge, a triangle peaking at the junction. The field points from the positive N-side charge toward the negative P-side charge.
Diffusion: carriers spreading from where there are many to where there are few, like ink in water.
Donor and acceptor ions: the fixed charged atoms left behind when carriers leave. Depletion region: the layer with almost no free carriers, only fixed charge.
Built-in potential: the voltage across the region once balance is reached, about 0. 7 volts in silicon. Drift: carriers moving because of an electric field.
Join P and N silicon. Electrons cross from N to P, and holes cross from P to N. When an electron meets a hole, it fills it and both disappear (recombination).
The N side is left with fixed positive ions and the P side with fixed negative ones. The field from them pushes carriers back.
When drift equals diffusion, the region stops growing. That is the whole idea.
"The depletion region forms because electrons diffuse from the N side to the P side and holes go the other way.
Each carrier that leaves exposes a fixed ionized dopant, positive donors on the N side and negative acceptors on the P side.
That fixed space charge makes an electric field that pushes carriers back, and the field grows until drift balances diffusion.
What's left is a carrier-free layer with a built-in potential of about 0. 7 volts for silicon. Reverse bias widens it, forward bias narrows it."

Common semiconductor materials. The question: What materials are typically used for semiconductors?
Semiconductors are made from several materials, and silicon is by far the most common. Each material has its own band gap and its own strengths.
Silicon wins on cost and ease of manufacture. Others, like gallium arsenide, are chosen when a special property is worth the cost: speed, light emission or high voltage.
Think of choosing a pan to cook with. A plain steel frying pan does almost every job well and is cheap, so most kitchens use it.
A copper saucepan heats faster, but costs more, so you use it only when speed matters. Silicon is the steel pan, and the others are the specialty pans.
The analogy only covers cost versus special ability, and not the actual physics.
On a log scale each material is a steep straight-ish line.

Germanium has the highest intrinsic density at room temperature and the highest leakage; silicon sits at 10^10; GaAs and especially SiC are many orders lower, which is why SiC devices can still behave as semiconductors at 500 degrees Celsius+ while silicon parts are normally rated only to about 150-175 degrees Celsius junction temperature (leakage climbs steeply above that, and lightly doped regions approach intrinsic behaviour near 200-250 degrees Celsius).
Band gap: the energy needed to free an electron, in eV (electron-volts, a tiny unit of energy). Mobility: how fast carriers move in a field.
Direct band gap: a gap where electrons can give off light easily, which suits LEDs and lasers. III-V compound: a mix of elements from groups III and V, such as gallium arsenide.
Wide-bandgap: materials with a large gap that handle high voltage and heat.
Compare gaps. Silicon has a band gap of about 1. 12 eV, which works well at room temperature. Germanium has about 0.
66 eV, which makes it leaky, so it is mostly used mixed with silicon (silicon-germanium) for fast radio-frequency (RF) circuits.
Gallium arsenide moves electrons faster and gives off light, so it suits RF and LEDs. That is the whole idea.
"Silicon is the workhorse because it's cheap, forms a great oxide, and has a good 1. 12 eV gap. Germanium is the older, leakier, 0. 66 eV material, now mostly used in SiGe.
III-V compounds like GaAs, InP and GaN are used for RF and optoelectronics because they have high electron mobility and direct bandgaps that emit light.
Silicon carbide and gallium nitride are wide-bandgap materials around 3. 3 eV used for high-voltage, high-temperature and fast power switching.
The choice is a trade between cost and a specific property."

What doping is and how it is done. The question: What is doping?
Doping means adding a tiny, controlled amount of another element to a semiconductor on purpose. Pure silicon barely conducts.
A few impurity atoms give it many more free carriers, and they set the carrier type: electrons for N-type or holes for P-type.
Doping is how chip makers build every diode, transistor and resistor on a chip.
Think of a nearly empty dance floor with only a handful of dancers. Adding a few more dancers makes it far livelier, and a small number of extra dancers has a big effect.
Dopant atoms are those extra dancers. You do not change the room, only invite a few guests.
The analogy is loose: the dopants also set whether the new carriers are electrons or holes.
The standard doping sequence. The mask decides where doping happens, implantation sets the dose and depth, and the anneal activates the dopants and repairs damage.
Anneals also let dopants diffuse a little, which engineers must budget.
Dopant: the impurity atom added on purpose. Carrier: a free electron or hole that can move and carry current. N-type and P-type: silicon with extra electrons, or extra holes.
Intrinsic: pure silicon with no doping. Ion implantation: firing electrically charged dopant atoms into the silicon slice (wafer), then heating it to repair the damage.
Silicon has about 5 times 10 to the 22 atoms per cubic centimeter (cm³). Add just one phosphorus atom per million silicon atoms.
That is 5 times 10 to the 16 dopant atoms per cm³, each giving one free electron.
Pure silicon has only about 10 to the 10 free carriers per cm³, so doping raises the number about five million times. That is the whole idea.
"Doping is deliberately adding a tiny, controlled amount of impurity atoms to a semiconductor to set its carrier type and concentration.
Pure silicon has only about 10 to the 10 carriers per cm³, so I add phosphorus or arsenic, which each donate an electron for N-type, or boron, which creates a hole for P-type.
A few parts per million is enough to raise conductivity by orders of magnitude.
It's done by ion implantation or diffusion followed by an anneal, and it's how every junction, channel and resistor on a chip is made."

How doping improves performance. The question: How does doping improve performance?
Doping improves silicon in four ways. It raises conductivity, since it adds many free carriers.
It makes the behavior steady, since the carrier count is fixed by the dopants and not by temperature.
It lets you choose electrons or holes, which is needed for diodes and transistors. And it lets you tune each region of a device for its own job.
Think of a river and a dam with adjustable gates. Pure silicon is like a trickle, whose flow changes a lot with weather.
Doping is like building controlled channels: more flow, a steady flow, and different channels for different jobs.
You can open one wide for low resistance and keep another narrow for high voltage. The analogy fails on one point: too much doping also makes things worse.
The undoped curve climbs about eight orders of magnitude over this range, which would make a resistor or junction unusable.
The doped curves are flat until the intrinsic density catches up: about 450-500 K for 10 to the 14 doping and about 600-700 K for 10 to the 16 .
That flat region is why doped devices are predictable. (Dopant freeze-out below roughly 100 K is not modelled.)
Conductivity: how easily a material carries current. It rises with the number of carriers.
Intrinsic carriers: free carriers in pure silicon, about 10 to the 10 per cm³ at room temperature. Doping level: dopant atoms per cm³, which sets the carrier count.
Junction: where N-type meets P-type. Breakdown voltage: the reverse voltage at which a junction starts to conduct heavily.
Pure silicon has about 10 to the 10 carriers per cm³. Dope it with 10 to the 16 phosphorus atoms per cm³. That is a million times more carriers.
The resistivity (the resistance of a 1 cm cube, in ohm-centimeters) falls from hundreds of thousands of ohm-centimeters to about half an ohm-centimeter.
The count now depends on the dopants, so it barely moves with temperature. That is the whole idea.
"Doping improves silicon in several ways.
It raises the carrier density by many orders of magnitude, so resistivity drops from hundreds of kilohm-centimetres to well under an ohm-centimetre.
It makes the carrier density set by design and stable over temperature instead of by thermal generation.
It lets me choose N or P so I can build junctions and transistors, and it lets me tune threshold, breakdown, gain and contact resistance.
The trade-off is that heavy doping lowers mobility and breakdown voltage."

Which elements are used as dopants. The question: What elements are typically used for doping?
Dopants are the elements added to silicon to make it N-type or P-type. Silicon has four outer electrons.
An element with five outer electrons gives an extra electron, which makes N-type. An element with three leaves a missing electron, which makes P-type.
You can find the right elements by looking at the periodic table.
Picture a square dance in which every dancer needs exactly four partners' hands. If a newcomer with five hands joins, one hand is left free.
If a newcomer with only three hands joins, one hand is missing. The free hand is an extra electron, and the missing one is a hole.
The analogy breaks down since atoms bond with electrons, not hands, but the counting works.
Dopants for a Group IV host sit one column on either side. Left column (one electron short) makes holes, right column (one extra electron) makes free electrons.
Elements in the same column as the host are isoelectronic and do not dope.
Valence electrons: the outer electrons that form bonds. Silicon has four. Donor: a dopant with five valence electrons that gives an extra electron, N-type.
Acceptor: a dopant with three valence electrons that makes a hole, P-type. Group III, IV and V: columns of the periodic table, with three, four and five valence electrons.
Doping: adding impurities on purpose.
Phosphorus is in Group V, with five valence electrons. Replace one silicon atom with it, and four electrons bond to neighbors while the fifth is free. That is a donor.
Boron is in Group III, with three, so one bond lacks an electron. That is an acceptor. Arsenic is another donor and boron is the usual acceptor. That is the whole idea.
"In silicon, donors are Group V atoms, with an extra valence electron: phosphorus, arsenic and antimony give N-type.
Acceptors are Group III atoms with one fewer: boron mainly, and gallium, aluminium or indium in special cases, give P-type.
Arsenic diffuses slowly so it's used for shallow source and drain; phosphorus diffuses faster and goes in wells; boron is the standard P-type dopant.
In compound semiconductors the dopants differ, such as silicon and magnesium in GaN."

Charge carrier mobility. The question: What is charge mobility?
Mobility tells you how fast a charge carrier moves for a given push from the electric field.
A higher mobility means carriers move faster, so the material conducts better and devices can switch faster.
Carriers keep bumping into vibrating atoms and impurities along the way, and those collisions limit the speed.
Picture walking across a room while pushed by a steady breeze. In an empty room you reach a good steady speed.
In a crowded room you keep bumping into people, and you move more slowly with the same breeze.
The breeze is the electric field, you are the carrier, and the crowd is the vibrating atoms and impurities.
The analogy fails at very high fields, where the speed stops increasing at all.
At low field the lines follow micro E (slope 1 on this log scale). Above a few kV/cm the curves bend over and flatten at v sat , while the dashed line keeps climbing.
Holes are slower at low field but saturate to a similar order of velocity, so the NMOS/PMOS gap closes in short-channel devices.
The hole saturation velocity is somewhat lower than electrons; the exact value depends on the model.
Drift velocity ( v d ): the average speed of carriers along the field. Electric field ( E ): the push on charge, in volts per cm.
Mobility ( micro ): speed per unit field, v d equals micro E , in cm²/V·s. Scattering: a carrier bouncing off a vibrating atom or an impurity.
Doping: adding impurities, which scatter carriers.
In lightly doped silicon, electron mobility is about 1350 cm²/V·s. Apply a field of 100 volts/cm. The drift velocity is 1350 times 100 equals 1. 35 times 10 to the 5 cm/s.
Holes in silicon have a mobility of about 480, so at the same field they drift at 4. 8 times 10 to the 4 cm/s, about three times slower. That is the whole idea.
"Mobility is how quickly carriers drift per unit of electric field: v d equals micro E , in cm²/V·s.
It equals q tau over m^ , so it depends on how long a carrier travels between scattering events and how light it is.
In silicon it's about 1350 for electrons and 480 for holes at room temperature, and it drops with higher temperature from lattice scattering and with higher doping from impurity scattering.
Conductivity is q(n micro n plus p micro p) , and at high field the velocity saturates near 10 to the 7 cm/s."

Majority carriers in P-type vs N-type. The question: What charge carriers are dominant in P-type semiconductors vs N-type semiconductors?
The majority carrier is whichever carrier is plentiful in a doped semiconductor. In N-type material it is electrons. In P-type material it is holes.
The doping sets the majority count. The other type is still there, as the minority carrier, but in tiny numbers.
Both matter, because the minority carriers do the work inside diodes and transistors.
Picture a school where almost every student is a left-hander, with just a few right-handers. The left-handers are the majority, and they set the character of the school.

Electron vs hole mobility. The question: Which charge carriers are more mobile: holes or electrons?
Mobility tells you how quickly a carrier moves when pushed by an electric field.
In silicon, electrons are more mobile than holes: about 1350 versus 480 in the same units, a ratio of roughly 2. 8. That one fact has big practical effects.
N-type devices are faster and conduct better than P-type devices of the same size.
Picture two runners crossing a field. The electron runs a smooth, simple track.
The hole has to move by a more crowded route, where neighbors keep passing the gap along, and it ends up slower. Same push, different path, so a different speed.
The analogy is only a picture: a hole is really an empty spot, and its "heaviness" comes from the way the silicon's energy bands are shaped.
Electrons have one conduction-band curve of moderate curvature.
Holes occupy the valence band, where the heavy-hole and light-hole branches meet at the top (degenerate at k equals 0 ).

The flat heavy-hole curve corresponds to a large effective mass; holes populate it heavily because it has a larger density of states, and they scatter readily between branches and into the nearby split-off band.
The parabolic picture is only a rough sketch; real silicon has six anisotropic conduction valleys and warped valence bands.
Mobility ( micro ): how fast a carrier drifts per unit of field. Effective mass: how heavy a carrier acts when pushed. Heavier means slower.
Majority carrier: the plentiful carrier type. NMOS and PMOS: transistors whose current is carried by electrons or by holes.

Say an NMOS transistor whose conducting channel is drawn 1 µm wide gives some amount of current. A PMOS of the same width carries holes, so it gives only about 1/2. 8 as much.
To match the NMOS, you make the PMOS about 2. 8 times wider, so roughly 2. 8 µm. In practice designers use about two to three times. That is the whole idea.

That's why PMOS devices are drawn wider than NMOS, NPN transistors beat PNP, and N-type material has lower resistance at the same doping."

Why N-type has lower resistance. The question: Why do N-type semiconductors typically have lower resistance?
N-type silicon has lower resistance than P-type silicon when both are doped by the same amount. Resistance depends on how many carriers there are and how fast each one moves.
With equal doping, the counts are about equal. But electrons move faster than holes, so N-type conducts better.
Picture two toll roads with the same number of cars. On one road the cars drive at 60 km/h and on the other they crawl at 20 km/h.
In an hour, the faster road moves more cars past the booth, so it carries more traffic. Equal car counts, different speeds, different flow. The analogy holds at equal doping.
At very heavy doping, the crowd of impurity atoms slows both kinds of carrier, and the speed gap shrinks.

As ionized-impurity scattering takes over (above about 10 to the 17 ), both mobilities converge toward their minimum values and the ratio decreases.
It never reaches 1 in this model; heavily doped P-type is still more resistive than N-type at equal doping.

How a diode works (PN junction). The question: How does a diode work?
A diode is a part that lets current flow easily in one direction and blocks it in the other.
Inside, it is a piece of silicon that is P-type on one side and N-type on the other, joined together. The join forms a barrier.
Pushing the right way lowers the barrier, and current flows. Pushing the wrong way raises it, and almost nothing flows.
Picture a turnstile at a subway gate, or a check valve in a water pipe. Push one way and it swings open, and people or water pass through. Push the other way and it locks shut.
A diode does that for current. The analogy breaks down in one place: a real diode needs a small push, about 0. 6 to 0.
7 volts in silicon, before it opens fully, like a stiff valve spring.
At equilibrium the junction is surrounded by a carrier-free depletion region holding fixed ions: negative acceptors on the P side, positive donors on the N side.
Their field points from N to P and pushes holes back to P and electrons back to N, opposing diffusion.
Anode and cathode: the P side and the N side. Forward current flows anode to cathode. Forward bias: the anode is more positive than the cathode, which lowers the barrier.
Reverse bias: the cathode is more positive, which raises the barrier. Depletion region: the carrier-free layer at the junction.
Forward voltage: the drop across a conducting diode, about 0. 7 volts for silicon.
Connect a 5 volts source, a 1 kilohms resistor and a silicon diode in series, with the diode pointing the right way. The diode drops about 0. 7 volts, so the resistor gets 4.
3 volts and the current is 4. 3 milliamps. Flip the diode around, and the current falls to a tiny leakage, nanoamps. That is the whole idea.
"A diode is a PN junction. Where P and N meet, carriers diffuse across and recombine, leaving a depletion region of fixed ions and a built-in barrier of a bit under a volt.
Forward bias lowers the barrier, and current grows exponentially, about ten times per 60 millivolts, so silicon looks 'on' around 0. 6 to 0. 7 volts.
Reverse bias raises the barrier and only a tiny leakage current flows, until breakdown. That's the Shockley equation: I equals I S(e to the V over nV T-1) ."

Diode use cases. The question: What are some use cases of a diode?
A diode lets current go one way and not the other, and engineers use that in many ways.
It can turn AC (current that keeps reversing) into DC (current that flows one way), block a battery that is plugged in backwards, or absorb a voltage spike.
A few special diodes do other jobs, such as emitting light. This page asks you to list the uses and say which diode property each one relies on.
Picture a one-way street. You can use it to keep traffic from going the wrong way, as in a rectifier. You can use it to stop a car from backing out, as in battery protection.
And you can give runaway traffic a side road to drain into, as a flyback diode does for a coil. All of those come from one rule: traffic goes one way.
The analogy leaves out the small toll a diode charges in voltage.
Group applications by the property they exploit. In an interview this gives you a structure to work through instead of a random list, and each branch has its own trade-off.
Rectifier: a diode circuit that turns AC into DC. Flyback diode: a diode across a coil that gives its current a safe path when switched off.
Zener diode: a diode designed to conduct in reverse at a set voltage. Forward drop: the voltage lost across a conducting diode, about 0. 7 volts in silicon.
Schottky diode: a diode with a lower forward drop.
Say a user might plug a battery in backwards. Put a diode in series with the supply. Plugged correctly, current flows, and the diode drops about 0. 7 volts.
Plugged backwards, the diode blocks, and the circuit is safe. The price is power: with 2 amps, the diode wastes about 0. 7 volts times 2 amps = 1. 4 watts. That is the whole idea.
"I group diode uses by the property they exploit. One-way conduction gives rectifiers, reverse-polarity protection, OR-ing two supplies, and flyback diodes across inductive loads.
Controlled breakdown gives Zener references and TVS surge clamps, plus the ESD diodes on every IC pin.
And the junction itself makes LEDs, photodiodes, varactors and temperature sensors.
The main cost is the forward drop, so in power paths I'd use a Schottky or an ideal-diode MOSFET."

Diode operating regions. The question: What are the different operation regions?
A diode acts differently depending on the voltage across it, and the three cases are called operating regions. Forward bias means it conducts. Reverse bias means it blocks.
Breakdown means a large reverse voltage makes current flow again. Knowing which region a diode is in tells you which simple model to use.
Picture a gate in a fence. Walk toward it from the front, and it swings open once you push hard enough. Walk toward it from the back, and it stays shut.
Push from the back with a bulldozer, and the gate breaks and lets everything through. Those are forward bias, reverse bias and breakdown.
The analogy fails in one way: a real diode's breakdown is reversible if you keep the current low.
The same physical device in three regimes. Forward: exponential conduction, voltage pinned near 0. 7 volts. Reverse: essentially zero current (nA).
Breakdown: steep reverse conduction, voltage pinned near minus V Z. Each region has a different hand model.
Anode and cathode: the diode's two ends, its P side and its N side. Forward bias: the anode is more positive than the cathode, so the diode conducts.
Reverse bias: the cathode is more positive, so the diode blocks and passes only leakage. Breakdown: a strong reverse field causes sudden current.
Operating region: which of the three cases the diode is in right now. Zener diode: a diode designed to work in breakdown.
Look at three cases for a silicon diode. Feed it forward from 5 volts through a resistor: it is forward biased and on, and for hand analysis it holds about 0. 7 volts.
Put minus 12 volts across a diode rated for 100 volts: it is reverse biased and off, like an open switch. Feed a 5.
1 volts Zener with 8 volts backwards through a resistor: it is in breakdown and holds about 5. 1 volts. That is the whole idea.

7 volts for silicon it's on, and I model it as a 0. 7 volt drop.
Reverse bias: the barrier rises, the depletion region widens, only nanoamps of leakage flow, so I treat it as open.

To find a diode's operating region, you work out the voltage across it, anode minus cathode, and compare it with two numbers: the turn-on voltage, about 0.
7 volts, and the breakdown voltage. Above turn-on, it is on. Between the two, it is off. Below minus the breakdown voltage, it is in breakdown.

Kinds of diodes. The question: What are the different kinds of diodes?
There are many kinds of diodes, and each is tuned for a different job. Some are built to conduct one way as efficiently as possible. Some are built to work in reverse breakdown.
Some use the junction to make or sense light, or to act as a tunable capacitor. You choose among them by trading forward drop, speed, leakage and voltage rating.
Think of a toolbox of one-way valves. One is a big, heavy valve for high pressure but slow to react. One is a light, quick valve for small flows.
One opens at very low pressure but leaks a little. All do the same basic job, but you pick the one that fits the pipe.
The analogy leaves out the special kinds, like LEDs, which also give off light.
Three families.
The first is about efficiency and speed when conducting; the second about controlled breakdown; the third about using the junction's optical or capacitive behaviour.
Each leaf is a different point in the trade-off space.
Rectifier diode: a standard diode for power, such as the 1N4007. Schottky diode: a metal-to-semiconductor diode with a low forward drop, around 0. 3 volts.
Zener and TVS diodes: diodes made to operate in reverse breakdown. LED and photodiode: diodes that give off light, or turn light into current.
Varactor: a diode used as a voltage-controlled capacitor.
You need a diode to carry 1 amps in a power path. A silicon diode drops about 0. 7 volts, so it wastes 0. 7 watts. A Schottky drops about 0. 3 volts, so it wastes about 0.
3 watts. For the power path, the Schottky is the better pick, as long as its higher reverse leakage is acceptable. That is the whole idea.
"I group them by job.

Conduction: standard rectifiers like the 1N4007 for high voltage but slow; small-signal 1N4148 for fast, low-current switching; ultrafast recovery for switching power; Schottkys for low forward drop and no reverse recovery but more leakage; and silicon carbide Schottkys for high-voltage power.
Breakdown: Zeners for references and clamps, TVS diodes for surge and ESD. And optical or capacitive: LEDs, laser diodes, photodiodes, solar cells and varactors."

A silicon diode needs about 0. 6 to 0. 7 volts across it before it conducts a useful current. That number is not magic. It comes from how the current rises with voltage.
The current is exponential in voltage, but it starts from an extremely tiny value, so you must push the voltage fairly high to reach milliamps.
Other diodes have different voltages because their barriers differ.
Picture climbing a very long staircase where each step multiplies your reward by ten. You start with almost nothing at the bottom.
You need to climb about eleven steps before the reward is large enough to matter. Each step costs about 60 millivolts. The voltage you climbed is the forward voltage.
The analogy is a little loose, since the rise is smooth and not in steps.

Forward voltage ( V F ): the voltage across a diode when it conducts normally.

Exponential: here, current rising about ten times for each 60 millivolts. Band gap: the energy gap of the material, which sets the barrier height. Decade: a factor of ten.

That is the whole idea.

Building an ideal diode. The question: How can you build an ideal diode?
An ideal diode would conduct forward with no voltage drop and block perfectly in reverse. A real diode always drops some voltage. You can get close by using other parts.
For small signals, an op-amp can hide the drop. For power, a MOSFET with a small controller acts like a diode with a drop of only millivolts.
Picture a revolving door that a helper watches. A normal diode is like a stiff one-way flap that always takes some effort to push.
The helper, the controller, senses when someone wants to enter and pushes the door open for them, and locks it the moment anyone tries to go backward.
The analogy fits closely: the helper is the control circuit, and the door is the MOSFET.
The first question to ask is signal or power.
Signal circuits use feedback to hide the diode drop; power circuits replace the diode with a MOSFET channel and add control to decide when it's on.
Forward drop: the voltage lost across a conducting diode. Op-amp: an amplifier chip with huge gain.
Wired with feedback (its output connected back to its input), it keeps correcting its output until it matches the input.
Superdiode: a diode placed inside an op-amp's feedback loop, so the op-amp cancels the drop.
MOSFET: a transistor switch turned on and off by the voltage on its control pin (the gate). R DS(on) : the small resistance of a MOSFET when it is on.
Body diode: the diode that is built into a MOSFET, pointing one way.
Take round example numbers. Say a power path carries 2 amps. A plain silicon diode drops about 0. 7 volts, so it wastes 0. 7 times 2 equals 1. 4 watts.
Now use a MOSFET with an R DS(on) of 10 milliohms and a controller that turns it on only when current should flow forward. The drop is 2 times 0. 01 equals 0.
02 volts, and the loss is about 0. 04 watts. That is the whole idea.

The NPN transistor symbol is a small picture with three leads: base, collector and emitter. The key detail is the arrow on the emitter.

BJT terminals: base, collector, emitter. The question: What are the terminals?
A BJT, or bipolar junction transistor, has three terminals. The base is the control terminal.
A small current into the base controls a much larger current flowing from the collector to the emitter.
The three terminals are not interchangeable, because the three layers inside are built differently, with different doping and size.
Picture a faucet. The handle is the base, the supply pipe is the collector, and the spout is the emitter.
A small twist of the handle controls a large flow of water from the pipe to the spout.
You could not swap the handle and the spout and expect the same result, because they are built differently.
The analogy breaks down since in a BJT the handle also draws a little current.

Real devices are laid out vertically with the emitter on top in a planar process.
Base: the thin middle layer and the control terminal. Emitter: the heavily doped layer that sends carriers into the base.
Collector: the layer that collects the carriers that cross the base. Current gain ( beta ): collector current divided by base current. Doping: how many impurity atoms a layer has.

The collector then carries about 100 milliamps, and the emitter passes the sum, about 101 milliamps. A small current controls a large one. That is the whole idea.

A small base current controls a large collector current.
They aren't symmetric: the emitter is heavily doped, the base is thin and lighter, and the collector is lightly doped and large to handle voltage and heat.
In an NPN, base and collector current go in and emitter current comes out, with the collector most positive and the base about 0. 7 volts above the emitter."

Use cases of a BJT. The question: What are some use cases of a BJT?
BJTs are used in two main ways. As a switch, a small base current turns a bigger load on and off, such as a relay or an LED.
As an amplifier, a small signal at the base becomes a larger signal at the collector.
Inside chips, BJTs also make references and temperature sensors, because their base-emitter voltage is very predictable.
Picture a light switch with a remote helper.
The microcontroller pin is too weak to power a relay directly, so it works the switch of a stronger helper, which does the heavy lifting. That is the switch use.
For the amplifier use, picture turning a small volume knob and hearing a much bigger sound.
The analogy leaves out the base current limit and the small voltage the helper itself needs.

7 volts instead of letting it spike to hundreds of volts. See "Diode use cases" for diode use cases.
Switch: a use where the transistor is fully on or fully off. Amplifier: a use where the output is a larger copy of a small input.
Saturation: fully on, with a very small voltage across it. Base resistor: a resistor that sets how much base current flows.
Current gain ( beta ): collector current divided by base current.

The base resistor sees about 3. 3 minus 0. 7 equals 2. 6 volts, so 2. 6 volts over 7 milliamps about 370 ohms. A 330 ohms resistor is a good choice. That is the whole idea.

BJT vs MOSFET comparison. The question: What is the difference between a BJT and MOSFET?
A BJT and a MOSFET both let a small control signal switch or shape a larger current. The key difference is the control. A BJT is controlled by a current into its base.
A MOSFET is controlled by a voltage on its gate, which draws almost no steady current.
That leads to different strengths: BJTs for precision analog, and MOSFETs for switching and digital logic.
Picture two ways of steering a boat. With a BJT, a person must keep pushing on the tiller the whole time to hold the course. That takes steady effort.
With a MOSFET, you set the rudder with a quick nudge and it stays there, with almost no ongoing effort.
The analogy breaks down since a MOSFET gate does need a brief pulse of charge each time you switch it.
At every current the BJT has more transconductance.

The BJT line is a straight line of slope 1 ( g m proportional to I C ); the MOSFET follows the same slope at very low current (weak inversion, with a ratio 1 over n lower) then bends over to a square-root law ( g m proportional to square root of I D ) in strong inversion.
At 1 milliamps the BJT has 38. 7 mS versus 6. 3 mS for this MOSFET (overdrive square root of 2I D over k equals 0. 32 volts).

A bigger device (higher W over L ) raises the square-root branch and keeps the MOSFET in weak inversion up to higher currents, so its g m gets closer to the BJT's (but never above I D over (nV T) ), which is why analogue MOS designers use large, low-current devices when they need gain per milliamp.
Current-controlled: the output is set by a steady input current. Voltage-controlled: the output is set by an input voltage with almost no current.
Gate: the MOSFET's control terminal, insulated from the channel. R DS(on) : the resistance of an on MOSFET, which can be a few milliohms.
Saturation voltage ( V CE(sat) ): the small voltage left across a fully on BJT, about 0. 1 to 0. 3 volts.
Take the example used further down this page: switching 5 amps. A fully on BJT keeps about 0. 3 volts across it, so it wastes 0. 3 times 5 equals 1. 5 watts.
It also needs about 0. 5 amps of steady base current (a gain of 10), which wastes roughly another 0. 35 watts. A MOSFET with an R DS(on) of 10 milliohms wastes 5 squared times 0.
01 equals 0. 25 watts, and it needs no steady gate current. That is the whole idea.
"A BJT is current-controlled: base current into a forward-biased junction controls collector current, with a gain around 100.
A MOSFET is voltage-controlled, with an insulated gate that draws essentially no DC current.
The BJT has higher transconductance per milliamp, better matching and lower noise, so it suits precision analogue.
The MOSFET has very low on-resistance, no base drive, positive temperature coefficient for current sharing, and scales to VLSI, so it dominates switching and digital."

The vertical axis is the collector current. You draw several curves, one for each value of base current.
Each curve rises quickly, then flattens, and a bigger base current gives a higher curve.

Each handle setting gives a different steady flow. The handle is the base current, and the steady flow is the collector current.

How a BJT works. The question: How does it work?
A BJT works by letting a small current at the base steer a much larger flow of carriers from the emitter to the collector.
In an NPN, electrons flow from the emitter into a very thin base. Most of them cross the base and get swept into the collector.
A few are lost along the way, and the base current replaces them.
Picture rolling balls across a narrow strip of sticky ground, with a steep downhill slope just past it.
The strip is so narrow that almost every ball makes it across and drops down the slope. Only a few get stuck on the way.
The roller is the emitter, the sticky strip is the base, and the slope is the strong electric field at the collector junction.
The analogy breaks in one place: carriers do not roll in straight lines but wander randomly across the base (diffusion).
A schematic band diagram.

The forward bias lowers the emitter-base barrier so electrons (blue) spill into the base's conduction band; they diffuse across the thin base along the flat part of the diagram and then "fall" down the steep slope of the reverse-biased collector junction.
The drawing is qualitative and not to scale.
Forward-biased junction: a junction pushed in the direction where the barrier is lowered. Minority carrier: electrons in the P-type base are the scarce carrier there.
Recombination: an electron falling into a hole, so both stop being free carriers. Base width: how thin the base is. A thinner base loses fewer carriers.
Current gain ( beta ): collector current divided by base current.
Take an NPN with a gain of about 100. The emitter sends 101 electrons into the base. Because the base is thin, 100 of them cross to the collector.
The cost is about one hole from the base: it is used up by recombination, or it leaks back into the emitter. The base current resupplies that one hole.
So the collector current is about 100 times the base current. That is the whole idea.
"In an NPN the forward-biased base-emitter junction injects electrons from the heavily doped emitter into the thin base.
Most diffuse across before recombining, and the field of the reverse-biased base-collector junction sweeps them into the collector.
That gives a collector current set by V BE , I C equals I Se to the V BE over V T , nearly independent of V CE .
A small base current supplies the holes lost to recombination and back-injection, so I B about I C over beta with beta 100 ."

NPN vs PNP transistors. The question: What is the difference between an NPN and PNP?
NPN and PNP are the two flavors of bipolar junction transistor (BJT), a part that uses a small current to control a larger one. They do the same job with every polarity flipped.
An NPN switches on when its base is a little above its emitter, and a PNP switches on when its base is a little below its emitter.
Think of two doors that open in opposite directions. The NPN door opens when you push the base up above the emitter, and the PNP door when you pull it down below.
Both let a big flow through once open. The analogy breaks down on speed: electrons move more easily than holes, so the NPN is usually the faster, higher-gain door.
The NPN conducts when V in is more than 0. 7 volts above V out (sourcing current from +12 volts to the load); the PNP conducts when V in is more than 0.
7 volts below V out (sinking current to -12 volts). Between plus or minus 0. 7 volts neither conducts, which creates the dead zone and crossover distortion.
Base, emitter, collector: the three terminals. A small current at the base controls a larger current between collector and emitter.
Electrons and holes: the two kinds of charge carrier. A hole is a missing electron that acts like a moving positive charge.
Electrons do most of the carrying in an NPN, holes in a PNP. Forward-biased junction: a junction is the boundary between two differently treated silicon layers.
Forward-biased means pushed the way that lets current through, about 0. 7 volts for silicon.
Low-side / high-side switch: a switch placed between the load and ground, or between the supply and the load.
Put an NPN's emitter on ground. A base at 0 volts keeps it off, and a base at about 0. 7 volts or more starts to turn it on. Now put a PNP's emitter on a 5 volts supply.
A base at 5 volts keeps it off, and a base at about 4. 3 volts starts to turn it on. The NPN naturally sits on the ground side of a load, and the PNP on the supply side.
That is the whole idea.
"NPN and PNP are doping mirror images. NPN is N-P-N with electrons as main carriers; PNP is P-N-P with holes. An NPN conducts when the base is 0.
7 volts above the emitter, current flows into the collector and out of the emitter, and it's the natural low-side switch. A PNP conducts when the base is 0.
7 volts below the emitter, with current into the emitter, and it's the natural high-side switch.
Because holes are less mobile than electrons, PNPs are slower with lower gain, so NPNs are preferred when you have the choice."

BJT modes of operation. The question: What are the different modes of operation?
A BJT has two junctions inside it, one between base and emitter and one between base and collector. A junction is the boundary between two differently treated layers of silicon.
Its "mode" just says whether each junction is pushed forward (letting current through) or reversed (blocking it).
The mode tells you whether the transistor is acting as an open switch, an amplifier, or a closed switch.
Picture a faucet. Fully closed is cutoff: nothing flows. Partly open is the active mode: the flow follows how far you turn the handle, so the transistor can amplify.
Wide open is saturation: the flow is limited by the pipe, not the handle. Reverse-active is like plumbing the faucet in backward. It works, but poorly.
A quick triage you can do with a multimeter. V BC equals V BE-V CE , so " V CE< 0. 3 volts with V BE about 0. 7 volts" means the collector junction is forward biased by about 0.
4 volts or more, i. e. saturation.
Forward-biased / reverse-biased: a junction that conducts, or one that blocks. V BE : the voltage from base to emitter. About 0. 7 volts when the junction is conducting.
V CE : the voltage from collector to emitter. Cutoff: both junctions reversed. No current, like an open switch. Saturation: both junctions forward. V CE drops to roughly 0.
2 volts, like a closed switch. Active region: base-emitter forward, base-collector reverse. Collector current is beta (the current gain, often around 100) times base current.
Connect a 1 kilohms resistor from a 5 volts supply to the collector of an NPN, with the emitter on ground.
With the base at 0 volts, the transistor is in cutoff, no current flows, and the collector sits at 5 volts. Now drive the base hard.
The transistor saturates, V CE falls to about 0. 2 volts, and the current is (5-0. 2) over 1 kilohms about 4. 8 milliamps, set by the resistor. That is the whole idea.
"A BJT's mode comes from the bias on its two junctions. Cutoff: both reverse, no current, open switch. Forward-active: base-emitter forward, base-collector reverse, V BE about 0.
7 volts and I C equals beta I B , the amplifier mode. Saturation: both forward, V CE about 0. 2 volts, current limited by the circuit, closed switch.
Reverse-active: roles of emitter and collector swapped, with poor gain. I tell them apart by V BE and V CE , and for a switch I check beta I B against the load current."

BJT current gain (beta). The question: What is current gain/beta?
Current gain, called beta, tells you how many times bigger a transistor's collector current is than its base current.
It is the number that makes a BJT useful: a tiny base current controls a much larger collector current.
Beta is typically 50 to 300 for a small-signal transistor, and it is not a precise value.
Think of a small tap that controls a big water main through a valve.
A trickle through the tap lets a flood through the main, and the flood is always a rough multiple of the trickle. But the multiple is not exact.
It differs from one valve to the next and changes with temperature. So a good plumber never designs a system that depends on one exact multiple.

beta is low at tiny currents (recombination in the depletion region steals base current), peaks in the middle (here around 1 milliamps) and falls again at high current (high-level injection, base widening).
The curve is an illustrative formula, not a specific part; the shape matches typical datasheet h FE plots. Operate in the flat region and don't rely on beta at the extremes.
Beta ( beta ): collector current divided by base current, I C over I B . Alpha ( alpha ): collector current divided by emitter current. Just under 1.
Base current ( I B ): the small current into the base that controls the transistor. Forward-active region: the mode where beta applies.
Forced beta: a deliberately low gain, such as 10, that you design with in a switch so it saturates reliably.
Suppose beta is 100 and you push 10 microamps into the base. The collector current is 100 times that: 1 milliamps. The emitter current is the sum of the two, 1. 01 milliamps.
So alpha is 1 over 1. 01 , about 0. 99. The page's formula beta equals alpha over (1- alpha) turns alpha back into beta: with alpha rounded to 0. 99 it gives 0. 99 over 0.
01 equals 99 , which is 100 apart from the rounding. That is the whole idea.
"Beta is the ratio of collector current to base current in forward-active mode, typically 50 to 300 for small-signal transistors. It's linked to alpha, I C over I E (about 0.
99), by beta equals alpha over (1- alpha) . It comes from the fraction of injected carriers that reach the collector: a thin base and a heavily doped emitter give high beta.
It's not a precise constant: it varies a lot between parts and with current and temperature, so good designs use feedback, like emitter degeneration, instead of relying on it."

Draw NMOS and PMOS symbols. The question: Draw a PFET/NFET symbol.
A MOSFET is a transistor controlled by a voltage on its gate. Engineers draw it with a standard symbol, and the symbol itself tells you which type it is.
The N-channel (NMOS) and P-channel (PMOS) symbols are almost identical, and the one clue that separates them is the direction of a small arrow.
Picture the symbol as a tiny diagram of the device. A plate on the left is the gate, held apart from the channel by a gap, which stands for the insulating oxide.
The channel is a broken vertical line on the right with drain at the top and source at the bottom.
The arrow points from the P side to the N side (P and N are the two kinds of specially treated silicon). It points in for NMOS and out for PMOS.
NFET on the left (arrow into the channel, drain on top), PFET on the right (arrow out of the channel, source on top).
In both, the body is tied to the source, which creates the drawn body diode. For the NFET it points source to drain, for the PFET drain to source.
Either way it's reverse-biased in normal operation.
Gate (G): the control terminal, insulated from the rest of the device. Drain (D) and source (S): the two ends of the channel that current flows between.
Body (B): the piece of silicon the channel forms in. The arrow sits on this line. Enhancement mode: no channel until you apply gate voltage. A broken channel line shows this.
Body diode: a built-in one-way valve for current (a diode) from source to drain, often drawn on power MOSFETs.
To draw an NMOS in words: a gate line goes to a vertical plate, a small gap follows, then a broken vertical channel line.
The drain leaves the top, the source leaves the bottom, and the body arrow points into the channel.
For a PMOS, point the arrow out, and usually flip it so the source is at the top, toward the supply. That is the whole idea.
"An NFET symbol is a gate plate separated from a broken channel line, drain on top, source on the bottom, and an arrow on the body pointing into the channel.
The PFET is the same with the arrow pointing out, and I flip it so the source is on top at the supply.
The arrow is the body-channel PN junction pointing from P to N, the broken line means enhancement-mode, normally off, and the gap shows the gate is insulated.
Discrete parts also show the body diode from source to drain."
Quick check. On a standard enhancement-mode MOSFET symbol, the arrow on the body points into the channel. What type is it?
MOSFET terminals and their roles. The question: What are the terminals?
A MOSFET has four terminals: gate, drain, source and body. The gate is the control, and a voltage on it decides whether current can flow from drain to source.
It does that by creating or removing the channel, a thin conducting path between drain and source. The body is the silicon the channel forms in.
On discrete parts the body is wired to the source inside the package, which is why you usually see only three pins.
Think of a garden hose with a pinch valve. Water enters at the source, leaves at the drain, and the gate is a hand squeezing the hose from the outside through a thin wall.
The hand never touches the water, and it takes no flow to hold the squeeze. The body is the ground the hose lies on.
The analogy breaks down on one point: the hand here is an electric field, not a push.
Lateral NMOS. The gate is separated from the body by a thin oxide (grey), so it couples only through an electric field.
Source and drain are identical N+ islands; the body is the P-type silicon underneath. With enough gate voltage, an N-type inversion layer (dashed) bridges source and drain.
Gate: the control terminal, insulated by a thin oxide, so it draws almost no DC current. Source: where the charge carriers enter the channel. Voltages are measured from it.
Drain: where the carriers leave the channel. Body (bulk, substrate): the silicon under the channel.
Threshold voltage ( V t ): the gate-to-source voltage where the channel starts to form.
Take an NFET with its source on ground and an LED and resistor from the supply to its drain. Say its threshold is about 2 volts.
With the gate at 0 volts, no channel forms and the LED is off. Raise the gate to 5 volts, the channel forms, current flows from drain to source, and the LED lights.
The gate itself carries almost no current. That is the whole idea.
"Four terminals: gate, drain, source and body. The gate is insulated by the oxide, draws no DC current, and its voltage relative to the source creates or removes the channel.
The source supplies the carriers and is the reference for V GS and V DS . The drain collects them and usually connects to the load. The body is the silicon the channel lives in.
Discrete parts tie it to the source internally, which is why they have three pins and a body diode."

Why source and body are tied. The question: Which two terminals are often connected together and why?
On almost every discrete MOSFET, the source and the body are shorted together inside the package.
This keeps the junctions around the channel safely blocked and keeps the threshold voltage steady. The price is a built-in diode from source to drain, called the body diode.
Think of a high-jump bar whose height is measured from the floor. If the floor under the jumper could sink, the jump needed to clear the bar would keep changing.
The body is that floor, and the threshold voltage is the bar height. Bolting the floor to the source keeps the bar where the datasheet says.
The catch is that the bolt also creates a one-way flap, the body diode, that lets current slip backward when the voltage is reversed.
A P+ body contact sits right next to the N+ source and one metal strap shorts them. The two red diodes are the body-source and body-drain junctions (anode = P body).
Shorting S to B leaves the body-source diode permanently at 0 volts. The body-drain diode remains and becomes the "body diode" between S and D.
Body (substrate): the silicon the channel is built in. PN junction: the boundary between P-type and N-type silicon (two differently treated kinds).
It acts like a diode, a one-way valve for current. Body effect: the threshold voltage shifts when the source is not at the same voltage as the body.
Body diode: the diode formed between body and drain once the body is tied to the source. V SB : the voltage from source to body.
Tie an NFET's body to its source, so V SB equals 0 . The threshold voltage then stays at its normal value, and the source-body junction can never conduct by accident.
Now pull the drain below the source by more than about 0. 7 volts while the gate is off. The body diode conducts anyway, so one MOSFET can block current in only one direction.
That is why battery protection circuits put two MOSFETs back to back. That is the whole idea.
"Source and body. Discrete MOSFETs short them internally.

It keeps the source-body PN junction from ever forward-biasing, and it removes the body effect: if the source sits above the body, the threshold voltage goes up, so with V SB equals 0 the threshold stays put.
The cost is the body diode from source to drain, so one FET only blocks one direction.
In ICs, NMOS bodies usually share the grounded substrate, so you often can't tie them and have to live with the body effect."
