MOSFET use cases. The question: What are some use cases of a MOSFET?
A MOSFET is a voltage-controlled switch or valve, and it is used in three big places.
It switches power on and off, it forms the logic gates (the tiny yes/no decision circuits) inside every chip, and it works as an amplifier or adjustable resistor in analog circuits.
It is popular because a tiny voltage on its insulated gate controls a lot of current.
Think of a light switch that needs no effort to hold. You flick it with a voltage, and it stays on without you pushing.
A small signal from a microcontroller flips the switch for something large, like a motor. Billions of these tiny switches, wired in pairs, make up a processor.
Sorting by operating region explains the "why."
Switches flip between cutoff and triode, amplifiers and current sources sit in saturation, and analog switches use triode as a variable resistor.
Switch: a part that is either fully on or fully off. Gate drive: the voltage and current you supply to the gate to turn the MOSFET on or off.
Low-side switch: a switch between the load and ground. CMOS: logic built from paired N-channel and P-channel MOSFETs.
R DS(on) : the resistance between drain and source when the MOSFET is fully on.
A 3. 3 volts microcontroller pin cannot power a 12 volts motor directly. Put an NFET between the motor and ground, and connect the pin to its gate.
Pin high turns the NFET on, and the motor runs. Say the motor draws 1 amps and the NFET has 10 milliohms of R DS(on) : it drops 1 times 0. 01 equals 0. 01 volts and wastes only 0.
01 watts. That is the whole idea.
"Three main areas.
Switching: low-side NFETs driving motors, relays and LEDs from a GPIO, PFET high-side load switches, and the switches in buck converters, H-bridges and synchronous rectifiers.
Digital: every CMOS gate and memory cell.

Analog: in saturation it's a voltage-controlled current source for amplifiers, current mirrors and LDO pass elements, and in triode it's a voltage-controlled resistor for analog switches and level shifters.
The insulated gate and low on-resistance are why it fits all of them."
Quick check. In which operating region does a MOSFET used as an on/off load switch spend its 'on' time?
Why MOSFETs are so widely used. The question: Why are MOSFETs used so often?
MOSFETs are everywhere because they are easy to drive, waste little power, and switch fast. The gate is insulated, so once it is charged it needs almost no current to stay on.
When fully on, the transistor acts like a small resistor. And in digital chips, paired N-channel and P-channel devices draw almost no power when idle.
Picture a door held open by a latch instead of by your hand. You give it one push, and then it stays open with no effort.
A BJT (the older bipolar transistor, which needs a steady control current) is more like holding the door open the whole time.
The latch comparison is not perfect, since the MOSFET gate does need a burst of charge each time it switches.
At high voltage the MOSFET's square-law I²R loss overtakes the IGBT's near-fixed drop once current is high enough (here about 8 amps). Below the crossover the MOSFET wins.
At low voltage (30–100 volts), MOSFET R DS(on) is so small that the MOSFET wins at essentially every current. Numbers are illustrative, not from a specific datasheet.
Gate capacitance: the gate acts like a small capacitor, a part that stores charge. It takes current only while charging or discharging. R DS(on) : the on-resistance.
Power lost is I to the 2R . Majority carrier: the main charge carrier. MOSFETs use only one type, so no stored charge slows them down.
CMOS: paired N- and P-channel MOSFETs where one is always off. Switching loss: energy wasted each time a switch changes state.
Carry 10 amps through a MOSFET with 5 milliohms of on-resistance. The power lost is 10 squared times 0. 005 equals 0. 5 watts. A saturated BJT dropping, say, 0.
3 volts at the same current would waste 10 times 0. 3 equals 3 watts. The MOSFET also needs no steady gate current, while a power BJT needs a steady base current.
That is the whole idea.
"Four reasons. The gate is insulated, so it's voltage-driven and draws no current to stay on, which makes it trivial to drive from logic.
When it's on it's just a small resistor, milliohms in modern parts, so conduction loss is low and paralleling works because R DS(on) rises with temperature.
It's a majority-carrier device, so it switches fast without storage time. And for digital, CMOS pairs draw almost no static power and MOSFETs scale down to billions per chip."
Quick check. What is the main reason a MOSFET can be driven directly from a microcontroller pin while a power BJT usually can't?
BJT vs MOSFET (MOSFET perspective). The question: What is the difference between a BJT and MOSFET?
A BJT and a MOSFET both act as electronic switches or amplifiers, but you control them differently. A BJT needs a steady base current to stay on.
A MOSFET needs only a voltage on its insulated gate. That one difference explains most of why MOSFETs dominate switching.
Think of two ways to keep a door open. A BJT is like holding it with your hand: as long as you keep pushing, it stays open.
A MOSFET is like setting a latch: you push once and it stays. The comparison fails on one point. A MOSFET gate still needs a short burst of current each time it switches.
The BJT's g m grows linearly with current; a MOSFET's grows only as √I, and you need a much wider device (bigger k n, i. e. , more W/L) just to approach the BJT.
This is why bipolar input stages are still used in low-noise and high-gain analog.
Base current: the steady current a BJT needs. About collector current divided by beta, the BJT's current gain (often about 100).
Gate capacitance: why the MOSFET gate takes current only during switching. V CE(sat) and R DS(on) : a BJT's fixed drop when on, versus a MOSFET's resistance when on.
Transconductance: how much output current changes per volt of input. BJTs have more per milliamp. Saturation: in a BJT it means fully on.
In a MOSFET it means constant-current mode.
Say you want to carry 1 amps. A BJT with a beta of 100 needs about 10 milliamps of base current the whole time it is on.
A MOSFET needs essentially zero current once the gate has charged. Neither is free, but the MOSFET's DC drive cost is far lower. That is the whole idea.
"A BJT is current-controlled through a forward-biased junction: it needs continuous base current, roughly I C over beta , and when on it has a fixed-ish V CE(sat) .
A MOSFET is voltage-controlled through an insulated gate: no DC gate current, and when on it's a resistor, R DS(on) . MOSFETs switch faster and parallel easily.
BJTs have more transconductance per milliamp and lower noise, so they still win in some analog.
And watch the names: BJT saturation is fully on, MOSFET saturation is the amplifier region."

MOSFET I-V curves. The question: Draw IV curve for MOSFET
The I-V curves of a MOSFET are graphs showing how much drain current flows for each drain voltage, with one curve per gate voltage.
They summarize the whole behavior in one picture. You read from them when the device is off, when it acts like a resistor, and when it acts like a constant current source.
Picture a family of hills, one for each gate voltage. Each starts at the origin, climbs steeply, and then levels off into a plateau. Higher gate voltages give higher plateaus.
A dashed curve through the point where each hill levels off separates the climb on the left from the plateau on the right.

The slight upward tilt in saturation is channel-length modulation.

Saturation region: the flat part, where current barely depends on V DS . Overdrive: V GS-V t , how far the gate is above threshold.
Channel-length modulation: the slight upward tilt of the flat part.

"I'd plot I D against V DS with a curve for each V GS . Below threshold there's no current.

Above it, each curve rises roughly linearly from the origin, that's triode where the FET is a voltage-controlled resistor, then flattens into saturation where I D equals 1 over 2 k n(V GS-V t) squared .

How a MOSFET works. The question: How does it work?
A MOSFET is a switch where the gate voltage builds a conducting path in the silicon. With the gate off, the source and drain are cut off from each other.
With enough gate voltage, a thin layer under the gate turns into a channel that connects them. The gate never touches that channel. It acts through an electric field.
Picture two ponds separated by dry land, with a flat metal plate hovering over the land.
Charge the plate and the ground beneath it fills with electrons, forming a shallow strip of water that joins the ponds.
The ponds are the source and drain, and the strip is the channel. Remove the charge and the strip dries up. One limit of the picture: the plate adds no water itself.
Its charge only pulls electrons already in the silicon up to the surface.
An NMOS with the gate above threshold and a small V DS.
The positive gate has pushed holes away (orange depletion region of ionized acceptors) and pulled a thin sheet of electrons to the surface (the channel).
Without that sheet, source-body-drain is N-P-N: two back-to-back diodes, so nothing flows.
Channel: the thin conducting layer that forms under the gate. Threshold voltage ( V t ): the gate voltage where the channel forms.
P-type and N-type: silicon treated so that it carries current mainly with positive "holes" or mainly with electrons.
Depletion region: the area where the gate field pushes away the free charges that were there. Inversion: the body surface flipping from P-type to N-type under the gate.
Triode and saturation: resistor-like and constant-current behavior.
Take an N-channel MOSFET with a threshold of about 2 volts.
With the gate at 0 volts, the path from source to drain is N, then P, then N, which is two back-to-back diodes (one-way valves for current facing opposite ways), so no current flows.
Raise the gate to 5 volts and the surface under it flips to N-type. Now there is a continuous path, and a voltage between drain and source drives current through it.
That is the whole idea.
"Take an NMOS: a P-type body with N-type source and drain, and a gate on a thin oxide in between. With no gate voltage, it's two back-to-back diodes, so no current.
A positive gate voltage first pushes holes away, then, past threshold, pulls enough electrons to the surface to form an N-type channel linking source and drain.
V DS drives current through it, and more overdrive means more channel charge and lower resistance. At high V DS the channel pinches off at the drain and the current saturates.
The gate controls everything through the field, with no DC current."

N-channel vs P-channel MOSFET. The question: What is the difference between an N-channel and P-channel?
N-channel and P-channel MOSFETs are the two mirror-image types of the same switch.
In an N-channel device the conducting path is made of electrons, and in a P-channel device it is made of holes.
Each one turns on with the opposite gate voltage, and each one likes to sit on the opposite side of a load.
Think of right-handed and left-handed scissors. They do the same job, but everything about how you hold them is mirrored.
Push the N-channel gate up above its source and it turns on. Pull the P-channel gate down below its source and it turns on.
Unlike scissors, the pair are not equally good: electrons move more easily than holes, so the N-channel one carries more current for the same size.
The NMOS sits between the load and ground (source at the low side); the PMOS sits between VDD and the load (source at the high side).
Each wants its source at its respective rail so the gate-source voltage is easy to generate from logic levels.
N-channel (NMOS): a MOSFET whose channel carries electrons. Source usually at ground. P-channel (PMOS): a MOSFET whose channel carries holes. Source usually at the supply.
Hole: a missing electron in silicon that acts like a positive charge carrier. Mobility: how easily a carrier moves. Electrons are about 2 to 3 times more mobile than holes.
Threshold ( V t ): the gate-to-source voltage that turns the device on.
Run both from a 5 volts supply. An NMOS has its source on ground, so a gate at 5 volts gives V GS equals plus 5 volts and it turns on.
A PMOS has its source on 5 volts, so a gate at 0 volts gives V GS equals -5 volts and it turns on, while a gate at 5 volts gives V GS equals 0 and it stays off.
At equal size, if the NMOS carries 2. 5 milliamps, the PMOS carries about 1 milliamps. That is the whole idea.
"The difference is the carrier in the channel.
An N-channel FET has an electron channel in a p-type body, turns on with the gate above the source by more than Vt, and its source usually sits at ground.
A P-channel FET is the mirror image: hole channel, gate must go below the source, source usually at the supply.

Because holes are about 2 to 3 times less mobile than electrons, a PMOS needs to be 2 to 3 times wider to match an NMOS, so NMOS is the default and PMOS is used where it simplifies high-side drive or for the pull-up in CMOS."
Quick check. What forms the conducting channel in a P-channel enhancement MOSFET?
Enhancement vs depletion mode MOSFET. The question: What is the difference between enhancement-mode and depletion mode?
The two modes differ in whether a channel already exists with zero gate voltage. An enhancement-mode MOSFET has no channel until you apply a gate voltage, so it starts off.
A depletion-mode MOSFET has a channel built in during manufacturing, so it starts on. Almost every MOSFET you buy is enhancement mode.
Picture two doors. The enhancement door is normally locked, and you have to push a button to open it.
The depletion door is normally open, and you have to push a button to close it. Many designs prefer the locked door, because if power is lost the circuit fails safely off.
The analogy fails on one point: for an N-channel depletion door, the button is a negative gate voltage.
The only structural difference is the thin implanted n-layer (shaded strip under the gate in the right-hand device).
It gives the depletion device a conducting path at zero gate bias; the enhancement device must have the gate create it.
Channel: the thin conducting layer between source and drain. Threshold voltage ( V t ): the gate voltage where the device changes state. Enhancement mode: normally off.
For N-channel, V t is positive. Depletion mode: normally on. For N-channel, V t is negative. Normally off / normally on: the state with the gate at 0 volts.
Say an N-channel enhancement MOSFET has V t equals plus 1 volts. At V GS equals 0 it is off, and at V GS equals 2 volts it is on.
Now say an N-channel depletion MOSFET has V t equals -2 volts. At V GS equals 0 it is already on, and you must pull the gate below -2 volts, say to -3 volts, to turn it off.
Use enhancement parts as switches. Use depletion parts where something must work before everything else powers up. That is the whole idea.
"The mode tells you whether a channel exists at zero gate voltage.
Enhancement mode has no channel at V GS equals 0 , so it's normally off and you apply a gate voltage above V t to create one. That's nearly every MOSFET.
Depletion mode has a channel implanted at fabrication, so it conducts at zero gate voltage and you apply a gate voltage of the opposite polarity to cut it off.
For an N-channel that means a negative threshold. The equations are identical, just with a negative V t , and depletion parts are used for start-up circuits and current sources."

MOSFET modes of operation. The question: What are the different modes of operation?
A MOSFET works in one of three regions, and two simple comparisons tell you which. If the gate is below threshold, it is off (cutoff).
If the gate is above threshold and the drain-source voltage is small, it acts like a resistor (triode).
If the drain-source voltage is larger, it acts like a constant current source (saturation).
Think of a faucet that is off, then opens, then reaches a maximum flow. At first the flow depends on both the handle and the pressure behind it.
Past a certain point, more pressure does not add flow, because the handle sets the limit. Switches work at the first two settings. Amplifiers work at the flat setting.
A warning: a MOSFET's "saturation" means flow is capped, not that it is fully on.
Each curve rises through the origin (triode), bends, and goes flat once it meets the dashed red parabola I D equals 1 over 2 kilovolts DS squared (saturation).
Left of and above the parabola is triode; right of and below it is saturation. The flat segments are spaced like V ov squared : 1, 4, 9 times 1 milliamps.
Cutoff: gate below threshold, so no channel and almost no current. Triode (linear) region: channel connects fully, and the device acts as a variable resistor.
Saturation: channel pinches off at the drain, and the current stays almost constant. Overdrive ( V ov ): V GS-V t . How far the gate is above threshold.
Pinch-off: the channel narrowing to a point at the drain end.
Say V t equals 2 volts. At V GS equals 1 volts the gate is below threshold, so it is in cutoff. At V GS equals 4 volts the overdrive is 2 volts.
If V DS is 1 volts, that is smaller than 2 volts, so the device is in triode and acts like a resistor.
If V DS is 5 volts, that is larger than 2 volts, so it is in saturation and the current is fixed by the gate. That is the whole idea.
"There are three regions. In cutoff, V GS is below threshold, there's no channel, and the device is open.
In triode, V GS is above threshold but V DS is less than the overdrive, so the channel spans the whole device and it behaves like a voltage-controlled resistor.

In saturation, V DS is bigger than the overdrive, the channel pinches off at the drain, and the current flattens at about half k times overdrive squared, so it acts like a gate-controlled current source.
Switches use cutoff and triode, amplifiers use saturation."
Quick check. An NMOS has V t equals 1 volts, V GS equals 3 volts, and V DS equals 0. 5 volts. Which region is it in?
Find the MOSFET region and load line. The question: Given Vgs and Vt, how will the FET behave? What operating region will it be in? Load-line analysis.
To find which region a MOSFET is in, you guess one region, calculate with it, and check whether the answer agrees with the guess.
The load line is the picture of the circuit's side of the problem. The operating point is where the circuit's line crosses the transistor's curve.
Picture a tug of war between two rules. The transistor says "my current is this much for this gate voltage".
The resistor says "my current depends on how much voltage is left over for me". The two rules only agree at one point, like two roads crossing at one intersection.
That intersection is where the circuit settles.
The gate source V GS sets which transistor curve applies; R D and V DD draw the load line. V D equals V DS because the source is at ground.
Cutoff, triode, saturation: the three regions. Overdrive ( V ov ): V GS-V t . Load line: the straight line I D equals (V DD-V DS) over R D set by the circuit.
Operating point (Q-point): the crossing of the load line and the transistor's curve. Check step: after guessing saturation, confirm that V DS at least V ov .
Take a supply V DD equals 5 volts, a drain resistor R D equals 1 kilohms, V t equals 1 volts and a size factor k equals 2 milliamps/V² (set by how big the transistor is).
Set V GS equals 2 volts. The overdrive is 1 volts, and guessing saturation gives I D equals 1 over 2 times 2 times 1 squared equals 1 milliamps.
Then V DS equals 5-1 equals 4 volts, which is at least 1 volts, so the guess was right.
If instead V GS equals 5 volts, saturation would want 16 milliamps, but 1 kilohms from 5 volts can supply at most 5 milliamps. So the guess fails, and the FET is in triode.
That is the whole idea.
"First compare V GS to V t : below it, cutoff.
Above it, assume saturation, compute I D equals 1 over 2 k(V GS-V t) squared , get V DS equals V DD-I DR D , and check that V DS is at least the overdrive.
If it's not, the device is in triode and I re-solve with the triode equation.
The load line is the straight line I D equals (V DD-V DS) over R D , and the operating point is where it crosses the transistor's curve for that V GS ."

MOSFET body diode: origin and effects. The question: What is the internal body diode? Where does it come from?
The body diode is a diode, a one-way valve for current, that exists inside every MOSFET because of how it is built.
It sits between the body (the silicon the channel is built in) and the drain.
In a typical power N-channel MOSFET it points from source to drain, so even with the gate off, current can flow backward through it.
It matters because it can waste power or save you, depending on the circuit.
Imagine a one-way flap built into the wall of a pipe. The main valve is the MOSFET channel, and it can open or close.
But the flap lets water slip backward whenever the pressure is reversed, whatever the valve is doing. You did not add the flap. It came from the way the pipe was made.
A simplified planar cell. The p-body (red) meets the n⁻ drift region (blue) along the green lines: that PN junction is the body diode.
Because the source metal contacts both the n⁺ source and the p-body, the junction sits between source (anode) and drain (cathode).
When the gate is high, a channel forms at the p-body surface under the gate (purple), linking the n⁺ source to the drift region, and electrons then flow down to the drain.
Not to scale.
Body diode: the PN junction between body and drain. Anode / cathode: the two ends of a diode. Current flows easily from anode to cathode.
Freewheeling: letting an inductor's current keep flowing through a path when the switch opens. An inductor is a coil that resists any sudden change in its current.
Dead time: a short gap when both switches in a half-bridge (two switches stacked between supply and ground) are off.
Synchronous rectification: turning the channel on so current avoids the diode's 0. 7 volts drop.
Take an NMOS with its source on ground and its gate at 0 volts, so it is off. Now let the circuit pull current out of the drain, trying to drag it below ground.
The body diode turns on, current flows from source to drain, and the drain stops about 0. 7 volts below ground, even though the gate says off.
With 2 amps through it, that is about 2 times 0. 7 equals 1. 4 watts of heat. That is the whole idea.
"The body diode is the PN junction between the MOSFET's body and its drain, there because of how the transistor is built.
With the body tied to the source, an NMOS has a diode with its anode at the source and cathode at the drain, so the FET can't block voltage in the reverse direction, and a PMOS is the opposite.
It matters in half-bridges: during dead time inductor current flows through it at 0.
7 to 1 volts and it has reverse-recovery charge, so we turn the channel on for synchronous rectification, and use back-to-back FETs when we need two-way blocking."

Why MOSFET gates fear overvoltage. The question: Why are MOSFETs sensitive to overvoltage conditions applied at the gate?
A MOSFET gate is a metal plate separated from the silicon by an extremely thin layer of glass (silicon dioxide).
That glass is a good insulator, but it is so thin that a modest voltage can break it. Once it breaks, the gate is permanently shorted and the transistor is dead.
Picture a sheet of ice over a pond. Thin ice holds a small weight with no problem, but there is a limit. Go past it and the ice cracks, and it never heals.
The oxide works the same way. The danger is made worse because the gate is like a tiny capacitor, a part that stores charge.
It has so little room for charge that a small bit of static makes a huge voltage.
With only 1 ohms in the loop the gate overshoots 12 volts by 60% (to about 19 volts), right up to the 20 volts rating; adding resistance damps it. Critical damping at about 6.
3 ohms gives a clean edge but slower switching.
Real gates also ring via source inductance that couples the drain current into V GS (common-source inductance), which is not included here.
Gate oxide: the thin glass layer under the gate. Breakdown: the permanent failure when the electric field is too strong. Electric field: voltage divided by thickness.
Thin oxide means a high field even at low voltage. ESD: electrostatic discharge, a brief static zap, such as from a fingertip.
Absolute maximum V GS : the datasheet limit you must never exceed.
Glass breaks at a field of roughly 10 MV/cm.
If the oxide is 5 nm thick, that is 5 times 10 to the -7 cm, so the breakdown voltage is about 10 to the 7 times 5 times 10 to the -7 equals 5 volts.
A 5 volts spike on a gate that thin is fatal.
So we add protection: a series resistor, a Zener (a diode that clamps the voltage at a set level) across gate and source, and a pull-down resistor so the gate is never left unconnected.
That is the whole idea.
"The gate is a capacitor with a very thin oxide, a few nanometers in logic and tens of nanometers in power FETs, so even a few volts makes a very high field.
Silicon dioxide breaks down at about 10 MV/cm and the damage is permanent, which is why V GS maximums are only around ±8 to ±20 volts.
Plus the gate has no DC path and tiny capacitance, so a small ESD charge gives hundreds of volts, and gate-loop ringing or Miller coupling can overshoot the drive.
I protect it with a gate resistor, a Zener clamp, a pull-down, and ESD diodes."

MOSFET W/L ratio and its effects. The question: What is W/L ratio? How does it impact FET performance/behavior?
W/L is the width of a MOSFET's channel divided by its length. Width is how many carriers (the electrons or holes that carry current) can flow side by side.
Length is how far they have to travel. A bigger W/L carries more current. The cost is a bigger gate, which loads whatever drives it.
Think of a road. Width is the number of lanes, and length is how long the road is. More lanes means more cars per minute. A longer road means more resistance to getting through.
So a wide, short road moves the most traffic. But widening the road also costs more land, and here the land is gate area, which means more capacitance.
Left: one transistor; current flows left to right across the gate length L , and W is the gate stripe's extent.

Right: layout designers build a big W from several parallel gate fingers with shared source/drain strips ( W total = number of fingers times finger width), which keeps the gate resistance low and the cell compact.
Width (W): how wide the channel is, across the direction of current. Length (L): the distance between source and drain.
Transconductance ( g m ): how much drain current changes per volt of gate change. On-resistance ( R on ): the resistance of the channel when fully on.
Gate capacitance: grows with gate area, W times L .
Say a MOSFET with W over L equals 10 carries 1 milliamps at some gate voltage and has an on-resistance of 1 kilohms. Double it to W over L equals 20 at the same gate voltage.
Now it carries 2 milliamps, and its on-resistance is 500 ohms. But its gate capacitance also roughly doubles, so the stage driving it works harder. That is the whole idea.
"W/L is channel width over channel length, and it sets the transistor's strength.
In the model k equals micro C oxW over L , so drain current, transconductance and conductance all scale with W/L, and on-resistance scales with L/W.
The cost is gate capacitance, which grows with W times L, so a stronger device loads its driver and uses more dynamic power.
You use wider devices for speed and drive, longer L for output resistance and matching, and in CMOS you make the PMOS about 2 to 3 times wider to match the NMOS."

Identify an unnamed analog circuit. The question: Often times, I'm given an unnamed circuit and asked to explain how it works and what type of circuit it is.
Here are a few of them I've gotten (and know what they're called):
Identifying an unnamed circuit means working out what it does from its shape. You do not guess a name first.
You find the supply, ground, input and output, then look for a few telltale patterns. Each pattern points to a known building block.
Think of a detective looking at a room. First they note the doors and windows, which are the ports.
Then they look for clues: feedback loops, clocks with capacitors, or matching pairs of transistors. Each clue narrows the list of suspects.
The job is not done when you have a name. You must also say what it does and what limits it.
A decision flow for classifying an unnamed circuit. It is a thinking aid, not a replacement for tracing signals. If two answers fit, say both and say what you'd check.
Feedback: sending part of the output back to the input to control it. LDO: a low-dropout regulator. It holds a steady output voltage using feedback.
Charge pump: a clocked circuit of switches and capacitors that produces a higher or inverted voltage. Current mirror: matched transistors that copy one current into another.
Diode-connected: a transistor with gate tied to drain so it acts like a diode, a one-way valve for current.
You see two identical MOSFETs with their gates tied together, and one has its gate tied to its own drain. That is a current mirror.
Say you push 100 microamps through the diode-connected one. If the second transistor is twice as wide, it copies and scales the current to about 200 microamps.
That is the whole idea.

"I find the ports and look for the telltale features: feedback to an amplifier input means regulation, like an LDO with V out equals V ref(1 plus R 1 over R 2) ; a clock with flying capacitors and diodes is a charge pump giving about 2 volts in minus drops; two matched FETs with a diode-connected reference is a current mirror copying current by the W/L ratio; a single NMOS with pull-ups either side is a level shifter; and series R, L with a shunt C is a second-order low-pass with a corner at 1 over (2 pi square root of LC ) .
Then I state what it does, the key equation, and its limit."

CMOS and the CMOS buffer. The question: What is CMOS? Draw a CMOS buffer.
CMOS builds logic from pairs of transistors that work as opposites. A PMOS network connects the output to the supply, and an NMOS network connects it to ground.
For any steady input, exactly one network is on. A CMOS buffer is two inverters in a row, which cleans up a signal and adds drive strength.
Imagine a see-saw with a person at each end. When one end is down touching the ground, the other end is up. They are never both down.
A CMOS stage is like that: either the output is tied up to the supply or tied down to ground, and never both at once (apart from a brief moment while it switches).
This is why no steady current flows from supply to ground.
PMOS source on V DD, NMOS source on ground, gates shorted together as the input, drains shorted together as the output.
For either steady input, one transistor is off, so there is no DC path between the rails.
CMOS: complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor, using both PMOS and NMOS together. Inverter: a gate whose output is the opposite of its input.
Pull-up / pull-down: connecting the output to the supply, or to ground. Rail: a supply line, V DD or ground.
Buffer: a stage that outputs the same logic value, with more drive strength.
Use a 3. 3 volts supply. In the inverter, an input of 3. 3 volts turns the NMOS on and the PMOS off, so the output goes to 0 volts.
An input of 0 volts turns the PMOS on and the NMOS off, so the output goes to 3. 3 volts. Now chain two inverters.
The first flips the signal and the second flips it back, so the output equals the input. The second one is often bigger, so it can drive a heavier load. That is the whole idea.

"CMOS means complementary MOS: every gate has a PMOS pull-up network to V DD and an NMOS pull-down network to ground, driven by the same inputs, so exactly one side is on at a time and there's no static current.
The basic cell is the inverter: PMOS on top, NMOS on the bottom, gates tied as input, drains tied as output.
A single stage always inverts, so a buffer is two inverters in series, usually with the second one sized up to drive a heavier load."

Why CMOS is used everywhere. The question: Why are these so often used?
CMOS dominates because it uses almost no power while it is sitting still.
In each gate (a tiny logic circuit), one transistor is always off, so there is no steady path from the supply to ground. Energy is spent only when a signal changes.
That makes it practical to put billions of gates on one chip.
Picture a water gate in a canal that has two doors: an upper door and a lower door. They are never open together.
Water only moves in a burst when you swap which door is open, and it sits still the rest of the time. Older logic was like leaving a tap trickling whenever the output was low.
The cost of CMOS is that every swap costs a burst, so faster switching uses more power.
In resistor-load (or depletion-load) NMOS logic, whenever the input is high the transistor is on and current flows straight from V DD through R L to ground for as long as the output stays low.
Static power: power used while nothing is changing. In CMOS, only leakage. Dynamic power: power used when signals change, about CV squared each cycle.
C is the capacitance being charged (how much charge a wire or input soaks up per volt) and V is the supply. Leakage: a tiny current that flows even when a transistor is off.
Noise margin: how much unwanted voltage a logic level can tolerate before it is misread. Fan-out: how many inputs one output drives.
Take one CMOS inverter whose output is held high, then held low. Both times one transistor is off, so no current flows from supply to ground.
It only draws energy at the moment it changes. Say it drives a 1 fF load (a femtofarad, a tiny capacitance) at 1 volts.
Each full cycle costs about CV squared equals 1 fF times 1 volts squared equals 1 fJ. That is the whole idea.
"Mainly power. In CMOS the PMOS pull-up and NMOS pull-down are complementary, so one is always off and there's no static current, only leakage.
You pay energy only when a node switches, about CV squared per cycle.
On top of that, outputs swing rail to rail for big noise margins, inputs are gates that draw no DC current so fan-out is huge, and MOSFETs scale and integrate densely.
The costs are dynamic power at high frequency, leakage at small nodes and ESD sensitivity."

PMOS high side, NMOS low side. The question: What type of MOSFETs are typically used on the high-side? What about the low-side? Why?
In CMOS the PMOS goes on top, connected to the supply, and the NMOS goes on the bottom, connected to ground. A MOSFET turns on based on the voltage between its gate and source.
This placement keeps each source at a fixed rail (the supply or ground), so each transistor gets the full gate drive and passes a strong signal.
Think of two people, one pulling a rope up and one pulling down. The person at the bottom has the best leverage pulling the output down to the floor.
The person at the top has the best leverage pulling it up to the ceiling. Put them in each other's places and each one runs out of strength before reaching the end of the rope.
The PMOS source is pinned to V DD and the NMOS source is pinned to ground, so a plain 0/V DD gate signal always gives the on device the full V GS = V DD, no matter what the output is doing.
V GS : the gate-to-source voltage that controls a MOSFET. High side / low side: the switch next to the supply, or next to ground.
Source follower: a stage where the source follows the gate, minus a threshold. Strong / weak level: a level that reaches the rail, or one that stops short.
Bootstrap: a trick that raises a gate above the supply.
Use a 5 volts supply and a threshold V t equals 1 volts (the gate-to-source voltage needed to turn a transistor on).
A low-side NMOS has its source at 0 volts, so a 5 volts gate gives V GS equals 5 volts and it pulls the output fully to 0 volts.
A high-side PMOS has its source at 5 volts, so a 0 volts gate gives V GS equals -5 volts and it pulls the output fully to 5 volts.
Swap the NMOS to the top and its source is the output, so it turns off once the output reaches about 5-1 equals 4 volts. That is the whole idea.
"PMOS on the high side, NMOS on the low side, because a MOSFET is controlled by V GS and you want each source tied to a fixed rail.
The NMOS source sits at ground, so a gate at V DD turns it fully on; the PMOS source sits at V DD , so a gate at 0 volts turns it fully on.
Swap them and each becomes a source follower that loses a threshold voltage.
In power stages, though, the high side is often an NMOS anyway for its lower on-resistance, using a bootstrap driver."

TTL vs CMOS logic families. The question: TTL vs CMOS?
TTL and CMOS are two families of digital logic chips. TTL is built from bipolar transistors and draws current all the time.
CMOS is built from paired MOSFETs and draws almost nothing when idle. Their voltage thresholds for "high" and "low" differ, so connecting them needs care.
Imagine two languages that use the same words but draw the line between "loud" and "quiet" at different volumes.
A listener from one may miss the other's "loud" if it stops just short of their line. That is what can happen at a TTL-to-CMOS connection.
The fix is a translator, a chip designed to accept one language and speak the other.
Q1 is the input transistor (its emitter is the input; NAND gates use a multi-emitter Q1).
Q2 is a phase splitter that drives the totem pole: Q3 + diode pull the output up, Q4 pulls it down. The diode makes sure Q3 is off when Q4 is on.
Every DC path here draws current, which is where TTL's static power comes from.
TTL: transistor-transistor logic, a bipolar family such as 74LS. CMOS: logic built from complementary MOSFETs.
Input thresholds: the lowest voltage an input is sure to read as "high", and the highest it is sure to read as "low". In between, the reading is not guaranteed.
Noise margin: the gap between what an output guarantees and what an input needs. 74HCT: CMOS with TTL-compatible input thresholds.
A 5 volts TTL output only guarantees at least 2. 4 volts for a high. A 74HC input on 5 volts needs about 3.
5 volts, which is 70% of its supply, before it is sure to read a high (datasheets often quote 3. 15 volts, measured at a 4. 5 volts supply).
So the TTL signal might not be read as high at all. A 74HCT input accepts anything above about 2. 0 volts as high, so it works.
The usual choice today is CMOS, since it is faster and uses less power. That is the whole idea.
"TTL is bipolar logic: multi-emitter BJT inputs and a totem-pole NPN output, 5 volts only. CMOS uses complementary MOSFETs.
TTL draws static current, a few mW per gate, and its inputs source current; CMOS draws almost nothing static and its inputs are high impedance but must not float.
TTL thresholds are fixed at 0. 8 and 2. 0 volts with outputs guaranteed only to 2. 4 volts, while CMOS swings rail to rail with thresholds that scale with V DD .
So a TTL output can't reliably drive a 5 volts HC input, which is what HCT parts fix."

Shoot-through in CMOS gates. The question: What is shoot-through on a CMOS logic gate? How can it be prevented?
Shoot-through is when both transistors in a CMOS stage are on at once, so current flows straight from the supply to ground instead of into the load.
It happens briefly on every switching edge. It becomes a real problem when edges are slow, when an input floats, or when two power switches overlap.
Picture a two-door airlock, where the outer door and inner door should never be open together.
While someone swaps doors, there is a moment when both are slightly open and the wind blows straight through. The longer the swap takes, the more wind passes.
Fast switching makes the overlap short.
Current is zero below V tn (NMOS off) and above V DD minus V tp (PMOS off), and peaks at the switching threshold.
The area under this curve, swept by the input edge, is the charge wasted on each transition. A slow edge sweeps it slowly, so more charge is wasted.
Shoot-through (crowbar current): current from supply to ground through both transistors. Switching threshold: the input voltage where the output flips, near half the supply.
Floating input: an input connected to nothing, which can sit at a middle voltage. Schmitt trigger: an input stage that gives a sharp internal edge from a slow signal.
Dead time: a deliberate gap with both switches off.
Use a 5 volts inverter where each transistor needs 1 volts of gate drive to turn on: the NMOS gate 1 volts above ground, the PMOS gate 1 volts below the 5 volts supply.
As the input rises from 0 volts, the NMOS turns on once the input passes 1 volts. The PMOS stays on until the input passes 4 volts.
For input voltages between 1 volts and 4 volts, both are on, and current flows supply to ground. A fast edge crosses this window quickly. A floating input can sit in it all day.
That is the whole idea.
"Shoot-through is when the PMOS and NMOS in a CMOS stage are on at the same time, so current goes straight from V DD to ground.
It happens during every input transition, between V tn and V DD minus V tp , peaking near mid-rail. It's worst with slow edges or floating inputs.
Prevent it with fast edges, Schmitt-trigger inputs, tied-off unused pins, and in drivers or power stages by giving each FET its own gate signal with break-before-make dead time."
Quick check. For a CMOS inverter with V DD = 3. 3 volts and V tn = V tp = 0. 7 volts, over what input range are both FETs conducting?
CMOS power and efficiency analysis. The question: CMOS efficiency analysis. How does operational frequency impact efficiency? What about logic/swing levels? Rise/fall times?
CMOS wastes very little power because it only takes energy when it switches.
Each time an output charges and discharges its load, it burns a fixed amount of energy that depends on the load and the supply voltage.
Average power is that energy times how often it happens.
Think of filling and emptying a bucket. Filling it costs a bucket's worth of energy from the supply. Emptying it throws that away.
The bigger the bucket, the higher the water level, and the more often you do it, the more you spend. The level matters most, because the cost goes up with its square.
Dynamic power is quadratic in supply voltage. Dropping from 3. 3 volts to 1. 8 volts cuts it by (1. 8 over 3. 3) squared equals 0. 30 .
A reduced swing from a high supply (dashed) only saves linearly, so the low swing should come from a low supply. Drag C or f: the curves scale in proportion, but the 0.
30 ratio between 3. 3 volts and 1. 8 volts never changes. Voltage is the only lever that acts quadratically.
Dynamic power: power burned while switching, P equals alpha C V DD squared f . Activity factor ( alpha ): the fraction of cycles that the node actually toggles.
Capacitance ( C ): how much charge the load soaks up per volt, like the width of the bucket. Measured in farads; 1 picofarads is a millionth of a millionth of a farad.
Frequency ( f ): how many cycles per second. 1 megahertz is a million per second. Leakage: a small current that flows even when idle.
Take a 10 picofarads load toggling every cycle ( alpha equals 1 ) at 1 megahertz from a 2 volts supply.
Power is 10 picofarads times 4 volts squared times 1 megahertz equals 40 µW.
Drop the supply to 1 volts and the power becomes 10 picofarads times 1 times 1 megahertz equals 10 µW, a quarter. Doubling the frequency would only double the power.
That is the whole idea.

"CMOS has no DC path in steady state, so power is mostly dynamic: every low-to-high transition draws CV DD squared from the supply, half stored on the load and half burned in the PMOS, and the discharge burns the stored half in the NMOS.
Average power is alpha CV DD to the 2f : linear in frequency, quadratic in supply and swing, independent of transistor resistance.
Rise and fall time only matter through short-circuit current, which grows with slow edges, plus there's leakage that doesn't depend on frequency.
Halving the supply cuts dynamic power by four."
Quick check. Charging a capacitor through a resistor from a fixed supply V , how much energy is dissipated in the resistor?
Achieving faster slew rates in CMOS. The question: How can you achieve faster slew rates?
Slew rate is how fast a signal's voltage can change. For a capacitive load it equals the current you can supply divided by the capacitance.
So to get faster edges, supply more current, reduce the capacitance, or make the voltage swing smaller.
Picture filling a balloon with a hose. A wider hose fills it faster, and a smaller balloon fills sooner. You get a fast fill by using a big hose on a small balloon.
But a big hose gushing suddenly makes a jolt, just as fast electrical edges cause spikes and ringing.
Same 50 picofarads load, three driver strengths. Rise time scales linearly with R on : wider drivers give proportionally faster edges.
Past a point, other limits (package inductance, previous stage) take over.
Slew rate: how fast the voltage changes, in V per second ( dV over dt ). Load capacitance: how much charge the load soaks up per volt, from traces, pins and inputs.
Measured in farads; 1 picofarads is a millionth of a millionth of a farad. Drive strength: how much current an output can supply, set by its W over L .
Fan-out: how many inputs the output drives, which adds load. Ground bounce: a voltage spike on ground caused by large fast current changes.
Say an output can deliver 10 milliamps into a 10 picofarads load.
The slew rate is I over C equals 10 milliamps over 10 picofarads equals 10 to the 9 volts/s, which is 1 volts per nanosecond. A 3. 3 volts swing then takes about 3. 3 nanoseconds.
Double the drive current to 20 milliamps and the edge becomes twice as fast. That is the whole idea.
"Slew rate is I over C , so to go faster I increase drive current, reduce capacitance, or reduce swing.

In CMOS that means wider output transistors for lower on-resistance, more gate overdrive or a higher supply, and a tapered chain of inverters, each about 3 to 4 times larger than the last, to drive big output devices.
I'd also cut the load capacitance by shortening traces and reducing fan-out.
The trade-off is peak current, ground bounce, ringing and EMI, so I'd choose the slowest edge that meets timing."
Quick check. Which change does NOT make a CMOS output edge faster?
CMOS input ESD and overvoltage protection. The question: Design CMOS input protection circuits against ESD/overvoltage events.
CMOS inputs are fragile because their gate oxide is very thin. A static zap can push amps for a few nanoseconds at thousands of volts.
Protection gives that current a safe path to the supply or ground before it can hurt the gate.
It works in layers: on-chip diodes, a small series resistor, and extra parts on the board.
Picture a dam with a spillway beside it. When a flood arrives, the spillway diverts the water around the delicate machinery instead of through it.
Diodes at the pin are the spillways. The series resistor is a narrow channel that slows what is left. The cost is that the spillway and channel slow down normal traffic.
D 1 and D 2 are the big primary clamps at the pad (anode of D 2 at ground, cathode of D 1 at V DD ). R s separates them from the small secondary clamps D 3 / D 4 at the gate.
If the pad goes above V DD + a diode drop the current goes into V DD ; below ground, out of ground.
ESD: electrostatic discharge, a brief high-voltage static pulse.
Clamp diode: a diode (a one-way valve for current) that conducts when the pin goes above the supply or below ground.
Rail clamp: a big device between supply and ground that carries ESD current away. TVS diode: an external part that clamps surges at a connector.
Series resistor: limits current into the clamp diodes.
Say a 3. 3 volts chip's pin is accidentally driven to 12 volts. The upper clamp diode holds the pin near 4 volts, about one diode drop (0. 7 volts) above the supply. A 3.
3 kilohms series resistor then sees about 8 volts, so the current is about 8 over 3. 3 kilohms about 2. 4 milliamps. That is a small, safe fault current. That is the whole idea.
"I'd use layers. At the pad, two big diodes steer ESD current to V DD or ground, with a rail clamp between the rails to sink it.
Then a series resistor of a few hundred ohms and a small secondary clamp at the gate, which see only what leaks through.
On the board, a TVS at the connector for IEC-level events, and a series resistor sized so that a DC overvoltage only pushes a milliamp or two through the clamp diode.
The cost is added capacitance and RC delay, so I check it against the signal speed."
Quick check. What does a diode from the pad to V DD do in an input protection circuit?
CMOS buffer driving a series RC load. The question: Draw voltage/current output waveforms for a CMOS buffer connected to a series RC load.
Which FETs are conducting during a positive/negative step?
A CMOS buffer drives its output to either the supply or ground.
When it is wired to a resistor and capacitor in series, each switch of the output charges or discharges the capacitor through the resistor.
The result is a rounded voltage on the capacitor and a short spike of current at each edge.
Think of filling a bucket through a narrow hose. At first the bucket is empty, so the water rushes in fast. As the bucket fills, the flow slows to a trickle.
When you swap the tap for an outlet, the bucket empties the same way: fast at first, then slower. The hose is the resistor and the bucket is the capacitor.

This output stage is an inverter, so the input falls (1 to 0) and the output rises: M P conducts (current flows from V DD down through the PMOS into the output and on through R to the capacitor, shown by the animated flow).
M N is off.
Buffer output: acts like a switch to V DD or to ground, giving a square wave. Capacitor: a part that stores charge, and whose voltage cannot jump instantly.
Time constant ( RC ): the time scale of the charging, resistance times capacitance. Exponential: a curve that changes fast at first and then slows.
Steady state: when nothing is changing and no current flows.
Say V DD equals 5 volts, R equals 1 kilohms and C equals 1 microfarads, so RC equals 1 milliseconds.
On the rising edge the capacitor is empty, so the full 5 volts sits across the resistor and the current starts at 5 over 1 kilohms equals 5 milliamps.
After 1 milliseconds the capacitor reaches about 63% of 5 volts, which is about 3. 2 volts, and the current has fallen to about a third.
After about 5 milliseconds the current is nearly zero. The falling edge is the mirror image with the current flowing the other way. That is the whole idea.
"Treat the buffer as a switch to V DD or ground.
On the positive step the PMOS is on and the NMOS is off: current V DD over R flows from the supply into the capacitor and decays with tau equals RC while the capacitor voltage rises exponentially.
On the negative step the NMOS is on and the PMOS is off: the capacitor discharges through the resistor into the NMOS, so the current reverses and again decays.
The output is a square wave, the capacitor voltage is a rounded square wave, and the current is alternating decaying spikes at each edge, zero in between."
Quick check. During the positive step of the buffer output into a series RC load, which transistor conducts?
Swapped PMOS and NMOS in a CMOS stage. The question: What happens if you swap the high-side PFET and the low-side NFET?
In a normal CMOS inverter the PMOS sits on top and the NMOS sits on the bottom. If you swap them, the circuit still conducts, but the output no longer reaches the rails.
Each transistor shuts itself off before the output gets all the way to its target. The circuit also stops inverting.
Picture climbing a ladder whose rungs vanish as you climb. Each step up removes a bit of your footing. You get most of the way and then there is nothing left to push against.
The swapped NMOS does this near the top. Its gate drive shrinks as its own source rises, so it stalls a threshold short of the supply.
Normal CMOS. Sources are at the rails, so the gate-source voltage of the active device is the full V DD and the output reaches the rails.
Source follower: a stage whose source copies the gate voltage minus a threshold. Threshold voltage ( V t ): the gate-to-source voltage needed to turn on.
Rail-to-rail: an output that swings all the way from ground to supply. Body effect: the threshold rising when the source is not at body voltage.
Non-inverting: the output follows the input instead of flipping it.
Use a 5 volts supply and give both transistors a 1 volts threshold ( V tn equals V tp equals 1 volts), with the NMOS now on top. Drive the input to 5 volts.
The output rises until it is about 5-1 equals 4 volts, and then the NMOS has no gate drive left and stops. Drive the input to 0 volts.
The PMOS at the bottom pulls the output down only to about 1 volts, one threshold above ground.
So the output swings from about 1 volts to 4 volts, and follows the input instead of flipping it. That is the whole idea.
"Swapping them puts the NMOS on top and the PMOS on the bottom, so each source is the output node.
The NMOS then can only pull the output up to V DD-V tn , since it turns off once its V GS falls to V t , and the PMOS can only pull it down to V tp .
So the output no longer reaches the rails, the body effect makes it worse, the edges get slower near the limits, and the stage becomes non-inverting.
That's why CMOS has the PMOS on top: its source sits at V DD so it gets full gate drive."
Quick check. With the NMOS on top (drain at V DD ) and gate at V DD , what is the highest the output can go (ignoring body effect)?
Common-mode vs differential gain, CMRR. The question: What is common-mode and differential gain? What are their ideal values?
A differential amplifier is meant to amplify the difference between two inputs and ignore what they have in common.
The "common-mode" part is the average of the two inputs, which is often noise. The common-mode rejection ratio (CMRR) says how well the amplifier ignores that average.
Imagine two people carrying a tray on a bumpy bus. The tray tilts only if they lift unevenly. If both rise and fall together, the tray stays level.
A good amplifier is like a tray that reacts only to the uneven lift. A real one is a bit wobbly, so some of the shared bump leaks through.
V 2 goes to the non-inverting input through the R 3 over R 4 divider and V 1 to the inverting input.
If R 4 over R 3 equals R 2 over R 1 equals 10 the circuit amplifies V 2-V 1 by 10 and exactly cancels any common-mode voltage.
Differential voltage ( V d ): the difference between the two inputs. Common-mode voltage ( V cm ): the average of the two inputs.
Differential gain ( A d ): how much the difference is amplified. Op-amps ("What an op-amp is and how it works") are the usual building block.
Common-mode gain ( A cm ): how much the average leaks to the output. Ideally zero. CMRR: the ratio A d over A cm . Higher is better.
Often given in decibels (dB), where every 20 decibels is another factor of 10.
Say the inputs are 5. 001 volts and 4. 999 volts. The difference is 2 millivolts and the average is 5 volts. An amplifier with A d equals 10 should output 20 millivolts.
An ideal one ignores the 5 volts average. A real one with CMRR of 100 decibels, which is a ratio of 100,000, has A cm equals 10 over 100 000 equals 0. 0001 , so it adds 5 times 0.
0001 equals 0. 5 millivolts of error to the 20 millivolts. Build the same gain from four 1% resistors, though, and the CMRR can fall to about 275 (49 decibels).
Then the 5 volts average adds about 180 millivolts, swamping the signal. That is the whole idea.
"Split two inputs into a difference and an average.
Differential gain is the gain on the difference and common-mode gain is the gain on the average, so the output is A dV d plus A cmV cm .
Ideally A d is large (or the designed gain) and A cm is zero, so the common-mode rejection ratio A d over A cm is infinite.

In practice mismatch leaves a small A cm : a four-resistor difference amp with 1% resistors and a gain of 10 has a worst-case CMRR of about 275, or 49 decibels, which is why precision designs use matched networks or instrumentation amps."
Quick check. What is the ideal common-mode gain of a differential amplifier?
Gain-bandwidth product. The question: What is the gain-bandwidth product?
The gain-bandwidth product (GBW) is a single number that says how much gain an op-amp (a standard amplifier chip) can give at what frequency.
Gain means how many times bigger the output is than the input. For most op-amps, gain times bandwidth stays constant.
So if you ask for more gain, you get less bandwidth, and the other way around.
Picture a fixed amount of paint. You can spread it thick over a small wall or thin over a large wall, but the total stays the same.
Gain is the thickness and bandwidth is the area. The analogy holds along the sloped part of the op-amp's gain curve.
It does not describe very low frequencies, down to steady (DC) signals, where the gain is flat.
Open-loop gain (top curve) is flat at 100 decibels until 10 hertz, then falls 20 decibels/decade, hitting 0 decibels at 1 megahertz.
Closing the loop for a gain of 10 (20 decibels) flattens the response up to about 100 kilohertz, where it meets the open-loop line. Gain 100 (40 decibels) gives 10 kilohertz.
All the curves share the same roll-off line: gain times bandwidth is constant. Drag GBW: every closed-loop corner slides with it.
Drag G₂ toward 1000: its flat region shrinks in exact proportion, but it still meets the same open-loop line.
Open-loop gain: the op-amp's raw gain with no feedback. Closed-loop gain: the gain set by the feedback network. Bandwidth: the range of frequencies the amplifier handles well.
Dominant pole: the low frequency where the gain starts to fall. Unity-gain frequency: where the gain drops to 1. It equals the GBW.
Take an op-amp with a 1 megahertz GBW. Set up a gain of 10, and the bandwidth is about 1 megahertz over 10 equals 100 kilohertz.
Set up a gain of 100, and the bandwidth is about 10 kilohertz. A gain of 1 has about 1 megahertz.
Pick the op-amp by multiplying the gain you need by the highest frequency you need, then add margin. That is the whole idea.
"The gain-bandwidth product is the constant you get by multiplying gain by frequency along the amplifier's roll-off.
A voltage-feedback op-amp has a huge DC gain with a dominant pole at a low frequency, then falls 20 decibels per decade, so gain times frequency is constant and equals the unity-gain frequency.
With feedback, closed-loop bandwidth is the GBW divided by the closed-loop noise gain, so a 1 megahertz op-amp running at a gain of 10 gives about 100 kilohertz.
I use it to pick an op-amp: the gain I need times the highest signal frequency, with margin."

What sets slew rate and rise time. The question: What determines slew rate and rise/fall time?
Slew rate and rise time are two different speed limits. Slew rate is the largest rate the output can change, set by how much current is available to charge a capacitor.
Rise time is how long a small, well-behaved step takes, set by bandwidth. Which one limits you depends on the size of the step.
Picture filling a bathtub through a valve that opens smoothly. For a small top-up, the level eases in at a pace set by how quickly the valve responds.
For a big fill, the valve is wide open and you are limited by the most water the pipe can carry per second, so the level climbs in a straight line.
The valve's response is the bandwidth limit, and the pipe's maximum flow is the slew limit.
The compensation capacitor connects the output of the second stage back to the high-impedance node between the stages.
The first stage must supply (or sink) the current that charges C c .
Slew rate: the maximum rate of change of the output, in volts per microsecond (V/µs; a microsecond is a millionth of a second).
Rise time: the time for the output to go from 10% to 90% of a step. Bandwidth: roughly the highest frequency the amplifier handles well (its minus 3 decibels point).
It sets the rise time of small signals. Tail current ( I tail ): the fixed current the op-amp's first (input) stage runs on.
Compensation capacitor ( C c ): the capacitor inside the op-amp that the current charges.
Say an op-amp has 10 microamps of tail current and a 20 picofarads compensation capacitor. The slew rate is I over C equals 10 microamps over 20 picofarads equals 0.
5 volts per microsecond. A big 10 volts step then ramps in a straight line for 10 over 0. 5 equals 20 microseconds. Its rise time, the middle 8 volts from 10% to 90%, is 8 over 0.
5 equals 16 microseconds, however much bandwidth the part has. A tiny step stays under the slew limit, so only the bandwidth sets how fast it moves. That is the whole idea.
"Slew rate is the largest-signal limit: the maximum dV/dt, set by the current available to charge a capacitor.
In an op-amp it's the input stage tail current divided by the compensation capacitor, I over C c , like 10 microamps over 20 picofarads gives 0. 5 volts per microsecond.
Rise time is the small-signal limit from bandwidth, about 0. 35 over the -3 decibels bandwidth, or 2. 2 RC.
Small steps are bandwidth-limited exponentials; big steps ramp linearly at the slew rate, taking about 0.
8 times the step over SR, and big fast sines get distorted into triangles."

Pros and cons of fast vs slow slew rates. The question: Pros/cons of fast/slow slew rates?
A fast slew rate means the voltage changes quickly, and a slow one means it changes gently. Fast edges give clean timing and less loss in power switches.
Slow edges are quieter and cause less electrical noise. Most designs pick the slowest edge that still meets timing.
Think of a car stopping at a light. A hard stop gets you there sooner but throws the passengers forward and screeches the tires. A gentle stop is smooth but takes more road.
Fast electrical edges are the hard stop: quick, but with jolts such as ringing, spikes and radiated noise.
Envelopes of the harmonic amplitudes.
Between 32 megahertz and 318 megahertz the gap between the two envelopes widens, and above 318 megahertz it stays at a constant 20 decibels (10x, the ratio of the edge times).
Radiated emissions in the 100-1000 megahertz range, where EMC limits bite, fall accordingly.
Slew rate: how fast a voltage changes, in V/ns or V/µs. EMI: electromagnetic interference, unwanted radio-frequency noise.
Ringing and overshoot: oscillation and spikes after a fast edge. Ground bounce: a brief ground voltage shift caused by a quickly changing current.
Crosstalk: a signal leaking into a neighboring trace.
Say an output drives a 10 picofarads load (a small capacitance that must be charged) with a 3. 3 volts swing. If the edge takes 1 nanoseconds, the slew rate is 3.
3 volts/ns and the charging current is C dV over dt equals 10 picofarads times 3. 3 volts over ns equals 33 milliamps. If the edge takes 10 nanoseconds, the current is 3.
3 milliamps. The fast edge gives 10 times the current spike, and with it more noise and ringing. The slow edge costs timing margin. That is the whole idea.
"Fast slew rates give better timing margin, less jitter, lower switching loss in power stages and less distortion in amplifiers.
The cost is more high-frequency content, so more EMI, ground bounce, crosstalk, ringing and overshoot, and you start to need termination.
Slow slew rates are quiet and easy on EMC but eat timing margin and raise switching loss.
So I choose the slowest edge that meets timing and tune with drive strength or a series resistor."
Quick check. Which is a typical cost of faster edge rates?
Biasing an amplifier. The question: How to bias an amplifier?
Biasing means setting a transistor's steady (DC) voltages and current so that a signal can swing up and down without being clipped.
You choose a resting point, usually near the middle of the available voltage range. The signal then moves around that point.
A good bias also stays put when the transistor's properties change.
Picture a swing at rest hanging from its chains. If you want it to move equally forward and backward, it should start at the center.
Starting at the far edge means it can only go one way. The bias is the resting position of the swing, and the signal is the push on top.
R 1 over R 2 fix the base at about 1. 65 volts; R E sets the emitter current; R C puts the collector near 7 volts.
C 1 and C 2 couple the signal in and out while blocking DC; C E bypasses R E at signal frequencies.
Bias / operating point (Q-point): the DC voltages and current when no signal is applied. Headroom: the room the signal has to swing before it clips.
Voltage-divider bias: two resistors that set the base voltage. Emitter resistor ( R E ): turns the emitter voltage into a stable emitter current.
Negative feedback: a self-correcting effect that holds the current steady.
Take a BJT, where a small base current controls the current from collector to emitter. Use a 12 volts supply and aim for 1 milliamps. Choose R E equals 1 kilohms.
The emitter sits at 1 milliamps times 1 kilohms equals 1 volts, so the base sits about 0. 65 volts higher, at about 1. 65 volts. A divider holds the base there.
A 5 kilohms collector resistor drops 5 volts, so the collector rests at 12-5 equals 7 volts. If the current tries to rise, the emitter voltage rises and pulls it back.
That is the whole idea.
"Biasing sets the DC operating point so the transistor stays active and the signal can swing symmetrically.

For a BJT I use voltage-divider bias with an emitter resistor: the divider sets the base voltage, I E equals (V B-V BE) over R E , so the current depends on resistors, not on beta , and the emitter resistor gives negative DC feedback.
The divider current is about ten times the base current, and the collector sits near mid-supply. Coupling capacitors pass the signal, and a bypass capacitor restores gain.
For a MOSFET it's a gate divider with a source resistor, and for an op-amp on a single supply the input sits at half the rail."
Quick check. What is the purpose of biasing an amplifier?
Why BJTs are often used for amplifiers. The question: Why are BJTs more often used for amplifiers than MOSFETs?
BJTs are popular for amplifiers because they turn a small change in input voltage into a large change in output current. That ratio is called transconductance.
At the same current, a BJT has several times more of it than a MOSFET. That means more gain, and often less noise, per milliamp.
Think of two gas pedals. One is very sensitive: a light touch changes the speed a lot. The other needs a big push for the same change. The BJT is the sensitive pedal.
The catch is that the sensitive pedal is a bit jumpy and nonlinear, and the BJT also draws a little current at its input.
BJT g m rises linearly with current (a straight line on log-log axes with slope 1); the MOSFET's rises as the square root (slope 1/2). At 1 milliamps the BJT gives 38.
7 mS vs 8 mS for a wide MOSFET and 2 mS for a small one. To reach the BJT's g m a MOSFET needs either far more current or a far larger W/L, which means more gate capacitance.
The MOSFET curve cannot exceed the weak-inversion limit I D over (nV T) (28 mS per mA, not drawn).
Transconductance ( g m ): change in output current per volt of input change.
BJT g m : I C over V T , where V T about 26 millivolts is the "thermal voltage", a fixed value at room temperature. Overdrive ( V ov ): how far a MOSFET gate is above threshold.
Input-referred noise: noise expressed as if it were added at the input. It falls as g m rises. Bias current: the small DC current drawn at the input of the BJT.
Run both at 1 milliamps. The BJT gives g m equals I C over V T equals 1 milliamps over 26 millivolts about 39 mS (millisiemens, meaning milliamps per volt).
A MOSFET with half a volt of overdrive gives g m equals 2I D over V ov equals 2 milliamps over 0. 5 volts equals 4 mS. That is about ten times less.
So for gain and low noise at the same current, the BJT wins. For no input current and easy integration, the MOSFET wins. That is the whole idea.
"Mostly because of transconductance. A BJT's g m is I C over V T , about 39 mS per milliamp, whereas a MOSFET's is 2I D over V ov , around 4 to 10 mS.
So a BJT gives more gain per stage, more bandwidth per mA, lower input-referred voltage noise, a higher intrinsic gain ( V A over V T in the thousands) and better offset matching.
The costs are base current, a more nonlinear exponential law and temperature drift.
MOSFETs win on input resistance, integration and power, so in CMOS ICs they dominate, and in weak inversion they approach BJT efficiency."

What an op-amp is and how it works. The question: What is an opamp? How does it work?
An op-amp is an amplifier with two inputs and one output. It takes the difference between the inputs and multiplies it by a huge number. On its own this is too big to be useful.
With feedback from the output back to one input, it becomes a precise amplifier whose gain you choose with resistors.
Picture someone steering a boat by watching a flag. They turn the wheel hard whenever the flag is off-center, and straighten up when it is centered.
The harder they react, the more tightly they hold the course. An op-amp does the same: it pushes the output as hard as needed until the two inputs match.
Two inputs, one output, and two supply pins. The output is the gain times the voltage difference between the inputs, limited by the supplies.
Inverting / non-inverting input: the two inputs, marked minus and plus. Open-loop gain ( A ): the raw gain, typically 100,000 or more.
Negative feedback: sending part of the output back to the minus input. Rail: the supply voltage the output cannot exceed.
Closed-loop gain: the gain of the whole circuit, set by the feedback resistors.
Without feedback, a 1 millivolts difference times a gain of 100,000 would try to make 100 volts, so the output hits a rail.
Now add feedback with R f equals 9 kilohms from the output to the minus input, and R g equals 1 kilohms from the minus input to ground. Apply 0. 1 volts to the plus input.
The output settles where the divider returns 0. 1 volts to the minus input, which is 1 volts. The gain is 1 plus 9 over 1 equals 10 . That is the whole idea.
"An op-amp is a high-gain differential amplifier: the output is a huge gain, around 10 to the 5 or more, times the difference between its two inputs.
Open-loop it just saturates, so you wrap negative feedback around it.
Then it forces the two inputs to nearly the same voltage, and the closed-loop gain is set by external resistors, roughly 1 over beta , instead of by the op-amp's own loose gain.
Inside it's an input differential pair, a gain stage with a compensation capacitor, and an output stage."

Op-amp symbol and its two inputs. The question: Draw an opamp. What are the two input terminals?
The op-amp symbol is a triangle with two inputs on the flat side and one output at the point. The plus input is non-inverting, so the output moves the same way.
The minus input is inverting, so the output moves the opposite way. Supply pins are often left off the drawing, but they are always there.
Think of a tug of war over a marker that shows the output. The plus team pulls the marker up, and the minus team pulls it down.
Whichever input has the higher voltage wins, and because the op-amp's gain is huge, even a tiny difference moves the marker a long way.
The symbol puts minus on top by convention, but that can be flipped, so always trust the signs.
The triangle points in the direction of signal flow. The two input pins are on the flat side, the output is the apex, and the supply pins go top and bottom.
The signs are inside the triangle next to each input.
Inverting input (minus ): raising it makes the output go down. Non-inverting input (+): raising it makes the output go up. Output: the point of the triangle.
Supply pins: positive and negative power connections, often not drawn. Negative feedback: wiring the output back to the minus input.
Draw the triangle pointing right. Put a minus sign on the upper input and a plus sign on the lower input.
Add the output on the right, and optionally the positive supply on top and negative supply at the bottom. If the plus input is 1. 001 volts and the minus is 1.
000 volts, the output swings high. Swap the two voltages and it swings low. That is the whole idea.
"An op-amp is a triangle pointing in the direction of signal flow. Two inputs on the flat side: the minus input is inverting, the plus input is non-inverting.
One output at the tip. The output is the gain times plus minus minus.
So a signal into plus comes out in phase and a signal into minus comes out inverted, which is why negative feedback is wired back to the minus input.
I'd also add the two supply pins, positive on top and negative on the bottom."

Connections needed to wire an op-amp. The question: What connections are required to wire up an opamp?
An op-amp needs a few connections before it does anything useful: power, two inputs, an output, a feedback path, and a decoupling capacitor.
Without feedback it works as a comparator (its output just slams high or low depending on which input is bigger), not as a smooth amplifier.
Without a defined steady (DC) voltage at each input, it drifts to a rail, one of the supply limits. And without decoupling, supply noise gets in.
Think of a lamp. It needs a power cord, a switch you control, and a bulb. A lamp with a loose cord flickers. Unplugging one wire leaves it dark.
In the same way, each missing op-amp connection gives its own symptom, from a stuck output to oscillation.

The seven connections: +supply, minus supply, two decoupling capacitors (one per supply, right at the pins), inverting input via R in , feedback R f from output to the inverting input, and a DC path for the + input (here, ground).
Signal path and power path are separate jobs.
Supply pins: V+ and Vminus . Vminus is ground in a single-supply design. Floating input: an input connected to nothing, which will drift.
Feedback path: a resistor from output to the minus input. Decoupling capacitor: usually 100 nanofarads at the supply pins, supplying fast current.
Common-mode range: the input voltages the part can handle.
Take a single 5 volts supply. Connect V+ to 5 volts with a 100 nanofarads capacitor right next to it, and Vminus to ground. Bias the plus input at 2.
5 volts with two equal resistors. Run a feedback resistor from the output to the minus input.
Now every pin has a defined connection, and the output has room to swing both ways around 2. 5 volts. That is the whole idea.
"Beyond the two inputs and the output, an op-amp needs a positive and negative supply, so power pins, with a 100 nanofarads decoupling capacitor close to them.
For a linear amplifier it also needs a feedback path from the output to the inverting input.
Both inputs need a DC path to a defined voltage, because bias current flows into them and a floating input drifts to a rail.
Then I check the common-mode range and output swing, and in single-supply designs I bias the signal to mid-rail."

The three ideal op-amp rules. The question: What are the three rules of an ideal opamp?
The three ideal op-amp rules are a shortcut for analyzing circuits. The inputs draw no current.
The output is a perfect voltage source: it holds its voltage whatever current is drawn.
And the gain is infinite, which with negative feedback (the output wired back to the minus input) forces the two inputs to the same voltage.
Real parts only approximate these rules.
Imagine a very picky referee who keeps changing the score until both teams are tied.
The referee cannot be stopped from correcting any gap, however small, so the teams always end up tied. The op-amp does this to its inputs, using its output as the adjustment.
The "virtual short" is the tie.
With the + input grounded and a virtual short, the minus node is at 0 volts.
The current I equals V in over R in cannot enter the op-amp (rule 1), so it flows through R f and produces V out equals -IR f .
Input impedance: how hard it is for current to flow into the input. Ideally infinite. Output impedance: ideally zero, so the output holds its voltage under load.
Open-loop gain: ideally infinite. Virtual short: the two inputs sit at the same voltage under negative feedback.
Virtual ground: a minus input held at 0 volts because the plus input is grounded.
Build an inverting amplifier with R in equals 1 kilohms and R f equals 10 kilohms, plus input grounded. Apply V in equals 0. 5 volts.
The minus input is at 0 volts by the virtual short, so the input current is 0. 5 over 1 kilohms equals 0. 5 milliamps. No current enters the op-amp, so all 0.
5 milliamps goes through R f . The output is -0. 5 milliamps times 10 kilohms equals -5 volts, a gain of -10 . That is the whole idea.
"The ideal op-amp has infinite input impedance, so no current flows into the inputs; zero output impedance, so the output is an ideal voltage source; and infinite gain.
With negative feedback, infinite gain forces the difference between the inputs to zero, the virtual short, so V plus equals V - . With these I can solve a circuit with just KCL.
For an inverting amp the minus node is a virtual ground, the input current all flows through the feedback resistor, and the gain is -R f over R in ."

Inverting and non-inverting op-amp circuits. The question: Draw an inverting/non-inverting opamp circuit.
There are two basic ways to wire an op-amp as an amplifier. In the inverting circuit, the signal goes to the minus input through a resistor and the output is flipped.
In the non-inverting circuit, the signal goes straight to the plus input and the output has the same sign. In both, two resistors set the gain.
Think of two ways to use a lever. In one, you push the input end down and the other end goes up. That is the inverting amp.
In the other, the output end moves the same way as your hand, but always at least as far. That is the non-inverting amp, which cannot give a gain below 1.
Plus input grounded, signal into the minus node through R in , feedback R f from output to the minus node. The dot marks the summing node where I in meets I f .
Inverting amplifier: gain -R f over R in . Output has the opposite sign. Non-inverting amplifier: gain 1 plus R f over R g . Output has the same sign.
Virtual short: both inputs at the same voltage. Feedback resistor ( R f ): connects the output back to the minus input. Input impedance: how much the circuit loads its source.
Use R f equals 100 kilohms and 10 kilohms for the other resistor, with V in equals 0. 1 volts. The inverting amp has gain -100 over 10 equals -10 , so the output is -1. 0 volts.
The non-inverting amp has gain 1 plus 100 over 10 equals 11 , so the output is plus 1. 1 volts.
The inverting circuit loads the source with 10 kilohms, while the non-inverting one barely loads it at all. That is the whole idea.
"Inverting: plus input to ground, signal through R in into the minus node, R f from the output back to that node. The minus node is a virtual ground, so gain is -R f over R in .
Non-inverting: signal on the plus input, and R f and R g form a divider from output to ground feeding the minus input.
The virtual short makes V out(R g over (R g plus R f)) equals V in , so gain is 1 plus R f over R g .
Inverting has input impedance R in and can attenuate; non-inverting has very high input impedance and gain of at least 1."
