DC gain of an op-amp. The question: What is the DC gain of an ompamp?
The DC gain of an op-amp is how much it amplifies very slow signals. Open loop, it is huge: from about 100,000 to a million.
But in a real circuit, what matters is the closed-loop gain, which feedback sets with resistors. The op-amp's own gain just has to be big enough to make the error small.
Think of a powerful but sloppy motor steering a car while you watch the road and correct.
You keep correcting until the car is where you want it, so your eyes, not the motor, set the path. A stronger motor just leaves a smaller leftover wobble.
The feedback resistors are your eyes, and the op-amp's open-loop gain is the motor.
Two op-amps with the same 1 megahertz GBW but different DC gain.
The higher- A 0 part has its pole at 1 hertz instead of 10 hertz, so at any frequency above 10 hertz their gains are identical.
Extra DC gain buys accuracy only at very low frequency. The phase falls to minus 90° by about ten times the pole frequency.
Open-loop DC gain ( A 0 ): the gain with no feedback at zero frequency. Closed-loop gain: the gain set by the feedback network.
Loop gain: the open-loop gain divided by the closed-loop gain. It sets the error. Dominant pole: the low frequency where the gain starts to fall.
dB: 20 times the log of the gain ratio. 100,000 is 100 decibels.
Take A 0 equals 100 000 and a closed-loop gain of 10. The loop gain is 100 000 over 10 equals 10 000 , so the gain error is about 1/10,000, or 0. 01%.
For a closed-loop gain of 1000 the loop gain is only 100, so the error is about 1%.
Also, a 1 megahertz GBW with this A 0 means the gain starts falling at 1 megahertz over 100 000 equals 10 hertz. That is the whole idea.
"Open loop, an op-amp's DC gain is very large, typically 10 to the 5 to 10 to the 6 , or 100 to 120 decibels, though it's loosely specified.
In a circuit what matters is the closed-loop gain, set by the feedback resistors: 1 over beta , such as 1 plus R f over R g .
The finite open-loop gain only adds a small error of about G over A 0 , so a gain of 10 on a 10 to the 5 part is off by 0. 01%.
And that high gain only holds at low frequency: a dominant pole rolls it off at 20 decibels per decade down to unity at the GBW."

Open-loop op-amp: the comparator. The question: How does an open-loop opamp behave? What type of circuit is it?
An op-amp with no feedback compares its two inputs and pushes the output hard to one rail or the other. If the plus input is higher, the output goes to the positive rail.
If the minus input is higher, it goes to the negative rail or ground. That is a comparator: it answers "which input is bigger?" with a one or a zero.
Think of a doorbell button with a spring. Press even slightly past the threshold and it clicks fully on. Release below it and it clicks fully off. There is almost no in-between.
An open-loop op-amp is like that. The trouble comes if you hold the button right at the click point: small shakes make it flutter.
The output is a rail-to-rail square wave. It flips to +12 volts when the sine goes above the 0. 3 volts reference and back to minus 12 volts when it falls below.
The duty cycle is not 50% because the reference isn't zero: the output is high for the fraction of the cycle where sine theta 0. 3 .
The sine is drawn at 1 volts peak, so it's tiny relative to the output; the transitions look instantaneous because the gain makes the linear window only ±120 µV wide.
Comparator: a circuit that outputs a high or low depending on which input is larger. Rail: the supply voltage at which the output stops.
Threshold: the voltage on one input that the other is compared against. Hysteresis: using two different thresholds, one for rising and one for falling.
Schmitt trigger: a comparator with hysteresis, made by feeding part of the output back to the plus input (positive feedback).
Say a 5 volts op-amp has 2. 5 volts on the minus input as the threshold, and a signal on the plus input. At 2. 6 volts the output slams to 5 volts. At 2.
4 volts it goes to 0 volts. If the signal hovers near 2. 5 volts with a little noise, the output chatters. Adding positive feedback gives hysteresis, so it switches cleanly.
That is the whole idea.
"Open loop, the op-amp's gain of 10 to the 5 or more acts on the tiny difference between its inputs, so the output slams to a rail depending on which input is higher.
That makes it a comparator, a one-bit ADC. The linear region is only ~100 µV wide.
Noise near the threshold causes chatter, so you add positive feedback for hysteresis, a Schmitt trigger.
In practice, dedicated comparators are better than op-amps for this because of faster recovery and logic-compatible outputs."

Why prefer non-inverting op-amp stages. The question: Why are non-inverting configurations often preferred?
An op-amp is a chip that amplifies the difference between its two inputs, plus and minus.
A stage adds resistors that feed part of the output back to the minus input to set the gain. There are two ways to wire it.
In the non-inverting way, the signal goes straight into the plus input and the output has the same sign.
In the inverting way, the signal goes through a resistor into the minus input and the output flips sign.
Most of the time you prefer the non-inverting way because it barely loads whatever feeds it.
Think of reading the level in a water tank. A clear glass gauge on the side lets you see the level without taking any water out. That is the non-inverting input.
A pipe that drains water out of the tank to measure it is the inverting input: you change the tank by measuring it.
This only matters for a weak source: a huge lake barely notices a small drain.
In (a) the sensor drives the high-impedance + input and the buffer follows it.
In (b) the same sensor drives R in into a virtual ground, so its 10 kilohms simply adds to R in and the gain is cut in half.
Input impedance: how hard it is for current to flow into an input. Higher means the input takes less current and disturbs the source less.
Source resistance: the resistance inside the thing driving the input, such as a sensor. Gain: output voltage divided by input voltage.
Op-amp: see "What an op-amp is and how it works". The two circuits are compared in "Inverting and non-inverting op-amp circuits".
A sensor puts out 1 volts and has 10 kilohms of resistance inside. Feed it into an inverting stage with a 10 kilohms input resistor.
The sensor's own 10 kilohms adds to that resistor, so the gain is cut in half, as if only 0. 5 volts had arrived. Now feed it into the plus input of a non-inverting stage.
That input draws almost no current, so nearly the full 1 volts arrives. That is the whole idea.
"Non-inverting stages are often preferred because the input goes straight into the op-amp's high-impedance plus terminal, so they don't load the source or turn its resistance into a gain error.
They also don't invert, can be built as a unity-gain buffer, and for the same signal gain have slightly better bandwidth.
The downsides: the gain is at least one, and both inputs swing with the signal, so common-mode range and CMRR matter.
For summing or low-impedance sources, the inverting stage is just as good."

Bode magnitude and phase of a first-order filter. The question: Draw mag/phase response of a first-order filter.
A Bode plot shows how a filter treats every frequency. It is two graphs stacked together.
The top one shows how much of the signal gets through (the magnitude), and the bottom one shows how much the signal is delayed (the phase).
Both use a logarithmic frequency axis, so each tick is ten times the last.
Imagine a road that runs flat for a while and then bends into a downhill slope of constant steepness. The flat part is the frequencies the filter lets through.
The bend is the corner frequency. The slope is how fast the filter shuts out higher frequencies.
In real life the bend is rounded, and the straight-line sketch is only an approximation.
With no load, the circuit is a divider between R and the capacitor's impedance 1 over (j omega C) . Low frequency: Z C to infinity so V out equals V in .
High frequency: Z C to 0 so V out to 0 .
Corner frequency: ( f c ): the frequency where the filter starts to cut. For an RC filter it is 1 over (2 pi RC) . Decibel (dB): a log scale for ratios.
0 decibels means unchanged, and -20 decibels means one tenth of the voltage. Decade: a factor of ten in frequency.
Phase: how far the output wave is shifted in time relative to the input, measured in degrees. Low-pass filter: passes low frequencies and cuts high ones.
Take an RC low-pass with a corner at 1 kilohertz. At 100 hertz the output is almost the full input (about 0 decibels) and the phase is about -6 degrees.
At 1 kilohertz the output is 0. 707 of the input (-3 decibels) and the phase is exactly -45 degrees.
At 10 kilohertz the output is about one tenth (-20 decibels) and the phase is about -84 degrees. That is the whole idea.
"For a first-order low-pass I'd draw magnitude in dB and phase versus log frequency.
Magnitude is flat at 0 decibels, is 3 decibels down at the corner f c equals 1 over (2 pi RC) , and then falls at minus 20 decibels per decade.
Phase goes from 0 to minus 90 degrees, with exactly minus 45 at the corner.
A high-pass is the mirror image: rising 20 decibels per decade up to the corner then flat, phase from +90 to 0, +45 at the corner."

First-order LPF and HPF circuits. The question: Draw a circuit for a first-order LPF/HPF.
A first-order filter is one resistor and one capacitor (or, less often, an inductor, which is a coil) that lets some frequencies through and blocks others.
A low-pass filter passes slow signals and cuts fast ones. A high-pass filter does the opposite.
The only difference between them is which part sits in series and which goes to ground.
For the low-pass, picture a bucket fed through a narrow pipe. Slow changes in the water supply fill and empty the bucket, so the level follows them.
Fast flutters are too quick for the narrow pipe, so they get averaged out. For the high-pass, picture a rubber membrane across a pipe.
A steady push stretches it and then nothing more flows, but a quick back-and-forth push passes right through.
Same two parts, swapped. In the low-pass, the capacitor to ground diverts high frequencies.
In the high-pass, the series capacitor blocks low frequencies and the resistor to ground sets the DC level. Both have f c equals 1 over (2 pi times 10 kilohms times 15.
9 nanofarads ) about 1 kilohertz.
Capacitor: stores charge. It blocks steady (DC) current but lets changing signals pass. Corner frequency: where the output has dropped to 70. 7% of its passband value.
For RC it is 1 over (2 pi RC) . Series / to ground: in series sits in the signal path. To ground connects the output node to 0 volts.
Loading: whatever you connect to the output draws current and shifts the filter's behavior. Buffer: an amplifier stage that copies a voltage without drawing current from it.
Use R equals 1. 6 kilohms and C equals 100 nanofarads. The corner is 1 over (2 pi times 1600 times 10 to the -7) , about 1 kilohertz.
Put R in series and C to ground, take the output across C, and you have a low-pass. Swap their places and you have a high-pass with the same corner. That is the whole idea.
"The RC low-pass is a series resistor with a capacitor to ground, output across the capacitor. The capacitor shorts out high frequencies.
The high-pass swaps them: series capacitor, resistor to ground, output across the resistor, so the capacitor blocks DC. Both have a corner at 1 over (2 pi RC) .
You can build the same filters with an inductor, series L plus a resistor to ground for a low-pass, but RC is usually preferred.
And note that loading shifts the corner, so buffer it or use an active stage if needed."

Roll-off rate of a first-order low-pass. The question: What is the dropoff rate of a first-order low-pass filter?
Roll-off is how quickly a filter's output shrinks once you pass the corner frequency. A first-order low-pass rolls off at -20 decibels per decade.
In plain terms, every time you multiply the frequency by ten, the output voltage drops to one tenth.
Picture walking down a staircase where every step is the same height. Each step is a tenfold jump in frequency, and each step down is the same 20 decibels drop.
The staircase never gets steeper or shallower. That is why a log-frequency graph shows a straight line.
The staircase only starts right at the corner, so close to the corner the real curve is gently rounded.
The curve hugs the dashed asymptote more than an octave away from the corner. The largest deviation is 3 decibels at f c .
From 10 kilohertz to 100 kilohertz the plot falls exactly one 20 decibels step per decade.
Roll-off: how fast the output falls above the corner. Larger slope means a sharper filter. Decade: a factor of ten in frequency. Octave: a factor of two in frequency.
For a first-order filter that is about -6 decibels. Decibel (dB): 20 log 10 of a voltage ratio. -20 decibels is one tenth.
Corner frequency: the point where the output is down 3 decibels.
Take a low-pass with a 1 kilohertz corner and feed in a 1 volts wave. At 10 kilohertz, the output is about 0. 1 volts (-20 decibels). At 100 kilohertz it is about 0.
01 volts (-40 decibels). Double the frequency instead, from 10 kilohertz to 20 kilohertz, and the output halves, from 0. 1 volts to about 0. 05 volts. That is the whole idea.
"A first-order low-pass rolls off at 20 decibels per decade, about 6 decibels per octave, above its corner.
The reason is that for f much greater than f c the magnitude is just f c over f : ten times the frequency gives one tenth of the amplitude, which is minus 20 decibels.
It's the capacitor behaving like a short, so the filter acts as an integrator.
The slope is asymptotic: minus 3 decibels at the corner and minus 20 decibels at ten times the corner. Each extra pole adds another 20 decibels per decade."

What bandwidth characterizes. The question: What does the bandwidth characterize?
Bandwidth is the range of frequencies a circuit can pass without cutting them down much.
We usually measure it between the two points where the output is 3 decibels below its normal level (about 70. 7% of the voltage).
It tells you how quickly a system can respond, so it is also a limit on how fast a signal can change.
Think of a road with several lanes. A wider road carries more traffic at once. Likewise, a wider bandwidth carries more kinds of signals, and faster changes, through the circuit.
But a wide road also lets in more roadside noise, so you don't build it wider than you need.
A simple band-pass built from a 1 kilohertz high-pass and a 10 kilohertz low-pass. Because the two stages overlap, the passband peaks about 0. 8 decibels below 0 decibels at 3.
2 kilohertz, and the minus 3 decibels points (measured from that peak) fall at about 0. 84 kilohertz and 11. 8 kilohertz.
The bandwidth is therefore about 11 kilohertz, the centre is f 0 equals square root of f Lf H about 3. 2 kilohertz and Q equals f 0 over BW about 0. 3 .
A low Q means a wide, shallow band-pass; a narrow-band filter has a high Q .
Bandwidth: the width of the frequency range that passes, from the lower -3 decibels point to the upper one.
Passband: the range of frequencies the circuit passes at about full strength. -3 decibels point: where the output is 70. 7% of the passband level.
Rise time: how long an edge takes to go from 10% to 90% of its final value. Gain-bandwidth product: for an op-amp, gain times bandwidth stays about constant.
A system with bandwidth B has a rise time of about 0. 35 over B . A 100 megahertz oscilloscope therefore has a rise time of 0. 35 over (100 times 10 to the 6) equals 3.
5 nanoseconds. If you feed it a faster edge, you will still see an edge of about 3. 5 nanoseconds on the screen. That is the whole idea.
"Bandwidth is the range of frequencies a system passes within 3 decibels of its passband gain: DC to the corner for a low-pass, upper minus lower edge for a band-pass.
It characterizes speed: rise time is about 0. 35 over the bandwidth. It also sets how much noise gets in and, through Shannon, how much information you can send.
For an op-amp, closed-loop bandwidth is about GBW over gain."

What is the approximate true rise time?
The minus 3 decibels point and how much passes. The question: What is the 3 decibels rolloff point? What happens after that? How much of the signal gets through?
The -3 decibels point is the frequency where a filter's output has dropped to 70. 7% of its normal voltage. At that point half of the power gets through.
It is the standard way to say "this is where the filter starts to cut."
Picture slowly closing a tap. At first the flow barely changes. At the -3 decibels point it has dropped noticeably but not to nothing, and past that it keeps shrinking.
There is no brick wall: a signal just above the corner still gets through with most of its strength. The tap picture breaks down for the exact 70.
7%, which comes from the math, not from any physical rule of taps.
At the minus 3 decibels frequency the output peaks at 0. 707 volts (30% less than the input) and is delayed by an eighth of a period, 125 microseconds at 1 kilohertz.
It is clearly still a sine wave of significant amplitude, which is why "cutoff" is not "stop".
Corner frequency: ( f c ): the -3 decibels frequency. For an RC filter it is 1 over (2 pi RC) . Decibel (dB): a log scale for ratios. -3 decibels is a voltage ratio of 0. 707.
Half-power point: the same point, seen as power. 0. 707 squared equals 0. 5 . Passband: the range where the signal passes nearly unchanged.
Roll-off: how the output keeps falling past the corner.
Feed a 1 volts wave into a low-pass with a 1 kilohertz corner. At 1 kilohertz the output is 0. 707 volts, with half the input power. At 10 kilohertz the output is about 0.
1 volts. At 100 hertz it is about 0. 995 volts, nearly the full input. That is the whole idea.
"The 3 decibels point is where the gain has dropped to 0. 707 of the passband, which is half the power. For an RC filter it's 1 over (2 pi RC) with 45 degrees of phase shift.
After that the response keeps falling at 20 decibels per decade for a first-order filter: it's not a cliff. At the corner 70.
7 percent of the voltage and 50 percent of the power get through; at twice the corner about 45 percent; at ten times about 10 percent, which is minus 20 decibels."
Quick check. An RC low-pass must have no more than 1% amplitude error at the highest signal frequency of 2 kilohertz. What minimum corner frequency is needed (approximately)?
Ways to raise a clock frequency (PLL). The question: What can you use increase clock frequency?
A PLL (phase-locked loop) is a circuit that makes a fast clock out of a slow, accurate one. You start with a cheap, stable reference such as a crystal.
The PLL multiplies its frequency by a number you choose, usually a whole number. It is used because crystals can't directly make very high frequencies cheaply and accurately.
Imagine a slow drummer keeping perfect time, and a fast drummer who plays 40 beats for each of the slow drummer's beats.
The fast drummer listens to the slow one and nudges the pace so that every 40th beat lands exactly on the slow drummer's beat.
The fast drummer is as steady as the slow one, just 40 times faster. The picture breaks down in that a real PLL adds a little timing wobble of its own.
The VCO output is divided by N and compared with the reference.
When they match, f out over N equals f ref , so the output is exactly N times the crystal frequency, with the crystal's long-term accuracy.
Reference clock: the slow, stable source, usually a crystal. VCO: voltage-controlled oscillator, the fast oscillator whose speed is set by a control voltage.
Divider: a counter that divides a frequency by N . Jitter: tiny cycle-to-cycle timing errors in a clock. PLL: the whole loop. How it works is on "How a PLL works".
Start with a 25 megahertz crystal and a divide-by-40 in the feedback path.
The loop forces the divided VCO clock to match 25 megahertz, so the VCO itself must run at 25 times 40 equals 1000 megahertz, which is 1 gigahertz.
Change N to 20 and you get 500 megahertz from the same crystal. That is the whole idea.
"A PLL, used as a frequency multiplier. A stable low-frequency reference like a crystal feeds a loop containing a VCO and a divide-by-N in the feedback path.
The loop locks the divided VCO to the reference, so the output is N times the reference: 25 megahertz times 40 gives 1 gigahertz.
It's preferred over a very high-frequency crystal because it's flexible and the reference is clean and cheap.
Simpler options exist, like an XOR-based doubler or a higher-frequency oscillator, but a faster clock costs power, timing margin and jitter."
Quick check. Which circuit is most commonly used to generate a high-frequency clock from a low-frequency crystal reference?
How a PLL works. The question: How does a PLL work?
A PLL is a feedback loop that makes an oscillator follow a reference clock.
It keeps checking whether the oscillator is early or late compared with the reference, and nudges it to fix the difference.
When the difference stops changing, the loop is "locked", and the output is an exact multiple of the reference.
Picture a cyclist trying to stay level with a friend. If the cyclist falls behind, pedal harder. If they pull ahead, ease off.
After a while they ride side by side at the same speed. The cyclist's pedaling effort is the control voltage.
The picture is loose in one way: the PLL compares when clock edges arrive, so it holds a timing gap steady, not a distance.
The classic charge-pump PLL. The closed path VCO to ÷N to PFD to charge pump to loop filter to VCO is a negative-feedback loop.
Locked, f fb equals f ref and so f out equals Nf ref .
Phase detector: compares edge timing of two clocks and outputs how early or late one is. Loop filter: smooths the detector's output into a steady control voltage.
VCO: an oscillator whose frequency depends on its control voltage. Lock: the state where the divided output matches the reference in frequency with a steady timing offset (phase).
Feedback divider: divides the output by N before comparing.
Reference is 25 megahertz and N equals 40 . Suppose the VCO starts at 900 megahertz. Divided by 40, that is 22. 5 megahertz, slower than the 25 megahertz reference.
The detector sees the feedback is late, the control voltage rises, and the VCO speeds up.
This continues until the VCO reaches 1 gigahertz, where the divided clock is exactly 25 megahertz and the correction stops. That is the whole idea.
"A PLL is a feedback loop that locks an oscillator's phase to a reference.
A phase-frequency detector compares the reference to the VCO output divided by N and generates pulses proportional to the phase error.
A charge pump and loop filter turn that into a control voltage, which steers the VCO.
When the divided clock has the same frequency as the reference and a constant phase offset, the control voltage stops changing: it's locked, and the output frequency is N times the reference.
The VCO's integration of frequency into phase is why the loop can lock with zero phase error."
Quick check. In a locked PLL, which condition holds?
PLL building blocks and their roles. The question: What blocks does a PLL have?
A charge-pump PLL has five blocks joined in a loop. Each has one job: compare, convert, smooth, oscillate, divide.
Knowing the role of each block lets you see what goes wrong when one of them is imperfect.
Think of tuning a guitar string against a reference note. Your ear notices the string is flat (compare). Your hand turns the peg a bit (convert and smooth).
The string changes pitch (oscillate). You then listen again. The loop filter plays the role of your steady hand: it keeps the peg from jerking.
The guitar picture breaks down at the divider: a real PLL compares against a clock divided down from its output.
Each arrow is labelled with the type of signal. The PFD is the only place where the digital (edge) domain is converted to the analog (charge/voltage) domain via the charge pump.
Locked: f vco over N equals f ref over R .
Phase-frequency detector (PFD): compares reference and feedback edges and outputs UP or DOWN pulses.
Charge pump: turns those pulses into current pushed into, or pulled from, the loop filter. Loop filter: a resistor and capacitors that smooth the current into a control voltage.
VCO: the oscillator that makes the output clock. Divide-by-N: the feedback counter that sets the multiplication ratio.
Walk one trip around the loop with a 25 megahertz reference and N equals 40 . The feedback clock is late, so the PFD makes UP pulses.
The charge pump turns them into current, and the loop filter turns that into a higher control voltage.
The VCO speeds up toward 1 gigahertz, and the divider turns it back into a clock near 25 megahertz. That is the whole idea.
"A charge-pump PLL has a reference oscillator, a phase-frequency detector, a charge pump, a loop filter, a VCO, and a divide-by-N feedback divider.

The PFD turns the timing error between reference and divided VCO into UP/DOWN pulses, the charge pump turns those into current, the loop filter integrates it into a control voltage, the VCO converts that to frequency, and the divider feeds it back.
Fractional-N adds a sigma-delta modulator on the divider, and there's usually an output divider and a lock detector."
Quick check. Which block closes the PLL feedback loop and makes the output a multiple of the reference?
Draw a PLL block diagram. The question: Draw a block diagram.
A PLL block diagram is a loop of boxes with one signal going around.
The reference goes in, the output comes out, and a copy of the output (divided down) goes back to be compared with the reference.
Drawing it means putting the right boxes in the right order and labeling the signals.
Picture a one-way circular track with five stations in order: phase detector, charge pump, loop filter, VCO, and divider.
The reference clock joins at the first station, and the output is taken off right after the VCO.
Everything going around the loop is the correction signal that keeps the output in step.
The loop reads left to right through the forward path (PFD to charge pump to loop filter to VCO) and returns along the bottom through the divider.
The signals are labelled on the wires. When locked, f fb equals f ref and so f out equals Nf ref .
f ref : the reference clock frequency that enters the loop. Feedback path: the branch that carries the divided output back to the detector.
UP / DOWN pulses: the detector's outputs telling the VCO to speed up or slow down. Control voltage: ( V ctrl ): the smoothed voltage that sets the VCO's frequency.
Lock condition: f out over N equals f ref .
The smallest version has four things in words: a phase detector, a loop filter, a VCO, and a divide-by- N in the return path. The reference enters the detector.
The detector output goes through the filter into the VCO. The VCO output is the PLL output, and it is also divided by N and sent back to the detector.
With f ref equals 10 megahertz and N equals 5 , locked output is 50 megahertz. That is the whole idea.

"Left to right: reference clock into a phase-frequency detector; its UP and DOWN outputs drive a charge pump; that feeds a loop filter, an R–C network; the filter's control voltage drives the VCO, whose output is f out.
A divide-by-N block takes f out and feeds it back to the second input of the PFD, closing the loop.
I'd label f ref, UP/DOWN, the pump current, V control, f out and f out over N, and write f out equals N times f ref as the lock condition."

PLL locking too fast or too slow. The question: What happens if your PLL locks too fast or too slow?
How fast a PLL settles is set by its loop bandwidth. A wide bandwidth makes the PLL lock quickly and follow the reference closely. A narrow one makes it slow but calm.
Both extremes cause problems, so the designer picks a compromise.
Think of steering a car. If you jerk the wheel at every bump, you correct instantly but also react to every little disturbance, and the car wobbles.
If you steer very gently, the ride is smooth but you are slow to get back to the lane after a real change. A good driver is somewhere between.
In a PLL the "bumps" are noise on the reference.
The same loop with omega n scaled by 10 each time.
The slow loop (red) is still settling after 150 microseconds, the 50 kilohertz loop settles in ~16 microseconds, and the 500 kilohertz loop is done in about 1.
6 microseconds (it looks like a vertical line). All overshoot by the same 21% because the damping is the same. Bandwidth buys time, not shape.
Loop bandwidth: how fast the loop can respond to errors. Lock time: how long the loop takes to settle after start-up or a frequency change.
Jitter: small random timing errors in the output clock. Spur: an unwanted tone in the output, often at the reference frequency. Damping: how quickly oscillation dies out.
Too little means overshoot and ringing.
Say the reference is 1 megahertz. A rule of thumb keeps the loop bandwidth below about a tenth of that, so under 100 kilohertz.
Settling takes roughly a few times 1 over bandwidth , so a 100 kilohertz loop settles in tens of microseconds, while a loop ten times narrower takes about ten times longer.
The wide loop passes more reference noise. The narrow loop lets more VCO drift and noise through. That is the whole idea.
"It's the loop bandwidth trade-off.

Too fast, meaning wide bandwidth, and the output inherits reference and charge-pump noise multiplied by N, reference spurs, and may overshoot or even go unstable as the bandwidth nears the reference frequency.
Too slow and the lock time gets long, so startup and frequency changes lag, and the loop can't suppress the VCO's own noise and drift, so jitter rises, and it can't track input jitter.
The sweet spot is where the two noise contributions are equal, with damping near 0. 7, and bandwidth well under a tenth of the reference."
Quick check. A PLL has a very narrow loop bandwidth. Which problem is most likely?
Why a crushed clock window hurts. The question: Why is crushing the clock window bad? How can this impact other circuits that may be connected to the clock?
The "clock window" is the time you get in each clock cycle to send data through the logic and have it caught safely at the other end.
If you shrink that window, by running faster or by letting the clock wobble, the data may not arrive in time. Then the chip makes errors.
Picture a relay race where each runner has one second to carry the baton and hand it over. The hand-over only works if the next runner is ready.
If the runner takes longer, or the starting signal comes at a slightly different time each lap, then some hand-overs fail.
The track doesn't care about the average lap; it only cares about the worst one.
One 1 nanoseconds cycle drawn to scale.
Launch clock-to-Q (120 picoseconds), logic (600 picoseconds), setup (60 picoseconds), skew (40 picoseconds) and jitter (50 picoseconds) add to 870 picoseconds, leaving 130 picoseconds of slack.
Crushing the window means eating that green slack.
Setup time: how long data must be steady before the clock edge arrives. Jitter: cycle-to-cycle variation in the clock edge timing.
Skew: a difference in clock arrival time between two flip-flops. Metastability: a flip-flop output hovering between 0 and 1 because the data changed too close to the clock edge.
Flip-flop (flop): a tiny memory cell that grabs its input at each clock edge and holds it until the next.
A 1 gigahertz clock gives a 1 nanoseconds window. The launching flop takes 0. 2 nanoseconds to put out new data, the logic 0. 5 nanoseconds, setup 0.
1 nanoseconds, and skew plus jitter 0. 1 nanoseconds. That totals 0. 9 nanoseconds, so the margin is 0. 1 nanoseconds. Now let the PLL add another 0. 15 nanoseconds of jitter.
The total becomes 1. 05 nanoseconds, which is more than the window, so the margin is -0. 05 nanoseconds and the data is captured wrong. That is the whole idea.
"I take the clock window as the time you have each cycle for launch, logic, setup, skew and jitter.

If you crush it, with a faster clock, jitter, duty-cycle error or PLL overshoot, you get setup and hold violations and metastability in synchronous logic, minimum-pulse-width failures in flops and memories, SNR loss in ADCs through aperture jitter, and eye closure and bit errors in serial links and DDR.
Circuits see the worst cycle, not the average, so the failures are intermittent. You fix it with margin, cleaner clocks and holding logic in reset until lock."
Quick check. Which problem is NOT fixed by reducing the clock frequency?
What kind of load is a SoC/CPU?. The question: What type of load (resistive, inductive, capacitive) can a SoC/CPU typically be characterized as?
A SoC or CPU is made of millions of tiny CMOS switches. Each switch charges and discharges a small capacitor every clock tick.
So the best description of the chip as a load is a current sink (something that draws current) whose demand changes quickly, controlled by what the software is doing.
It is mostly capacitive in nature, but you rarely model it as a plain capacitor.
Imagine a city's water supply. At night, demand is a trickle. When everyone's alarm goes off, thousands of taps open at once and demand jumps in seconds.
The pipes and the water tower have to cope with the jump. The chip is the city, and the board's power supply is the pipe.
The picture breaks down because the chip's demand can change in nanoseconds.
The load is the die: a workload-controlled current source in parallel with on-die capacitance. The resistance and inductance (orange) are the delivery path.
The die capacitance supplies the first few nanoseconds of any current step; the inductance and resistance determine how quickly the rest can arrive.
CMOS: the type of transistor logic used in nearly all chips. Load: whatever draws current from a supply.
Dynamic power: the power used charging and discharging those tiny capacitors. It grows with the voltage squared and with the clock frequency. Transient: a quick change in current.
Droop: the temporary dip in the supply voltage when current jumps.
A core runs at 0. 9 volts and draws 54 amps. That is 48. 6 watts, and by Ohm's law, 0. 9 over 54 about 17 milliohms, so the chip looks like a 17 milliohms resistor.
But then the code goes idle and the current drops to almost nothing while the voltage stays at 0. 9 volts. The "resistance" just jumped, so it was never a real resistor.
That is the whole idea.
"A SoC is best described as a capacitive, time-varying current sink. It's CMOS, so power goes into charging and discharging capacitance every cycle: alpha C V squared f .
On average it looks resistive, like 17 milliohms for a 54 amp core, but that's just V over I, and it changes with the workload. It isn't really inductive.
The inductance is in the package and board, and with fast current steps it causes droop, which is why the supply needs low impedance and lots of decoupling."
Quick check. Which description best fits a CMOS SoC as seen by its power supply?
Maximum power transfer condition. The question: What is the condition for maximum power transfer?
Maximum power transfer says: a source delivers the most power to a load when the load's resistance equals the source's own internal resistance.
It is for situations where the available power is small and you want to catch as much of it as possible, like a radio antenna. It is not what you want for a power supply.
Picture a battery with some resistance inside. If the load is a tiny resistor, a big current flows but almost no voltage appears across the load.
If the load is a huge resistor, the voltage is high but almost no current flows. Power is voltage times current, so it is small at both ends and largest somewhere in the middle.
That middle is where the load matches the source.
The source is fixed; only R L is adjustable. The load voltage is V sR L over (R s plus R L) and the current is V s over (R s plus R L) . Power is their product.
Source resistance: ( R s ): the resistance inside the source. Load resistance: ( R L ): the resistance of the thing being powered. Matched: R L equals R s .
Efficiency: the fraction of total power that goes to the load. Impedance: the general word for how strongly a circuit opposes current, covering resistance and more.
A 10 volts source has R s equals 10 ohms. With R L equals 10 ohms the current is 0. 5 amps, so the load gets 0. 5 squared times 10 equals 2. 5 watts.
That is the peak, V s squared over (4R s) . With R L equals 1 ohms the load gets only about 0. 83 watts. With R L equals 100 ohms it also gets about 0. 83 watts.
At the match, the source's own resistor burns 2. 5 watts too, so efficiency is 50%. That is the whole idea.
"Maximum power goes to the load when the load resistance equals the source resistance, or for AC when Z L equals Z s^ .
The load power is V s to the 2R L over (R s plus R L) squared , and setting the derivative to zero gives R L equals R s , with P max equals V s squared over (4R s) .
The catch is that efficiency is only 50% at that point, so it's used in RF and signal chains, not in power supplies, where you want low source impedance instead."
Quick check. A fixed source with R s equals 8 ohms drives a variable resistive load. For which R L is load power maximum?
Why many capacitors on a power rail. The question: Often times on a power rail, there are many capacitors connected to ground. What are these capacitors and why are there so many?
Why can you just put one massive capacitor?
Those small capacitors next to a chip are decoupling capacitors. They act as little local energy reserves.
A chip pulls current in sharp bursts that the distant regulator cannot supply fast enough. The capacitors cover each burst so the voltage on the rail doesn't dip.
Think of a restaurant kitchen. A big delivery truck (the regulator) is slow to arrive. So each cook keeps a small bowl of ingredients right at the station.
A single huge container across the kitchen would be too far to reach quickly. Many small bowls placed close to each cook work better.
The bowls are the capacitors, placed right at the chip's pins.
The three series elements of a real capacitor.
Reactances omega L and 1 over omega C have opposite signs, so they cancel at one frequency, the SRF; beyond it the part is inductive.
Decoupling capacitor: a capacitor placed close to a chip's supply pins to supply fast current bursts.
ESL: the small unwanted inductance (a resistance to fast changes in current) of a real capacitor and its mounting. ESR: the small unwanted series resistance of a real capacitor.
Self-resonant frequency: above it, a capacitor acts like an inductor. Impedance: how strongly a part opposes changing current at a given frequency.
Suppose one capacitor and its mounting have 5 nanohenries of inductance. At 100 megahertz its inductive impedance is 2 pi times 10 to the 8 times 5 times 10 to the -9 about 3.
1 ohms. Put ten of them in parallel and the inductance divides by ten, giving about 0. 31 ohms. That is ten times lower impedance at that frequency. That is the whole idea.
"They're decoupling capacitors, acting as local charge reservoirs so fast current bursts don't pull the rail down.
There are many because a real capacitor has ESR and inductance, so each one is only a low impedance over a limited band, above its self-resonant frequency it looks like an inductor.
Paralleling several small parts divides the inductance and gives low impedance out to hundreds of megahertz.
One massive capacitor has a big package and long path, so it's inductive exactly where the chip needs help."
Quick check. What is the main job of the many small capacitors on a processor's power rail?
What is bulk capacitance?. The question: What is bulk capacitance?
Bulk capacitance is a large capacitor, tens to thousands of microfarads, placed where power enters a board or at a regulator. It is a local energy tank.
It covers the slower, bigger demands that the regulator needs a few microseconds to catch up with.
Think of a water tower in a town. The pump at the reservoir cannot change speed instantly. When demand surges, the tower's stored water covers the gap until the pump catches up.
A tower is too big and too far away to handle quick flicker at each tap, though. For that you need the small local buckets, which are the small ceramic capacitors.
The capacitor hierarchy. Each stage covers a time (or frequency) band: bulk covers microseconds to milliseconds, ceramics the nanoseconds to microseconds.
The regulator's own bandwidth defines where bulk takes over from the loop.
Bulk capacitor: a big capacitor that holds a large reserve of charge. Droop: the dip in voltage when a load suddenly asks for more current.
Hold-up: keeping the output alive during a brief loss of input power. ESL: a tiny built-in inductance (a resistance to fast changes in current) in every real capacitor.
It makes big capacitors poor at handling very fast changes. Capacitance: how much charge a capacitor stores per volt. Loop bandwidth: how quickly the regulator's feedback reacts.
A 100 kilohertz loop needs roughly 1. 6 microseconds to respond.
A load suddenly asks for 2 amps more. A regulator with a 100 kilohertz loop needs about 1 over (2 pi times 100 kilohertz ) about 1. 6 microseconds to react.
During that gap the capacitor alone supplies the extra current, and its voltage sags. The sag is roughly current times time divided by capacitance. To keep it under 0.
1 volts you need C about 2 times 1. 6 micro s over 0. 1 volts about 32 microfarads. Twice the capacitance halves the droop. That is the whole idea.
"Bulk capacitance is the large capacitance, tens to thousands of microfarads, at a board's power entry or a regulator's input or output.
It's the local energy tank: it supplies load steps while the regulator catches up, smooths converter input ripple, and provides hold-up.
You size it from C equals I change in t over change in V or from energy. It's slow, though.
Big capacitors are inductive above a few hundred kilohertz, so small ceramics handle the fast stuff."
Quick check. Which description best matches bulk capacitance?
Inductive flyback and protection. The question: What is inductive flyback? When can this be unwanted? When can it be wanted? How can you protect against it?
Inductive flyback is a voltage spike that appears when you suddenly cut the current through a coil. A coil, or inductor, resists changes in its current.
If you open a switch, the coil pushes a huge voltage in whatever direction keeps the current going.
In a relay (a switch worked by a coil) it can destroy the driving transistor, so you add a diode to give the current a safe path.
In a boost converter the same effect is used on purpose.
Picture a long pipe full of fast-moving water. If you slam a valve shut, the moving water has nowhere to go and produces a huge pressure spike, called water hammer.
The inductor's current is the moving water, and the switch is the valve. A bypass pipe next to the valve gives the water somewhere to go, like the flyback diode.
While Q1 is on, current flows down through the coil and Q1.
When Q1 opens, the coil keeps the same current direction (I L, down), which forces the switch node above V S and turns D1 on.
The current then circulates coil to node to D1 to the supply side (I D) and decays.
Inductance: how strongly a coil resists changes in current. L di over dt : the voltage across an inductor. Faster current change means bigger voltage.
Flyback (freewheel) diode: a diode (a one-way valve for current) across the coil that gives current a path when the switch opens.
Zener / TVS / snubber: parts that clamp or absorb a voltage spike at a chosen level.
A relay coil has L equals 1 millihenries and carries 0. 1 amps. A transistor cuts the current in 1 microseconds. The spike is L di over dt equals 10 to the -3 times 0.
1 over 10 to the -6 equals 100 volts, from a circuit that might run on 12 volts. With a diode across the coil, the current circulates through the diode instead.
The coil's reverse voltage is held to about 0. 7 volts, so the transistor sees only about 12. 7 volts: the supply plus one diode drop. That is the whole idea.
"Inductive flyback is the voltage spike when you suddenly interrupt current through an inductor.
Since v equals L di over dt , the inductor forces the current to continue by driving its voltage as high as needed, up to kilovolts if there's no path.
It's unwanted with relays, motors and solenoids, where it can kill the driver, so you add a freewheel diode, or a diode with a Zener or a TVS, or a snubber.
It's wanted in boost and flyback converters and ignition coils, which use that voltage deliberately to transfer energy."
Quick check. A transistor switches off current in a relay coil. What produces the voltage spike?
PWM and its characteristics. The question: What is PWM? What are its characteristics?
PWM (pulse-width modulation) controls how much power a load gets by switching a signal fully on and fully off, over and over, very fast.
The fraction of each cycle that the signal is on is the duty cycle. A higher duty cycle means more average power.
It is popular because a switch that is either fully on or fully off wastes very little energy.
Picture flicking a light switch on and off many times a second. If it is on for 30% of each cycle, your eye sees a light that is 30% as bright. Nothing in the bulb is "partly on".
It is just averaged. The load acts like a low-pass filter: it can't follow the rapid switching, so it responds to the average.
The wave spends 30% of each 1 milliseconds period high. The average (orange) is 1. 5 volts but the RMS (green) is 2. 74 volts, which matters when the load is a heater or lamp.
Notice the signal itself never sits at 1. 5 volts. Drag D toward 90%: the average rises linearly, the RMS more slowly, and the gap between them closes as the wave approaches DC.
Drag D down to 5%: the RMS is more than four times the average.
Duty cycle: ( D ): the fraction of the period that the signal is high, t on over T . Period and frequency: T is the time of one on-off cycle, and f equals 1 over T .
Average value: D times V , what a slow load responds to. RMS value: V square root of D , what matters for heating a resistor.
Low-pass filter: smooths the pulses into their average.
A 5 volts signal switches at 1 kilohertz, so the period is 1 milliseconds. It is high for 0. 3 milliseconds each cycle, so D equals 0. 3 . The average is 0. 3 times 5 equals 1.
5 volts. The RMS value is 5 square root of 0. 3 about 2. 74 volts. A heater would warm as if driven by 2. 74 volts, while a filter would output 1. 5 volts. That is the whole idea.
"PWM is switching a signal fully on and off at a fixed frequency and varying the on-time fraction, the duty cycle D . The average is D times V , for example 1.
5 volts from a 5 volts signal at 30%, but the RMS is V square root of D , which sets heating. A filter or a slow load averages it.
The main benefit is efficiency, since the switch is either on or off. Frequency is the trade-off: higher means smaller filters but more switching loss and EMI."
Quick check. Why is PWM control of a power load more efficient than a linear (series-resistor) approach?
Wide-bandgap semiconductors: SiC, GaN. The question: What novel semiconductors are being explored for power electronics? What are their tradeoffs?
Silicon carbide (SiC) and gallium nitride (GaN) are semiconductors with a much wider "bandgap" than silicon.
That lets a power transistor made from them block high voltage while being thinner.
The result is less resistance and faster switching than silicon, so power converters can be smaller and more efficient.
Think of a dam holding back water. A stronger material lets you build a thinner wall for the same height of water.
In a power transistor, the "wall" is a layer that blocks voltage.
Wide-bandgap materials withstand about ten times the electric field, so that layer can be much thinner, and the current has a shorter path through it when the transistor is on.
The dam picture breaks down on cost: the new materials are pricier.
Each material follows R on sp proportional to V B squared , but the lines are separated by orders of magnitude because of E c to the 3 .
At a given V B , SiC and GaN sit about 300-1000 times below silicon.
These are theoretical limits for the drift region only; real devices are well above them, and silicon superjunction closes some of the gap at 600-900 volts.
Bandgap: the energy an electron needs to jump into a conducting state. It is measured in electron-volts (eV): silicon is 1. 12 eV, and SiC and GaN are about 3. 3 eV.
Breakdown field: the most voltage per unit of thickness (electric field) a material can take before it fails. On-resistance: the resistance of a transistor when it is on.
Lower means less heat. Switching loss: energy wasted each time the transistor turns on or off. dv/dt, di/dt: how fast voltage and current change. Higher with these devices.
Compare two transistors rated for the same voltage. The silicon one needs a thick blocking layer.
The SiC or GaN one needs about a tenth as thick, so it has far lower on-resistance and much less capacitance to charge.
Less resistance means less conduction heat, and less capacitance means faster, cheaper switching. That is the whole idea.
"The main ones are silicon carbide and gallium nitride, with gallium oxide and diamond in research.
Their wide bandgap gives a critical field about ten times silicon's, so the drift region can be much thinner.
That gives much lower on-resistance for a given voltage, smaller capacitances and faster switching, so higher efficiency and frequency with smaller magnetics.
SiC fits high voltage, GaN fits up to roughly 650 volts and MHz.
The trade-offs are cost, gate drive constraints, reliability maturity and layout sensitivity because of very fast edges."
Quick check. Why do wide-bandgap semiconductors allow lower on-resistance at a given blocking voltage?
Ways to step voltage up or down. The question: What are some ways to step up/down voltage? What about for a power rail?
To step a voltage up or down, you use a regulator or converter. Some simply burn the extra voltage as heat (a linear regulator).
Others shuffle energy with a switch and an inductor or capacitor so that very little is lost (a buck, boost, or charge pump).
The right choice depends on current, efficiency, noise, size, and cost.
Think of the gears on a bicycle. A different gear changes the balance between force and speed without creating energy.
A switching converter does the same with voltage and current: it can trade a higher voltage for a lower voltage and a higher current, and the power in and out stays almost the same.
A linear regulator is more like riding the brakes: it throws the extra away.
A first-pass decision tree. The question that really drives the branch is "what is the load current, and what efficiency can I afford?"
, because it separates the linear options from the switching ones.
LDO: low-dropout linear regulator, which drops the extra voltage across a transistor.
Buck converter: a switching step-down converter built around an inductor, a coil that stores energy. Boost converter: a switching step-up converter.

A voltage divider only gives its expected output when nothing draws current from it. A power rail exists to supply current, and that current changes.
So the output of a divider moves around as the load changes. For a rail you want a regulator, which holds its output steady.
Think of a water pipe with a narrow restriction in it, and a tap after the restriction. With the tap closed, the pressure at the tap is full.

The divider's resistors are the restriction, and the load is the tap.

Design a power supply. The question: Design a power supply.
Designing a power supply means turning a source (such as a 12 volts adapter) into the steady voltages your circuit needs.
The design follows from the requirements: input range, output voltages, currents, and how clean the output must be.
So the first step is always asking questions, then picking the converter type that fits.
Think of planning a trip. You first decide where you are going, how many people are coming, and how much luggage you have. Only then do you choose a car or a train.
A supply design works the same way: needs first, parts second. The trip picture breaks down because supply parts also need protection against accidents, like short circuits.

Protection: features that prevent damage, such as current limit, a gentle turn-on (soft start), and shutting off when the input is too low or the chip too hot.

Supply overshoot and undershoot. The question: Why is supply voltage overshoot/undershoot often undesired? When can it be tolerated?
What type of loads are more sensitive to overshoot/undershoot?
Undershoot is when a supply voltage dips below its nominal value. Overshoot is when it rises above. Both usually happen when the load changes suddenly or the supply starts up.
Undershoot makes circuits fail to work. Overshoot can damage them or wear them out.
Imagine the water level in a bathtub with a tap and a drain. If someone suddenly pulls the plug, the level dips before the tap catches up.
If the tap is turned up too hard, the level overshoots the rim. A heater tolerates such swings, but a processor does not.
A stylised response. A load step causes the voltage to dip, ring and settle; a release causes the opposite polarity.
The size of the first excursion is set by C , ESR, ESL and the loop crossover; the ringing and settling time by phase margin. The numbers are illustrative.
Undershoot / droop: a temporary dip below nominal. Overshoot: a temporary rise above nominal. Transient: a quick change, such as a load step.
Margin: spare room before something fails. Brown-out: a dip deep enough to reset or corrupt a chip.
A 1. 0 volts core rail has a 5% tolerance, which is 50 millivolts. A load step makes it sag to 0. 95 volts.
The logic gates (the chip's tiny switching circuits) slow down, and if the timing margin was smaller than that slowdown, the chip makes errors.
If instead the rail overshoots to 1. 05 volts, the chip's switching power rises by roughly 10%, since it scales with the voltage squared ( 1. 05 squared about 1. 10 ).
That is the whole idea.
"Undershoot makes logic slower, because gate delay rises as the supply drops, so you get timing failures, brown-outs, bad memory writes and analogue errors.
Overshoot stresses devices, since it can exceed absolute-maximum ratings, and it increases power as V squared .
It's tolerable for loads with wide input range or their own regulation, like motors, heaters or LEDs, and for brief events within spec.
Low-voltage digital cores, PLLs, ADC references and RF are the most sensitive, since 5% of 0. 8 volts is only 40 millivolts."

Parameters to track in a supply. The question: What parameters would you want to track in a power supply?
A power supply has many numbers worth tracking.
They fall into groups: how accurate the output voltage is, how clean and steady it is, how efficient it is, how hot it gets, and how it behaves during start-up and faults.
You track different numbers during design and in the running product.
Think of a health check-up. The doctor does not look at one number.
Temperature, pulse, and blood pressure each say something different, and together they show whether you are healthy.
A supply's output voltage, ripple, efficiency, and temperature are its vital signs.
A checklist tree. In an interview, speak branch by branch; each leaf names a parameter you would measure or monitor.
The right-hand side of every branch is a question about the load: is the voltage right, clean, cool and safe?
Load regulation: how much the output changes as the load current changes. Line regulation: how much the output changes as the input voltage changes.
Ripple and noise: small unwanted wiggles on the output. Efficiency: output power divided by input power. Quiescent current: what the supply draws with no load.
A supply takes 12 volts at 0. 5 amps, so the input power is 6 watts. It delivers 5 volts at 1 amps, which is 5 watts.
The efficiency is 5 over 6 about 83 % , and 1 watts becomes heat. If the output reads 5. 00 volts with no load and 4. 95 volts at full load, the load regulation is 1%.
That is the whole idea.

Beyond that, start-up behaviour like soft-start and inrush, and protection thresholds: current limit, under-voltage lockout, thermal shutdown and power-good.
At runtime I'd monitor voltage, current, temperature and fault flags."

Specs for buying or designing a supply. The question: When buying/designing a power supply, what specs do you look out for?
When buying or designing a supply, start from the load. The supply's specifications are the load's needs plus some margin.
You ask what voltage, how much current (steady and peak), how clean, and from what input. Then you check that the supply covers all of those, in the worst case.
Think of buying a vehicle. You do not start with the brand. You start with what you need to carry, how far, and on what roads. Then you compare the specs that matter for that.
A supply's rated power is like a truck's load rating: you do not run it at the limit all day, and heat in a closed box lowers what it can carry.
A spec comes from four directions: the load, the source, the environment and non-technical constraints.
Selection or design happens in the middle; verification at the corners closes the loop.
Continuous current: the current the supply can deliver indefinitely. Peak current: a higher current allowed only briefly. Derating: lowering the allowed output when it is hot.
Efficiency: output over input power. Margin: spare capacity above what you need.
A load needs 5 volts at 2 amps continuous, with a brief 3 amps peak. A common rule is to load a supply to only 70 to 80% of its rating.
At 80%, the rating must be at least 2 over 0. 8 equals 2. 5 amps. At 70% it is 2 over 0. 7 about 2. 9 amps.
So pick a 3 amps supply, and check that it can handle the 3 amps peak and still works at the hottest surrounding air temperature. That is the whole idea.
"I'd start from the load and spec the output voltage and tolerance, continuous and peak current, ripple and noise, regulation and transient response.
Then efficiency including no-load power, the input range and surge/inrush behaviour, protections like over-current and over-temperature, thermal derating, and certifications and cost.
I'd size continuous current at about 70-80% of the rating, cover the peak, and verify under worst-case load, input and temperature."

Energy conservation in power design. The question: Why is energy conservation important? How is it applicable?
Energy conservation says energy cannot be created or destroyed. In a power circuit, the power going in equals the power coming out plus the power lost as heat.
It is useful twice: as a quick way to find unknown currents, and as a reminder that every loss is heat you must deal with.
Think of a bank account. Money deposited equals money withdrawn plus fees. The fees never vanish: they go to the bank.
In a converter, the "fees" are lost power, and they go to the air as heat. You can use the account books to find a missing number without checking every transaction.
Everything that enters must leave as useful output or as heat (plus any change in stored energy, which averages to zero in steady state). equals P out over P in .
Power: ( P equals VI ): energy per second. Efficiency: ( ): P out over P in . Loss: P in minus P out , which becomes heat. Stored energy: a capacitor stores 1 over 2 CV squared .
Inductor: stores energy in current.
A converter makes 3. 3 volts at 2 amps from 12 volts. The output power is 3. 3 times 2 equals 6. 6 watts. At 90% efficiency, the input power is 6. 6 over 0. 9 about 7. 3 watts.
The input current is 7. 3 over 12 about 0. 61 amps. It takes in less current than it delivers, because the input voltage is higher. That is the whole idea.
"Energy conservation says input power equals output power plus losses, almost always heat: P in equals P out plus P loss . It's a tool and a goal.
As a tool, it gives me unknown currents: a 90% efficient converter making 6. 6 watts from 12 volts draws 0. 61 amps.
As a goal, wasted energy is heat and battery life: an LDO from 12 to 3. 3 volts at 2 amps wastes 17 watts while a buck wastes under 1 watts."

Name some voltage regulators. The question: Name some voltage regulators.
Voltage regulators come in a few families. Linear regulators drop the extra voltage across a transistor and waste it as heat.
Switching regulators use a switch and an inductor and waste very little. Charge pumps use capacitors only. Shunt regulators hold a voltage by soaking up extra current.
You pick one by comparing efficiency, noise, size, and current.
Suppose you must lower the water pressure from a high-pressure main. You could throttle it with a valve and waste the pressure (linear).
You could pulse the flow rapidly into a tank (switching). You could pass it along in small buckets (charge pump). Or you could dump the extra to a drain (shunt).
Each works, with different costs.
The same job (hold the output constant) done four ways.
The branch tells you what is physically absorbing or moving the energy, which is what sets efficiency, noise and whether the output can be above the input.
Linear regulator / LDO: drops the extra voltage across a transistor that acts like a variable resistor. Quiet but wasteful.
Switching regulator: moves energy in chops using an inductor. Charge pump: moves energy using switched capacitors, with no inductor.
Shunt regulator: holds a voltage by diverting extra current, such as a Zener or TL431. Isolation: no direct electrical connection between input and output.
Make 3. 3 volts at 1 amps from 12 volts. The output is 3. 3 watts. A linear regulator draws 1 amps from 12 volts, which is 12 watts, and wastes 8. 7 watts. A buck at 90% draws 3.
3 over 0. 9 about 3. 7 watts and wastes about 0. 4 watts. That is the whole idea.
"I'd group them by how they work. Linear regulators, like a 7805, LM317 or an LDO, burn the excess voltage as heat, so they're simple and quiet but only step down.
Switching regulators use an inductor and a switch, buck to step down, boost to step up, buck-boost for both, flyback for isolation, and they hit roughly 90 percent efficiency.
Charge pumps use capacitors to double or invert a voltage at low current. And shunt regulators like a Zener or TL431 hold a voltage by absorbing extra current."

Buck converter vs LDO trade-offs. The question: What is the difference between a buck converter vs LDO? What are the tradeoffs?
An LDO and a buck both lower a voltage, but in different ways. An LDO acts like an adjustable resistor that burns off the extra voltage as heat.
A buck chops the input rapidly and averages it with an inductor and capacitor, so the energy is passed along instead of burned. The buck is far more efficient for big drops.
The LDO is simpler and quieter.
Think of slowing a car on a hill. The LDO is like holding the brakes: you stay at the speed you want, but all the extra energy turns into hot brakes.
The buck is more like the regenerative braking of an electric car, which stores the energy back in the battery.
The car picture breaks down on noise: the buck's chopping makes electrical noise that the quiet LDO does not.
In the LDO, the whole load current passes through the pass transistor with V in-V out across it. Multiply the two and you have the loss.
The error amplifier compares the feedback voltage with the reference and drives the pass gate; if V out rises, the amp output rises and turns the PMOS off a little.
LDO: low-dropout linear regulator. Efficiency is about V out over V in . Buck converter: a switching step-down converter. Ripple: leftover switching wiggle on a buck's output.
EMI: electromagnetic interference, the noise a switcher radiates. Inductor: the coil that stores energy between switch pulses.
Convert 12 volts to 3. 3 volts at 1 amps. The output power is 3. 3 watts. The LDO draws 1 amps at 12 volts, so it takes 12 watts and wastes 8. 7 watts, which is 27. 5% efficient.
A buck at about 90% takes 3. 7 watts and wastes about 0. 4 watts. That is the whole idea.
"An LDO burns the extra voltage as heat in a series pass element, so its efficiency is about Vout over Vin, and it only steps down.
A buck switches and uses an inductor to transfer energy, so it's around 90 percent efficient regardless of the voltage drop.
The trade is that the LDO is tiny, quiet and fast, while the buck needs an inductor, has ripple and EMI, and needs careful layout.
Big drop or high current, buck; small drop or noise-sensitive load, LDO."

When an LDO beats a buck. The question: When can an LDO be more efficient than a buck converter?
An LDO beats a buck when the voltage drop is small, or when the load is tiny.
An LDO's efficiency is about V out over V in , so if that ratio is higher than the buck's efficiency, the LDO wins on efficiency.
It also wins when a buck's fixed overhead is bigger than the load itself.
Think of moving house. For a big load, a large truck is efficient.
For one small parcel, the truck's fixed cost (fuel just to start the engine, the driver) is far more than the cargo, and a bicycle courier is better. The buck is the truck.
Its overhead is the controller and switching losses that are there whatever the load.
The LDO line crosses the buck line at V in equals V out over c . Left of it the LDO is better, right of it the buck wins.
The region of interest is narrow: a few hundred millivolts above V out .
Dropout: the minimum gap between input and output voltage that an LDO needs to keep regulating. Break-even: the point where two options are equally efficient.
Quiescent current: the current a regulator draws just to run. Switching overhead: losses a buck pays every cycle regardless of load. Headroom: the input minus output voltage.
A buck is 90% efficient. An LDO matches that when V out over V in equals 0. 9 . For a 3. 3 volts output, that is an input of 3. 3 over 0. 9 about 3. 67 volts.
Below that input, as long as it stays above the LDO's dropout, the LDO is better. From a 3. 6 volts battery, the LDO gets 3. 3 over 3. 6 about 92 % . That is the whole idea.
"An LDO is more efficient when the voltage drop is small or the load is tiny.
Its efficiency is about Vout over Vin, so it beats a buck whenever that ratio is higher than the buck's efficiency, like 3. 6 volts down to 3. 3 at 92 percent.
At very light loads, a buck's own quiescent current and switching overhead can exceed the load, so a nano-amp-class LDO can win.
At a big drop and real current, the buck always wins."

AC-AC, AC-DC, DC-DC, DC-AC converters. The question: What type of circuits can convert AC-AC/AC-DC/DC-DC/DC-AC?
Power converters are sorted by what goes in and what comes out. AC-AC changes one AC into another. AC-DC (a rectifier) turns wall power into DC.
DC-DC changes one DC voltage into another. DC-AC (an inverter) makes AC from DC. Real products often chain two of them.
Think of AC and DC as two different currencies, and a converter as a money changer.
Some keep the same currency but change the amount, like breaking a big bill into coins (a transformer or a DC-DC converter).
Others change between currencies (a rectifier or an inverter).
A laptop charger changes wall AC to DC, and inside the laptop another changer makes the small voltages the chips need.
Four conversions around one hub, the DC bus. Most real systems go AC to DC bus, then DC-DC for electronics or DC-AC for motors and grid-tied outputs.
A frequency-changing AC-AC converter usually goes through the DC bus (AC-DC-AC).
AC: current that reverses direction back and forth, like wall power. DC: current that flows in one direction. Rectifier: turns AC into DC.
Inverter: turns DC into AC, usually by switching transistors on and off in a fast pattern (an H-bridge with PWM).
Transformer: steps AC voltage up or down and isolates the two sides.
Take a wall adapter that powers a small gadget. First, an AC-DC stage turns the wall AC into a DC voltage. Next, a DC-DC stage steps that DC to the exact voltage the gadget needs.
A motor drive does the reverse at the end: it makes DC from the wall, then an inverter makes variable AC to spin the motor. That is the whole idea.
"It's a grid by input and output. AC to AC is a transformer, variac, or TRIAC phase control.
AC to DC is a rectifier, usually a diode bridge plus a filter capacitor, often with a PFC stage.
DC to DC is linear regulators, charge pumps and switching converters like buck, boost and flyback. DC to AC is an inverter: an H-bridge or three-phase bridge with PWM.
They chain: a wall adapter is AC-DC then DC-DC, and a motor drive is AC-DC then DC-AC."

Bridge rectifier operation. The question: What is a bridge rectifier? How does it work?
A bridge rectifier is four diodes in a diamond that turns AC into DC that only goes one way. The AC connects across two corners, and the load across the other two.
Whichever way the AC is pushing, two diodes steer the current through the load in the same direction.
Picture a pipe with water sloshing back and forth, and four one-way flap valves arranged so that, whichever way the water is pushed, it passes through a side chamber in the same direction.
The chamber is the load. The water still pulses, but it never reverses. That pulsing is the ripple, and a capacitor works as a small tank that smooths it.
Positive half-cycle. Terminal A is high.
Current (animated) leaves A, passes through D1 (green) to the positive rail, goes down through the capacitor and load, and returns through D4 (green) to terminal B.
D2 and D3 are reverse biased: D2 has B at its anode but the rail is higher.
Diode: a part that lets current through in only one direction. Half-cycle: half of one AC wave, either the positive or the negative half.
Peak voltage: the highest voltage of the AC wave. Reservoir capacitor: a capacitor that charges at the peaks and feeds the load between them.
Ripple: the leftover wiggle on the DC output.
Feed a 10 volts peak sine into a silicon bridge. Two diodes are in the path, each dropping about 0. 7 volts, so the output peaks at about 10 minus 1. 4 equals 8. 6 volts.
At 60 hertz, the output pulses 120 times per second, because both half-cycles now push the same way. That is the whole idea.
"A bridge rectifier is four diodes in a diamond: AC across one diagonal, load across the other.

On one half-cycle two diodes conduct and on the other half-cycle the other two do, but current always goes through the load in the same direction, so you get the absolute value of the input, pulsating DC at twice the line frequency.
Two diodes are in the path, so you lose about 1. 4 volts, and you add a capacitor to smooth it, with ripple of about I over 2fC."

Why step-down regulators dominate. The question: In many embedded systems, why are step-down regulators more common than step-up regulators?
Most power rails inside a device are stepped down from a higher voltage, because the sources are usually higher than what the chips need.
Chip voltages keep falling, since lower voltage saves a lot of power. Moving power at high voltage and converting down near the load also wastes less in the wires.
Think of a water tower on a hill. It is easy to let water run down to many houses and lower its pressure with valves at each tap. Pushing water uphill needs a pump and extra work.
Electronics is similar: getting from a high voltage down to a low one is the natural, simple direction.
Almost every arrow is a step-down. The one place a step-up would appear is when a battery replaces the adapter and sags below the 3. 3 volts or 5 volts rail.
Step-down: output voltage lower than input. Rail: a supply line at a particular voltage. I to the 2R loss: heat in a wire, which grows with the square of the current.
Chip switching power: the power chips use to flip their tiny switches. It scales with V squared , so lower voltage means much lower power.
Boost converter: a step-up converter, harder to design than a buck.
A 10 watts load at 1 volts draws 10 amps. At 12 volts, the same power needs only about 0. 83 amps. Through a trace of 10 milliohms, the 10 amps case loses 10 squared times 0.
01 equals 1 watts, while the 0. 83 amps case loses about 0. 007 watts. So bring the power in at 12 volts and convert down right next to the load. That is the whole idea.
"Because supplies are usually higher than what the chips need, and chips keep going lower in voltage to save CV-squared-f power.
Distributing at a higher voltage also means less current and less I-squared-R loss, so you convert down at the point of load.
Step-down converters are also simpler: a buck has continuous output current and no right-half-plane zero, while a boost has higher input current, a pulsed output and no short-circuit isolation.
Step-up shows up when a battery dips below the rail."

Power supply efficiency: definition, measurement. The question: What is efficiency in a power supply? How can it be measured? Why is it important?
Efficiency is the share of the energy you take from a source that actually reaches the load. It is output power divided by input power.
Whatever does not reach the load is loss, and it all turns into heat. Efficiency tells you how warm the supply gets and how long a battery lasts.
Imagine pouring water from a jug into a leaky bucket. Whatever arrives in the bucket is the useful part, and the rest spills.
Efficiency is the ratio of what arrives to what you poured.
To measure it you have to measure both flows at the same time, and not just once, since the leak changes with how fast you pour.

Model parameters are illustrative, not a specific part. Drag P₀ down to 5 milliwatts and the efficiency at 10 milliamps rises from 51% to above 80%.
Drag R up and the peak moves left and the full-load efficiency drops.

Pin, Pout, efficiency: find the third. The question: Given two of the following: input power, output power, and efficiency, calculate the third value that isn't given.
Input power, output power, and efficiency are tied together by one equation: efficiency equals output power divided by input power. Know any two, and you can find the third.
The input is always larger than the output, because some power is lost as heat.
Picture pouring water through a leaky funnel. If you pour in 10 liters and 8. 2 liters come out, the efficiency is 82%.
If you want 5 liters out and the funnel is 90% efficient, you must pour in more than 5.
The most common mistake is forgetting that: the thing you pour in is bigger than what you get.
Each line is P in equals P out over . The lines always sit above the ideal line; the vertical gap between a line and the ideal line is the loss.
At 50% efficiency the gap equals P out itself.
Input power: ( P in ): power taken from the source. Output power: ( P out ): power delivered to the load. Efficiency: ( ): P out over P in , between 0 and 1.
Loss: P in minus P out . Stage: one converter in a chain.

Where lost power goes and why it hurts. The question: What happens to any lost power? Why is this bad?
Power that a converter takes in but does not deliver does not vanish.
It turns into heat inside the transistors, the inductor, the copper traces (the board's wiring), and the controller.
That heat raises the temperature of the parts, which hurts reliability, performance, and battery life, and forces you to add heatsinks or fans.
Rub your hands together hard. The friction wastes some effort and your hands warm up. The harder you rub, the hotter they get. A converter's losses are the friction.
And just as your hands can only lose heat to the air so fast, a chip's temperature rises until enough heat escapes. If it cannot lose enough, it overheats.
The thermal-electrical analogy. P loss (a current source in watts) flows through theta JC and theta CA (resistors in °C/W) to ambient (a voltage source in °C).
The voltage at the top node is T J equals T A plus P( theta JC plus theta CA) . Anything that lowers either resistor, or lowers the current source, lowers T J .
Power loss: input power minus output power, turned into heat. Thermal resistance: how many degrees a part warms per watt of heat, in °C/W.
Junction temperature: the temperature of the silicon inside the package. Thermal shutdown: the chip turns itself off to avoid damage.
Efficiency: see "Power supply efficiency: definition, measurement".
A regulator loses 1. 5 watts, and its package has a thermal resistance of 40 degrees Celsius/W. The temperature rise is 1. 5 times 40 equals 60 degrees Celsius.
In a 70 degrees Celsius enclosure, the silicon reaches 130 degrees Celsius, close to the 125 to 150 degrees Celsius limit that many chips have. That is the whole idea.
"Lost power becomes heat. The energy not delivered to the load is dissipated in FET and inductor resistance, switching transitions, magnetic cores and the controller's bias.

That raises junction temperature by loss times thermal resistance, which risks thermal shutdown and shortens component life, shifts parameters like on-resistance, wastes battery energy, and forces larger heatsinks and more cost.
So I compute the loss and check junction temperature at worst-case ambient."

Quiescent current of a regulator. The question: What is quiescent current?
Quiescent current (Iq) is the small current a regulator draws just to stay alive, even with nothing connected to its output.
It runs the regulator's own circuits: a reference voltage to compare against, an amplifier that checks the output, and control logic. It is tiny, but it never switches off.
For a device that sleeps most of the time, Iq can be most of the energy used.
Think of a car idling at a red light. It is going nowhere, yet the engine still burns fuel every second. For a long trip the idling hardly matters.
For a car that sits waiting nearly all day, idling is nearly all the fuel. The regulator's Iq is the idling fuel.
The input current splits into two paths: I out flows through the pass element to the load, and the remaining I GND flows through the regulator's internal circuits to ground.
At no load, I GND equals I q .
Quiescent current (Iq): the current a regulator uses with no load. Ground current: the same current as seen leaving through the ground pin of an LDO.
Standby / sleep: a low-power state where the load draws very little. Load current: what the circuit actually draws from the output.
Light-load efficiency: efficiency when the load is small.
A coin cell holds 220 milliamp hours. A microcontroller sleeps at 2 microamps behind a regulator with an Iq of 50 microamps, so the total is 52 microamps.
The cell lasts about 220 over 0. 052 about 4200 hours, roughly 176 days.
With a 1 microamps part the total is 3 microamps, and the cell lasts about 73,000 hours, over 8 years in theory.
And if the load draws 10 microamps, a 50 microamps Iq means only 10 of every 60 microamps does useful work, so efficiency is below 17% (about 15% once the voltages are counted).
That is the whole idea.
"Quiescent current is what a regulator draws from its input just to operate, with no load: the bias for the reference, error amp, feedback divider and control.
For an LDO it's the ground-pin current.
It matters because it never goes away: in a battery device that sleeps at microamps, it can dominate standby current and light-load efficiency.
For example, 50 microamps on a coin cell kills standby life, so for always-on rails you pick nanoamp-class parts."
