Handling and disposing of LiPos. The question: Why is it important to properly handle and dispose LiPos?
A LiPo packs a lot of energy into a soft, thin pouch with a flammable liquid inside.
Handling it carelessly can short it out or damage it internally, and the damage is not always visible.
Safe handling means protecting the terminals and the pouch, storing it half-charged and charging it carefully.
Safe disposal means taking it to battery recycling, never the regular trash.
Picture a loaded mousetrap in a thin paper bag. It is harmless while it sits still. Toss it in a pocket with your keys and something may set it off.
A crushed or punctured pack is similar: the harm can come right away or later. A pack that looks fine after a drop may still be damaged inside.
The dangerous region is any low-resistance contact: wire, tool, coin.

The contact dissipates a maximum of V squared over (4R int) equals 88 watts when its resistance matches the cell's, and the cell itself heats even more at the lowest contact resistances (the red curve runs off the top of the chart, to about 340 watts at 1 milliohms).
Together that is hundreds of watts split between a small cell and a few grams of metal.
Short circuit: an unintended low-resistance path across the terminals that lets huge current flow ("Short-circuiting a LiPo"). Storage voltage: about 3.
8 volts per cell, roughly half full ("LiPo storage charge"). Swelling: a puffed pouch caused by gas, a sign of damage to retire.
Take-back point: a collection spot or recycler that accepts lithium batteries safely.
Balance lead: the extra connector on a multi-cell pack ("Balance charging and when it is needed").
A loose 2 Ah cell with 50 milliohms internal resistance is dropped in a pocket, and a key touches both terminals with a 20 milliohms contact. The current is 4. 2 over (0.
05 plus 0. 02) equals 60 amps. The contact point heats at about 60 squared times 0. 02 equals 72 watts, which is why this can start a fire.
Putting caps or tape over the terminals avoids it. At end of life, tape the terminals and take the pack to a battery drop-off. That is the whole idea.
"LiPos are soft pouch cells holding a lot of energy and a flammable electrolyte, so puncture, crush, heat or shorted terminals can start an internal short and thermal runaway, even hours later.
So I store them insulated, at a partial charge, cool, in a fire-safe bag, charge them only with the right charger and never unattended, and retire swollen ones.
At end of life they go to battery recycling, with the terminals taped and the pack discharged, never in household trash where compactors crush them and start fires."
Quick check. Why must lithium batteries not go into household trash?
Why puncturing a LiPo is dangerous. The question: Why is it so dangerous to puncture LiPos?
Puncturing a LiPo is dangerous because it creates a short circuit inside the cell itself. The object pushes through the thin layers and connects the two electrodes.
The cell's energy then flows through that tiny spot as heat, which can trigger thermal runaway: venting, fire and toxic fumes. The danger can also show up hours later.
Imagine a stack of metal foils separated by sheets of tissue paper. Push a nail through the stack and it touches foils that were meant to stay apart.
Electricity now has a direct path through the nail, right in the middle of the stack. Nothing outside the stack can stop it, because the connection is on the inside.
A fuse on the outside wires cannot see it.
A pouch cell is a sandwich of thin layers.
The nail connects the aluminium and copper sides through the separator, so the stored energy discharges through the nail and the layers around it.
The red path never leaves the pouch, so nothing connected to the external terminals can interrupt it.
Internal short circuit: the two electrodes connected inside the cell ("LiPo cell materials").
Separator: the thin film, only some tens of micrometers thick, that keeps the electrodes apart. Pouch cell: a cell in a soft foil bag with no rigid case ("What LiPo stands for").
Thermal runaway: self-feeding heating that ends in venting and fire ("Dangers of lithium batteries and prevention").
External protection: fuses and protection circuits in the outside wiring. They cannot interrupt an inside short.
Take a full cell at 4. 2 volts with 50 milliohms of internal resistance. A nail makes a short of 100 milliohms. The current is 4. 2 over (0. 05 plus 0. 1) equals 28 amps.
The heat in the short is about 28 squared times 0. 1 equals 78 watts, packed into a spot about a millimeter across.
That melts the separator around it, which makes the short larger, and it starts the heating loop. That is the whole idea.
"A LiPo is a thin stack of electrodes separated by a micron-scale separator in a soft foil pouch.
A puncture bridges the electrodes, creating an internal short: the cell's energy dumps through a tiny spot, heating it fast, melting the separator and starting thermal runaway.
Air and moisture entering make it worse.
No protection circuit or fuse can help because the short is inside the cell, and damage can be delayed, so punctured or crushed cells should be treated as dangerous."
Quick check. What is the layer that keeps a charged anode and cathode from touching inside a LiPo?
LiPo overcharge and overdischarge damage. The question: What happens if you overdischarge/overcharge a LiPo?
Both overcharging and over-discharging damage a lithium cell, in different ways. Overcharging is the dangerous one: above about 4.
2 volts it can plate metal, make gas and heat, and lead to fire. Over-discharging, below about 3. 0 volts and certainly below 2.
5 volts, wears the cell out and can create a hidden hazard for the next charge. So a cell has a safe window, and everything around it is built to enforce it.
Picture a water tank with a pump. Overfill it and it overflows, which is a big mess and a hazard.
Run it completely dry and the pump grinds itself up, and the damage may only show when you start it again. The tank is safe in the middle.
For a series pack there is a twist: you may see the total level look fine while one tank is overflowing and another is dry.
The window is narrow. Above the red line you are in overcharge; below the orange line in overdischarge.

The curve is schematic: real cells are steeper at both ends and flat through the middle, which is why voltage alone is a poor SoC gauge ("Determining state of charge and why it's hard") but a good limit detector.
Overcharge: pushing a cell above about 4. 2 volts ("What happens when a LiPo is overcharged"). Over-discharge: draining a cell below about 3.
0 volts ("LiPo cell voltage range and why"). Lithium plating: metallic lithium depositing on a full anode.
SEI layer: a protective film on the anode that breaks down in over-discharge.
Per-cell monitoring: watching each cell's voltage, not just the pack total ("Cell balancing: why, when, what if missing").
A 2S pack reads 7. 4 volts in total, which is the normal nominal value for two cells. But the cells can be unequal: 4. 4 plus 3. 0 equals 7. 4 volts. One cell is well above its 4.
2 volts limit, where it can plate and make gas. The other sits at the 3. 0 volts floor, where more discharge starts to damage it. The total looked fine.
Only per-cell monitoring catches it. That is the whole idea.
"Overcharging above about 4.
2 volts pulls too much lithium out of the cathode, plates lithium on the anode and oxidizes the electrolyte, so you get gas, swelling, heat and potentially thermal runaway.
Overdischarging below about 3 volts breaks down the anode's protective layer and can dissolve the copper collector, which then forms dendrites on recharge and risks an internal short.
So overcharge is the immediate hazard and overdischarge is silent damage with a delayed one, and protection ICs, chargers and cutoffs exist to avoid both."
Quick check. What is the typical upper charge voltage per cell for a standard LiCoO2/NMC LiPo?
Short-circuiting a LiPo. The question: What happens when you short circuit a LiPo?
A LiPo cell has very low internal resistance, only milliohms. So if you connect its terminals directly with a wire, the current is huge.
Only that small internal resistance limits it. All of that current heats the cell and the wiring, and it can lead to venting and fire within seconds.
Protection has to be fast and built in.
Picture a full water tank whose only outlet is a short, very wide pipe.
Open it straight to the outside and the water rushes out, held back only by that pipe, which barely slows it.
The cell's internal resistance is that pipe: it is tiny, so the current is enormous.
The picture breaks in one way that matters: spilled water just makes a puddle, while the battery's current turns into heat inside the cell itself.
The only things limiting the current are R int and R ext . A fuse in series is the intended last resort. The animated flow shows the short loop.
Short circuit: a direct low-resistance path across the battery terminals. Internal resistance: the cell's own resistance, usually milliohms ("Battery internal resistance").
Ohm's law: I equals V over R , so a small resistance gives a large current. I²R heating: heat equals current squared times resistance.
Fuse / protection IC: parts that cut the circuit quickly when current is too high ("Why charging and monitoring ICs matter").
Take a single cell at 4. 2 volts with 50 milliohms of internal resistance, shorted with a thick wire. The current is 4. 2 over 0. 05 equals 84 amps. For a 2 Ah cell that is 42C.
The heat inside the cell is 84 squared times 0. 05 about 350 watts. That would warm a small cell by several degrees every second. A 4S hobby pack with 20 milliohms in total at 16.
8 volts would carry about 840 amps. That is the whole idea.
"A LiPo has milliohm-level internal resistance, so a short is limited almost only by that: one 4.
2 volts cell at 50 milliohms gives about 84 amps, and a 4S hobby pack with 20 milliohms gives around 840.
That puts hundreds of watts to kilowatts of I to the 2R into the cell and wiring, heating it by many degrees per second toward venting and thermal runaway.
So you need layered protection: a properly rated fuse, a fast short-circuit-detecting protector IC, cell-level devices, and wiring and connectors that prevent shorts."
Quick check. Why must a pack fuse have a DC voltage rating at or above the pack voltage?
Why heat is a big concern for LiPos. The question: Why is heat such a big concern?
Heat is the big enemy of a lithium battery for three reasons. Current flowing through its internal resistance makes heat inside the cell. Heat speeds up aging.
And at high enough temperatures the cell can start heating itself in a runaway, which ends in fire. So designs keep cells inside a safe temperature window and get the heat out.
Think of a crowded room. Every person gives off a little heat, and the vents carry it away. With a few people, the room stays comfortable.
Pack in more people, or block the vents, and the room keeps warming up. A cell works the same way, with the current as the crowd and the surface as the vents.
If heat is made faster than it leaves, the temperature keeps rising.
With a 0. 5 eV activation energy the acceleration at 45 degrees Celsius is about 3. 4x, close to the 2x-per-10 degrees Celsius heuristic (4x over 20 degrees Celsius).
It is a trend line, not a spec: a different mechanism (or a different temperature range) gives a different slope.
The takeaway: a pack cycled at 45 degrees Celsius wears out several times faster than at 25 degrees Celsius.
Joule heating: heat made when current flows through resistance, equal to I to the 2R ("Battery internal resistance"). Internal resistance: the cell's own opposition to current.
Thermal runaway: self-feeding heating that ends in venting and possible fire ("Dangers of lithium batteries and prevention").
Aging: the slow loss of capacity, which speeds up as temperature rises ("LiPo aging and end of life").
NTC thermistor: a temperature sensor that the charger or BMS watches ("Temperature effects on LiPo performance").
Take a 2 Ah cell with 50 milliohms of resistance, discharged at 3C, which is 6 amps. The heat is 6 squared times 0. 05 equals 1. 8 watts. Say a small sealed pack sheds about 0.
1 watts for each kelvin of warming. Then it settles about 1. 8 over 0. 1 equals 18 K above the surrounding air.
At 20C, which is 40 amps, the heat would be 80 watts, and a 40 g cell would warm by about 2 degrees every second without strong cooling. That is the whole idea.
"Heat is a concern for three reasons. Current through the cell's internal resistance makes I squared R heat inside a small sealed package.
Higher temperature speeds up the side reactions that age the cell, roughly doubling degradation per 10 degrees as a rule of thumb.
And above about 80 to 130 degrees the cell's decomposition reactions are exothermic, so heat makes more heat and you get thermal runaway.
So we limit charge and discharge temperature, monitor with NTCs, derate, and design for heat removal and propagation barriers."
Quick check. What is thermal runaway?
What motors and solenoids are, and uses. The question: What is a motor/solenoid? What can they be used for?
A motor turns electrical energy into spinning motion. A solenoid turns it into a short push or pull in a straight line. Both are built from a coil of wire.
When current flows through the coil, it makes a magnetic field, and that field makes a force.
Motors are used for anything that spins or drives, and solenoids for things like locks and valves.
Picture a door lock. A solenoid is like a little piston: switch it on and it snaps a bolt a few millimeters, switch it off and a spring pushes the bolt back.
A motor is more like a wheel that keeps being pushed around. Electromagnets give the pushes, and as the wheel turns, the pushes are timed so they keep going in the same direction.
Electrical model of a brushed DC motor: coil resistance R, coil inductance L, and a back-EMF source E proportional to speed (orange).
A solenoid is the same circuit without the speed-dependent E (its inductance changes as the plunger moves instead).
Everything about startup current, steady-state current and flyback follows from this one loop.
Actuator: a device that turns an electrical signal into motion or force. Coil: many turns of wire. Current in it makes a magnetic field.
Plunger: the movable iron rod inside a solenoid that the field pulls in.
Brushed DC motor: a simple motor that uses brushes and a commutator (a switch that turns with the shaft) to keep the current direction right as it spins.
Inductive load: a load made of a coil, which resists sudden changes in current ("What is inductance?")
Think of a 12 volts door-lock solenoid whose coil has 24 ohms of resistance. By Ohm's law the current is 12 over 24 equals 0. 5 amps, which is 6 watts.
Switch it on and the plunger pulls the bolt. Switch it off and a spring returns it.
A small fan motor on the same 12 volts supply would instead spin continuously, and it would draw less current once it is up to speed than when it starts. That is the whole idea.
"A motor converts electrical energy into rotation and a solenoid converts it into a short linear push or pull, both using a coil that creates a magnetic field.
A solenoid is a coil with a movable plunger and a spring, good for locks, valves and relays.
A motor has coils on a rotor in a magnetic field, so current produces torque, used for fans, pumps, wheels and drones.
Electrically both are inductive loads, a resistance in series with an inductance, and a motor also produces a back-EMF."
Quick check. Which description best matches a solenoid?
How motors and solenoids work. The question: Describe how a motor/solenoid works.
Both devices rely on two facts: current in a wire makes a magnetic field, and a magnetic field pushes on a current-carrying wire.
A solenoid uses the field to pull an iron plunger. A motor places a coil in a magnetic field so the force turns it, and keeps flipping the current so the turning continues.
A spinning motor also makes a voltage of its own that pushes back.
Think of pushing a child on a playground roundabout. To keep it going, you must push at the right moment on each turn.
If you pushed the same way at the wrong moment, you would slow it down.
A brushed motor has a part called a commutator that does the timing: it flips the current in the coil every half turn so the push is always the same way around.
Force falls as 1 over g squared with gap and rises as I squared : at 2 mm the 0. 5 amps curve gives 0. 98 N, halving the current gives one quarter (0. 25 N).
Real solenoids saturate near zero gap, so the curve flattens at small g , and designers shape the plunger tip to get a flatter force-stroke curve.
Magnetic field (B): the region where magnets and currents feel force. Torque: a twisting force. In a brushed motor it is proportional to current ( tau equals K t I ).
Commutator: the switch on the rotor that reverses the coil current each half turn.
Back-EMF: the voltage a spinning motor generates, proportional to speed, that opposes the supply. Air gap: the space the plunger has to close.
A solenoid's pull is strongest when it is small.
A solenoid has 500 turns, 0. 5 amps, a 1 cm² plunger and a 2 mm gap. The pull is about 1 N. Shrinking the gap to 1 mm makes it about 4 N, so a solenoid pulls harder as it closes.
For a motor with K t equals 0. 009 N·m/A, a current of 2 amps gives a torque of 0. 009 times 2 equals 0. 018 N·m. As the motor speeds up, back-EMF rises and the current falls.
That is the whole idea.
"Both use the fact that current makes a magnetic field and a field pushes on current.
A solenoid is a coil with an iron plunger that the field pulls in to close the air gap, with a spring to return it; force grows with turns times current and gets much stronger as the gap shrinks.
A brushed motor has a rotor coil in a magnet's field, so F equals BIL on each side gives torque proportional to current, and the commutator flips the current so torque stays one way.
The spinning coil also makes a back-EMF proportional to speed."
Quick check. What does the commutator in a brushed DC motor do?
Why coils are used in motors and solenoids. The question: Why are coils often used? What is so special about that configuration?
A single loop of wire makes only a tiny magnetic field.
Winding the wire into many turns makes each turn add its field to the others, so the total field grows with the number of turns.
That lets a small current from a modest supply produce a useful force. This is why motors and solenoids are built from coils, and why they behave like inductors.
Picture one person pushing a heavy cart. They barely move it. Two hundred people all pushing in the same direction move it easily.
Each turn of a coil is one pusher, and they all push the field the same way inside the coil.
The picture is only partly right: more turns also store more energy and slow down how quickly the current can change.
The field grows linearly with the number of turns at a fixed current. Two hundred turns of a 1 cm loop give about 12.
6 mT, 200 times a single turn; an iron core would multiply this by micro r until saturation.
Turn: one loop of wire. N is the number of turns. Ampere-turns ( NI ): turns times current. It sets how strong the magnetic push is.
Inductance ( L ): how strongly a coil resists changes in current. It grows as N squared ("What is inductance?")
Iron core: iron in the middle of a coil, which can make the field hundreds or thousands of times stronger. Winding: the coil of wire in a motor or solenoid.
A single loop of radius 1 cm carrying 1 amps makes about 63 µT at its center.
Wind 200 turns of the same loop and keep 1 amps, and the field is about 200 times 63 micro T equals 12. 6 mT. That is 200 times larger, with the same current.
The same ampere-turns can also come from fewer thicker turns at a higher current, or more thinner turns at a lower current, and, for the same amount of copper, the heating stays about the same.
That is the whole idea.

"A coil multiplies the magnetic effect of the current: each turn carries the same current and their fields add in the same direction inside the coil, so field and force scale with ampere-turns NI, and iron inside makes it far stronger.
The same configuration is an inductor with L proportional to N squared, so these loads store energy and resist current changes.
For fixed copper and ampere-turns, more turns means less current and more voltage with similar loss, so you pick turns to match the supply."
Quick check. Why does winding a wire into N turns increase the magnetic field for a given current?
When a motor or solenoid draws most current. The question: When does a motor/solenoid draw the most current?
A DC motor draws the most current when it is not turning: at the moment it starts, or when its shaft is jammed.
A spinning motor makes its own voltage that opposes the supply, called back-EMF. At zero speed there is no back-EMF, so only the winding's small resistance limits the current.
A DC solenoid is simpler: it draws its largest current at steady state, once it has settled.
Think of starting a loaded bicycle from a standstill. The first push takes the most effort. Once you are rolling, the bike helps carry you, and the effort drops.
A motor behaves the same way. Starting and getting up to speed takes a big gulp of current. A jammed shaft is like holding the bike still against the pedals: it keeps gulping.
At t = 0 the rotor is stationary so E equals 0 and the only things between the supply and the loop are R and L.
The current then climbs with tau e equals L over R while E rises with speed and chokes it off.
Back-EMF: the voltage a spinning motor generates, proportional to speed, opposing the supply. Stall current: the current when the shaft cannot turn, equal to V over R .
Winding resistance: the small resistance of the motor's coil. Time constant ( L over R ): how fast current builds up in a coil ("Inductor at t = 0⁺ and DC steady state").
Inrush current: the large current right after switching on.
Use a 12 volts supply and a motor with 1 ohms of winding resistance. At rest, there is no back-EMF, so the current is 12 over 1 equals 12 amps.
When the motor is spinning freely at nearly full speed, the back-EMF might be 11. 5 volts. The current is then (12 minus 11. 5) over 1 equals 0. 5 amps.
The inductance delays the rise by a few milliseconds, so the actual peak is a bit under 12 amps. That is the whole idea.

"A motor draws the most current when it's stalled or just starting, because there's no back-EMF to oppose the supply: I equals V minus K e omega over R, so at zero speed it's V over R, say 12 amps for 12 volts and 1 ohm, versus half an amp at free-running speed.
Inductance only delays it by a few milliseconds. The same goes for a jammed or heavily loaded motor.
A DC solenoid draws its maximum, V over R, at steady state once the plunger is seated."
Quick check. When does a brushed DC motor draw its maximum steady current?
When a motor or solenoid draws least current. The question: When does a motor/solenoid draw the least amount of current?
A DC motor draws the least current when it spins freely at its top speed with nothing to push against.
By then its own back-EMF almost cancels the supply voltage, so only a small current is left to overcome friction.
A solenoid draws no current when it is off, and the smallest useful current is a low holding current once it has pulled in.
Imagine pedaling a bike on a smooth flat road at your top speed. You barely push, just enough to beat the friction and the wind. Add a hill or a headwind and you must push harder.
A free-running motor is in that easy state. If something pushes the bike downhill faster than you can pedal, the bike pushes you, and the motor can even act as a generator.
Current falls linearly with speed. The line would reach zero at the ideal speed V over K e = 600 rad/s (grey line), but friction demands 0.
5 amps, so a real free-running motor settles at 575 rad/s (orange line).
Beyond 600 rad/s the line goes negative: the motor is being driven by the load and pushes current back to the supply.
No-load speed: the speed a motor reaches when it has no mechanical load.
Back-EMF: the voltage a spinning motor generates, close to the supply at no load ("When a motor or solenoid draws most current").
Friction and windage: the small drag from bearings and air that a free-running motor still overcomes. Holding current: the lower current that keeps a solenoid pulled in.
PWM: switching the voltage on and off quickly so the average voltage and current are lower.
With a 12 volts supply and a 1 ohms motor, the current at stall is 12 amps. At no load, the back-EMF is about 11. 5 volts, so the current is (12 minus 11. 5) over 1 equals 0.
5 amps. A 24 volts, 48 ohms solenoid draws 24 over 48 equals 0. 5 amps and 12 watts while on. Once pulled in, switching it with 20% PWM cuts the average current to 0. 2 times 0.
5 equals 0. 1 amps, and the power to about 0. 48 watts (current squared times resistance, because the coil smooths the current). That is the whole idea.

"For a motor, the steady-state minimum is at no load and top speed: the back-EMF almost equals the supply, so the current is just what's needed to overcome friction, about half an amp versus 12 amps at stall in my example.
The absolute minimum is the instant of turn-on, when the inductor makes the current start at zero.
If the shaft is driven faster than no-load speed, the current goes negative: regeneration. For a solenoid it's zero when off, or the small PWM hold current once it has pulled in."
Quick check. In steady state, when does a brushed DC motor draw least current?
Steady state at minimum and maximum current. The question: Describe what happens to a motor/solenoid at steady-state under minimum and maximum current draw?.
"Steady state" means the motor has settled and nothing is still changing. In that state, how much current a motor draws depends on how fast its shaft is turning.
Held still (stalled), it draws the most current. Spinning freely with no load, it draws the least.
Picture a hose filling a tank from the bottom. The water level in the tank pushes back against the hose. With an empty tank, water rushes in.
As the level rises, the flow slows to a trickle. A spinning motor makes its own "level", called back-EMF, that rises with speed and pushes back against the supply.
The analogy breaks down in one place: the motor builds that push by spinning, so a stalled motor has none.
At the left (stall) the red copper-loss curve equals the input, so all 144 watts is heat.
Moving right, the back-EMF absorbs more of the input and the blue mechanical output rises, peaking at 36 watts at 300 rad/s (half the free speed), then falls to zero at the ideal speed.
The ratio of blue to grey is the efficiency: 50% at the power peak, higher still beyond it.
Steady state: everything has settled, so the current is no longer changing. Back-EMF: the voltage a spinning motor generates that opposes the supply.
Stall: the shaft is held still, so speed is zero. No-load: the shaft spins freely and nothing but friction slows it. Winding: the motor's coil of copper wire.
Its resistance, in ohms (Ω), limits the current at stall. Inductor: a coil that resists changes in current. Once the current stops changing, it drops no voltage.
Use a 12 volts supply and a motor winding of 1 ohms. Stalled, there is no back-EMF, so the current is 12 volts / 1 ohms = 12 amps .
The power is 12 volts times 12 amps = 144 watts, and all of it becomes heat. Spinning freely, suppose the back-EMF reaches 11. 5 volts. Only 0.
5 volts is left across the winding, so the current is 0. 5 amps . That is the whole idea: more speed means more back-EMF, which means less current.
"At steady state the inductor drops nothing, so the winding is its resistance plus back-EMF.

At maximum current the motor is stalled: no back-EMF, I equals V over R, maximum torque, and all the input power V squared over R, 144 watts in my 12 volts, 1 ohm example, becomes winding heat, so it burns out in seconds.
At minimum current it's free-running: back-EMF nearly equals the supply, current is just friction, about half an amp, and the power goes into friction and windage.
A solenoid's steady state is always V over R unless you reduce the voltage."
Quick check. In DC steady state, what is the voltage across the winding inductance?
Motors and solenoids as electrical loads. The question: What type of loads are motors/solenoids?
Motors and solenoids are inductive loads. Each is a coil of wire, so electrically it acts like a resistor in series with an inductor.
An inductor is a part whose current cannot change instantly. That one fact explains most of the odd behavior of these loads.
Think of pushing a heavy shopping cart. It does not reach full speed the instant you push, and it does not stop the instant you let go. It keeps rolling.
Current in a coil behaves like the cart's motion: it ramps up gradually and keeps going when you try to cut it off.
The analogy has a gap: a motor also generates its own voltage once it spins, which a plain cart does not.
The resistor jumps to 12 amps at once. The inductive load (blue) starts at zero and takes about 5 tau to settle at 12 amps.
The capacitor (orange) is the mirror image: a 12 amps inrush that decays.
Motors and solenoids are the blue curve (in steady state at least); battery-fed capacitor banks are the orange one.
Inductor: a coil that stores energy in a magnetic field and resists changes in current. Inductive load: any device built from a coil, such as a motor, solenoid or relay.
Flyback (inductive kick): the voltage spike when you suddenly interrupt coil current. Back-EMF: the voltage a spinning motor generates that opposes the supply.
Solenoid: a coil with a movable iron plunger that gets pulled in when current flows.
Connect a 12 volts supply to a coil with 1 ohms of resistance and a little inductance. At the instant of turn-on, the current is 0 amps, not 12 amps.
It then climbs over a few milliseconds toward 12 volts / 1 ohms = 12 amps. Now open the switch.
The coil still "wants" 12 amps, so it produces a large voltage spike across the switch until the energy is used up.
That is the whole idea: current ramps, and it fights being cut off.
"Motors and solenoids are inductive loads: a coil resistance in series with an inductance, plus for a motor a back-EMF that depends on speed.

The inductance means the current can't change instantly, so it ramps with L over R and, when you switch off, the stored energy causes a voltage spike across the switch, so you need a flyback diode or snubber.
In AC the current lags the voltage, giving a power factor below one. A motor is also a dynamic load because its current depends on speed and mechanical load."
Quick check. What best describes a solenoid as an electrical load?
Flyback voltage. The question: What is flyback voltage?
Flyback voltage is the voltage spike you get when you suddenly cut the current through a coil, like a motor or relay. A coil stores energy while current flows.
If the switch opens, that energy must go somewhere, so the coil pushes its voltage as high as needed to keep the current going. The fix is to give the current a safe path.
Imagine a long, heavy pipe full of moving water with a valve at the end. Slam the valve shut and the water's momentum cannot just vanish. Pressure spikes and the pipe can burst.

What back EMF is. The question: What is back EMF?
Back-EMF is the voltage a motor generates simply because it is spinning. A motor and a generator are the same device.
When the shaft turns, the coil moving through a magnetic field makes a voltage. In a motor, that voltage pushes against the supply, which is why it is called "back".
It is what keeps a spinning motor from drawing huge current.
Imagine pushing a playground merry-go-round with a friend who runs along the rim. At the start, the merry-go-round is still, so you push hard.
As it speeds up, it moves away from your hand, and you can push less and less. The faster it goes, the less your push matters.
Back-EMF works the same way: speed reduces the net push of the supply. The analogy has one gap: the motor creates this opposition itself.
The two curves add to the supply at every speed. At stall the red curve is the whole 12 volts (maximum current).
As speed rises the back-EMF takes over and the resistive drop (hence current) shrinks. The slope is K e : steeper means a higher-voltage, lower-speed motor.
EMF: electromotive force, a voltage produced by a source. Here the source is the spinning coil. Back-EMF: the voltage a spinning motor generates, opposing the supply.
It equals K e omega : speed times a fixed number for each motor, K e . omega (omega): shaft speed in radians per second. One full turn is about 6. 28 radians.
Stall: shaft held still, so back-EMF is zero. Flyback voltage: a different effect, the spike when coil current is interrupted.
Take a 12 volts motor with a 1 ohms winding. Suppose K e equals 0. 02 volts per rad/s. Stalled, back-EMF is 0 volts, so the current is 12 volts / 1 ohms = 12 amps.
At 300 rad/s, back-EMF is 0. 02 times 300 = 6 volts. The net voltage is 12 minus 6 = 6 volts, so the current is 6 amps . At 575 rad/s, back-EMF is 11.
5 volts, so the current is only 0. 5 amps. That is the whole idea: faster spin means more back-EMF and less current.
"Back-EMF is the voltage a spinning motor generates: a coil moving in a magnetic field induces a voltage proportional to speed, e equals K e omega, and by Lenz's law it opposes the supply.
So the current is V minus back-EMF over R: huge at stall, small at speed, and voltage essentially sets speed while current sets torque.
It also gives free speed information for sensorless control and is what makes regenerative braking possible.
It's different from flyback voltage, which is the spike from interrupting the coil current."

What inrush current is. The question: What is inrush current?
Inrush current is the big surge a device draws in the moment it is switched on, before it settles to its normal running current.
For a motor, the surge happens because it is not spinning yet.
A motor that is not spinning makes no back-EMF, so nothing holds the current back except the winding resistance (the resistance of the motor's copper coil).
Think of a crowd waiting at a stadium gate. When the gate opens, people pour in fast. After a minute the flow calms to a steady trickle.
The gate-opening rush is the inrush, and the steady trickle is the running current. For a motor, the rush lasts until the shaft speeds up, tens of milliseconds for a small one.
The analogy breaks in one way: the crowd's rush is a backlog of waiting people, while the motor's surge comes from missing back-EMF, which builds up as the shaft speeds up.
The motor's inrush flows through the source and wiring resistance R s (battery internal resistance plus wires and connector).
The rail seen by the logic electronics drops by I R s during the start.
Inrush current: the peak current at turn-on, higher than the steady running current. Back-EMF: the voltage a spinning motor makes against the supply.
Stall current: the current with the shaft held still, V over R . Soft start: raising the voltage slowly at turn-on so the surge stays small.
Brownout: the supply voltage sagging because of heavy current.
A 12 volts motor has a 1 ohms winding. Running under load, it draws 5 amps.
At the instant of start, the shaft is still, so back-EMF is 0 volts and the current is 12 volts / 1 ohms = 12 amps . That is 2. 4 times the running current.
With no load, the running current might be only 0. 5 amps, so the surge is 24 times the running current. That is the whole idea: inrush is the stall current seen at turn-on.
"Inrush current is the surge a load draws when first switched on, above its steady running current.

For a motor it's because at standstill there's no back-EMF, so only the winding resistance limits the current, roughly V over R, 12 amps for a 12 volt, 1 ohm motor versus maybe 5 amps running; it lasts until the rotor speeds up.
AC solenoids also have it, while the plunger is open.
It sags supplies and trips protection, so you handle it with soft start, current limiting, series resistance or an NTC, and bulk capacitance."

A motor's current is high whenever its speed is low compared to the supply voltage. That is the one rule behind every peak.
Startup, stall, a jammed shaft and a heavy load all drag the speed down. Some less obvious cases, like reversing direction, can be even worse. Solenoids peak in simpler ways.
Picture pushing a shopping cart. A cart that is already rolling away from you needs only a light push. A cart that is standing still needs a big shove.
A cart rolling toward you that you want to turn around needs the biggest effort of all, because you must stop it and push it back.
The motor's current is that effort: low speed means a lot, and reversed speed means even more.
The analogy breaks down because here the effort is electrical current, which heats the winding.

It only controls how fast the current can change.
So a motor's starting surge is not a contradiction: the current does start at zero and rise smoothly, but it rises very fast, to a very large value.
Think of a heavy flywheel on a car engine. It cannot jump to full speed instantly, so it takes a moment to get going. But it does not decide the top speed. The engine does.
The inductor is the flywheel: it sets how fast the current ramps. The winding resistance and the missing back-EMF set the final value.
The analogy has one gap: the electrical ramp is far faster than anything mechanical.

Back-EMF: the voltage a spinning motor makes against the supply. Inrush: the large current right after turn-on.
Mechanical time constant: how long the rotor (the spinning part) takes to speed up.

That is the whole idea: the inductor sets the ramp rate, and the resistance sets the peak.

Motor vs generator. The question: What is the difference between a motor and generator?
A motor and a generator are physically the same machine. The only difference is which way the energy flows. In a motor, electrical power goes in and the shaft turns.
In a generator, you turn the shaft and electrical power comes out.
Think of a bicycle with a hub dynamo. When you pedal, the wheel turns the dynamo and the light glows.
In principle, feeding the right kind of electricity into that same dynamo would push the wheel instead. Same machine, energy flowing the other way.
The analogy has one gap: real machines are often tuned for one job, so one direction works better than the other.
Motor mode at 500 rad/s: the supply (12 volts) exceeds the back-EMF (10 volts), so 1 amps flows into the machine.
Electrical input 12 watts = 2 watts heat in R + 10 watts mechanical output.
Motor: turns electrical power into mechanical power. Generator: turns mechanical power into electrical power. Back-EMF: the voltage a spinning motor generates against the supply.
It is speed times a motor constant: E equals K e omega , with speed omega in radians per second.
Regenerative braking: when the shaft is driven faster than the supply "expects", the motor feeds energy back.
No-load speed: the speed where back-EMF equals the supply, so no current flows.
Take a motor with K e equals 0. 02 volts per rad/s, on a 12 volts supply. Its no-load speed is 12 / 0. 02 = 600 rad/s.
At 300 rad/s, back-EMF is 6 volts, below the supply, so current flows in and it acts as a motor .
If you force the shaft to 700 rad/s, back-EMF is 14 volts, above the supply, so current flows out and it acts as a generator .
That is the whole idea: the same device switches roles at the speed where back-EMF equals the supply.
"A motor and a generator are the same machine with the energy flowing in opposite directions. A motor converts electrical power to mechanical: current in the field makes torque.
A generator converts mechanical to electrical: moving conductors in a field make a voltage. Inside every running motor there's also a back-EMF K e omega .
If you drive the shaft faster than V over K e , that back-EMF exceeds the supply, the current reverses and it regenerates. So the difference is just the sign of the power."

Motor vs solenoid. The question: What is the difference between a motor and solenoid?
Both motors and solenoids are coils that turn electricity into motion using magnetic force. A motor spins continuously.
A solenoid has a plunger that pulls in a short distance, then stops. Use a motor when you need steady turning and a solenoid when you need a quick push, latch or valve.
A motor is like a ceiling fan: it keeps turning as long as the power is on. A solenoid is like a doorbell hammer or a door latch. It snaps once and holds.
Both are "magnet machines", but one makes a loop of motion and the other makes a single stroke.
The analogy has a limit: a fan runs freely, while a solenoid holding a latch is using power the whole time without moving.
A low-side N-MOSFET switches the coil.
D1 sits across the coil with its cathode on the +12 volts side, so it is reverse-biased while the coil is energised and conducts the coil current when Q1 opens.
A motor drops in where the coil is.
Motor: a coil-and-magnet machine that gives continuous rotation. Solenoid: a coil with an iron plunger that moves a short distance when current flows.
Inductive load: a coil-based load, so it kicks back when switched off. Back-EMF: the voltage a spinning motor makes against the supply.
Flyback diode: a diode across the coil that absorbs the kickback.
Say a 12 volts solenoid coil has 24 ohms of resistance. Once settled, it draws 12 volts / 24 ohms = 0. 5 amps, which is 6 watts.
The plunger moves once, then the coil just sits there turning those 6 watts into heat while it holds.
A 12 volts motor with the same winding would draw less current once it spins, because its back-EMF fights the supply.
That is the whole idea: both are coils, but one is built for continuous rotation and one for a short stroke.
"Both are coils that turn current into mechanical force and both are inductive loads that need flyback protection.
A motor makes continuous rotation with torque proportional to current and a back-EMF that limits its current as it speeds up.
A solenoid pulls an iron plunger in over a short linear stroke: force goes roughly as current squared and rises sharply as the gap closes.
Motors for continuous motion, solenoids for short on/off pushes like valves and latches. Holding a solenoid on costs I to the 2R continuously, so we use peak-and-hold PWM."

Parts of a brushed motor, rotating vs static. The question: What are the parts of a motor? Which parts rotate and which parts remain static?
A brushed DC motor has two groups of parts. The static parts (the stator) stay still: the housing, the magnets, the brushes and the end caps.
The rotating parts (the rotor) turn: the shaft, the wire-wound core and the commutator. Knowing which is which explains how the motor works.
Picture a bicycle wheel with fixed brake pads touching the rim. The wheel (rotor) spins, and the pads (brushes) stay put and rub against it.
In the motor, the "rim" is a ring of copper segments called the commutator, and the pads carry electric current into it instead of slowing it down.
The analogy has a twist: the pads also help flip the current direction as the wheel turns.
Side cutaway of a small PM brushed motor. Blue/red: static magnets inside the steel can. Orange: everything that rotates (shaft, laminated core with windings, commutator).
Green: static brushes with springs pressing down on the rotating commutator, wired to the two terminals. Bearings carry the shaft; their outer races are fixed.
Stator: the stationary part: housing, magnets, brush holders. Rotor (armature): the rotating part: shaft, iron core and copper coils.
Commutator: a ring of copper segments on the shaft, each wired to a coil. Brush: a stationary contact, often carbon, pressed against the commutator.
Bearing: a part that lets the shaft turn smoothly in the housing.
Imagine one wire loop between two magnets. Its two ends connect to two half-ring copper segments. Two fixed brushes touch those segments.
Current flows in through one brush, around the loop, and out through the other, so the loop is pushed and starts to turn.
After half a turn, the segments swap places under the brushes, so the current in the loop reverses and the push keeps going the same way.
That is the whole idea: the brushes stay still and the commutator turns under them.
"A brushed DC motor has a stator that doesn't move: the housing, the permanent magnets or field windings, the end caps, the brush holders and the brushes.
The rotor, or armature, spins: the shaft, laminated iron core, copper windings and the commutator. Bearings let the shaft turn.
The brushes stay still and press on the rotating commutator to feed current into the windings and reverse it each half turn, so torque stays in one direction.
That sliding contact is also what wears out."

Types of motors and their uses. The question: Name a few types of motors. What are they each used for?
There are several kinds of motors, and each is built and driven differently.
The right choice depends on what you need most: simple and cheap, efficient and long-lived, exact position, or running straight from wall-outlet (mains) power.
Knowing the main types lets you pick the right one for a job.
Think of a toolbox. A hammer, a screwdriver and a wrench all turn effort into work, but each is best for a different task. Motors are the same.
A brushed motor is the cheap all-purpose tool, a stepper is the precise one, and a brushless motor is the efficient long-lasting one.
The analogy has one limit: some jobs, like a servo, combine a motor with sensing and control, which is more like a tool with a built-in gauge.
Family tree by supply and commutation. A servo is a layer on top of any of these; it is defined by the feedback loop, not the machine.
Brushed DC motor: spins when you apply DC (steady one-way current, like from a battery), with sliding contacts called brushes switching the coil current.
Brushless DC (BLDC) motor: magnets on the spinning part (rotor), with an electronic controller switching the coils.
Stepper motor: moves in fixed steps, so you can position it without feedback. Servo: a motor plus a sensor and a control loop, so you can command position or speed.
Open loop / closed loop: control without or with feedback from a sensor.
Three jobs, three motors. A toy car wheel only needs to spin, so a cheap brushed motor works. A 3D printer axis must stop at exact spots.
A stepper with 200 steps per turn moves 360° / 200 = 1. 8° per step, with no sensor needed. A drone propeller needs efficiency and long life, so it uses a brushless motor.
That is the whole idea: match the motor type to the need.
"Brushed DC: simple, cheap, voltage sets speed, good for toys, pumps and automotive actuators.
Brushless DC: electronic commutation, efficient and long-lived, used in drones, fans, drives and EVs.
Steppers move in discrete steps with holding torque, so they're used for open-loop positioning such as 3D printers.
AC induction motors run off mains and are rugged, used in appliances and industry. Servos are any motor plus feedback and a control loop for position.
Plus special ones like voice coils and vibration motors. I'd choose based on precision, efficiency, life and cost."

What are linear motors?. The question: What are linear motors?
A linear motor makes force in a straight line instead of torque (a turning force) on a shaft. It is like a normal motor that has been cut open and rolled out flat.
A stationary track holds magnets, and a sliding part carries coils. Switching the coils in order pushes the slider along the track with no gears or screws in between.
Imagine slicing a cardboard tube lengthwise and unrolling it into a flat sheet. The curved wall of the tube becomes a straight strip.
A linear motor does the same to a rotary motor: the round stationary part becomes a straight track, and the spinning part becomes a slider.
The analogy has one catch: the flattened version needs a position sensor along the track, since there is no shaft to put a rotation sensor on.
A flat PM linear motor.
Three coil groups (A, B, C) on the forcer are energised in sequence by position-dependent currents, creating a travelling magnetic wave that pulls the forcer along the alternating-pole magnet track.
The encoder gives the position needed for commutation and closed-loop control.
Forcer (slider): the moving part that carries the coils. Track: the stationary strip of alternating magnets.
Lorentz force: the push on a wire carrying current through a magnetic field: F equals BIL , field strength B (in teslas, T) times current I times wire length L .
Direct drive: no gearbox, belt or screw between motor and load. Linear encoder: a sensor that reports position along the track.
Suppose a wire 0. 2 m long sits in a 0. 5 T field and carries 10 amps. The force is F equals BIL = 0. 5 times 10 times 0. 2 = 1 N .
Double the current to 20 amps and the force doubles to 2 N.
That straight-line push is what moves the slider, and the force is proportional to current just like torque in a rotary motor.
That is the whole idea: force from current in a magnetic field, laid out in a line.
"A linear motor is a rotary motor unrolled flat: a magnet track and a coil carrier, the forcer, that moves along it.
Force is proportional to current, F equals K fI , and the moving coil generates a back-EMF K ev , same as a rotary motor.
The big win is direct drive: no lead screw, belt or gearbox, so no backlash and very high speed and precision.
The downsides are cost, heat, limited force without gearing, strong magnet attraction and needing a linear encoder. Think wafer stages, voice coils and maglev."

Phone vibration motors (ERM and LRA). The question: What sort of motors are typically used for phone's vibration motor?
Phone buzzers come in two kinds. An ERM is a tiny motor with a lopsided weight, so it shakes as it spins.
An LRA is a coil that pushes a small weight back and forth on a spring, like a tiny speaker. LRAs give sharper, more controllable buzzes and are common in modern phones.
An ERM is like a washing machine with all the laundry bunched on one side: the unbalanced spin shakes everything.
An LRA is like pushing a child on a swing at just the right rhythm: small pushes at the right pace make a big swing. The swing example also shows the catch.
Push at the wrong rhythm and little happens, so the LRA must be driven at its resonant frequency.
Force grows with the square of speed, so doubling voltage (and so speed) gives about four times the force and doubles the vibration frequency.
You cannot have "strong but low-frequency" buzz from an ERM.
ERM: eccentric rotating mass, a small motor with an off-center weight. LRA: linear resonant actuator, a coil driving a mass on a spring.
Resonance: the natural rhythm at which a mass on a spring moves most easily. Frequency (Hz): how many shakes happen per second. 100 hertz means 100 per second.
Haptics: using vibration to give touch feedback.
An ERM spinning at 6,000 rpm (revolutions per minute) turns 6,000 / 60 = 100 times a second, so it shakes at 100 hertz.
Spin it faster and it buzzes harder and higher, since strength and frequency are tied together.
An LRA driven at its resonance of, say, 200 hertz moves back and forth every 1/200 = 5 milliseconds. It starts and stops in a few milliseconds, so you get a crisp tap.
That is the whole idea: ERM is simple and a bit mushy, LRA is sharp and programmable.
"Two kinds.
ERMs are tiny brushed DC motors with an off-centre weight; the force is m e omega squared , so strength and frequency rise together with voltage, and they're a bit slow to spin up.
LRAs are voice-coil actuators: a mass on a spring driven by an AC signal at its resonance, around 150 to 250 hertz.
They respond in milliseconds, so they give crisp, programmable haptics, and amplitude is independent of frequency. Most modern phones use LRAs with a haptic driver IC."

Put them together and the motor's behavior plots as straight lines. Torque is highest at zero speed and falls steadily to zero at the top speed.

The band pulls hardest when stretched the most, and the pull fades smoothly to zero as the cart reaches the spot where the band goes slack.
A motor's pull fades the same way: strongest when stalled, zero at its no-load speed.
The analogy has one gap: in a motor, changing the supply voltage slides the whole line, which a rubber band cannot do.

No-load speed: the speed where torque falls to about zero.
Take a 12 volts motor with 1 ohms winding and K t equals K e equals 0. 02 . Stalled, the current is 12 amps and the torque is 0. 02 times 12 = 0. 24 N·m .
The no-load speed is about 12 / 0. 02 = 600 rad/s . Halfway, at 300 rad/s, back-EMF is 6 volts, the current is 6 amps, and the torque is 0. 12 N·m, which is half.
The points fall on a straight line. That is the whole idea: one straight line between stall and no-load.
"With V equals IR plus K e omega and T equals K tI , torque falls linearly with speed from stall torque K tV over R at zero rpm to zero at the no-load speed V over K e .
Current is proportional to torque, so it's highest at stall and lowest at no-load. Back-EMF rises with speed, so the remaining voltage across the winding, IR , shrinks.
Peak power is at half stall torque and half no-load speed, but efficiency peaks at low torque near no-load speed, so you design to run in that region and never sit at stall."

Torque is current, speed is voltage. The question: What electrical parameter corresponds to high torque? Why? What about high RPM?
For a DC motor, torque follows current, and speed follows voltage. More current through the winding gives more twisting force.
More voltage lets the motor spin faster before its back-EMF catches up with the supply. This is the simplest way to think about what a motor controller is doing.
Think of a treadmill you are running on. You choose the belt speed with a dial: that is the voltage.
How hard you have to push to keep up depends on the incline or load: that is the current and torque. A steeper hill means more effort at the same speed.
The analogy has a gap: on a real motor, a heavier load also slows the speed a little.
The electrical port (V, R, L) in series with a back-EMF source E that stands for the mechanical side. Current through that source sets the torque; its voltage is set by the speed.
Torque ( T ): the twisting force, in newton-meters (N·m). It is current times a motor constant: T equals K tI . Back-EMF ( E ): the voltage the spinning motor makes.
It is speed omega (in radians per second, rad/s) times a motor constant: E equals K e omega .
Voltage balance: the supply voltage equals the drop across the winding's resistance ( IR ) plus the back-EMF. Stall: shaft held still, so the current is maximum.
PWM duty: switching the supply on and off very fast; the fraction of time it is on sets the average voltage.
Use a 12 volts motor with R equals 1 ohms and K t equals K e equals 0. 02 . At 0. 5 amps, the torque is 0. 02 times 0. 5 = 0. 01 N·m, and the speed is (12 minus 0. 5 times 1) / 0.
02 = 575 rad/s . Load it to 5 amps, and the torque is 0. 1 N·m, ten times more. The speed drops to (12 minus 5) / 0. 02 = 350 rad/s .
That is the whole idea: current sets torque, and voltage (minus the IR drop) sets speed.
"Torque goes with current and speed goes with voltage.
The Lorentz force on the winding gives T equals K tI , so more current means more torque; that's why stall, the highest torque, is also the highest current, V over R .
Spinning generates a back-EMF K e omega that opposes the supply, so omega about (V minus IR) over K e : speed tracks voltage, minus a load-dependent drop.
K t and K e are the same number in SI units, by energy conservation."

How to spec a brushed motor. The question: How do you spec a motor?
Choosing a motor means starting with the job, not the motor. First work out how much twisting force (torque) and how much speed the load needs.
Then pick a motor, and usually a gearbox, that delivers that with some safety margin.
Finally, check that the supply and the driver (the circuit that switches the motor's power) can handle the current.
It is like picking a vehicle for moving house. First you decide what you must carry and how far. Only then do you choose a van or a truck.
A sports car is fast but cannot carry a sofa. A motor works the same way: a high-speed motor is a poor match for a slow, heavy load unless a gearbox sits between them.
The analogy has one gap: motors also get hot, so how long you run them matters.
Spec flow. Iterate on the gear ratio and winding until all four motor checks pass, then size the electronics and verify on the bench.
Torque: the twisting force at the shaft, in newton-meters (N·m): force in newtons (N) times the lever arm in meters. Gear ratio ( N ): how many motor turns make one output turn.
It trades speed for torque. Duty cycle: the fraction of time the motor is actually running. Stall current: the current with the shaft held still, V over R .
Margin: extra capacity beyond the calculated need, for battery sag and heating.
A robot wheel has a 0. 05 m radius and must push with 2 N. The torque at the wheel is 2 times 0. 05 = 0. 1 N·m .
The wheel should turn at 20 rad/s (radians per second; one turn is about 6. 28 radians).
Suppose the chosen motor runs best near 400 rad/s, so pick a gear ratio of 400 / 20 = 20:1 . The motor then supplies 0. 1 / 20 = 0. 005 N·m. With K t equals 0.
02 N·m/A, that is 0. 005 / 0. 02 = 0. 25 amps . That is the whole idea: work from the load back to the motor.
"I work from the load backwards. Get the output torque and speed, continuous and peak, plus duty cycle, supply voltage, size and life.
Pick a gear ratio that sets motor torque as load torque over N and motor speed as N times load speed.
Then check the motor: continuous torque under its rated continuous value, peak under stall, and enough voltage for back-EMF plus IR with margin.
Current is torque over K t , which sizes the driver, and stall current is V over R . Then check thermal, brush life, noise, mounting and cost, and verify on the bench."

Motor noise and how to reduce it. The question: Why are motors so noisy? How can you reduce this noise?
A motor makes two kinds of noise. Acoustic noise is sound you can hear. Electrical noise is voltage spikes that spread through wires and upset nearby circuits.
In a brushed motor, the electrical noise mostly comes from the brushes switching current in the coils. The fix is to calm the spikes at the source.
Picture a washing machine thumping on a thin floor. The thump travels through the floor into the rooms next door, just as motor spikes travel through shared wires.
You can soften the thump at the source with a rubber mat, or keep the machine away from the quiet room.
The analogy has a limit: electrical noise can also radiate through the air, like radio static.
The standard fix.

C1 (differential) is soldered across the motor terminals, with ferrite beads (or a few µH) in each lead to form an LC filter; C2 and C3 (small ceramics, a few nF) tie each terminal to the motor case for common-mode currents.
All three sit on the motor, not on the PCB.
EMI: electromagnetic interference, electrical noise that disturbs other circuits. Commutation: the brushes switching current from one coil to the next as the motor turns.
Arcing: tiny sparks at the brushes. Inductance: how strongly a coil fights a change in its current by making a voltage, in henries (1 microhenries is a millionth).
Bypass capacitor: a small part that stores charge and soaks up fast spikes, in farads (1 nanofarads is a billionth). Ferrite bead: a part that blocks fast noise on a wire.
Illustrative numbers for a small 6 volts motor: a brush switches a 50 microhenries coil, and its current drops by 0. 5 amps in 1 microseconds (a millionth of a second).
The faster the change, the bigger the voltage: L di over dt = 50 microhenries times 0. 5 amps / 1 microseconds = 25 volts , about four times the supply.
This happens hundreds to thousands of times per second. A 100 nanofarads capacitor right across the motor terminals gives that fast current a place to go.
That is the whole idea: fast current changes make spikes, and you absorb them where they start.
"Motor noise has electrical and acoustic parts.

Electrically, brush commutation interrupts inductive coil current, so L di over dt spikes and arcs produce broadband noise that couples onto the leads and the supply, along with PWM edges and start-up current steps.

I'd suppress at the source with a 100 nanofarads ceramic across the terminals plus small capacitors to the case, add ferrite beads to make an LC filter, then use decoupling, twisted leads and a star ground.
Acoustically, raise PWM above 20 kilohertz and choose better bearings or mounting."

What is arcing?. The question: What is arcing?
An arc is an electrical spark that jumps through air (or another gas) between two conductors that are close but not touching.
The gas heats up and becomes a glowing, conducting plasma. Arcs appear when the voltage across a gap gets high enough, and a common cause is opening a switch on a coil.
Think of the shock you get from a doorknob after walking on carpet. Air is normally an insulator.
But when the electrical push across it gets strong enough, it suddenly breaks down and a spark flows. An arc is the same breakdown, except that it can keep burning.
The analogy has a gap: a static shock is brief, while an arc on a steady (DC) supply can persist because the voltage never passes through zero.
Left of the minimum, the gap is too small for the electrons to ionise enough gas. Right of it, higher pressure or gap needs more voltage.
At atmospheric pressure ( p equals 760 Torr) a 10 µm gap has pd equals 0. 76 Torr·cm: about 300 volts.
A 1 mm gap ( pd equals 76 ) needs about 5 kilovolts by this fit; a measured value for a uniform 1 mm air gap is more like 4–5 kilovolts, consistent with ~3–4 kilovolts/mm.
For very small gaps (below a few µm) the fit isn't reliable and field emission dominates.
Arc: a sustained electrical discharge through a gas, hot and glowing. Breakdown: the moment an insulating gas starts to conduct.
Plasma: gas that has been ionized (charged) so it conducts. Inductive current: current through a coil, which resists stopping.
Snubber: a small circuit that absorbs the spike across a contact.
Air breaks down at roughly 3 million volts per meter in larger gaps. A 1 mm gap therefore needs roughly 3,000 volts to spark.
Now a switch opens in series with a coil carrying 1 amps.
The coil insists on keeping 1 amps flowing, so the voltage across the opening gap climbs until the gap breaks down, and an arc forms.
A diode (a one-way valve for current) across the coil gives the current a path instead, so the gap never sees that voltage.
That is the whole idea: an arc is a gap breaking down, and coils push the voltage high enough to cause it.
"Arcing is a discharge through ionised gas between two conductors, hot plasma that conducts at a low voltage once it's lit.

It starts either from breakdown of a gap by high voltage, or, the common case, when you interrupt current in an inductor: v equals L di over dt drives the opening gap's voltage up until air breaks down, and DC has no zero crossing to put it out.
It erodes contacts and brushes, makes EMI, and can start fires. Fix it by giving the current another path, a flyback diode, RC snubber, TVS, or by using a solid-state switch."

What are brushes?. The question: What are brushes?
Brushes are the stationary contacts of a brushed motor. They are small blocks, usually carbon, pressed by springs against a spinning ring of copper segments called the commutator.
They do two jobs: they carry current from the fixed terminals into the spinning coils, and they help flip the current in each coil at the right moment.
Picture a pencil lead pressed against a spinning bicycle rim. The lead stays still, the rim slides past it, and the lead stays in contact.
In the motor, the rim is the commutator and the pencil lead is the brush, carrying electricity instead of marking paper.
The analogy has one gap: the brush also has to switch from one copper segment to the next, which a pencil never does.
End view of a 6-segment commutator. Brushes (green, static, spring-loaded) touch segments 2 and 5.
Each armature coil is connected between two adjacent segments, so the coils form two parallel paths from the + brush to the minus brush (one round each side of the ring).

As the ring turns, each brush briefly bridges two adjacent segments, shorting the coil between them while it passes the neutral axis; after 60° the brushes sit on the next pair of segments and that coil has moved into the other path, so its current has reversed.
Brush: a stationary conductor, often carbon, that slides on the commutator. Commutator: copper segments on the rotor, each wired to a coil. Rotor: the spinning part of the motor.
Contact voltage drop: the voltage a carbon brush loses as current passes through it, roughly 0. 5–1 volts per brush.
Brushless motor: a motor that switches current electronically instead.
Take one wire loop spinning between magnets, with its ends on two half-rings and two fixed brushes touching the half-rings.
Half a turn later, each brush has slid onto the other half-ring, so the current in the loop reverses. That reversal keeps the push in the same direction.
The brushes also waste a little voltage. Take the top of the usual range, 1 volts per brush: the current passes through two brushes, so 2 volts is lost.
At 2 amps, that is 2 volts times 2 amps = 4 watts . That is the whole idea: brushes bring in power and flip the current.
"Brushes are the stationary conductive contacts, usually carbon, spring-pressed against the commutator on the rotor.

They feed current from the motor terminals into the spinning windings, and together with the commutator's segments they reverse the current in each coil at the right angle, so the torque stays in one direction.
The trade-off is that they wear, drop about a volt, create friction and spark slightly, which makes noise. Brushless motors avoid this by switching electronically."

What brushes are made of. The question: What are brushes made out of?
Most motor brushes are made of carbon, usually a carbon-graphite mix.
Graphite conducts electricity and also slides very smoothly, so it works as its own lubricant on the copper commutator.
Some brushes mix in metal powder for more current, and tiny motors use thin metal fingers.
Think of a pencil. The "lead" is really graphite, and it writes because thin layers slip off as you slide it.
That same slipperiness makes graphite gentle on the commutator and leaves a thin lubricating film.
The analogy has a limit: unlike a pencil, a brush must also carry current, so its material has to balance conductivity, wear and friction.

With a roughly constant drop per brush, contact loss grows linearly with current ( 2 volts bI ), while the blocks' own ohmic loss ( I to the 2R with R about 5 milliohms) is small by comparison: about 1 watts at 10 amps against 20 watts of contact loss for carbon.
The drops used (1. 0 volts and 0. 3 volts) are typical round numbers for the two families, not data for a specific grade.
Graphite: a form of carbon with slippery layers that conducts electricity. Carbon-graphite brush: the common general-purpose brush material.
Metal-graphite brush: graphite mixed with copper or silver for lower resistance. Commutator: the copper segments the brush slides on.
Contact voltage drop: the voltage lost across the brush contact, roughly 0. 5–1 volts per carbon brush.
Take a carbon brush that drops about 1 volts.
A motor on a 12 volts supply has two brushes in the current path, so it loses about 2 volts, which is 2 / 12, about one sixth of the supply.
For a car starter, that waste matters at very high current, so it uses metal-graphite brushes with a much lower drop.
A tiny toy or camera motor often uses thin precious-metal fingers instead. That is the whole idea: pick the brush material to match the current and size of the motor.
"Most brushes are carbon-graphite.
Graphite is conductive and a natural solid lubricant, so it slides with low friction and leaves a stable film on the copper commutator, and the slightly resistive carbon helps commutation.
Variants: electrographite for better performance, metal-graphite with copper or silver for lower drop and higher current in low-voltage motors, and precious-metal fingers in tiny motors.
It's a trade-off between conductivity, drop, hardness and wear, set by current density and speed."

Concerns about brushes. The question: What are some concerns about brushes?
Brushes cause four kinds of trouble. They wear out, because they rub on a moving surface. They lose some voltage and make electrical noise.
They create friction and sometimes squeal. And their dust and sparks can cause problems in some environments.
These are the reasons designers sometimes choose brushless motors instead.
Think of the brake pads on a bicycle. They grip a spinning rim, so they slowly wear away, make dust, and sometimes squeal.
Brushes rub on the commutator in much the same way, and every bit of wear shortens the motor's life.
The analogy has one gap: brushes also carry current, so sparking and voltage drop come on top of the mechanical wear.
The reactance voltage rises linearly with speed because the commutation time shrinks.
At 6000 rpm it is a small fraction of the brush drop; near 30,000 rpm it is comparable, so commutation worsens, sparks appear and the brush grade and position become critical.
(A simplified model: real commutation depends on the brush width, the resistance of the film and the field in the neutral zone.)
Brush wear: the slow loss of brush material from rubbing and sparking. Contact voltage drop: the voltage lost where a brush touches the commutator, roughly 0.
5–1 volts per carbon brush. Arcing: small sparks at the contact. Commutator: the ring of copper segments on the spinning shaft that the brushes rub on.
Spring pressure: the force pushing the brush onto the commutator. Brushless motor: a motor with no sliding contacts.
Suppose a motor's brushes last 2,000 hours, and the motor runs 8 hours a day. That gives 2,000 / 8 = 250 days, so less than a year before the brushes need attention.
If the product must last years, you either change the brushes, derate the motor (lower speed or current), or switch to a brushless motor.
That is the whole idea: every brush concern comes from a sliding, sparking contact.
"The concerns are wear and finite life, electrical drop and loss, arcing noise, and speed and current limits. Brushes wear and make dust, typically thousands of hours.
They drop about a volt each, which matters at low voltage. Commutation of an inductive coil causes sparks and EMI.
Too much current density overheats them, and at high speed they bounce. Humidity, altitude and contamination change their behaviour and sparks are an ignition risk.
So pick the grade, suppress noise, derate, or go brushless."

Why brushes wear out. The question: Why do brushes wear out?
Brushes wear out because they slide on a moving surface and also carry current through it.
Three things remove material: rubbing friction, tiny sparks, and chemistry in the air and on the surface.
These effects feed each other, which is why a motor can seem fine and then fail quickly.
Think of rubbing a pencil eraser on a table. The harder you press, and the longer you rub, the more of it you wear away.
A brush works like that eraser against the spinning commutator. Add sparks and a dry or dirty surface, and the wear gets faster.
The analogy has a gap: an eraser has no sparks, and sparks roughen the surface, which then wears the brush even faster.
With these assumed numbers the brush reaches the 6 mm wear limit at about 7400 h (0. 3 N), 4400 h (0. 5 N) and 2200 h (1. 0 N).
Life is inversely proportional to spring force and to speed. The real wear coefficient k s differs by grade and condition by orders of magnitude; the scaling is the useful part.
Friction wear: material rubbed off by sliding, roughly force times distance. Arcing: small sparks as the brush switches between segments.
Film: a thin layer on the commutator that lubricates the brush. Spring force: how hard the brush presses on the commutator. Commutator: the copper segments the brush slides on.
Friction wear is roughly proportional to contact force times sliding distance. Double the spring force and the wear doubles.
Run the motor twice as fast and the brush slides twice as far each second, so the wear rate doubles again. Both together give about 2 times 2 = 4 times the wear.
A rough commutator makes the brush bounce, which causes sparks, which make it rougher. That is the whole idea: force, distance, sparks and surface condition all add up.
"Brushes wear from three things at once. Mechanical: friction against the moving commutator removes material in proportion to spring force times sliding distance.
Electrical: commutation sparks erode the contact, and current heats the contact spots.
Chemical and environmental: graphite needs a film and humidity to lubricate, so dry air, altitude, oil or silicone make it wear fast.
A rough or out-of-round commutator makes the brush bounce, which makes sparks, which makes everything worse."

Replace the brushes or the motor?. The question: When should you replace brushes vs replace the whole motor?
When a brushed motor stops working because its brushes are worn, you must decide whether to replace the brushes or the whole motor.
It depends on whether the brushes can be replaced at all, what condition the rest of the motor is in, and what each option costs.
Also ask why the brushes wore out, or the new ones will fail the same way.
It is like a worn tire on a car. If the rest of the car is healthy, you replace the tires. If the engine and frame are also worn out, you buy a different car.
A sealed toy motor is more like a disposable item, where the "tire" cannot be changed at all.
The analogy has a gap: with a motor you must inspect the commutator and bearings to know how healthy the rest is.
Decision flow. Serviceability and commutator condition come first; windings and bearings next; economics last.
"Fix the root cause" applies on every path where the brush failure was premature.
Serviceable: designed so you can open it and change the brushes. Brush kit: a set of replacement brushes and springs. Commutator: the copper segments the brushes slide on.
It should be round and evenly colored. Bearings: the parts the shaft turns in. They should have no play (looseness) or noise.
Root cause: the real reason the part failed, such as overload or arcing.
Take a power drill with worn brushes. Its brush holders are easy to reach. The commutator is smooth with an even brown film, and the bearings are quiet.
So you replace the brushes and the drill is nearly like new. Now take a small sealed toy motor with worn brushes.
The brushes are part of the can and cannot be changed, so you replace the motor.
That is the whole idea: replace the brushes if they are accessible and the rest is healthy, otherwise replace the motor.
"It depends on serviceability, condition and cost.
If the motor has accessible brush holders and a standard kit, and the commutator is round with a good film, the bearings and windings are fine, then replacing the worn brushes restores it cheaply.
If the commutator is grooved, burnt or below minimum size, or windings or bearings are failing, or the motor is a sealed consumable, replace the motor.
Compare repair cost over the extra life with the new-motor cost, and fix the cause of the wear."

How brushes stay in contact. The question: How do brushes maintain contact with the commutator?
Brushes stay in contact with the commutator because springs push them against it. Each brush sits in a holder that lets it slide in and out.
As the brush wears shorter, the spring pushes it further forward, so contact stays firm. A flexible wire braid carries the current so the spring does not have to.
Think of a mechanical pencil. The lead sits in a sleeve, and as you write and it wears down, the lead is pushed forward so it always touches the paper.
A brush works the same way: the spring keeps feeding it toward the commutator as it shortens.
The analogy has one gap: a brush needs a controlled, fairly constant force, not just any push.
A spring-loaded brush in its holder.
The spring supplies the normal force F N ; the flexible pigtail (red) carries the current to the terminal so the spring and the sliding fit of the holder are not current paths.
The brush face rides on the commutator; the part of the brush below the dashed line is the length that will wear away, over which the spring must keep pushing it down.
Brush holder: a guide or box that lets the brush slide freely. Spring: the part that pushes the brush onto the commutator.
Pigtail: a flexible copper braid carrying current from the brush to the terminal. Contact force: how hard the brush presses. Too low causes bouncing and sparks.
Too high wears things fast. Commutator: the copper segments the brush rides on.
A new brush is 12 mm long and sits in its holder with a spring behind it. After a long time it wears down to 6 mm.
The spring has extended 6 mm further forward and is still pressing the brush against the commutator.
The current does not pass through the spring: it travels through the pigtail, so the spring stays cool and the brush moves freely.
That is the whole idea: a spring feeds the brush forward as it wears.
"Springs push the brushes onto the commutator.
Each brush slides in a holder box, and a spring behind it, a coil spring, a constant-force strip spring, or a torsion arm, keeps a set pressure, around 1. 5 to 2.
5 psi for carbon, as the brush wears down. A flexible copper pigtail carries the current so the spring doesn't. In small motors the brush is itself a springy metal finger.
Too little force means bounce and sparking, too much means fast wear and friction."
