How BLDC motors work. The question: How do BLDC motors work?
A brushless DC motor puts the magnets on the spinning part and the coils on the fixed part. Because the coils never move, no brushes are needed to feed them.
Instead, electronics switch the current through the coils in a repeating order, and the magnet on the rotor keeps chasing the moving magnetic field.
Picture a carrot on a stick held in front of a donkey. The donkey keeps walking toward the carrot, and you keep moving the stick a little ahead.
The rotor magnet is the donkey, and the changing field from the coils is the carrot.
The analogy has a gap: the controller must know where the rotor is, so it knows when to move the carrot.
The BLDC control loop in one picture. The rotor moves, the position code changes, and the controller steps the stator field forward again.
Nothing mechanical decides when to switch.
Stator: the fixed part holding the coils. Rotor: the spinning part holding the permanent magnets. Phase: one of the three groups of coils, usually named A, B and C.
Hall sensor: a sensor that detects the rotor magnet's position. Commutation: switching which coils are powered, here done by electronics. Compare "What are brushes?"
Power two of the three phases. This makes a magnetic field pointing in one direction, and the rotor magnet swings to line up with it.
Just before it arrives, the controller powers a different pair of phases. The field jumps ahead by 60 electrical degrees, and the rotor follows.
(On the simplest motor, with one pair of magnet poles, electrical degrees equal real degrees of turn.)
There are six such steps, and 6 times 60° = 360° makes one electrical revolution. That is the whole idea: switch the field ahead of the rotor, again and again.
"A BLDC motor has permanent magnets on the rotor and three coils on the stator, so there's no brush or commutator.
An electronic inverter energises two of the three phases at a time to create a stator field, and steps to the next pair every 60 electrical degrees so the rotor keeps chasing the field.
It knows the rotor position from Hall sensors or from back-EMF.
So it's really a three-phase synchronous motor, but because the torque goes with current and speed goes with voltage, it behaves like a DC motor."
Quick check. In a BLDC motor, where are the permanent magnets and where are the windings?
Controlling BLDC motors. The question: How do you control BLDC motors?
Controlling a BLDC motor has three layers. First, work out which coils to power, based on where the rotor (the spinning magnet) is.
Second, use PWM to set how much voltage the coils get. Third, run control loops on speed and current.
Six-step is the simple method; field-oriented control is the smooth, efficient one.
Think of pushing a child on a swing. You need to push at the right moment in the swing, which means watching where the swing is. That is commutation, with a sensor as your eyes.
How hard you push sets how high the swing goes. That is the voltage or current.
The analogy has one gap: a motor needs a push in a new direction six times per electrical turn, not just once per swing.
Everything in BLDC control fits this loop. Position feedback feeds both commutation (fast) and the speed loop (slow).
Current feedback closes the inner loop and doubles as the overcurrent protection.
Commutation: choosing which of the three coil groups (phases) to power as the rotor turns. PWM: switching the supply on and off very fast.
The fraction of time it is on, the duty, sets the average voltage. Hall sensor: a position sensor, so the controller knows the rotor's sector.
Six-step control: a simple method that powers two phases at a time from a lookup table. Field-oriented control (FOC): a smoother method that controls the current's angle and size.
Say a motor runs from a 24 volts supply. Three Hall sensors each report on or off, and together they tell the controller which of six sectors the rotor is in.
A lookup table then says which two phases to power. If the PWM duty is 50%, the coils see an average of 12 volts, so the motor runs at about half speed.
A control loop measures the speed and nudges that duty up or down to hold the speed you asked for.
That is the whole idea: read the position, switch the phases, and PWM the voltage.
"I think in three layers. Commutation chooses the active phases from rotor position, using Hall sensors, back-EMF zero-crossings or an encoder.
Modulation uses PWM on a three-phase bridge to set the voltage. On top are a current loop and a speed loop.

The simple version is six-step with Hall sensors, which is cheap but has torque ripple; the high-performance version is field-oriented control, which regulates the d and q currents for smooth, efficient torque."
Quick check. In six-step BLDC control with Hall sensors, what do the Hall sensors provide?
BLDC from a microcontroller. The question: How do you control a BLDC motor from a microcontroller? What other components do you need?
A microcontroller (MCU) cannot drive a BLDC motor directly. Its pins give only milliamps, and the motor needs amps at 12 volts or more.
So you place a power stage between them: gate drivers and six MOSFET switches. The MCU sends small timing signals; the power stage does the heavy lifting.
Think of the power steering in a car. Your hands turn the wheel with little force, but the hydraulic booster does the real work of moving the heavy wheels.
The MCU is your hands, and the gate driver and MOSFETs are the booster.
The analogy has one gap: the MCU also listens for feedback, such as rotor position and current, to know what the motor actually did.
The signal chain. Six logic PWM lines leave the MCU, the driver converts them into proper gate waveforms, and the bridge drives the motor.
Hall, current and fault signals return to the MCU on the left and bottom pins.
MOSFET: a transistor (a part a small signal can turn on and off) used as a fast, powerful switch.
Half-bridge: two MOSFETs stacked between the supply and ground, with one motor phase (coil group) connected between them.
PWM: switching on and off very fast, so the fraction of on-time sets the average voltage. Gate driver: a chip that delivers the burst of current needed to switch MOSFETs fast.
Dead-time: a short pause so the two switches of a half-bridge are never both on. Shunt resistor: a tiny resistor used to measure current.
Say a motor draws 3 amps from a 12 volts supply, and an MCU pin can supply about 20 milliamps (a typical figure). The motor needs 3 / 0.
02 = 150 times more current than the pin can give.
The chain is: MCU makes six PWM signals, the gate driver boosts them, three half-bridges (six MOSFETs) switch the supply, and the motor turns.
Hall sensors and a current shunt report back to the MCU. That is the whole idea: the MCU commands, the power stage delivers.
"I can't drive a BLDC from GPIO.
I need a three-phase bridge of six N-MOSFETs, a gate driver to level-shift and supply gate current, and an MCU with complementary PWM and dead-time to command it.
Feedback comes from Hall sensors or back-EMF, a shunt plus amplifier for current, and a divider for bus voltage.
I'd add a hardware overcurrent trip into the timer's break input, a bulk DC-link capacitor, and local supplies.
Or I'd use an integrated BLDC driver and just supply PWM and Halls."

Brushless vs brushed advantages. The question: What are some advantages of brushless vs brushed motors?
A brushed motor switches its coil current with a sliding contact (brushes). A brushless motor does the same job with electronic switches.
Nearly every advantage of brushless comes from removing that sliding contact: longer life, better efficiency, less noise, and higher speed and power.
The price is a more complex controller.
Think of two doors. One has a rubbing seal that scrapes the floor each time it swings, so it wears out, squeaks and wastes effort. The other opens with no contact at all.
The brushed motor is the scraping door, and the brushless motor is the contactless one.
The analogy has one gap: the contactless door needs a smart control system, just as a brushless motor needs a controller.
Every brushed-motor limitation traces back to one of two root causes: the sliding contact (the four-way branch on the left) and having the hot winding on the rotor (the pair of boxes on the right).
Commutation: switching the coil current as the rotor (the spinning part) turns. Mechanical in a brushed motor, electronic in a brushless one.
Brush wear: the slow loss of brush material by rubbing and sparking. EMI: unwanted electrical noise that disturbs nearby circuits.
Contact voltage drop: the voltage lost where the brushes touch the commutator, typically about 1–2 volts for the pair.
Power density: how much power you get for the motor's size and weight.
Suppose the two brushes together drop about 1 volts, the low end of the usual range. On a 12 volts motor, 1 / 12 is roughly 8% of the input power lost at the brushes.
On a 3 volts motor, the same 1 volts is 1 / 3, about 33% . A brushless motor has no brush drop, so it wastes none of it. It also needs no brush replacement.
The cost is a controller: a set of electronic switches, a way to sense the rotor's position, and software to run them.
That is the whole idea: removing the sliding contact fixes wear, loss and noise.
"Brushed motors commutate mechanically; brushless motors commutate electronically, and nearly every advantage follows from that.
No brushes means no wear, so longer life, no arcing, so less EMI and no sparks, and no brush friction or voltage drop, so higher efficiency.
The winding sits on the stator against the housing, so it cools better and handles more continuous power, and top speed isn't limited by the commutator.
The cost is the controller: a three-phase bridge, sensing and firmware, so brushed is still the cheap, simple choice for low-duty or low-cost applications."
Quick check. What is the fundamental difference between brushed and brushless DC motors?
Motor poles and performance. The question: What are the poles of the motor? How can they impact performance?
Poles are the magnetic north and south regions on the rotor, arranged N, S, N, S around the rim.
The number of pole pairs decides how many electrical cycles happen in one turn of the shaft.
More poles give more torque at lower speed, but they require a faster electrical frequency for the same rpm (revolutions per minute).
Think of a bicycle in a low gear. Your legs spin the pedals many times for each turn of the wheel, and you push with more force.
More poles act like a lower gear inside the motor: for each shaft turn, the controller must cycle the current more times, and the motor gives more torque for its size.
The analogy has a limit: a real gear multiplies torque exactly, while extra poles help only through a better magnetic design, and add losses.
Same rotor diameter, different pole counts. With 2 poles one turn of the shaft is one electrical cycle; with 14 poles, one shaft turn is seven electrical cycles.
The stator fields and the Hall pattern repeat seven times per turn, so the rotor only needs to move 1/7 of a turn to advance one full electrical cycle.
Pole: one magnetic north or south region on the rotor. Pole pair ( p ): one north and one south pole together.
Electrical frequency: how many electrical cycles per second the controller drives, f equals p times rpm over 60 .
Electrical cycle: one full north-then-south pass of the rotor's magnets past a coil. The controller must drive one current cycle for each.
Cogging: a slight notchy feel as the rotor magnets are pulled toward the iron of the fixed part (stator).
A 14-pole motor has 14 / 2 = 7 pole pairs. At 30,000 rpm, the shaft turns 30,000 / 60 = 500 times per second. The electrical frequency is 7 times 500 = 3,500 hertz , or 3.
5 kilohertz. A 2-pole motor at the same speed has only 1 pair, so its electrical frequency is 500 hertz.
Higher electrical frequency means more switching loss and more heating in the motor's iron, but more torque from a compact motor.
That is the whole idea: poles trade torque against electrical frequency.
"Poles are the permanent-magnet poles on the rotor; p pole pairs means p electrical cycles per revolution, so f e equals p times rpm over 60 .
More poles gives more torque at lower speed for the same size, thinner back-iron, finer Hall resolution and, with the right slot count, less cogging.
The cost is a higher electrical frequency for the same rpm, which raises iron and switching losses and demands a faster controller.
Few poles suit very high speed; many poles suit gimbals, drones and direct drive."

Specifying a BLDC motor. The question: How do you spec a BLDC motor?
Specifying a BLDC motor means working backward from the load. Work out the torque and speed you need, and the supply you have.
Then choose a motor whose constants fit, check it does not overheat, and add the practical details such as sensors, size and mounting.
Think of choosing a car engine for a trailer. You first decide how heavy the load is and how fast you must tow it.
Then you check the engine can deliver that power without overheating, and the fuel tank (here, the battery) can keep up.
The analogy has one gap: with a motor, the battery voltage also limits top speed, because the back-EMF must stay below it.
The spec flows from the application to the motor, and loops back if any check fails. The voltage check and thermal check are the two that most often change the choice.
Mechanical power: torque times angular speed, P equals T omega . Torque constant ( K t ): newton-meters (N·m) of torque per amp of current.
Back-EMF: the voltage the spinning motor makes. Duty: the fraction of time the controller's switches are on. It sets the average voltage the motor sees.
Headroom: spare supply voltage left over for acceleration and disturbances. Continuous rating: the torque the motor can hold without overheating.
You need 0. 5 N·m at 3,000 rpm (revolutions per minute). One turn is 2π about 6. 28 radians, so the speed is 3,000 times 2π / 60 about 314 rad/s, so the power is 0.
5 times 314 about 157 watts . With K t equals 0. 06 N·m/A, the current is 0. 5 / 0. 06 about 8. 3 amps . The back-EMF is 0. 06 times 314 about 19 volts, and with about 1.
25 volts lost in the winding's resistance the motor needs about 20. 1 volts. On a 24 volts supply, that is 20. 1 / 24, around 84% duty, leaving some headroom.
That is the whole idea: torque sets current, speed sets voltage.
"I work backwards from the load: continuous and peak torque, speed, duty and supply voltage. Power is T omega .
I choose K t so that the current at continuous torque is within the continuous rating and the back-EMF plus IR at top speed is under about 85% of the supply.
Then I check heating, I to the 2R times thermal resistance, and peak torque against the current limit.
Finally I check sensors, pole count and frequency, size, bearings, environment and the controller."

What is an ESC. The question: What is an electronic speed controller (ESC)?
An ESC (electronic speed controller) is the box between the battery and a brushless motor.
It turns a simple throttle command, like "50%", into the precisely timed switching the motor needs.
Inside are six electronic switches (MOSFETs) that feed the motor's three coil groups (phases), run by a small computer chip (a microcontroller).
It also protects the motor and battery.
Think of the coxswain in a rowing boat. The captain just says "harder" or "easier". The coxswain turns that into exact timing, telling each rower when to pull.
The ESC does the same for the motor's three phases. The analogy has a gap: the ESC also works out the timing by listening to the motor itself, rather than by being told.
Four ports. Battery power in, a command in, three phases out. The dashed lines are optional: telemetry back and a 5 volts supply for the controller.
ESC: the controller that drives a brushless motor from a throttle input. Inverter: a stage of switches that makes three-phase drive from a DC battery.
PWM: fast on-off switching that sets the average voltage. BEC: a small regulator in the ESC that makes 5 volts for other electronics.
Telemetry: data sent back, such as rpm, current and temperature.
A drone's flight controller sends a throttle value of 50%.
The ESC senses where the rotor (the spinning magnet) is, usually from back-EMF, picks which two phases to power next, and switches them with PWM so they are on 50% of the time (50% duty).
From a 16 volts battery, the motor sees an average of about 8 volts, so it spins at roughly half speed.
If the current gets too high or the battery too low, the ESC cuts back to protect itself. That is the whole idea: throttle in, correctly timed three-phase power out.
"An ESC is the electronics that sits between a battery and a motor and converts a throttle command into power for the motor.
For a brushless motor it's a three-phase inverter, six MOSFETs plus a microcontroller, that senses rotor position, usually from back-EMF, commutates the phases in sequence and PWMs them to set speed.
It also adds protection like current limiting and undervoltage cutoff, often a 5 volts BEC, and telemetry.
Inputs are battery power and a command signal; outputs are three motor phases."

Why brushless motors need ESCs. The question: Why are ESCs often required for brushless motors?
A brushless motor has no commutator, so nothing mechanical switches its coils. Without that switching, the rotor (the spinning magnet) just locks in place.
Something electronic must power the right coils at the right moment, and that is the ESC's main job. It also sets the speed and protects the motor.
Hold a magnet on top of a table, and move another magnet underneath. The top magnet follows as long as you keep moving the lower one ahead.
If you stop and hold the lower magnet still, the top magnet snaps into line and stays there.
A brushless motor fed a steady DC voltage is like that: the rotor magnet locks onto the fixed field.
The analogy has one gap: the motor's field must be moved electrically, not by hand.
With a fixed stator field the torque always points toward the alignment point at 0°. The rotor does a damped swing and sits there.
To keep spinning, the controller must keep moving the zero point ahead of the rotor, so the torque stays near its peak at about 90° behind the field.
Commutator: the mechanical switch in a brushed motor. Stator field: the magnetic field made by the fixed coils. ESC: the electronic controller that moves that field.
Back-EMF: the spinning motor's voltage, which limits current. Sensorless: finding the rotor position from back-EMF instead of sensors.
Suppose (illustrative numbers) you connect 12 volts DC across two wires of a small brushless motor with 0. 2 ohms per winding (coil).
The rotor swings into line with the field and stops. Now there is no back-EMF, so the current is limited only by resistance: 12 volts / (0. 2 + 0.
2) Ω = 30 amps , which soon overheats the windings. With an ESC, the field keeps moving, the rotor keeps turning, and back-EMF holds the current down.
That is the whole idea: the field must keep moving ahead of the rotor.
"Because a brushless motor has no commutator. In a brushed motor the brushes switch the coil current automatically as the rotor turns.
With permanent magnets on the rotor and fixed coils, something electronic has to do that switching, and that's the ESC.
Plain DC just creates a fixed field, so the rotor locks to it and draws huge current.
The ESC reads rotor position, steps the phase currents, sets speed with PWM, limits current and protects the battery and motor."
Quick check. What is the main reason a brushless motor needs an ESC?
ESC vs single-phase motor driver. The question: What is the difference between an ESC and a single-phase motor driver? What additional functionality may an ESC offer?
A simple motor driver (an H-bridge) takes a direction and a speed setting and lets a brushed motor do the rest, because the brushes switch the coils.
The speed setting is a PWM duty: the fraction of time the power is switched on. An ESC for a brushless motor has to do the coil switching itself.
So it needs three pairs of switches, position sensing, and firmware (software built into the chip) that decides what to switch next.
An H-bridge is like a reversing switch on a toy train: forward, reverse, faster, slower. The train does the rest.
An ESC is more like a conductor directing every musician in sequence, listening to the room to know when to cue the next one.
The analogy has one gap: the ESC also includes everything the reversing switch does, such as setting the speed with PWM.
An H-bridge. Q1 and Q4 on drive the motor one way; Q3 and Q2 on drive it the other way; both low-sides on is brake.
Compare with the three-phase bridge in "How BLDC motors work": it has a third leg and nothing like "one motor between two midpoints".
H-bridge: four switches that drive a brushed motor in either direction. Half-bridge: one pair of switches. An ESC has three, one per motor wire.
Commutation: choosing which coils to power as the rotor (the spinning part) turns. Hall sensor: a sensor that tells the controller where the rotor is.
DShot: a digital throttle protocol used by many ESCs.
For a brushed motor, an H-bridge has 4 switches. You tell it "forward, 50% duty" and the motor runs. It needs no idea where the rotor is.
For a brushless motor, an ESC has 3 half-bridges, which is 6 switches .
Every few degrees of rotor movement, it must choose one of six switching states, based on Hall sensors or back-EMF. That choice is the extra intelligence.
That is the whole idea: the ESC is a driver plus commutation.
"A single-phase driver is an H-bridge: it gives a brushed motor a direction and a PWM duty, and the commutator does the smart part mechanically.
An ESC drives three phases with six switches and must do the commutation itself, so it needs rotor position from Hall sensors or back-EMF, and firmware for startup and sequencing.
ESCs also add a throttle protocol, braking and regeneration, current and thermal protection, a BEC, and telemetry."
Quick check. How many switches are in a three-phase ESC power stage versus an H-bridge?
ESC components and subsystems. The question: What components/subsystems does an ESC have?
An ESC can be split into four groups of parts. The power path carries the battery current to the motor. The control path decides what to switch and when.
The sensing parts measure the motor and battery. The support parts make small supply voltages and keep everything safe.
Think of the ESC as a body. The MOSFETs (power switches) are the muscles that do the heavy work. The microcontroller (a small computer chip) is the brain that decides what to do.
The sensing circuits are the senses, telling the brain what is happening. The regulators are the digestion, turning the battery's energy into the small supplies the brain needs.
The analogy has one gap: the whole thing also needs fast capacitors close to the muscles.
The ESC as a set of blocks.
Power flows top to bottom through the bridge to the motor; information flows back from the back-EMF network and the shunt to the MCU, which closes the loop through the gate drivers.
The regulators hang off the DC link.
DC link capacitors: charge stores at the battery input that supply the sudden bursts of current. Gate driver: a chip that switches the MOSFETs quickly and safely.
Bootstrap: a small capacitor and diode that give the upper switches the extra voltage they need to turn on. Shunt: a tiny resistor used to measure current.
BEC: a regulator that makes 5 volts for outside electronics.
Follow one command through. The throttle signal goes into the microcontroller. The microcontroller sends six fast on/off (PWM) signals to the gate driver.
The gate driver switches the six MOSFETs, which push current to the motor.
A 1 milliohms shunt carrying 30 amps produces 30 millivolts (30 amps times 1 milliohms), which a comparator (a circuit that flags when a voltage crosses a limit) watches for overcurrent.
Resistor dividers on each motor wire let the firmware see back-EMF. A regulator makes 5 volts and 3. 3 volts for the logic.
That is the whole idea: power, control, sensing and support, all linked by firmware.
"An ESC has four groups of parts. The power path: input connector, DC-link capacitors and a three-phase bridge of six MOSFETs.
The control path: a microcontroller running commutation, with a gate driver, bootstrap and dead-time between it and the FETs.
The sensing: back-EMF dividers into comparators or ADC, a shunt for current, and voltage and temperature sensors.
And the support: a BEC and logic regulators, throttle input conditioning, telemetry and protection firmware."
Quick check. Why are capacitors placed right next to the ESC's MOSFETs?
Interfacing with ESCs. The question: How do you interface with ESCs? What other components/controllers are needed? How do they communicate?
An ESC has a simple physical interface: power in from the battery, three wires out to the motor, and a signal wire plus ground from the controller.
What matters most is the language the controller uses on the signal wire. Older systems use pulse widths. Modern ones send digital packets.
The old method is like holding a button down for a certain length of time to say how much power you want. A short press means little, a long press means a lot.
The new method is like sending a written note with a checksum, so mistakes are caught.
The analogy has a gap: the pulse method relies on exact timing, so noise and calibration errors matter, while the digital note is much more robust.
A drone's signal and power topology (two of four motors shown). Power runs battery to distribution board to each ESC, and the flight controller is a low-power consumer.
Each ESC also gets its own throttle line from the flight controller (the arrows from the flight controller to each ESC); an optional telemetry wire back is not drawn.
RC PWM: a 1 to 2 milliseconds pulse, repeated, where the width is the throttle. DShot: a digital throttle protocol that sends a packet of 16 bits (each bit is a single 1 or 0).
CRC: a short check code that catches transmission errors. Arming: a safety step where the ESC wants to see minimum throttle first.
Failsafe: what the ESC does if the signal disappears.
With RC PWM, a 1 milliseconds pulse means zero throttle and 2 milliseconds means full. A 1. 5 milliseconds pulse is halfway, 50% .
With DShot, the packet has 16 bits: 11 for throttle, 1 to ask for telemetry (data sent back, like rpm), and 4 for the CRC.
At 150,000 bits per second, that packet takes 16 / 150,000, about 107 microseconds. The controller must also share a common ground (the 0 volts reference wire) with the ESC.
That is the whole idea: the controller sends a command, and the ESC reads it.
"The ESC takes battery power, a signal-plus-ground from the controller, and optionally returns telemetry; three wires go to the motor.

The command is either an analog RC pulse of 1 to 2 milliseconds, Oneshot or Multishot for faster updates, or digital DShot, which sends a 16-bit packet with 11-bit throttle and a CRC at 150 to 1200 kbit/s.
Bigger systems use UART or CAN. The controller is usually a flight controller or MCU with timer and DMA outputs, and the ESC needs a common ground, arming and a failsafe."

Design an ESC. The question: Design an ESC.
Designing an ESC is a sequence of choices that start with what it must do. First list the requirements: motor, battery voltage, current, command interface and size.
Then pick an architecture, size the key parts (MOSFETs, shunt, capacitors), write the firmware, and test it carefully.
It is like designing a bridge. You do not start by choosing steel. You start by asking what load it must carry and how far it must span.
Then you choose the structure, calculate the size of each part, and test it before anyone drives on it.
The analogy has one gap: an ESC's "load" includes heat, so thermal checks are as important as electrical ones.
The architecture I would draw.
Power flows from the battery down through the bridge; BEC and gate supplies hang off the input rail; the MCU gets position (back-EMF) and current feedback and commands the gate driver.
Requirements: voltage, current, interface, size and cost the design must meet.
R ds(on) : a MOSFET's resistance when switched on, which sets how much heat it makes while conducting. Shunt: a tiny resistor used to measure current.
Dead-time: a short pause so the two switches on one motor wire are never on at once.
Bootstrap: a capacitor circuit that gives the upper switches the extra voltage they need to turn on.
Say the target is a 4S LiPo battery (four lithium cells in series, 16. 8 volts when full) and 30 amps continuous. Each MOSFET has 2. 5 milliohms on-resistance.
Two are in the current path, so the loss is I to the 2R = 30² times 0. 005 = 4. 5 watts . A 1 milliohms shunt gives 30 millivolts and loses 30² times 0. 001 = 0. 9 watts.
An efficient switching regulator (a buck converter) makes the 5 volts supply, because a linear regulator, which burns the extra voltage as heat, would waste far more.
That is the whole idea: requirements first, then size each part with simple numbers.
"I'd clarify the spec first: say 4S, 30 amps continuous, 60 amps burst, DShot input, 5 volts BEC.

Architecture: sensorless six-step on a small MCU, three half-bridges of 40 volts low- R ds(on) MOSFETs, a three-phase gate driver with bootstrap and dead-time, back-EMF dividers, a low-side shunt and a buck BEC.
Sizing: about 7 watts total loss at 30 amps, bus capacitors for 15 amps ripple, 1 microfarads bootstrap.
Then firmware for startup and protections, and a test plan: double-pulse, thermal, desync, regen."
Quick check. Why would you choose a 40 volts MOSFET for a 4S (16. 8 volts max) ESC?
Specifying an ESC. The question: How do you spec an ESC?
Specifying an ESC means matching it to the motor and the battery.
Check that its voltage rating covers the battery, that its current rating covers what the motor really draws (plus margin), and that it speaks the right command protocol.
Then check the extras: whether it can switch fast enough for the motor's speed, the BEC, size, cooling and protections.
It is like buying an extension cord or power strip. You add up what will be plugged in, then choose one rated well above that. A cord rated just at the limit will overheat.
The same goes for an ESC: rate it above the measured load, not the number on the motor's label.
The analogy has a gap: an ESC can also be destroyed by too much voltage, not just too much current.
Spec an ESC from the application inward: battery and motor determine the electrical needs; features and packaging follow; bench validation closes the loop.
Any failure at the end sends you back to a larger rating or better cooling.
Cell count (S): the number of battery cells in series. A 4S LiPo is 4 times 4. 2 volts = 16. 8 volts fully charged.
Continuous current rating: the current the ESC can carry without overheating. Burst rating: a short-term current limit, only meaningful with stated test conditions.
Protocol: the throttle language, such as DShot. BEC: the built-in 5 volts supply for outside electronics.
A 4S pack is 4 times 4. 2 = 16. 8 volts, so the ESC must be rated for at least 4S. Suppose you measure 38 amps at full throttle. Add 25 to 50% margin: 38 times 1.
25 about 48 amps and 38 times 1. 5 = 57 amps. So pick an ESC in the 50 amps class or above.

Then check speed: a motor with a 34,000 rpm (revolutions per minute) no-load speed and 7 pole pairs (north-south magnet pairs) needs its coils switched through 34,000 times 7 / 60 about 4,000 cycles per second (4 kilohertz).
The ESC must handle that. That is the whole idea: voltage, current, protocol and speed must all match.
"I start from the battery and motor. Voltage: the ESC must be rated for the pack's maximum, 16. 8 volts for 4S, with margin.
Current: take the motor's measured full-throttle current on the real prop, and choose an ESC with continuous rating 25 to 50% above it, checking burst duration.
Then compatibility: protocol like DShot, firmware that supports the motor's electrical rpm, BEC if needed, protections, telemetry.
Finally the practical side, size, cooling, wires and I'd verify temperature on a bench test."

What is a stepper motor. The question: What is a stepper motor?
A stepper motor moves in small, fixed steps. Each pulse sent to its driver (the electronics that power its coils) turns the shaft by one step.
By counting pulses, you know how far it has turned, usually without any position sensor. It can also hold its position firmly when stopped.
Think of the second hand on a ticking clock. It does not sweep smoothly. It jumps a fixed amount on each tick, and counting ticks tells you the time passed.
A stepper works the same way, with each pulse as a tick.
The analogy breaks down at one point: a clock cannot be overloaded, but a stepper pushed too hard silently skips a step and loses count.
Where steppers sit in the motor family, and the subdivision inside steppers. The hybrid, bipolar stepper (NEMA 17 and similar) is the one you will meet in practice.
Step: one fixed angular move of the shaft, caused by one pulse. Phase: one of the motor's coil groups. Most steppers have two.
Holding torque: the turning force that keeps the shaft in place when the coils are powered but the motor is still.
Open loop: control by counting pulses, with no sensor to check the result. Missed step: a step the motor fails to make, so the position count is wrong.
A common stepper turns 1. 8° per step. A full turn is 360° / 1. 8° = 200 steps . To rotate a quarter turn, send 200 / 4 = 50 pulses . To rotate half a turn, send 100.
If you then stop sending pulses but leave the coils powered, the shaft stays put against a push, up to the holding torque.
That is the whole idea: one pulse, one step, and the count tells the position.
"A stepper is a brushless motor that moves in fixed angular steps, one per pulse to the driver, so you can position it by counting pulses, usually open loop.
The common hybrid type has two phases and 50 rotor teeth, giving 1. 8 degrees per step, 200 per revolution.
It has high holding torque at standstill, but torque falls with speed and it can lose steps if overloaded. Windings are bipolar or unipolar."
Quick check. What does a stepper motor do on each pulse from the driver?
How a stepper motor works. The question: How does it work?
A stepper motor works by moving a magnetic field in small jumps and letting the rotor (the spinning part, which carries a magnet) chase it.
Powering one coil makes the rotor line up with it. Powering the next coil moves the target slightly, and the rotor follows.
Repeating the sequence turns the shaft one step at a time.
Imagine a compass needle surrounded by electromagnets. Switch on the one to the north, and the needle swings to point at it.
Switch it off and the one to the east on, and the needle swings 90° to face east. Keep stepping around the ring, and the needle turns around in jumps.
The analogy has a gap: real steppers have many small teeth, so each step is much smaller, such as 1. 8°.
A simplified four-pole PM stepper (real hybrids have many more teeth, same idea). Energising coil A as an N pole attracts the rotor's S end to the top.
Turning A off and energising B moves the equilibrium 90° clockwise; the rotor follows. Energising A' next carries it another 90°. Reversing the sequence reverses the direction.
Phase: one of the fixed coil groups, turned on or off in a sequence. Full step: a move made by switching whole phases on.
Microstepping: sharing the current smoothly between the two phases so the rotor settles between full steps, for smoother motion. Open loop: counting pulses without feedback.
Missed step: the rotor falls behind when the load is too big.
A typical stepper (the common "hybrid" kind) has two phases and 50 teeth on its rotor. The angle from one tooth to the next, the tooth pitch, is 360° / 50 = 7. 2° .
A full cycle of the four-state sequence moves the rotor one tooth pitch, so each of the four steps is 7. 2° / 4 = 1. 8° .
Run the sequence the other way and the motor turns the other way. That is the whole idea: step the field, and the rotor follows.
"A stepper moves by walking a magnetic field in small jumps.
Energise a coil and the rotor, a magnet or toothed iron, aligns with it; switch to the next coil and the equilibrium moves one step, so the rotor follows.
In a 2-phase, 50-tooth motor, four steps make one electrical cycle, 7. 2 degrees, each step 1. 8. Driving the phases as sine and cosine gives microsteps.
It runs open loop by counting pulses, and the driver uses current chopping from a high supply voltage so the coil current can build quickly at speed."
Quick check. In a stepper, what makes the rotor move from one step to the next?
Stepper motor applications. The question: What are its applications?
Steppers are used wherever you want accurate, repeatable positioning at low to moderate speed without paying for feedback sensors.
You tell them how many steps to move, and they go there. 3D printers, computer-controlled cutting machines (CNC), camera focus and medical pumps are all good examples.
Think of walking to a spot by counting steps. If each step is exactly 0. 5 m, then 20 steps takes you 10 m, with no tape measure. A stepper works like that.
The analogy has a gap: if a stepper slips and misses a step, it does not notice, so the count is quietly wrong from then on.
A rough decision tree.
Steppers sit in the low-cost, low-to-moderate speed corner where open-loop counting is enough, with closed-loop steppers extending that corner when a missed step is not acceptable.
Open-loop positioning: moving to a position by counting steps, without a sensor. Microstep: a fraction of a full step, made by splitting the current between the motor's two coils.
Holding torque: strong torque at standstill that holds position. Lead screw: a threaded rod that turns rotation into straight-line motion.
Closed-loop stepper: a stepper with an added encoder that catches missed steps.
A 3D printer belt drive uses a pulley with 20 teeth spaced 2 mm apart, so one turn moves the belt 40 mm.
The stepper has 200 steps per turn, with 16 microsteps each, so 3,200 microsteps per turn. That gives 3,200 / 40 = 80 microsteps per mm , or 40 / 3,200 = 0. 0125 mm (12.
5 µm) per microstep. No encoder is needed. That is the whole idea: known angle per step gives known distance.

"Steppers are used where I want accurate positioning at low to moderate speed without feedback: 3D printers and CNC axes, printers and scanners, camera focus mechanisms, syringe pumps, valves and dampers, telescope mounts and gauge needles.
They fit because position equals step count, they hold torque at standstill, they give high low-speed torque without a gearbox, and they're cheap with simple drivers.
They're a poor fit for high speed, high efficiency or applications where a missed step is unacceptable without an encoder."

Stepper advantages over other motors. The question: What are its advantages compared to other types of motors?
The main advantage of a stepper is that it gives accurate, repeatable positioning without feedback.
A brushed or brushless (BLDC) motor spins at a speed set by voltage, so you need a sensor and a control loop to stop at the right place. A stepper moves a fixed angle per pulse.
That makes it cheap and easy to use.
Picture a staircase versus a ramp. On a staircase, you can only stand on certain steps, so counting steps tells you your height.
On a ramp, you can stop anywhere, so you need to look and judge where you are. A stepper is the staircase and a DC motor is the ramp.
The analogy has a gap: if you are pushed hard enough, a stepper can skip a step without telling you.
Shapes, not data. A stepper's usable torque collapses with speed because winding inductance slows the current and back-EMF eats the voltage.
A brushed DC motor's torque only falls linearly towards its no-load speed, and a BLDC with field control holds it flat up to base speed.
If your operating point is to the right of about 600 to 1000 rpm, the stepper is usually the wrong motor.
Open loop: control with no position feedback. Holding torque: torque at zero speed that holds the position. Encoder: a sensor that reports the shaft's position.
Missed step: a step the motor fails to make under overload. Control loop: electronics that compare where the motor is with where it should be, and correct it.
A stepper has 200 steps per turn and drives a lead screw (a threaded rod that turns rotation into straight-line motion) that moves 2 mm per turn. Each step moves 2 / 200 = 0.
01 mm. To move a carriage 10 mm, send 10 / 0. 01 = 1,000 pulses . No encoder or tuning is needed, and the carriage holds position when it stops.
That is the whole idea: one pulse is one known movement.

"A stepper's big advantages are open-loop positioning without an encoder or tuning, full holding torque at standstill, high torque at low speed so it can drive loads directly, no brushes, and low cost with a simple step/dir interface; error also doesn't accumulate.
The downsides are torque falling with speed, low efficiency and heat because it always draws full current, resonance, and silent missed steps.
So steppers win on cost and simplicity at low speed, and servos or BLDCs win on speed, efficiency and knowing their position."

Stepper from a microcontroller. The question: How do you control a stepper motor from a microcontroller? What other components do you need?
A stepper motor turns in small, fixed steps: one electrical pulse, one step.
A microcontroller pin can only supply a few milliamps, but the motor needs an amp or two, so you put a driver chip in between.
The microcontroller only sends "step" pulses and a "direction" level. The driver does all the heavy electrical work.
Picture a foreman and a crane operator. The foreman (the microcontroller) never touches the crane. He just shouts "one notch!" and "this way!"
The operator (the driver) has the strength and the controls to actually move the load.
The analogy breaks in one place: the foreman never sees where the crane ended up, so if it slips, he does not know.
Only STEP, DIR and ENABLE (plus microstep-select lines, not wired here) come from the MCU.
The driver draws motor current from its own supply, decoupled by a bulk capacitor right at the VMOT pin, and drives each coil with an H-bridge (outputs 1 amps/1B and 2 amps/2B).
All grounds are common.
Stepper motor: a motor that moves a fixed small angle for each pulse. Driver: a chip that pushes current through the motor's coils (windings), in both directions, and limits it.
STEP / DIR: the two control wires. Each pulse on STEP moves one step (or one microstep); the level on DIR picks the direction.
Microstepping: splitting each full step into smaller slices, such as 16, for smoother motion.
Current limit: the maximum winding current you set on the driver, usually near the motor's rated current.
Homing: driving to a limit switch to set position zero, because the motor never reports its position.
Take a 200-step motor and set the driver to 16 microsteps. One turn then needs 200 times 16 equals 3200 pulses.
To turn once per second, the microcontroller sends 3200 pulses per second, about one every 312 microseconds.
That is the whole idea: pulses in, motion out, with a driver in the middle.
"I use a step/direction driver such as an A4988, DRV8825 or TMC2209: it contains the dual H-bridge, current chopper and microstep sequencer.
The microcontroller sends STEP pulses, a DIR level, an enable and microstep-select lines.
I add a separate motor supply well above the rated voltage, say 24 volts, with a bulk capacitor at the driver, a common ground, and a current limit set via VREF.
In firmware I generate steps with a timer, ramp acceleration, and use limit switches for homing."

Specifying a stepper motor. The question: How do you spec a stepper motor?
Specifying a stepper means choosing a motor that can actually do your job. You start from what the load needs: how much twist (torque), how fast, and how precisely.
Then you check that a candidate motor can deliver that twist at that speed.
Do not trust the big holding-torque number on the datasheet, because a stepper's torque drops as it spins faster.
Think of a person pushing a heavy cart. Standing still, they can push very hard. Once the cart must move fast, they run out of breath and push much less.
Holding torque is the standing-still push. The speed curve is the running push, and that is the one that matters.
The analogy breaks in one place: a stepper that runs out of push silently loses steps instead of slowing down.
The spec flow. The loop back to motor selection is normal: an inertia or thermal check often forces a different winding, frame or supply voltage.
Torque: the twisting effort a motor delivers, in newton-meters (N·m). Holding torque: torque at standstill. It is the zero-speed number only.
Pull-out torque: the most torque the motor gives at a given speed without skipping steps.
Torque-speed curve: the datasheet graph of pull-out torque at each speed, for a given supply voltage. Lead screw: a threaded rod that turns rotation into straight-line motion.
Its lead is the distance moved per turn.
A motor lifts a 2 kg carriage on an 8 mm lead screw that is about 35% efficient. Lifting it takes about 20 N. The screw turns that into about 0.
075 N·m of motor torque, once you allow for its losses. Double it for margin: 0. 15 N·m. Moving at 50 mm/s is 6.
25 screw turns per second, so a 200-step motor runs at 1250 full steps per second. Now read the torque-speed curve at your supply voltage, at 1250 steps per second.
If it shows at least 0. 15 N·m, the motor passes. That is the whole idea.
"I work backwards from the load: compute the torque including friction, gravity and acceleration, for example T equals FL over (2 pi ) for a lead screw, and the step rate needed for the speed.
Then I pick a motor whose pull-out torque at that speed and my supply voltage is at least 1. 5 to 2 times the requirement, not just a big holding torque.
I check inertia ratio, winding inductance versus speed, rated current and heating at hold, resolution with microsteps, frame size and shaft loads, and whether I need a closed-loop version."

How steppers hold position. The question: How do stepper motors hold a certain position?
A stepper holds its position by magnetism.
When you keep a steady current flowing in the right coils, the rotor (the turning part) settles into the spot where it lines up with the magnetic field.
If something pushes it away, a magnetic pull brings it back. No sensor or feedback is involved. The cost is that the current must keep flowing, which makes heat.
Picture a marble resting at the bottom of a shallow bowl. Nudge it and it rolls back to the middle, and the harder you push, the stronger the pull back, up to a point.
Push it over the rim and it drops into the next bowl along. The coils make the bowl, and the "holding torque" is how steep the bowl gets before the rim.
The analogy breaks in one place: switch the current off and the bowl nearly vanishes.
Near zero the torque is a straight spring line with stiffness 22. 5 N·m/rad. It bends over and peaks at ±1. 8° (one full step, 90° electrical) at the holding torque.
Beyond that the torque falls and reaches zero at 3. 6° (the red dashed line, unstable); push further and the torque reverses and drags the shaft to the next equilibrium 7.
2° away. The black marker shows the deflection for a 0. 2 N·m static load; the orange dashed lines mark the ±1. 8° torque peaks.
Holding torque: the largest twist the energized motor resists without slipping. Restoring torque: the pull back toward the resting spot when the shaft is pushed away.
Detent torque: the weak holding left when the power is off. Lost step: the rotor jumps to a different resting spot after an overload, and the controller does not know.
Hold current: the current kept in the coils while the motor is stationary.
Take a motor with 0. 45 N·m of holding torque. A load of 0. 225 N·m, half the limit, pushes the shaft only about 0. 6 degrees off its spot, and it stays there.
Raise the load above 0. 45 N·m and the shaft slips by 7. 2 degrees, or a multiple of it. Meanwhile, holding at 1. 7 amps through its two 1. 5 ohm coils burns about 8.
7 watts with no mechanical work. Halving the current cuts the heat to a quarter but also roughly halves the holding torque. That is the whole idea.
"A stepper holds position by magnetic alignment.

With the right coils energised with steady current, the rotor sits in a stable equilibrium, and any displacement creates a restoring torque like a spring, roughly T h sine (N r change in theta) , so no feedback is needed.
Holding torque is the peak of that restoring torque; beyond it the rotor slips by whole electrical cycles.
The cost is continuous current and heat; reducing the current reduces holding torque in proportion. With power off only the small detent torque remains."

What is a servo motor?. The question: What is a servo motor?
A servo motor is a motor packaged with a sensor and a small controller, so it can go to a position you ask for and stay there. The sensor reports where the shaft really is.
The controller compares that with where you wanted it and drives the motor to shrink the difference. "Servo" describes this feedback loop, not a special kind of motor.
Reach for a cup with your eyes open. Your eyes see how far your hand is from the cup.
Your brain turns that gap into a push: a big gap means a big move, and a tiny gap means a tiny move. When the gap reaches zero, you stop.
The analogy breaks in one place: the servo's controller follows a simple rule and is not clever, so a badly tuned one can overshoot and wobble.
The servo loop. Everything in the top-to-bottom chain is the same as an ordinary motor drive; the arrow from the sensor back to the error junction is what turns it into a servo.
Feedback: measuring the output and using that measurement to correct the input. Setpoint: the position you are asking the servo to reach. Error: setpoint minus measurement.
The controller acts on this. Controller: the rule that turns error into a motor command. The simplest pushes in proportion to the error. The common industrial one is called PID.
RC servo: the small hobby servo, commanded by a 1 to 2 milliseconds pulse repeated about every 20 milliseconds.
A hobby servo travels 90 degrees across pulse widths from 1. 0 to 2. 0 milliseconds. You send 1. 5 milliseconds, which means the middle: 45 degrees.
The shaft now sits at 30 degrees, so the error is 15 degrees. The controller drives the motor toward larger angles.
As the shaft approaches 45 degrees the error shrinks, the drive shrinks with it, and the motor stops at zero error. That is the whole idea: a motor plus feedback.
"A servo motor is a motor with a position sensor and a controller built around it, so it goes to a commanded angle and holds it.
The controller compares the command with the sensor reading and drives the motor to shrink the error.
Hobby servos use a small DC motor, gearbox and potentiometer, commanded by a 1 to 2 milliseconds pulse every 20 milliseconds. Industrial ones use brushless motors with encoders.
The feedback is what makes it a servo, not the motor type."
Quick check. What makes a motor system a servo?
How a servo works inside. The question: How does it work?
Inside a hobby servo are a small motor, gears, a position sensor on the output shaft, and a control chip. You send a pulse whose width says the angle you want.
The chip reads the sensor to learn the actual angle, then runs the motor in whichever direction closes the gap. It stops when the two agree.
Imagine steering a boat toward a lighthouse. The lighthouse is the target, and your compass reading is the sensor.
If the lighthouse is far off to the left, you turn the wheel hard left. As you line up, you ease the wheel back toward straight.
When you point right at it, you hold the wheel still. A servo's chip does the same with the motor, many times a second.
Each character is 0. 5 milliseconds, so the frame shown is 20 milliseconds. The three signals are three different commands: widths of 1. 0, 1. 5 and 2. 0 milliseconds.
The servo ignores the frame period and just times how long the line stays high.
Pulse width: how long the signal stays high in each pulse. For a hobby servo it is about 1 to 2 milliseconds, sent every 20 milliseconds, and it sets the target angle.
Potentiometer: a variable resistor on the output shaft. Its voltage tells the chip the angle. Error: target angle minus actual angle.
H-bridge: the switches that let the chip run the motor either way. Deadband: a tiny error range where the chip does nothing, so the motor does not twitch back and forth.
Suppose 1. 0 milliseconds means 0 degrees and 2. 0 milliseconds means 180 degrees. You send 1. 5 milliseconds, so the target is 90 degrees.
The potentiometer says the shaft is at 60 degrees, so the error is +30 degrees and the chip drives the motor forward.
At 85 degrees the error is only 5 degrees, so the drive is gentler. At about 90 degrees the error falls inside the deadband and the drive stops. That is the whole idea.
"The servo measures the width of a 1 to 2 milliseconds pulse that arrives every 20 milliseconds and treats it as a target angle.
A potentiometer on the output shaft reports the actual angle.
The control chip subtracts them to get an error and drives an H-bridge so the motor turns toward the target, roughly proportional to the error, stopping inside a small deadband.
A gearbox trades motor speed for torque. Push on the shaft and the error returns, so it pushes back."

Servo motor applications. The question: What are its applications?
Servos are used wherever something must sit at a chosen position, or follow a chosen motion, and stay accurate even when the load pushes back.
Examples run from a model-airplane flap to a factory robot arm. If you only need to spin something at a steady speed, use a plain motor.
If you only need a short on-off push, use a solenoid.
Think of the steering in a car. You turn the wheel to an angle and the wheels must hold that angle, even when bumps shove them.
That is a servo job: a position, held against disturbances. The ceiling fan above you only needs to spin, and a door latch only needs one quick push.
Neither needs to know a position, so a servo would be wasted on them.
A rough decision chart. Servos win when position or trajectory matters and the load is not guaranteed to be benign, because only a closed loop knows when it has failed to arrive.
Servo: a motor with a sensor and controller that goes to a commanded position and holds it. Trajectory: a path of positions over time, which the servo is asked to follow.
Disturbance rejection: pushing back when something tries to move the output. Torque: the twisting effort at the joint, in newton-meters (N·m).
Stall torque: the most torque the servo gives at zero speed. It is not the torque you can use continuously. Solenoid: a coil that gives a short on-off push.
A robot arm holds a 0. 5 kg payload 0. 30 m from the joint. With the arm horizontal, the joint must supply 0. 5 times 9. 81 times 0. 30 equals 1. 47 N·m.
The arm's own weight raises that to about 1. 9 N·m. Pick a servo with at least double that for acceleration and margin, roughly 3. 8 N·m of stall torque.
That is the whole idea: say what the job needs, then size from torque.

"Servos go wherever something has to be at a position or follow a trajectory and hold it against load: RC steering and control surfaces, robot arm joints, camera pan-tilts and gimbals, CNC and 3D printer axes, pick-and-place machines, throttle and valve actuators.
I'd use a servo when I need angle or trajectory with disturbance rejection. A plain motor is for constant speed and a solenoid for on-off strokes.
Sizing starts with joint torque, force times lever arm, with about 2x margin."

Servo advantages over other motors. The question: What are its advantages compared to other types of motors?
A servo's big advantage is that it measures where it is.
Because of that, it reaches its target under any load, it pushes back when disturbed, and it knows when it has failed to arrive.
A stepper only counts steps and trusts that it got there. A plain motor has no idea where it is. The price of the servo's advantage is cost, extra parts, and tuning.
Imagine walking across a dark room by counting exactly 20 paces. That is a stepper. If you slip once, you never find out, and you end up in the wrong spot.
A servo is the same walk with the lights on: you look, see you are short, and take another step. The analogy breaks in one place: the lights cost money.
The sensor, the drive and the tuning all add expense, so for easy jobs counting paces is fine.
Shapes, not data for any specific motor.
The stepper's torque has halved by about 1200 rpm in this model; the servo stays flat until it reaches rated speed, with a dashed peak envelope for short bursts.
The brushed DC at fixed voltage falls linearly from stall torque to no-load speed because back-EMF eats the voltage.
Open loop / closed loop: running without feedback, or with a measured result fed back to correct it. Following error: the gap between commanded and actual position.
A big one raises a fault. Stepper: a motor that moves a fixed step per pulse and never checks where it ended up. Phase (winding): one of a motor's coils of wire.
Current through it makes heat.
Compare two motors sitting still, holding a position. A stepper with 1. 5 amps in each of two phases, 2 ohms each, burns 2 times 1.
5 squared times 2 equals 9 watts in its windings, even with no load. A servo holding a balanced load draws almost nothing, because its current follows the load.
Now overload both: the stepper silently loses steps, and the servo shows a following-error fault.
That is the whole idea: feedback buys accuracy, fault detection and efficient current use.
"A servo's advantage is feedback: it knows where it is, so it's accurate under any load, holds position by pushing back and reports when it fails to arrive.
Its torque stays flat out to rated speed with brief higher peaks, whereas a stepper's torque falls with speed.
It's efficient because current follows load, while a stepper burns full current at rest.
Disadvantages are cost, complexity and tuning, so I'd pick a stepper for simple light low-speed jobs."

Controlling a servo from an MCU. The question: How do you control a servo motor from a microcontroller? What other components do you need?
A hobby servo needs two things from you: a timing signal and a proper power supply.
The signal is a short pulse sent every 20 milliseconds, and its width (1 to 2 milliseconds) says which angle you want. The microcontroller makes this pulse with a hardware timer.
The power must come from a separate supply, because a servo can pull an amp or more and would crash the microcontroller's own supply.
Think of the servo as a worker who reads a note you pass every 20 milliseconds. The note's wording is the pulse width, and it needs no strength from you.
But the worker also needs a big meal, which is the power. If you try to feed the worker from your own small lunchbox (the microcontroller's regulator), you go hungry and faint.
Both of you must also stand on the same floor, the common ground, or the note means nothing.
Three connections matter. The signal goes through a small series resistor. The servo's V+ comes from its own supply with a bulk capacitor across the servo's pins.
All grounds join at one rail so the MCU's ground reference and the servo's return current do not share a long, resistive path.
Hardware timer / PWM: a counter in the chip that produces exact pulses with no help from the program. Prescaler: a divider that slows the timer's clock to a convenient tick.
Stall current: the current drawn when the shaft is blocked. Size the supply for this. Bulk capacitor: a large capacitor next to the servo that supplies brief current spikes.
Common ground: all grounds joined, so the signal has a shared reference.
With a 16 megahertz clock, use the prescaler to divide by 16, giving a 1 megahertz timer. Each tick is 1 microseconds.
To command the middle position, end each pulse after 1500 ticks, which is 1. 5 milliseconds.
Feed the servo from its own 5 to 6 volts supply, with a 470 microfarads capacitor beside it and the ground tied to the microcontroller's ground. That is the whole idea.
"I generate a 50 hertz pulse with the MCU's hardware timer, 1 to 2 milliseconds wide, e. g. 1 megahertz tick, period 20,000, compare 1000 to 2000.
The servo gets its own 5 to 6 volts supply sized for stall current, with a bulk capacitor near it, because the MCU can't supply those spikes.
Grounds are common, and I put a few hundred ohms in series with the signal. For a DIY servo from a DC motor I'd add an H-bridge, encoder and a PID loop."

How to spec a servo motor. The question: How do you spec a servo motor?
Specifying a servo means turning a mechanical job into a motor choice using numbers.
You work out the motion the load needs, then the torque that motion demands, both the peak and the average heating torque.
Then you pick a gear ratio, check that the motor and its supply can reach the speed, and add margin.
Think of choosing a bicycle gear for a hill. The hill and your rider weight set the push you need.
A low gear trades speed for push, so the rider's legs (the motor) can spin quickly and lightly while the wheel turns slowly and strongly.
But even in the best gear, you cannot pedal all day at your sprint effort. Sprinting is peak torque. Sustainable effort is continuous torque.
The speed ramps up to 10. 5 rad/s then back down. The torque is 1. 50 N·m while accelerating and flips to -1. 30 N·m while braking (friction helps stop the load).
The motor must supply the peak, and heating follows the RMS of this torque over the full cycle including dwell.
Inertia: how hard a load is to spin up or slow down, in kg·m². Torque equals inertia times angular acceleration.
Peak torque: the most torque for a short burst, needed to accelerate the load. Continuous torque: what the motor can supply forever without overheating.
RMS torque: the average heating effect of torque over the whole cycle. Compare it to the continuous rating. Gear ratio ( N ): how many motor turns for one output turn.
Through the gears, the motor feels the load's inertia divided by N squared .
Move a load with inertia 0. 02 kg·m² by 90 degrees in 0. 3 seconds.
Speeding up and slowing down evenly gives an angular acceleration of about 70 rad/s² (a radian is about 57 degrees). The acceleration torque is 0. 02 times 70 equals 1.
4 N·m, plus 0. 1 N·m of friction, so the peak is about 1. 5 N·m. Over a 1 seconds cycle with a long rest, the RMS torque is only about 0. 77 N·m. The motor needs peak above 1.
5 and continuous above 0. 77, with margin. That is the whole idea.
"I'd work from the load: compute the motion profile, then peak torque as inertia times acceleration plus friction and gravity, and RMS torque for thermal duty.
Pick a gear ratio, remembering reflected inertia drops as N squared. Check the motor's torque-speed curve covers the peak and the RMS is below continuous with margin.
Then supply voltage and current, feedback resolution, size and environment. For a hobby servo it's torque in kg·cm with 2x margin, speed in s per 60 degrees, and voltage."

Why servos are so precise. The question: How are servo motors so precise in their movement?
A servo is precise because it never trusts the motor. It measures where the shaft really is, compares that with the command, and keeps correcting until the error is nearly zero.
So the precision comes from the sensor and the loop, not from how well the motor behaves.
Be careful about one word, though: resolution (the sensor's smallest step) is not the same as accuracy (being at the true position).
Think of cruise control in a car. Without it, a hill slows you down and you end up wherever the road takes you.
With it, the car measures its speed, sees the drop, and adds throttle until the speed matches the setting.
The analogy also shows the catch: if the speedometer itself reads wrong, cruise control holds the wrong speed very precisely.
Each extra bit halves the step.
Beyond about 17–20 bits, extra resolution mostly shows sensor noise and mechanical imperfection rather than real position information, which is why you also see accuracy specified in arc-seconds.
Encoder: a sensor that reports the shaft angle as a count. Resolution: the smallest position step the sensor can report. Accuracy: how close the position is to the true one.
Stiffness: how little the shaft moves when a load pushes on it. A loop that pushes harder for each bit of error is stiffer.
Integral term: a control part that keeps increasing the drive until the steady error reaches zero. Backlash: the free play between meshing gears.
A 17-bit encoder splits one turn into 2 to the 17 equals 131 072 counts, so each count is about 0. 0027 degrees.
Put it on the motor behind a 10:1 gearbox, and the output steps are ten times finer, about 0. 00027 degrees. Now give the gearbox 0.
5 degrees of backlash and hang a 100 mm arm on it. That slop lets the arm tip wander about 0. 87 mm, and the encoder on the motor cannot even see it.
That is the whole idea: feedback gives the precision, and the mechanics limit it.
"A servo is precise because it measures the shaft position and keeps correcting the error, so precision comes from the sensor and loop, not the motor.
A high-resolution encoder, say 17 bits is about 0.
003 degrees, gearing that makes output steps finer, high loop gain for stiffness and an integral term that drives steady-state error to zero.
Resolution isn't accuracy though: backlash, flex, friction and sensor error set the real limit."

Motor and solenoid failure modes. The question: What are some failure modes of motors/solenoids? How can they be avoided?
Motors and solenoids are coils of copper wire that turn current into motion. They fail in four main ways.
They overheat, because current turns into heat when the motion is blocked. They make voltage spikes when switched off, because a coil resists sudden changes in current.
They wear mechanically, and they suffer from the environment. Each failure has a standard cure, such as current limiting, a flyback diode, or a duty-cycle limit.
Picture a water pipe with a heavy flow. Slam the tap shut and the moving water has nowhere to go, so pressure spikes and can burst a fitting.
That is the voltage spike from switching off a coil.
Now picture pushing hard against a wall: you spend lots of effort and nothing moves, so all of it becomes heat in your muscles. That is a stalled motor.
Most root causes fall into four buckets. Thermal and electrical stress are controlled by the drive; mechanical wear and environment by design and maintenance.
Stall: the shaft cannot turn. With no back-EMF, only the coil's (winding's) resistance limits the current. Back-EMF: the voltage a spinning motor generates against the supply.
Flyback diode: a diode across the coil that gives its current a safe path when the switch opens. Duty cycle: the fraction of time a solenoid is energized. It limits heating.
A 12 volts motor has a 2. 4 ohm winding. At stall it draws 12 over 2. 4 equals 5 amps and dissipates 5 squared times 2. 4 equals 60 watts.
That heat goes into about 30 g of copper, which warms by roughly 5 degrees Celsius per second.
From 25 degrees Celsius it reaches 155 degrees Celsius in about 25 seconds, which is the limit for common insulation.
Separately, switching off 1 amps in a 10 millihenries coil in 10 microseconds would give a 1 kilovolts spike with no diode or other clamp. That is the whole idea.
"Main failure modes are thermal, electrical and mechanical.
Stall or overload makes current V over R, and the winding overheats in seconds, so use current limiting, thermal protection and stall detection.
Switching off the coil produces an inductive spike that kills drivers, so use a flyback diode or snubber.
Brushes, bearings and plungers wear or stick, and solenoids burn out if held on beyond their duty cycle, so pull in at full voltage and hold with PWM. Derate and add fuses."
Quick check. Why does a stalled motor draw so much current?
Dangers of motors and solenoids. The question: What are some dangers when using motors/solenoid?
Motors and solenoids are dangerous for three groups: people, the equipment, and the rest of the system.
People can be pinched, entangled, burned, shocked, or hurt by a sudden restart. Equipment can be wrecked by voltage spikes, regeneration, or overheating.
The cure is to reduce the energy and force involved, then add protections that work even when the software fails.
Think of a spinning bicycle wheel held off the ground. Even after you stop pedaling, it keeps turning for a long time and will catch a finger or a sleeve.
The wheel is full of stored energy that does not vanish when you cut the power. Motors, springs, raised loads, and capacitors all hold energy like that.
Energy grows with the square of speed.
Tripling speed gives nine times the energy, so a spinning load needs guarding even if the motor is small, and coasting to a stop after power-off takes time unless a brake is applied.
Stored energy: energy held in a spinning rotor, a spring, a coil, or a capacitor that remains after the power is cut.
E-stop: an emergency stop that removes power by hardware, independent of the controller. Fail-safe: a design where a failure leaves the load in a safe state.
Regeneration: a decelerating or back-driven motor acting as a generator and pushing energy back to the supply.
Gate pulldown: a resistor that holds the transistor (the electronic switch driving the motor) off while the microcontroller pin floats, connected to nothing, during reset.
A hobby servo with 20 kg·cm of torque (twisting force), or 1. 96 N·m, pushes with 1. 96 over 0. 02 equals 98 N at the end of its 20 mm arm (the horn).
A small motor's rotor (its spinning part) at 3000 rpm can store about 9. 9 J and keeps spinning after power-off. Now the microcontroller resets with no gate pulldown.
The pin floats, the transistor may turn on, and the motor lurches.
That is the whole idea: find the energy and force, then limit it with protection that does not depend on firmware.
"Dangers are to people, equipment and the system.

People: pinching and entanglement, a 20 kg·cm servo gives about 100 N at 2 cm; unexpected restart after a reset; burns from stalled motors; shock from mains or high-voltage supplies; fire from battery shorts.
Equipment: inductive spikes that kill drivers, regeneration that raises the supply, stall overheating.
Mitigation: low voltage, guards, torque and current limits, hardware e-stop, flyback clamps, safe defaults."
