What to measure on a motor or solenoid. The question: What properties do you want to measure when using a motor/solenoid?
Before adding sensors to a motor or solenoid, ask what each reading is for.
There are three purposes: protecting it (current, temperature, supply voltage), controlling it (speed, position, torque), and checking its health (power, efficiency, vibration, trends).
Many of these can be worked out from cheap electrical readings. Current is the single most useful one.
Think of a car dashboard. The temperature gauge protects the engine. The speedometer lets you control the car. The trip computer's fuel economy tracks health over time.
The analogy breaks in one useful way: a motor often needs no dedicated gauge, because current and voltage already carry the information.
Three electrical measurements (I, V, R) yield torque, speed, power, heating, stall detection and winding temperature. Dedicated sensors improve accuracy but are not always needed.
Torque constant ( K t ): newton-meters of torque per amp of current. Torque is roughly K t times I . Back-EMF: the voltage a spinning motor generates. It tells you speed.
Winding temperature: the hottest, most critical temperature. Copper's resistance rises about 0. 39% per degree Celsius, so resistance reveals it.
Efficiency: mechanical output power divided by electrical input power. Current signature: the shape of coil current over time. A solenoid's shows a dip when the plunger moves.
A motor on 12 volts draws 2 amps while giving 0. 04 N·m at 3000 rpm. Electrical power in is 12 times 2 equals 24 watts.
At 3000 rpm the shaft turns at about 314 rad/s (radians per second; one turn is 2π radians), so power out is 0. 04 times 314 equals 12. 6 watts.
Efficiency is about 52%, and the other 11. 4 watts is heat. Separately, a winding that reads 2. 0 ohms cold and 2. 6 ohms hot has warmed by about 76 degrees Celsius.
That is the whole idea: a few electrical readings give torque, power, and temperature.
"I'd measure by purpose. Protection: current, winding temperature and supply voltage.
Control: speed and position from an encoder or back-EMF, and torque, which comes from current since torque is about Kt times current.
Health: input power, efficiency, vibration, and trends like winding resistance, which also gives temperature.
For solenoids I'd add the current waveform and stroke time to know whether the plunger actually seated. Current is the single most valuable measurement."
Quick check. Which single measurement gives torque, stall detection and overload protection for a DC motor?
Monitoring a motor with sensors. The question: How can these properties be monitored? What sensors/components can you use?
To monitor a motor, you build a small sensing chain for each quantity you care about. A sensor turns the physical thing into a tiny electrical signal.
An amplifier or filter makes the signal usable. Then an ADC (a converter from voltage to a number) hands it to the microcontroller.
For current, the usual sensor is a very small resistor called a shunt. For temperature, it is often a thermistor.
Imagine measuring how fast water flows in a pipe by squeezing in one short, narrow section and reading the tiny pressure difference across it.
The difference is small, so you attach a magnifying gauge to make it readable. The shunt is the narrow section, and the amplifier is the magnifier.
Every quantity has the same skeleton. Note the parallel hardware path: fast faults must not wait for the ADC and firmware loop.
Shunt resistor: a tiny resistor in the current path. Its voltage drop, V equals I times R , measures the current.
Current-sense amplifier: an amplifier built to boost that small voltage drop. ADC: a converter that turns a voltage into a number the microcontroller can read.
NTC thermistor: a resistor whose resistance falls as it warms. It is cheap and sensitive. Gain: how many times an amplifier multiplies its input voltage.
Pass 10 amps through a 5 milliohms shunt. The drop is 10 times 0. 005 equals 0. 05 volts, or 50 millivolts. The shunt also burns 10 squared times 0. 005 equals 0. 5 watts.
An amplifier with a gain of 50 turns 50 millivolts into 2. 5 volts, which fits a 3. 3 volts ADC. A 12-bit ADC splits 3. 3 volts into 4096 steps of about 0.
8 millivolts, so each step is about 3. 2 milliamps of motor current. That is the whole idea: small signal, amplify, digitize.
"One chain per quantity. Current: low-value shunt, current-sense amplifier and ADC, with a comparator for fast trips, or a Hall sensor if I need isolation.
Temperature: NTC thermistor on the housing through a divider, RTD or thermocouple for accuracy or range, IR if contactless.
Speed and position: encoder or Hall sensors into a timer. Bus voltage: divider to ADC. Vibration: accelerometer.
I'd synchronise sampling to the PWM, filter, and watch common-mode voltage and layout."
Quick check. What is the role of the current-sense amplifier in a shunt measurement?
Acting on motor monitoring data. The question: How would you alter the behavior of the motor/solenoid based on the observed data?
Acting on monitoring data means turning a reading into a response that fits how bad and how fast the problem is. A short circuit needs an instant hardware cutoff.
A slow overheating needs a gentle reduction in current and, if it keeps rising, a shutdown. A stall needs a stop and a few retries.
You choose thresholds carefully, so the system does not trip on harmless events.
Picture a bucket with a small hole in the bottom. Water poured in is the heat made by current. Water leaking out is the heat the motor sheds to the air.
A short burst of extra pouring is fine. Pour too much for too long and it overflows: overheating. The protection watches the water level, not the instantaneous pour rate.
Every response has a natural timescale set by the physics it protects against.
Fast electrical events need analogue hardware; slow thermal events are better handled by a model that remembers history.
Hardware trip: a simple circuit that shuts off the motor's power switches within microseconds and keeps them off, with no firmware involved.
I to the 2t model: a running total of squared current over time, which estimates accumulated heat. Derating: smoothly lowering the allowed current as temperature rises.
Hysteresis: different trip and reset points, so the system does not chatter on and off.
Blanking: ignoring a signal briefly, such as start-up inrush, so it does not look like a fault.
Take a 2.

4 ohm winding that settles 5 degrees Celsius warmer for each watt, may rise at most 105 degrees Celsius, and heats with a 2-minute time constant (the time to get about two-thirds of the way to its final temperature).
It can carry about 2. 96 amps forever. At 5 amps it reaches the limit after about 52 seconds. At 4 amps it takes about 95 seconds.
So the controller tolerates a short 5 amps burst, and trips only if the overload lasts. One fixed current threshold cannot do that. That is the whole idea.
"I'd match the response to severity. Shorts trip a hardware comparator immediately. Overcurrent gets cycle-by-cycle limiting.
Slow overload and heat use an I squared t or thermal model to derate smoothly, then shut down with hysteresis.
Stall, meaning high current and no motion for a set time, stops the drive, retries a few times and latches.
I'd also compensate for supply droop, limit decel to avoid regeneration, run solenoids at peak then hold current, and log events for maintenance."
Quick check. Why add hysteresis to an overtemperature shutdown?
Measuring motor or solenoid current. The question: How do you determine how much current a motor/solenoid is drawing?
To measure the current in a motor or solenoid, the usual method is a shunt: a very small resistor in the current path.
The current makes a small voltage across it, V equals I times R . An amplifier scales that voltage up so the microcontroller's ADC (its voltage-to-number converter) can read it.
The catch is that "current drawn" depends on where you measure, because a PWM drive chops the current into pulses.
Picture a ring road with a toll booth at the entrance. While the entrance gate is open, cars flow in and keep circling the ring.
When it shuts, the cars already on the ring keep circling. An entrance counter sees only cars coming through the gate. A counter on the ring sees them all.
The entrance counter is the supply shunt, and the ring counter is a shunt in series with the motor.
The orange shunt R hs sees the pulsed supply current; the blue shunt R ls sees the motor current only while Q1 conducts.
Neither sees the free-wheel current circulating through D1 and the motor.
To see it you put the shunt in series with the motor itself (in-line), at the cost of a switching common-mode voltage.
Shunt resistor: a precision resistor of a few milliohms. Its voltage drop measures current. Current-sense amplifier (CSA): an amplifier that scales up that small drop.
PWM and duty cycle ( D ): PWM switches the supply fully on and off very fast. The duty cycle is the fraction of each period it is on.
Free-wheel current: the current that keeps circulating through a diode across the motor (the flyback diode) when the switch is off.
Say the current is up to 20 amps and the shunt is 2 milliohms. At full current it drops 20 times 0. 002 equals 0. 04 volts, or 40 millivolts.
An amplifier with a gain of 75 turns 40 millivolts into 3. 0 volts. On a 12-bit (4096-step) ADC each count is about 5. 4 milliamps.
A separate trap: if the motor current is a smooth 4 amps at 50% duty, a bench supply shows only about 2 amps. That is the whole idea.
"Most commonly a milliohm-scale shunt resistor plus a current-sense amplifier into the ADC: 20 amps through 2 milliohms is 40 millivolts, gain 75 gives 3 volts.
Low-side is simple but only sees on-time current; high-side or in-line sees more but needs a high-common-mode amplifier.
Hall sensors give isolation, MOSFET R DS(on) sensing saves a part but drifts with temperature.
Because PWM chops the current I sample mid on-time or filter, and calibrate offset at zero current."
Quick check. Which arrangement can see the free-wheeling (diode) current of a PWM-driven DC motor?
Detecting motor or solenoid temperature. The question: How can you detect the temperature of a motor/solenoid?
You can detect the temperature of a motor or solenoid in several ways.
The cheap, common choice is an NTC thermistor, a resistor that changes with heat, read through a voltage divider. Fancier sensors trade cost for accuracy or range.
A thermal fuse or switch can protect the coil with no electronics at all. The winding is also its own thermometer, because copper's resistance rises with temperature.
Think of taking a fever temperature. A thermometer on the skin of your forearm reads lower than your core, and it takes minutes to catch up when the fever spikes.
A motor is the same. The copper winding is the core, and the housing is the skin. During a stall the winding heats within seconds, while the housing lags far behind.
So place the sensor as close to the winding as you can.
Sensor location sets the thermal lag. For overload protection you want the sensor as close to the winding as possible (or a model).
A housing sensor is fine for ambient and cooling checks, but too slow for stall events.
NTC thermistor: a resistor whose resistance falls as it warms. Voltage divider: two resistors in series. The voltage at their midpoint depends on their ratio.
Self-heating: the sensor warming itself from the current you pass through it, which skews the reading.
Thermal lag: the delay between the winding's temperature and the sensor's reading.
Put a 10 kilohms NTC on top of a 10 kilohms resistor, across 3. 3 volts. The midpoint reads 2. 643 volts. That means the NTC is 10 times (3. 3 over 2. 643 minus 1) equals 2.
49 kilohms, which corresponds to about 60 degrees Celsius. Now use the winding itself: a coil that is 2. 0 ohms cold and 2. 6 ohms hot has warmed by about 76 degrees Celsius.
And if a housing sensor lags 10 seconds behind a winding heating at 5 degrees Celsius per second, it under-reads by 50 degrees Celsius.
That is the whole idea: pick the sensor, then mind where it sits.
"The common options are an NTC thermistor in a divider, cheap and sensitive, an RTD like Pt100 for accuracy, a thermocouple for high temperatures, or an IC sensor for board temperature.
For protection a thermal fuse or bimetal switch needs no electronics. And since copper resistance rises about 0.
4 percent per kelvin, I can infer average winding temperature from its resistance.
I'd embed the sensor in the winding if I can, because housing sensors lag, and watch for self-heating and linearisation."
Quick check. Which sensor has a resistance that falls as temperature rises and is widely used on motor windings for firmware readout?
Which motor temperatures matter. The question: Which temperatures do you want to/can you measure?
A motor has several different temperatures, and each one matters for a different reason. The copper winding matters most, because its insulation fails if it gets too hot.
In a permanent-magnet motor, the magnets matter too, because heat weakens them.
Bearings, brushes, the housing, and the drive's transistors (its electronic switches) each have their own limit. Some can be measured directly.
Others, such as a spinning rotor, must be estimated.
Think of a car. The engine coolant, the oil, the brakes, and the tires each have their own safe temperature, and each fails in its own way.
You read some from a gauge, but you can only guess the temperature of the tire's inner rubber.
A motor is the same: a set of parts, each with its own limit, and some parts you cannot reach with a sensor.
Heat sources feed a network of thermal resistances and capacitances. The winding is the hottest and fastest-changing node; the housing is the slowest and coolest.
Rotor heat leaves mainly through the air gap and shaft, which is why the rotor can run hotter than the stator in some designs, and why it is hard to measure.
Hot spot: the hottest point in the winding. It sets the insulation's life. Insulation class: a standard maximum winding temperature, such as class F at 155 degrees Celsius.
Remanence: the strength of a magnet's field. It falls as the magnet warms. Demagnetization: permanent loss of magnet strength from too much heat.
Junction temperature: the temperature of the silicon inside a transistor. Thermal resistance: degrees of temperature rise per watt of heat flowing.
Neodymium (NdFeB) magnets lose about 0. 12% of their strength per degree.
Heat them by 100 degrees Celsius and the motor's torque per amp drops by 12%, so the motor needs about 13. 6% more current for the same torque.
Separately, a transistor carrying 20 amps through 8 milliohms dissipates 20 squared times 0. 008 equals 3. 2 watts.
With 30 degrees Celsius per watt of thermal resistance, its junction sits 96 degrees Celsius above the room, about 121 degrees Celsius in a 25 degrees Celsius room.
That is the whole idea: several limits, several sensors, plus some estimation.
"Several temperatures matter. The winding, average and hot spot, limits insulation life, so I embed a thermistor or use resistance.
The stator and housing lag but are easy to measure. For permanent-magnet motors the rotor magnets matter: NdFeB loses about 0.
1 percent flux per kelvin and can demagnetise, but you can't sense it directly, so I estimate it.
Bearings have a grease limit, brushes wear, and the MOSFET junction has to be computed from power and thermal resistance. Rotating parts need IR, telemetry or models."
Quick check. Which temperature most directly limits the life of a motor's insulation?
Contactless temperature of moving motors. The question: Since the motor/solenoid may be moving, you might not always want physical contact between the sensor and motor/solenoid.
What are some contactless ways to measure temperature?
When a part is spinning or hard to reach, you can measure its temperature without touching it. The main way is infrared (IR).
Every warm surface gives off invisible heat radiation, and an IR thermometer, a small thermopile sensor, or a thermal camera reads it.
The big catch is that shiny bare metal gives off very little, so it reads far too cold.
You can also infer temperature electrically, from the copper coil's resistance or from the magnets' back-EMF.
Picture a polished mirror and a matte black cloth sitting in the same warm room. The cloth looks like itself. The mirror mostly shows its surroundings instead.
An IR sensor sees bare metal the same way: it picks up the reflected room, not the metal's own heat.
A strip of matte tape on the metal acts like the black cloth, and the sensor then sees the real surface.
The reading collapses as emissivity falls.

The curve includes the reflected 25 degrees Celsius surroundings and assumes the instrument's reflected-temperature setting is also 25 degrees Celsius, so as ε to 0 the reading tends to the background temperature (it is the formula above).
Hotter surroundings or reflections of hot parts push it in other directions.
For bare metal the practical fix is to change the emissivity: tape, paint, or an oxidised or anodised patch.
Emissivity: how well a surface gives off heat radiation, from 0 to 1. Matte paint is about 0. 95. Polished metal might be 0. 1.
Thermopile sensor: a small, cheap IR sensor that gives a voltage when it absorbs heat radiation. Spot size: the area the sensor averages. A 10:1 sensor at 0.
3 m sees a 30 mm circle. Back-EMF: the voltage a spinning motor generates. Warmer magnets make less of it at the same speed, so it reveals magnet temperature.
Aim an IR thermometer, set for emissivity 0. 95, at objects that are truly at 100 degrees Celsius in a 25 degrees Celsius room. A matte black surface reads 100 degrees Celsius.
A surface with emissivity 0. 5 reads about 70. 5 degrees Celsius. Polished metal with emissivity 0. 1 reads only about 35. 8 degrees Celsius.
That is the whole idea: IR is easy to use and easy to fool.
"Infrared: a thermopile sensor or IR thermometer reads the surface from a distance, and a thermal camera gives an image.
The catch is emissivity: black or painted surfaces are around 0. 95 but shiny metal might be 0. 1, so a bare shaft at 100 degrees Celsius can read about 36 degrees Celsius.
Fix with matte tape or paint.
Without optics, I can infer temperature from winding resistance or back-EMF constant, use a thermal model, or use telemetry or fibre-optic sensors on rotors.
Watch spot size and reflections."
Quick check. Why does a polished metal shaft read too cold on an IR thermometer set for emissivity 0. 95?
How motors degrade with age. The question: How do motors perform as they age?
As a motor ages, almost everything gets a little worse, and the symptoms point to the cause. Bearings and grease wear, so friction rises. In a brushed motor the brushes wear down.
Winding insulation slowly breaks down with heat. Magnets can lose strength.
The result is the same motor drawing more current for the same job, running hotter and noisier, and wasting more power.
The best defense is to log measurements and watch the trend.
Think of an old bicycle. The chain dries out, the bearings get gritty, and the brake pads rub. You pedal harder for the same speed, you get warmer, and it squeaks.
Each of those faults leaves its own sign: a gritty hub sounds different from a rusty chain.
The ageing mechanisms all feed back into more current and heat, which accelerates the same mechanisms.
This positive feedback is why degradation tends to accelerate near the end of life and why catching early symptoms pays off.
No-load current: the current needed to spin the motor with no load. It measures friction. Torque constant ( K t ): torque per amp. Weaker magnets lower it.
Bathtub curve: failure rate over life, high at the start, low and flat in the middle, then rising at wear-out. Insulation: the thin coating on the winding wire.
Heat slowly breaks it down.
A 12 volts motor has a 1. 2 ohms winding and makes 0. 02 N·m per amp. It carries a 0. 04 N·m load. New, it needs 0. 15 amps just to beat friction, so it draws 0. 04 over 0.
02 plus 0. 15 equals 2. 15 amps and runs near 4500 rpm at about 73% efficiency. Age it: 10% weaker magnets, friction current up to 0. 4 amps, and 5% more resistance.
It now draws about 2. 6 amps, runs slightly faster, and is only about 61% efficient. Weak magnets do not make a slower motor. They make a hungrier one. That is the whole idea.
"Motors drift as they age. Bearings wear and grease degrades, so friction and no-load current rise, with more noise and heat.
Brushes shorten and the commutator grooves, increasing contact resistance and sparking.
Insulation ages and can short turns; magnets can lose strength, lowering the torque constant so you need more current per newton-metre.
Efficiency falls, a 73 percent motor might drop to 61. Reliability follows a bathtub curve, so I'd trend current, vibration and temperature to catch wear-out early."
Quick check. Which change is a typical sign of bearing wear?
Stresses on a motor over its life. The question: What kind of stress may a motor experience in its lifetime?
Over its life, a motor faces four families of stress. Thermal stress is steady heat plus repeated heating and cooling.
Electrical stress is start-up surges, reversals, and voltage spikes. Mechanical stress is start-stop shocks, side loads, vibration, and overspeed.
Environmental stress is moisture, dust, and chemicals.
Many of these wear the motor by the count of events, not by hours of running, so you must start from how it will actually be used.
Bend a paper clip back and forth. One bend does nothing. Ten bends do nothing visible. But a few dozen and it snaps, even though no single bend was hard.
Motor stresses work like that: each start, each heat-up, each reversal does a tiny bit of damage that adds up.
All four stress families come from the same duty profile.
A design review should ask for the profile first, since a datasheet cannot know whether the motor will be started twice a day or twice a second.
Back-EMF: the voltage a spinning motor generates. It opposes the supply and grows with speed. Inrush current: the surge at start-up, before back-EMF builds up. It is V over R .
Plugging: reversing the supply on a spinning motor to brake it. Back-EMF adds to the supply.
Thermal cycling: repeated heating and cooling that fatigues solder, brush wires, and adhesives. Duty profile: the real pattern of loads, speeds, starts, and ambient conditions.
A 12 volts motor has a 1. 2 ohms coil (winding) and runs at 2 amps. At the instant of start, back-EMF is zero, so the current is 12 over 1. 2 equals 10 amps.
That is five times the running current and 25 times the heating. Now spin it to no-load speed, where back-EMF is 12 volts, and reverse the supply.
The current starts at (12 plus 12) over 1. 2 equals 20 amps, twice the stall current.
Separately, 20% overspeed raises the stress in the spinning rotor by 44%, because stress grows with speed squared.
That is the whole idea: list the stresses, put numbers on them, and design for the real duty profile.
"Four groups. Thermal: steady heat ages insulation and cycling fatigues joints. Electrical: inrush is V over R, so a 12 volts, 1.
2 ohm motor sees 10 amps at start, 25 times the heating of a 2 amps run; plugging can double stall current; plus inductive spikes and PWM edges stressing insulation and bearings.
Mechanical: start-stop shocks, side loads, vibration, overspeed. Environmental: moisture, dust, chemicals.
I'd soft-start, protect, derate, seal and qualify with cycling and life tests."
Quick check. A motor passes a constant-load life test but fails early in the field with frequent starts. What does this suggest?
Thin coil wire versus high current. The question: Motor/solenoids often require many loops in the coils, so the coil wires will be very thin.
Motors/solenoids also draw lots of current, possibly more than the coils can support. How do you reconcile this? Do coils on the motors always burn out?
It sounds as if a coil of many thin turns must carry a big current, but it is the reverse.
More turns of thinner wire means more resistance, so at a given voltage the current is smaller.
A coil's force depends on ampere-turns, which is the number of turns times the current. Designers choose the number of turns to fit the supply voltage.
Big currents appear only at start-up, stall, or overload. Coils burn out only when heat outruns cooling.
Think of pushing water through a garden hose. A longer, thinner hose lets less water through at the same pressure.
Winding more turns of thinner wire is like swapping in a longer, narrower hose: the flow (current) drops sharply.
To get the same push from the coil, you pair that long thin hose with a higher-pressure supply.
With heat dissipation fixed at 0. 54 watts, current falls as 1 over V ( I equals P over V ). Higher supply voltage means more turns of thinner wire carrying less current.
In every case the ampere-turns are 200 and the current density is 4 amps/mm².
Ampere-turns ( NI ): turns times current. It sets how strongly a coil magnetizes. Current density ( J ): current per square millimeter of wire. It sets the heating.
Back-EMF: the voltage a spinning motor generates against the supply. It cuts the running current. Duty cycle: the fraction of time a solenoid may stay energized.
Take a coil with room for about 2 cm³ of copper and a limit of 4 amps/mm². The copper fills a 50 mm² cross-section, so 4 amps/mm² allows 200 ampere-turns.
On 5 volts you wind about 1860 turns, which draws about 108 milliamps. On 12 volts you wind about 4460 turns of thinner wire, which draws about 45 milliamps.
Both make 200 ampere-turns. At 4 amps/mm², copper heats at only about 0. 08 degrees Celsius per second.
At 20 amps/mm² it heats at about 2 degrees Celsius per second, so a stall heats the coil 100 degrees Celsius in under a minute. That is the whole idea.
"The premise is off: many turns of thin wire gives higher resistance and lower current, and force depends on ampere-turns, so you pick turns to match your supply. 4500 turns of 0.
12 mm wire draws about 45 milliamps at 12 volts.
Large currents occur only at start, stall or overload; a running motor's back-EMF limits current, and solenoids are rated by duty cycle.
Coils don't always burn out; they fail when heat outruns cooling, so designers hold current density to a few amps per square millimetre and protect against stall."
Quick check. At a fixed supply voltage, what happens to the current in a coil if you wind twice as many turns of thinner wire in the same space?
Why measure motor/solenoid speed and position. The question: When/why would knowing the speed and/or position of a motor/solenoid be useful?
The voltage you apply to a motor does not set its speed or position. It only sets what the motor tries to do. Load, supply voltage, and temperature all change the result.
Speed and position measurements let you hold a speed, reach a position, switch a brushless motor's windings at the right moment, and detect stalls and wear.
For a solenoid, you learn whether the plunger arrived.
Think of a shower. Setting the tap to one position does not fix the water temperature. If someone flushes a toilet elsewhere, the water changes with no change at the tap.
To keep it right, you test the water with your hand and adjust. That hand is the sensor, and your adjusting is the feedback.
With a fixed 6. 28 volts the speed falls linearly with load (red).
A speed loop measures the sag and raises the PWM duty to hold 3,000 rpm (blue) until the 12 volts rail is exhausted at about 0. 114 N·m.
Beyond that point no controller can help, which is why sizing the motor and supply still matters.
Back-EMF: the voltage a spinning motor generates against the supply. It grows with speed.
Open loop / closed loop: driving with no measurement, or measuring the result and correcting. Speed droop: the drop in speed as load torque rises at a fixed voltage.
Commutation: switching current between a brushless motor's windings in step with the rotor position. Stall: the shaft is stopped while the drive pushes current.
Take a 12 volts motor with a 1 ohms winding. Each rad/s of speed (radian per second, about 9. 5 rpm) makes 0. 02 volts of back-EMF, and each amp makes 0. 02 N·m.
With no load it spins at 12 over 0. 02 equals 600 rad/s, about 5730 rpm. Add a 0. 1 N·m load and it needs 5 amps.
That drops 5 volts across the winding, leaving 7 volts for back-EMF, so speed falls to 350 rad/s, about 3340 rpm. The voltage did not change.
If the shaft stops entirely, the current is 12 over 1 equals 12 amps. That is the whole idea: open-loop speed wanders, so you feed the measurement back.
"Voltage only sets what a motor tries to do.

Load, supply and temperature change what it actually does, so for speed control, positioning, BLDC commutation, stall and jam detection and diagnostics you need to measure speed or position and close the loop.
For a solenoid the equivalent is knowing the plunger arrived, how hard it hit, and whether it jammed, so you can drop to a hold current, soften the landing and flag faults."
Quick check. A brushed DC motor is driven with a fixed PWM duty. Its load torque doubles. What happens to the steady-state speed?
Measuring motor RPM. The question: How can you measure the RPM of a motor?

The usual way to measure a motor's rpm is a sensor that gives pulses as the shaft turns, such as an encoder (a slotted disk read by a light sensor) or a Hall sensor (a magnetic sensor) that sees a magnet go by.
Pulses per second, divided by pulses per revolution, gives revolutions per second, and you multiply by 60 for rpm. The real skill is in how you count the pulses.
You can also get speed from a motor's own back-EMF with no sensor at all.
Think of taking someone's pulse. You can count the beats for 15 seconds and multiply by 4. Or you can time the gap between two beats and divide into 60.
When the heart beats fast, counting for a window works well. When it beats very slowly, you only catch one or two beats in the window, so timing one gap is better.
A pulse train and a gate window.
In the frequency method you count the pulses that fall inside the window (here a handful); with few pulses per window, each missing or extra pulse is a large percentage of the reading.
In the period method you instead count fast clock ticks between two consecutive pulse edges.
PPR: pulses per revolution of the sensor. A single magnet gives 1. Gate (frequency) method: count pulses in a fixed time window. It works well at high speed.
Period method: time the interval between two pulses with a fast clock. It works well at low speed.
Input capture: a timer feature that records the clock value at each pulse edge, so software delays do not add error.
Back-EMF: the voltage a spinning motor generates, proportional to speed.
A Hall sensor gives 1 pulse per revolution, and the motor turns at 3000 rpm. That is 50 pulses per second, one every 20 milliseconds.
With a 100 milliseconds window you catch only 5 pulses, and one miscount is a 20% error.
With a 1 megahertz clock timing one pulse period, you count 20,000 ticks, so one tick is only 0. 005%. That is the whole idea.
"I'd get a pulse train from an encoder, a Hall sensor on a magnet, or an optical interrupter, and convert with rpm equals 60 times frequency divided by pulses per rev.
At high speed I count pulses in a fixed window; at low speed I time the period between pulses with a hardware timer. No sensor?
Back-EMF is proportional to speed, so I can measure terminal voltage during a PWM off-time. For lab checks I'd use an optical tach on a reflective mark."
Quick check. Which counting method gives better relative resolution at very low speed?
Determining motor position. The question: How can you determine the position of a motor?
To know where a motor shaft is pointing, pick a sensor that fits the job. An absolute sensor tells you the angle the moment it powers up.
An incremental sensor only counts movement, so it needs a starting reference.
Some motors need no extra sensor: a stepper counts its steps, and a brushless motor's Hall sensors give a rough angle.
Always ask about resolution, absolute versus relative, environment, and cost.
Think of a hotel hallway. Absolute sensing is like door numbers: step out of the elevator and you instantly know where you are.
Incremental sensing is like counting your steps from the elevator.
It can be very precise, but if you lose count, or leave the building and return, you must walk back to the elevator to start over. That return trip is homing.
A first-pass selection tree. Most small actuators end up in "magnetic angle sensor" (absolute) or "incremental encoder with a homing switch".
Absolute sensor: reports a unique angle at power-up, such as a potentiometer (a variable resistor), magnetic angle sensor, or absolute encoder.
Incremental encoder: outputs pulses as the shaft turns, so the controller keeps a running count.
Homing: moving to a known reference, such as a limit switch or index pulse, to set zero.
Resolution vs accuracy: the smallest step the sensor reports, versus how close it is to the true angle.
A 12-bit absolute magnetic sensor splits one turn into 2 to the 12 equals 4096 positions, so each is 360 over 4096 equals 0. 088° .
Incremental: a 12-line encoder gives 4 countable edges per line, so 48 counts per motor turn. Through a 30:1 gearbox that is 48 times 30 equals 1440 counts per output turn, 0.
25° each. A brushless motor's three Hall (magnetic) sensors give 6 readings per magnetic cycle.
With 7 pole pairs (north-south magnet pairs), that is 42 readings per turn, so it knows its position only to about 8. 6°. That is the whole idea.
"I'd pick between absolute and incremental. Absolute options are a potentiometer, a magnetic angle sensor (12 bits or more, contactless) or an absolute encoder.
Incremental means an optical quadrature encoder, which needs homing at power-up. Brushless motors have Hall sensors good for commutation (about 60 electrical degrees).
Steppers count steps if they don't slip. The gear ratio multiplies output resolution but adds backlash. I'd choose on resolution, absolute versus relative, environment and cost."
Quick check. What must an incremental encoder system do after power-up?
Rotary encoder and speed measurement. The question: What is a rotary encoder? How can it be used to measure motor speed?
A rotary encoder turns shaft rotation into electrical signals. The common type is an incremental quadrature encoder.
It outputs two on-off signals (square waves), A and B, that are a quarter of a cycle apart.
Counting the edges gives how far the shaft turned, and which wave comes first gives the direction. Dividing the count change by the elapsed time gives speed.
An absolute encoder outputs a unique code at each angle instead.
Picture a striped belt sliding past two eyes that are placed a quarter of a stripe apart. As the belt moves one way, the first eye sees each stripe edge first.
Move the belt the other way and the second eye sees it first. So the order tells you direction.
Every change at either eye is an edge you can count, so one stripe gives four counts.
Forward rotation: A rises first, then B rises a quarter cycle later. Each of the four edges per cycle is a count, so one line equals four counts.
If the shaft reverses, B leads A and the same state machine counts down.
Lines (PPR): how many cycles of channel A occur per revolution. Quadrature: two signals 90° apart. Their order gives the direction.
CPR: counts per revolution after decoding every edge, which is 4 times the lines. Index pulse (Z): one pulse per revolution, used for homing.
Hardware quadrature counter: a timer mode that counts up and down by itself, without the program handling each edge.
Take a 1024-line encoder decoded on all edges, so CPR is 4 times 1024 equals 4096 . At 3000 rpm, that is 50 rev/s, or 204,800 counts per second.
Read the counter every 1 milliseconds and you get about 205 counts. One count is 60 over (4096 times 0. 001) equals 14. 65 rpm, which is 0. 49% at this speed.
At 30 rpm the same window holds only about 2 counts, so the speed estimate hops in steps. That is the whole idea.
"A rotary encoder converts shaft rotation into electrical pulses.

An incremental quadrature encoder gives two square waves, A and B, 90 degrees apart, so the phase order gives direction and counting every edge gives four times the line count, plus an index pulse once per rev.
For speed I count edges over a fixed window, rpm equals 60 times counts over CPR times window, or time between edges at low speed.
Absolute encoders give a unique code for each angle."
Quick check. In a quadrature encoder, how is direction determined?
Measuring solenoid speed. The question: How can you measure the speed of a solenoid?
A solenoid's moving part, the plunger, travels a few millimeters in a few milliseconds. You cannot use a spinning-speed sensor (tachometer) on it, because nothing spins.
Instead you time the plunger between two known points, or track its position and see how fast it changes, or read its motion from the coil's own current.
The coil trick works because a moving plunger generates a small voltage that opposes the supply.
Think of timing a sprinter with two cones and a stopwatch. Start the watch at the first cone, stop it at the second, and divide the distance by the time.
Two sensors along the stroke do the same job.
The analogy breaks in one place: the plunger speeds up all the way to the end stop, so the average speed over the whole stroke is far lower than its speed at impact.
With a constant 24 volts the current first rises like a normal RL circuit, then falls as the plunger accelerates and generates speed voltage, hits a minimum at the moment of arrival (19.
5 milliseconds), then climbs toward 2 amps with the higher closed-state inductance. Without the plunger moving (blocked plunger) the curve would just keep rising.
Plunger (armature): the moving iron part of the solenoid. Stroke: how far the plunger travels. Transit time: the time to cross the stroke or a set segment.
Motional EMF: the voltage the moving plunger generates in the coil. It grows with speed and opposes the supply.
Current dip: the dip in coil current during pull-in, caused by that voltage. The dip ends at arrival.
A plunger crosses a 10 mm stroke in 8 milliseconds. Its average speed is 0. 010 over 0. 008 equals 1. 25 m/s. Now put two gates 5 mm apart and read a 2.
5 milliseconds gap between them. The speed there is 0. 005 over 0. 0025 equals 2 m/s. With no added sensor at all, drive the coil with a steady voltage and watch the current.
It rises, dips while the plunger moves fast, and climbs again once the plunger stops. That is the whole idea.
"I'd time the plunger between two known points: optical or Hall gates a set distance apart, velocity equals distance over time, with a hardware timer.
Or I differentiate a position sensor like a linear Hall or LVDT, with filtering.
Without a sensor, the coil gives velocity through the motional back-EMF, i dL over dx v , which makes a dip in the current during the stroke.
Lab check with a high-speed camera or laser."
Quick check. Which term in the coil voltage equation carries plunger velocity information?
Measuring solenoid position. The question: How can you measure the position of a solenoid?
How you measure a solenoid plunger's position depends on what you need to know.
If you only need "home or extended," a limit switch, reed switch, or Hall switch with a small magnet is enough.
For a continuous position you can use a linear Hall sensor, an LVDT (a precise contactless sensor), a sliding potentiometer, or an optical strip.
Or you can use the coil itself, because its inductance rises as the plunger closes the gap.
Think of a trombone. The pitch of a note tells you how far the slide is out.
A solenoid coil works similarly: its inductance, an electrical "pitch," changes as the plunger slides in.
You send a small test pulse and read the response to learn the position, with no extra sensor.
Start from the resolution you need.
In practice most on/off solenoids use a switch; proportional valves use an LVDT; low-cost products try self-sensing first and add a sensor only if accuracy demands it.
Inductance: how strongly a coil resists a change in its current. More iron inside the coil means more inductance, so the current rises more slowly.
Hall switch: a magnetic sensor with an on-off output. A magnet on the plunger triggers it. Linear Hall sensor: gives a voltage that follows the magnetic field.
Its output does not change in a straight line with distance. LVDT: a set of coils around an iron core fixed to the plunger. Its output follows the position, with no contact.
An example solenoid has 48 millihenries of inductance with the plunger open and 170 millihenries when closed.
Apply a 5 volts test pulse for 100 microseconds, short enough that the plunger does not move. The current rises by V t over L . Open, that is 5 times 0. 0001 over 0.
048 equals 10. 4 milliamps. Closed, it is only 2. 9 milliamps. A simple threshold on that current can tell you "closed" without any added part. That is the whole idea.
"For just home or extended, a limit switch, reed or Hall switch.
For continuous position: a linear Hall sensor with a magnet on the plunger (nonlinear, so linearise), an LVDT (precise, contactless, needs excitation), a linear pot, or an optical strip.
Sensorless: inductance depends on air gap, so a small test pulse measures L and hence position, best near the closed end.
I'd pick on resolution, linearity, temperature drift and space."
Quick check. Which sensor is best if you only need to know whether a solenoid plunger is fully extended?
BEMF speed sensing for motors and solenoids. The question: How can you use BEMF to measure motor/solenoid speed?
A spinning motor is also a generator. The voltage it generates, called back-EMF, is proportional to its speed.
So if you can read that voltage by itself, you have a speed sensor with no extra part. The trouble is that while current flows, other voltage drops hide it.
The usual fix is to measure when the current has stopped. For a solenoid the matching effect is weaker and depends on the plunger's position.
Think of a bicycle dynamo that lights a lamp. Pedal faster and the lamp gets brighter, because the dynamo makes more voltage at higher speed. A motor shaft acts like that dynamo.
To read it cleanly, you disconnect the power for an instant and measure what the spinning shaft produces on its own.
Switch Q₁ drives the motor from the battery; D₁ freewheels the motor current when Q₁ turns off.
A divider from the motor terminal to the ADC lets the MCU read the terminal voltage. During Q₁-off, once the diode current has stopped, that voltage equals the back-EMF.
Back-EMF: the voltage a spinning motor generates, E equals K e omega . It is proportional to speed.
K e : the back-EMF constant, in volts per rad/s of speed (radians per second; one turn is 2π radians).
Off-time sampling: reading the terminal voltage while a PWM drive (one that switches on and off rapidly) is off and the current has died away.
Freewheel (flyback) diode: carries the winding's current after the switch opens.
A motor has K e equals 0. 02 volts per rad/s. At 3000 rpm, which is 314 rad/s, it generates 0. 02 times 314 equals 6. 28 volts. Turn the PWM switch off.
After the freewheel current dies, about 0. 13 milliseconds for a small example motor, the open terminal voltage is that 6. 28 volts.
Two resistors scale it down for the microcontroller's ADC (its voltage-to-number converter), and you divide by K e to get speed. At 300 rpm it is only 0.
63 volts, which is why the method struggles at low speed. That is the whole idea.
"Back-EMF is proportional to speed, E equals Ke omega.

The terminal voltage is IR plus L di/dt plus E, so I measure it when the current is zero: switch the drive off during the PWM off-time, wait for the freewheel current to decay, and sample the terminal through a divider into an ADC.
Speed is that voltage over Ke. Otherwise subtract the I times R drop during on-time. It fails at low speed and drifts with temperature, because R rises about 0. 4% per degree."
Quick check. When can the motor terminal voltage be read directly as back-EMF?
How to drive an inductive load. The question: How do you drive an inductive load?
A motor, solenoid, or relay coil is an inductor, which resists any sudden change in its current.
The simplest safe way to drive one is a MOSFET switch between the load and ground, controlled by a microcontroller pin.
Always add a flyback diode across the load, so the current has somewhere to go when the switch opens. You vary speed or hold force with PWM.
Size the switch for the starting surge, not the running current.
Picture a heavy truck that cannot stop instantly. A runaway-truck ramp gives it somewhere safe to slow down. The coil's current is the truck's momentum.
The switch opening is the brake. The flyback diode is the escape ramp. Without one, it hits whatever is ahead: the MOSFET.
The standard low-side drive. D 1 across the load (cathode to V S ) is reverse-biased while Q 1 is on and takes over the inductor current when Q 1 turns off.
R g tames gate ringing and limits GPIO current; R pd keeps Q 1 off when the pin floats.
MOSFET: a transistor used as a fast electronic switch. Flyback (freewheel) diode: a diode across the load that carries the coil's current after the switch opens.
Inrush / stall current: the big current at start-up or when stuck, V over R , because a still motor makes no back-EMF (opposing voltage).
PWM duty cycle: in PWM the switch flips on and off rapidly. The fraction of time on sets the average voltage.
Time constant: L over R , the time for the coil's current to fall to about 37% of its starting value.
A 24 volts solenoid coil of 24 ohms and 100 millihenries draws 1 amps, and stores 1 over 2 times 0. 1 times 1 squared equals 50 mJ.
When the MOSFET turns off, the diode catches that current. It decays with a time constant of 0. 1 over 24 equals 4. 17 milliseconds, falling from 1 amps to 0. 1 amps in about 9.
6 milliseconds. To hold the plunger cheaply, run PWM at 33% duty: the average is 8 volts, so it holds with about 0. 33 amps instead of 1 amps. That is the whole idea.

"I'd use a logic-level N-MOSFET as a low-side switch with the load between the supply and the drain, a gate resistor and pull-down, and a flyback diode across the load so the inductor current has a path when the FET turns off.
Size the FET for voltage margin and stall or inrush current, then use PWM for speed or hold current.
For two directions or protection and diagnostics, step up to an H-bridge or a driver IC."
Quick check. For a low-side N-MOSFET driving a coil from V S , where does the flyback diode go?
Adding motor braking to a drive. The question: What if you need motor braking?
A single switch can only let a motor coast, so it slows down on friction, which can take seconds.
To brake, you give the motor's own generated voltage a path to push current through.
The simplest way is to connect the motor's two terminals together by turning on the drive's bottom (low-side) switches.
The motor then works as a generator into its own winding and slows itself down. This braking is strong at high speed and fades to nothing at standstill.
Picture a spinning merry-go-round with a paddle dipped in thick syrup. The faster it spins, the harder the syrup pushes back, and as it slows, the drag fades.
It slows quickly at first and then creeps to a stop. A shorted motor is that paddle, and the drag grows in proportion to speed.
Coasting barely slows in 0. 4 seconds. Dynamic braking falls exponentially (95% of the speed gone in about 0.
14 seconds) but the last bit is slow because torque vanishes with speed.
A current-limited plugging stop has constant deceleration and reaches zero in about 52 milliseconds, but only if the drive switches off exactly then.
Model: J equals 2 times 10 to the -5 kg·m², K equals 0. 02 , R equals 1 ohms , b equals 2 times 10 to the -5 N·m·s/rad.
Coast: both terminals open. Only friction slows the motor. Dynamic braking: shorting the terminals, so the motor's back-EMF drives a current that opposes the rotation.
Back-EMF: the voltage a spinning motor generates, E equals K e omega . Plugging: applying reverse drive voltage while spinning forward. It brakes harder but is riskier.
A motor has K e equals 0. 02 volts per rad/s and a 1 ohms winding, and spins at 3000 rpm, or 314 rad/s. Its back-EMF is 0. 02 times 314 equals 6. 28 volts.
Short the terminals and the brake current starts at 6. 28 over 1 equals 6. 28 amps.
For a small rotor, the speed then falls to about 37% every 48 milliseconds (the time constant), against about 1 seconds when coasting.
Plugging with 12 volts reversed would start at (12 plus 6. 28) over 1 equals 18. 3 amps and must be cut at zero speed, or the motor spins backward. That is the whole idea.
"A single low-side switch can only coast.
To brake I give the motor's back-EMF a short-circuit path: in a half-bridge, turn on the low-side FET; in an H-bridge, turn on both low sides.
The motor then acts as a generator into its own resistance and stops in a time constant of tens of milliseconds instead of seconds.
I'd check the brake current, E over R, against FET and winding ratings, limit it with PWM if needed, and remember braking has no holding torque at standstill."
Quick check. A drive uses one low-side MOSFET. Turning the MOSFET off will:
Driving a motor in both directions. The question: What if you need to drive the motor in both directions?
To run a DC motor both ways, you must reverse the current through it. The standard circuit is an H-bridge: four switches arranged around the motor like the letter H.
Closing one diagonal pair sends current one way through the motor. The other pair sends it back. A PWM signal on one switch sets the speed.
The one forbidden state is turning on both switches on the same side.
Imagine a toy car with a battery you can flip by hand. One way it goes forward. Flipped, it reverses.
An H-bridge flips the battery electronically, using four switches, two at a time.
The danger is like shorting the battery with a wire: if the top and bottom switch on one side close at once, they short the supply.
Forward: Q₁ and Q₄ on. Current runs from V M through Q₁, left to right through the motor, and down through Q₄ to ground. Reverse swaps to Q₃ and Q₂.
The animated wires show where current flows.
H-bridge: four switches in an H shape, with the motor as the crossbar. Shoot-through: both switches on one side (one leg) on at once, shorting the supply.
PWM: switching fully on and off very fast. The fraction of time on (the duty) sets the average voltage.
Dead time: a short gap between one switch turning off and its partner turning on.
Call the switches Q1 and Q2 on the left (top, bottom) and Q3 and Q4 on the right. With 12 volts, Q1 and Q4 on gives forward at +12 volts.
Q3 and Q2 on gives reverse at minus 12 volts. Both low sides on, Q2 and Q4, shorts the motor and brakes it. All off is coast.
Q1 and Q2 together is the forbidden state: with two 10 milliohms switches, the short is 12 over 0. 02 equals 600 amps on paper.
For speed, chop one switch at 50% duty and the motor sees an average of 6 volts. That is the whole idea.
"An H-bridge: four switches around the motor. Turning on the top-left and bottom-right sends current one way; top-right and bottom-left the other way. PWM one switch for speed.
Never turn on both switches of one leg, so I add dead time or use a driver IC with shoot-through protection.
Body diodes carry freewheel current, both low sides give braking, all off is coast. The MCU drives it with PWM plus a direction pin or two inputs."
Quick check. In an H-bridge with switches Q1 (top-left), Q2 (bottom-left), Q3 (top-right), Q4 (bottom-right), which pair drives the motor forward and which the reverse?
Kinds of motor braking. The question: What are the different kinds of motor braking?
There are five ways to slow a motor. Coasting just removes power and lets friction act. Dynamic braking shorts the motor so it acts as a generator and burns its energy as heat.
Plugging applies reverse voltage for the fastest stop, at a high current. Regenerative braking sends the energy back into the supply.
Mechanical brakes use friction and are the only kind that hold at standstill.
Think of stopping a car. Coasting is slow and uncontrolled. Downshifting to let the engine drag the car is like dynamic braking: it works well at speed and fades as you slow.
Slamming into reverse is like plugging: abrupt, and it drives you backward if you hold it. A hybrid that charges its battery while slowing is regenerative.
Friction brakes are mechanical, and only the parking brake holds you on a hill.
Electrical braking uses the motor as a generator, with the energy burned (dynamic, plugging) or returned (regen).
Mechanical brakes are independent of the motor's electrical state, which is why they are used for holding and safety.
Dynamic braking: shorting the motor, or loading it with a resistor, so its generated current opposes the rotation.
Plugging: reversing the applied voltage while the motor is still spinning forward. Regenerative braking: returning the motion's energy to the supply through the drive's switches.
Holding torque: the torque available at zero speed.
A small 12 volts motor with a 1 ohms winding makes 0. 02 volts per rad/s of speed and 0. 02 N·m per amp. It spins at 3000 rpm, holding about 0. 99 J of motion energy.
Shorted, it brakes with 6. 28 amps and 0. 126 N·m, but at 100 rpm the torque has faded to 0. 0042 N·m. Plugging would start at about 18. 3 amps. Now hang a 0.
01 N·m load on the shaft. The shorted motor still turns at about 25 rad/s, roughly 240 rpm, so electrical braking alone cannot hold a load still.
That is the whole idea: compare torque against speed, current, and where the energy goes.

"Five kinds: coast, which is just letting friction work; dynamic braking, shorting the terminals or adding a resistor so the motor dissipates its energy as a generator; plugging, reversing the voltage for the fastest stop at high current; regenerative braking, returning energy to the supply with a bridge; and mechanical brakes for holding torque and fail-safe.
Electrical braking loses torque as speed drops, so combine it with a mechanical brake for holding."
Quick check. Which braking method returns energy to the power source?
Protection for inductive load drives. The question: What sort of protection circuitry do you need?
A motor or solenoid drive must survive faults, not just work on the bench. You protect it in layers. A flyback diode or clamp handles the voltage spike when the switch opens.
Resistors on the MOSFET's gate (its control pin) keep the switch under control. A current limit and a fuse handle stalls. Thermal shutdown handles overheating.
Supply protection handles reverse polarity, surges, and regeneration. A safe default state handles processor crashes.
Think of a car's safety systems. The crumple zone, seat belts, and airbags each handle a different part of a crash.
In a drive, each part answers one specific fault, and the layers overlap, so one failure does not destroy the drive.

A low-side drive with its protection layers: fuse F₁ in series with the supply, a TVS and bulk capacitor on the rail, flyback diode D₁ across the motor, gate resistor and pull-down, and a low-side sense resistor feeding a comparator or amplifier for current limit.
Each part answers a specific fault.
Flyback diode: a diode across the coil that gives its current a safe path when the switch opens.
Zener / TVS diode: a diode that blocks until a set voltage, then conducts, clamping spikes to that voltage.
Slow-blow fuse: a fuse that tolerates a brief inrush but opens on a sustained overload. Regeneration: a slowing motor acting as a generator and pushing its supply voltage up.
A 10 millihenries coil on 12 volts carries 1 amps (so it is 12 ohms) and stores 1 over 2 times 0. 01 times 1 squared equals 5 mJ. With a plain diode clamp, the current falls to 0.
1 amps in about 1. 58 milliseconds. Add a 36 volts Zener in series with the diode and that drops to about 0.
21 milliseconds, but the MOSFET now sees the supply plus 36 volts plus the diode's 0. 7 volts: 12 plus 36. 7 equals 48. 7 volts, so choose a 60 volts part.
Separately, a 12 volts, 1 ohms motor that stalls draws 12 amps and dissipates 144 watts, so it needs a current limit and a timeout.
That is the whole idea: one layer per fault, each with a number.
"Layers. For the kick, a flyback diode, or a diode plus Zener or TVS for faster release. For the gate, a series resistor, pull-down and maybe a gate Zener.
For over-current, a sense resistor with current limit, plus a fuse; motors stall at V over R. Thermal shutdown.
On the supply side, reverse-polarity protection, a TVS for surges and bulk capacitance for regeneration. In bridges, dead time.
Plus a capacitor across brushes for noise and a safe default off."
Quick check. What is the main purpose of the flyback diode across a motor or solenoid?
Drive switch trade-offs: EMR, SSR, MOSFET, BJT, IGBT.
The question: Tradeoffs between different drive circuits: electromechanical relay (EMR), solid-state relay (SSR), MOSFET, BJT, insulated-gate bipolar transistor (IGBT), etc.
You can switch a motor or solenoid with a mechanical relay, a solid-state relay (SSR), a MOSFET, a BJT, or an IGBT.
They differ in power wasted while on, switching speed, ease of driving, and whether they isolate (electrically separate) the load from the logic.
For a 12 volts PWM motor, use a MOSFET.
Think of a wall light switch versus an electronic dimmer. The wall switch is a mechanical relay.
It clicks slowly, wears out, cannot flicker thousands of times a second, and fully separates the circuits.
The dimmer is like a MOSFET: silent, fast, and long-lived, and it can vary the average power. But it does not isolate the circuits.
At low voltage the 10 milliohms MOSFET is far below everything else even at 20 amps (4 watts).
A high-voltage MOSFET has a quadratic loss that overtakes the IGBT's near-linear loss above a crossover current (5.
3 amps for these made-up models), which is why IGBTs take over at high voltage and current, but only for moderate switching frequency.
The BJT's linear loss ignores switching and storage effects. All models are illustrative, not datasheet values.
Relay (EMR): a small electromagnet that moves metal contacts. Almost no loss when on and full isolation, but slow, and it wears. SSR: a solid-state relay.
Light carries the signal inside it, so it isolates. No moving parts. MOSFET: a transistor switch that acts like a tiny resistor when on, so its loss is I squared R .
BJT / IGBT: transistor switches that drop a roughly fixed voltage when on, so their loss is that voltage times the current.
PWM: rapid on-off switching that sets the average power.
Compare what each switch wastes carrying 5 amps. A MOSFET with 10 milliohms loses 5 squared times 0. 01 equals 0. 25 watts. A BJT dropping 0.
3 volts, plus the current that keeps it on, loses about 1. 9 watts. A relay's contacts lose under 1 watts, plus about 0. 4 watts in the coil. A typical SSR dropping 1.
2 volts loses 6 watts, and an IGBT at 1. 3 volts loses about 6. 5 watts.
For a 12 volts motor with 20 kilohertz PWM, only the MOSFET both switches fast enough and wastes almost nothing. That is the whole idea.
"Relay: contacts, zero on-state loss, isolation, AC or DC, but slow, wears, can't PWM, and DC inductive arcs hurt.
SSR: isolated, silent, but about a volt drop (triac types) and AC-only unless MOSFET-based. MOSFET: voltage-driven, milliohm resistance, fast, the default for low-voltage PWM.
BJT: cheap, current-driven, 0. 2 to 0. 7 volts drop. IGBT: high voltage and current with constant drop, slower. 12 volts motor: MOSFET. Mains: relay or SSR.
400 volts inverter: IGBT or SiC."
Quick check. Which device is the best choice for a 20 kilohertz PWM drive of a 12 volts motor?
Faster solenoid drive: velocity and cycle rate. The question: What optimizations can you do for solenoid drives to increase plunger velocity and cycle rate?
A solenoid's cycle time is pull-in time plus release time plus return time.
To speed up pull-in, you over-excite it: apply a much higher voltage for the first few milliseconds, then drop to a low hold current.
To speed up release, drain the coil's current faster with a Zener or TVS clamp instead of a plain diode. The limits are coil heating and the transistor's voltage rating.
Picture a bucket. A higher-pressure hose fills the bucket faster, which is over-excitation. A bigger drain empties it faster.
The plain diode is a thin drain: the coil's stored energy trickles away slowly. A Zener or TVS is a wide drain. A thin trickle keeps a full bucket topped up: the hold current.
With 72 volts the current ramps to about 4 amps and the plunger closes at 7. 5 milliseconds, then the drive drops to a 6 volts average (0. 5 amps) hold.
The rated-voltage curve reaches the end of stroke at 19. 5 milliseconds.

The fall in current just before closure in each curve is the speed voltage of the accelerating plunger ("Measuring solenoid speed"); on the 72 volts curve the drive also drops to the hold level at the moment of closure.
Over-excitation (peak-and-hold): a high pull-in voltage or current first, then a lower, regulated hold current.
Flyback clamp: the part that sets the coil's reverse voltage at turn-off. A plain diode gives about 0. 7 volts.
A Zener or TVS diode blocks until a set voltage, then conducts, so it holds a much higher voltage. Hold current: the lower current that keeps a closed plunger shut.
With almost no air gap left, it needs far less.
Take a 24 volts solenoid with a 12 ohms coil, so 2 amps at rated voltage. Driven at 24 volts steady, it closes in about 19. 5 milliseconds.
With 72 volts applied until it closes, it takes about 7. 5 milliseconds. Then hold at 0. 5 amps, which dissipates 0. 5 squared times 12 equals 3 watts instead of 48 watts.
On release, a plain diode lets the plunger start leaving about 28 milliseconds after turn-off.
A 60 volts clamp cuts that to about 4 milliseconds, or about 1 milliseconds from the hold current. The cycle shrinks from about 65 milliseconds to about 22.
5 milliseconds, roughly 15 hertz up to 44 hertz. That is the whole idea.
"Cycle time is pull-in plus release plus return.
For pull-in I over-excite: a high voltage for the first few milliseconds, then PWM down to a hold current, since force goes as current squared and a closed plunger needs much less.
For release I replace the plain flyback diode with a Zener or TVS so the coil sees a high reverse voltage and the current collapses fast.
Add soft landing to stop bounce, and mechanical tweaks: lighter plunger, right spring. Watch coil heating and FET voltage rating."
Quick check. Why does applying a higher voltage for the first few milliseconds speed up solenoid pull-in?
Specifying a motor/solenoid driver IC. The question: If you're using a driver IC, how do you spec it? What properties should you look for?
Specifying a driver IC (the chip that switches the motor's current) means turning your load and your supply into a datasheet checklist. Check the voltage range, including spikes.
Check the continuous current by heat, not by the headline number. Check the interface, the protections, and the package.
A "3 amps" driver may not deliver 3 amps for long on your board.
Think of a car rated "200 km/h". It hits that briefly on a test track, not all day in desert heat. A driver's "peak current" is like the top speed.
Its continuous current depends on how well the chip sheds heat on your board. The datasheet shows the test-track number, and you must work out the desert number.
The first decision is integrated versus gate-driver.
Integrated parts are simpler, smaller and include protections; gate drivers scale to power but put the FET choice and layout on you ("Specifying discrete transistors for a drive").
On-resistance: the resistance of the chip's switches when on. Hot, it is 1. 4 to 1. 7 times the 25 degrees Celsius value.
Thermal resistance: how many degrees the chip warms per watt, which depends on your board's copper. Junction: the silicon inside the chip. Its temperature is the one that matters.
Thermal shutdown: the chip turns itself off when too hot, then back on once it cools.
A 12 volts motor has a 1 ohms winding, so it stalls at 12 amps, and it runs at 2 amps. The IC has 0.
4 ohms of hot on-resistance, 40 degrees Celsius/W of thermal resistance, and a 3. 6 amps current limit, in 60 degrees Celsius surroundings.
Running at 2 amps loses 2 squared times 0. 4 equals 1. 6 watts, so the junction reaches 60 plus 64 equals 124 degrees Celsius, which is acceptable. At the 3.
6 amps limit during a stall, it loses 5. 2 watts and wants to rise about 207 degrees Celsius, so thermal shutdown cycles.

What limits switching frequency. The question: What limits the switching frequency?
A switching drive is limited by whichever of several things runs out first.
The main limit is heat: each switching transition wastes a little energy, so losses grow in step with frequency.
Fixed delays, like dead time and the minimum pulse width, eat a bigger share of each shorter period.
The circuit that drives the switch, the timer, and electrical noise (EMI) also set ceilings.
There is a lower limit too, because slow switching gives large ripple and audible whine.
Think of stirring a pot of soup. Stir faster and the soup stays smoother, which is lower ripple, but your arm tires faster, which is heat.
Each stroke also has fixed pauses at each end while you reverse. When the strokes are long, the pauses barely matter.
When you stir very fast, the pauses become most of each stroke.
Conduction loss is constant, switching losses grow linearly with frequency (on a log axis the curve bends upward). With a 1.
3 watts thermal budget (horizontal line: ΔT = 65 degrees Celsius at 50 degrees Celsius/W) the ceiling is near 257 kilohertz for this FET and edge speed.
Shortening the edges or lowering the voltage moves the ceiling up ("Increasing the switching frequency"). The model ignores the rise of R DS(on) with temperature.

Drag the edge time up to 300 nanoseconds and the ceiling falls to about 95 kilohertz; drag the conduction loss up to 1 watts instead and it falls to about 86 kilohertz, because less of the budget is left for switching.
Switching loss: energy wasted each time the switch changes state, because for a moment it carries current and voltage at once.
Dead time: a deliberate gap where both switches of a pair are off, so they never overlap. Minimum on-time: the shortest pulse the circuit can reliably make.
Current ripple: the wiggle in motor current from switching on and off. Faster switching shrinks it. Thermal budget: how much heat the part can shed without getting too hot.

Fixed times bite sooner: 200 nanoseconds of dead time on each of two edges is 0. 8% of a 20 kilohertz period, but 40% of a 1 megahertz period. That is the whole idea.
"Mainly loss and timing.
Switching loss, half V I times rise-plus-fall time times f, plus gate-drive, C oss and diode recovery losses, all scale with frequency and add to conduction loss until the thermal limit.
Then dead time, minimum on-time and blanking eat a bigger share of a shorter period, gate drivers can only supply so much current, and the timer resolution caps the frequency.
EMI rises too. The lower bound is ripple and audible noise, so motors typically run 20 to 50 kilohertz."

Increasing the switching frequency. The question: How do you increase the switching frequency?
Before raising the switching frequency, ask whether you need to, because every step costs efficiency and adds electrical noise (EMI).
Make each switching transition faster and less wasteful, with a stronger gate drive (the circuit that flips the transistor), better transistors, and a tight layout.
Shrink fixed delays. Or let the load see a higher frequency while each switch keeps its old rate, by staggering two sets of switches.
Think of two rowers sharing a boat. Each one pulls at a modest stroke rate, so each tires slowly.
But because they alternate, the boat feels a stroke twice as often, and the ride is smoother.
Interleaving and unipolar PWM work the same way: the load sees double the frequency, but each switch keeps its original rate and loss.

A smaller one switches it faster. Ringing: a brief overshoot and wobble after a very fast edge, from stray inductance in the wiring.
Unipolar PWM: an H-bridge pattern where the motor sees pulses at twice the rate each switch runs.

Draw an H-bridge circuit. The question: Draw an H-bidge circuit.
An H-bridge is two legs side by side, drawn like the letter H.
Each leg has a high-side switch from the supply down to a middle node, and a low-side switch from that node to ground.
The motor sits between the two middle nodes, as the crossbar of the H.
A good drawing also shows the transistors (usually MOSFETs), their built-in diodes, and the gate drivers that switch them.
Picture a canal with four gates, two on each side, and a channel across the middle that holds a paddle wheel.
Open the top-left and bottom-right gates, and water flows across the channel one way. Open the top-right and bottom-left gates, and it flows the other way, so the wheel reverses.
Open both gates on the same side and the water rushes straight from supply to drain without touching the wheel.
The H. S1/S3 form the left leg (midpoint A) and S2/S4 the right leg (midpoint B). The motor is the crossbar.
Closing S1 and S4 puts A at V M and B at ground; closing S2 and S3 does the opposite.
Node: a connection point in a circuit. Leg (half-bridge): one high-side and one low-side switch in series, with the output at the midpoint.
Body diode: the diode built into every MOSFET. It gives the motor's current a path when switches turn off.
Shoot-through: both switches in one leg on at once, which shorts the supply. Dead time: a brief gap with both switches of a leg off, between transitions.
Label the switches S1 (top left), S2 (top right), S3 (bottom left), and S4 (bottom right), with 12 volts as the supply.
S1 and S4 on puts the left node at 12 volts and the right at 0 volts, so the motor gets +12 volts. S2 and S3 on reverses it to minus 12 volts.
Both low sides on, S3 and S4, shorts the motor to brake it. All off, it coasts. S1 and S3 together is the forbidden short.
For real parts, add body diodes and gate drivers with dead time. That is the whole idea.
"An H-bridge is two half-bridges: each leg has a high-side and a low-side switch, and the motor sits between the two middle nodes.
Turn on top-left plus bottom-right and current flows one way; top-right plus bottom-left reverses it; both low sides shorts the motor for braking; all off lets it coast.
With MOSFETs I draw NFETs low and PFETs, or bootstrapped NFETs, high, include the body diodes for the inductive freewheel path, and add gate drivers with dead time so one leg never shoots through."

Draw a half-bridge circuit. The question: Draw a half-bidge circuit.
A half-bridge is two switches in series between the supply and ground, with the output taken from the node between them. When the top switch is on, the output is at the supply.
When the bottom one is on, it is at ground. Flip between them quickly, and the average output is the fraction of time the top is on, times the supply.
Picture flicking a mixer handle very fast between hot and cold. If hot is on a quarter of the time, the water comes out a quarter of the way from cold to hot.
The duty cycle sets the average. Never open both taps at once into the same pipe: that connects the hot supply straight to the cold drain. In a half-bridge, that is shoot-through.
Two ideal switches from V M to ground; the node between them is the output. A load connects from SW to ground (or elsewhere, see below).
Switch node: the junction between the two switches. It is the output. Duty cycle ( D ): the fraction of each period the high side is on. Average output is D V M .
Dead time: a short gap with both switches off between transitions, so they never overlap. Body diode: the diode built into each MOSFET (transistor switch).
It carries the load current during dead time. Inductive load: a load with a coil, like a motor, whose current cannot change instantly.
With a 12 volts supply and a 25% duty cycle, the output averages 0. 25 times 12 equals 3 volts. Put a motor with 1 millihenries of inductance on it, switching at 20 kilohertz.
Its coil smooths the current, which wiggles by only about 0. 11 amps each cycle. With 100 nanoseconds of dead time on each edge, 5 amps flowing through a 0.
7 volts body diode wastes only 0. 7 times 5 times 200 nanoseconds times 20 kilohertz equals 14 milliwatts. That is the whole idea.
"A half-bridge is two switches in series from the supply to ground, with the output at the middle node.
High side on gives the supply, low side on gives ground, both off lets an inductive load clamp through a body diode.
I'd use two NFETs with body diodes, a bootstrapped gate driver for the high side, and dead time so the two never overlap.
The average output is duty cycle times supply, and with an LC filter it becomes a buck converter."

How a half/H-bridge works. The question: How does a half/H-Bridge work?
A half-bridge is two switches stacked between the supply and ground, with the output wire taken from the point between them.
Close the top switch and the output connects to the supply; close the bottom one and it connects to ground.
Flip between the two very fast and a motor sees an average voltage, so you can set its speed.
An H-bridge is two of these with the motor between them, so current can run either way.
Picture a tap that feeds a pipe from a high tank and a drain valve that dumps the pipe to the ground. Open the tap, then the drain, many times a second.
The water in the pipe settles to an in-between level set by how long the tap stays open.
The motor's coil acts like a heavy water wheel: it will not stop or start instantly, so it smooths the flicker.
Where it breaks: when the top switch opens, the coil's current keeps flowing, so the bottom switch must give it a path.
High side on. Current flows from V M through Q H and SW into the motor and down to ground. The winding stores energy: L di over dt equals V M-iR .
PWM: switching at a steady rate while changing how long each "on" lasts. Duty cycle ( D ): the fraction of each cycle the top switch is on. D equals 0.
25 means on 25% of the time. Inductor (winding): a coil that resists sudden changes in current, so its current cannot jump.
Freewheel path: the route the coil's current takes when the top switch opens, through the bottom switch or a diode built into it.
Dead time: a short gap with both switches off so they never conduct together.
Use a 12 volts supply and a motor on one half-bridge. Keep the top switch on for 25% of each cycle.
The output is 12 volts for a quarter of the time and 0 volts for the rest, so the average is 0. 25 times 12 equals 3 volts. That is the whole idea.
"A half-bridge connects the output to the supply or to ground, and PWM duty sets the average output.
The inductive motor current can't stop when the top switch opens, so it freewheels through the bottom FET or its body diode.
An H-bridge is two half-bridges with the motor in between: one leg high and the other low gives one direction, the opposite gives reverse, and PWM on one leg, or on both in anti-phase, sets speed.
Dead time keeps both FETs in a leg from conducting together."

H-bridge vs half-bridge trade-offs. The question: What is the difference between an H-bridge and half-bridge? What are the tradeoffs?
A half-bridge is one pair of switches with a single output. The load must connect that output to something fixed, such as ground.
An H-bridge is two such pairs, and the load sits between the two outputs.
That extra control of the load's second end is what lets an H-bridge reverse a motor, at the cost of more parts and more loss.
Think of pushing a child on a swing. With a half-bridge you can only push from one side of a fixed post, so the swing goes one way.
With an H-bridge you have a helper on each side, so you can push either way, and you can also hold the swing still. The helper costs a second wage and adds a little drag.
Where it breaks: a half-bridge can still brake a motor by shorting it; it just cannot reverse it.
Only the H-bridge covers the full plus-or-minus range with the full supply.
The split-rail half-bridge covers both polarities but only half the range; the ground-referenced half-bridge is one-sided.
Half-bridge: two switches, one output node. H-bridge (full bridge): two half-bridges with the load floating between their outputs.
Floating load: a load with neither end tied to a fixed rail, so you control both ends.
Conduction loss: heat from current flowing through the small resistance of a switch that is on, P equals I squared R .
Plugging / braking: stopping a motor by shorting it or by driving it backward.
Take a 12 volts supply and a 5 amps load. Each switch that is on has 20 milliohms (0. 02 ohms) of resistance.
A half-bridge with the load to ground has one switch in the current path: 5 squared times 0. 02 equals 0. 5 watts. An H-bridge has two in series: 5 squared times 0. 04 equals 1.
0 watts. The half-bridge gives 0 to 12 volts, so a motor turns one way; the H-bridge gives -12 volts to +12 volts, so it can reverse. That is the whole idea.
"A half-bridge is one leg of two FETs; it drives a load between its output and a fixed rail, so the load sees zero to the supply and a motor only turns one way.

An H-bridge is two legs with the load floating between them, which gives plus or minus the full supply, so reverse, brake and regeneration, but it needs twice the FETs and drivers, and has twice the conduction loss.
Use a half-bridge for fans, solenoids and bucks, an H-bridge for reversing motors and bipolar drive."
