Braking a motor with half/H-bridges. The question: How can you brake a motor using a half-bridge? What about an H-bridge? Which can brake the motor faster?
How does this stress the motor?
A spinning motor is also a generator: it makes its own voltage, called back-EMF, that grows with speed.
To brake it you give that voltage a path to push current through, or you drive the motor backward.
Shorting the two motor wires together is one way; applying reverse voltage ("plugging") is a harder, faster one.
A half-bridge can only short the motor, while an H-bridge can do both.
Picture a heavy flywheel spinning in a workshop. You can let it coast, drag a gentle brake pad on it, or throw the machine into reverse.
The brake pad grips hardest when the wheel is fast and fades as it slows.
Reverse gives a much harder stop, but it strains the gears and the engine, and if you keep the reverse on after the wheel stops, it spins up backward.
The analogy leaves out one thing: with a motor, plugging also draws extra energy from the supply.
With both low-side FETs on, the motor terminals are shorted through the two FETs and the ground path.
The rotating armature (E) pushes current round this loop; the current is E over (R a plus 2R DS(on)) .
After forward drive (current A to B), the braking current flows the other way, B to A through the winding, then down through Q 3 and up through Q 4 , so its torque opposes the rotation.
The high-side devices stay off.
Back-EMF ( E ): the voltage a spinning motor generates, proportional to its speed. Coast: all switches off; only friction slows the motor.
Short-circuit (dynamic) brake: both motor wires tied together; the current is E over R .
Plugging: applying reverse voltage while still spinning; the current is (V plus E) over R . Stall current: V over R , the current when the spinning part (rotor) is held still.
Take a 12 volts motor with 1 ohms winding resistance, spinning at full speed so that its back-EMF is 12 volts. Shorting the wires gives a current of 12 over 1 equals 12 amps.
Plugging adds the supply to the back-EMF, so the current is (12 plus 12) over 1 equals 24 amps, twice as much, and the motor stops faster.
On this page's example motor, plugging stops it in about 35 milliseconds, while the short brake takes about 115 milliseconds to fall to 10% of its speed. That is the whole idea.
"I'd brake with a half-bridge by turning on the low-side FET, which ties both motor terminals to ground, so the back-EMF drives current through the winding and the motor slows.
An H-bridge can do that with both low sides, or can plug by applying reverse voltage, which makes current (V plus E) over R , about twice as much, and stops several times faster.
The stress is peak current, winding heating, a torque jolt on the gears and brushes, and with plugging you must cut the drive at zero speed or it reverses."

Asymmetrical half-bridge vs symmetrical H-bridge. The question: When can you use an asymmetrical half-bridge? When do you need a symmetrical H-bridge?
A half-bridge is one pair of switches that connects its output to the supply or to ground.
"Asymmetrical" here means the two halves do unequal jobs: either the two switches are sized differently, or the load only ever sees one polarity.
A symmetrical H-bridge has four equal switches and drives a load in both directions.
Imagine two workers sharing a shift. One works 90% of the day and the other 10%. You would give the busy one the better tools, not split the budget evenly.

A buck converter (a circuit that steps a voltage down by switching) is like that at low duty cycle: the low-side switch carries current most of the time, so it deserves a bigger, lower-resistance switch.
But if both workers must do the same job in turn, as in a reversing motor or a transformer, you want identical workers.
The gain from asymmetry grows as the duty cycle moves away from 50% and is symmetric about it (a low-side-dominated converter and a high-side-dominated one both gain).
At 50% duty there is nothing to gain.
Duty cycle ( D ): the fraction of each cycle the high-side switch is on. On-resistance ( R DS(on) ): the small resistance of a switch that is on; current through it makes heat.
Conduction loss: heat from current in that resistance, P equals I squared R times the fraction of time it conducts.
Unipolar vs bipolar: the load sees one voltage polarity, or both. Volt-seconds: voltage multiplied by time; a transformer needs these to average to zero.
Take a buck converter with D equals 0. 1 and a 10 amps load. Two equal 10 milliohms switches give 10 squared times (0. 1 times 0. 01 plus 0. 9 times 0. 01) equals 1. 0 watts.
Now keep the same total switch size but make the high side 20 milliohms and the low side 6. 67 milliohms. The loss becomes 100 times (0. 1 times 0. 02 plus 0. 9 times 0.
00667) equals 0. 8 watts, a 20% saving. At D equals 0. 5 equal switches are already the best. That is the whole idea.

"An asymmetrical half-bridge is one where the two FETs differ or where the load only sees one polarity, so I'd use it for unidirectional loads and buck converters at lopsided duty cycles; resizing the FETs to match the duty cycle cuts conduction loss, 20% at D = 0.

I need a symmetrical H-bridge when the load must see both polarities or zero DC average: reversing motors, voice coils, class-D speakers and transformers, where equal FETs and symmetrical drive are the right choice."

High-side NFET advantages and challenges. The question: What are the advantages of using a high-side NFET? What additional challenges are presented?
A high-side switch sits between the supply and the load. An N-channel FET (NFET) is the better switch: lower resistance and cost than a P-channel one of the same size.
The catch: an NFET turns on when its gate (control pin) is a few volts above its source (the pin current leaves by).
On the high side the source is the output, which rises to the supply when the FET is on. So the gate needs a voltage above the supply.
Picture a person who must stay 10 meters above a platform that rises with the water level. When the platform is at 24 meters, the person must be at 34 meters.
A ladder fixed to the ground tops out at 24 and never gets them there. You need a ladder that rides up with the platform.
The riding ladder costs parts, board area and limits on how long the switch can stay on.
The gate must sit 10 volts above the source whenever the FET is on. When the source is at 24 volts the gate is at 34 volts, above the supply rail.
Drive from ground-referenced logic and the high side never turns on.
Gate-source voltage ( V GS ): the gate voltage measured against the source, not against ground. On-resistance ( R DS(on) ): the resistance of the FET when it is on.
Lower means less heat. Bootstrap: a capacitor charged at low voltage, then lifted with the source to give the gate its extra voltage.
Switch node: the output point between the high-side and low-side switches. Charge pump: a small circuit that makes a voltage above the supply, so the FET can stay on indefinitely.
Take a 24 volts supply and an NFET that needs 10 volts of V GS to be fully on. When it conducts, its source is at 24 volts, so the gate must be at 24 plus 10 equals 34 volts.
A 10 volts ground-referenced driver gives V GS equals 10 minus 24 equals -14 volts, so the FET stays off. The payoff: at 10 amps a 10 milliohms NFET wastes 10 squared times 0.
01 equals 1 watts, while a 25 milliohms P-channel FET wastes 2. 5 watts. That is the whole idea.
"An NFET is the better switch because electrons are two to three times more mobile than holes, so for the same die it has lower on-resistance and gate charge, and it's cheaper with more choices.
The challenge on the high side is that its source is the switch node, so the gate has to be a few volts above the supply, which needs a floating gate supply: a bootstrap capacitor or charge pump.
That limits duty cycle and complicates start-up, and adds undershoot and dv/dt issues."
Quick check. Why does an N-channel power MOSFET generally have lower R DS(on) than a P-channel one of the same die size?
Drive circuit for a high-side NFET. The question: Design a circuit to properly drive a high-side NFET. Why is it needed?
A high-side NFET needs its gate about 10 volts above its source, and its source rides up to the motor supply. So you need a small gate supply that moves with the switch node.
The usual answer is a bootstrap: a diode and a capacitor beside a gate-driver chip.
The capacitor charges while the low side is on, then floats up with the switch node and powers the gate drive.
Fill a bucket at ground level, then carry it up in an elevator to the 24th floor.
The water still stands the same height above the bucket's floor, even though the bucket is now high above the ground.
The capacitor is the bucket, and the 10 volts charge is the water. A one-way valve (the diode) stops the water draining back down.
The bucket slowly leaks, so it cannot stay up there forever without a refill.
With a fixed gate rail, V GS drops linearly as the source rises and the FET turns itself off before the source gets to 7 volts. A bootstrapped supply holds V GS near 9.
6 volts for any V SW .
Switch node (SW): the junction between the high-side and low-side FETs, where the motor connects.
Bootstrap capacitor ( C boot ): the capacitor between the driver's boot pin and SW that holds the floating gate supply.
Bootstrap diode: lets current charge the capacitor, and blocks it when SW rises. Gate charge ( Q g ): the charge needed to turn the FET fully on.
Charge pump: a circuit that makes a supply above the rail, so the FET can stay on 100% of the time.
Use a 24 volts bridge, a 10 volts driver supply and a FET with Q g equals 40 nC. While the low side is on, SW is near 0 volts, so the capacitor charges through a 0.
4 volts diode to about 9. 6 volts. When SW jumps to 24 volts, the boot pin sits near 33. 6 volts and the gate gets its 9. 6 volts. To keep the voltage from sagging more than 0.
5 volts, the capacitor needs at least 40 nC over 0. 5 volts equals 80 nanofarads, so use about 470 nanofarads. That is the whole idea.
"A high-side NFET needs its gate about 10 volts above its source, and the source is the switch node, so I need a gate supply that floats with it.
I'd use a half-bridge driver with a bootstrap: a fast diode from the 10 volts supply to a capacitor that sits between the boot pin and the switch node.
It charges when the low side is on and lifts the gate drive when the high side turns on. Size it as gate charge over allowed droop, about 0.
5 microfarads for 40 nC, add a gate resistor and a gate-source pull-down, and use a charge pump if I need 100% duty."

PFET and NFET on together: shoot-through. The question: What happens if you turn both the PFET and NFET on the same side at the same time? How do you prevent this? 1
Shoot-through is when the top and bottom switches in the same leg are on at the same time.
That connects the supply straight to ground through both switches, with no load in the way. The current spikes, the switches heat up, the supply sags and parts often die.
It can happen even when the control logic looks correct, so you add a deliberate gap, called dead time, plus other safeguards.
Picture a canal lock with a gate at each end. If the upstream gate and the downstream gate are open together, water rushes straight through and floods everything.
The safe rule is to close one gate fully before you open the other. Dead time is the pause between "close" and "open".
The analogy leaves out one trick: a fast voltage jump at the middle node can push a gate open by itself, like a gust slamming a door.
With both gates asserted the current runs from V M through Q P and Q N to ground and never touches the load.
The only limits are the FETs' saturation currents, the loop inductance and the supply impedance.
Leg: a high-side and a low-side switch sharing one output node. Dead time: a short interval, tens to hundreds of nanoseconds, when both switches are off.
Turn-off delay: the time a switch takes to actually stop conducting after its gate is told to turn off.
Miller turn-on: a fast voltage jump at the output leaks through the FET's internal capacitance into its gate and briefly turns the "off" switch on.
CMOS inverter: a PFET and NFET with joined gates, which has the same overlap issue on a small scale.
A 24 volts leg has two switches, each with 20 milliohms of on-resistance. If both are fully on, the ideal current is 24 over (0. 02 plus 0. 02) equals 600 amps.
Real FETs limit their own current, so it is lower, but still tens of amps or more.
Add 100 nanoseconds of dead time at each transition and neither switch is on while the other turns off, so the short never forms. That is the whole idea.
"Turning on the PFET and NFET in the same leg shorts the supply to ground through two on-resistances, so you get big current spikes, heat, rail droop and often a dead FET.
It happens with overlapping gate edges, tied gates, mismatched turn-off and turn-on delays, or Miller-coupled dv/dt.
I prevent it with separate gate drives and dead time, a driver with built-in shoot-through protection, faster turn-off than turn-on, stiff gate pull-downs, and current limiting as a backstop."
Quick check. What is shoot-through?
Drive an inductive load from a GPIO. The question: Design a circuit to drive an inductive load from a microcontroller GPIO.
A microcontroller pin can supply only a few milliamps at 3. 3 volts. A solenoid or relay needs hundreds of milliamps at a higher voltage.
So the pin controls a transistor switch, and the transistor carries the load current.
A coil also fights any sudden stop in its current, so you add a diode to give that current a safe path when the switch opens.
Think of a small lever that opens a big water valve: your finger only needs a tiny push. The coil is like a long, heavy pipe full of moving water.
If you slam a valve shut, the water hammers the pipe. A bypass loop lets the water keep circulating and slow down gently. The diode is that bypass loop.
The coil's stored energy ends up as heat in the coil and diode.
The flyback diode sits across the load with its cathode on the +12 volts side.
R g (100 to 220 ohms) limits the GPIO current and damps ringing; R pd (10 to 100 kilohms) keeps the gate low whenever the pin is not driving.
GPIO: a general-purpose pin on a microcontroller that you set high or low in software.
Logic-level MOSFET: a transistor switch whose control pin (the gate) turns it fully on at logic voltages such as 3. 3 volts.
Low-side switch: a switch between the load and ground, so the gate voltage is simply measured from ground.
Flyback diode: a diode across the coil that conducts when the switch opens. Gate pull-down: a resistor from gate to ground that keeps the switch off when the pin is not driving.
Drive a 12 volts solenoid with a 24 ohms coil. The current is 12 over 24 equals 0. 5 amps, far more than a pin can give.
Put a logic-level NFET between the coil and ground and connect the pin to its gate through about 220 ohms. Place a diode across the coil, cathode to +12 volts.
When the FET turns off, the coil's 0. 5 amps circulates through the diode and fades over a few milliseconds. The drain stays near 12 volts instead of spiking to hundreds of volts.
That is the whole idea.
"I'd use a low-side logic-level N-channel MOSFET: load from the supply to the drain, source to ground, GPIO to the gate.

A flyback diode across the load takes the inductive kick, a 100 k pull-down on the gate keeps it off when the MCU is in reset, a 100 to 220 ohms series gate resistor limits GPIO current and ringing, and a bulk capacitor supports the supply.
If the load is on a different or noisy supply, add isolation between the MCU and the gate."
Quick check. In a low-side FET switch for a solenoid, where does the flyback diode go?
Why a gate pulldown resistor. The question: Why would a pulldown resistor be necessary?
A MOSFET's gate (its control pin) is insulated from the rest of the transistor, so it acts like a tiny capacitor that draws almost no steady current.
If nothing drives it, it does not sit at zero: it keeps whatever voltage it last had and drifts with leakage and noise.
A pulldown resistor from gate to ground gives that gate a defined path to 0 volts, so the switch stays off whenever the microcontroller is not driving it.
Imagine a swing door with no latch and no spring. It could sit open, closed or halfway, depending on the draft. A pulldown is a spring that always pulls the door shut.
Pushing the door open on purpose takes only a little extra effort.
The analogy leaves out one limit: a weak spring cannot hold the door against a strong gust, like a fast voltage jump on a bridge.
With the GPIO high-impedance (reset or input), leakage and coupled noise (the arrow) have nowhere to go except R pd .
They create V equals I leakR pd : 100 nanoamps through 100 kilohms is 10 millivolts, nowhere near the threshold.
High-impedance (Hi-Z) pin: a pin that is not driving high or low, as in reset or input mode. Floating: a wire with no steady connection, so leakage and pickup set its voltage.
Threshold voltage ( V th ): the gate voltage where the transistor starts to conduct.
Linear region: the half-on state where the FET drops real voltage while carrying current, so it heats up.
Pulldown resistor: a resistor, here 10 to 100 kilohms, from gate to ground.
A 12 volts supply drives a 24 ohms coil through a FET. If the floating gate leaves the FET half on and 0. 25 amps flows, the coil drops 0. 25 times 24 equals 6 volts.
The FET drops the other 6 volts, so it dissipates 6 times 0. 25 equals 1. 5 watts, a lot for a small package.
With a 100 kilohms pulldown, the gate sits at 0 volts when the pin is Hi-Z, and the FET stays off. When the pin drives 3. 3 volts, the pulldown draws only 3.
3 over 100 k equals 33 microamps. That is the whole idea.

"A MOSFET gate is a capacitor with a huge DC resistance, so if the driving pin is in reset, booting or set as an input, the gate floats and drifts with leakage and noise, and can drift above threshold.
Then the FET half-turns on and either fires the load at power-up or sits in its linear region burning power.
A 10 to 100 kilohms pulldown from gate to source gives the gate a defined path to ground so it defaults off, and costs only microamps when the pin drives it high."
Quick check. Why is a pulldown resistor placed from gate to source on a low-side NFET driven by a GPIO?
Gate series resistor and parasitic oscillation. The question: Why would you want a series resistor between the GPIO and MOSFET gate?
What is parasitic oscillation in the context and where can it arise from? What does the series resistor do?
A MOSFET's gate (its control pin) acts like a small capacitor, which stores charge, and the wire leading to it acts like a small inductor, which resists changes in current.
A fast edge pushed into that pair makes it ring, like a bell, and the gate voltage can overshoot.
A small resistor in series with the gate soaks up that energy, limits the driver's current and slows the edge a little.
Parasitic oscillation is the same ringing, but sustained, when the transistor's own gain and feedback keep it going.
Picture a heavy door on a spring. Shove it and it bounces back and forth many times before it settles. A shock absorber on the hinge turns the bouncing into one smooth swing.
The series resistor is the shock absorber. Too little and the door still bounces. Too much and the door creeps shut slowly.
Where it breaks: a transistor can pump energy back into the bounce, so it can keep oscillating instead of ringing once.
A series RLC. The step from the driver sees R drv plus R g , the loop inductance L g (orange) and the gate capacitance.
Lowering R without lowering L makes the loop ring; raising R damps it.
Gate capacitance ( C iss ): the capacitor the driver must charge to turn the FET on. Loop inductance ( L ): inductance of the bond wire, lead and trace feeding the gate.
Ringing: a decaying wobble after a fast edge. Damping: how quickly a wobble dies out; a resistor adds it.
Critical damping: the smallest resistance, R equals 2 square root of L over C , that gives no overshoot.
Take a gate loop with L equals 20 nanohenries and C equals 1 nanofarads. It rings at about 36 megahertz.
Critical damping needs R equals 2 square root of 20 nanohenries over 1 nanofarads equals 2 times 4. 47 about 9 ohms, so a resistor near that value stops the overshoot.
The resistor also protects the pin. A 3. 3 volts pin with 25 ohms of output resistance and no gate resistor would try to push 3. 3 over 25 equals 132 milliamps.
With 220 ohms added, the peak is about 13. 5 milliamps. That is the whole idea.

"The gate is a capacitor, and the wire and package feeding it add nanohenries of inductance, so a fast driver edge makes a series LC that rings at tens of megahertz and overshoots the gate; with enough gain and feedback through the Miller capacitance it can even oscillate.
A series gate resistor damps the loop, requiring R at least 2 square root of L over C , caps the GPIO's peak current, and slows the edge to cut dv/dt and EMI, at the cost of some switching loss."
Quick check. Why does a fast driver edge into a MOSFET gate through a short wire often ring?
Why isolation matters, and its trade-offs. The question: Why is isolation important? What are the tradeoffs?
Isolation means two circuits exchange signals with no direct electrical connection between them. Light, a magnetic field or a tiny capacitor carries the message instead of a wire.

You use it to keep dangerous voltages away from people and from the microcontroller, to stop a power-stage failure from spreading, and to keep heavy switching currents from disturbing the logic's ground.
It costs money, board space, speed and a second power supply.
Picture a castle with a moat. Messengers can signal across with lamps, but nobody can walk over, and floodwater on the far side cannot flow in. That keeps the king safe.
The price is real: you need people on both banks, a way to feed the far side, and the lamp signals are slower than shouting across a hall.
The analogy leaves out one leak: very sudden surges can still splash across the moat through the tiny capacitance of the barrier.

Information crosses the barrier (PWM and enable one way, a fault flag the other), but the DC path does not: the fault voltages, spikes and ground shifts of the power stage stop at the barrier (the dotted link ending in a cross), so the MCU and the user-accessible parts tied to it stay on the safe side.
Galvanic isolation: no direct conductive path between two circuits. Ground bounce: a voltage appearing on a shared return wire from current changes, v equals L di over dt .
Isolation barrier: the insulating gap, rated for a working voltage, that separates the two sides.
Creepage and clearance: the required distances along a surface and through air between the two sides.
CMTI: how fast a voltage jump across the barrier the isolator tolerates without glitching.
A 24 volts motor controller shares one ground wire between the motor and a 3. 3 volts microcontroller.
Ten amps changing in 100 nanoseconds through 10 nanohenries of that wire gives 10 nanohenries times 10 amps over 100 nanoseconds equals 1 volts.
That shifts the microcontroller's ground by a third of its supply. Separately, if the power FET fails short, 24 volts can reach a pin rated for about 4 volts.
A barrier solves both, at the cost of an isolator, a second supply and some delay. That is the whole idea.

"Isolation matters for safety (keeping hazardous voltage away from people and logic), for protection (a shorted FET can't put the motor rail on the MCU pin), and for noise, because switching current on a shared ground shifts the MCU's reference by volts.
It also gives floating references for high-side drives and sensors.

The trade-offs are cost, area, an isolated power supply, delay and limited bandwidth, optocoupler aging, and the barrier's capacitance, which still passes fast common-mode transients, so I'd choose by CMTI, speed and voltage rating."
Quick check. Which is NOT a primary reason to isolate a microcontroller from a power stage?
Which kinds of isolation to use. The question: What sort of isolations would you want?
"Which kind of isolation" has several answers, because it depends on what has to cross the barrier. Logic and PWM signals can use an optocoupler or a digital isolator.
A bridge's gate drive needs an isolated gate driver. Analog measurements need an isolated amplifier.
Communication links need isolated versions of their interface chips, and the far side's power needs an isolated power converter.
Then the safety standard decides how strong the barrier must be.
Imagine passing messages across a river with no bridge.
You could flash a lamp at the other bank (optical), tap a drum so the pulse travels through a thin wall (magnetic), or touch a thin plate that wiggles one on the far side (capacitive).
All work; they differ in speed, price and how well they ignore a storm. The far bank also needs its own food supply: the isolated power converter.
The first question is what has to cross; each answer has a standard device family.
Optocoupler: an LED and a light sensor in one package; light crosses the gap. Digital isolator: a chip that sends logic across a tiny capacitive or magnetic barrier.
Isolated gate driver: a gate-driver chip with a barrier between its control side and output side.
Insulation grade: functional, basic, double or reinforced; the standard sets which you need.
Pulse-width distortion: the difference between rising and falling delay, which warps short pulses.
Take a 20 kilohertz PWM with 12-bit resolution. One step of duty is 1 over (20 kilohertz times 4096) equals 12. 2 nanoseconds.
A digital isolator with about 5 nanoseconds of pulse-width distortion barely disturbs that.
A slow optocoupler with 500 nanoseconds of distortion makes the low bits meaningless, so the digital isolator is the better pick.
That is the whole idea: match the device to the signal, then match the rating to the standard.
"It depends on what crosses the barrier and how strong it needs to be. For logic and PWM I'd use a digital isolator, or an optocoupler if it's slow.
For a high-voltage bridge, an isolated gate driver with an isolated supply. For motor current sensing, an isolated amplifier or delta-sigma modulator.
For buses like CAN or RS-485, an isolated transceiver, and for power, an isolated DC-DC.
The grade is set by the standard: basic or reinforced insulation for mains, with working voltage, CMTI, delay and creepage as the selection parameters."
Quick check. Which isolation device is the best fit for a 20 kilohertz PWM with 12-bit resolution?
Opto-isolation and its trade-offs. The question: What is opto-isolation? What are its tradeoffs?
An optocoupler is an LED and a light sensor sealed in one package with an insulating gap between them.
Current through the LED makes light, the sensor on the other side sees it and conducts, and no electrical connection crosses the gap.
The main number to know is the current transfer ratio, how much output current you get per unit of LED current. It is cheap and robust, but it is slow, and it weakens with age.
Imagine signaling across a canyon with a flashlight. A friend on the far side has a light sensor and reacts when the beam arrives. The two of you share no wire, only light.
Over the years the flashlight bulb dims, so the beam gets weaker, and the sensor eventually misses it. The sensor is also slow compared with a wire.
Heat makes the bulb dim faster.
Current through the LED (set by R LED ) produces light that drives the phototransistor.
OUT is pulled low when the LED is on and saturated, and pulled to V CC2 by R pull when the LED is off.
The two grounds are separate (the chassis-style ground symbol marks the isolated side). Note the output is inverting with respect to the input.
Optocoupler: an LED plus a photodetector in one insulating package. Phototransistor: a transistor switched by light instead of by an input current.
Current transfer ratio (CTR): output current divided by LED current, I C over I F . Pulse-width distortion: unequal rise and fall delays that stretch or shrink a pulse.
CMTI: how fast a common-mode voltage jump the part tolerates without a false output.
Drive the LED with 5 milliamps from a 3. 3 volts pin and a resistor: (3. 3 minus 1. 2) over 5 milliamps equals 420 ohms. A new part with 50% CTR can then sink 0.
5 times 5 equals 2. 5 milliamps. After years of aging and heat, CTR may fall to 20%, and the same 5 milliamps gives only 1 milliamps.
If the output's pull-up resistor (which holds the line high) needs 2. 5 milliamps to pull the output low, the circuit now fails.
So you design for the worst-case CTR, not the nominal one. That is the whole idea.
"An optocoupler is an LED and a photodetector, usually a phototransistor, in one package with an insulating gap, so only light crosses and the two sides are galvanically isolated.
The key spec is CTR, output current over LED current, which varies with temperature and drops with age.
Trade-offs: slow with distorted pulse widths, milliamps of input current, limited common-mode immunity, and aging, in return for low cost, simplicity and a high isolation rating.
For fast or long-life interfaces a digital isolator is better."
Quick check. What does the CTR of an optocoupler specify?
Design an opto-isolated gate drive. The question: Describe/draw/design an opto-isolation circuit.
An opto-isolated gate drive lets a microcontroller switch a power transistor with no electrical connection between them. The pin lights an LED.
A phototransistor (a transistor switched by light) on the other side sees it, and a small buffer stage then pushes current into the power FET's gate.
You size the LED resistor, size the output stage for an aged part, make the buffer fast enough to charge the gate, and choose the polarity so a reset leaves the FET off.
Picture a person flashing a small lamp to tell a crane operator across a yard to lift. The lamp signal is weak and the crane needs real power.
So the operator uses the signal to work a big lever. The phototransistor's weak output is the lamp signal, and the buffer transistors are the big lever.
The crane also needs its own power: an isolated supply.
GPIO high drives I F equals (3. 3-1. 2) over 200 equals 10. 5 milliamps. The pin low, or high-impedance at reset, means no current: LED off. This is the default-safe polarity.
LED series resistor ( R LED ): sets the LED current, (V pin minus V F) over I F .
End-of-life CTR: the lowest transfer ratio the part will have after aging and heat; the value to design with.
Emitter follower: a transistor stage whose output copies its input voltage and can supply more current.
Isolated supply: a power source for the output side that shares no conductor with the microcontroller side.
Gate pulldown: a resistor that holds the FET off if nothing drives the gate.
A 3. 3 volts pin drives the LED at 10 milliamps, so R LED equals (3. 3 minus 1. 2) over 10 milliamps equals 210 ohms, and you use 200 ohms.
At 20% end-of-life CTR the phototransistor passes 0. 2 times 10. 5 equals 2. 1 milliamps. A plain pull-up of 5. 6 kilohms feeding a 2 nanofarads gate has a time constant of 5.
6 k times 2 nanofarads equals 11 microseconds, far too slow, and it is also inverting.
So use an emitter-follower output, which is non-inverting and off by default, then add a buffer stage. That is the whole idea.
"I'd bias the LED at about 10 milliamps from the GPIO: (3. 3 minus 1. 2)/10 milliamps is 210 ohms, so 200 ohms, active-high so reset means off.

On the output side I'd run the phototransistor from an isolated 12 volts as an emitter follower into a pulldown, which is non-inverting, defaults off and goes to about 11 volts at end-of-life CTR, then buffer it with an NPN/PNP pair into a 10 ohms gate resistor with a gate-source pulldown, because a plain pull-up into a gate is microseconds slow.
Then verify CTR margin, delays and CMTI."
Quick check.

What is galvanic isolation?. The question: What is galvanic isolation?
Galvanic isolation means two circuits have no direct conductive path between them, so no steady current can flow from one to the other.
They can still exchange information or power, using light, a magnetic field or an electric field across a thin gap.
It lets the two sides sit at very different voltages and keeps a fault on one side from reaching the other.
It is not perfect: fast voltage jumps can still leak across the small capacitance (charge-storing ability) of the barrier.
Picture two rooms separated by a thick glass wall. You can wave, and the person inside sees you. You can tap on the glass and they feel the vibration. But nobody can walk through.
A very hard slam, though, can rattle things on the other side. That slam is a fast voltage edge passing through the barrier capacitance.
The analogy leaves out power: the far room still needs its own heater, meaning its own supply.
Information (and energy) crosses through a transmitter, a non-conductive coupling medium and a receiver. The two grounds are separate and can sit at different potentials.
Conductive path: a route where steady (DC) current can flow, such as a wire or a shared ground.
Barrier capacitance ( C iso ): the small capacitance across the gap, around 1 picofarads in a signal isolator.
Common-mode voltage: a voltage that appears on both wires of one side relative to the other side's reference.
CMTI: the fastest common-mode voltage edge the isolator tolerates without error.
Working voltage: the voltage the barrier can withstand continuously, which is lower than the short test voltage.
Take a 1 picofarads barrier.
A capacitor passes no steady current at all, and at 1 megahertz it still acts like a 1 over (2 pi times 10 to the 6 times 10 to the -12) equals 159 kilohms resistor.
But a fast edge of 50 volts/ns pushes 1 picofarads times 50 volts over ns equals 50 milliamps across, which can cause glitches.
So isolation blocks steady and slow stuff well and fast edges poorly. That is the whole idea.

"Galvanic isolation means two circuits have no direct conductive path, so no DC current, yet they still exchange signal or power through light, a magnetic field or an electric field across a capacitor.
It lets the two sides sit at completely different voltages, breaks ground loops and contains faults.
But the barrier has a little capacitance, so fast common-mode transients still cross, it has a finite voltage rating, and the far side still needs its own isolated supply."
Quick check. What defines galvanic isolation?
High-side PFET challenges at high supply voltage. The question: What are some challenges when using a high-side PFET and a much higher supply voltage to power the motor?
A P-channel FET (PFET) on the high side turns on when its gate (control pin) is pulled a few volts below its source, and its source sits at the supply.
So the gate signal is measured from the supply, not from ground. With a 48 volts supply and a 3. 3 volts microcontroller, the pin cannot drive the gate directly.
You need a level shifter and a clamp so the gate is never pulled too far, and you accept slow, lossy switching.
Picture a ceiling light with a pull cord hanging from the ceiling. To switch it on, you pull the cord about 10 cm down from the ceiling. A microcontroller pin that only reaches 3.
3 volts above the floor is like someone who can only reach the floor: they yank the cord far past its limit and snap it. The gate oxide is the cord.
The GPIO can only pull the gate between 0 and 3. 3 volts, but the source is at 48 volts.
In both logic states V GS is hugely negative: the PFET is permanently on and the gate oxide is overstressed. A gate that never rises near 48 volts can never turn the device off.
Gate oxide: the thin insulating layer under the gate; too much voltage across it punches through.
Level shifter: a circuit that turns a ground-referenced logic signal into a gate drive referenced to the supply.
Gate-source rating: the largest V GS the gate survives, typically 20 volts. Zener clamp: a diode that limits the gate-source voltage to about its rated value.
Connect a 3. 3 volts pin straight to the gate of a PFET whose source is at 48 volts. Then V GS equals 3. 3 minus 48 equals -44. 7 volts.
The FET is always on, and the gate is far beyond a 20 volts rating.
With a small NFET level shifter, a 10 kilohms resistor and a 12 volts Zener, the gate is held 12 volts below the source when on, and at the supply when off.
The on-state current is (48 minus 12) over 10 k equals 3. 6 milliamps. That is the whole idea.
"A PFET high-side switch needs its gate pulled below the supply, so with a 48 volts motor and a 3.
3 volts MCU the logic can't drive it directly: V GS would be minus 45 volts, always on and beyond the gate rating.
You need a level shifter, a small NFET rated for the full supply, a Zener clamp so the gate-source never exceeds about 12 volts, and resistors that make turn-on and turn-off slow and lossy.
Add the PFET's higher on-resistance, supply transients, Miller coupling and shoot-through, and it's good for low-frequency switching, not fast PWM."
Quick check. Why is a Zener often placed from gate to source of a high-side PFET on a 48 volts bus?
Design a high-side PFET drive. The question: Design a circuit to properly drive a high-side PFET. Why is this needed?
To switch a high-voltage load with a PFET from a 3. 3 volts pin, you build a small circuit around its gate.
A small NFET, driven by the pin, pulls the PFET's gate down through a resistor. A pull-up resistor from gate to source keeps the PFET off by default.
A Zener diode (one that conducts above a set voltage) from gate to source stops the gate being pulled too far. It switches slowly, so it suits on/off load switching and slow PWM.
Think of a window blind with a pull cord, a spring and a stopper. The spring (pull-up resistor) keeps the blind closed. A person (the NFET) tugs the cord to open it.
The stopper (Zener) prevents tugging so far that the cord breaks. When the person lets go, the spring closes it again.
Spring and tug are both gentle, so the blind moves slowly: slow switching and heat.
With Q2 off, R gs holds the PFET gate at the bus: V GS equals 0 , off. With Q2 on, R c pulls the gate node down until the Zener clamps V GS at minus 12 volts.
The Zener's cathode is on the source (bus) side. Q2 is a low-side switch exactly like "Drive an inductive load from a GPIO", with a gate resistor and a pulldown.
D fw gives the motor current a path (anode at ground) when Q1 turns off.
Level-shifting NFET: a small transistor, source at ground, that the pin turns on to pull the PFET gate down.
R c : the resistor between that NFET and the PFET gate; it sets turn-on speed and standing current. R gs : the gate-to-source pull-up that holds the PFET off.
Gate Zener: clamps V GS at about -12 volts when on. Standing current: current that flows the whole time the switch is on.
Take a 48 volts bus, a 5 amps motor and a 3. 3 volts pin. With the pin low, the NFET is off and R gs holds the gate at 48 volts, so the PFET is off.
With the pin high, the NFET pulls the gate node down until the 12 volts Zener clamps it at 36 volts, so V GS equals -12 volts.
The standing current is (48 minus 12) over 10 k equals 3. 6 milliamps, which dissipates about 130 milliwatts in R c .
The gate time constant is 10 k times 2 nanofarads equals 20 microseconds, so this is fine near 1 kilohertz and poor beyond. That is the whole idea.
"PFET source on the bus, drain to the load.
A small 100 volts NFET level shifter, driven from the GPIO through a series resistor with a pulldown, pulls the PFET gate down through a 10 k resistor.
A 10 k pull-up from gate to source holds the PFET off, and a 12 volts Zener from gate to source clamps V GS so it can't exceed the rating at any supply voltage.
That gives about minus 12 volts of V GS when on and 0 when off, with 3. 6 milliamps standing current at 48 volts.
It's fine up to about 1 kilohertz; beyond that add a push-pull stage."

Ways to measure current. The question: How can you to measure current?
You cannot see current directly, so every method turns it into something you can measure, usually a voltage.
One way is to let the current flow through a small resistor and measure the voltage across it. Another is to measure the small magnetic field the current makes.
A third is to reuse a resistance already in the circuit. Each trades cost, accuracy, power loss and electrical isolation.
Think of counting traffic on a road. You can put a toll booth across the road and count each car as it slows down. That is accurate, but it slows traffic.
A camera beside the road does not disturb traffic but costs more and can be fooled. The toll booth is a shunt resistor and the camera is a magnetic sensor.
The analogy leaves out one wrinkle: some magnetic sensors only see cars that are changing speed, meaning AC.
Two physical handles, current-induced voltage drop and current-induced field, produce all the common sensing methods.
Everything on the resistance branch dissipates power and connects electrically to the circuit; everything on the field branch is isolated.
Shunt resistor: a small, precise resistor placed in series with the load. Insertion loss: the voltage drop and power the sensor adds to the circuit.
Current sense amplifier: an amplifier that boosts a tiny voltage riding on a larger bus voltage.
Hall-effect sensor: a chip that outputs a voltage in proportion to the magnetic field of the current.
Current transformer: a transformer whose primary is the conductor; it works with AC only.
Put a 10 milliohms shunt in series with a 5 amps load. By Ohm's law, the voltage across it is 5 times 0. 01 equals 50 millivolts. The heat it makes is 5 squared times 0.
01 equals 0. 25 watts. That 50 millivolts is small for a 3. 3 volts, 12-bit ADC (the chip that turns a voltage into one of 4096 numbers), whose step is about 0.
8 millivolts, so you add an amplifier first. For the same 5 amps, a Hall sensor would add almost no loss and would isolate the circuit, but it costs more and drifts.
That is the whole idea.
"You convert current to a voltage.

The common ways are a series sense resistor with an amplifier, which is cheap, accurate and DC-capable but dissipates power; using an existing resistance like a MOSFET's Rds(on) or inductor DCR, which is free but inaccurate; and magnetic sensing, Hall sensors or current transformers, which give isolation and low loss but cost more and drift.
For a low-voltage board I'd default to a shunt plus a current sense amplifier."

Why measure current. The question: Why do you want to measure current?
Current is the quantity that heats wires, makes motor torque and tells you how much battery charge has moved. Voltage alone often cannot show these things.

So products measure current for four jobs: protection (shut down on a short), control (regulate a power converter or motor), monitoring (battery charge and power) and diagnostics (spot a stalled motor or a broken wire).
The job decides how fast and how accurate the measurement must be.
Think of the water meter on a house. It spots a burst pipe because flow suddenly jumps (protection). It can tell a pump how hard to work (control).
It adds up the total for the bill (monitoring). And a flow of zero while a tap is open tells you something is blocked (diagnostics).
A burst pipe needs a fast alarm, but billing needs a precise total. The analogy leaves out the heat: in electronics, the flow itself causes damage by warming the pipes.
Four jobs for the same measurement.
Each job puts a different demand on the sensor: speed for protection, bandwidth and linearity for control, low offset for monitoring, moderate accuracy for diagnostics.
Overcurrent protection: shutting off when current exceeds a safe limit. Torque constant ( k t ): how much twisting force (newton-meters) a motor makes per amp.
Coulomb counting: adding up current over time to track battery charge. Stall current: the large current a motor draws when its shaft cannot turn.
Offset: a small constant error in the reading, which adds up when you integrate.
Short a 12 volts supply through 10 microhenries of wiring. The current rises at V over L equals 12 over 10 micro H equals 1.
2 amps per microsecond, so it reaches 12 amps after 10 microseconds. A trip circuit with a 1 microseconds delay catches it near 1 or 2 amps over the limit.
A slow check every 100 microseconds would let it reach about 120 amps. Now take battery tracking: a 10 milliamps offset on a 2 Ah cell is 0. 01 times 1 over 2 equals 0.
5 % of capacity per hour. That is the whole idea.
"Four reasons. Protection, because current is what overheats and destroys hardware, so you need a fast overcurrent trip.
Control, because converters use inductor current for current-mode control and motors produce torque proportional to current.
Monitoring, because integrating current gives battery state of charge and multiplying by voltage gives power. And diagnostics, like detecting a stalled motor or missing load.
The purpose sets the spec: protection wants speed, metering wants low offset, control wants bandwidth."

Magnetic current sensing pros and cons. The question: How does inductive/magnetic current sensing work? What are its pros and cons?
Magnetic current sensing reads the magnetic field that a current makes, instead of the voltage it drops across a resistor.
That gives you electrical isolation and almost no power loss. A Hall sensor reads the field directly and works for steady (DC) and alternating (AC) current.
Current transformers and Rogowski coils respond only to changing current, so they work for AC only. The price is higher cost, offset drift and poor accuracy at small currents.
Imagine feeling the wind from a fan without touching it. A Hall sensor is like a flag that leans steadily as long as the wind blows, so it reports steady wind too.
A current transformer is like a pinwheel that only spins while the wind speed is changing: a steady wind gives it nothing. Both keep your hand away from the fan.
Stray wind from other fans, meaning nearby wires and magnets, adds error to both.
Hall principle.

A bias current flows along the plate; the field from the measured conductor pushes the moving carriers sideways (Lorentz force), so a voltage appears across the plate, between the edges perpendicular to both the bias current and B.
It is proportional to B and therefore to the measured current; its sign depends on the carrier type.
Because V H depends on B itself, not on its rate of change, this works at DC, unlike induction.
Hall effect: a magnetic field pushes moving charges sideways in a thin plate, making a small voltage proportional to the field.
Current transformer (CT): the measured wire passes through a ring with an N -turn coil, which carries I p over N .
Burden resistor: the resistor across a CT's coil that turns its current into a voltage.
Rogowski coil: a coil whose output follows how fast the current changes, so a circuit must add it up over time.
A wire carrying 10 amps makes a field of B equals micro 0 I over (2 pi r) equals 0. 2 mT at 1 cm, which is tiny, so real sensors use a core or a close conductor to concentrate it.
For a CT with 1000 turns, 10 amps in the wire gives 10 over 1000 equals 10 milliamps in the coil. A 100 ohms burden turns that into 0. 01 times 100 equals 1 volts.
A steady DC current would give no output at all, because nothing is changing. That is the whole idea.
"Magnetic sensing measures the field around the conductor instead of a voltage drop. Hall sensors detect the field directly and work at DC and AC.
Current transformers and Rogowski coils use Faraday induction, so they only see AC. The big advantages are isolation, almost no insertion loss and high current range.
The downsides are cost, size, offset and temperature drift, sensitivity to stray fields, and poor accuracy at small currents compared with a shunt."

Current sensing tradeoffs compared. The question: Describe tradeoffs between different current sensing mechanisms.
There is no single best current sensor. Each method trades accuracy, power loss, speed, DC ability, isolation and cost.
A shunt resistor with an amplifier is the accurate, cheap default but wastes power as current grows and has no isolation.
Reusing the resistance of a transistor switch is free but rough. Magnetic sensors give isolation and handle large current but cost more and are poor at small currents.
You pick by the current, the isolation need and the smallest current you care about.
Think of choosing a vehicle. A bicycle is cheap, precise and fine for a light load, but it is hopeless for hauling bricks.
A truck carries any load but is costly and clumsy for small trips. A shunt is the bicycle and a magnetic sensor is the truck.
Using the free resistance of a MOSFET is like borrowing a neighbor's bike: no cost, but you cannot count on its condition.
Many boards combine two: a cheap fast path and a precise slow one.
A first-pass decision flow.
It is a heuristic, not a law: exceptions such as a 5 amps mains line (CT or isolated shunt amplifier) or a 150 amps battery pack with a busbar shunt are common.
Insertion loss: the voltage and power a sensor takes from the circuit, I squared R for a shunt. Offset: a small fixed zero error, which matters more as the current gets smaller.
DC capability: whether the sensor can read steady current. Isolation: no conductive path between the measured circuit and the electronics.
Rds(on) sensing: using a MOSFET's own on-resistance as the sense resistor.
A 2 milliohms shunt at 100 amps burns 100 squared times 0. 002 equals 20 watts, but at 10 amps it burns only 0. 2 watts, so shunts stop scaling at high current.
Now compare small-current accuracy. A 10 milliohms shunt with a 100 µV amplifier offset has an equivalent error of 0. 0001 over 0. 01 equals 10 milliamps.
A Hall sensor with 66 millivolts per amp and 15 millivolts of offset has an error of about 227 milliamps. At 100 milliamps, the shunt is much better. That is the whole idea.
"A shunt plus current-sense amp is the accurate, cheap, DC-capable default, but it dissipates I-squared-R and has no isolation.
Rds(on) or inductor DCR sensing is lossless and free but only 10 to 20 percent accurate, so it's for protection.
Hall and CT sensors give isolation, no loss and high current range, but cost more, drift, and are poor at low current, and CTs are AC only.
I'd choose by current level, isolation need, accuracy at the lowest current, and power budget."

How a sense resistor works. The question: How does a sense resistor work to sense current?
A sense resistor is a small, precise resistor placed in series with the load, so all the load current flows through it.
By Ohm's law the voltage across it is the current times its resistance. Because you know the resistance, measuring that voltage tells you the current.
The voltage is tiny, so an amplifier boosts it and an ADC turns it into a number the firmware can use.
Picture a short, slightly narrow section in a long water pipe. All the water has to pass through it, and the pressure drops across it in proportion to the flow.
Read the pressure drop and you know the flow. The narrow section must stay only slightly narrow, or it would choke the pipe and waste energy.
The analogy leaves out one trap: you must read the pressure right at the two ends of the narrow section, not somewhere further along the pipe.
The load current flows down through R s. The voltage V s across it (+ at the top) equals I·R s; the amplifier takes the difference and multiplies it by G.
Shunt (sense resistor): a low-value resistor in series with the load used to turn current into voltage. Sense voltage: the voltage across the shunt, V s equals I R s .
Current sense amplifier: an amplifier that boosts the small difference across the shunt.
Kelvin connection: attaching the sense wires right at the resistor's pads so only the resistor is measured.
ADC: the converter that turns the amplified voltage into a digital number.
Let 5 amps flow through a 10 milliohms resistor. The voltage across it is 5 times 0. 01 equals 50 millivolts, and it wastes 5 squared times 0. 01 equals 0. 25 watts.
A current sense amplifier with a gain of 50 turns that into 2. 5 volts, which fits a 3. 3 volts ADC. Firmware reverses the steps: divide by 50, then by 0. 01, to get back 5 amps.
That is the whole idea.
"A sense resistor is a small precise resistor in series with the load. All the load current flows through it, so the voltage across it is I times R .
I measure that millivolt-level drop with a current sense amplifier and an ADC and divide by the resistance to get current.
It's small to limit loss, a few milliohms, and I connect the sense lines directly to its pads, Kelvin style, so only the resistor is in the measurement."

Sense resistor pros and cons. The question: What are its pros and cons?
A sense resistor is simple, cheap, tiny and very linear: its voltage is exactly proportional to the current. It works from DC up to high frequencies and it shrugs off overloads.

Its drawbacks are side effects: it wastes power and drops voltage in the supply path, its small signal is easily swamped by amplifier offset, its resistance drifts with heat, and a fast current edge makes its tiny inductance add a false spike.
It also gives no electrical isolation.
Think of a speed bump on a road. It is cheap, it always works and it responds to every car the same way.
But every car has to slow down, which wastes energy, and a very busy highway would turn into a traffic jam. And the bump itself warms up and changes its behavior.
At a fixed sense voltage, loss grows linearly with current.
100 millivolts at 100 amps is 10 watts, which is why designers lower the sense voltage and rely on a low-offset amplifier at high current.
Insertion loss: the voltage and power the sensor takes from the circuit. TCR: how much the resistance changes with temperature, in parts per million per °C.
ESL: the tiny series inductance every real resistor has, a few nanohenries. Offset floor: the smallest current you can tell from zero, V os over R s .
Kelvin sensing: taking the sense voltage at the resistor's own pads.
A 5 milliohms shunt at 30 amps wastes 30 squared times 0. 005 equals 4. 5 watts, so it does not scale to high current.
Now the small-signal side: a 100 µV amplifier offset on a 10 milliohms shunt is 0. 0001 over 0. 01 equals 10 milliamps, so you cannot trust readings near that value.
Finally, a fast edge: with 5 nanohenries of inductance and a 10 amps step in 100 nanoseconds, the extra spike is 5 nanohenries times 10 amps over 100 nanoseconds equals 0.
5 volts, five times the 0. 1 volts real signal from 10 amps in 10 milliohms. That is the whole idea.
"Sense resistors are cheap, small, linear and accurate, they work from DC to high frequency, and they handle overloads.

The downsides are that they dissipate I to the 2R and drop voltage so they don't scale to very high current, their tiny signal means amplifier offset limits low-current accuracy, resistance drifts with temperature, parasitic inductance corrupts fast edges, and there's no isolation.
They also need Kelvin routing and a CSA that handles the common-mode voltage on the high side."

Specifying a sense resistor. The question: How do you spec a current sense resistor? What happens if it's too big/small?
Choosing a sense resistor means finding a value that fits inside a window. If it is too large, it wastes power, drops the load voltage and heats up.
If it is too small, the signal at low current disappears into noise and the amplifier's offset (its small built-in zero error).
The allowed drop and power at full current set the upper limit; the smallest current you must measure sets the lower limit. Then you pick power rating, tolerance and construction.
Picture adjusting the opening of a turnstile that counts people. Too narrow and it jams the crowd and gets hot. Too wide and the counter cannot tell a person from a gust of wind.
In between, it counts well without slowing anyone. Sometimes no setting works, and you need a better counter.
The design flow. When the window is empty, the fix is never "pick a number anyway" but to change something: a lower-offset amplifier, more resolution, or range switching.
Sense voltage: the voltage across the shunt at full current, I max R s . Power derating: running a part well below its rated power, so it stays cool and accurate.
Equivalent offset current: V os over R s , the smallest current distinguishable from the amplifier's offset. TCR: how much the resistance drifts with temperature.
Four-terminal resistor: a part with separate pads for current and sensing.
Take I max equals 10 amps with a drop of at most 100 millivolts and a power budget of 0. 5 watts. The drop limit gives 0. 1 over 10 equals 10 milliohms. The power limit gives 0.
5 over 100 equals 5 milliohms, so the upper bound is 5 milliohms. Now require 1% accuracy at 0. 1 amps. With a 100 µV offset, the lower bound is 10 to the -4 over (0. 01 times 0.
1) equals 100 milliohms, which is above the upper bound, so the window is empty. With a 5 µV zero-drift amplifier the lower bound drops to 5 milliohms, and the design works.
That is the whole idea.
"I find the allowed window for the resistance. The upper limit is set by voltage drop and power at maximum current, R at most (V drop over I max P over I max squared) .
The lower limit is set by the smallest current I need to measure: the signal must beat amplifier offset, so R at least V os over ( I min) .
Then I pick a low-TCR, low-ESL part rated at least twice the dissipation. Too big wastes power and drops voltage; too small loses low currents in offset and noise."

Sense resistor from ADC range. The question: Given a range of input currents and ADC input voltage range, find an appropriate sense resistor value.
An ADC is the chip that turns a voltage into a number, and it can only read up to a set voltage.
To pick a sense resistor from that range, you ask what resistor makes your biggest current produce a voltage just under the ADC's full-scale.
That gives R s equals V FS over (k times I max) , where k is a headroom factor such as 1. 1. Then you check the answer for power, voltage drop and resolution.
Often the answer is silly, which tells you to use a small shunt and an amplifier instead.
Picture filling a measuring cup from a tap through a funnel. The cup's size is the ADC's range.
You pick a funnel so that the heaviest flow you expect fills the cup almost to the brim, but never overflows.
If the funnel needed to do that is absurd, say it would hold back the whole house's water pressure, you add a pump (an amplifier) and use a gentler funnel.
The funnel also wastes pressure, which for the resistor means voltage drop and heat.
At full scale the shunt dissipates V sense times I max . With a 3. 3 volts direct ADC input, 1 amps already costs 3. 3 watts.
With 50 millivolts into an amplifier it costs 50 milliwatts. This is the fundamental reason current is sensed with a small shunt plus gain.
Full-scale ( V FS ): the largest voltage the ADC can read. Headroom ( k ): spare margin, such as 10%, so an overload does not clip the ADC.
LSB: one step of the ADC, V FS over 2 to the N . Burden: the voltage and power the resistor takes from the load.
Bidirectional sensing: current in both directions, with zero set at mid-scale.
Take a 3. 3 volts ADC and a 100 milliamps maximum current, with 10% headroom. Then R s equals 3. 3 over (1. 1 times 0. 1) equals 30 ohms, so use the standard 27 ohms.
It would drop 2. 7 volts and waste 0. 27 watts, which is useless in a supply path. Now take an ADC that accepts only ±250 millivolts and a 10 amps maximum. Then R s equals 0.
25 over (1. 1 times 10) equals 22. 7 milliohms, so use 20 milliohms, which gives 200 millivolts at 10 amps.
That is the whole idea: the ADC's input range decides what works directly.
"I take the ADC full-scale voltage, divide by the maximum current with about 10 percent headroom, and that gives the largest resistor: R s equals V FS over (1. 1 I max) .
Then I check power I to the 2R , voltage drop, and resolution per LSB. If the result is silly, like 27 ohms at 100 milliamps, I use a small shunt and an amplifier instead.
For bidirectional current I use half the range, since zero sits at mid-scale."

High-side vs low-side current sensing. The question: What is the difference between high-side and low-side current sensing? What are the advantages/disadvantages of each?
When do you need to use one vs the other?
Low-side sensing puts the sense resistor between the load and ground. High-side puts it between the supply and the load.
Low-side is simple and cheap, but it lifts the load's ground a little and cannot see a short from the load to ground.
High-side keeps the load grounded and sees every fault, but the amplifier must handle the bus voltage on both its inputs.
The choice depends on whether the load must be grounded and which faults you must catch.
Imagine a water meter on a building's pipes. A meter at the tap (high side) counts all the water that leaves the supply, even if a pipe leaks straight into the ground.
A meter at the drain (low side) only counts water that reaches the drain, so a leak that bypasses the drain goes unseen.
But the tap meter sits under full water pressure, so it must be sturdier: that is the high-side amplifier.
Low-side. The shunt's bottom end is ground, so both amplifier inputs are within millivolts of 0 volts.
The load's own ground is the shunt's top node, which sits IR s above true ground.
High-side sensing: shunt in the supply path, between source and load. Low-side sensing: shunt in the return path, between load and ground.
Common-mode voltage: the voltage both amplifier inputs share relative to ground.
CMRR: the amplifier's ability to ignore common-mode voltage, in decibels (dB); each 20 decibels is ten times better.
Ground lift: the voltage I R s by which a low-side shunt raises the load's ground.
A low-side 10 milliohms shunt carrying 5 amps lifts the load's ground by 5 times 0. 01 equals 50 millivolts.
That is the price for a simple circuit, plus it misses a load wire shorted to ground. Now take a high-side shunt on a 48 volts bus with a 10 millivolts signal.
To keep the error under 100 µV, the amplifier's CMRR must satisfy 48 over 10 to the CMRR over 20 at most 0. 0001 , which needs about 114 decibels.
An amplifier with 80 decibels would add 48 over 10 to the 4 equals 4. 8 millivolts of error, half the signal. That is the whole idea.
"Low-side puts the shunt between load and ground: simple, cheap, near-zero common-mode, but it lifts the load's ground by IR s and can't see a short-to-ground fault.
High-side puts it between supply and load: load stays grounded and short-to-ground is detected, but the amplifier must handle bus-level common-mode voltage and have good CMRR.
I use high-side when the load must be grounded or for protection, and low-side when a small ground shift is fine and I want simplicity."

Sensing current with MOSFET Vds. The question: How can you use drain-source measurements of a MOSFET to determine current? What are the pros and cons of this setup?
A MOSFET that is fully on behaves like a small resistor, called R DS(on) .
So if you measure the voltage across its two power pins (drain and source) while it conducts, you can compute the current, I equals V DS over R DS(on) .
This adds no extra resistor, no extra loss and no extra parts, which is why it is popular for overcurrent protection.
It is not very accurate, because R DS(on) changes a lot with temperature.
Imagine a pipe that already has a valve in it, and the valve is fully open but still slightly narrow.
You can read the small pressure drop across that valve to estimate the flow, with no new part in the pipe.
The estimate is rough: when the valve warms up it swells and narrows, so the same pressure drop now means less flow.
Also, just after the valve opens the water sloshes, so you wait a moment before trusting the reading.
The comparator's non-inverting input watches the FET's drain; the other input is a threshold.
While the FET is on, V DS = I·R DS(on), so crossing V th means the current exceeded V th/R DS(on). A real design adds blanking, a filter, and a clamp.
R DS(on) : the resistance between drain and source when the FET is fully on. Triode region: the operating region where the FET acts like a resistor.
Blanking time: a short delay after turn-on during which the reading is ignored. Body diode: the diode inside the FET, which can carry current while the FET is off.
Comparator: a circuit that flips its output when a voltage crosses a set threshold.
A FET has R DS(on) equals 5 milliohms at 25 degrees Celsius. At 30 amps the drain-source voltage is 30 times 0. 005 equals 150 millivolts.
Set a comparator at 150 millivolts and it trips at 30 amps when cold. At 125 degrees Celsius the resistance rises by about 1. 68 times, to 8.
4 milliohms, so the same 150 millivolts is reached at only 0. 15 over 0. 0084 equals 17. 8 amps. The threshold slides with temperature. That is the whole idea.
"A fully-on MOSFET is a small resistor, so I equals V DS over R DS(on) .
You measure drain-source voltage with a comparator or amplifier and get current with no added loss, part or board space, which is why it's used for overcurrent protection.

The cons are accuracy: R DS(on) rises 50 percent or more when hot and varies part to part, it only works while the FET is fully on and after the switching edge settles, and the signal is just tens of millivolts.
Good for protection, poor for metering."

What a current sense amplifier is. The question: What is a current sense amplifier (CSA)?
A current sense amplifier (CSA) is a chip built to read the tiny voltage across a shunt resistor. It does three things.
It multiplies that small difference by a precise fixed gain, like 20 or 50. It ignores the large bus voltage that both shunt terminals sit on.
And it outputs a voltage measured from ground, ready for an ADC (a voltage-to-number converter).
It is one chip because precisely matched resistors are hard to get from loose parts.
Imagine measuring the height of a single step at the top of a very tall tower. You do not care how tall the tower is, only how big the step is.
A CSA is a person who climbs up, measures only the step, and reports the number back at ground level in a form you can read easily.
The tower's height is the bus voltage that gets ignored. The person's ruler has a tiny zero error, which matters for very small steps.
The chain inside and around a CSA. The first block deals with the large common-mode voltage, the second applies the precise gain, and the last presents a signal the ADC can use.
Gain (V/V): how many times the amplifier multiplies the small difference, such as 50. Common-mode voltage: the voltage both shunt terminals share relative to ground.
CMRR: how well the amplifier ignores that shared voltage, in decibels (dB). Input offset: a small built-in zero error that sets the lowest current you can trust.
REF pin: sets the output level at zero current, so negative currents can be shown.
A 10 milliohms shunt carries 5 amps, so the voltage across it is 5 times 0. 01 equals 50 millivolts. A CSA with a gain of 50 turns that into 50 times 0. 05 equals 2.
5 volts, which fits a 3. 3 volts ADC. If the amplifier has a 100 µV offset, the output error is 50 times 100 micro V equals 5 millivolts, which corresponds to 100 micro V over 0.
01 equals 10 milliamps of current. The rule is V out equals G times I times R s plus V ref . That is the whole idea.

"A current sense amplifier takes the small voltage across a shunt, rejects the large common-mode bus voltage it sits on, multiplies the difference by a precise fixed gain like 20 or 50, and outputs a ground-referenced voltage for an ADC or comparator, often with a reference pin for bidirectional current.
Inside it's a difference amplifier with trimmed matched resistors, so V out equals G I R sense plus V ref .
Key specs are gain error, offset, common-mode range, CMRR and bandwidth."

When you need a CSA. The question: When do you need a CSA?
You need a current sense amplifier when the raw voltage across the shunt cannot go straight into the ADC.
Maybe the signal is only tens of millivolts and the ADC step is about a millivolt, so resolution is poor. Maybe the shunt sits on a 24 or 48 volts bus the ADC cannot tolerate.
Or the current reverses and the signal needs shifting to mid-scale. You can skip it if the ADC accepts tiny signals directly or you only need a rough trip point.
Think of reading a thermometer whose markings are far too small to see. You hold a magnifying glass over it so the markings fill your view.
The amplifier is the magnifying glass: it makes a tiny signal fill the ADC's range.
But a magnifying glass magnifies smudges as well, and these are the amplifier's own offset and noise.
And if the thermometer sits behind a high fence (the bus voltage), you need a glass that sees over it.
Directly connected, the shunt signal barely lifts off the axis (50 millivolts at 5 amps, under 2 percent of the ADC range).
With a gain of 50 the same signal covers about 76 percent of full-scale. Without amplification, most of the ADC's resolution is thrown away.
Resolution (A/LSB): the smallest current change the ADC can tell apart. Common-mode range: the voltage range at the inputs where the amplifier still works.
Level shift: moving a signal's zero point to suit an ADC that reads only positive voltages.
Delta-sigma ADC: a converter with a small differential input range, often used directly on shunts. Offset: a zero error that amplification does not remove.
Take a 10 milliohms shunt, a 5 amps maximum, and a 12-bit ADC with 3. 3 volts full scale. The ADC step is 3. 3 over 4096 equals 0. 806 millivolts.
Connected directly, one step equals 0. 806 millivolts over 0. 01 equals 80. 6 milliamps, and the whole 5 amps uses only about 62 codes. With a gain of 50, one step is 1.
6 milliamps and 5 amps reads 2. 5 volts. So the amplifier recovers resolution that the ADC would throw away. That is the whole idea.

"You need a CSA when you can't feed the shunt voltage straight into the ADC: the signal is millivolts and the ADC step is about a millivolt, so resolution is poor; the shunt sits on a high-side bus voltage the ADC can't tolerate; or the current is bidirectional and needs a level shift.
A gain of 50 turns 50 millivolts into volts and also rejects common-mode noise.
I don't need one if the ADC has a small differential range or a PGA, or if I only need a comparator trip."

CSA versus a regular op-amp. The question: What is the difference between a CSA and a regular opamp?
A current sense amplifier is really an op-amp (a general-purpose amplifier chip) wired as a difference amplifier, with the properties this job needs built in.
Its gain-setting resistors sit on the same chip and are trimmed to match. Its inputs can sit far above its own supply voltage, so it works on a high-side bus.
And its offset is often microvolts, not millivolts. A plain op-amp with loose resistors is more flexible and fine when the bus is low and accuracy is modest.
Think of a pair of shoes. Two shoes made together as a matched pair fit each other well.
Two shoes bought separately in the same size can still differ a little, and the mismatch makes you limp.
In a difference amplifier, the four resistors are the shoes: if they are not matched, the bus voltage leaks into the reading. On-chip resistors are the matched pair.
Input range is a separate limit: a regular op-amp's inputs must stay inside its own supply.
Higher gain makes the same resistor tolerance look better (CMRR ∝ 1+G) but even G = 200 needs about 0. 05 percent matching to reach 100 decibels. Discrete 0.
1 percent resistors land at 82 decibels for G = 50; an on-die trimmed network gets to 100 decibels or more.
Difference amplifier: an op-amp with four resistors that subtracts two inputs. Matched resistors: resistors whose ratios agree very closely, which gives high CMRR.
CMRR: how well the amplifier ignores voltage common to both inputs, in dB. Input common-mode range: the voltage range the inputs tolerate, usually limited by the supply.
Zero-drift amplifier: a design that cancels offset continuously, to a few microvolts.
Build a difference amplifier with gain 50 and 0. 1% resistors. Its worst-case CMRR is about (1 plus 50) over (4 times 0. 001) equals 12 750 , which is 82 decibels.
On a 48 volts bus the leakage is 48 over 12750 equals 3. 8 millivolts, which is 7. 5% of a 50 millivolts signal.
A CSA with 120 decibels CMRR leaks only 48 over 10 to the 6 equals 48 µV, 0. 1% of the signal.
The offset gap is similar: 1 millivolts on a 10 milliohms shunt is a 100 milliamps error, while 100 µV gives 10 milliamps. That is the whole idea.
"A CSA is a difference amplifier in an IC, but built for shunt sensing: its gain-setting resistors are on-die and trimmed so CMRR is 100 to 120 decibels, where discrete 0.
1 percent resistors give only about 80 decibels; its inputs can sit above its own supply so it works on a high-side bus; and its offset is microvolts rather than millivolts.
A plain op-amp is more flexible and fine when the bus is within the supply and accuracy is modest."

How to spec a CSA. The question: How do you spec a CSA?
Speccing a current sense amplifier means turning your system's needs into a short list of numbers and checking each against the datasheet.
Start with where the shunt sits and how high the bus voltage can spike. Pick a gain that fills the ADC without overflowing it.
Check that the amplifier's own errors are small next to your smallest current, and that it is fast enough. Then add up all the errors and compare with your accuracy target.
Imagine buying a ruler for a job.

It must be long enough to reach the object (the common-mode range), have the right scale so the object fills the page (the gain), and have fine enough marks that a tiny object is not a blur (the offset).
It must also be quick to read if the object is moving (the bandwidth). A ruler can fail on any one of these, and its markings can be slightly off (gain error).
The unidirectional part is flat at its low-swing floor for any negative current (and for the first few tens of mA if the floor is above zero), so it can't see charging or regeneration.
With REF = 1. 65 volts the output moves both ways, but each direction gets only about half the ADC range, so the usable gain is lower (here ±2. 0 volts on a 1.
65 volts centre would clip at +16 amps, which is why you may choose G = 20).
Common-mode range: the input voltage range where the amplifier works and meets its specs. Gain and gain error: the multiplier and how far the real value strays from it.
Input offset ( V os ): a zero error that sets the minimum current, V os over R s . CMRR: how well the amplifier ignores the bus voltage.
Output swing: how close the output can get to ground and to the supply.
Take a 24 volts motor, 20 amps maximum, and a 2 milliohms shunt, which gives 40 millivolts. With a 3. 2 volts usable output, the largest gain is 3. 2 over 0.
04 equals 80 , so choose the standard 50, giving 2. 0 volts. A 100 µV offset means 100 micro V over 0. 002 equals 50 milliamps of error, which is 5% at 1 amps.
A CMRR of 100 decibels on 24 volts adds 24 over 10 to the 5 equals 240 µV, or 120 milliamps, so you would want about 110 decibels or better. That is the whole idea.
"I'd work from system requirements to parameters. Topology fixes the common-mode range I need.
The shunt and ADC range set the gain, limited by output swing and rounded to what's available.
Offset divided by the shunt gives my minimum current, so I check it against my lowest current, and CMRR against the bus voltage.
Then bandwidth at that gain against my PWM or protection time, output swing and REF, supply and protection.
Finally I do an error budget with shunt tolerance and tempco to make sure it meets accuracy."
Quick check. Which spec most directly determines the lowest current you can measure accurately with a given shunt?
Choosing CSA gain from ranges. The question: Given a range of input currents, a sense resistor value, and ADC input voltage range, find an appropriate CSA gain.
Choosing the gain means making the biggest current you expect land just below the top of the amplifier's usable output range.
You compute the shunt voltage at full current, divide the usable output limit by it, and round down to a gain the part actually offers.
Then you check what that gives you in resolution at the low end. If the current can reverse, you measure the room from the reference voltage to the nearer limit instead.
Think of zooming a camera so the subject fills the frame. If you zoom too little, the subject is a small speck and the picture wastes detail.
If you zoom too far, the edges of the subject are cut off. The right zoom lets the biggest subject just fit.
The gain is the zoom, and clipping at the top of the output is the cut-off edge.
The analogy leaves out one wrinkle: the zoom also magnifies the camera's own dust, which is the amplifier's offset and noise.
Each gain's line rises until it hits the output limit. At the 5 amps marker, G = 50 is still on its slope (2.
5 volts), while G = 100 and G = 200 have already flattened, meaning the top of the current range is lost. The G = 20 line wastes more than 60 percent of the ADC range.
Gain ( G ): how many times the amplifier multiplies the shunt voltage. Usable output range: the smaller of the ADC range and the amplifier's output swing, minus headroom.
Standard gain steps: gains a part family offers, such as 20, 50, 100 and 200. LSB: one ADC step, giving change in I equals V LSB over (G R s) per count.
Clipping: the output sticking at its limit when the signal is too large.
Take a 10 milliohms shunt and a 5 amps maximum, so the shunt voltage is 5 times 0. 01 equals 50 millivolts. The amplifier can swing to 3. 2 volts, so G max equals 3. 2 over 0.
05 equals 64 . Round down to a standard gain of 50. Then 5 amps gives 50 times 0. 05 equals 2. 5 volts, and one 12-bit ADC step is 0. 806 millivolts over (50 times 0.
01) equals 1. 6 milliamps. A gain of 100 would give 5 volts and clip near 3. 2 amps. That is the whole idea.
"Maximum gain is the largest usable output voltage divided by the shunt voltage at full current: G max equals V out max over (I maxR s) .
Usable means within both the ADC range and the CSA's output swing, with some headroom. I round down to a standard gain such as 20, 50, 100 or 200, and check amps per LSB.
Example: 5 amps on 10 milliohms gives 50 millivolts, so with a 3. 2 volts swing G max is 64 and I'd choose 50, giving 2. 5 volts.
For bidirectional current I measure from the reference to the nearer limit."
