Why protect against over/undervoltage and overcurrent. The question: How/why do you want to protect against overcurrent and/or over/undervoltage conditions?
Every part has limits, and real systems regularly go beyond them. Too much current heats wires and parts, because heat grows with the square of the current.
Too much voltage punches through the thin insulating layers inside parts. Too little voltage makes logic misbehave and transistors run half on.
Protection is whatever stops those things: a fuse, a clamp, or a supervisor chip that holds the system in reset while the supply is low.
You stack several layers so one failure does not destroy everything.
Think of a house. The circuit breaker is the overcurrent protection: it cuts power before the wires overheat.
A surge protector is the overvoltage protection: it absorbs a spike from a lightning strike.
And when the lights dim and the fridge stutters during a brownout, that is the undervoltage problem. Nothing burns, but equipment behaves strangely.
The analogy leaves out one thing: in a circuit board the protection parts are tiny, so they must be chosen for the energy of the fault.
Heating rises faster than I squared (the exponent is 1 over 0. 44 about 2. 27 ).
Doubling the current from 1 amps to 2 amps raises this trace from about 13 degrees Celsius to about 64 degrees Celsius above ambient.
A short circuit doesn't just run hotter, it leaves the safe region entirely.
Drag the width to 20 mil: the same 2 amps now heats it by only about 20 degrees Celsius, because cross-section enters with an exponent of 0. 725.
Joule heating: heat from current in a resistance, P equals I squared R . Absolute maximum rating: the limit past which a part may be damaged.
TVS diode: a clamp that absorbs short, high-energy voltage spikes. UVLO (undervoltage lockout): holding a circuit off until the supply is high enough.
Brown-out: a supply sag below the operating minimum, but not to zero.
Short a 5 volts rail through 10 milliohms. The ideal current would be 5 over 0. 01 equals 500 amps, which would dissipate 500 squared times 0. 01 equals 2.
5 kilowatts in a few millimeters of copper. A real supply cannot deliver that, but even a few amps can burn a thin trace. Doubling any current quadruples the heating.
Now the other end: a microcontroller rail that sags below its minimum may run garbage or half-write its saved settings, with no smoke at all. That is the whole idea.
"Every component has limits, and real systems leave the nominal range: shorts, hot-plug spikes, wrong adapters, sagging batteries.
Overcurrent is a heating problem since power goes as I squared R. Overvoltage causes breakdown of oxides and capacitors. Undervoltage makes logic misbehave and FETs run half on.
So I layer protection: a fuse or eFuse and TVS at the input, current limit and thermal shutdown in the regulator, and a supervisor or UVLO so the system only runs when the rails are healthy."
Quick check. Why is overcurrent so damaging compared with a modest voltage increase in a conductor?
Design an over/undervoltage and overcurrent detector. The question: Design a circuit to detect overcurrent and/or over/undervoltage conditions.
A fault detector watches a rail and raises a flag when something is wrong.

For voltage you build a window comparator: a resistor ladder scales the rail down, and two comparators (circuits that flip their output when one voltage passes another) check it against a reference, one for too high and one for too low.
For current you put a small shunt in the rail, amplify its voltage and compare that to the same reference.
A little hysteresis keeps the output from chattering, and you check that tolerances still give acceptable trip points.
Think of a thermostat with two limits. The heater should come on below 18 degrees and an alarm should sound above 25. Between them everything is fine. That band is the window.
A tiny gap between the "on" and "off" temperatures stops the heater clicking on and off when the room sits right at the limit. That gap is hysteresis.
The ladder gives two taps.
The upper tap feeds the UV comparator's inverting input (fault when it falls below V ref ); the lower tap feeds the OV comparator's non-inverting input (fault when it rises above V ref ).
R h feeds the OV output back to the + input so the release point sits below the trip point. The OR gate merges both into one FAULT line.
Window comparator: two comparators that flag when a signal is outside a lower and an upper limit. Voltage reference: a stable voltage, such as 1.
24 volts, that the scaled rail is compared against. Resistor ladder: resistors in series whose taps give fixed fractions of the rail.
Hysteresis: different rising and falling trip points, made with a little positive feedback.
Shunt and current sense amplifier: a small series resistor and an amplifier that scales its voltage.
Take a 12 volts rail, a 1. 24 volts reference, and a ladder of standard resistors totaling 99 kilohms whose bottom resistor is 8. 87 kilohms. The overvoltage trip is about 1.
24 times 99 k over 8. 87 k equals 13. 85 volts. A second tap sets the undervoltage trip near 9. 9 volts. For current, a 5 milliohms shunt and a gain of 50 turn 4.
96 amps into 50 times 0. 005 times 4. 96 equals 1. 24 volts, so the comparator trips at 4. 96 amps, wasting only 4. 96 squared times 0. 005 equals 0. 12 watts.
That is the whole idea.
"I'd use a window comparator: a resistor ladder from the rail with two taps, each going to a comparator against a 1.
24 volts reference, one for overvoltage and one for undervoltage, with a little hysteresis so it doesn't chatter.
The trip is the reference times the total divider over the lower part.
For current I'd put a milliohm shunt in the rail, amplify it with a current-sense amp, and compare to the same reference.
Then I'd OR the outputs into one fault line, check the tolerances, and add a small filter against glitches."
Quick check. What does hysteresis do in a voltage-monitor comparator?
What to do when a fault is detected. The question: If an overcurrent and/or over/undervoltage condition is detected, what can you do?
Detecting a fault is only half of protection; you also have to decide what to do.
The options run from gentle to drastic: flag it to the software, limit the current, shut down, disconnect the faulty branch, or clamp the voltage.
After a shutdown you choose how to restart: stay off until reset, retry automatically, or retry slowly (hiccup).
The response must be as fast as the hazard, and must leave the system safe.
Think of a small kitchen fire. First you notice and warn the household (flag). Then you turn down the heat (limit).
If it grows, you turn off the gas (shut down) or close the door to that room (disconnect).
After the fire is out, you either wait for someone to say it is safe to cook again (latch-off), or you try the stove again after a pause (retry).
In electronics you may also need time to save data before the power goes.
Severe, fast faults go to a hard response; slow or partial faults get a soft one. The restart policy depends on whether the fault is expected to clear.
Reporting is the last step in every branch.
Latch-off: the output stays off after a fault until power is cycled or reset. Auto-retry: the output switches back on after a delay and trips again if the fault remains.
Hiccup mode: retry with a very low duty cycle, so average fault power is small. Foldback: a current limit that falls as the output voltage falls.
Crowbar: a device that deliberately shorts the rail on overvoltage so a fuse opens.
A linear regulator (one that burns off extra voltage as heat) makes 5 volts from 12 volts and is limited to 2 amps. In a hard short it wastes 12 times 2 equals 24 watts.
In hiccup mode it stays on for 3 milliseconds and off for 150 milliseconds. The duty is 3 over 153 equals 1. 96 % , so the average fault power is about 0. 02 times 24 equals 0.
47 watts, and the part survives. When the short is removed, the next retry succeeds and the output stays on. That is the whole idea.
"It depends on how bad the fault is. The gentlest is to just flag it so firmware can react. Then limiting, like current limit or foldback.
Then shutdown, either latched or with auto-retry or hiccup so a persistent short sees only a few percent duty.
For overvoltage I can clamp with a TVS or crowbar a rail and blow a fuse, or disconnect the load.
I match the response speed to the hazard, and in an embedded system I use the warning to go to a safe state and save data before power is lost."
Quick check. Which restart policy leaves the output off after a fault until power is cycled or reset?
Protecting a power supply from overcurrent and overvoltage. The question: How/why do you need to protect a power supply from overcurrent/overvoltage?
A power supply must survive faults from outside (shorts, overloads, input spikes) and from inside (a shorted switch, or a broken resistor in the feedback path that reports the output voltage).

A buck converter (a switching circuit that steps voltage down through a coil, the inductor) limits current on every cycle, but a hard short can still let the coil current creep upward, so controllers add a valley limit, hiccup mode and thermal shutdown.
For overvoltage you also need a clamp or crowbar that does not depend on the regulator.
Imagine climbing a staircase where each step up is two stairs but each step back down is only one and a half.
Every cycle you gain half a stair, so you keep going up even though each step is small.
That is the inductor current in a hard short: it rises a little more than it falls each cycle.
The fix is to skip steps up until you have come back down far enough: the valley limit.
Each cycle the current steps up by 0. 383 amps in 150 nanoseconds and decays only 0.
276 amps over the long off-time, so the current staircases upward even though the controller has already reduced the on-time to its minimum.
The peak limit cannot stop it: the on-time is already at its minimum (and inside the blanking time), so the current keeps climbing until resistive drops balance the slopes or the inductor saturates.
Peak current limit: turning the switch off each cycle when the inductor current hits a ceiling.
Valley current limit: skipping the next cycle until the current has fallen below a threshold. Hiccup mode: repeated short restarts with long pauses during a persistent fault.
OVP (overvoltage protection): stopping switching when the output rises above a set level. Crowbar: a device that shorts the rail on overvoltage to force a fuse to open.
Short the output of a 12 volts buck with a 4. 7 microhenries inductor.
The switch cannot stay on for less than 150 nanoseconds, and in that time the current rises by 12 times 150 nanoseconds over 4. 7 micro H equals 0. 383 amps. During the 1.
85 microseconds it is off, only a 0. 7 volts diode drop pulls it down, removing about 0. 7 times 1. 85 micro s over 4. 7 micro H equals 0. 276 amps. The net gain is 0.
107 amps per cycle, so it reaches 5 amps in about 47 cycles. That is the whole idea.

"For overcurrent, a cycle-by-cycle peak limit stops the inductor from saturating, plus a valley limit or frequency foldback because in a hard short the inductor only has a diode drop to ramp down and current can ratchet up.
Then hiccup and thermal shutdown.
For overvoltage, the controller's OVP on the feedback turns off the high side, but since a shorted FET or an open feedback resistor defeats that, I'd add an independent clamp or crowbar and a fuse.
On the input: fuse, TVS, reverse protection, UVLO and soft start."
Quick check. What does a cycle-by-cycle peak current limit do in a buck converter?
Over/undervoltage on an embedded system. The question: What happens if you get an over/undervoltage on an embedded system?
When a microcontroller's supply leaves its allowed range, two different things happen.
Too low a voltage causes malfunction: logic slows down, the processor can run garbage, and a write to flash (the memory that keeps settings) can be cut halfway.
Too high a voltage causes damage: thin insulating layers inside the chip break down, and a pin pushed above the supply can trigger latch-up.
So you add a brown-out reset, a supervisor, series resistors and clamps on inputs, correct power-up order, and firmware guards.
Think of a cook at a stove. With too little heat the food is only half cooked, and nothing looks burnt, but the meal is wrong.
That is undervoltage: the chip still runs, but badly. With far too much heat the pan burns and cracks: overvoltage damage.
A good cook stops cooking if the gas pressure drops too low (brown-out reset). The analogy leaves out one hazard: a pin driven while the chip is off partly powers it.
A 1. 1 volts dip from 3. 3 volts (down to about 2. 2 volts) crosses the 2. 7 volts BOR threshold, so the chip is reset cleanly rather than running in the marginal band.
Without BOR (or with the threshold set at 1. 8 volts) the chip would run through the dip at reduced margins.
The numbers are examples: BOR levels and minimum operating voltages are device-specific.
Brown-out reset (BOR): holds the chip in reset while the supply is below a threshold. Supervisor: an external chip that monitors the rail and releases reset after a delay.
Clamp diodes: protective diodes on each pin that conduct if the pin goes above the supply or below ground.
Latch-up: an unintended structure inside the chip that switches on and shorts the supply until power is removed.
Back-powering: powering a chip through a pin's clamp diode while its supply is off.
A 3. 3 volts microcontroller has a BOR threshold of 2. 7 volts. If the rail dips to 2. 2 volts for a moment, the chip is reset cleanly instead of running in the unreliable band.
Now an exposed input: a 12 volts signal feeds a pin that clamps near 3. 6 volts. A 1 kilohms series resistor limits the clamp current to (12 minus 3. 6) over 1000 equals 8.
4 milliamps, which the diodes can survive. That is the whole idea.
"Undervoltage makes the system misbehave: slower logic, corrupted RAM, half-written flash, weak I/O, so you add brown-out reset and a supervisor.
Overvoltage damages it: breakdown above the absolute maximum, and a pin above Vdd forward-biases the ESD diodes and can trigger latch-up.

So I use brown-out detection, series resistors and clamps on exposed inputs, proper power sequencing, and a fuse or OVP on the rail, plus firmware that resets on brown-out and avoids flash writes when the supply is weak."
Quick check. What is the main purpose of a brown-out reset (BOR) in a microcontroller?
Limiting the current a load can draw. The question: How can you protect a load from pulling too much current?
To limit the current a load can draw, you put something between the supply and the load that bounds it, from simple to smart. A series resistor works for an LED.
A fuse opens once on a big fault. A resettable PTC resets when it cools.
For real power rails you use an active limiter: a transistor in series with the load that a sense resistor throttles, or a one-chip version called an eFuse.
Some loads, like LEDs and motors, are limited by their drivers by design.
Think of a water tap with a flow restrictor. A narrow pipe (series resistor) always restricts flow, even when you want plenty. A fuse is a safety valve that bursts once.
An active limiter is a smart valve that opens fully for normal use but squeezes shut when the flow tries to exceed a set value. Squeezing hard makes the smart valve hot.
And filling an empty tank looks like a burst pipe for a moment, even though nothing is wrong.
On log-log axes the melting time falls with the square of the current: ten times the current opens the fuse a hundred times faster.

This is why a fuse is excellent against hard shorts and poor against small overloads (near the rated current heat escapes as fast as it is generated, the I to the 2t approximation breaks down, and opening times become very long or infinite).
Fuse I to the 2t : current squared times time, the heat that melts the fuse, so big faults open it faster.
PTC (polyfuse): a resettable device whose resistance rises sharply when it heats. Sense resistor: a small series resistor whose voltage measures the current.
Inrush current: the brief large current to charge input capacitance, I equals C dV over dt .
For an LED on 5 volts with a 2 volts drop at 20 milliamps, a series resistor of (5 minus 2) over 0. 02 equals 150 ohms does the job. For a power rail, use a series FET with a 0.
6 ohms sense resistor. When the sense drop reaches about 0. 6 volts, a transistor throttles the FET, so the limit is 0. 6 over 0. 6 equals 1 amps.
In a hard short from 12 volts, the FET carries 1 amps while dropping about 12 volts, so it dissipates about 12 watts, and it needs thermal protection. That is the whole idea.
"Match it to the fault. A fuse is cheap and reliable but one-shot, a PTC polyfuse resets, and a series resistor only suits things like LEDs because of the drop and heat.
For real rails I'd use an active limiter: a pass FET with a sense resistor and a transistor that throttles the gate at about 0.
6 volts across the sense resistor, so the limit is roughly 0. 6 over R, or an eFuse that integrates the limit, soft-start, thermal shutdown and a fault flag.
Loads like LEDs and motors get constant-current drivers or current chopping, and inrush needs soft-start."
Quick check. What is the main difference between a fuse and a PTC polyfuse?
What a PCB is and where it's used. The question: What is a PCB? Name some applications.
A printed circuit board, or PCB, is a flat insulating board with copper conductors on it.
Components are soldered to pads on the board, and the copper traces connect them in the pattern the design requires.
It replaces a tangle of loose wires with something repeatable, compact and easy for machines to assemble.
PCBs range from a one-layer board in a remote control to a board with twenty layers in a server.
Picture a city map printed on a board. The streets are copper traces, the buildings are components, and the doors of the buildings are pads where the solder goes.
A via is a tunnel or ramp that takes a road from one level to another. Every board made from the same map has exactly the same streets, which is the whole point.
The analogy leaves out that streets here are not perfect: a trace has a little resistance, inductance and capacitance, and these matter at high speed.
A top view of a small board. Components (U1, R1) are soldered to orange pads.
Solid traces connect pads on the top layer; a via drops a signal to another layer (dashed), where it continues as a trace.
Mounting holes, board outline and silkscreen labels complete the picture. Soldermask covers everything except the pads.
Trace: a copper conductor on a PCB layer. Pad: exposed copper where a component lead is soldered. Via: a plated hole that connects copper on different layers.
FR-4: the common fiberglass-epoxy material that insulates and supports the copper. Soldermask and silkscreen: the protective coating over the copper and the printed labels on top.
A common board is FR-4, 1. 6 mm thick, with 1 oz copper, which is about 35 µm thick. That copper has about 0.
49 milliohms for every "square" of trace (a piece as long as it is wide). A trace 0. 25 mm wide and 50 mm long is 200 squares, so its resistance is about 200 times 0.
00049 equals 0. 098 ohms. The same trace on the outer layer carries roughly 0. 9 amps for a 10 degrees Celsius temperature rise. So a trace is a real conductor with real limits.
That is the whole idea.
"A PCB is an insulating board, usually fibreglass-epoxy FR-4, with copper traces etched on it that connect components soldered to pads.
Vias connect layers, soldermask protects the copper and silkscreen labels the parts.
We use them because they're repeatable, compact, machine-assembled and let you control impedance and return paths.
They're in everything from remote controls to servers, from a single layer up to twenty or more layers."
Quick check. What is a via?
PCB vs breadboard vs perfboard vs wiring vs IC.
The question: What are the tradeoffs of PCBs vs solderless breadboards vs soldered breadboards vs just soldering everything together with wires vs ICs?
A breadboard, a perfboard, point-to-point wiring, a PCB and an IC are different ways to build the same circuit, and each suits a different stage of a project.
A breadboard is fastest to change but has flaky contacts and extra stray capacitance and inductance. Perfboard and point-to-point are permanent but slow and hard to repeat.
A PCB is repeatable and compact. An IC costs the most to start but is cheapest per unit at huge volume.
Think of designing a house. A pencil sketch is quick to change but is not a house (the breadboard). A cardboard model is sturdier but each one is hand-made (perfboard).
A printed blueprint lets any builder make an identical house (the PCB). Building a factory that stamps out whole houses (the IC) only pays off if you sell enough of them.
The analogy leaves out electrical behavior: each step also changes how fast and how cleanly the circuit can run.
The decision is driven by what you need next.
A PCB is the default for anything that will be built more than a handful of times; a custom IC is justified only by volume or performance that discrete parts cannot reach.
Solderless breadboard: a plastic board with spring clips, so parts push in and need no solder.
Perfboard / point-to-point: soldered builds with a hole grid, or with parts wired directly together. Parasitic: unintended resistance, inductance or capacitance from the build.
NRE (non-recurring engineering): the one-time cost of design and tooling. Break-even volume: the number of units at which a higher-NRE, lower-unit-cost option becomes cheaper.
On a breadboard, a 100 mm jumper adds about 100 nanohenries of inductance, and the rows add about 10 picofarads.
Together they resonate near 1 over (2 pi square root of 10 to the -7 times 10 to the -11 ) equals 159 megahertz, so fast edges ring.
For cost, suppose a PCB has 150 USD of setup and 5 USD per unit, and hand wiring costs 25 USD per unit with no setup.
They match when 5 plus 150 over n equals 25 , so at n equals 7. 5 units. Above about eight units, the PCB wins. That is the whole idea.
"A breadboard is fastest to change but has flaky contacts and a few picofarads and nanohenries of parasitics, so it's for exploration at low frequency.
Perfboard or point-to-point is permanent but slow and not repeatable. A PCB takes days to fab but is repeatable, compact, with controlled impedance and cheap at volume.
An IC has the biggest up-front cost but the best size, power and performance at high volume. So you progress from breadboard to PCB, and to an IC only when volume justifies it."
Quick check. Which option is best for quickly testing an idea at low frequency?
PCB versus IC. The question: What is the difference between a PCB and IC?
An IC (integrated circuit) is a tiny piece of silicon where transistors and their wiring are built together at nanometer scale, then sealed in a package.
A PCB is the larger board that the packaged ICs, resistors, capacitors and connectors are soldered onto, with copper traces wiring them together.
The IC is where the active work happens: switching, amplifying and computing. The PCB mostly connects. ICs take months and a lot of money to make, and they cannot be modified.
PCBs take days and can be reworked.
Think of a city. The PCB is the street map: roads connect buildings, and you can add a bridge or close a road with a small effort.
The IC is a skyscraper with billions of tiny rooms and corridors inside, all built at once from a master plan. You cannot move a wall once the tower is built.
Inside the tower the corridors (wires) are very thin and resistive, while city streets are wide.
A transistor sits inside a die, the die in a package, packages on a PCB, PCBs in a product.
Each step multiplies the length scale by roughly 10 to 1000, and each step adds parasitics that the lower level did not have.
Die: the piece of silicon cut from a wafer that holds the integrated circuit. Package: the housing with pins or balls that lets a die be soldered to a board.
Photolithography: patterning with light, used at nanometer scale for ICs. Metal stack: the layers of on-chip wiring above the transistors.
Parasitics: unwanted resistance, inductance and capacitance.
Compare the wires. An on-chip copper wire 1 µm wide and 0. 2 µm thick has a resistance of about 85 ohms per millimeter. A PCB trace 0. 25 mm wide and 35 µm thick has only about 1.
7 times 10 to the -8 over (0. 25 times 10 to the -3 times 35 times 10 to the -6) equals 1. 9 milliohms per millimeter, about 40,000 times less.
But chip distances are around 100 times shorter and the loads are tiny, so chips are faster and use less power overall. That is the whole idea.
"An IC is a piece of silicon with transistors and nanometre-scale wiring fabricated together, put in a package.
A PCB is the board that ICs and other parts are soldered onto, with copper traces connecting them. So ICs are the active devices and a PCB is mostly interconnect and support.
IC features are nanometres to microns, PCB traces about a tenth of a millimetre.
ICs take months in a cleanroom with huge tooling cost and can't be modified, while PCBs take days and can be reworked."
Quick check. Which statement correctly describes the relationship between ICs and PCBs?
Parasitic elements on a PCB. The question: What are the parasitic elements present on a PCB?
A PCB trace is not an ideal wire. Every trace, via and plane has a little unwanted resistance, inductance and capacitance, called parasitics.
They are tiny at low frequency but matter at fast edge rates.
Inductance is the one that usually causes trouble, and it depends on the whole current loop, including the return path.
So the main layout rules are: keep loops small, keep a solid ground plane under signals, keep traces short, and put small supply capacitors close to each chip.
Picture a garden hose. Water has inertia, so a sudden push at one end takes time to reach the other, which is like inductance resisting a change in current.
The hose also swells slightly under pressure, which is like capacitance storing charge. And the narrow bore causes friction, which is resistance.
Slow flows never notice any of it; rapid pulses do. Where it breaks: in a circuit the current loops back, and a bigger loop means more inductance.
A short trace is a pi network: series resistance and inductance, with its capacitance to the plane split between the two ends.
Each element is small, but at 100 megahertz the 14 nanohenries is 9 ohms, comparable to the circuit impedance.
Parasitic: an unintended R, L or C that comes from physical structure. Loop inductance: inductance of the whole current path including its return; smaller loop, lower value.
Ground bounce: a voltage disturbance on a ground connection from L di over dt . Ground plane: a solid copper layer that gives every signal a close return path.
Via: a plated hole between layers, with about 1 nanohenries and 0. 5 picofarads of its own.
A 50 mm trace in standard copper, 0. 25 mm wide, has a resistance of about 0. 1 ohms. Over a ground plane it has roughly 0.
29 nanohenries per millimeter, so about 14 nanohenries, and about 5. 8 picofarads of capacitance.
At 1 gigahertz, 14 nanohenries is 2 pi times 10 to the 9 times 14 times 10 to the -9 equals 90 ohms, so it no longer acts like a plain wire.
In a power loop of 23 nanohenries, a current change of 1 amps in 10 nanoseconds makes 23 nanohenries times 1 amps over 10 nanoseconds equals 2. 3 volts of spike.
That is the whole idea.
"Every feature on a board has parasitics. Traces have resistance, about 0. 1 ohm for 50 millimetres in 1 oz copper, and inductance of roughly 0.
3 nanohenries per millimetre over a plane, which really depends on the loop area. They have capacitance to planes and neighbours, about 0.
1 picofarad per millimetre, which causes crosstalk.
Vias add about a nanohenry and half a picofarad, pads and component packages add more, the laminate has dielectric loss, and surface leakage matters on high-impedance nodes.
So I keep loops small, use a solid ground plane and place decoupling close."

Types of PCBs, trade-offs and uses. The question: What are the different types of PCBs? What are their tradeoffs and applications?
A PCB (printed circuit board) is the flat board that holds electronic parts and links them with copper tracks.
Products need different things: cheap, small, bendable, or able to handle heat or radio signals.
Each type trades cost against density, performance or shape, so you pick the simplest one that does the job.
Think of buildings. A garden shed is cheap and fine for a few tools. An apartment tower packs many people onto a small plot, but costs far more.
A tent folds up and moves, but cannot carry much. The analogy breaks in one place: board features combine, so one board can be many-layered and bendable at once.
Cross-sections of six common types. Orange is copper, grey-green is dielectric or prepreg, purple is polyimide and the heavy grey base is aluminium.

Note the plated through-hole in the double-sided and multilayer boards, the tiny microvias and buried via in HDI, the thin bendable polyimide between rigid parts in rigid-flex, and the thin dielectric on a thick metal base in metal-core boards.
Layer count: how many copper layers the board has. More layers give more room for tracks and for solid power and ground sheets ("Choosing the PCB layer count").
FR-4: the standard fiberglass-and-epoxy board material, cheap and used for most boards ("What "FR4" means").
Flex board: a board built on thin bendable plastic (polyimide) instead of stiff fiberglass ("Flex PCBs: construction, trade-offs, uses"). HDI: high-density interconnect.
Tiny laser-drilled holes and fine tracks that pack parts closely. Metal-core board: copper over a very thin insulating layer on an aluminum base, which carries heat away well.
A TV remote has few parts and slow signals, so one copper layer is enough. That single-sided board is the cheapest type. A 3 watts LED is a different problem: heat.
Its heat must pass through the board's insulating layer to escape. Through 1.
6 mm of plain FR-4 under a 1 cm² pad, that layer alone would make the LED about 160 degrees Celsius hotter than the far side of the board.
A metal-core board's insulator is only 0. 1 mm thick and conducts heat better, so the rise is only about 1. 5 degrees Celsius.
Same job, different board, chosen by the requirement. That is the whole idea.
"By layer count: single-sided is cheapest for simple products, double-sided is the default, multilayer adds planes for signal integrity and density.
By rigidity: rigid, flex for bending, and rigid-flex combining both.
By material: FR-4 for most, PTFE or Rogers-type laminates for RF, ceramic for high temperature, metal-core with an aluminium base for LEDs and power.
And HDI with microvias for dense designs like phones. I'd choose the simplest type that meets density, thermal, RF and form-factor needs."
Quick check. Which board type is best for a low-cost remote control with simple routing?
Flex PCBs: construction, trade-offs, uses. The question: What is a flex PCB? What are its tradeoffs and applications?
A flex PCB is a circuit board built on a thin, bendable plastic film instead of stiff fiberglass.
It does the job of a cable and its connectors, but as one thin part that folds into tight spaces.
The price is that it costs more and must be designed so the copper tracks do not crack when bent.
Think of a paper clip. Bend it once and it is fine. Bend it back and forth and it snaps, because the metal wears out a little each time. Flex copper tracks behave the same way.
A gentle, wide curve stresses the metal far less than a sharp crease, so flex design is mostly about keeping bends gentle.
The analogy is loose on one point: flex copper is a special soft kind made to last much longer than a paper clip.
A double-sided flex cross-section (thicknesses exaggerated).
The two copper layers sit close to the neutral axis in the centre of the stack, so they see small strain when the board bends.
Coverlay replaces soldermask, with an opening at the left end exposing pads or fingers. A stiffener under the right-hand region supports a connector or part.
The curve at the bottom shows the flexible region.
Polyimide: the heat-resistant plastic film that forms the flexible base ("PCB insulation materials and trade-offs").
Rolled-annealed (RA) copper: copper foil made to survive repeated bending better than normal copper.
Coverlay: a polyimide film with adhesive that covers the tracks and replaces soldermask ("What soldermask is and does").
Stiffener: a rigid piece glued under parts or a connector so that area does not flex. Bend radius: the radius of the curve. A bigger radius means a gentler bend.
Strain: how much the copper stretches, as a fraction of its length.
When a board bends, copper far from the middle of its thickness stretches more, and a tighter bend stretches it more.
The strain is about d over R , where d is the copper's distance from the middle and R is the bend radius. Say the copper sits 0. 025 mm from the middle.
At a 1 mm radius the strain is 0. 025/1 = 2. 5%, acceptable only for a single bend. At a 10 mm radius it is 0. 25%, a level the page treats as workable for repeated bending.
That is the whole idea.
"A flex PCB is a circuit on a polyimide film instead of rigid fibreglass, with rolled-annealed copper traces, a coverlay instead of soldermask, and stiffeners where parts go.
It's thin, light and bendable, so it fits tight 3D spaces, handles dynamic flexing like hinges, and replaces cables and connectors, which improves reliability under vibration.
The trade-offs are higher cost, delicate handling, special design rules like a large bend radius, and less density than rigid boards.
It's used in phones, cameras, medical devices and aerospace."

PCB layers and their materials. The question: What are the layers of a PCB? What are they made of?
A circuit board is a flat sandwich of thin copper sheets and insulating layers, pressed together into one solid piece.
The copper carries current, the insulation keeps the copper layers apart, and coatings on the outside protect it and label it.
Knowing what each layer is made of lets you predict how the board behaves.
Think of a layered sandwich. Thin slices of cheese (copper) sit between slabs of bread (the insulating layers). The bread is glass cloth soaked in epoxy glue.
Some slabs come already baked hard, and others are a sticky spread that melts in the oven and glues the sandwich together.
A glossy glaze on top (soldermask) and writing in icing (silkscreen) finish it.
The analogy is loose on one point: the copper is etched into tracks and shapes, not left as full slices.
A 4-layer board cross-section (thicknesses not to scale). The three dielectric layers (two prepregs and a core) separate four copper layers.
Soldermask and silkscreen cover the outside; a plated via barrel connects layers.
The thick core gives mechanical stiffness; the thin prepregs set the spacing between outer signal layers and the inner planes, which sets controlled impedance.
Core: a rigid, fully hardened sheet of glass and epoxy with copper on one or both faces. Prepreg: glass cloth with partly hardened epoxy.
It melts under heat and pressure and glues layers together. Ounce (oz) of copper: a foil weight. 1 oz is about 0. 035 mm thick ("Best conductor material for PCB layers").
Soldermask: the green coating that covers copper except at the pads, where parts are soldered ("What soldermask is and does").
Silkscreen: the white ink text and symbols printed on top ("The silkscreen (legend) layer"). Surface finish: a thin coating on exposed pads that keeps them easy to solder.
Stack a common 4-layer board from the top down. Top copper is 0. 035 mm and prepreg is 0. 2 mm. The inner copper is 0. 0175 mm and the core is 1. 0 mm. Then come another 0.
0175 mm of inner copper, 0. 2 mm of prepreg and 0. 035 mm of bottom copper. These add up to 1. 505 mm. Two soldermask coats of 0. 025 mm add 0. 05 mm, giving 1.
555 mm, which is the ordinary 1. 6 mm board. That is the whole idea.
"A rigid PCB is copper foil layers on FR-4, which is fibreglass cloth in epoxy.
Multilayer boards are built from cores, which are cured laminate with copper on both sides, and prepreg, partly cured glass-epoxy that bonds the layers under heat and pressure.
Outside, there's soldermask, a green epoxy coating that covers everything but the pads, silkscreen ink for labels, and a surface finish such as ENIG or HASL on the pads.
Vias are plated holes connecting the layers. A typical 1. 6 millimetre four-layer board has 35 micron outer copper and 0. 2 millimetre prepreg."

Best conductor material for PCB layers. The question: What material would I want for conduction layers?
Traces are the thin metal paths on a circuit board that carry current between parts.
The best metal for them is copper, because it conducts almost as well as silver, costs far less, and is easy to etch, plate and solder.
The metal and the trace size set how much current a trace can carry and how hot it gets.
Think of a water pipe. A wide pipe carries more water with less effort than a narrow one.
A trace is a flat pipe for current: wider and thicker means less resistance and more current before it heats up.
The analogy breaks on one point: a trace's heat comes from the current pushing through the metal's resistance, and a pipe has nothing like that.
Resistivity of candidate metals (shorter is better). Copper (highlighted) is within 6% of silver; gold and aluminium are about 1.
5 times worse; nickel and tin are many times worse, which is why they are used only as thin layers (barrier, solder), not as conductors.
Resistivity: how strongly a material resists current, whatever its shape ("What resistance is", "What resistance depends on").
Copper weight (oz): foil thickness named by weight per area. 1 oz is about 0. 035 mm thick. Sheet resistance: the resistance of one square patch of foil, any size of square.
For 1 oz copper it is about 0. 49 milliohms (thousandths of an ohm). Temperature rise: how many degrees a trace heats above its surroundings when carrying current.
Etching and plating: the processes that carve traces out of foil and build up copper inside holes.
Take a 1 oz copper trace 1 mm wide and 100 mm long. You can cut it into 100 squares of 1 mm by 1 mm, so its resistance is 100 times 0. 49 milliohms = 49 milliohms.
Carry 2 amps and it drops 2 times 0. 049 equals 0. 098 volts, about 0. 1 volts. The page's sizing formula says 3 amps needs a 1 oz trace about 1.
37 mm wide for a 10 degrees Celsius rise. That is the whole idea.
"Copper, almost always. It has the second-lowest resistivity of any practical metal, about 1. 7 times ten to the minus eight ohm-metres, close to silver but vastly cheaper.
It's ductile, easy to etch and to electroplate, solders well and conducts heat. Standard foil is 35 microns, one ounce.
Silver is costly and tarnishes, gold is worse and very expensive so it's only a thin finish, and aluminium is hard to solder and plate.
So copper for traces, with the width set by the current."
Quick check. Which metal is the standard conductor on PCBs?
Gold versus copper for PCB conductors. The question: What are the tradeoffs of using gold vs copper on the conduction layers?
Copper carries the current on a circuit board. Gold appears only as a very thin coat on the pads, the bare spots where parts are soldered.
Gold is not a better conductor than copper (it resists current about 1. 45 times more), and it costs thousands of times more per gram.
What gold does well is resist corrosion, so the pads stay clean, flat and easy to solder.
Picture a steel beam in a bridge with a thin coat of rust-proof paint. The beam does the real work, and the paint just protects it.
On a board, copper is the beam and a gold layer about 0. 1 µm thick is the paint. Underneath sits a thin layer of nickel that stops the copper from creeping into the gold.
The analogy is loose on one point: the gold dissolves into the solder during assembly, so it protects the pad only until then.
An ENIG-finished pad in cross-section (not to scale). Copper carries the current. A few microns of nickel stop copper diffusing into the gold. A gold layer of only about 0.
1 µm keeps the nickel from oxidising until soldering, when it dissolves into the molten solder and the solder bonds to the nickel.
Resistivity: how much a material resists current, whatever its shape. Gold is 2. 44 and copper 1. 68, in units of 10 to the -8 ohms·m ("Best conductor material for PCB layers").
Noble metal: a metal such as gold that does not rust or tarnish. ENIG: electroless nickel, immersion gold.
A common pad finish with a very thin gold layer over nickel ("PCB layers and their materials"). Embrittlement: weakening of a solder joint when too much gold dissolves into it.
Make the same trace out of both metals. Gold resists 2. 44 / 1. 68 = 1. 45 times more, so to match 35 µm of copper you would need about 51 µm of gold.
Even a gold layer only as thick as the copper, 35 µm over 100 cm², weighs about 6. 8 g, against 3. 1 g of copper. At roughly USD 100 per gram, that gold costs hundreds of dollars.
The ENIG finish uses only about 15 mg over the same area. That is the whole idea.
"Copper for the conductors, gold only as a thin finish.
Gold is actually a worse conductor, about 45% higher resistivity, and thousands of times more expensive per unit mass, so gold traces make no sense.
Its advantage is that it's noble: it doesn't oxidise, so pads stay solderable and contacts stay low resistance. That's why we use ENIG, nickel with about 0.
1 micron of gold, and gold-plated edge connectors. Downsides are softness, it dissolves into solder and can embrittle joints above a few percent, and the nickel adds loss at GHz."
Quick check. Which statement is correct?
PCB insulation materials and trade-offs. The question: What materials are often used for the insulation materials? What are their tradeoffs?
The insulating material between a board's copper layers is called the dielectric.
It holds the layers apart, but it also shapes how fast signals travel, how much of a fast signal is lost, how well heat escapes, and whether the board survives soldering.
The standard material, FR-4, is cheap and fine for most boards. Special materials are used when a job needs less signal loss or better heat flow.
Think of the surface of a road. Ordinary asphalt is cheap and works well at city speeds. A race car at top speed needs a much smoother track, and a good one costs far more.
Signals behave the same way. At low frequency FR-4 is fine. At several GHz (billions of cycles per second) it quietly eats away part of the signal, so you pay for a better "road".
The analogy is loose: the loss comes from the material soaking up energy and turning it into heat, not from friction.
At 5 gigahertz, FR-4 loses about 0.
4 decibels per inch in the dielectric alone (a 10 inch trace loses 4 decibels, plus conductor loss), while a ceramic-filled RF laminate loses about 0.
07 decibels/inch and PTFE about 0. 015. Because the curves are straight lines on log-log axes, the ratio between materials is constant.
The mid-loss curve is representative of "low-loss" epoxy-glass grades: exact values are product-specific.
Dielectric constant ( r ): how strongly the material stores electric field. It sets trace widths and signal speed ("Dielectrics and permittivity").
Loss tangent ( delta ): how much signal energy the material absorbs. Smaller is better ("Dielectric losses and their mechanisms").
Glass transition ( T g ): the temperature where the resin turns soft and expands quickly. Decibel (dB): a ratio scale for loss.
3 decibels is half the power, 10 decibels is a tenth. FR-4: glass cloth in epoxy, the standard board material ("What "FR4" means").
Send a 5 gigahertz signal along a 10 inch trace. On FR-4 the dielectric alone loses about 0. 41 decibels per inch, so 10 inches lose about 4 decibels.
That leaves about 40% of the power. On a ceramic-filled RF (radio-frequency) laminate with 0. 07 decibels per inch, the same trace loses about 0. 7 decibels and keeps about 85%.
At 1 gigahertz FR-4 loses only about 0. 08 decibels per inch, which is why it is fine for most products. That is the whole idea.
"The default is FR-4, glass-fibre in epoxy: cheap, strong and easy to process, with a dielectric constant around 4. 3 and a loss tangent around 0.
02, fine up to about a gigahertz. Its limits are high-frequency loss, a permittivity that varies, a modest glass transition and poor heat conduction.
Alternatives: high-Tg FR-4 for lead-free assembly, polyimide for flex and heat, PTFE or ceramic-filled laminates with loss of 0. 001 to 0.
004 for RF, ceramics for heat and high temperature, and metal-core for LEDs. It's a trade between loss, temperature, thermal conduction and cost."
Quick check. What is FR-4 made of?
What "FR4" means. The question: What does "FR4" mean?
FR-4 is the standard material most circuit boards are made from.
It is woven glass cloth soaked in epoxy resin and baked hard, with a flame retardant added so it stops burning when a flame is removed. The name does not mean four layers.
The 4 is just an old grade number.
Think of a fiberglass boat hull. Glass cloth gives the strength and stiffness, and hardened resin glues the cloth into one solid sheet and keeps it from soaking up water.
FR-4 is the same kind of sheet, thin and flat, with copper bonded to its faces. The flame retardant is an extra ingredient in the resin.
The analogy breaks in one place: flame retardant means "stops burning on its own", not "fireproof".
Left, the structure: woven glass yarns (the two yarn directions, drawn in two colors) with epoxy filling the spaces.
Right, the name: FR for flame retardant, 4 for the grade number.
The sibling G-10 is the same composite without the flame retardant, so it is flammable and rarely used for modern PCBs.
Flame retardant (FR): formulated so the material self-extinguishes. UL 94 volts-0 is the usual rating. Epoxy: the resin that hardens to bond the glass and insulate.
Glass cloth: woven glass fiber that gives strength and stiffness ("PCB layers and their materials"). G-10: the same glass and epoxy sheet with no flame retardant.
Glass transition temperature ( T g ): the temperature where the resin turns soft. Standard FR-4 is about 130 to 140 degrees Celsius ("PCB insulation materials and trade-offs").
Take a bare FR-4 sheet 100 mm by 100 mm and 1. 6 mm thick. Its volume is 10 cm times 10 cm times 0. 16 cm = 16 cm³. At about 1. 85 g/cm³ it weighs about 30 g. A standard 0.
035 mm copper foil on both faces would add only about 6 g. It is cheap, stiff and easy to drill and plate, which is why almost every ordinary board uses it.
That is the whole idea.
"FR-4 means Flame Retardant grade 4. FR means the laminate is self-extinguishing, tested to UL 94 volts-0; the 4 is just a grade number in the NEMA system, not four layers.
It's woven fibreglass in epoxy resin, the standard PCB substrate: strong, cheap, easy to process, with a dielectric constant around 4. 3, loss tangent around 0.
02, and a glass transition around 130 to 180 degrees depending on grade. It's the flame-retardant version of G-10."
Quick check. What does the "FR" in FR-4 stand for?
Why PCBs are green; other colours. The question: Why are PCBs often green? What other colors could they be?
The color of a circuit board is the color of its soldermask, the thin coating over the copper. The fiberglass underneath is a pale tan.
Green is the default because it is the oldest, cheapest and best-tuned coating, and it is easy to inspect. Other colors work the same electrically.
They just trade away some cost, visibility or convenience.
Think of a car's paint. Red paint and gray paint do not change how the engine runs. But a dark color can hide a scratch that a light color would show. A board is the same.
The coating color changes nothing about the circuit, but black hides traces and solder problems from your eyes and from inspection cameras.
The analogy breaks in one place: a car paint choice rarely affects how readable its labels are, while a board's text color must contrast with the mask.
The same mini board (a trace, two pads and a legend) over six mask colours.
Notice how the trace (the mask over copper appears lighter) is clearly visible on green, red, blue and yellow, is low-contrast on white, and almost vanishes on black.
The legend needs the right colour too: white text on green, red, blue and black; black text on white and yellow.
Soldermask: the polymer coating over the copper that sets the board color ("What soldermask is and does").
Contrast: how clearly features such as traces and text stand out against the mask. AOI (automated optical inspection): cameras that check boards, usually tuned to green.
Silkscreen: the printed text layer on top, which needs the right color against the mask ("The silkscreen (legend) layer").
Laminate: the fiberglass-epoxy board underneath, which is not the colored part ("PCB layers and their materials").
Order two identical prototypes, one green and one black. Electrically they behave the same. Now one trace is cut by mistake.
On the green board you can see the trace and the cut under a lamp. On the black board the trace almost vanishes, so you hunt longer.
White text works on green but not on a white mask, which needs black text.
So use green while developing, and pick a colored mask for the final product only if the look is worth the harder inspection. That is the whole idea.
"The colour is the soldermask, the polymer coating over the copper, not the fibreglass.
Green is the default because it's the most mature and cheapest mask chemistry, it gives good contrast with copper and white silkscreen, it's easy on the eyes, and inspection systems are tuned to it.
There's also some military-spec folklore.

Other colours, red, blue, black, white, yellow, work electrically the same: black looks premium but hides traces and makes debugging harder, white is good for LED reflectivity, and the rest are cosmetic."
Quick check. What gives a PCB its colour?
The silkscreen (legend) layer. The question: What is the layer with text called?
The silkscreen, also called the legend, is the layer of ink printed on top of a board, usually white.
It carries the human-readable labels: part names like R1 and U3, outlines, polarity marks, pin-1 dots, test point names and the board revision.
It exists so that the people who build, probe and repair the board can find and orient every part.
Think of the street names and landmarks on a map. The roads exist without them, but nobody could find their way. The silkscreen labels a crowded board the same way.
A map is useless if the labels sit under a building or cover the road.
In the same way, silkscreen text hidden under a part, or ink spilled on a solder pad, causes mistakes and soldering problems.
Left, good practice: the IC has a body outline and a pin-1 dot, the refdes sits just outside the body so it stays readable after assembly, and the resistor's outline stops short of its pads.
Right, bad practice: the text is tiny and sits inside the body (hidden once the part is placed), the pin-1 mark is missing, the outline is faint, and the label for R1 runs across a pad.
The ink on the pad would be clipped by the fab, cutting the text, and any ink left would hinder the solder.
Reference designator: the label tying a part to the schematic, such as R1 or C5. Polarity mark: a symbol showing which way a part must face, like a diode bar or a "+".
Pin 1: the dot or mark showing where a chip's first pin is. Legend / nomenclature: other names for the silkscreen layer ("PCB layers and their materials").
Soldermask: the coating the ink is printed on, never on pads ("What soldermask is and does").
Picture a board with one LED and a resistor named R1.
The silkscreen draws the resistor's outline, prints "R1" beside it (not under it), and puts a mark next to the LED's cathode side.
An assembler can now place and orient both parts without the schematic. A common rule of thumb is text at least 1 mm tall with strokes at least 0.
15 mm wide, which is 15% of the height, and ink kept about 0. 15 to 0. 2 mm away from pads. That is the whole idea.
"It's the silkscreen, also called the legend or nomenclature: a layer of ink, usually white epoxy, printed on top of the soldermask.
It carries reference designators, component outlines, polarity and pin-1 marks, test points, connector labels, and the board name and revision.
Keep it off the pads, because ink on a pad blocks soldering and the fab will clip it, use legible sizes, and choose a colour that contrasts with the mask.
It's what lets people assemble and debug the board."
Quick check. What is the layer of text on a PCB called?
What soldermask is and does. The question: What is soldermask?
Soldermask is the thin polymer coating over a circuit board's copper, with openings only where you want to solder or make contact.
Solder sticks to bare copper but not to the mask.
So the mask keeps solder on the pads, stops it from bridging between close-spaced pins, and protects the copper from corrosion and accidental shorts.
Imagine a baking tray with a non-stick coating, except for small bare patches. Spread melted butter on it and the butter pools only on the bare patches.
The soldermask is the non-stick coating and the pads are the bare patches. The strip of coating between two patches keeps the butter in each patch apart.
The analogy is loose on one point: the mask is also a permanent protective skin, not just a tool for assembly.
Exposed areas of the mask polymerise and stay; unexposed areas (over the pads) dissolve in the developer.
The pattern comes from your mask layers in the Gerber files, so every opening you draw is exactly where copper is exposed.
Soldermask opening: the hole in the coating over a pad. It is a bit larger than the pad.
Mask expansion: how much larger the opening is than the pad on each side, to allow for alignment error (about 0. 05 mm is typical).
Solder dam: the strip of mask left between two neighboring pads. LPI mask: liquid photoimageable mask, put on wet, exposed to UV and developed.
Tented via: a via covered by mask so solder and flux stay out. Pitch: the center-to-center distance between neighboring pins.
The solder dam is the pitch minus the pad width minus twice the expansion. For 0. 5 mm pitch, 0. 25 mm pads and 0. 05 mm expansion, the dam is 0. 5 - 0. 25 - 0. 1 = 0.
15 mm, comfortable. For 0. 4 mm pitch and 0. 2 mm pads it is 0. 4 - 0. 2 - 0. 1 = 0. 10 mm, right at the usual limit. That is the whole idea.
"Soldermask is the thin polymer coating over the copper on a PCB, the green layer, with openings at the pads. It's an LPI epoxy about 20 to 30 microns thick.
It stops solder bridging between pads and keeps solder on the pads during assembly, protects the copper from oxidation and moisture, and insulates the traces.
In layout you set the opening slightly bigger than each pad, keep a minimum mask dam between fine-pitch pads, and usually tent the vias.
It's different from solder paste and from the silkscreen."
Quick check. What is the main purpose of soldermask during assembly?
PCB layers in a stackup and their materials. The question: What are the layers of a PCB? what are they made of?
A multilayer circuit board is built up from alternating layers of copper and insulation, stacked in a fixed order and pressed into one solid piece.
The copper layers carry signals, power and ground. The insulating layers keep the copper apart and hold the board flat.
How thick the insulation is between two copper layers decides important things later, such as how wide a trace must be.
Think of plywood. Thin planks are glued together with glue that is runny when hot and hard when cured.
In a board, a core is like a finished plank that is already hard, and prepreg is the half-cured glue layer that melts, flows into every gap and then sets.
Press the stack under heat and you get one solid sheet. Unlike plywood, the board has copper that is etched into patterns before it is pressed in.
A typical 4-layer stackup.
Note the symmetry about the centre core, the thin prepreg layers between outer copper and the inner planes (that thickness sets trace impedance), and the plated via running from L1 to L4.
Where it passes the ground and power planes there is a clearance gap (antipad) so it does not short to them.
Core: a fully cured glass-epoxy sheet with copper already bonded to both faces. Prepreg: glass cloth with partly cured epoxy. It melts and glues cores and foils together.
Stackup: the ordered list of every layer and its thickness ("PCB layers and their materials").
Reference plane: a solid copper layer, usually ground, that a fast trace runs next to ("Which layers should be ground").
Impedance: the ratio of voltage to current a fast signal sees on a trace, in ohms (Ω). It depends on trace width and insulation thickness.
A common 4-layer board is, top to bottom: top copper, thin prepreg, inner copper, thick core, inner copper, thin prepreg, bottom copper. Say a top-layer trace sits on 0.
2 mm of prepreg above a plane. The page's quick formula (IPC-2141) says it must be about 0. 335 mm wide for 50 ohms. Put the same trace 1.
6 mm above its plane, as on a 2-layer board, and it needs about 3 mm of width. Thinner insulation means a narrower trace for the same impedance. That is the whole idea.
"A PCB is a stack of copper layers separated by FR-4 glass-epoxy.
From the top: silkscreen, solder mask, top copper, a prepreg glue layer, inner copper, a thick cured core, more inner copper, prepreg, bottom copper, mask and silkscreen.
Copper carries signals and current, FR-4 insulates and gives stiffness, mask protects against solder bridges, silkscreen is labeling. Plated holes link the layers.
The dielectric thicknesses matter most electrically, since they set impedance and plane coupling."
Quick check. In a multilayer PCB, which material acts as the adhesive that bonds cores and outer foils together during lamination?
Choosing the PCB layer count. The question: How to choose how many layers for PCB?
Layer count is the number of copper layers in a circuit board.
You choose it from what the board must do: how dense its connections are, how fast its signals switch, how much power it carries, and what it may cost.
Start with two layers and add more only when you can name a specific reason.
Think of a road network. Two roads that cross need a bridge. A big interchange stacks several levels of overpasses so everything gets through, but each level costs a lot.
Board layers work the same way: more layers give room for crossing connections, but each pair adds cost.
The analogy breaks in one place: extra layers also add solid ground sheets that make fast signals cleaner, which has no road equivalent.
Top view of BGA pads (circles).
The outer rows can leave on the top layer, but the channels between pads hold only one trace, so deeper rows must drop through vias onto inner signal layers.
That is where layer count comes from.
BGA (ball grid array): a chip with a grid of solder balls underneath instead of pins on its edges. Pitch: the center-to-center distance between neighboring balls.
Escape routing: getting every signal out from under a dense chip ("Components that need more PCB layers"). Via: a plated hole that carries a signal to another layer.
Its round copper pad takes up space. Plane: a whole layer of solid copper used for ground or power ("Which layers should be ground", "Which layers for power planes").
Take a BGA with a 16 by 16 grid of balls at 0. 8 mm pitch. Each via pad is 0. 45 mm across, so the gap between pads is 0. 8 - 0. 45 = 0. 35 mm. A 0. 1 mm trace with 0.
1 mm clearance on each side needs 0. 30 mm, so one trace fits through each gap, but not two. That lets each layer bring out about two rows of balls.
Of the 8 rows from edge to center, the middle 6 by 6 balls are power and ground, so 5 rows carry signals.
That needs 3 signal layers, plus 2 planes, and boards come in even counts, so 6 layers. That is the whole idea.
"I'd choose the fewest layers that satisfy routing, signal integrity and EMI, and I'd name the reason for each layer.

It also keeps the stack symmetric and uses thicknesses the fab can build at a sensible cost.

On a 4-layer board that means ground on layer 2, just under the top signals. On a 6-layer board it means ground on layers 2 and 5.

All three come from placing the trace right next to a solid copper plane, ideally ground.

Which layers for power planes. The question: Which layers should power planes be on?
A power plane is a whole layer of copper that carries a supply voltage, such as 3. 3 volts, across the board.
It goes on an inner layer, right next to a ground plane, with the thinnest insulation the stackup allows.
Packed that close, the two planes act like a large capacitor with very little inductance, which helps feed the chips' sudden current demands.
Think of a town's water supply. Pumping water from a distant reservoir takes time, and the pipes resist sudden demand.
A water tower right in town answers instantly when everyone turns on a tap. The plane pair is the tower, sitting right beside the chips.
The decoupling capacitors are buckets you carry in, and they do most of the work at lower frequencies.
The analogy breaks in one place: the planes store only a little charge, and what makes them useful is that they can deliver it very fast.
Which element dominates at which frequency.

At low frequency the regulator and bulk capacitors set the impedance; mid-band ceramic capacitors take over; above roughly 100 megahertz only the plane pair and the package and on-die capacitance are effective.

Capacitance: how much charge two nearby conductors store per volt. Closer plates store more ("What capacitance is").
Inductance: how strongly a path resists a sudden change in current. Impedance: how much the supply's voltage moves per amp of sudden current, in ohms. Lower is better.

Target impedance: the PDN impedance you must stay under so the supply does not sag too much.
A 3. 3 volts supply may sag 5%, which is 0. 165 volts, when a chip suddenly draws 1 amps more. So the target is 0. 165 volts / 1 amps = 0. 165 ohms.
A 100 mm by 100 mm plane pair with 0. 1 mm of insulation has about 3. 8 nanofarads of capacitance. At 500 megahertz its impedance is about 0. 084 ohms, under the target.
With 1 mm of insulation it is 0. 38 nanofarads and 0. 84 ohms, five times over. That is the whole idea.

In four layers that's layer 3 under the layer 2 ground; in six layers, layer 4 next to the layer 5 ground.

Components that need more PCB layers. The question: What components would require a higher layer count?
Some parts force a board to have more layers. A dense chip with hundreds of tiny solder balls underneath needs room to route every signal out.
Fast interfaces like DDR memory need a solid copper plane next to each routing layer. Chips with many supply voltages need extra power layers.
Simple parts like small microcontrollers do not, which is why a hobby board can have only two layers.
Imagine a packed stadium with narrow aisles. Each aisle holds only so many people side by side, so the crowd in the middle cannot all leave at once.
You would need several tiers of walkways to get everyone out.
A dense chip is the crowd, the gaps between its pads are the aisles, and each board layer is another tier of walkways.
The analogy is loose: a board also needs whole layers for planes that carry no signals at all.
With a 0. 8 mm pitch only one trace fits between the via pads, so each signal layer can free about two rows. Smaller features cost money; this is a fab-capability decision.
BGA (ball grid array): a chip package with a grid of solder balls underneath it. Pitch: the center-to-center distance between neighboring balls.
Via pad: the round copper landing of a plated hole that takes a signal to another layer.
Escape routing: getting each signal out from under the chip ("Choosing the PCB layer count").

"Dense, fast or power-hungry parts push the layer count up. Fine-pitch BGAs need extra layers to escape their signals, roughly two rows of balls per layer at 0. 8 mm pitch.

General PCB routing rules of thumb. The question: What are some general rule of thumbs for board routing?
PCB routing rules of thumb are a short checklist of habits that prevent most layout problems. Place the parts well first. Route the most important connections first.
Give every signal a solid ground path beneath it, keep loops small, put decoupling capacitors right at the chip pins, and size traces for the current.
Each rule has a physical reason, so you can bend one when you know it.
Think of cooking a big meal. A good cook sets out ingredients and tools before turning on the stove. A poor setup means running across the kitchen with hot pans.
Board layout works the same way: good placement makes good routing easy, and clever traces cannot rescue bad placement.
The analogy is loose: in a kitchen you can carry things anywhere, but a signal's return path must always be continuous.
A fixed routing order, from the nets that matter most to those that matter least.
Each step uses up routing resources, so you give the best resources (short paths, clean reference planes) to the nets that need them.
Return path: the route the current takes back to its source, usually the plane under the trace ("Which layers should be ground").
Loop area: the area enclosed by a signal and its return. Smaller loops radiate and pick up less.
Decoupling capacitor: a small capacitor next to a chip pin that supplies quick bursts of current ("Decoupling capacitors and when needed").
Crosstalk: unwanted coupling between nearby traces ("How signals couple and how to prevent it"). Sheet resistance: the resistance of one square patch of copper foil, about 0.
49 milliohms for standard 1 oz foil.

At 1 mm wide it is 50 squares, about 24 millivolts. So you check both heat and voltage drop. That is the whole idea.

Floorplanning subsystems on a PCB. The question: How do you decide which subsystems go where on a PCB?
Floorplanning means deciding where each functional block goes on the board before drawing any traces.
You group circuits by job, separate the noisy ones from the sensitive ones, put each power supply near the part it feeds, and keep connectors where the enclosure needs them.
Clever routing cannot fix a bad floorplan.
Think of zoning a city. You put the noisy factory away from the hospital and the school, you put the power station near the factories it serves. Board blocks work the same way.
A switching power supply is the factory, a precision measurement circuit is the hospital, and the traces are the roads.
The analogy breaks in one place: on a board every "road" also needs a clean return path beside it.

Noisy blocks (switcher, motor driver) are at one side, the digital core is in the middle, the analog and RF sections sit in their own corners, and the connectors line the bottom edge.
Note that nothing sensitive is adjacent to the switcher.
Functional partitioning: grouping circuits by role, such as power, digital, analog and RF ("When and why to separate grounds").
Noise source and victim: a block that gives off interference, and one that suffers from it.
Linear regulator: a simple supply that lowers a voltage by burning the difference as heat. Switching regulator (buck): a supply that lowers a voltage by switching rapidly.
It wastes little power but is electrically noisy. Thermal resistance: how many degrees a part heats up per watt it burns, in °C/W ("Reducing component heating on the board").

18 watts, so in the same package it heats up about 11 degrees Celsius, but it makes electrical noise instead.
Either way the choice shapes the floorplan: keep the hot linear part away from a precision voltage reference that drifts with temperature, and keep the noisy buck away from sensitive inputs.

I start from the block diagram, mark noisy blocks (switching supplies, clocks, drivers), sensitive ones (ADC, reference, RF receive) and hot ones, and place connectors and mounting holes per the enclosure.

Then I let the signal flow run in a line through the board, keep noisy and sensitive blocks apart, put each supply close to its load, decoupling and crystals at their ICs, and keep the ground plane solid.
I check the ratsnest and thermals, then route."

What PCB grounding is and why it matters. The question: What is grounding on a PCB? Why is it so important?
On a circuit board, ground is two things at once.
It is the zero-volt reference that every voltage is measured against, and it is the route that every current takes to get back to its source.
The schematic shows one ground symbol, but on the board it is real copper with real resistance and inductance.
So current flowing in ground creates small voltages of its own, and those can disturb other circuits.
Imagine two apartments sharing one drain pipe. When one tenant empties a full bathtub, the other tenant sees the water level in their sink bob up and down.
Two circuits sharing a ground conductor behave the same way: one circuit's current moves the other circuit's zero.
The analogy is loose on one point: for fast changes the trouble comes from the pipe's "inertia" (inductance), not just its narrowness.
Both loads return through the same ground segment Z g .
Whatever current load A draws (including its fast switching steps) develops a voltage across Z g , and that voltage appears in series with load B's reference.
That's common-impedance coupling.
Return path: the route current takes back to its source to complete the loop ("KCL and KVL explained").
Reference: the node called 0 volts, against which other voltages are measured. Inductance: a conductor's resistance to sudden changes in current.
A changing current through it creates a voltage, L times (rate of change).
Common-impedance coupling: two circuits sharing a conductor, so one's current shows up as voltage for the other ("Ground potential differences across a board").
Ground plane: a solid copper layer that gives a return path with very low resistance and inductance ("Ground plane pros and cons").
A digital block's current jumps by 100 milliamps in 2 nanoseconds through a ground trace with 10 nanohenries of inductance.
The voltage across the trace is L di over dt equals 10 nanohenries times 0. 1 amps over 2 nanoseconds equals 0. 5 volts.
A sensor sharing that ground sees its zero jump by half a volt.
Even steady current matters: a 1 mm wide, 50 mm long trace of standard copper is about 24 milliohms, so 1 amps drops 24 millivolts. That is the whole idea.
"Ground on a PCB is the reference node and the return path for every current.
It's real copper with resistance and inductance, so return currents create voltage drops, I·R at low frequency and L·di/dt at high frequency.
If circuits share a ground conductor they couple through it, which shows up as noise, offset errors, resets or emissions.
A solid ground plane, short low-inductance connections, and keeping large currents away from sensitive references are how you control it."

Basic grounding layout techniques. The question: Describe some basic grounding layout techniques.
Basic grounding techniques are layout moves that give every return current a short, well-defined, low-inductance path. Use a solid ground plane under the signals.
Connect each ground pad to the plane with a via right at the pad. Keep decoupling capacitor loops as small as you can. Keep noisy and sensitive circuits apart by placement.
Each move shrinks a loop or stops two circuits sharing one.
Picture an emergency exit. A door beside the room lets people out quickly. One at the end of a long corridor delays them.
A ground via touching the pad is the door beside the room.
A ground connection that first runs several millimeters of trace is the long corridor, and each millimeter adds about a nanohenry.
The analogy breaks in one place: you must build the short path on purpose, because the current has no other way out.
Same capacitor and plane, two connections. On the left the via touches the capacitor pad and goes straight to the adjacent plane: tiny loop.
On the right the ground leg runs several millimetres to a via, adding trace inductance (about 1 nanohenries/mm) to the loop.
Via: a plated hole that connects layers. A short one to the nearest plane has very little inductance. Inductance: resistance to sudden changes in current, in nanohenries (nH).
A current step through it makes a voltage spike.
Decoupling loop: the path from a capacitor to the chip pin and back through the plane ("Placing and routing decoupling capacitors").

Stitching vias: vias that tie ground layers and copper fills together ("Ground stitching vias").

5 nanohenries of loop inductance lets the supply dip by L change in I over change in t equals 1. 5 nanohenries times 0. 1 amps over 2 nanoseconds equals 75 millivolts.
The same capacitor with its ground via 5 mm away has 6. 5 nanohenries, and the dip is 325 millivolts. A 3. 3 volts supply with a 5% window allows only ±165 millivolts.
Moving the via to the pad fixes it. That is the whole idea.

A solid ground plane right next to the signal layers, never cut by slots; a via at every ground pad, placed right at the pad; the shortest possible loop for decoupling capacitors, since each millimetre of trace is about a nanohenry; separate noisy and sensitive returns by placement rather than by cutting the plane; a star point only where I need one; and stitching vias so no ground pour is floating.
The goal is small loops and no shared impedance between circuits."

Ground plane pros and cons. The question: What is a ground plane? Pros/cons?
A ground plane is a continuous layer of copper tied to ground, usually right under the signal layers. It is the reference and the return path for everything above it.
Its big benefit is a return path with very low resistance and inductance that keeps current loops small.
Its costs are extra layers, unwanted capacitance on nearby sensitive points, and trouble if you cut slots in it.
Picture a wide, smooth floor in a big hall. Wherever you walk, you can come straight back, so your round trip stays short.
But a floor sits close to everything, so it also touches things you wanted to keep apart. A crack in the floor forces you to walk around it, which is a slot forcing a detour.
The analogy is loose: a fast return current flows directly under its trace, not wherever it likes.
The benefits all come from one property: a large, low-impedance conductor sits a small distance from the signals.
The same property causes the costs: it also sits close to everything else, so it adds capacitance, shares currents, and needs to stay unbroken.
Return path: the route current takes back to its source ("Which layers should be ground"). Plane vs pour: a plane is a nearly solid layer.
A pour is copper fill on a signal layer, broken up by traces. Sheet resistance: the resistance of one square patch of copper, any size, about 0. 48 milliohms for standard foil.
Parasitic capacitance: unwanted capacitance between a trace or pad and the plane ("Parasitic elements on a PCB").
Slot or split: a gap in the plane that makes the return current detour.
For the benefit, compare resistances. A 0. 25 mm wide, 100 mm long trace is 400 squares, so about 400 times 0. 48 = 192 milliohms.
A plane over the same distance is about 1 square, so about 0. 48 milliohms. For the cost, a 1 mm² pad 0. 2 mm above the plane adds about 0. 19 picofarads.
On a sensitive amplifier input with a 1 megohms resistor, it is enough to slow the circuit and make it ring. So you cut the plane away under that one spot. That is the whole idea.
"A ground plane is a solid copper layer used as the reference and return path.
Pros: very low impedance, tiny return loops so less radiation, pickup and crosstalk, controlled-impedance traces, shielding between layers, heat spreading, and capacitance with a nearby power plane.

Cons: extra layers and cost, parasitic capacitance on high-impedance or RF nodes, shared-impedance noise if big currents flow through it, damage if you cut it, possible plane resonance, and thermal issues when soldering."

Ground stitching vias. The question: What is ground stitching?
Ground stitching means placing vias that tie ground copper on different layers together, in rows or grids. This makes them act as one.
It also gives return current a short path when a signal changes layers, and it keeps loose copper islands from acting as antennas.
The key rule is to space the vias no more than about one twentieth of a wavelength apart at the highest frequency you care about.
Think of a quilt. Two layers of fabric bunch up and gap unless you stitch them together.
Ground planes work the same way: two planes joined only far away behave like two separate plates with a gap between them.
Stitching vias are the stitches, and the closer they are, the more the layers act as one.
The analogy breaks in one place: the right stitch spacing for a board depends on signal frequency, which a quilt does not have.
Four common uses: an edge fence, a fence along an RF trace, return vias beside a layer-changing signal via, and stitching of pours.
Spacing along each fence is set by the highest frequency to be contained.
Via: a plated hole that connects copper on different layers. Wavelength: the distance a wave travels during one cycle: speed divided by frequency.
In a board it is shorter than in air. Via fence: a row of stitching vias that forms a wall along a trace or the board edge ("Why a ground plane shields signals").
Return via: a ground via beside a signal via so the return current can change layers too ("Layers for high-speed signal routing").
Ground island: a poorly connected patch of ground copper, which can radiate or pick up noise.
In an FR-4 board a signal on an outer layer travels at about 1. 68 times 10⁸ m/s, a bit over half the speed of light.
At 1 gigahertz the wavelength is about 168 mm, so one twentieth of it is 8. 4 mm. At 2. 4 gigahertz the wavelength is about 70 mm, so the spacing must be about 3. 5 mm.
That is the whole idea.
"Ground stitching means connecting ground layers and pours together with vias in a regular pattern.
It removes floating islands, gives return currents a short path at layer changes, forms a via fence for shielding RF or sensitive traces and the board edge, and reduces plane resonances.
The spacing rule of thumb is about a twentieth of a wavelength in the board at the highest frequency of concern, which is around 8 mm at 1 gigahertz and 3. 5 mm at 2.
4 gigahertz in FR-4."
