Ground plane vs ground traces. The question: What are the tradeoffs between using a ground plane vs ground traces to connect all ground potentials?
There are two ways to distribute ground on a board. A ground plane is a solid copper layer that every ground connection drops into through a via.
Ground traces are routed connections, such as a chain, a star or a grid. The plane has far lower resistance and inductance and keeps each signal's return loop small.
Traces make sense on cheap one- or two-layer boards, or where you want a deliberately separate return.
Imagine a neighborhood where everyone must walk home. With a plane, it is an open field, and each person walks a short, direct route home.
With ground traces, it is one narrow lane that all the neighbors share, so the last house on the lane has everyone else's foot traffic in the way.
The analogy is loose: a fast return current follows the path right under its own signal.
With a daisy chain, segment R g1 carries all three currents (300 milliamps, 15 millivolts), R g2 carries two (200 milliamps, 10 millivolts) and R g3 one (100 milliamps, 5 millivolts).
Each node's ground sits above the source ground by the sum of upstream drops, and any change in I 1 moves G2 and G3.
Daisy chain: loads connected in a row on one ground trace, so each later load sees the earlier loads' currents ("Ground potential differences across a board").
Star grounding: a separate trace from each load to one common point ("Star grounding"). Ground grid: ground traces in both directions tied together with vias, a middle option.
Loop area: the area between a signal and its return. Radiation grows with it.
Common-impedance coupling: voltage made in a shared conductor that appears in another circuit's reference ("What PCB grounding is and why it matters").
Put three 100 milliamps loads on a daisy-chained ground trace, with 50 milliohms per segment. The first segment carries all 300 milliamps, so it drops 15 millivolts.
The second carries 200 milliamps and adds 10 millivolts, so the second load's ground sits 25 millivolts up. The third adds 5 millivolts, so it sits 30 millivolts up.
Any change in the first load's current moves the other two. On a plane the same currents spread out and the drops are tens of times smaller. That is the whole idea.
"A ground plane gives much lower impedance than ground traces: about 0.
5 milliohms per square and sub-nanohenry spreading, versus roughly 190 milliohms and 140 nanohenries for a 100 mm thin trace.
It also puts the return directly under each signal, so loops are small, and it avoids the common-impedance buildup of a daisy chain.
Traces cost less and let you force a deliberate single-point return, so they're right for one- or two-layer boards and for things like a shunt measurement.
Otherwise I use a plane, or a ground grid as a compromise."

Other jobs of a ground plane. The question: In addition to providing a common reference potential, what are some other functionalities of ground planes?
A ground plane does much more than serve as zero volts. It is the return path for signals, which keeps loops small.

It sets the impedance of the traces above it, shields layers from each other, adds capacitance with a power plane, spreads heat, gives static-discharge current an easy path, balances the copper so the board stays flat, and acts as the other half of an antenna.
Cutting the plane weakens every one of these jobs.
Think of a Swiss army knife: one tool, many uses. Each of the plane's jobs uses a different property of one large copper sheet.
A knife with a snapped blade loses only that function. A plane with a slot cut in it loses several functions at once, because all its jobs depend on it staying continuous.

One plane, many jobs: signal return and fields (return path, impedance, shielding, EMI), power integrity (decoupling), and the jobs that just need a big conductor (heat spreading, ESD; mechanical balance and antenna counterpoise are covered below).
All of them depend on the plane staying continuous.
Return path: the route current takes back to its source, directly under the trace at high frequency ("Which layers should be ground").
Controlled impedance: a trace built to a set ratio of voltage to current for fast signals, which needs a plane beneath it ("Layers for high-speed signal routing").
Shielding: keeping fields from one circuit out of another ("Why a ground plane shields signals").
ESD (electrostatic discharge): a sudden spark of static current, like the zap from a doorknob. Inductance: resistance to sudden changes in current.
A fast current change through it creates a voltage.
Take ESD. A standard 8 kilovolts test spark delivers about 30 amps, rising in about 0. 8 nanoseconds. That is about 37. 5 amps per nanosecond.
The voltage across a ground connection is L di over dt , inductance times the rate of change. With 1 nanohenries of inductance it is about 38 volts.
With 5 nanohenries of thin trace, about 188 volts. A via right at the protection part keeps the spike small. For the antenna job, a quarter-wave antenna at 2.
4 gigahertz is about 31 mm long and needs a ground sheet to work against. That is the whole idea.

"Beyond being the reference, a ground plane is the return path that keeps loops small, so it cuts radiation, pickup and crosstalk; it defines trace impedance; it shields between layers; next to a power plane it adds high-frequency decoupling capacitance; it spreads heat; it gives ESD and surge currents a low-inductance path; it balances copper to limit warp; and it's the counterpoise for antennas.
Cutting it up gives up all of those at once."

Why a ground plane shields signals. The question: Why can you use your ground plane to shield your signals?
A ground plane shields because it is a good conductor, and a good conductor does three things to nearby fields. It stops electric field lines, so they do not reach the other side.
It carries the return current, whose magnetic field cancels most of the trace's own.
And at higher frequencies, above a few MHz, currents induced in the copper soak up what is left.
A solid plane between two layers cuts the coupling between them a lot, as long as it has no slots or holes.
Picture a thick wall between two noisy rooms. A hole or gap in the wall lets sound leak straight through, and a thin wall does little against deep rumbles.
A ground plane is that wall. Slots and holes leak, and a thin copper plane does almost nothing against slow magnetic fields, such as 50 hertz hum from mains wiring.
Electric-field shielding in one picture. Without the plane, field lines from the aggressor terminate on the victim, which is capacitive coupling.
With a grounded plane between them, the lines terminate on the plane instead.
Electric field: the push a voltage exerts across space. Its field lines end on a conductor ("What capacitance is").
Return current: the equal and opposite current in the plane under a trace. Its field cancels the trace's field.
Mutual capacitance: the small capacitance between two traces that couples a signal from one to the other ("How signals couple and how to prevent it").
Aggressor and victim: the trace that makes the noise, and the trace that picks it up. Aperture: a slot or hole in the shield through which fields leak.
An aggressor trace swings 3. 3 volts and couples through 0. 5 picofarads to a victim input that has 5 picofarads to ground.
The capacitances split the voltage, so the victim sees 3. 3 times 0. 5 over (0. 5 plus 5) equals 0. 30 volts.
Put a grounded plane between them and the direct coupling falls to about 0. 05 picofarads (the page assumes a tenth). Now the victim sees 3. 3 times 0. 05 over (0.
05 plus 5) about 0. 033 volts, about nine times less. That is the whole idea.
"A ground plane is a good conductor, so it shields in three ways.
Electric field lines terminate on it instead of passing through, so a plane between two layers kills capacitive coupling.
The return current under the trace is equal and opposite to the signal current, so their magnetic fields cancel and the net field falls off fast.
And above a few MHz eddy currents absorb the field: about 47 decibels for 1 oz copper at 100 megahertz.
It only works if the plane is continuous, since slots and edges leak, and it does little against low-frequency magnetic fields."
Quick check. Why does a grounded plane between two signal layers reduce capacitive crosstalk?
Typical ground plane layers and why. The question: Which layers typically have ground planes and why?
By convention, ground goes on layer 2, directly under the top signals, and on the layer next to the bottom.
On bigger boards you add more ground planes so that every signal layer has one beside it.
The reason is that a fast signal's return current runs right under it, and a thin gap between the signal layer and a ground plane gives tight return loops and narrow traces.
On a 2-layer board, ground is the bottom layer.
Think of a restaurant where every table must sit next to an aisle so the servers can reach it. A routing layer is a table, and a ground plane is the aisle beside it.
The closer the aisle, the easier the service. The analogy is loose: the plane also shields and stores charge.
The usual ground positions (blue).

Notice the pattern: L2 is always ground; the layer just inside the bottom is ground in boards of four or more layers (except S/G/P/S); each inner signal layer has a ground neighbour; power (orange) sits next to ground.
The 2-layer board is the exception, with only one plane.
Reference plane: the plane next to a signal layer that carries its return current ("Which layers should be ground").
Prepreg: the thin glue layer between outer copper and the first plane ("PCB layers in a stackup and their materials").
Impedance: the ratio of voltage to current a fast signal sees on a trace, in ohms (Ω). It is set by trace width and distance to the plane.
Stripline: an inner trace sandwiched between two planes ("Layers for high-speed signal routing").
Symmetric stackup: layers mirrored around the center so the board stays flat ("Choosing a board stackup").
Compare where the plane sits for a 50 ohms trace, using the page's quick formula (IPC-2141). With ground 0. 2 mm below on layer 2, the trace is 0. 335 mm wide. With the plane 1.
6 mm away on the far side of the board, the same impedance needs about 2. 99 mm, close to 3 mm. A 0. 335 mm trace can squeeze out between the closely spaced pins of a small chip.
A 3 mm trace cannot. That is the whole idea.

"Ground goes on layer 2, directly under the top signals, and on the layer next to the bottom, with more ground planes added so every inner signal layer sits next to one: layers 2 and 5 on six layers, for example.

The reason is return current: outer layers have thin prepreg, so a plane there gives tight return loops and narrow 50 ohm traces; ground beside power adds decoupling capacitance; and inner grounds shield signal layers from each other.
I keep the outer layers for parts and routing, and use stitched pours there."

Why ground probe points matter. The question: Why are ground probe points important?
A ground probe point is a small ground pad placed right next to a test point, so an oscilloscope probe can touch both with a very short ground connection.
It matters because the probe's ground lead becomes part of the circuit you are measuring.
A long lead acts as an inductor, and together with the probe tip's capacitance it rings on fast edges. You then see ringing on the screen that is not really on the board.
Imagine measuring the water pressure in a pipe through a long, floppy hose.
Every time the pressure jumps, the hose wobbles, and your gauge shows the wobble as well as the pressure. A short, stiff connector gives a true reading.
A long ground clip is the floppy hose, and a spring tip on a nearby ground pad is the short connector.
The analogy is loose: the "wobble" is an electrical resonance between the lead's inductance and the tip's capacitance.
The step source charges the probe tip capacitance through R s , and the charging current returns through the ground-lead inductance.
That's a series RLC whose output across C p is what the scope displays; if L g is large the response overshoots and rings.
Oscilloscope: an instrument that draws voltage against time on a screen. Ground lead inductance: about 1 nanohenries for each millimeter of lead.
Inductance resists sudden changes in current. Probe tip capacitance: the roughly 10 picofarads a standard probe adds at its tip.
Ringing: a decaying wobble after a fast edge, as energy sloshes between inductance and capacitance.
Resonant frequency: the rate of that wobble, f 0 equals 1 over (2 pi square root of LC ) .
Use the probe tip's 10 picofarads.
A 150 mm alligator-clip ground lead is about 150 nanohenries, so f 0 equals 1 over (2 pi square root of 150 nanohenries times 10 picofarads ) is about 130 megahertz.
A 1 nanoseconds edge contains frequencies up to about 350 megahertz, so it sets off that ring.
A spring ground of about 15 mm is 15 nanohenries, which gives about 411 megahertz, and the overshoot falls from about 52% to about 7%.
The board did not change, only the ground path. That is the whole idea.
"The probe's ground lead is a real inductor, about 1 nanohenries per millimetre, and with the probe's roughly 10 picofarads tip capacitance it forms an LC circuit.
A 150 mm clip lead resonates near 130 megahertz and shows about 50% overshoot on a fast edge that isn't really there; it also picks up magnetic fields through its loop.
A ground pad right next to the test point, with a spring ground, brings the resonance up to hundreds of MHz and cleans up ripple and edge measurements.
Ground points also serve production test and debug."

When and why to separate grounds. The question: When/why should you separate your ground reference potentials?
Separating grounds is a tool for specific problems, not a default.
You do it for safety isolation, to break ground loops between pieces of equipment, to keep large or noisy return currents out of a sensitive reference, and to steer static sparks to the metal case.
On a single board you usually do not cut the plane. You place noisy and quiet circuits in different regions of one plane and join them at one deliberate point.
Picture a street where heavy trucks and bicycles both head for the same town center.
Sharing a lane, the trucks shove the cyclists around, so each gets its own lane and they meet at one intersection.
The analogy breaks in one place: a signal that crosses between separated grounds loses its return path, so crossings must happen at the join.
The motor's 5 amps returns through its own conductor R pg to the star point at the supply.
The quiet load returns through a different trace, so the 50 millivolts across R pg never appears in series with its reference.
Compare with "What PCB grounding is and why it matters", where both loads shared the return.
Common-impedance coupling: a shared conductor turns one circuit's current into voltage for another ("What PCB grounding is and why it matters", "Ground potential differences across a board").
Galvanic isolation: no wired connection at all between two circuits. Signals cross by light or magnetism.
Ground loop: a closed loop of ground connections that picks up interference. Star point: the one place where separate returns join ("Star grounding").
ADC: a chip that turns a voltage into a number. Its smallest step is called an LSB.
A motor draws 5 amps through a shared ground conductor of 10 milliohms. The drop is 5 times 0. 010 = 50 millivolts. A 16-bit ADC with a 3.
3 volts range splits it into 65,536 steps of about 50 µV each, so that shift is an error of about 990 steps.
Giving the motor its own return, joined to the ADC's ground at one point, keeps the 50 millivolts out of the measurement. That is the whole idea.

"I separate grounds for specific reasons: safety isolation, breaking ground loops between systems, keeping large or noisy return currents out of a sensitive reference like a shunt or an ADC, different voltage references, and chassis/ESD handling.
On one board I usually partition by placement over a single plane and join returns at one deliberate point rather than cutting the plane.
Where the separation is real, signals cross through isolators. The cardinal sin is a split that fast signals cross, because they lose their return path."
Quick check. Which is a legitimate reason to separate grounds?
Ground layout schemes. The question: What are some ground layout schemes?
A ground layout scheme is the way you wire ground on a board.
In single-point grounding, every circuit returns to one common point, either in a chain or in a star with a separate path for each circuit.
In multipoint grounding, a solid ground plane lets every circuit connect to ground at the nearest spot. Most modern boards use a plane with careful placement.
Think of drainage in a neighborhood. In a chain, all the houses empty into one shared pipe, so the last house feels everyone else's flow.
In a star, each house has its own pipe to the treatment plant, so none affects another.
In a plane, the whole neighborhood sits on a tiled floor with drains everywhere, so water leaves right where it lands.
The analogy is loose: for fast signals a star's long pipes resist sudden changes (inductance), and the plane wins.
In a daisy-chain ground, the return current of the noisy Load B flows through R g2 and then R g1.
The sensitive Load A shares R g1, so its ground reference moves by (I A + I B)·R g1 every time B changes current.
Common-impedance coupling: a shared ground segment turns one circuit's current into noise for another ("What PCB grounding is and why it matters").
Inductance: resistance to changing current. It matters more the faster the current changes. Impedance: resistance and inductance together, in ohms, at a given frequency.
Star ground: each circuit has its own return to a common point ("Star grounding"). ADC and LSB: a chip that turns a voltage into a number, and its smallest step.
Take a 50 mm ground trace, 0. 25 mm wide in standard copper.
Its resistance is about 98 milliohms and its inductance about 60 nanohenries, so above roughly 250 kilohertz the inductance dominates. At 1 megahertz its impedance is about 0.
39 ohms. A 10 milliamps return current then shifts the ground by about 4 millivolts. A 12-bit, 3. 3 volts ADC has steps of 0. 8 millivolts, so that is an error of about 5 steps.
One square of plane is only about 1. 6 milliohms at 1 megahertz, so the same current gives about 0. 02 millivolts. That is the whole idea.
"The main ground layout schemes are single-point, which can be series daisy-chain or parallel star, multipoint, which is a solid ground plane, and hybrids.
Star grounding keeps circuits from sharing return impedance and suits low-frequency analog. A plane gives the lowest inductance and is the right answer for fast digital.
In practice I use a solid plane, partition the board so noisy and quiet circuits don't share return paths, and join sections at one controlled point."
Quick check. Which scheme gives each circuit its own dedicated return path to one common point?
Star grounding. The question: What is star grounding?
Star grounding gives every circuit its own separate return path, and all those paths meet at one single point, like spokes meeting at a hub.
It works because ground copper has resistance and inductance.
If a noisy and a sensitive circuit share part of a return, the noisy current makes a voltage in the sensitive one's reference. In a star, they share only the hub.
Picture a bicycle wheel. No two spokes share any length, so a knock on one does not travel along another.
In a chain of rods joined end to end, a pull at the far end passes through every rod. A star is the wheel. A daisy chain is the chain of rods.
The analogy breaks for fast signals, where long spokes act as inductors and form large loops.
Each load returns through its own leg (R gA, R gB, R gC) to the hub. The sensor's reference differs from the hub only by its own tiny current times R gA.
The motor's amps never flow through the sensor's leg.
Return current: the current that flows back to the source through ground ("KCL and KVL explained").
Common-impedance coupling: voltage across a shared return segment that appears in other circuits' references ("What PCB grounding is and why it matters").
Daisy chain: circuits returning along one shared ground wire, one after another ("Ground layout schemes").
Inductance: resistance to sudden changes in current, which grows with wire length. Ground loop: a second path between two grounds that encloses an area and picks up noise.
Three loads return current to ground: a power stage at 1 amps, logic at 20 milliamps and a sensor at 100 microamps. Each ground segment is 20 milliohms.
In a daisy chain with the sensor farthest out, the segment nearest the hub carries all three currents, about 1. 02 amps, so it alone lifts the sensor's ground by about 20.
4 millivolts. The other segments bring it to about 20. 8 millivolts.
In a star, the sensor's own leg carries only its 100 microamps, so it shifts by just 100 micro A times 20 milliohms equals 2 micro V. That is the whole idea.
"Star grounding gives every circuit its own return path to one common point, so no two circuits share a return segment.
That matters because ground has resistance and inductance, and a shared segment turns one circuit's current into noise on another's reference.
It works best at low frequency, where legs are resistive, and for mixing power, digital and analog.
The risks are long inductive legs at high frequency and accidental second connections that make ground loops."

Combined vs separate analog, digital, power grounds. The question: What are the tradeoffs between combining analog, digital, and power grounds vs separating them?
Should analog, digital and power circuits get separate grounds or share one solid ground plane? Splitting keeps noisy return currents out of the quiet analog copper.
But every signal that crosses the split loses its return path right beneath it, which makes a big loop.
The usual default is one solid plane, with the board arranged so noisy and quiet currents stay apart.
Imagine a building with a quiet library wing and a noisy workshop wing. A solid wall stops the noise, but anyone carrying things between wings must detour to the single door.
Or you can leave the building open and put the workshop and library at opposite ends, so people rarely cross. A solid plane with careful placement is the open building.
The analogy is loose: the detour matters because current must always complete a loop.
Left, a signal trace crosses the gap between split planes: the high-frequency return current (red dashed) must travel around to the bridge, enclosing a large loop.
Right, the same signal is routed over the bridge so the return runs right beside it and the loop stays small.
Return current: the current flowing back to its source, right under the signal at high frequency ("Ground plane pros and cons").
Split ground: a plane cut into separate analog and digital areas joined at a narrow bridge. Inductance: resistance to sudden changes in current.
A bigger loop has more, about 1 nanohenries per millimeter of detour.
Partitioning by placement: putting analog, digital and power circuits in separate regions of one plane ("When and why to separate grounds").
AGND and DGND pins: a converter chip's analog and digital ground pins. Normally both go to the same plane.
A 3. 3 volts clock edge draws 8 milliamps in 1 nanoseconds. It crosses a split, and its return current must detour 80 mm to the bridge.
At about 1 nanohenries per millimeter that adds about 80 nanohenries, so the spike is L di over dt equals 80 nanohenries times 8 milliamps over 1 nanoseconds equals 0. 64 volts.
Over an unbroken plane the loop is only a few nH, giving about 16 to 40 millivolts. The split made it 16 to 40 times worse. That is the whole idea.
"Combining grounds gives every signal a short, low-inductance return right beneath it, which is simple and robust, but noisy return currents can pass through quiet areas if placement is sloppy.
Separating them keeps noisy currents out of the analog region, but any signal crossing the split loses its return path, which creates loops, crosstalk and EMI.
My default is one solid plane partitioned by placement, with separate grounds only for isolation, very high currents or precision low-frequency work, joined at one deliberate point."
Quick check. What is the main risk of splitting a ground plane in mixed-signal PCBs?
Ground potential differences across a board. The question: What happens if your ground plane potential differs throughout your board?
On a real board, ground is not one single point at one voltage.
It is a network of copper with resistance and inductance, and current flowing through it creates small voltage differences between places.
Every logic level and every analog reading is measured against a local ground.
So a few hundred millivolts of difference shifts what a receiving chip sees, eating its safety margin, and shows up as error in measurements.
Measure a table's height with a ruler. If the ruler stands on a floor 5 cm higher than the table's floor, you get the wrong answer.
A receiver measures against its own ground pin, so if its floor is not level with the driver's, it reads wrong.
The analogy is loose: here the floor level moves with the current flowing through it, so the error changes with the load.
The driver pushes V OH relative to its own ground, but the return current has to flow through the ground impedance Z g to get back.
The voltage across Z g is subtracted from what the receiver sees relative to its ground.
Ground impedance: the ground path's resistance and inductance ("What PCB grounding is and why it matters").
Logic thresholds: the voltages above which a receiver reads "1" ( V IH ) and below which it reads "0" ( V IL ).
Noise margin: the headroom between the voltage a driver sends and the receiver's threshold. Common-mode: a voltage shared by both wires of a pair.
Receivers that compare the two wires ignore it. ADC and LSB: a chip that turns a voltage into a number, and its smallest step.
Take 3. 3 volts logic with V IH = 2. 0 volts and V IL = 0. 8 volts. With matching grounds, a 3. 3 volts high has 1. 3 volts of margin and a 0 volts low 0. 8 volts.
Offset the receiver's ground by 600 millivolts and one margin shrinks: to 0. 7 volts for highs, or to only 0. 2 volts for lows. For a 12-bit, 3.
3 volts ADC, with steps of about 0. 81 millivolts, a 1 millivolts ground shift is an error of about 1. 2 steps. That is the whole idea.
"Every voltage on the board is measured against a local ground, so if grounds differ, I get errors everywhere.
Logic levels arrive shifted, so noise margin shrinks and I get bit errors or false triggers. Analog measurements shift by the offset, which can be several LSBs.
Large or fast offsets can exceed pin ratings, cause latch-up, or drive cables as antennas and fail EMC.
It comes from current times ground impedance, so the fix is to lower that impedance and keep noisy returns apart."

Sources of ground potential variation. The question: What can be the source of ground plan potential variation?
Voltage differences appear across ground for a few distinct physical reasons. Resistive drop is steady current flowing through the resistance of ground copper.
Inductive drop is fast-changing current flowing through ground inductance. Path distortion is slots, splits and crowded via areas that force current to detour.
And coupled sources are fields and outside connections that push voltage into ground. Knowing which one you have tells you which fix to use.
Think of a road network. A narrow road slows every car a little: that is resistive drop.
A heavy truck that must suddenly change speed shoves everything around it: that is inductive drop, where the fast change is the problem.
A road closure forces a long detour: path distortion. And a loud concert next door shaking the whole street is coupling.
Each problem needs a different fix: widen the road, slow the truck, reopen the road or soundproof the street.
DC drop grows linearly with current and with the number of squares.
Even a few milliohms matter: 5 amps through a 20-square trace gives about 49 millivolts, a large error for a precision converter, while an open plane keeps it near 7 millivolts.
Sheet resistance: the resistance of one square patch of copper, any size, about 0. 49 milliohms for standard 1 oz foil. Inductance: resistance to sudden changes in current.
The voltage it makes is V equals L di over dt , inductance times the rate of change. Ground bounce: a ground shift when many outputs switch at once.
Plane discontinuity: a slot, split or via cluster that forces return current to detour ("Ground plane pros and cons").
Ground loop: a closed ground path that picks up magnetic fields ("Ground potential differences across a board").
For the resistive source, 5 amps flowing across 3 squares of 1 oz copper gives 5 times 3 times 0. 49 milliohms about 7. 4 millivolts.
For the inductive source, a 1 nanohenries connection carrying a current that changes by 1 amps per nanosecond gives L di over dt equals 1 nanohenries times 1 amps over ns equals 1 volts.
Same ground, different mechanism: the first needs more copper, the second needs a smaller loop and closer decoupling capacitors. That is the whole idea.
"I group the sources into resistive, inductive and coupled.
Resistive is IR drop through copper, about half a milliohm per square for one-ounce copper, made worse by neck-downs, vias and connectors.
Inductive is L di/dt from fast current: simultaneous switching, switching-regulator loops, package pins and connectors, and it's usually larger on fast boards.
Coupled covers return paths detoured by slots, shared returns, ground loops picking up magnetic fields, and external injection like ESD or a cable at another potential."

Keeping ground variation small. The question: How do you avoid too much variation?
To keep ground voltage differences small, you attack from two sides.
Make the ground path low in resistance and inductance: a solid plane close to the signals, no slots or narrow necks, and plenty of vias.
And make the currents in shared ground paths small and local: decoupling capacitors at the pins, tiny switching loops and slower edges.
Keep noisy and quiet circuits apart, and check with probe points.
Think of quieting a noisy street. You can widen the road so traffic flows easily: that is lowering the ground's resistance and inductance.
You can cut the number of cars and their speed: that is lowering the current and how fast it changes. Sending trucks away from the school is partitioning.
A sound meter outside the school is the probe point. The analogy is loose: ground has no "street" of its own, only the copper you give it.
A typical four-layer stackup keeps a continuous ground plane just 0. 1-0. 2 mm below the top signal layer.
The tiny gap makes the signal-return loop thin, so its inductance per square is only a fraction of a nanohenry. Compare with a 1-nH-per-mm trace with no nearby plane.
Inductance: resistance to sudden changes in current, in nanohenries (nH). It makes a voltage L di over dt .
Decoupling capacitor: a nearby capacitor that supplies fast current so it does not flow through the plane ("Placing and routing decoupling capacitors").
Ground bounce: a ground shift when many outputs switch together. ADC and LSB: a chip that turns a voltage into a number, and its smallest step.
Error budget: the allowed ground shift, from which you work backward to milliohms and nanohenries.
A 12-bit, 3. 3 volts ADC has steps of about 0. 81 millivolts, so half a step is about 0. 4 millivolts.
If 100 milliamps of return current crosses a shared path, its resistance must be under 0. 4 millivolts / 0. 1 amps = 4 milliohms, about 8 square patches of standard copper at 0.
49 milliohms each. For ground bounce, say 8 outputs each switch 20 milliamps in 1 nanoseconds, and the shift must stay under 100 millivolts.
Then the shared inductance must be at most 0. 1 volts over (8 times 20 milliamps over ns ) equals 0. 625 nanohenries. That is the whole idea.
"I keep ground variation small by lowering the impedance and shrinking the currents.
Impedance: a solid unbroken plane right under the signal layers, no slots or neck-downs, stitching vias at layer changes, and many ground pins on connectors.
Currents: tight decoupling at every power pin, compact switching loops, slower edges and fewer simultaneous switches.
Then I partition by placement so noisy returns stay away from sensitive analog, and I budget the allowed millivolts back to milliohms and nanohenries."

Designing for ground disturbance resilience. The question: How can you design your system to be more resilient against ground disturbances?
Good layout shrinks ground disturbances but never removes them, so a robust system is designed to keep working when ground moves.
Send signals on two wires and compare them, so a shared offset cancels. Use isolation when two grounds cannot be tied together.
Make measurements relative to the same supply that powers the sensor, so a shift cancels. Add margin with filters, and recover from corrupted data with error checks and retries.
Imagine two boats on a tide that rises and falls. If you measure each boat's height above the seabed, the tide ruins both numbers.
If you measure the distance between the boats, the tide cancels out. A differential receiver measures only the difference between two wires and ignores what they share.

Capacitor self-resonant frequency in decoupling. The question: What is a capacitor's self resonant frequency? Why is this important?
The self-resonant frequency (SRF) is the frequency where a real capacitor stops acting like a capacitor. Every real capacitor has a tiny built-in inductance.
Below the SRF, the capacitor part wins and the part helps the supply. Above it, the inductance wins and the part acts like an inductor.
So the SRF marks the edge of the capacitor's useful band for decoupling.
Picture a weight hanging on a spring. Push it back and forth slowly and you mostly feel the spring's stiffness. Shake it very fast and you mostly feel the weight's inertia.
At one rhythm in between, the two cancel and the weight moves with almost no effort; only friction is left.
For a capacitor, the spring is the capacitance, the inertia is the inductance, the friction is the ESR, and that special rhythm is the SRF.
At any capacitance, adding mounting inductance pulls the SRF down by square root of L . Moving from 0. 5 nanohenries to 5 nanohenries costs a factor of 3.
2: a 100 nanofarads capacitor goes from 22. 5 megahertz to 7. 1 megahertz. This is the plot to keep in mind when someone asks "does the datasheet SRF apply?"
ESL: the small inductance inside every real capacitor ("Realistic capacitor model and parasitics"). ESR: the small resistance inside a capacitor. It sets the impedance at the SRF.
Self-resonant frequency: f 0 equals 1 over (2 pi square root of LC ) ("Capacitor self-resonant frequency").
Mounting inductance: extra inductance from pads, traces and vias, which lowers the SRF on a real board ("Sources of parasitic inductance in decoupling").
Impedance: how strongly a part opposes alternating current, in ohms.
Take a 100 nanofarads capacitor with 0. 5 nanohenries of inductance. Then f 0 equals 1 over (2 pi square root of 0. 5 times 10 to the -9 times 10 to the -7 ) , which is about 22.
5 megahertz. Below that it is capacitive. At 22. 5 megahertz its impedance is just its ESR. Above that it is inductive.
Now pads, traces and vias raise the total inductance to 3 nanohenries, and the SRF on the board drops to about 9 megahertz. That is the whole idea.
"SRF is where a capacitor's parasitic inductance and capacitance resonate: 1 over (2 pi square root of LC ) .
Below it the part is capacitive, at it the impedance is just the ESR, and above it the part is an inductor. A 100 nanofarads ceramic with 0.
5 nanohenries resonates around 22 megahertz.
It matters because it marks the useful band, so I choose values whose SRFs cover the range, and remember mounting inductance lowers the SRF on the real board."

When not to use decoupling capacitors. The question: When should you not use decoupling capacitors?
A capacitor next to a chip is the right default, but not an absolute rule. Some regulators and amplifiers become unstable if you add more capacitance than the datasheet allows.
A big capacitor can also cause a huge surge of current at power-on. And a capacitor on a signal line is not decoupling at all. It just slows the signal down.
Think of shock absorbers on a car. The right ones smooth a bumpy road. The wrong ones make the car bounce or fight the steering.
The same part that helps in one setup hurts in another. A capacitor is a shock absorber for voltage, so you match it to what it is attached to.
When a live supply is connected, the cable inductance, the capacitor's ESR and its capacitance form a series RLC.
Ceramic capacitors have tiny ESR, so the circuit is lightly damped.
Inrush current: the surge that flows into an empty capacitor when power is first applied.
Stability: whether a regulator or amplifier settles to a steady output instead of ringing or swinging on its own.
ESR window: the range of internal resistance some regulators need in their output capacitor to stay stable.
Capacitive load limit: the most capacitance an amplifier or reference can drive without ringing. Hot-plug: connecting a live supply to a board whose capacitors are empty.
Plug a 12 volts supply into a board with 100 microfarads of capacitance, and let the voltage rise over 1 milliseconds.
The current that fills the capacitor is i equals C dV over dt equals 100 micro F times 12 volts over 1 milliseconds equals 1. 2 amps.
That can trip a protection circuit sized for a small load. If the voltage jumps up instantly, the surge is far bigger, limited only by wiring resistance. That is the whole idea.
"Decoupling is the default, so the exceptions are specific.
Don't add capacitance beyond what the datasheet allows: LDOs with ESR windows, references and op-amp outputs with capacitive-load limits.

Be careful where capacitance causes problems: hot-plugged inputs where ceramic plus cable inductance overshoots toward twice the input, large capacitors that cause inrush, and bad value mixes that create anti-resonance.
And never decouple a signal line, because that is just a low-pass filter."

Rules of thumb for routing high-speed signals. The question: What are some rules of thumb when routing high-speed signals?
A fast signal on a circuit board travels down the trace like a wave.
It stays clean only if the path keeps the same shape the whole way and the return current has a smooth path back.
Every routing rule protects one of those two things: a solid plane underneath, one trace width, few vias, no dead-end branches, and space from neighbors.
Imagine a ball rolling down a smooth, even gutter. It arrives cleanly. Add a gap, a narrow spot or a side branch, and part of its motion bounces back.
Fast signals do the same at every bump. What matters is how fast the edge is, not how often the signal repeats.
Below the line a trace may be treated as a wire; above it, as a transmission line that needs controlled impedance and probably termination.
Modern 100 picoseconds edges push the threshold to a few millimetres, which is why almost every trace on a fast board is "a transmission line".
Rise time ( t r ): how long a signal takes to go from low to high.
Transmission line: a trace long enough, compared with the edge, that the signal must be treated as a wave ("Characteristic impedance explained").
Characteristic impedance ( Z 0 ): the ratio of voltage to current the wave sees, set by trace width, height above the plane and board material.
Return path: the route current takes back to its source. At high speed it is the plane right under the trace ("Ground plane pros and cons").
Stub: a dead-end branch that reflects part of the signal. Crosstalk: unwanted coupling from a neighboring trace.
A signal edge takes 1 nanoseconds to rise. On ordinary board material it travels about 5. 9 picoseconds per millimeter.
A trace counts as a transmission line when its one-way delay is more than about t r over 6 , here about 167 picoseconds. That is a critical length of 167 over 5. 9 about 28 mm.
Longer traces need the full set of rules. That is the whole idea.
"High-speed routing is about keeping the trace a uniform transmission line with a clean return path.

I route on a solid reference plane without crossing splits, keep one width for controlled impedance, avoid stubs, minimise vias and put a ground via beside each signal via, use 45° bends, keep about three trace widths of spacing, match lengths on buses and pairs, and terminate if the trace is long compared with the edge.
What counts is rise time, not clock frequency: if the one-way delay is more than a sixth of the rise time, it's a transmission line."

Vias in high-speed traces. The question: Should you put vias through high-speed traces?
A via is a small plated hole that carries a signal from one board layer to another. At slow speeds it acts like a plain wire.
For very fast edges it is a small bump in the path: a little inductance, a little capacitance and a leftover dead-end piece of barrel. That bump reflects part of the edge.
How much that matters depends on the edge speed.
Picture a smooth garden hose with one short kink and a dead-end side pipe. Slow water barely notices. A sudden splash hits the kink, and part of it bounces back.
The return current also has to change layers with the signal, so it needs its own path nearby.
The signal enters on L1, travels down the barrel to L3 and leaves. Everything below L3 (red shading) is an open stub.
The dashed square shows the anti-pad clearance in L2 (every plane the barrel passes has one); these clearances set the via's shunt capacitance.
The adjacent green ground via lets the return current move between the planes.
Via barrel: the plated tube between layers. It adds about 1 nanohenries of inductance (which resists fast changes in current) on a 1. 6 mm board.
Via stub: unused barrel left beyond the layer where the signal exits ("Via types and their tradeoffs"). Back-drilling: drilling out the stub from the far side of the board.
Return (ground) via: a ground via beside the signal via so the return current can follow.
Reflection: the part of an edge that bounces back where the impedance changes ("Reflections and why they matter").
Say a via adds 1 nanohenries in a 50 ohms line. The reflected fraction is roughly L over (2 Z 0 t r) . Here 1 nanohenries over 100 ohms equals 10 picoseconds.
For a 1 nanoseconds edge, 10 picoseconds / 1 nanoseconds is 1 percent. For a 100 picoseconds edge, it is 10 percent.
The same via is harmless on a slow bus and a real problem on a fast link. That is the whole idea.
"I avoid vias on fast signals where I can, because each one adds around 1 nanohenries of series inductance, a few tenths of a picofarad of shunt capacitance and a stub that resonates.
A 1 nanohenries via reflects about 1% of a 1 nanoseconds edge but about 10% of a 100 picoseconds edge, so it depends on edge rate.
When I must use one I keep the count low, put a ground via next to it for the return current, shorten or back-drill the stub, and make the two vias in a differential pair identical."

Shape of high-speed traces: bends and widths. The question: What shape should these high-speed traces be? Why?
A trace's impedance depends on its width and its height above the reference plane. Anywhere the shape suddenly changes, a little of a fast edge bounces back.
So you route traces at constant width, turn corners with 45 degree cuts or smooth arcs, and avoid stubs and sharp angles.
A square 90 degree corner is a small effect, but it costs nothing to avoid.
Picture a river of constant width flowing around a bend. If the bank makes a sharp square corner, a small eddy forms there, but the river mostly carries on.
If a wide pool or a side channel appears, the flow is disturbed far more. A smooth curve keeps the flow even. A square corner is the eddy. A stub or wide pad is the pool.
A 90° bend only becomes a percent-level reflection when the edge is tens of picoseconds. At 1 nanoseconds edges the effect is 0. 03%: invisible.
So the rule is "free insurance", not an emergency.
Characteristic impedance ( Z 0 ): the impedance a signal sees along a trace, set by width, height above the plane and board material ("Changing a trace's characteristic impedance").
Shunt capacitance: extra capacitance from a trace to the plane. Extra copper adds it.
Reflection: the part of an edge that bounces back at an impedance change ("Reflections and why they matter"). Mitered corner: a corner with the outer tip cut at 45 degrees.
Stub: a dead-end branch, a far bigger discontinuity than a corner ("Sources of reflection on a PCB and fixes").
A square corner on a 0. 36 mm trace, 0. 2 mm above the plane, has about half a trace width squared of extra copper. That adds roughly 12 fF of capacitance.
In a 50 ohms line, the reflection is Z 0 C over (2 t r) . For a 100 picoseconds edge, that is 50 times 12 fF over 200 picoseconds equals 0. 3 percent.
For a 30 picoseconds edge it reaches about 1 percent. That is the whole idea.
"Straight where possible, and 45° mitres or curves when they have to turn, with constant width, no stubs and no acute angles.
A 90° corner puts extra copper over the plane, which is a little capacitance and a small impedance dip.
For a 50 ohms line that's around ten femtofarads, so well under a percent of reflection for a 100 picoseconds edge, mostly negligible below several GHz.
It costs nothing to route it right, though, and it matters on multi-gigabit nets. The bigger offenders are stubs, abrupt width changes and wide pads."

Serpentining for bus synchronization. The question: What is serpentining? Why is it important for synchronization?
Serpentining means adding zig-zag length to a trace on purpose. In a bus, the receiver reads every data bit at the moment a clock or strobe edge arrives.
If some bits travel a shorter route, they arrive early and squeeze the time window. Adding length to the short traces makes all signals arrive together.
Think of runners in a relay who must all hand off at the same moment. If one runner has a shorter path, you make that runner take a winding route so everyone arrives together.
The winding must not bunch up, or runners on neighboring bends cut across to each other. So the bends need space between them.
The receiver samples on each rising clock edge. D0 changes well before the edge and stays valid after: lots of setup and hold margin.
D1 arrives late: it changes closer to the edge so setup margin shrinks.
D2 is so late that its transition (the x region) coincides with the sampling edge: setup violation, so the bit may be read wrong. Serpentining pulls D1 and D2 back toward D0.
Skew: the difference in arrival time between signals that should arrive together. Unit interval (UI): the time of one bit, equal to 1 divided by the data rate.
Setup and hold time: how long data must be stable before and after the sampling edge ("Setup and hold times (SI view)"). Propagation delay: time per unit length, about 5.
9 picoseconds per millimeter on outer-layer FR-4 traces. Speed-up: when tight meander legs couple, so the signal arrives earlier than the length suggests.
A signal moves at about 6 picoseconds per millimeter on FR-4. A trace that is 6 mm shorter than its neighbors arrives about 35 picoseconds early. At 3. 2 Gb/s a bit lasts 312.
5 picoseconds. Take away 150 picoseconds for setup and hold and 50 picoseconds for jitter, and 112. 5 picoseconds remains for all skew. That is roughly 19 mm of length.
So you add meanders until every trace is within that budget. That is the whole idea.
"Serpentining means adding zig-zag length to the shorter traces in a group so that all the signals arrive within the timing budget.
In a clocked bus the receiver samples data relative to a clock or strobe, so skew eats directly into setup and hold.
On FR-4 it's about 6 picoseconds per millimetre, so a few mm of mismatch is tens of ps.
I match delay rather than length, keep meander legs at least three or four trace widths apart to limit self-coupling, and place them near where the mismatch arises."

Differential pair and its tradeoffs. The question: What is a differential pair? What are some tradeoffs?
A differential pair is two wires that carry opposite versions of one signal. When one goes up, the other goes down by the same amount.
The receiver looks only at the difference between them. Noise that lands on both wires equally cancels out in that subtraction.
The price is double the pins and traces, and a need to keep the two wires closely matched.
Imagine two people holding the ends of a rope, with a flag in the middle that shows how far apart their hands are.
If a gust of wind pushes both people the same way, the gap between their hands does not change, so the flag stays put.
Only when they move in opposite directions does the flag move. The analogy breaks down if one person is delayed. Then the wind and the signal get mixed together.
Each line swings ±0. 2 volts around a 1. 2 volts common-mode level (LVDS-like). The receiver sees ±0. 4 volts of differential signal, twice the per-line swing.
The common-mode level (dashed) doesn't move: all of the information is in the difference.
Differential voltage ( V d ): V P minus V N . This is the signal. Common-mode voltage ( V cm ): the average (V P plus V N) over 2 . It carries no data.
CMRR: how strongly a receiver ignores common-mode noise, often given in dB ("How differential signals improve noise immunity").
Skew: a timing difference between the two wires of a pair.
Mode conversion: when imbalance turns some of the signal into common-mode noise ("Differential pair skew: why it matters, how to fix").
Differential impedance ( Z diff ): the impedance between the two wires, often 100 ohms ("Characteristic impedance explained").
Drive V P equals 1. 4 volts and V N equals 1. 0 volts. The receiver sees V d equals 0. 4 volts. The common-mode level is (1. 4 plus 1. 0) over 2 equals 1. 2 volts. Now 0.
5 volts of noise lands equally on both wires, so they read 1. 9 volts and 1. 5 volts. The difference is still 0. 4 volts, and only the common-mode level moved.
That is the whole idea.
"A differential pair is two complementary traces where the data is the voltage difference between them.
Noise that hits both lines equally is common-mode and gets subtracted out, the opposite currents make the pair radiate less, and you get a bigger signal difference for a given swing.

The costs are double the pins and traces, strict length matching and constant spacing, differential termination, and the fact that any skew converts signal into common-mode noise, so it must be routed carefully."

Routing differential pairs: layout guidelines. The question: How should it be routed? What are some layout guidelines that may differ from single-ended high-speed signals?
You route a differential pair as one object, not as two separate wires.
Both traces run side by side on the same layer, with the same spacing, the same length, the same vias and the same surroundings.
Anything that makes one trace see a different world than the other turns part of the signal into noise. The width and the gap together also set the pair's impedance.
Think of two dancers who must move in perfect mirror image. They stay the same distance apart, take the same number of steps and turn at the same moment.
If one has to walk around a table while the other goes straight, the mirror breaks. Pair routing is the same. Keep them together, and fix any difference right where it appears.
Pulling the pair closer requires narrower traces for the same 100 ohms.
Narrow traces have more conductor loss and are harder to fabricate consistently, which is why many designs choose moderate coupling ( s about w to 2w) rather than very tight.
Values come from the model behind the lab below; your fab's field solver gives the final numbers.
Differential impedance ( Z diff ): the impedance between the two traces, often 100 ohms (90 ohms for USB) ("Common characteristic impedance values").
Spacing: the gap between the two traces. Unlike single-ended routing, it helps set the impedance.
Intra-pair skew: the difference in arrival time between the two traces ("Differential pair skew: why it matters, how to fix").
Mode conversion: when imbalance turns some of the signal into common-mode noise.
Ground (return) vias: ground vias placed beside signal vias at layer changes so the return current can follow ("Vias in high-speed traces").
Say the board has 0. 2 mm of dielectric under the traces. A trace width of about 0. 24 mm with a 0. 2 mm gap gives roughly 100 ohms differential.

So you add a small jog on the inner trace right after the bend. That is the whole idea.

The big differences from single-ended routing are that matching is within the pair and done locally at each bend or via, spacing sets the impedance, and there should be no stubs or one-sided obstacles.
Anything asymmetric converts differential signal into common-mode."

Differential pair skew: why it matters, how to fix. The question: Why is it important that signals for both lines of the diff pair arrive to the source at the same time?
What happens if they don't arrive at the same time? How can you ensure that they do arrive at the same time?
The receiver of a differential pair expects the two wires to be exact mirror images at the same instant.
If one wire arrives late, for a moment the two wires do not mirror each other, and part of the signal turns into common-mode, which is the same-direction motion on both wires.
That hurts the eye, adds jitter and makes the pair radiate more noise. You fix it by making both traces arrive together.
Picture two rowers in a boat who must pull their oars together. If one is late, the boat does not just slow a little. It also wobbles sideways, because the pulls no longer cancel.
The sideways wobble is the common-mode noise. The forward motion barely changes, which is why the damage is easy to miss.
The common-mode trace (red) should be a flat 1. 2 volts. With a 40 picoseconds skew it develops a pulse of 80 millivolts: V s over 2 change in t over t r equals 0. 2 times 0. 4 .
The differential edge (green) now takes t r plus change in t equals 140 picoseconds instead of 100 picoseconds to complete.
That pulse repeats on every edge and is a clock-rate-related common-mode current.
Skew: the time difference between the two lines of a pair ("Serpentining for bus synchronization"). Common-mode: voltage or current that moves both lines the same way.
It radiates well ("Common-mode voltage of a differential pair"). Mode conversion: signal turning from differential into common-mode because of imbalance.
CMRR: how well a receiver rejects common-mode noise that arrives from outside.

For a larger 25 picoseconds skew, with a 0. 4 volts swing and a 100 picoseconds edge, that is 0. 2 times 0. 25 equals 50 millivolts on every edge.
The receiver's CMRR cannot remove it, because the pair made it inside the channel. That is the whole idea.
"If the two lines of a pair don't arrive together, part of the differential signal turns into common-mode.
That's a voltage the receiver ignores, but it's also current that radiates and a signal-dependent disturbance, so skew costs eye width, adds jitter and creates EMI.
The mode conversion, in S-parameter terms, goes as tan of pi times frequency times skew, so 20 picoseconds at 5 gigahertz is about minus 10 decibels.
To avoid it I match the pair in delay, locally at each bend and via, keep everything symmetric, and verify with TDR or an eye diagram."

Serpentining a differential pair. The question: What is serpentining? Why is it important for diff pairs?
Serpentining a differential pair means adding a small zig-zag of extra length to the shorter trace so both traces arrive at the same time.
You add it right where the difference appears, such as just after a bend. If the whole pair needs to be longer, you meander both traces together so they stay equal.
Imagine two people walking side by side around a curve. The person on the outside walks farther. To arrive together, the inside person takes a small detour right after the curve.
If they waited until the end, they would have been out of step the whole way. And the detour must stay close, so they remain a pair.
(A) after a bend the outer (black) trace is longer, so a small jog on the inner (orange) trace restores equality. (B) To lengthen both traces equally, meander the pair as a pair.
(C) Avoid: a long detour of one trace pulls it away from its partner, raises the differential impedance and creates a fresh asymmetry.

Jog: a small zig-zag added to the shorter trace to give it extra length. Pitch: the center-to-center distance between the two traces, equal to width plus gap.
Coupled meander: a serpentine in which the whole pair winds together, so both traces gain equal length.

Transmission line components on a PCB. The question: Describe transmission line components on a PCB.
On a circuit board, a fast signal travels along a copper trace as a wave.
The wave needs two conductors: the trace itself, and a solid reference plane under it that carries the return current. A layer of insulation (the dielectric) sits between them.
The shape of this sandwich sets the line's impedance and how fast the signal moves.
Think of a water slide with a smooth channel. The slide's width and slope decide how the water flows, and it flows the same way along its whole length.
Bumps or gaps make the water splash back. The trace plus plane is the channel. Its size sets the impedance, and any via, pad or connector along the way is a bump.
In all three the signal conductor (orange) and a return conductor (blue) with a dielectric between them form the line; thin lines indicate where the electric field goes.
Microstrip's field is partly in air so waves travel faster; stripline's all in FR-4; GCPW adds coplanar returns to tighten the field.
Reference (return) plane: the solid copper layer beside the trace. The signal's return current flows in it ("Ground plane pros and cons").
Dielectric: the insulating layer between trace and plane, often FR-4 with r about 4. 3 . L' and C': inductance and capacitance per unit length of the line.
They set the impedance and the delay ("Characteristic impedance explained").
Characteristic impedance ( Z 0 ): square root of L' over C' , the impedance a wave sees along the line.
Microstrip and stripline: a trace on an outer layer, versus a trace buried between two planes ("Choosing a board stackup").
Take a typical 50 ohms microstrip on FR-4. It has about L' equals 0. 30 nanohenries per millimeter and C' equals 0. 12 picofarads per millimeter. Then Z 0 equals square root of 0.
30 nanohenries over 0. 12 picofarads equals square root of 2500 equals 50 ohms . The delay per millimeter is square root of L'C' equals square root of 0.

"A PCB transmission line is a signal trace over a reference plane with FR-4 dielectric between them.
It's microstrip if it's on an outer layer, stripline if buried between two planes.

Electrically it's a ladder of series R and L and shunt C and G per unit length; Z 0 equals square root of L' over C' and delay is square root of L'C' , about 50 ohms and 6 picoseconds/mm for a typical trace.
Along the path you also have lumped pieces, vias, pads, connectors and terminations, which are the places that cause reflections."

Common characteristic impedance values. The question: What are some common characteristic impedance values?
Characteristic impedance is the fixed ratio of voltage to current for a wave traveling down a line.
A handful of standard values are used everywhere: 50 ohms for most RF and board traces, 75 ohms for video, and 90, 100 or 120 ohms for differential pairs depending on the interface.
The standard for each interface sets the number. You pick the board stackup and trace width to hit it.
Think of garden hoses and nozzles. If the hose and the nozzle are the same size, the water flows through without splashing back. If they differ, some water bounces back.
Impedance values work the same way: everything along the signal path (driver, trace, cable, receiver) should use the same standard, so nothing reflects.
The red curve (loss, normalised to its minimum) bottoms out near 77 ohms and the green curve (power handling, normalised to its maximum) peaks near 30 ohms.
At 50 ohms loss is about 1. 10 times the minimum and power is about 0. 86 times the maximum. Cable and instrument makers settled on it, and the PCB world inherited it.
Characteristic impedance ( Z 0 ): square root of L' over C' , set by the line's geometry and materials, not its length ("Characteristic impedance explained").
Differential impedance ( Z diff ): the impedance between the two traces of a pair, about twice the odd-mode impedance ("Differential pair and its tradeoffs").
Reflection coefficient ( ): the fraction of a wave that bounces back at a mismatch, (Z 2 minus Z 1) over (Z 2 plus Z 1) ("Impedance matching: what, why, when").
Tolerance: the allowed error, usually about 10 percent on a board. Controlled impedance: a board ordered with a target impedance that the fab checks on a test coupon.
A 60 ohms trace connects to a 50 ohms system. The reflection coefficient is (60 minus 50) over (60 plus 50) equals 0. 09 . So about 9 percent of the wave bounces back.
For a 10 percent tolerance, the worst case is about 5 percent. On a short trace with slow edges, you will not notice it. On a long, fast channel, small reflections add up.
That is the whole idea.
"50 ohms single-ended is the default for RF and most PCB traces, 75 ohms for video.
For differential pairs, 100 ohms is the usual value, covering Ethernet, SATA, HDMI, PCIe and LVDS, with USB at 90 ohms, and 120 ohms for CAN and RS-485.
DDR has its own 40-60 ohms single-ended values. 50 ohms comes from the coax compromise between lowest loss near 77 ohms and highest power handling near 30 ohms.
In practice the standard sets the target and I set the stackup and width to hit it within about ±10%."
