Why avoid radiated EMI. The question: Why do I want to avoid radiated EMI?
Radiated EMI is noise that leaves your board as radio waves. You avoid it for four reasons. The law limits it, and a product that fails cannot be sold.
It disturbs other equipment, including your own radios. A board that radiates well also picks up noise well. And fixing it late is costly, while good layout is nearly free.
Imagine an apartment with thin walls. Your loud music gets out, and the neighbor's music gets in. Whatever lets sound leak out also lets it leak in.
That is reciprocity: a structure that sends well also receives well. The building rules are the regulators' limits, and your own ear is your own radio.
Each curve rises at 40 decibels/decade (because E proportional to f squared ) and sits 9. 5 decibels higher per tripling of area, 20 decibels higher per tenfold.
The 10 cm² loop crosses the limit near 48 megahertz, the 3 cm² loop near 87 megahertz and the 1 cm² loop only near 185 megahertz.
The limit line is stepped because the standard is. (Assumes the same 10 milliamps of harmonic current at each frequency, which is a simplification.)
Emission limit: the legal ceiling on how strong a field a product may radiate, measured at a set distance. FCC and CISPR publish these.
Common-mode current: current flowing the same direction on both wires of a cable, which makes the cable an antenna.
Loop area: the area enclosed by a current's outbound and return paths. A bigger loop radiates more. Reciprocity: a structure that radiates well also receives well.
Decibel (dB): a way to compare sizes. Every 20 decibels is a factor of 10 in field strength. Desense: noise lowering a receiver's sensitivity, so it hears weak signals worse.
Take 10 milliamps of current at 100 megahertz in a loop, measured 3 m away. A 1 cm² loop is about 11 decibels under the US limit for home products (FCC Class B), so it passes.
Make the loop 10 cm². Ten times the area gives a field 10 times stronger, and now it is about 9 decibels over, so it fails.
A 30 cm cable carrying only about 12 microamps of common-mode current at 100 megahertz also reaches the limit.
That is the whole idea: tiny currents in the wrong geometry fail tests.
"Mainly four reasons. It's regulated: you can't sell a product that fails FCC or CISPR limits.
It interferes with other radios, including your own, because noise in the Wi-Fi or GPS band desensitises your receiver.
By reciprocity, anything that radiates well also picks up interference well.
And it's a symptom of bad layout: big loops and cable common-mode current also cause ringing and crosstalk.
It's very sensitive too: about 12 microamps of common-mode current on a 30 centimetre cable can reach the limit at 100 megahertz."
Quick check. Which statement about radiated EMI and susceptibility is most accurate?
Board techniques to minimize radiated EMI. The question: What are some board-level techniques to minimize radiated EMI?
A circuit board radiates mostly from two things: current loops, and noise current on cables.
So the layout fixes are to make loops small, make edges only as sharp as the timing needs, damp ringing, and filter cables where they leave the board.
The first step is a solid ground plane right under fast signals.
Think of a megaphone. The bigger its opening, the farther it projects sound. A current loop is like the opening: more enclosed area means more radiation.
Speaking softly is like slowing the edges. A long pipe that carries sound outside is like a cable that carries noise out of the box.
Three families of fixes mapped to the physics. Spend effort in this order: loops (free), source (cheap), cables (cheap), shielding (expensive).
Loop area: the area enclosed by a signal's outbound path and its return path. A bigger loop radiates more. Ground plane: a solid copper layer at 0 volts.
Return current flows in it, right under the signal trace. Edge rate: how fast a signal switches. Slower edges carry less high-frequency energy.
Common-mode current: current flowing the same direction on both wires of a cable, which makes the cable an antenna.
Common-mode choke: a small part that blocks that same-direction current but passes the wanted signal.
Take a 10 cm trace running 0. 2 mm above a solid ground plane. The return current flows right under it, so the loop is 0. 2 mm times 100 mm = 20 mm², or 0. 2 cm².
Now cut a slot in the plane that forces the return about 1 cm away from the trace. The loop is about 10 cm times 1 cm = 10 cm².
That is 50 times the area, and radiation grows in proportion to area, so 50 times the field.
Separately, an edge three times slower shrinks the high-frequency part of the signal about three times. That is the whole idea: small loops, soft edges, quiet cables.
"I attack it by mechanism. Make loops small: solid ground plane under every fast signal, no splits, ground vias at layer changes, tight decoupling and a compact switcher hot loop.
Reduce the source: slow edges with series resistors or slew control, damp ringing with snubbers or gate resistors.
Deal with cables: common-mode chokes or ferrites and a proper chassis bond at the connector, and keep fast traces off the edge.
Shield cans are the last resort, because layout fixes cost nothing."
Quick check. Which layout change most directly reduces radiation from a fast signal trace?
External EMI and its impact on circuits. The question: What about external sources of EMI? How can they impact a circuit?
External EMI is interference that comes from outside your board: radio transmitters, nearby motors, noise from wall power (mains) and static zaps.
Every loop of copper and every cable acts as an antenna that picks it up.
The effects are unwanted voltage added to weak signals, steady offsets from rectification, resets and glitches in digital chips, and sometimes damage.
Connectors and inputs are the entry points.
Imagine rain falling on a yard full of open buckets. A bigger opening catches more rain. A long gutter, like a cable, funnels water in from far away.
Loops and cables on a board collect radio energy in the same way. The doors of the house are the connectors.
Induced voltage grows linearly with frequency.

At 100 megahertz and 10 volts/m, a 10 cm² loop sees 21 millivolts, as big as a 20 millivolts sensor signal; at 1 gigahertz the simple formula says over 200 millivolts, though the loop is no longer small compared with the wavelength so the real value saturates.
Shrinking the loop (area) is the direct fix.
Immunity: how well a circuit keeps working when outside interference arrives. Induced voltage: the unwanted voltage a field creates in a loop or wire.
Loop area: the area enclosed by a wire and its return path. The induced voltage is proportional to it.
Rectification: parts inside a chip pass current more easily one way than the other, so fast radio-frequency (RF) energy turns into a steady offset.
ESD: electrostatic discharge, a static zap with a very fast edge.
Suppose a strong radio field of 10 volts per meter at 100 megahertz hits a 10 cm² loop on a board. The induced voltage is about 21 millivolts.
If the loop carries a 20 millivolts sensor signal, the interference is as big as the signal.
The induced voltage is proportional to loop area, so shrinking the loop to 1 cm² cuts it to about 2 millivolts.
Even if the amplifier cannot respond at 100 megahertz, its input junctions can rectify the RF, so the reading shifts when a phone is nearby.
That is the whole idea: loops and cables collect interference, and junctions turn it into errors.
"External EMI is energy from phones, radios, motors, mains transients and ESD that couples in through loops, traces and cables.
A 10 volts/m field at 100 megahertz induces about 20 millivolts in a 10 square centimetre loop, as big as a sensor signal.
Semiconductor junctions also rectify RF, so a sensor's DC reading can shift when a phone is nearby. Digital lines can glitch, and ESD or surge can reset or damage the board.
So the connectors and high-impedance inputs are where I protect first."
Quick check. Which describes how a loop of PCB copper responds to an external magnetic field?
Board techniques to protect against EMI. The question: What are some board-level techniques to protect against EMI?
To protect a circuit from outside interference, you build layers. At the connector, you add a surge-clamping diode and a filter so noise is stopped where it enters.
At each sensitive input, you add a small filter and keep wires short. In the layout, you keep loops small and bond connector shells to the enclosure. Shielding comes last.
Think of a castle. The moat and gatehouse are the connector protection, and they stop most trouble at the border. An inner wall is the small filter at each sensitive input.
The treasure sits in the middle, away from the gate. A tall outer wall, the shield, is costly, so it comes last.
The TVS sits at the connector with the shortest possible return; the bead blocks RF from entering the board; the RC at the receiving end finishes the job before the amplifier.
All the shunt parts return to the same low-impedance reference.
TVS diode: a protective diode that clamps a surge or static zap to a safe voltage.
Low-pass filter: a circuit, such as a resistor and capacitor, that passes slow signals and blocks fast noise. Corner frequency: the frequency where a filter starts to cut.
For an RC filter it is 1 over (2 pi RC) . Ferrite bead: a small part that acts like a resistor for fast noise, absorbing it.
Chassis bond: connecting a connector's metal shell to the enclosure with a short, wide path.
Put a 1 kilohms resistor and a 1 nanofarads capacitor in front of a sensor amplifier. The corner is about 159 kilohertz, so a slow sensor signal passes.
Noise at 100 megahertz is about 630 times above the corner, and an ideal filter cuts it by about that factor (56 decibels).
Real capacitors lose effect at high frequency, so use short leads.

At the connector, the TVS needs a short, wide return: a loop with 10 nanohenries of inductance (how strongly wiring fights fast current changes) and a static edge rising 10 amps per nanosecond adds 100 volts.
That is the whole idea: stop noise at the entry, then harden the victim.
"I defend in layers.
At every connector: a TVS for transients with a short, wide return to chassis, a ferrite bead or common-mode choke for RF, and a small capacitor, all placed right at the connector.
At the victim: an RC filter at sensitive inputs, low and balanced source impedance, short high-impedance traces.
In the layout: solid planes for small loops, differential signalling, partitioning away from connectors, and chassis bonding of shells.
Shielding and firmware robustness (watchdog, filtered resets) come after."
Quick check. Where should ESD/transient protection for a connector pin be placed?
How signals couple and how to prevent it. The question: How can signals couple together? How can this be prevented?
Noise gets from one circuit to another in four ways. Two circuits can share a wire, so one's current creates a voltage the other sees.
A changing voltage can push current through the tiny capacitance between nearby conductors. A changing current can induce voltage in a nearby loop through the magnetic field.
Or noise can travel through space as radio waves. To prevent it, quiet the source, cut the coupling, or toughen the receiver.
Think of an apartment building. Two flats on one water pipe share pressure, so a neighbor flushing drops yours. That is shared wiring.
A thin shared wall passes bangs, like capacitance. Two linked chain rings tug each other when you pull one, like magnetic coupling.
A loud stereo heard across the street is radiation.
Four independent paths from the same aggressor to the same victim. A cure for one does nothing for the others, so diagnose the mechanism first.
Aggressor and victim: the circuit that makes the noise and the circuit it disturbs.
Shared impedance: a wire or ground path two circuits both use, so one's current makes a voltage for the other.
Mutual capacitance: two nearby conductors act like a tiny capacitor, two metal plates with a gap. Fast voltage changes on one push current into the other.
Mutual inductance: the magnetic link between two loops. A changing current in one induces voltage in the other.
Impedance of the victim: how hard the victim node is to push around. High impedance is the most vulnerable.
Say the mutual capacitance is 0. 5 picofarads and the victim wire has 4. 5 picofarads to ground. A 3.
3 volts edge in 1 nanoseconds divides between the two capacitances, so at most 3. 3 times 0. 5 / 5. 0 = 0. 33 volts reaches a high-impedance victim.
If the victim is a low-impedance 50 ohms line, it quickly drains the injected charge and sees only about 81 millivolts. A 1 kilohms line sees about 0. 30 volts.
That is the whole idea: find which path it is, then cut the cheapest link.
"There are four mechanisms. Conductive coupling through a shared impedance, like a common ground trace, where V equals IZ or L di over dt .
Capacitive coupling between conductors, i equals C m dv over dt , worst for high-impedance victims.
Inductive coupling between loops, v equals M di over dt , worst for large loops and long parallel runs. And radiation.
To prevent it: separate returns and planes for common impedance, spacing and shielding for capacitive, small loops for inductive, plus slower edges and a lower-impedance or differential victim."
Quick check. Two circuits share a ground trace and one circuit's digital current shifts the other's reference. Which coupling mechanism is this?
Board techniques to minimize coupling. The question: What are some board-level techniques to minimize coupling?
You can cut coupling (noise leaking from one trace to another) with layout choices, and most are free.
Keep each trace close to its ground plane so its fields stay trapped under it. Space noisy traces from sensitive ones, avoid long parallel runs, and cross at 90 degrees.
Give noisy and quiet circuits separate return paths. If a victim is very sensitive, add a grounded guard trace.
Hold a flashlight close to the floor and its pool of light stays small. Lift it higher and the pool spreads to neighbors. A trace's electric field behaves the same way.
The closer a trace is to the ground plane, the more its field ends right underneath it, and the less reaches the next trace.
So moving a trace nearer its plane often beats moving traces apart.
Same spacing, different dielectric height. When the plane is close, field lines from the aggressor terminate under it and little reaches the victim.
This is why "move the trace closer to the plane" is often more effective than "move the traces apart".
Reference plane: a solid copper layer, usually ground, that a trace's field and return current use.
Dielectric height ( h ): the thickness of insulation between the trace and its plane. 3 watts rule: keep trace centers at least three trace widths apart.
It is a quick guideline, not a guarantee. Guard trace: a grounded trace between aggressor and victim, tied down with vias. A floating guard can make coupling worse.
Return path: the route current takes back to its source.
A rough empirical rule says the coupled amount is about 1 over (1 plus (s over h) squared) , where s is the spacing between traces. Take traces 0. 3 mm apart. Over a plane 0.
1 mm below ( s equals 3h ), coupling is about 0. 1, a tenth. Over a plane 0. 4 mm below ( s over h equals 0. 75 ), it is about 0. 64.
So at the same spacing, a four times thinner dielectric cuts coupling about six times. Check critical nets with field-solver software.
That is the whole idea: keep traces near the plane first, then separate, then guard.

"Geometry first: keep traces close to their reference plane and separate aggressor and victim by several times that height, with the 3 watts rule as a check; avoid long parallel runs and cross at 90 degrees.
Then return paths: solid planes, separate returns for noisy and quiet circuits. For sensitive nets, a grounded, via-stitched guard.
Then slow aggressor edges, lower the victim's impedance, use differential pairs, and partition noisy and quiet sections apart."
Quick check. Which change most effectively reduces crosstalk between two microstrip traces without changing their spacing?
Clock and analog on adjacent layers. The question: If I have two traces on adjacent layers, one a clock and another a sensitive analog signal. How should I route these signals?
Suppose two signal layers sit back to back with no ground plane between them.
A clock trace (a fast on-off timing signal) on one layer and an analog trace (a small, smoothly varying signal) on the other then form a tiny capacitor wherever they overlap.
The fixes, best first, are a ground plane between the layers, crossing at 90 degrees so the overlap is tiny, and keeping the traces apart sideways.
Imagine a drummer upstairs and a reader downstairs, separated only by a thin floor. The more floor they share, the more thumping comes through.
If the drummer is over just one corner, little gets through. A thick carpet between them, which is the ground plane, helps most.
Top view of two adjacent layers superimposed.
Parallel routing makes the overlap equal to the full trace length; a perpendicular crossing makes it a single square of trace width squared.
Adjacent layers: two inner signal layers separated only by a thin insulating layer. Dielectric: that insulating layer between conductors.
Capacitance: two conductors that overlap with insulation between them form a capacitor. More overlap area and less spacing mean more capacitance.
90-degree crossing: running one trace straight across the other, so they overlap only in a small square.
Take two traces 0. 2 mm wide, separated by 0. 2 mm of insulation. If they run together for 50 mm, the capacitance is about 1. 9 picofarads (picofarads, trillionths of a farad).
The analog node has 10 picofarads to ground. A 3. 3 volts clock edge divides by the capacitances, so the analog node jumps by about 3. 3 times 1. 86 / 11. 86 = 0. 52 volts .
If the traces instead cross at 90 degrees, the overlap is only 0. 2 mm times 0. 2 mm. That is about 7 fF (femtofarads, thousandths of a pF), and the jump falls to about 2.
4 millivolts , 250 times smaller. That is the whole idea: overlap area sets the coupling, so remove the overlap or put a plane in the way.
"Directly overlapping traces on adjacent layers form a parallel-plate capacitor, so the clock injects C dv/dt into the analog node: roughly 1.
9 picofarads over 50 mm, which can put half a volt on a 10 picofarads node. Best fix is a ground plane between the layers.
If that's not possible, cross them at 90 degrees so the overlap is a tiny square, about 250 times less capacitance, and keep them laterally separated.
Then slow the clock edge, lower the analog node's impedance, and filter at the ADC."
Quick check. Two traces on adjacent layers with no plane between them run parallel for 50 mm. What is the dominant coupling mechanism?
Desense: what, why, and how to avoid. The question: What is desense? Why should it be avoided? What are some board-level techniques to avoid it?
Desense, short for desensitization, is when a radio receiver, such as Wi-Fi or GPS, loses sensitivity because noise raises the floor under the weak signals it is trying to hear.
The noise often comes from the product's own clocks, displays or power supplies. The result is shorter range and slower data.
It can pass legal emissions tests, because receivers are far more sensitive than those limits.
Picture trying to hear a whisper in a quiet room. If a fan starts humming, the whisper must now be louder to be heard, even though the fan is not loud.
The hum is the noise floor and the whisper is the weak radio signal. You can quiet the fan, move away from it, or close a door between you.
Interference only starts to matter within about 10 decibels of the noise floor, but is brutal beyond it: at equal power you lose 3 decibels, at +10 decibels you lose 10.
4 decibels. A target of I over N at most -10 decibels keeps desense below about 0. 4 decibels.
Receiver sensitivity: the weakest signal a receiver can still decode. Noise floor: the unavoidable background noise level that weak signals must rise above.
In-band: at the same frequencies the receiver listens to. Decibel (dB): a way to compare two powers. +3 decibels is double, +10 decibels is ten times.
Isolation: how many dB of separation you create between a noise source and the antenna or receiver.
Suppose in-band interference reaches the receiver at exactly the same power as its noise floor.
Total noise is then double, which is 3 decibels worse, so the receiver needs a 3 decibels stronger signal.
If the interference is 10 decibels below the noise floor, the loss is only about 0. 4 decibels.
In free space, a 3 decibels loss cuts range by about 29%, and a 1 decibels loss by about 11%. A common design goal is to keep interference at least 10 decibels below the floor.
That is the whole idea: desense is a noise budget.
"Desense is loss of receiver sensitivity caused by noise from elsewhere, usually the same product.
In-band interference adds to the thermal noise floor, and the sensitivity loss is 10 log of one plus I over N: 3 decibels when interference equals noise, 0.
4 decibels at 10 decibels below. It costs range and throughput and can pass regulatory tests because the receiver floor is tens of dB below the limits.
To avoid it: separate and shield the RF section, filter lines crossing zones, slow edges, plan clocks so harmonics miss the band, and keep the antenna away from noisy cables and displays."
Quick check. What is desense?
What EMI shields are and when to use them. The question: What are EMI shields? Why/when are they needed?
An EMI shield is a conductive barrier, such as a metal can soldered over a circuit, a metal case, or a cable's braid.
It goes around a noise source to keep energy in, or around a sensitive circuit to keep energy out.
Layout should fix problems first, because shields add cost, height and heat, and leak at seams. But reserve space for one at layout time.
Think of a soundproof booth. Put the drummer in it and the noise stays inside. Put the person recording in it and the noise stays out.
Either way, the booth is only as good as its door gaps and cracks.
Cross-section of a board-level shield. The can is soldered to a ground ring; vias connect that ring to the ground plane, so can plus plane enclose the noisy IC.
The RF section to the right is outside this can and would get its own.
Shield can: a small stamped metal cover soldered over part of a board. Source and victim: the circuit making the noise and the circuit it disturbs.
Ground fence: a ring of ground pads, linked to the ground layer with vias (plated holes), that the can is soldered to.
Aperture: any gap in a shield, such as a seam, vent or cable hole, that lets energy through. Shielding effectiveness: how much a shield reduces a field, in decibels (dB).
20 decibels is a factor of 10.
In theory, solid metal at 2. 4 gigahertz blocks well over 100 decibels. But real shields leak.
A slot of length l gives about 20 log 10( over 2l) dB, where is the wavelength, the length of one wave. At 2. 4 gigahertz, is about 125 mm.
A 10 mm slot gives only about 16 decibels, which is about a factor of 6. A 5 mm slot gives about 22 decibels, or a factor of 12. So the gaps, not the metal, set the result.
That is the whole idea: a shield is a last-resort closed box, limited by its holes.
"An EMI shield is a conductive barrier, usually a soldered metal can on the PCB or a conductive enclosure, that keeps electromagnetic energy from leaving a noisy circuit or entering a sensitive one.
I'd use it for RF sections, noisy sources I can't fix at the source, very sensitive analog, or to fix a compliance or desense problem.
But it adds cost, height, heat and rework difficulty and leaks at seams, so I treat it as a last resort after layout, filtering and edge control, while reserving footprint for it up front."
Quick check. Which statement best describes the role of a board-level EMI shield?
How EMI shields work. The question: How do EMI shields work?
A metal shield works in two ways. Most of a radio wave bounces off the metal surface, which is reflection.
The small part that gets in dies out inside the metal, because it makes eddy currents (circulating currents in the metal) that oppose it, which is absorption.
Electric fields are easy to block with grounded metal, slow magnetic fields are hard, and real shields are limited by leaks.
Picture a mirror in front of a dark curtain. The mirror bounces most light back. Whatever slips past is soaked up by the curtain. A thin mirror reflects as well as a thick one.
Slow magnetic fields are different: they reflect poorly, and a thin curtain barely absorbs them.
Most of the incident wave reflects at the surface (orange). What enters decays exponentially over skin depths (red), and what emerges (grey) is very small.
The shield's decibels are the sum of the reflected and absorbed fractions.
Reflection: the wave bouncing off the metal because the metal is so unlike air. Absorption: the wave fading as it passes through the metal.
Skin depth: how deep a field goes into a metal before it fades to about a third. It shrinks as frequency rises.
Eddy currents: circulating currents a changing field creates in the metal. Aperture: any gap in a shield, such as a seam or vent, that leaks. Decibel (dB): a way to compare sizes.
20 decibels is a factor of 10 in field strength.
Take a 35 µm copper foil. At 100 megahertz copper's skin depth is 6. 6 µm, so the foil is more than five skin depths thick.
It absorbs about 46 decibels (a factor of about 200), and reflection adds about 88 decibels. At 1 kilohertz the skin depth is 2. 09 mm, so the same foil absorbs only about 0.
15 decibels. Against slow, close magnetic sources use steel, a smaller loop, or distance.
That is the whole idea: reflection plus absorption, strong at radio frequencies, weak for slow magnetic fields.
"A shield works by reflection and absorption.
The metal's surface impedance is milliohms against 377 ohms for a far-field wave, so most of it reflects; what gets in is absorbed because eddy currents oppose it, decaying over a skin depth, 6.
6 microns for copper at 100 megahertz. Electric fields are easy to shield with any grounded conductor.
Low-frequency magnetic fields are hard, because reflection is weak and thin copper absorbs little, so you need high-permeability material or loop control.
And in practice leakage through seams and holes sets the real performance."
Quick check. Which two mechanisms mainly provide shielding in a solid metal shield?
What EMI shields connect to, and why. The question: What are EMI shields typically connected to? Why?
A shield only works if it is connected to the right place in the right way. A shield can on a board connects to the circuit's ground plane, all the way around its edge.
A cable shield or metal enclosure connects to the chassis, the product's metal frame, through the connector shell. A floating shield passes noise on.
Think of a bathtub. Noise current is water pouring in, and the shield's voltage is the water level. A wide, short drain keeps the level low.
A narrow, long drain, like a thin wire pigtail, lets the level rise until it overflows into the room, which is the sensitive circuit.
A tub with no drain, a floating shield, fills right up.
The noise source drives a displacement current through C s into the shield node.
A low-impedance Z g (short, wide ground connection) drains it to ground, so the shield node barely moves and the victim sees almost nothing through C v .
If Z g is large (a long pigtail) or absent (floating), the shield node swings and drives the victim.
Ground plane: a solid copper layer at 0 volts inside the board. Chassis: the metal frame or enclosure of the product.
Floating: connected to nothing, so its voltage drifts with whatever couples to it. Pigtail: a single thin wire used to connect a shield, which has a lot of inductance.
Inductance: how strongly a wire resists fast current changes. At 100 megahertz, a 10 nanohenries wire acts like about 6 ohms.
Say a noisy node swings 12 volts at 2. 4 volts per nanosecond, and a stray 1 picofarads capacitance (nearby metal passing fast voltage changes) links it to the shield.
That pushes a current of 1 picofarads times 2. 4 volts/ns = 2. 4 milliamps into the shield. At 100 megahertz, a 10 nanohenries pigtail is about 6.
3 ohms, so the shield swings about 15 millivolts. A connection through many short plated holes (vias), about 0. 5 nanohenries, is about 0. 3 ohms, which gives only about 0.
75 millivolts. A floating shield, with 5 picofarads to ground, would swing about 2 volts. That is the whole idea: give the noise current a short, wide way home.

"Board-level cans are connected to the PCB ground plane at many points around the perimeter; cable shields and enclosures are bonded to chassis with a 360 degree low-inductance connection at the connector.

Shielding an electric field means giving the displacement current a path to return, so the shield has to be grounded, and at RF the connection impedance matters: 10 nanohenries is 6 ohms at 100 megahertz.
A floating shield just floats to some potential and re-couples noise. For cables, RF wants both ends bonded; low-frequency audio may need one end to avoid ground loops."
Quick check. Why must an electric-field shield be connected to ground?
Where to place EMI shields. The question: Where should I place EMI shields?
Put a shield over the block that matters most and is easiest to isolate.
That is either a strong, localized noise source, like a switching regulator, or a very sensitive circuit, like a radio.
Build it as a cage: a can over a ring of ground pads, a fence of ground vias into the ground layers, and a solid ground plane underneath.
Signals cross the wall only through filters.
Think of a restaurant. Walling off the noisy kitchen quiets the dining room, and one wall serves every table.
Food and staff pass through a small hatch, which is the filtered crossing. An open archway would defeat the wall.
A typical placement. The regulator gets its own can (source shielding). The RF section is a two-compartment can so the PA and LNA don't talk through the cavity.
The wall sits on a stitched ground fence. The only lines through the walls are filtered (orange). The antenna stays outside with its keep-out.
The connector's lines are filtered where they enter the board, before they approach the cans.
Ground ring and via fence: a closed ring of ground copper under the can's wall, tied to the ground layers by closely spaced vias (plated holes).
Filtered crossing: a small filter part, such as a ferrite bead that soaks up fast noise, where a signal or supply passes through the wall.
Antenna keep-out: a clear zone around the antenna. A shield would block it and shift its tuning.
Cavity resonance: an empty metal box rings at certain frequencies and can amplify noise inside. Source and victim: the circuit making the noise and the circuit it disturbs.
Say a board has a switching regulator beside a 2. 4 gigahertz radio. The regulator is one strong source for many victims, so one can over it protects everything.
The can's ground contacts must be spaced at most over 20 apart, where is the wavelength. At 2. 4 gigahertz is about 125 mm, so 6. 25 mm. At 5 gigahertz it is about 60 mm, so 3 mm.
Signals leaving the can go through a filter. That is the whole idea: choose the single best thing to wall off, and keep the wall closed.
"I put the shield over the block that's most localised and matters most: the RF section, or a noisy source like a switching regulator or processor and memory, and sometimes sensitive analog.
It sits on a closed ground ring, stitched to the plane with a via fence so the planes form the floor and walls of a cage.
Anything crossing the wall gets filtered or goes through an inner layer.
I keep the antenna outside, watch clearance to parts and inductors, put test points outside, and keep compartments small so cavity resonances stay out of the band."
Quick check. Where should the antenna be relative to a shield can?
What is a Faraday cage?. The question: What is a faraday cage?
A Faraday cage is a closed metal box, solid or a fine mesh. It stops outside electric fields and radio waves from reaching the inside, and stops inside ones from getting out.
Charges in the metal shift until they cancel the field inside.
It leaks through holes that are large compared with the wavelength, and misses static magnetic fields and wires passing through.
Look at the door of a microwave oven. You can see your food through its little holes, because light waves are tiny compared with the holes.
But the microwaves, about 12 cm long, cannot fit through holes only a millimeter or two wide. A mesh stops a wave when the holes are much smaller than the wavelength.
An external field (blue) pushes free charges to the surfaces (red).
The induced charges produce a field inside the metal equal and opposite to the applied one, so the cavity sees none. Field lines end on the outer surface charge.
Free charges: electrons in metal that move freely when pushed by a field. Wavelength: the distance between two peaks of a wave. For the 2.
45 gigahertz microwave oven it is about 122 mm. Aperture: any hole, slot or seam in the cage.
Grounded cage: a cage connected to ground (the circuit's 0 volts reference), so charge from sources inside can drain away.
Penetration: a wire or cable passing through the cage, which carries outside fields in unless it is filtered.
The leakage through an opening of size l is about 20 log 10( over 2l) dB. That is the decibel scale, where 20 decibels means a field 10 times weaker.
The oven's wavelength is 122 mm. For a single 2 mm hole, the formula gives about 30 decibels, which is roughly 30 times weaker.
A big 20 mm opening gives only about 10 decibels, about 3 times weaker. That is the whole idea: a closed conductive shell blocks fields, limited by its openings.
"A Faraday cage is a closed conductive enclosure, solid or fine mesh, that keeps external electric fields and EM waves out of its interior, and internal ones in.
Free charges rearrange on the surface until the field inside the metal is zero, and for a charge-free cavity the interior field is zero too.
For waves, surface and eddy currents reflect and absorb them.
Holes leak in proportion to size versus wavelength, so a microwave oven's mesh door stops 12 cm waves; it doesn't stop static magnetic fields or whatever wires carry through."
Quick check. Why is the electric field zero inside a closed conducting shell in an external static field?
What a via is and why. The question: What is a via? Why are they needed?
A via is a small plated hole through a circuit board that connects copper on one layer to copper on another.
A board has several layers, and a trace can only run flat along one of them. A via lets a signal, power or heat move up or down between layers. It is not a perfect wire, though.
It has a little resistance (opposition to steady current), inductance and capacitance (it stores a little charge).
Think of an elevator in an office building. Each floor is a layer, and the hallways are traces. To get from one floor to another you need the elevator shaft, which is the via.
The shaft runs through every floor, even if you only stop at two, so it takes space on all of them. And the elevator is not instant: at high speeds it holds up traffic.
A through via on a 4-layer board. The barrel is a thin tube, so the middle is hollow.
It lands on pads on L1 and L4, while the plane layers have a void (antipad) so the barrel doesn't short to them.
Layer: one flat sheet of copper in the board's stack. Boards often have four or more. Trace: a copper line that carries a signal along one layer.
Barrel: the copper-plated wall of the hole, like a thin copper tube. Pad: a copper ring on a layer that the barrel connects to.
Inductance: how strongly a wire resists fast changes in current. 1 nanohenries is a billionth of a henry.
Take a common via: a 0. 3 mm hole through a 1. 6 mm board. Its resistance is only about 1. 3 milliohms, so 1 amps through it loses about 1. 3 millivolts.
Its inductance is about 1. 3 nanohenries. At slow speeds you can ignore it. At 1 gigahertz the same 1. 3 nanohenries acts like about 8 ohms, which is large.
That is why fast designs count their vias and put a ground via next to each signal via.
That is the whole idea: a via connects layers, but it is a small circuit element, not a free wire.
"A via is a plated hole that electrically connects copper on different layers of a PCB.
We need them because traces only run in 2-D on each layer, so signals have to drop through the stack to cross each other, reach power and ground planes, escape from BGAs, and move heat.
A via isn't ideal: a typical one is about a milliohm, around 1 nanohenries and a few tenths of a picofarad, so at high frequency I treat it as a small inductor and keep return paths close."
Quick check. What is the main purpose of a via on a multilayer PCB?
Connecting one signal across two layers. The question: If I have a signal on two separate layers, how can I connect them together?
To connect one signal across two layers, you use a via. The right setup depends on the signal. A slow signal needs just one via.
A power connection needs several vias in parallel, because each carries only about an amp.
A fast signal's return current must also change layers, so you put a ground via right next to the signal via.
Picture a train on a loop of track. The train goes out along one track and must come back along another.
If the outbound track climbs a hill through a tunnel, the return track should go through a tunnel right beside it.
If the return track takes a long road across town, the loop gets huge. The ground via is that second tunnel.
Return current (red) follows the signal in the L2 plane, hops through the ground via and continues in L3 under the L4 trace.
The ground via is drawn lighter because it sits beside the L4 trace, not on it; it never touches the signal copper.
The closer the ground via is to the signal via, the smaller the loop and the lower its inductance.
Via: a plated hole connecting copper on different layers. Return current: the current that flows back to the source. At high frequency it flows in the plane just under the trace.
Reference plane: the solid copper layer a signal's return current uses. Ground via: a via tied to ground, placed beside a signal via to give the return current a short path.
For a slow on/off control signal, one via is plenty. For power, a 0. 3 mm via carries roughly 0. 84 amps for a 10 degrees Celsius temperature rise, a conservative figure.
A 2 amps rail needs 2 / 0. 84 = 2. 4, so at least three vias. A 10 amps rail needs about 12.
For a fast signal, the loop made by the signal via and its nearest ground via acts like a small inductor, which resists fast changes in current. On a 1. 6 mm board it is about 1.
2 nanohenries with the ground via 1 mm away, and about 2. 4 nanohenries at 6 mm. That is the whole idea: the via is easy, but the return path and current count matter.
"I connect them with a via: a plated hole with pads on both layers, and I'd use the router's layer-change command to drop it.
For a slow signal one through via is fine, for power I use several in parallel, and for a fast signal I add a ground via right next to the signal via so the return current can change layers too.
If the stack-up allows, I'd use blind or microvias where space is tight."
Quick check. Which is the standard way to connect a trace on layer 1 to a trace on layer 4 of a PCB?
Via types and their tradeoffs. The question: What are the different types of vias? What are their tradeoffs?
There are four main kinds of via. A through via runs from the top of the board to the bottom. A blind via starts on an outer layer and stops inside.
A buried via connects inner layers only. A microvia is a tiny laser-drilled hole spanning one layer. Through vias are the cheapest and most robust.
The others save space or shorten stubs, but they cost more, so use through vias unless something forces you not to.
Think of a building. A stairwell that runs through every floor is a through via. It is cheap, but it uses space on every floor.
A staircase from the lobby to the second floor is a blind via. A staircase between two upper floors is a buried via. A short ladder between neighboring floors is a microvia.
Each via spans a different layer range. The buried via leaves both outer surfaces free.
The through via on the right is used only from L1 to L3, so the red lower barrel is an unused stub that rings at its quarter-wave frequency.
Through via: drilled through the whole board. Blind via: connects an outer layer to an inner layer and stops there.
Buried via: connects inner layers and is invisible from both outer surfaces. Microvia: a very small laser-drilled via that spans a single layer.
It lets chips with tightly packed pins route their wires out. Stub: the unused part of a through via barrel below the layer where the signal exits.
Say a fast signal goes from the top layer to an inner layer through a through via. The part of the barrel below the exit is a stub.
A stub rings at the frequency where it is a quarter of a wavelength long, c over (4 square root of r ) .
A 3 mm stub in typical board material rings near 12 gigahertz, a problem for a 25 Gb/s link (25 billion bits per second). A blind via or microvia has almost no stub.
But blind and buried vias need extra build steps, which cost money. That is the whole idea: through vias are the default, and the other kinds trade cost for density.

"The main types are through vias, which go top to bottom and are cheapest; blind vias, which go from an outer layer to an inner one; buried vias, which connect inner layers only; and microvias, which are tiny laser-drilled vias spanning one layer, sometimes stacked.

The tradeoff is cost and complexity against density and signal integrity: blind, buried and micro need extra lamination or laser steps, so I default to through vias and only go further when BGA pitch, layer count or stub resonance forces it."
Quick check. Which via connects two inner layers and is not visible from either outer surface?
Vias between inner layers. The question: If I need to via between inner layers, what type of vias would I use?
To connect two inner layers of a board, you use a buried via. It lives entirely inside the board and never shows on the top or bottom.
The board factory (fab) drills and plates it in a thin inner core before the board is pressed together. That extra build step makes it cost more.
In return it takes no space on the outer layers and leaves no stub.
Picture a staircase between two middle floors of a building. It does not reach the street or the roof, so it uses no ground-floor or roof space.
But it has to be built before the upper floors go on, and afterward you cannot see or repair it. A stairwell through every floor is simpler, but it cuts a hole in every floor.
The shaded centre core carries L3 and L4. The buried via is drilled and plated in that core alone, before the outer layers are laminated onto it, so its barrel is only 0.
2 mm long. The through via on the right spans all six layers and goes through the plane layers with antipads.
Buried via: a plated hole that connects inner layers only. Core: a thin insulating sheet with copper on both sides. It is the building block of the board.
Lamination: pressing the layers together with heat to form the finished board. Through via: a hole through the whole board. It touches every layer.
Stub: the unused part of a through via barrel, which can disturb fast signals. Inductance: how strongly a wire resists fast current changes.
Say you need to connect inner layers 3 and 4 of a six-layer board. A through via would run 1. 6 mm through all six layers, cut holes in both ground planes, and leave stubs.
Its inductance is about 1. 3 nanohenries, which at 5 gigahertz acts like about 41 ohms. A buried via in a 0. 2 mm core is only 0. 2 mm long. Its inductance is about 0.
1 nanohenries, 13 times lower, or about 3 ohms at 5 gigahertz, and it has no stub.
That is the whole idea: build the short connection inside the board, at the price of extra manufacturing steps.
"I'd use a buried via. It connects two inner layers, never reaches the surface, and is drilled and plated in a core before the final lamination.
That saves outer-layer space and avoids a stub, but it needs sequential lamination, so it costs more and can't be inspected or reworked.
If density or signal integrity doesn't justify it, a through via, possibly back-drilled, is the cheaper alternative."
Quick check. Which via type connects two inner layers and is not visible from either surface of the board?
When to use filled vias. The question: When would I want filled vias?
A filled via has its hole filled with epoxy (a hard resin) or copper and then covered with a flat copper cap. The surface is smooth, like an ordinary pad.
You use one when a via has to sit inside a solder pad, because an open hole steals solder. You also use them to stack microvias and move heat.
They cost more, so fill only where needed.
Picture a puddle of water sitting next to a drain. The water runs down the hole and leaves the puddle empty.
Melted solder behaves the same way, because the via's copper-lined hole pulls it in like a straw.
A filled via is a stopper pushed into the drain, sanded flat, and capped, so the puddle stays where it was meant to be.
Left: an open via in the pad lets solder run down the barrel and leaves a starved, voided joint.
Middle: the via is moved off the pad with a short dogbone and covered by mask, which is the cheapest fix when there is space.
Right: a filled via with a copper cap restores a flat pad so the via can stay in it.
Via-in-pad: a via placed directly in a component's solder pad, used when there is no room beside the pad. Solder wicking: liquid solder being pulled down into an open via.
Fill and cap: filling the barrel, sanding it flat, and plating copper over the top. Microvia: a tiny laser-drilled via spanning one layer.
Void: an empty bubble in a solder joint that weakens it.
Take a 0. 3 mm via with a 0. 25 mm finished hole in a 1. 6 mm board. Its inner volume is about 0. 079 mm³. A 0.
3 mm solder ball, the tiny bump under some chips, holds only about 0. 014 mm³. So an open via under a ball can swallow the solder of about 5 or 6 balls in the worst case.
In practice the barrel does not fill completely, but even part of that loss starves the joint and leaves voids. A filled and capped via keeps the solder on the pad.
That is the whole idea: filling fixes a specific problem, a hole that steals solder or breaks a stack.
"I use filled vias when a via has to sit in a solder pad, like under a BGA or QFN, because an open barrel wicks solder away and starves the joint.
The fab fills the barrel with epoxy and plates copper over it so the pad is flat. I also use copper-filled vias for stacked microvias in HDI and for better thermal conduction.
The cost is extra process steps, so I specify it only where it solves a problem."
Quick check. Why is an open (unfilled) via placed in a BGA pad a problem?
When to use plugged vias. The question: When would I want plugged vias?
A plugged via has its hole blocked with soldermask ink (the board's thin colored coating) or epoxy resin, so nothing can pass through.
It is not sanded flat and plated over, so its surface is not a good solder pad.
You use plugged vias to stop solder being sucked in or bridging between pads, to make a board airtight for vacuum test fixtures, and to avoid trapping chemicals.
For a via in a solder pad you need a filled and capped via instead.
Think of a pipe. Tenting is like stretching plastic wrap over the pipe's end. The pipe is still hollow, and the wrap can pop. Plugging is like pushing a cork into the pipe.
Nothing can pass and nothing can pop through, but the cork may stick up. Filling and capping is sanding the cork flush and covering it with a flat lid.
Only that is smooth enough to stand on.
A sketch of the IPC-4761 progression (simplified, one side shown). Types I and II leave the barrel hollow. Types III and IV block it.
Types V to VII fill it completely, and only VII ends with a copper cap that makes a flat solderable pad. Real cross-sections vary by fab.
Tenting: covering a via's opening with a film of soldermask, leaving the hole hollow. Plugging: blocking the hole with ink or epoxy.
Filled and capped: filled, sanded flat and plated over with copper. Solder wicking: solder being pulled into an open via.
Vacuum test fixture: a test jig that sucks the board against probes, so the board must be airtight. IPC-4761: the standard that names the types of via protection.
A vacuum fixture pulls on the board, so every open hole is a leak. A 0. 3 mm via has an opening of about 0. 07 mm².
A board with 2,000 open vias then has a total leak area of about 141 mm². That is small next to the board, but it can still defeat the vacuum, depending on the pump and gasket.
Plugging the vias seals them. That is the whole idea: a plug blocks the hole but does not make a flat pad.
"A plugged via has its barrel blocked with soldermask or epoxy, but it isn't ground flat or plated over like a filled via.
I use plugging to stop solder wicking and shorts near pads or on wave-soldered sides, to make the board airtight for vacuum test fixtures, and to avoid trapped chemicals or ingress.
It's not enough for via-in-pad, which needs filled and capped, and it costs more than tenting, so I use it only where tenting isn't robust enough."

Common via failure modes. The question: What are some common failure modes of vias?
Most vias fail from heat cycling. The board's resin, the plastic that holds it together, expands along its thickness much more than copper does.
Each time the board heats, the resin stretches the copper tube in the via, and after enough cycles it cracks.
That gives an intermittent open circuit, a break that comes and goes, which often shows up only when warm.
Other causes are manufacturing flaws, copper filaments growing between close vias, and too much current.
Bend a paper clip back and forth. It does not break the first time, but each bend leaves a little damage, and after enough bends it snaps.
The via's copper barrel is the paper clip, and each heating cycle is a bend. Bigger stretches break it in fewer cycles.
Strain grows slowly up to Tg and then steeply, because the resin's expansion rate jumps. A normal operating swing (25 to 125 degrees Celsius) imposes about 0.
4 %, but one lead-free reflow imposes about 2. 8 %, which is why assembly and rework consume part of the via's fatigue life before the product ships.
Values are typical; use your laminate's datasheet.
Barrel: the copper-plated wall of the via, a thin tube. Thermal cycling: repeated heating and cooling, from use or from soldering.
Expansion mismatch: resin grows faster with heat than copper, so they pull against each other. Fatigue: damage that builds up from repeated stretching until something breaks.
CAF: conductive anodic filament, a copper filament that grows inside the board between nearby vias in humid conditions, causing leakage.
Say the resin expands 60 millionths per °C along its thickness and copper expands 17. The difference is 43 millionths per °C.
Heat the board from 25 to 125 degrees Celsius, which is 100 degrees Celsius. The mismatch is 43 times 100 = 4,300 millionths, about 0. 43% stretch on the copper every cycle.
A lead-free soldering pass to 260 degrees Celsius is far worse, about 2. 8%, because the resin softens and expands several times faster at high temperature.
A cracked via can still pass a room-temperature continuity test. That is the whole idea: heat cycling slowly fatigues the barrel.
"The main via failures are barrel and corner cracks from Z-axis thermal expansion mismatch between FR-4 and copper, which show up as intermittent opens after thermal cycling or lead-free reflow.

Next are plating voids and thin plating in high-aspect-ratio holes, interconnect separation between barrel and inner pad, annular-ring breakout, and CAF, copper migration along glass fibres between close vias in humidity.
At assembly, open vias in pads wick solder, and too much current in too few vias overheats them.
I prevent these with low aspect ratio, enough plating, spacing, high-Tg material and via arrays."

When to avoid using vias. The question: When do I not want to use vias?
A via is not a free wire. Avoid or limit vias where their cost outweighs the routing convenience.
Fast edges and radio-frequency paths suffer because a via's inductance reflects part of the signal.
Solder pads suffer because an open via sucks solder away, and a via is a poor sole path for high current.
When you must use one, add a ground via beside it and keep layer changes few.
Think of a speed bump on a road. A slow cyclist hardly notices it. A speeding car gets thrown off, and the faster the car, the worse the jolt.
A via is a speed bump for signals, and what counts is how fast the signal's edge is, not how often it repeats.
A simple T model of a via. The two half-inductances are the barrel, and the capacitor is the pad-to-plane capacitance.
The characteristic impedance square root of L over C about 53 ohms is close to 50 ohms, so the via is not a bad match by itself; the trouble comes from edges fast enough to see the lumped elements.
Inductance: how strongly a via or wire resists fast changes in current. Rise time: how quickly a signal edge goes from low to high. Shorter means faster.
Reflection: part of a signal bounces back from a change in the path, such as a via. Stub: the unused part of a via barrel, which can resonate.
Return path: the route the signal's current takes back to the source. A layer change can disrupt it.
A typical via has about 1. 3 nanohenries of inductance, which is a billionth of a henry.
On a typical 50 ohms signal line, the worst-case reflection is roughly L over (2 Z 0 t r) . With a 1 nanoseconds edge (a billionth of a second) that is 1.
3 nanohenries / (2 times 50 ohms times 1 nanoseconds) = about 1. 3% reflected. With a 100 picoseconds edge the same via reflects about 13%.
The via did not change, but the faster edge sees it as a big bump. This is an upper-bound estimate.
That is the whole idea: judge a via by the signal's edge speed and by what else it affects.
"I avoid vias where their cost outweighs their convenience. On fast edges, a 1.

3 nanohenries via on a 50 ohm line can reflect up to roughly 13 percent of a 100 picosecond edge, so for multi-gigabit lanes, clocks and RF I stay on one layer or minimise layer changes, add ground vias, and remove stubs.
I also avoid open vias in solder pads, vias near board edges, single vias for power, and via fields that perforate planes."
Quick check. Which type of net is most sensitive to a via's parasitic inductance?
Vias on surface-mount pads. The question: Can you put a via on a surface-mount pad?
Can you put a via in a surface-mount solder pad? Yes, but you have to handle it. An open via pulls molten solder down the barrel during soldering.
That starves the joint and can leave bubbles. It is fine if the via is filled and capped, or is a tiny laser-drilled microvia. It is also normal on a chip's thermal pad.
Imagine gluing two boards together when one has a hole drilled in the middle of the glued area. The glue runs through the hole, and the joint is left dry.
Melted solder acts the same way: it flows into narrow channels. Filling and capping the hole fixes it, and so does moving the via beside the pad.
A typical exposed-pad pattern.
Paste (grey) is windowed into small areas between the vias so the part sits on controlled solder volume and the vias don't drain it (the real stencil would use larger windows where rules allow).
The vias carry heat down to a plane.
Via-in-pad: a via placed directly inside a solder pad. Dogbone: a short trace that connects a pad to a via set beside it.
Thermal pad: the exposed metal pad under a chip, used to carry heat into the board. Fill and cap: fill the barrel, sand it flat, and plate copper over it.
An open 0. 3 mm via through a 1. 6 mm board holds about 0. 079 mm³, and one 0. 3 mm solder ball holds about 0. 014 mm³.
So one open via can drain about five balls' worth of solder. On a chip's thermal pad, vias are still wanted to carry heat. Nine hollow 0.
3 mm vias together pass heat at about 21 degrees Celsius per watt. For a 2 watts chip that is about 43 degrees Celsius of temperature rise across them.
Sixteen vias give about 24 degrees Celsius. To keep solder from draining, use small vias, close them from the back, and print the solder paste in small patches.
That is the whole idea: allowed, but only with a plan for the solder.
"Yes, but not open. An open via in a pad wicks solder away and gives starved joints and voids.
So I either fill and cap it, use laser microvias, or move it off the pad with a short dogbone and tent it.
The normal exception is the thermal pad of a QFN or power part, where I use an array of small vias, tented on the back, with a windowed paste pattern."
Quick check. What is the main risk of an open via in a BGA pad?
Problems from too many vias. The question: What happens if you have too many vias?
Every via takes space and has a cost. A through via needs a pad on every layer and punches a clearance hole through every plane it passes. A few vias are fine.
Too many remove routing room, cut the planes into thin strips that force return currents to detour, raise the board factory's (fab's) price, and add places that can fail.
How many is too many depends on the board's density.
Punch a few holes in a paper towel and it still works as a sheet. Punch hundreds and the paper between the holes is just thin strips.
It tears easily, and anything that needs to cross it has to go around. A plane full of via holes is like that towel. It also takes the drilling machine longer, which costs money.
Area lost scales with count and with the square of antipad size. Cutting antipads from 1. 2 to 0. 8 mm saves more plane than removing a third of the vias.
This is why smaller drills and tighter antipads matter on dense boards.
Via: a plated hole connecting layers. Plane: a solid copper layer, often ground or power. Antipad: the clearance hole cut in a plane around a via that does not connect to it.
It is bigger than the drilled hole. Return path: the route a signal's current takes back to its source, usually in the plane under the trace.
Yield: the share of boards that come out of manufacturing good.
Say a 100 mm times 100 mm board has 2,000 vias, so each plane has an area of 10,000 mm². With 0. 8 mm antipads, each removes about 0.
5 mm² of copper, so 2,000 remove about 1,000 mm². That is 10% of every plane. With 1. 2 mm antipads the loss is about 23%. The antipad, not the drill, removes the copper.
If vias sit 1. 0 mm apart with 0. 9 mm antipads, the copper left between them is only 0. 1 mm wide, a narrow neck.
That is the whole idea: vias cost area, plane quality, money and reliability.

"Too many vias eat routing space because each has a pad on every layer, perforate the planes so antipads merge and break return paths, add inductive bumps on signals, raise drill cost and yield loss, and add more barrels that can fail.
I keep counts down, stagger vias so antipads don't line up, and use blind or microvias when density demands it."
Quick check. What does a through via remove from every plane layer?
Too many vias in a power plane. The question: What happens if you have too many vias through a power plane?
A power plane is a sheet of copper that carries current to chips. Every via that passes through it without connecting still cuts a clearance hole in it.
If the holes get close together, the copper between them becomes narrow necks.
Current must squeeze through, which adds resistance, voltage drop and heat, and also raises inductance (opposition to fast current changes).
You avoid it by staggering vias and shrinking the holes.
Picture a wide road with a row of concrete pillars across it. If the pillars are far apart, traffic flows around them with little trouble.
If they are packed close together, all the cars must squeeze through the narrow gaps, and traffic backs up.
The current in a plane is the traffic, and the gaps between holes are the narrow lanes.
A row of antipads (white circles) forces current (grey flow lines) to squeeze through the narrow webs between them (red marks the web width W ).
Along the row the copper cross-section drops to (p-d a) over p , so the current density there rises by p over (p-d a) .
Power plane: a solid copper layer that delivers a supply voltage across the board. Antipad: the clearance hole in a plane around a via that does not connect to it.
Neck: the narrow strip of copper left between two nearby holes. Sheet resistance: the resistance of one square of copper of any size.
For standard 1 oz (35 µm thick) copper it is about 0. 49 milliohms. IR drop: the voltage lost as current flows through resistance, V equals I times R .
A neck that is 10 mm long and 0. 1 mm wide is 100 squares long. Its resistance is 100 times 0. 49 milliohms = 49 milliohms. Carrying 3 amps, it drops 3 times 0. 049 = 0.
147 volts, which is 147 millivolts. That is a big loss on a 1 volts supply. A neck 1 mm wide is only 10 squares, 4. 9 milliohms, or 15 millivolts.
This is a worst case with all the current in one channel; real via fields have many channels in parallel. That is the whole idea: narrower copper means more resistance and heat.
"Each via that doesn't connect to a power plane still cuts an antipad hole.

Too many and the copper between holes becomes narrow necks, so resistance, IR drop and current density rise, causing hot spots; the plane inductance rises and signals referencing it lose their return path.
I stagger vias, shrink antipads, keep wide copper bridges, and use heavier copper or more planes."

Swiss cheesing a plane. The question: What is "swiss cheesing" a plane?
Swiss cheesing is slang for a plane that has so many clearance holes around its vias (plated holes) that it looks like Swiss cheese.
It happens under chips with dense via fields, and it is worst when holes line up in rows.
The copper between holes becomes thin necks, so resistance and inductance (opposition to steady and to fast-changing current) go up.
A row of merged holes also acts as a slot, which makes signal return currents detour and increases crosstalk (noise leaking between traces) and radiation.
Think of the perforated line between postage stamps. A straight row of small holes makes a weak line that tears. That is a slot.
Scattered, offset holes would leave the paper in one piece. Aligned via holes make the same weak line for current.
Left: antipads spaced at their own diameter touch along each row and merge into slots.
Right: holes of the same size, spread wider and offset from row to row, leave continuous copper channels (this layout also has fewer vias per unit area, which is part of why it works).
Antipad: the clearance hole in a plane around a via that does not connect to it. Slot: a long gap in a plane, made when holes in a row merge.
Web: the copper strip left between two neighboring holes. It is the pitch minus the hole diameter.
Return current: the current flowing back to its source, usually in the plane under the signal trace. Stagger: offsetting rows of vias so the holes do not line up.
Say vias sit 1. 0 mm apart and each antipad is 0. 9 mm wide. The web between them is only 1. 0 - 0. 9 = 0. 1 mm. A row of those is almost a slot.
Staggering the rows at the same via density, about one via per mm², raises the nearest spacing to about 1. 07 mm, so the narrowest web grows only to about 0. 17 mm.
The real gain is that no straight slot remains. To widen the webs, shrink the antipads: 0. 7 mm antipads leave 0. 3 mm.
That is the whole idea: align and pack holes carelessly and you cut the plane into strips.
"Swiss cheesing is a plane so perforated by via antipads that it looks like Swiss cheese, typically under BGAs when via rows align.
The copper between holes becomes narrow necks, raising resistance and inductance and creating slots that break return paths, so crosstalk and EMI worsen.
I stagger vias, shrink antipads, leave copper bridges, and use fewer or blind vias."
