Ground probes and ground test points. The question: What are ground probes on a PCB? Why are they needed? When should they be used?
A ground probe point is a pad on the board connected to the ground plane, placed right next to a signal test point.
A scope (oscilloscope, which draws voltage against time) measures the voltage between its probe tip and its ground clip, so a fast signal is only measured well if that ground connection is short.
A nearby ground pad lets you use a very short ground path.
Imagine measuring how a ball bounces using a long, floppy measuring stick. If the stick itself swings, you measure the stick's wobble as well as the ball.
A long ground lead is that floppy stick: it wobbles, and it also picks up stray noise like an antenna. A short connection to the ground pad is a stiff ruler.
The probe's input capacitance C in is charged through the ground lead's inductance L gnd (orange).
A fast edge excites a series LC resonance, f₀ = 1/(2π√(LC)) about 130 megahertz for 150 nanohenries and 10 picofarads.
The scope displays V scope, the voltage across C in, so it shows this ring even though the circuit doesn't have it.
Ground pad: a pad tied straight to the ground plane through vias (small plated holes), for connecting the probe's return.
Return path: the route the signal's current takes back to ground, which forms a loop with the signal. Inductance: a wire's resistance to fast changes in current.
A longer wire has more. Ringing: a signal wobbling back and forth after a fast edge. Ground plane: a large copper layer used as the common reference.
A 15 cm clip lead has roughly 150 nanohenries of inductance.

Together with the probe's 10 picofarads of input capacitance (its small built-in charge storage), it rings at about 130 megahertz, so a fast edge shows overshoot (the signal swinging past its true level) that is not really on the board.
A short ground spring of about 10 nanohenries rings near 500 megahertz, much further from the signal's content. The loop is also smaller, so it picks up less noise.
That is the whole idea.
"A ground probe point is a pad tied to the ground plane through vias, placed right beside a signal test point so a scope's ground can attach with a very short loop.
It's needed because a probe measures tip minus ground, and a long ground lead adds inductance that rings with the probe capacitance and picks up noise.
I use them next to any fast or sensitive test point and power rail. In fixtures, ground probes serve the same role for the tester's reference."

What test points are and what they do. The question: What are test points? What are their use cases?
A test point is a small, labeled connection to a net on the board.
It is usually a pad, a loop of wire or a via (a small plated hole), placed there so a person or a machine can measure or drive that net.
Without test points you must probe the legs of parts, which is slow, risky and often impossible on modern small parts.
Think of the valve on a car tire. You do not cut into the tire to check the pressure. The valve is a deliberate access point, and anyone with a gauge can use it.
A test point is the same idea for a signal.
The analogy has one catch: a valve costs almost nothing, but a test point takes board space and adds a small load to the signal, so you place them where they matter.
One pad serves many customers over the product's life. The more customers a net has (power rails, resets, programming lines), the stronger the case for a test point.
Net: all the copper that is electrically one connection. Bring-up: the first power-on and debugging of a new board.
Bed-of-nails fixture: spring pins that touch many test points at once in factory testing. Ground reference: a nearby ground point; a test point is useless without one.
Stub: the short spur of copper that a test point adds to a signal.
A 1 mm round pad sitting 0. 1 mm above a ground plane adds about 0. 3 picofarads of capacitance, a tiny bit of charge storage that slows fast edges.
On a slow power supply line (a rail) that is nothing. On a signal running at multiple gigabits per second it can matter.
So power rails, ground, reset, clocks, programming lines and key analog nodes nearly always get test points, and the fastest nets get a tiny pad or none. That is the whole idea.
"A test point is a deliberate, labelled pad, loop or via on a net so something can measure or drive it.

Engineers use them during bring-up and debug to probe rails and signals, factories use them for in-circuit and functional test, programming and calibration, and technicians use them for diagnosis in the field.
They cost a little area and, on fast nets, some capacitance, so I place them on the nets where observability matters most."

Types of PCB test points. The question: What are different types of test points?
Test points come in a few common styles, and the right one depends on who will measure and how fast the signal is.

The main styles are a flat surface pad, a through-hole loop or post, an exposed via (a small plated hole), a header or connector, and a coaxial connector (a shielded plug, like a TV cable's) for radio signals.
Each trades space, ease of use and effect on the signal.
Think of the ways to grab something: a flat tab you tap with a tool, a hook you can clip onto, a hole you slip a probe into, or a proper plug.
A factory machine wants a flat tab it can land on from below. A bench engineer wants a hook for a measuring clip. A radio signal wants a plug that does not disturb it.
The analogy has one limit: here every choice also loads the signal a little.
From left to right, a flat SMD pad, a through-hole loop, an exposed via and an RF coax connector. Notice how much height and area each takes and which side of the board it needs.
SMD pad: a flat copper pad on the surface, about 1 mm across, left uncovered by the board's green protective coating (solder mask).
Through-hole loop or post: a wire loop or pin soldered into a hole, easy to clip onto. Via test point: an exposed via used as a pad, saving space.
Header: a row of pins for programming or debug. Bed-of-nails fixture: factory spring pins that land on pads.
One board has four needs. A factory fixture needs flat pads about 1 mm wide, spaced at least 1. 27 mm apart.
The power rail gets a through-hole loop, so an engineer can clip an oscilloscope probe on it. A crowded corner uses an exposed via, which must not be covered or filled.
A fast radio signal gets a tiny pad or a coaxial connector. That is the whole idea.

"The main styles are SMD pads, which are small and fixture-friendly; through-hole loops or posts, which are easy to clip a scope onto; exposed vias for tight boards; headers and connectors for programming and debug; and RF connectors like SMA or U.
FL for high-speed signals. I pick by who measures it, a fixture, an engineer or a technician, and by how fast and sensitive the net is."

Layout guidelines for test points. The question: What are layout guidelines for test points?
Test points work only if a probe can land on them reliably. So the layout has rules about pad size, spacing, side of the board, and distance from tall parts.
The rules come from the size of the spring-loaded probes and the small errors in lining the board up. The factory's own guideline always overrides typical numbers.
Think of marked parking spaces. Each space must be big enough for the car, spaced so doors open, and kept clear of pillars.
If the spaces are too small or too close, cars scrape and miss. A test pad is a parking space for a probe.
The fixture plate is like a low ceiling: a tall part next to the pad is a pillar that blocks it. Putting all spaces on one level, the bottom, keeps the garage simple.
Pads sit on a regular grid with spacing at least the probe's receptacle size; a keep-out strip separates them from tall parts so the fixture plate can lie flat.
Ground pads (green) are scattered among signal pads (orange).
Pad: a bare copper circle, about 1 mm across, left uncovered by the green protective coating (solder mask). Pitch: the center-to-center spacing between neighboring pads.
Keep-out: space around a pad or tall part where nothing else may sit. Tooling holes: holes that align the board to the fixture.
Stub: the short spur of copper joining a pad to its net (the copper connection it tests). Ground pad: a pad on the ground net near signal pads, for a return connection.
A typical rule set: pads about 1 mm wide, centers at least 1. 27 mm apart, so the gap between neighboring pads is at least 0. 27 mm.
Keep about 1 mm away from small parts, more from tall ones, and about 3 mm from the board edge. Put every pad on the bottom and add two tooling holes at asymmetric spots.
Connect each pad straight onto its net with no stub. That is the whole idea.
"Make each test point a bare, flat pad of about a millimetre or more, on one side of the board, on a grid with at least about 1.
27 mm spacing, clear of tall parts and the edge, with tooling holes for alignment.
Connect it in-line to the net with minimal stub, put ground pads nearby, label it on the silkscreen, and check against the factory's DFT rules.
On fast nets, I keep the stub tiny or skip the pad."

When to use and skip test points. The question: When should/shouldn't you use them?
A test point earns its place only if what it tells you is worth what it costs. You use one where a fault would show up and you cannot see it any other way.
You skip or adapt it where it would harm the signal, create a safety problem, or duplicate access you already have. The decision is made net by net.
Think of putting inspection hatches in a building. You want one near the main water valve and the electrical panel, where problems start and where plumbers need access.
You would not cut a hatch where a window already shows the pipe, or in a spot where the hatch would weaken the wall.
A test point works like that: it gives a view, but it also takes space and may disturb the signal.
A per-net decision flow. Most nets end at "standard pad"; the interesting engineering is in the special-case branch.
Net: all the copper that forms one electrical connection. Power rail: a net that carries a supply voltage.
Boundary scan: using chips' own pin controls to check connections you cannot probe. Stub: a short spur of copper from the signal to the pad.
Reflection: part of a fast signal bouncing back because of a bump in the line.
A test pad adds about 0. 5 picofarads with its stub.
On a slow power rail this does nothing, so power rails, ground, resets, clocks, programming lines and key analog points all get test points.
On a fast signal line (a standard 50 ohms one) whose edge, the time to switch from low to high, is 100 picoseconds, a tenth of a nanosecond, the same 0.
5 picofarads reflects about 12. 5 % of the signal. So fast nets get a special in-line pad, a shielded coaxial connector, or no pad at all. That is the whole idea.
"I add test points where the information is worth the cost: rails, ground, resets, power-good, programming lines, slow buses and key analog nodes.
I skip or modify them on high-speed, RF, high-impedance and oscillator nets, where the pad adds capacitance and a stub, and on nets I can already see through a connector, boundary scan or self-test.
High-voltage nets need guarded points. I decide per net by value, user, alternatives and cost."

Test points on high-speed or sensitive signals. The question: Should you use test points on high-speed or sensitive signals? Why?
On the fastest and most sensitive signals, a test point is not free.
The pad adds a little capacitance (stored charge that blunts sharp changes) and a stub, and these disturb the signal you want to measure.
So for these signals you use a special kind of point, such as an in-line pad or a coaxial connector, or you use a built-in self-test instead of a pad.
Picture a fast channel of water with a small side basin cut into its bank. A smooth, slow flow barely notices the basin.
A sharp, rushing wave slaps into it, and part of the wave bounces back up the channel. A stub on a fast net is that basin. The faster the edge, the more the pad matters.
One caveat: a long stub also rings like a struck bell at certain frequencies (it resonates), which adds extra harm.
The line (50 ohms source, line, 50 ohms termination) with a test pad tapped on. Without R iso the 1 picofarads pad hangs straight on the line and reflects about 24.
5% at 100 picoseconds. With a 500 ohms resistor at the tap, the initial reflection is about minus 4. 8%, decaying with τ about (R iso + Z0/2)·C about 0.
5 nanoseconds, but the pad now sees a low-pass.
Edge: the fast rise or fall of a signal; its rise time is how quickly it changes. Stub: a short dead-end spur of copper joining the pad to the signal.
Reflection: part of the edge bouncing back from a bump in the line. In-line pad: a pad that the trace itself runs through, so there is no stub.
Built-in self-test (BIST): the chip checking its own link, so no probe is needed.
A pad with its stub adds about 0. 5 picofarads to a typical 50 ohms signal line. With a 100 picoseconds edge, about 12. 5 % of the step reflects. At 1 picofarads it is about 24.
5 %. A 10 mm open stub also resonates near 3. 75 gigahertz, and a 100 picoseconds edge carries frequencies up to about 3. 5 gigahertz. So the pad would visibly distort the signal.
The fix is an in-line pad, a tiny stub, or measuring at the receiver. That is the whole idea.
"I avoid or special-case them on fast and sensitive nets.
A pad plus stub adds roughly half a picofarad that reflects about 12% on a 50 ohm line at 100 picoseconds edges, and the stub can resonate and close an eye.
On sensitive analog nodes, pads and probes add loading, leakage and pickup.
So I use in-line pads, tiny stubs with an isolation resistor, coax footprints, buffered monitors or built-in eye scan and measure at the receiver."

Who and what uses test points. The question: Who/what uses test points?
Many different users rely on test points, both people and machines. Design engineers use them to debug. Factory fixtures use them to check boards.
Programming stations use them to load firmware. Field technicians use them for repairs. Each user needs something different, so you design the points with the user in mind.
Think of a public tap on a water main. A plumber, a city inspector and a meter reader may all use it, but each uses a different fitting.
A test point is the same: one connection, several users. A machine wants a flat, precise spot at a fixed spacing. A technician wants a labeled loop to clip onto.
A programmer wants a standard plug. Satisfying all of them takes a bit of planning.
The same copper pad is used at every stage. Early users are people with instruments; middle users are machines; late users go back to people. The design must work for all.
Bring-up: the first power-on and debugging of a new board. Bed-of-nails fixture: factory spring pins that land on pads.
Programming station: a station that loads firmware and a serial number. Calibration: injecting a known value and storing a correction.
Boundary scan (JTAG): a standard test port that lets a tool check connections between chips. Field technician: a person who repairs products after they have shipped.
Take the 3. 3 volts supply rail of one board. A design engineer clips an oscilloscope probe onto a loop on the top. The factory fixture lands on a flat bottom pad.
A field technician measures it with a meter at a labeled point. A programming station uses a standard debug header (a small plug) to load firmware.
The same net serves four users, each with a different fitting. That is the whole idea.
"Engineers during bring-up and validation use them with scopes and meters.
In production, in-circuit and flying-probe testers, functional test stations, programmers and calibration stations contact them, driven by test software that logs by serial number.
Boundary-scan controllers use the JTAG port. Afterwards, field technicians and failure-analysis engineers use them.
Each user needs something different, like fixture pads, clip loops or a programming header."

Prioritizing test points when space is short. The question: If you're short on board space, how do you prioritize which signals should have test points?
Space on a board is limited, so you cannot give every net a test point.
You rank the nets by how much each point is worth compared with what it costs, and you give pads to the highest-ranked ones first.
For the nets you skip, you write down how they are covered another way and what risk remains.
Think of packing a small suitcase for a trip. You pack the passport, phone and medicine first, because the trip fails without them. Then comfort items, and last the nice-to-haves.
If space runs out, you leave the extras at home, and you plan what you will do without them.
Choosing test points works the same way: essentials first, extras only if there is room.
The prioritisation flow. Mandatory items are removed from the competition first, then alternatives are subtracted, and only the leftover candidates are scored.
Net: all the copper that forms one electrical connection. Power rail: a net that carries a supply voltage.
Fixture pin: each test point on a factory fixture needs its own spring pin, which adds cost.
Boundary scan and built-in self-test: ways for chips to test connections without a pad. Fallback: another way the fault would still be caught if a net gets no pad.
Score each net from 1 to 5 for likelihood of a fault (L), severity (S) and unique information (I), then divide by cost (C). Score = L x S x I / C. The 3.
3 volts supply rail scores 5 x 5 x 5 / 1 = 125, so it gets a pad. A crystal, the part that sets a chip's clock, scores 2 x 1 x 1 / 5 = 0.
4, so it gets none, because a probe can stop it from running. Programming lines get pads anyway, since the factory needs them. That is the whole idea.
"I'd rank nets by value over cost. Value is fault likelihood times severity times how much information the pad gives that nothing else does.
Cost is area, signal-integrity impact and a fixture pin. That puts ground, main rails, reset, power-good and programming at the top, then clocks, console and key analog nodes.
I'd make space by sharing connector pins, using boundary scan or firmware readback, and bottom-side pad fields, and I'd review the list with the factory."

Detecting, finding and root-causing a PCB short. The question: If there's a short on the PCB, how can it be detected, found, and root caused?
A short is an unwanted low-resistance connection, such as between a supply and ground. Handling one has three steps: detect it, find where it is, and work out why it happened.
The whole time you limit the current, so the fault shows itself without burning anything.
Imagine a garden hose with a hidden leak. Turn the water on gently and you can follow the wet trail. Turn it on at full blast and you flood the garden.
A current-limited supply is the gentle flow.
The current takes the easiest route to the short, so the voltage along the copper is lowest near the fault, like water pressure that drops toward the leak.
Follow the drop to the spot.
A current source pushes 1 amps along a trace into a short (red). Each segment drops I·R, so the voltage falls toward the short.
Probing P1, P2 and onward with a millivolt meter shows the gradient and points at the fault. The short itself dissipates I²R = 20 milliwatts here.
Short: a connection with very low resistance that should not exist. Current limit: a supply setting that caps how much current can flow.
Milliohm: a thousandth of an ohm; shorts often read this low. Thermal camera: a camera that shows hot spots, where a short is heating up.
Bisecting: splitting the shorted connection into halves, by lifting links or parts, to see which half has the fault.
Set the bench supply to the board's normal supply voltage with a 1 amps current limit.
If the board has a 50 milliohms short, the supply hits its limit and the voltage sags to about 1 amps x 50 milliohms = 50 millivolts. Now follow the current.
A square patch of standard board copper (35 µm thick, called 1 oz), of any size, has about 0. 49 milliohms end to end. Across 5 such squares at 1 amps, the drop is about 2.
5 millivolts, which a sensitive meter can read. You step toward lower voltage until you reach the fault. That is the whole idea.
"I power from a current-limited supply or check resistance to ground to detect it.

To find it, inspect under magnification, then use physics: thermal camera or freeze spray for the hot spot, or force a known current and map the voltage drop along the copper, since copper is about half a milliohm per square.
I bisect the net by lifting links or removing parts.
For root cause I use microscope, X-ray or cross-section, ask whether it's a part, assembly or fab defect, and fix it at the source."

Measuring signals on a PCB. The question: How do you measure signals on a PCB? What are some considerations?
Measuring a signal on a board means choosing the right instrument and setting it up so it does not mislead you. A meter suits steady (DC) voltages.
A scope shows how a signal changes over time. A logic analyzer reads many digital lines.
The instrument and probe themselves can change what you see, through limited speed, loading and the ground connection.
Think of photographing a fast-moving ball. If the camera is slow, the ball is a smear, and you cannot tell its real shape.
A scope that is too slow smears a fast edge (a quick jump in voltage) in the same way. Also, if you hold the camera with a shaky, floppy strap, the shake shows up in the photo.
A long ground lead on a probe is that floppy strap, and it adds its own wobble.
Every block shapes the waveform. Loading happens at the tip, ringing in the ground return, bandwidth smoothing in the front end, and aliasing in the ADC.
Oscilloscope: an instrument that draws a signal's voltage against time. Bandwidth: how fast a signal the instrument can follow; higher is faster.
Rise time: how long a signal takes to go from low to high.
Probe loading: the probe itself drawing a little current or adding capacitance (stored charge that slows edges) at the point you measure.
Ground lead: the wire that connects the probe's return to the board's ground.
A scope's rise time is about 0. 35 divided by its bandwidth. A 200 megahertz scope has a rise time of about 0. 35 / 200 megahertz = 1. 75 nanoseconds.
If you measure a true 1 nanoseconds edge, the readings combine like the sides of a right triangle: the square root of (1 squared + 1. 75 squared) is about 2. 0 nanoseconds.
The scope makes the edge look twice as slow. A 1 gigahertz scope would show about 1. 06 nanoseconds. That is the whole idea.
"I pick the instrument by the quantity, DMM for DC, scope for dynamic signals, logic analyser for buses, then make sure the measurement doesn't lie.
That means scope bandwidth well above the signal's knee frequency (0.
35 over rise time), a probe whose resistance and capacitance don't load the node, and a short ground connection, because a long ground lead rings and picks up noise.
I measure at the receiver, using test points with nearby grounds, and sanity-check surprising results by changing the setup."
Quick check. Why is a 10 times passive probe preferred over 1 times for fast signals?
Measuring signals through test points. The question: How can test points be used to measure signals?
Measuring through test points means contacting the pads you placed for the purpose, along with a nearby ground pad.
You choose the signal, the instrument and the return connection first, then set up the instrument.
The same pads let you check voltage, ripple, timing, current and bus traffic, and even inject a signal.
Measuring at a prepared point is quicker and safer than poking at part legs.
Think of plugging a gauge into the service port on a machine, rather than cutting into a pipe. The port is made for the gauge, and it has a known reference.
A test point is the port, and its nearby ground pad is the reference.
Without the reference, the reading is meaningless, because a voltage is always a difference between two points.
The gauge picture has one gap: a careless probe can also short two close pads.
A repeatable workflow. The "plausible?" gate is where artifacts get caught: if the result changes when you change the probe or ground, it wasn't the signal.
Test point: a pad you can probe to reach a signal. Ground pad: a pad connected to ground where the probe's return connects. Ripple: the small leftover wiggle on a supply voltage.
Shunt: a small, known resistor that you measure the voltage across to find current. Injection: driving a test signal into a net through a test point.
Check a supply line (a rail) first: black meter lead on the ground pad, red on the rail pad. A 3. 3 volts rail with a 3 % tolerance should read between about 3. 20 volts and 3.
40 volts. To find the current, measure across the pads on a 10 milliohms shunt.
Reading 10 millivolts means 10 millivolts / 10 milliohms = 1 amps, and the shunt wastes 1 amps x 10 millivolts = 10 milliwatts. That is the whole idea.

"I connect the instrument's return to the ground pad next to the test point and measure with the right tool: a DMM for DC rails, a scope with tip-and-barrel and a bandwidth limit for ripple, several scope channels for sequencing, a logic analyser for buses, and a millivolt reading across a shunt's pads for current.
I can also use test points to force or inject signals. I watch for probe loading and slips, and sanity-check by changing the ground."
Quick check. For ripple on a rail, which scope setup is standard?
The ground loop in a measurement. The question: When measuring a signal, what is the ground loop?
When you measure with an oscilloscope (scope) probe, you connect two things: the tip to the signal and the ground lead to a ground point.
Together with the board's own return copper, these form a closed loop. That loop is part of the measurement.
It can ring after a fast edge and pick up noise, so what you see may not be what is really on the board.
Imagine holding a hula hoop up in the rain. The bigger the hoop, the more rain it catches.
A measuring loop catches stray magnetic fields from nearby switching wires in the same way, and bigger loops catch more. Now picture the loop as a long, springy rope.
A sudden jolt keeps it swinging for a while. A long ground lead behaves like that rope, ringing after each fast edge.
The probe presents its input capacitance C in to the node through the ground lead's inductance L lead (orange), and the scope displays V scope, the voltage across C in.
The loop is: source, tip, C in, L lead, board return and back to the source. A fast edge excites the LC resonance.
Loop: a closed path that current flows around, here made by the tip, the ground lead and the board return.
Return path: the route a signal's current takes back to where it started. Inductance: a wire's resistance to fast changes in current. A longer wire has more.
Probe capacitance: the probe tip's small ability to store charge, around 10 picofarads (picofarads) for a typical probe.
Ringing: a signal wobbling back and forth after a fast edge.
A 15 cm clip lead has roughly 150 nanohenries.
With 10 picofarads of probe capacitance, the loop rings at about 130 megahertz, and a fast edge shows overshoot (the signal swinging past its true level) that is not on the board.
A short spring tip of roughly 10 nanohenries rings near 500 megahertz, far above most of the signal.
The phrase has a second meaning: a mains ground loop, which adds 50 or 60 hertz hum when the scope and the board both connect to earth through the wall-socket wiring.
That is the whole idea.
"The ground loop is the closed loop made by the probe tip, the signal path, the ground lead and the board's return path.
It has inductance, about 1 nanohenries per mm, which rings with the probe's capacitance, and it has area, which picks up magnetic fields.
It's part of the measurement, not just the board. Separately, 'ground loop' can mean multiple earth connections that carry current and inject mains hum."
Quick check. In probing, what is 'the ground loop'?
Why the ground loop should be small. The question: Why should your ground loop be as small as possible?
A small measurement loop gives a truer picture. The loop is part of the circuit you are measuring, and its size sets how much it distorts the result.
A larger loop rings more after a fast edge, picks up more stray magnetic noise, and shares more copper with other currents. All three errors shrink when the loop shrinks.
Think of holding a hula hoop in the rain. A big hoop catches far more rain than a small ring. Now imagine the rain is the changing magnetic field around a nearby switching wire.
A big measurement loop catches a lot of it, and that shows up as a voltage on your screen.
One limit: real magnetic fields are not even, so the numbers below are rough estimates, but the trend holds.
Overshoot stays under about 2% for lead inductance up to about 10 nanohenries (ζ about 0. 8).
By 15 nanohenries it is about 7%, and it climbs steeply as the lead grows (30% at 50 nanohenries, 52% at 150 nanohenries). The curve is the probe artifact, not the circuit's.
Drag the probe capacitance down to 5 picofarads: the whole curve shifts to the left, so even a 10 nanohenries lead overshoots by about 12%.
Loop area: the area enclosed by the measurement path; more area catches more magnetic field. Inductance: a wire's resistance to fast changes in current; it grows with loop size.
Ringing: the wobble after a fast edge, caused by inductance and the probe's small charge storage (capacitance) together. Rise time: how long an edge takes to go from low to high.
Pickup: noise voltage induced in the loop by nearby changing currents.
Suppose a nearby wire 5 cm away carries 100 milliamps that switches in 5 nanoseconds.
A loop of 10 cm by 2 cm, which is 2,000 mm², would pick up about 160 millivolts in a rough estimate. A loop of 5 mm by 5 mm, which is 25 mm², would pick up about 2 millivolts.
The area ratio is 80, so the pickup drops by 80 times. You would think you had a noise problem with the big loop and none with the small one. That is the whole idea.
"Because the loop is part of the measurement.
Its inductance, about 1 nanohenries per mm, rings with the probe's capacitance (130 megahertz for a 150 nanohenries clip lead) and distorts fast edges.
Its area picks up magnetic fields in proportion to area, so a loop 80 times bigger sees 80 times more noise from a nearby switch node.
A longer return also shares copper with other currents and radiates and receives more. Small loop, accurate waveform."
Quick check. Which statement best explains why a small probe ground loop is preferred?
Reducing the measurement ground loop. The question: How can you reduce your ground loop?
To reduce the ground loop in a measurement, you make it shorter and smaller.
Remove the long clip lead and use a spring ground tip or the probe barrel touching a ground pad right next to the signal. Better probes and sockets help further.
Then check that the picture does not change when you shorten the loop more.
Think of shortening a leash. A long, loose leash lets a dog wander and swing wildly with every tug. A short leash keeps it tight. The probe's ground lead is the leash.
Pulling it tight to the ground pad stops the wild swinging, which is ringing, and also shrinks the area of the loop, which catches stray noise the way a hoop catches rain.
The point is the same each time: keep the return path short and close to the signal.
Four attack routes. The first two are the same action (a short, close ground connection) viewed in two ways: lower inductance and less area.
Spring ground tip: a short spring that contacts ground right beside the probe tip. Tip-and-barrel: touching the probe's metal barrel against ground instead of using a lead.
Ground pad: a pad connected to ground, placed next to a test point.
Differential probe: a probe that measures the difference between two points without using the scope's ground lead.
Noise-floor check: shorting the tip to ground to see how much noise the setup itself adds.
Replace a 150 nanohenries clip lead with a 10 nanohenries spring tip.
With 10 picofarads of probe capacitance and a 50 ohms source, the ringing moves from about 130 megahertz to about 500 megahertz.
The overshoot (the signal swinging past its true level) falls from about 52 % to about 2 %. Then do the check: short the tip to ground at the pad and look at the noise.
Shorten the loop again and see whether the waveform changes. When it stops changing, the loop is small enough. That is the whole idea.

"I'd shrink the loop in order of effectiveness: remove the long clip and use a spring ground tip or tip-and-barrel; ground at the nearest quiet ground pad, which I design in next to test points with vias to the plane; use soldered leads, SMA connectors or low-capacitance active probes for fast signals; and use differential or isolated probes for floating nodes.
For mains loops, one earth point or isolation, never lifting the safety earth. Then verify with a shorted-tip noise-floor check."
Quick check. Which is the single most effective quick fix for a ringing, noisy probe measurement of a fast edge?
What PCB rework is. The question: What is PCB rework?
PCB rework means going back to a board that is already built and changing it. You take a part off, put a new one on, or fix a bad connection.
It exists because boards sometimes come out wrong, and fixing one is often cheaper than scrapping it.
The catch is that rework melts the solder again, so the board gets another dose of heat it has to survive.
Imagine fixing one brick in a wall whose mortar has already set.
You have to soften the mortar around that brick without loosening its neighbors, and each repair leaves the wall a little weaker. A cheap wall you would just rebuild.
A board works the same way, except that solder really can be melted again, which is what makes the fix possible at all.
Rework is a loop with an economic gate at the start (is it worth it?) and an inspection gate at the end.
A failed inspection sends you back around, adding another thermal cycle to the board.
Solder: a metal that melts at a fairly low temperature and joins a part to the board. Pad: the small copper patch on the board that a part is soldered to.
Flux: a paste that cleans the metal so melted solder sticks to it. Preheat: warming the whole board gently first, so it is not shocked by local heat.
Rework, repair, modification: rework restores the original design, repair fixes damage, and modification deliberately changes the design.
A built board has a resistor of the wrong value. You put flux on it, preheat the board, and heat the part until its solder melts.
Common lead-free solder melts at about 217 degrees Celsius. You lift the part off, clean the pads, solder on the right resistor, and check it.
That second dose of heat is the cost of the fix. That is the whole idea.
"Rework is removing, replacing or modifying parts or connections on a board that's already been assembled.
Usually that's desoldering a bad component and soldering in a new one, or adding jumper wires for a design change.
It needs a controlled thermal profile, flux, preheat and ESD care, because every rework cycle stresses the pads and laminate.
It's a last resort that gets weighed against scrapping the board, and good layout makes it easier."
Quick check. Which statement best describes the difference between rework and modification?
Describing your rework experience. The question: Describe any rework experience you have.
The interviewer is asking, "Have you really fixed a circuit board, and what did you learn?" They are not checking a fact.
They want a short true story that shows you can find out what is wrong before touching anything, handle the repair carefully, and think about why the problem happened.
Even a small job makes a good story if you give real detail.
A good answer is a tiny detective story.
Something was broken, you looked for clues, you made the fix, you checked that it worked, and you worked out how to stop it happening again.
A weak answer skips the detective work and only says "I used a soldering iron." One honest slip-up in the story sounds more real than a story where nothing went wrong.
A rework story is a diagnosis story with a soldering step in the middle. Interviewers follow your reasoning along this chain; weak answers contain only the "Action" box.
Rework: removing, replacing or changing parts on a board that is already built. STAR: a story shape: Situation, Task, Action, Result.
Diagnosis: finding out which part or connection is the problem, usually by measuring, before you fix anything.
Root cause: the real reason the fault happened, not just the broken part you replaced. Verification: checking after the fix that the board really works.
Here is a skeleton to fill in with your own true details. "On my [project] , the [symptom] showed up. I measured [what you measured] and narrowed it to [the part] .
I replaced it using [your tools and method] . It did not go perfectly: [one honest slip and how you recovered] . I checked it by [how you verified] .
The root cause was [why it failed] , so I [what you changed so it will not recur] ." If your experience is small, say so. Never claim work you did not do. That is the whole idea.
"On my [project] board, a [part] failed, so I diagnosed it with a multimeter and thermal camera, then replaced it with a hot-air station: flux, preheat, low airflow, Kapton on the neighbours.
I lifted a pad on the first attempt, patched it with a wire, and learned to wait until every joint is liquid.
Afterwards I checked under the microscope, re-measured the rail, and fixed the footprint error that caused the failure."
Quick check. What is the main purpose of preheating the board before hot-air rework?
Types of rework on a PCB. The question: What sort of rework can be done on a PCB?
Rework comes in a few kinds, and each kind fits a different fault.
You can replace a part, add a wire to change a connection, change which parts are fitted, repair damaged copper, or clean up solder mess.
Think of fixing a road. Replacing a broken sign is swapping a part. Building a detour is adding a wire. Filling a pothole is repairing a lifted pad.
Sweeping up debris is cleaning off a solder bridge. A detour is fine for a slow footpath, but it adds extra distance, and on a fast highway that extra distance causes trouble.
A wire on a circuit is the same: harmless for slow signals, a problem for very fast ones.
Most bring-up fixes fall into one of five branches. The cheapest and safest branches (population changes) are the ones you can design in; the others need heat and skill.
Bodge wire (jumper): a thin wire added by hand to make a connection the board does not have.
Cut-and-jump: cutting a copper trace so a connection is removed, then adding a wire to connect somewhere else.
DNP (do not populate): a spot on the board left empty on purpose, so a part can be fitted later if needed. Inductance: how strongly a wire resists changes in current.
It only matters when the signal changes very fast. Lifted pad: a copper pad that has peeled off the board.
Suppose a reset signal was never connected to the chip that needs it. You solder a thin wire from the reset pad to the chip pin, and glue the wire down.
A 30 mm wire has about 30 nanohenries of inductance (a rough rule is 1 nanohenries per millimeter). At 1 megahertz that is only about 0.
19 ohms, and at 100 megahertz about 19 ohms. A reset line barely changes, so the wire is harmless. A 100 megahertz clock would be badly disturbed. That is the whole idea.

"I split rework into component replacement (through-hole, SMD, or BGA/QFN with a rework station), connection changes like cut-and-jump bodge wires, population changes like swapping values or fitting DNP parts, repairs of lifted pads or traces, and cleanup of bridges or coating.
Each has risks: wires add about a nanohenry per millimetre, so fine for slow signals and bad for fast ones, and every thermal cycle stresses the board."
Quick check. Which change is best done by swapping or populating a part rather than adding a wire?
Why PCB rework is needed. The question: Why may rework be needed?
Boards need rework for four reasons. Something went wrong when the board was built (a defect). The design itself had a mistake. A part was bad.
Or someone deliberately changed the design after boards were made. Knowing which one applies tells you what to fix, so the problem does not return.
Think of a long printed book. Even if the printer makes only one typo per 20,000 words, a whole book still ends up with a few.
A board is like that: each solder joint is one tiny chance to fail, and a board has hundreds or thousands of them.
The four causes match too: a printing slip (assembly defect), an author's mistake (design error), a bad batch of paper (component problem), and a revised edition (planned change).
Each cause points at a different part of the process. Treat the leaves as the fix; the rework itself is just a symptom.
Solder joint: one soldered connection between a part and the board. Defect: a joint or part that is not made correctly, such as two pins bridged by solder.
First-pass yield: the share of boards that work the first time with no rework. Root cause: the real reason a fault happens, as opposed to the symptom you repaired.
ECO (engineering change order): a formal design change made after boards exist. ppm: parts per million, so 50 ppm is 50 in every million.
Say a board has 1000 joints, and each has a 50 ppm chance of being bad. That is a chance of 0. 00005 per joint. Over the whole board, you expect 1000 times 0. 00005 = 0.
05 defects. About 95 boards in 100 come out clean, and about 5 in 100 need rework. Now suppose most of that rework is the same pad on the same part every time.
The fix is to correct that pad design, not to keep reworking. That is the whole idea.

"Rework is needed for four reasons: manufacturing defects like bridges, opens or tombstones, design errors like a wrong footprint or missing pull-up, component failures from ESD or bad lots, and changes like ECOs or obsolescence.
Even a tiny per-joint defect rate adds up: 1000 joints at 50 ppm gives about 5% of boards needing rework.
I try to find the root cause so we fix the process or the design, not just the board."
Quick check. A footprint error causes the same part to fail on every prototype board. Which category is this?
Designing a board for reworkability. The question: What can you do in your design to improve reworkability?
Designing for reworkability means laying out a board so that someone can later remove and replace a part without ruining the board.
In practice that means leaving room for the repair tool, letting heat reach the joint you want to melt, and building in options so a fix is a part swap instead of a wire.
Think of a house built to be repaired. There is open space around the water heater, an access panel in the wall, and labeled shutoff valves.
Boxed in behind drywall, the same heater still works, but fixing it means tearing things apart. A board is the same.
The dashed square is the area a rework nozzle (plus its airflow margin) occupies.
On the left, a tall capacitor and small passives sit inside it, so they would be heated, blown or shadowed. On the right the zone is clear and the same parts sit outside it.
Ask your assembler for nozzle sizes; the margin is typically a few millimetres around the part but is equipment dependent.
Keepout: an empty area left around a part so a tool can reach it. Nozzle: the tip of a hot-air tool that blows hot air onto a part to melt its solder.
Thermal relief: a pad joined to a big copper area through thin spokes, so less heat drains away.
DNP (do not populate): a footprint (the set of pads a part sits on) left empty on purpose so a part can be fitted later.
Zero-ohm link: a resistor of 0 ohms used as a jumper you can remove. BGA: a chip whose connections are small solder balls hidden underneath it.
Take a 15 mm BGA. Say the repair nozzle needs 3 mm of clear space on every side. The clear zone is then 15 + 3 + 3 = 21 mm across.
A tall capacitor 2 mm from the BGA sits inside that zone and would be heated or blocked, so you move it outside.
You also add an empty footprint for a second resistor, so changing a value later is a part swap, not a wire.
Heavy parts on the back side are another risk: melted solder may not hold them. That is the whole idea.

"I'd leave keepouts around BGAs and big parts so a nozzle can sit there, keep tall parts away, add thermal reliefs on plane-connected signal pins, and put alternate footprints and zero-ohm links where I expect changes.
I'd keep heavy parts off the bottom under rework areas because they can fall during reheat, avoid hiding parts under BGAs, add test points to diagnose faults, and mark pin 1 and polarity clearly."
Quick check. Why leave a keepout around a BGA?
Thermal relief pads and rework difficulty. The question: Often times many power components or ground components have thermal relief pads. How does this impact reworkability?
A pad that is joined solidly to a big copper plane is hard to desolder, because the plane carries the heat away as fast as your tool delivers it.
A thermal relief joins the pad to the plane through a few thin spokes, so less heat drains away and the solder melts more easily.
Thin spokes carry less current, so power pads often stay solid.
Imagine filling a bucket with a big hole in the side up to a marked line. Water level stands for temperature, and the marked line is the solder's melting point.
A big hole (a plane) means you must pour very fast. A thermal relief shrinks the hole. Preheating the board is like filling the bucket partway before you start.
Tool power flows into the joint node and out through two thermal resistances in series to the board temperature. The joint temperature rise is P times (R relief plus R spread) .
Removing the relief removes R relief (and shrinks the spread resistance because the pad touches the plane at a smaller radius), so the same power produces a smaller rise.
Copper plane: a large sheet of copper in the board, usually for power or ground. Thermal relief: a pad joined to a plane by thin spokes.
Melting point of solder: the temperature where it turns fully liquid, about 217 degrees Celsius for common lead-free solder.
Thermal resistance: how many degrees hotter the joint stays than the board for each watt of heat you push in, in K/W (a kelvin step equals a degree Celsius).
Preheat: warming the whole board first, so the tool has less temperature to add.
Say a solid pad has a thermal resistance of about 41. 4 K/W to the rest of the board. From 25 degrees Celsius you need 192 degrees more to reach 217 degrees Celsius.
That takes 192 ÷ 41. 4 about 4. 6 watts. Add a relief and the resistance rises to about 58 K/W, so you need only about 3. 3 watts.
Preheat to 120 degrees Celsius and the step is only 97 degrees, so the solid pad needs about 2. 3 watts. It is a rough model: trust the trends, not the exact watts.
That is the whole idea.

"Thermal reliefs make rework easier because a pad tied solidly to a plane sits on a heat sink; the plane carries away the heat from the iron or nozzle, so the joint struggles to reach solder liquidus.
Spokes limit that heat flow. But power and ground pads often need the low-resistance connection, so reliefs get omitted there and those joints become the hardest to rework.
I'd compensate with bottom preheat, a bigger tip or hot air, and flux."
Quick check. Why is a pad solidly connected to a plane harder to rework?
Eagle, Altium, KiCad, Allegro experience. The question: Do you have experience with Eagle/Altium/KiKad/Cadence Allegro?
The interviewer is asking which board-design programs you have really used, and whether you understand the steps every one of them shares.
Those steps are the same everywhere: draw the circuit, define the parts, lay out the board, check it, and send files to the factory.
A short, honest answer about one real board beats a long list of tool names.
It is like being asked which word processor you use. The real skill is writing; the programs differ mostly in menus and shortcuts.
A good answer names the program, says what you made with it, and admits which ones you have not touched. It also shows you could learn the team's program quickly.
The same loop exists in every tool.
The dashed arrow is the one that separates experienced designers: bring-up findings go back into the library and the checklists so the next board doesn't repeat the mistake.
ECAD: software for drawing circuits and designing circuit boards. Schematic: the circuit diagram, showing which parts connect to which.
Footprint: the pattern of copper pads on the board that a part is soldered onto. Layout: arranging the parts on the board and drawing the copper paths between them.
DRC (design rule check): an automatic check that the layout obeys the factory's limits, such as minimum spacing.
A similar check on the schematic is called ERC and catches things like unconnected pins. Gerber files: the standard files you send to the factory that makes the board.
Here is a skeleton to fill in with your own true details. "I used [tool] on [board] .
I made the footprints from the datasheets, drew the schematic and ran the checks, laid out the board with rules set to the factory's limits, and sent Gerber files.
When I first powered the board, I found [one mistake] , so I fixed [library or checklist] .
I have not used [other tools] , but the steps are the same, so I would learn the team's tool in a couple of weeks." Do not claim tools you have not used. That is the whole idea.
"I've used [tool] for [board] : library parts from datasheets, schematic with ERC, layout with design rules set to the fab's limits, DRC, then Gerbers, drill, BOM and pick-and-place.

I know the others conceptually: Eagle is simple and library-centric, Altium is integrated with strong rules and collaboration, KiCad is open source with Python scripting, and Allegro is the high-end constraint-driven tool.
The workflow is the same, so I'd ramp up on a new one in a couple of weeks."
Quick check. Which pair of tools in the question are most associated with open-source and with high-end constraint-driven design, respectively?
Describing your ECAD experience. The question: What experience do you have with ECAD software?
The interviewer wants to know how far you have taken a real board in design software, and whether you can explain the choices you made.
Name one project, describe a few decisions with reasons, say how you checked your work, and mention one mistake and what you changed afterward.
Think of giving a guided tour of one house you built. You say why the walls are where they are, how you checked that they stand, and which door you had to rehang.
A good answer in miniature is that tour: one board, three decisions, one check, one mistake.
Each rung builds on the one below. A strong intern answer usually owns rungs 1 to 5 on at least one board and has an opinion about 6.
Don't skip to the top: "constraint-driven DDR layout" without the lower rungs sounds hollow.
Footprint: the pattern of copper pads that a part is soldered onto. Stackup: the order and thickness of the copper and insulating layers inside the board.
Net class: a group of connections that share rules, such as how wide their copper paths (traces) must be.
DRC (design rule check): an automatic check of the layout against the factory's limits. BOM (bill of materials): the list of parts to buy, with part numbers.
Here is a skeleton with placeholders. "My project was [board and purpose] in [tool] . I made the footprints from datasheets and checked them against a 1:1 printout.
I chose a [number] -layer stackup because [reason, such as a ground layer under the signals] . I made the power traces wider, sized from the current they carry.
I ran the design rule check with the factory's limits, looked at the output files in a separate viewer, and had a classmate review the schematic.
When I first powered the board, [a real mistake] showed up, so I [fixed the board and the library] ."
Replace every bracket with something true, and delete any step you did not do. That is the whole idea.

"I've done [N] boards in [tool] , including [project] , end to end: libraries from datasheets, schematic with ERC, a four-layer stackup, net classes with trace widths sized from current, USB as a 90-ohm differential pair, DRC with the fab's rules, and Gerber, drill, BOM and pick-and-place.
At bring-up I found a footprint error, fixed the board with a bodge, and then fixed the library. I'm weaker on DDR and RF and want to learn them."
Quick check. Which statement best describes a footprint?
Scripting and automation in ECAD. The question: Do you have any scripting experience in ECAD?
Scripting means writing a small program that does repetitive board-design work for you, such as placing parts in a pattern or checking a parts list.
The interviewer wants to hear that you have automated something real and that you do it carefully.
If you have not, an honest answer plus a similar example (like a short Python program that reads a parts list) is fine.
Imagine drawing the twelve numbers around a clock face by hand. They would come out uneven.
A rule such as "put one number every 30 degrees around the circle" gives a perfect result every time, and the same rule handles sixty marks as easily as twelve.
A script is that rule, written so the computer applies it.
The first decision is whether the task is worth automating at all.
The second splits scripts into safe (read exported files) and risky (edit the live design), which determines how careful you must be.
Script: a short program that automates a task. API: the set of commands a design tool lets your code use to read and change the design.
BOM (bill of materials): the list of parts to buy. MPN (manufacturer part number): the maker's exact code for a part.
Export: a plain file (such as a CSV table) saved out of the tool. A script that only reads exports cannot damage your design.
Place 12 LEDs in a ring of radius 20 mm. Each LED goes 360° ÷ 12 = 30° further around the circle. The first sits at (20, 0) mm, the next at about (17. 3, 10) mm, and so on.
Neighbors end up about 10. 4 mm apart. A short loop does this exactly; by hand it is slow and uneven.
A safe second script reads the exported parts list and flags any line with no part number. In the interview, fill in your own version: "I wrote [script] in [tool] to [task] .
I ran it on a copy and checked the result with [DRC or a review] ." That is the whole idea.
"My scripting is [level] . I've done [e. g.
a KiCad Python script that places LEDs on a circle using x = cx + r cos θ, y = cy + r sin θ, and a BOM checker in Python that groups lines and flags missing part numbers] .
The other tools have hooks too: Altium scripting and API, Eagle ULPs, Allegro SKILL.
I'd run any editing script on a copy, check with DRC, and keep it in version control so releases are repeatable."
Quick check. Which kind of ECAD scripting is the safest to start with?
Design rule checks (DRC). The question: What are design rule checks (DRC)?

A design rule check, or DRC, is an automatic check that compares your board layout with a list of rules, such as the smallest gap between copper paths, the thinnest trace, and the smallest drill hole.
The rules come from what the factory can build and what your circuit needs. If the layout passes, it can be made. That does not prove the design is right.
Think of a spell checker. It underlines misspelled words, but it will happily accept a perfectly spelled sentence that says the wrong thing. DRC is the same.
It measures every gap and width quickly, and it never gets tired, but it cannot tell whether you wired the right pin to the right place.
DRC combines two rule sources (the fab's limits and your own electrical needs) with the layout.
A clean result is an input to release, not the conclusion; the right-hand box lists what DRC cannot cover.
Trace: a copper path on the board that carries a signal or power. Net: all the points that are wired together as one connection.
Clearance: the smallest allowed gap between copper of two different nets. Annular ring: the copper left around a drilled hole after the hole is made.
Fabricator: the factory that makes the bare board.
Say the fabricator can reliably make a 0. 1 mm gap and no smaller. You draw two traces from different nets only 0. 08 mm apart.
DRC flags them at once, because they might touch and connect two signals that must stay apart (a short). Now a hole. A pad 0. 6 mm wide with a 0. 3 mm drill has a ring of (0.
6 minus 0. 3) ÷ 2 = 0. 15 mm of copper around the hole. Drills wander a little and layers do not line up perfectly, so up to about 0. 1 mm can be lost, leaving as little as 0.
05 mm. So the factory's ring rule includes margin for this, and DRC flags any pad whose ring is smaller than the rule, telling you to enlarge it. That is the whole idea.

"DRC is an automated check of the PCB layout against rules: clearance between nets, minimum trace width, drill and annular ring, solder mask and silkscreen rules, board-edge distance and connectivity.
I set the rules from the fab's capability sheet plus my electrical needs, and run it after every routing session.
A clean DRC means it's manufacturable by those rules, not that it's correct, so I still need ERC, review and bring-up."

Common IC packages and trade-offs. The question: What are some common IC packages? What are their tradeoffs?
An IC (integrated circuit, or chip) package is the case around the chip. It protects the chip, connects its tiny contacts to pads on the board, and carries heat away.
Packages come in a few families (legs, flat pads, a grid of solder balls), and each trades off pin count, size, heat, and ease of soldering and inspection.
Think of parking cars. A package with legs around its edge is like parking along the curb: you can see every car, but only so many fit.
A ball grid is like a full parking lot: many more cars fit in the same area.
The catch is that cars in the middle are hidden from view and hard to get out, just as ball connections under a package are hard to inspect and repair.
A package decision usually starts with pin count and power, then asks about assembly capability.
Notice that prototype-friendliness can override density; many chips are offered in several packages for exactly that reason.
Package: the case around the chip, with the connections to the board. Pitch: the center-to-center spacing between neighboring pins or balls. Through-hole vs.
surface-mount: legs pushed through holes in the board, or contacts soldered flat onto pads on the surface.
QFN: a flat package with contacts on its underside edges and no legs sticking out. BGA: a package with a grid of solder balls underneath.
Exposed pad: a metal plate on the underside, soldered to the board to carry heat away.
Take a square body 10 mm on a side. Put pins around the edge at 0. 5 mm pitch. You get about 4 times 10 ÷ 0. 5 = 80 pins. Now fill the underside with balls at the same 0.
5 mm pitch. You get (10 ÷ 0. 5)² = 20 times 20 = 400 balls. The grid wins because its count grows with the area, while edge pins grow only with the perimeter.
Real parts have fewer. That is the whole idea.

"Packages fall into families: through-hole like DIP and TO-220, leaded SMD like SOIC and QFP, leadless like QFN with an exposed pad, area-array BGAs with balls under the package, and wafer-level or stacked packages for phones.
Moving along that list gives more pins per area, lower inductance and better thermals, but harder inspection, rework and PCB routing.
I choose by pin count, heat, speed and what my assembly process can handle, and use the hand-friendly option for prototypes."
Quick check. Which package type has solder joints hidden under the body and usually an exposed thermal pad?
Surface-mount vs through-hole. The question: What are the tradeoffs between surface-mount and through-hole packaging?
Through-hole parts have metal legs that go through holes in the board and are soldered on the far side.
Surface-mount parts sit flat on pads on the board's surface and are soldered there. Surface-mount parts are smaller and easy for machines to place.
Through-hole parts hold on much more strongly. Most boards use both.
Think of hanging things on a wall. Sticky tape is quick and works well for light things, and you can put tape on both sides of a thin panel.
A heavy mirror needs screws that go through the wall. Surface-mount is the tape and through-hole is the screw.
Tape is not weak in every way, though: for fast electrical signals the short, tidy connection is better.
In through-hole, the lead sits inside a plated barrel and the solder fills it, so the mechanical connection goes through the board.
In surface-mount only the small fillet between the pad and the terminal holds the part, so heavy or plugged parts are vulnerable.
SMD also leaves the other side and inner layers free for routing.
Lead: a metal leg on a part. Pad: a small flat copper patch on the board's surface that a part is soldered to.
Plated hole: a drilled hole lined with copper, which a through-hole lead is soldered into. Reflow: melting printed solder paste in an oven to solder surface-mount parts.
Inductance: how strongly a wire resists fast changes in current. Longer leads have more.
Consider a 100 nanofarads capacitor (a part that stores a little charge) used to steady a power supply. With long through-hole leads it adds about 10 nanohenries of inductance.
Mounted flat on pads it adds about 1 nanohenries. At 100 megahertz, 10 nanohenries acts like about 6. 3 ohms of opposition, and 1 nanohenries like about 0. 63 ohms.
The flat mount is ten times better at high speed, so supply-steadying capacitors are almost always surface-mount. Now a connector that people plug in a thousand times.
Its small solder joints on surface pads could crack or peel off, so connectors often keep through-hole pins. That is the whole idea.
"Surface-mount parts sit on pads and are placed by machine and reflowed, so they're small, cheap to assemble in volume, usable on both sides and have short leads and low inductance.

Through-hole parts go through plated holes and are wave or selectively soldered; they're bigger and costlier to assemble but mechanically strong and good for power, so connectors and heavy parts often stay through-hole.
Most boards are mixed. Prototypes favour through-hole for hand soldering."
Quick check. Which part is most likely to stay through-hole on a mostly SMD board?
Ball grid array packages and trade-offs. The question: What are ball grid array (BGA) packages? What are their tradeoffs?
A ball grid array, or BGA, is a chip package whose connections are small solder balls laid out in a grid on its underside, instead of legs around the edge.
The grid fits many connections into a small area and keeps each path short. The price is hidden joints and a board that needs careful design.
Picture a crowd standing in a grid on a floor, each person needing a path to the exit. The people at the edge walk out easily. People in the middle need gaps to squeeze through.
Pack them tighter and the gaps vanish. A BGA board is the same: every ball needs a path, and tighter spacing leaves less room.
A BGA is a die on a small multilayer substrate whose underside carries a grid of solder balls that mate with pads on the PCB.
The red bar marks the distance from the package centre: the farther a ball is, the more the thermal mismatch between substrate and board shears it, so corner balls are the weakest.
Pitch: the center-to-center spacing between neighboring balls. Reflow: heating the board so the balls and solder paste melt and form joints.
Escape routing: getting a copper path from each ball out to the edge of the grid or down to another board layer.
Via: a tiny plated hole that connects copper on different layers of the board. X-ray inspection: the way to check hidden joints, since nothing is visible from above.
Take a 10 mm square package with balls at 0. 5 mm pitch. The grid is 20 times 20, so it holds 400 balls. An edge-pin package of the same size and pitch holds only about 80 pins.
That is the density win. Now the routing. At 0. 8 mm pitch with pads half that size, the gap between pads is 0. 4 mm. A 0. 1 mm copper path (a trace) needs 0.
1 mm of clearance on each side, so 0. 3 mm total, and it fits. At 0. 5 mm pitch the gap is only 0. 25 mm, so it does not fit.
You then put a via inside the pad itself, which costs more. That is the whole idea.
"A BGA has solder balls in a grid under the package instead of leads at the edge.
It packs a lot of pins into a small area, has short, low-inductance connections, good heat flow into the board and self-aligns during reflow.

The costs are hidden joints that need X-ray, rework stations and reballing, tough escape routing that can force via-in-pad and more layers at fine pitch, and thermal-cycling fatigue, worst at the corner balls.
I use them when pin count or speed demands it and plan the board and assembly for them."
Quick check. What is the main reason a BGA fits more pins than a QFP of the same body size?
Die vs wafer vs package. The question: What is the difference between the die, wafer, and package?
A wafer is a thin round disc of silicon on which hundreds of copies of a circuit are built at the same time. Each copy, once cut out, is called a die.
A package is the case around a die: it protects the die and gives it connections you can solder to a board. They are the same silicon at three stages.
Think of baking cookies. The wafer is the whole sheet of dough. The dies are the individual cookies you cut from it. The package is the box each cookie goes in for shipping.
Cookies with a burnt spot get thrown away, and a bigger cookie is more likely to catch a burnt spot. Also, fewer big cookies fit on the sheet.
That is why chip cost depends so strongly on die size.
The wafer is the batch unit; the die is the functional unit; the package is the product unit.
Two test stages catch different faults: wafer sort stops bad dies from being packaged, final test catches assembly and packaging damage and bins parts by speed.
Wafer: the silicon disc, usually 300 mm across for modern chips. Die: one rectangular copy of the circuit, cut from the wafer. Package: the case and connections around the die.
Wafer sort: testing each die on the wafer before it is cut, so bad ones are not packaged. Yield: the share of dies that work.
A 300 mm wafer has an area of about 70,700 mm². Suppose each die is 100 mm². Dividing gives about 707, but dies at the curved edge do not fit, so you get about 640 whole dies.
Now make the die eight times bigger, 800 mm². Dividing gives about 88, and after edge losses about 65 dies. So an 8 times bigger die gives about 10 times fewer dies.
Add the fact that a bigger die is more likely to contain a flaw, and a big die costs far more than 8 times as much. That is the whole idea.
"A wafer is a thin disc of silicon, usually 300 millimetres, on which hundreds of identical circuits are fabricated at once. Each rectangular copy is a die.
The wafer is tested, cut into dies, and the good dies are mounted in packages, which connect the tiny die pads to board-scale balls or leads, protect the silicon, remove heat and make it solderable.
Dies per wafer is roughly wafer area over die area minus edge loss, so a bigger die costs disproportionately more."
Quick check. Which statement is correct?
Process node sizes and what 3nm means. The question: What are node sizes? What does "3nm process" refer to? Are transistors really that small?
A process node such as "3 nm" names a generation of chip manufacturing technology. Today the number is a marketing label. It is not the size of any part of a transistor.
A smaller number means a newer generation, which packs more transistors into the same area and generally uses power more efficiently.
Think of a "half-ton" pickup truck. The name once meant it carried about half a ton. Today it is just a size class.
A chip node name works the same way: it once matched a real length, and now it only says "this generation".
Unlike the truck name, a newer node does give a real gain, just not the one the number suggests.
If the names were literal linear dimensions, going from 28 nm to 3 nm would yield an 87 times density gain. An assumed 1. 7 times per generation gives 14 times .
The real gains from public foundry claims are somewhere in the lower curve's neighbourhood; the exact multiple is vendor-specific and not what the name implies. The 1.
7 times is an illustrative assumption, not a measurement.
Transistor: a tiny electronic switch. A modern chip has billions. Nanometer (nm): one billionth of a meter.
Process node: a named generation of chip manufacturing, such as "5 nm" or "3 nm". Transistor density: how many transistors fit in one square millimeter.
Pitch: the center-to-center spacing of repeated features, such as neighboring wires. Die: one chip's worth of silicon cut from a wafer.
If the names were literal lengths, shrinking from 5 nm to 3 nm would shrink each feature to 3/5 of its size. Area would shrink to (3/5)², so density would rise by (5/3)² about 2.
8 times . Real gains claimed by chip factories (foundries) per generation are closer to 1. 6 to 1. 8 times .
Real dimensions are also larger than the name: roughly 45 to 50 nm between neighboring transistors' gates (the part that switches it on and off), and about 20 to 30 nm between the tightest wires.
These are estimates. Some thin layers inside a transistor really are only a few nanometers thick, but the spacings that set density are ten times larger. That is the whole idea.
"A node name like 3 nm used to mean a real feature size, such as gate length or half-pitch, but since roughly the 2000 seconds it's a marketing label for a generation.

Real dimensions on a '3 nm' process are tens of nanometres, a contacted gate pitch around 45 to 50 nm and metal pitch about 20 to 30 nm, though a few features like fin or sheet thickness are a few nanometres.
Density gains per node are about 1. 6 to 1. 8 times , not the 2. 8 times the name would imply. Transistors are 3D now: FinFETs and gate-all-around, patterned with EUV."
