Series vs parallel termination tradeoffs. The question: What is the difference and tradeoffs of series vs parallel termination?
A fast signal travels down a wire as a wave. At an end that doesn't absorb it, part of the wave bounces back and garbles the signal.
A termination is a resistor that soaks up the wave so it can't bounce. Series termination puts that resistor at the sending end. Parallel termination puts it at the receiving end.
Push a wave down a long water trough. At a solid end wall, the wave bounces back. Parallel termination is a sponge beach at the far end: the wave dies on arrival.
Series termination is a soft pad at the pushing end: the wave bounces off the far wall, returns, and the pad soaks it up.
The gap in the analogy: a resistor at the far end also wastes steady power as heat while the signal is high.
Here is the key diagram for this question.
Characteristic impedance ( Z 0 ): the resistance a wire "looks like" to a wave traveling down it ("Characteristic impedance explained").
Reflection: the part of a wave that bounces back from a mismatched end ("Reflections and why they matter").
Driver output resistance: the small resistance inside the chip pin that sends the signal. Receiver: the chip input that reads the signal.
It draws almost no current, so to a wave it looks like an open end. Multi-drop: one wire with several receivers tapped along it.
Take a 3. 3 volts driver with 15 ohms of its own resistance, a 35 ohms series resistor, and a 50 ohms wire. The driver sees 15 + 35 = 50 ohms, matching the wire.
Those 50 ohms and the wire's 50 ohms split the voltage evenly, so the wave leaves at 1. 65 volts. The open receiver end doubles it to 3. 3 volts and bounces it back.
The sending end absorbs the bounce. A receiver tapped mid-wire would see only 1. 65 volts for a while, so this suits one receiver at the end. That is the whole idea.
"Series termination puts a resistor at the driver so driver plus resistor equals Z 0 : the line launches half the swing, the open end doubles it, and the reflection is absorbed at the source.
It's cheap, uses no DC power, but only works with receivers at the end, and the full level arrives after a round trip.
Parallel termination puts Z 0 at the receiver and absorbs the wave on arrival, so it suits multi-drop and fast links, but burns DC power, lowers the high level and loads the driver."
Quick check. With ideal series termination ( R drv plus R s equals Z 0 ) and an open far end, what voltage does the end receiver see once the first wave arrives?
Source vs sink termination and matching. The question: What is the difference and tradeoffs of source vs sink termination/matching?
A signal on a fast wire is a wave, and a wave bounces back from any end that doesn't absorb it. The sending end is the source and the receiving end is the sink.
"Matching" an end means giving it a resistance equal to the wire's own impedance, so it soaks up the wave instead of bouncing it. You can match the source, the sink, or both.
Each choice absorbs the bounce at a different place.
Picture throwing a ball down a long corridor. A catcher with a glove at the far end (sink matching) catches it on arrival, so nothing bounces.
With no catcher, the ball hits the far wall and returns, and the thrower catches it (source matching). Every catcher takes energy, though.
In a circuit the matching resistors form a divider, so matching both ends costs half the voltage.
The two schemes differ in time and place of absorption.
Source termination absorbs after a round trip (the sink sees full swing at t d , but a mid-line receiver sees half swing until the reflection passes).
Sink termination absorbs at the first arrival, so there is nothing to come back.
Characteristic impedance ( Z 0 ): the resistance a wire "looks like" to a wave traveling along it ("Characteristic impedance explained").
Reflection: the part of a wave that bounces back from a mismatched end ("Reflections and why they matter").
Source resistance: the driver's own output resistance plus any resistor added in series with it. Echo: a bounced wave that arrives again later, distorting the signal.
Divider: two resistances in a row that split a voltage between them.
Use a 3. 3 volts source with 50 ohms of source resistance and a 50 ohms wire. If the far end is open, the wave leaves at 1. 65 volts, doubles to 3.
3 volts at the receiver, and the bounce is absorbed at the source. Now add a 50 ohms resistor to ground at the receiver.
The wave is absorbed on arrival, nothing bounces, and the receiver sees 3. 3 times 50 over (50 plus 50) equals 1. 65 volts.
That is double matching: very clean, but only half the voltage. That is the whole idea.

"Source termination matches the driver so reflections coming back are absorbed at the near end: cheap, no DC power, but the full level only appears after a round trip, so it suits one receiver at the end.
Sink termination matches the receiver so the wave is absorbed on arrival: clean edges for every receiver, tolerant of driver impedance, but costs DC power and swing.
Doing both is double termination, standard in RF and on-die termination links, very forgiving, but the amplitude is only half the source voltage."
Quick check. Where is the reflected wave absorbed with source termination?
Real TL distributed RLGC model. The question: Draw real TL distributed model. What are its components on a real TL? How do they differ between ideal vs real?
A real wire carrying a fast signal can't be treated as one single resistor, because the signal needs time to travel along it.
So we model it as a long chain of tiny identical slices, each with four small effects built in. Two of the effects (resistance and inductance) act along the wire.
Two (capacitance and leakage) act between the wire and its return path, the second conductor that carries the current back. Together they set the wire's impedance, speed and loss.
Picture a long garden hose. The water has inertia, so it resists changes in flow: that is the inductance.
The hose walls bulge a little under pressure and store water: that is the capacitance. Rubbing against the walls wastes energy: that is the resistance.
Pinholes leak water out the side: that is the leakage. An ideal hose has no friction and no pinholes, so a pulse arrives unchanged, only delayed.
Series elements ( R' , L' ) sit in the signal path. Shunt elements ( C' , and G' drawn as its equivalent resistor 1 over G' ) sit between signal and return.
Orange marks the loss element in the dielectric. The ground symbol is the return conductor.
Per unit length: each value is given for one meter of wire, so a longer wire has more of it. R (resistance): energy lost as heat in the metal, along the wire.
L (inductance): the wire's resistance to a change in current, from the magnetic field around it.
C (capacitance): charge the wire stores against its return path, from the electric field between them.
G (conductance): a tiny leak through the insulation between wire and return path.
Characteristic impedance ( Z 0 ): the resistance the wire "looks like" to a traveling wave ("Characteristic impedance explained").
Take an ideal line with no loss, so R and G are zero. Say it has 250 nanohenries of inductance and 100 picofarads of capacitance per meter.
Then Z 0 equals square root of L over C equals square root of 250 nanohenries over 100 picofarads equals square root of 2500 equals 50 ohms.
The delay is square root of LC equals 5 nanoseconds per meter. Real wires add small R and G, and both grow with frequency. That is the whole idea.
"A real transmission line is a ladder of small sections, each with a series R' and L' and a shunt G' and C' per unit length.
L' and C' are the stored magnetic and electric energy and set Z 0 equals square root of L' over C' and the speed. R' is copper loss, G' is dielectric loss.
The ideal line sets R' and G' to zero, so no loss, no dispersion, and a constant real Z 0 .
A real one attenuates high frequencies more, from skin effect and dielectric loss, so edges slow down and round off."
Quick check. In the distributed RLGC model, which elements are in the series path along the line?
Controlling characteristic impedance. The question: How can I control the characteristic impedance of a TL?
Characteristic impedance is the resistance a circuit-board trace "looks like" to a fast signal moving along it. You don't add a part to set it.
The trace's shape and the board material set it. Designers pick the trace width and layer thickness to hit a target such as 50 ohms.
A fast edge moving along a trace must charge the next little stretch of trace, like filling a bucket just ahead of it. The trace and the copper plane under it form a capacitor.
A wider trace, or a plane closer underneath, makes a bigger bucket. A bigger bucket takes more current for the same voltage, which means lower impedance.
A taller gap does the opposite. The bucket covers capacitance only.
The trace also has inductance (it resists changes in current), and a closer plane lowers that too, which also lowers the impedance.
Microstrip cross-section with the four knobs labelled. Field lines between the trace and the plane set C' ; the current loop through trace and plane sets L' .
Not drawn: some fringing field also loops through the air above the trace, which is why eff< r (see the cross-section in "How R, L and C set Z0: microstrip vs coax").
Trace: a strip of copper on a circuit board that carries the signal. Reference plane: a solid copper layer beside the trace that carries the return current.
Dielectric: the insulating board material between the trace and the plane. Dielectric constant ( r ): how much a material boosts capacitance. A higher value means a bigger bucket.
Characteristic impedance ( Z 0 ): the resistance the trace "looks like" to a traveling wave ("Characteristic impedance explained").
Controlled impedance: a service where the board maker adjusts widths to hit a target impedance.
A trace 0. 39 mm wide, over a 0. 2 mm layer of common board material (FR-4) with a plane beneath, comes out near 50 ohms. Now make the layer twice as thick, 0.
4 mm, and keep the same width. The trace and plane are farther apart, so capacitance drops and the impedance rises to about 73 ohms. To get 50 ohms back, double the width to 0.
78 mm. That is the whole idea.
" Z 0 is square root of L' over C' , so I steer it with geometry and material.
For a PCB trace over a plane: wider trace or thinner dielectric means more capacitance and less loop inductance, so lower Z 0 . Higher r also lowers it.
Thicker copper acts like a wider trace. About 0. 39 mm over 0. 2 mm FR-4 is roughly 50 ohms on microstrip.
I'd confirm in a field solver and ask the fab for controlled impedance at ±10%. For coax it's set by D over d and the dielectric."
Quick check. For a microstrip over a plane, what happens to Z 0 if you make the trace wider (same dielectric)?
Standard termination and Z0 values. The question: What are some standard termination/characteristic impedances?
Every cable and circuit-board trace has a characteristic impedance, the resistance it "looks like" to a fast signal.
A few values are industry standards: 50 ohms for radio gear, test equipment and most single traces, and 75 ohms for video.
Pairs of wires use 90, 100 or 120 ohms depending on the interface. The numbers are agreements.
Everything in the signal path must share the same number, or parts of the signal bounce back.
Think of railway gauge, the spacing between the two rails. Every track, train and station on a route has to use the same gauge.
If two sections differ, the train can't cross smoothly. Impedance works the same way: cable, connector, board trace and chip input all have to agree. The analogy has one gap.
A small mismatch doesn't stop the signal. It just sends back a small echo.
Loss (red) bottoms out near 77 ohms; power capacity (green) peaks near 30 ohms. At 50 ohms you pay about 10% more loss than the minimum and keep 86% of peak power.
That's the compromise. At 75 ohms loss is at its minimum but power capacity has dropped to about 56%.
Characteristic impedance ( Z 0 ): the resistance a wire "looks like" to a signal traveling along it ("Characteristic impedance explained").
Single-ended: one signal wire measured against a ground or return path. Differential pair: two wires carrying opposite versions of one signal.
Its impedance is measured between the two wires.
Termination: a resistor at the end of a line, chosen to equal Z 0 so the signal is absorbed ("Impedance matching: what, why, when").
Reflection: the part of a signal that bounces back at a mismatch ("Reflections and why they matter").
Plug a 75 ohms video cable into a 50 ohms input on an oscilloscope (a measuring instrument). The size of the bounce is (50-75) over (50 plus 75) equals -0. 2 .
So a 1 volts step sends 0. 2 volts back, inverted. If both ends were 50 ohms, nothing would bounce.
The same idea holds for pairs: a USB pair is 90 ohms, and routing it at 100 ohms leaves a small mismatch. That is the whole idea.
"50 ohms is the default for RF, test gear and single-ended PCB traces, picked as a compromise between lowest loss near 77 ohms and highest power handling near 30 ohms in coax.
75 ohms is video, close to lowest loss. Differentials are mostly 100 ohms (Ethernet, HDMI, LVDS), 90 ohms for USB, about 85 ohms for PCIe, and 120 ohms for CAN and RS-485.
Terminations equal those values, so a 50 ohms line gets a 50 ohms load, and everything in the path has to share the number or you get reflections."
Quick check. Which impedance is the typical differential target for USB?
Parasitic R, L, C and Z0. The question: Describe the parasitic R, L, and C components that impact characteristic impedance.
"Parasitic" means a small unwanted effect that comes along with every real wire. Every trace has resistance, inductance and capacitance spread along its length.
The inductance and capacitance per meter decide its characteristic impedance, the resistance it looks like to a fast signal. The resistance just wastes a little energy.
Vias and pads add small extra bits of inductance or capacitance at single spots, and those spots can bounce part of a fast edge back.
Picture a signal as a wave moving down a canal. A side pool beside the canal soaks up some water as the wave passes, so the wave briefly weakens: that is extra capacitance.
A narrow stretch resists the flow and pushes back: that is extra inductance. A slow swell barely notices either. A sharp wave feels both.
A via or connector reduces to a series inductance plus a shunt capacitance in the middle of otherwise uniform line. The inductor lifts the local impedance, the capacitor drops it.
Parasitic: a small unwanted resistance, inductance or capacitance that comes with a real part or wire.
Per-meter inductance and capacitance ( L' , C' ): how much of each one meter of line has ("Real TL distributed RLGC model").
Characteristic impedance ( Z 0 ): the resistance the line looks like to a traveling signal, square root of L' over C' ("Characteristic impedance explained").
Via: a plated hole joining two board layers. It adds a little inductance. Pad: the copper patch a part is soldered to. It adds a little capacitance.
Rise time: how long an edge takes to go from low to high, often in picoseconds (ps, trillionths of a second).
A coax cable (a center wire inside a round shield) has 250 nanohenries of inductance and 100 picofarads of capacitance per meter.
Then Z 0 equals square root of 250 nanohenries over 100 picofarads equals 50 ohms. Now add a 0. 5 picofarads pad.
It dips the local impedance and reflects about 12% of a 100 picoseconds edge. A slow 500 picoseconds edge reflects only about 2. 5%.
The same pad is harmless at low speed and a problem at high speed. That is the whole idea.
"Per unit length, L' is the magnetic energy of the trace-plus-return loop, C' is the electric energy between trace and plane, and together they set Z 0 equals square root of L' over C' .
R' and G' add loss and only matter for Z 0 at low frequency.

On a real board the bigger problem is lumped parasitics from vias, pads and connectors: a shunt capacitance dips the impedance, a series inductance bumps it, and the size of the reflection depends on how that parasitic compares with the edge rate."

TL loss and distortion sources. The question: What are sources of loss and distortion in a TL? How can they be minimized or actively compensated for?
A fast signal gets weaker as it travels down a wire or circuit-board trace. That is loss. Fast-changing parts fade more than slow parts, so the signal also changes shape.
That is distortion. Sharp edges turn slow and rounded, and one bit smears into the next. Designers fight it with shorter paths and by boosting the fast parts.
Think of someone talking in the next room through a thick wall. Deep, slow sounds come through fine. Sharp sounds like "t" and "s" are muffled, so the words blur together.
A trace does the same to a bit stream: slow content passes, fast content fades. Turning up the volume doesn't help, because the low sounds get louder too.
You need to boost the sharp sounds specifically.
Conductor loss (blue) grows as square root of f , dielectric loss (orange) grows linearly. In FR-4 they cross near 0.
4 gigahertz in this model, and the linear term dominates beyond that. With a low-loss laminate (green), conductor loss stays dominant until about 9 gigahertz.
At 5 gigahertz FR-4 loses about 0. 53 decibels/in versus about 0. 2 decibels/in.
Loss: the signal getting smaller as it travels. It is measured in decibels (dB): 6 decibels is about half the height.
Distortion: a change in the signal's shape, not just its size.
Skin effect: at high frequency, current crowds into the outer surface of the copper, which raises its resistance ("Skin effect and where it matters").
Dielectric loss: energy soaked up by the insulating board material around the trace ("Dielectric loss and frequency").
Inter-symbol interference (ISI): the tail of one bit spilling into the next bit and confusing the receiver.
Pre-emphasis: boosting the fast parts of the signal at the sender ("Preemphasis: why and how").
A link sending 10 billion bits per second as 1, 0, 1, 0 makes a wave that repeats 5 billion times a second (5 gigahertz). A typical circuit board (FR-4) loses about 0.
53 decibels per inch at 5 gigahertz. Over 12 inches that is about 6. 4 decibels, so the alternating pattern comes out under half its original height.
A long run of identical bits is slow and passes nearly untouched. The receiver sees uneven bit heights that are hard to tell apart. That is the whole idea.
"Loss comes from conductor resistance (skin effect, roughness, rises as square root of f ), dielectric loss (rises roughly with f ), radiation, and energy lost to reflections at discontinuities.
Because the loss grows with frequency, the line is a low-pass filter, so edges smear and ISI closes the eye.
I minimize it with short, clean, impedance-controlled routing, smooth copper and low-loss laminate.
Then I compensate actively: pre-emphasis at the transmitter, CTLE and DFE at the receiver, or a retimer for long channels."
Quick check. Which statement about loss mechanisms in a PCB trace is correct?
Dielectric loss and frequency. The question: What are dielectric losses? Where do they come from and how does it vary with frequency?
The insulating material around a trace is not perfect.
When a fast signal's electric field (the push its voltage puts on charges nearby) flips back and forth, the material's tiny charges shift to follow it, and they lag a little.
That lag turns a small part of the signal's energy into heat. This is dielectric loss.
The faster the signal, the more flips per second, so the more energy is lost on each inch of board.
Squeeze a rubber ball over and over. Each squeeze wastes a little energy, and the ball warms up.
Squeeze twice as fast and you waste twice as much per second, because the ball loses the same small fraction on every squeeze.
The insulator behaves like that ball, and each field flip is a squeeze. The ball is a loose picture: the real lag comes from shifting charges, not rubbing.
Loss tangent (red) peaks where the dipoles can just barely follow the field, at omega tau about square root of s over infinity , here about 0. 096.
At the same time ' (blue, scaled by 1/50 for display) steps down from 4. 6 to 3. 8.
Away from the peak the loss falls off: either the dipoles follow easily (low frequency) or can't move at all (high frequency).
Dielectric: the insulating material between conductors, such as the fiberglass-epoxy of a circuit board ("Dielectrics and permittivity").
Polarization: tiny charges in the material shifting to follow the electric field. Loss tangent ( delta ): the fraction of stored energy lost as heat on each cycle.
Smaller is better. Attenuation: how much the signal shrinks per inch, in decibels (dB). Every 6 decibels roughly halves the signal's height.
FR-4: the standard, cheap circuit-board material. Its delta is about 0. 02.
FR-4 loses about 0. 1 decibels per inch from this effect at 1 gigahertz. At 5 gigahertz it loses about 0.
5 decibels per inch, five times more, because the loss grows in step with frequency. A 10-inch trace at 5 gigahertz loses about 5 decibels to the dielectric alone.
A low-loss board material with delta of 0. 004 is five times better than FR-4. That is the whole idea.
"Dielectric loss is heat generated in the insulator because the polarization of its molecules lags the alternating field.
It's captured by the imaginary part of the permittivity, and the ratio to the real part is the loss tangent, delta .
On a transmission line it acts as a shunt conductance G' equals omega C' delta , so the attenuation rises about linearly with frequency: roughly pi f square root of r delta over c .
For FR-4 that's around 0. 1 decibels/in at 1 gigahertz and 0. 5 decibels/in at 5 gigahertz, which is why high-speed boards use low-loss laminate."
Quick check. What does the loss tangent delta represent?
TL impedance vs frequency. The question: How does a TL's insertion impedance vary with respect to frequency?
"The impedance of a transmission line" can mean three different things. One is the line's own characteristic impedance, which stays about the same at high frequency.
The second is the impedance a source sees when it looks into a finite piece of line, and that changes with frequency unless the far end is matched.
The third is how much signal gets through, called insertion loss, which grows with frequency.
Picture pushing a child on a swing. Pushes in step with the swing help. Pushes out of step fight it. A mismatched line works like that.
A bounce comes back from the far end, and whether it helps or fights the outgoing signal depends on timing, so on frequency.
The source feels a different "push-back" at each frequency. With a matched end there is no bounce, so the feel never changes.
Below 100 megahertz the open line is a capacitor ( Z in about 1 over omega C' with C' equals 12 picofarads, falling with frequency).
At 415 megahertz it collapses to near a short, at 830 megahertz it spikes to an open, and it repeats.
The red lossy line shows the same pattern with the extremes softened: loss limits how deep the null and how high the peak can go, and grows with frequency.
Characteristic impedance ( Z 0 ): the resistance the line looks like to a single wave traveling along it ("Characteristic impedance explained").
Input impedance: what the source sees looking into the start of the line. It depends on the far-end load.
Matched: the far-end load equals Z 0 , so nothing bounces back ("Impedance matching: what, why, when"). Insertion loss: how much signal is lost passing through the line.
Delay: the time a wave takes to travel the length of the line.
Take a 50 ohms line with a 0. 6 nanoseconds delay. End it with a matched 50 ohms load, and the source sees 50 ohms at every frequency. Now end it with 100 ohms.
The input impedance swings between 100 ohms and 25 ohms as frequency rises, completing one swing about every 0. 83 gigahertz. That is because the bounce returns after a 1.
2 nanoseconds round trip, and 1 over 1. 2 nanoseconds about 0. 83 gigahertz. The 25 comes from 50 squared over 100 . That is the whole idea.
"I'd separate three things. The characteristic impedance is essentially constant with frequency above a few MHz, square root of L' over C' , with a small drift from loss.

The input impedance of a finite line depends on frequency through its electrical length: matched, it's Z 0 at all frequencies; unmatched, it oscillates, like an open line looking capacitive, then a short at the quarter-wave frequency, then open at the half-wave.
And insertion loss rises with frequency, roughly square root of f plus f terms, with ripples if there are reflections."

Skin effect and where it matters. The question: What is the skin effect? Where does it come up in TLs?
With steady current (DC), current spreads through the whole thickness of a wire.
As the frequency rises, the current crowds into a thin layer near the surface, and the middle carries almost none. This is the skin effect.
A thinner usable layer means less metal carrying current, so the wire's resistance goes up with frequency. It is a main reason copper loss grows at gigahertz speeds.
Picture a long hallway with a crowd moving along it. When everyone walks slowly, people fill the whole width.
When the crowd rushes, everyone hugs the walls and the middle of the hallway stays empty. The hallway is just as wide, but only the edges are used.
In a wire the cause is not crowding. A changing current builds a changing magnetic field, which pushes current out of the middle toward the surface.
Skin depth falls as 1 over square root of f : a straight line of slope minus 1/2 on log-log axes. The horizontal red line is 1 oz copper thickness (35 µm).
Where the copper curve falls to half of that, about 14 megahertz, the conductor starts to behave as a surface layer, and above that you're paying the square root of f penalty.
All four metals are within about 30% of each other (δ scales as √ρ), so the metal choice barely matters; the surface smoothness and plating do.
Skin depth ( delta ): how deep into the metal most of the current flows. It shrinks as frequency rises.
Eddy currents: small circling currents the changing magnetic field creates inside the metal. They cancel current in the middle.
AC resistance: a wire's effective resistance at high frequency, higher than its DC value.
Conductor loss: signal energy lost as heat in the copper ("TL loss and distortion sources").
Surface roughness: tiny bumps on the copper that lengthen the path current takes, so loss rises further.
For copper, the skin depth is about 66 micro m over square root of f over MHz . That is 66 µm at 1 megahertz, about 6. 6 µm at 100 megahertz, and about 2. 1 µm at 1 gigahertz.
A typical circuit-board trace is 35 µm thick. Above about 14 megahertz the skin is thinner than half the trace, so the middle goes unused.
From 100 megahertz to 1 gigahertz the skin gets about three times thinner, so the resistance rises about three times. That is the whole idea.
"The skin effect is high-frequency current crowding into a thin layer at the surface of a conductor.
Induced eddy currents oppose current in the middle and reinforce it at the edges.
The skin depth is delta equals square root of over pi f micro : 66 µm at 1 megahertz for copper, 2. 1 µm at 1 gigahertz.
Since the effective area shrinks, resistance rises as square root of f .
In transmission lines it's the dominant conductor loss: R' and attenuation grow as square root of f , current hugs the surfaces facing the plane, and roughness makes it worse."
Quick check. What causes the skin effect?
Preemphasis: why and how. The question: What is preemphasis? Why is it used? How can it be implemented?
A long trace or cable weakens the fast-changing parts of a signal more than the slow parts, so sharp edges arrive rounded and bits smear into each other.
Preemphasis fixes this at the sender. The transmitter deliberately exaggerates the fast parts, by about as much as the cable will take away.
The signal that arrives is then close to the one you wanted.
Imagine steering a heavy, sluggish car. To change lanes quickly, you yank the wheel hard at first and then ease it back once the car starts moving.
If you turned only to the final angle, the car would drift over slowly. Preemphasis does the same to a bit stream.
The first bit after a change is driven at full strength to overcome the sluggish line. Repeated bits are driven softer.
The sender can't exceed its maximum output voltage, so in practice repeated bits are turned down.
The red curve is the channel falling to about minus 8 decibels at 5 gigahertz. The blue dashed curve is the 2-tap FFE, rising by 6 decibels.
Their sum (green) is within about 2 decibels of flat out to Nyquist, instead of 8 decibels down.
Because the FFE boost is a cosine of frequency and the channel loss is smooth, a 2-tap filter approximates the inverse only roughly, so real links use 3 taps and a receiver CTLE/DFE as well.
Channel: everything the signal travels through, such as the trace, connectors and cable ("TL loss and distortion sources").
Transition: a bit that differs from the one before it, like a 0 followed by a 1.
Inter-symbol interference (ISI): the tail of one bit spilling into later bits and confusing the receiver. De-emphasis: driving repeated bits lower than transition bits.
It is the same trick as preemphasis, measured from a different reference. Boost: how much stronger the fast parts are than the slow parts, in decibels (dB).
6 decibels means twice the height.
Suppose the sender mixes 75% of the current bit with 25% of the opposite of the previous bit. A bit after a change comes out at full height, 1. 0. A repeated bit comes out at 0.
75-0. 25 equals 0. 5 . Fast switching is therefore 2 times, or 6 decibels, stronger than a long run of the same bit.
A channel that loses about 6 decibels on fast switching then evens it out. That is the whole idea.
"Preemphasis boosts the high-frequency part of the transmitted signal to cancel the low-pass response of a lossy channel, so the received signal is flat and ISI is small.
In the time domain it overshoots the first bit after a transition, or equivalently de-emphasizes repeated bits.
It's usually a short FIR filter in the driver, like y[n] equals (1-a)x[n]-a x[n-1] , which boosts Nyquist by 1 over (1-2a) . It can also be a passive RC network.
The cost is lower low-frequency swing, more high-frequency EMI and crosstalk, and coefficients that need tuning."
Quick check. Why is preemphasis applied at the transmitter of a lossy link?
Signal with and without preemphasis. The question: Draw the time-domain and frequency-domain spectrum of a signal with/without preemphasis.
Pre-emphasis changes a bit stream in a way you can see in two pictures. In the time picture, the first bit after a change stays at full height, but repeated bits are drawn lower.
In the frequency picture, the slow part of the signal is turned down while the fast part is left alone. The two pictures describe the same change.
A run of identical bits is slow, so lowering it lowers the slow part.
Think of the bass and treble knobs on a stereo. Slow, deep sounds are low frequency, and quick, sharp sounds are high frequency.
Pre-emphasis turns the bass down and leaves the treble alone. The song sounds brighter. Here, bass is the long runs of identical bits and treble is the edges where bits change.
A real driver has no knob, only weighted copies of the data.
The dashed grey trace is plain NRZ. The blue trace de-emphasizes: whenever a bit repeats (the 1 1 1 run and the 0 0 pairs), the level steps down to ±0. 5 after the first bit.
The transition levels are still ±1, so peak swing is unchanged and the driver doesn't clip.
The filter works by removing amplitude from the low-frequency bits, not by adding it to the edges.
Frequency: how fast something repeats. A long run of identical bits is slow, so it is low frequency. Spectrum: a chart of how much of the signal sits at each frequency.
NRZ: a bit stream with one fixed level per bit, high for 1 and low for 0. Transition: a bit that differs from the one before it.
De-emphasis: lowering repeated bits relative to transition bits ("Preemphasis: why and how").
Send the bits 0, 1, 1, 1, 0 as plain NRZ, with levels of minus 1 and +1. Now apply 6 decibels of de-emphasis (repeats drop to half height).
The first 1 follows a change, so it stays at 1. The next two 1 seconds are repeats, so they drop to 0. 5. The final 0 is a change, so it is back at minus 1.
The spectrum shows the same thing: the slow, low-frequency part falls by half in height, while an alternating 1010 pattern, which is all changes, is untouched.
That is the whole idea.
"Time domain: preemphasis keeps full swing on the first bit after a transition and lowers the following repeated bits, a shoulder after each edge.
Frequency domain: the NRZ sinc-squared spectrum is multiplied by a high-pass shape, so DC drops by 6 decibels while the Nyquist region stays put.
Since the channel is a low-pass, the two combine to a flatter overall response, and at the receiver the isolated bits and long runs reach more similar levels, which opens the eye."
Quick check. In a 2-tap de-emphasis with a equals 0. 25 , what is the amplitude of a repeated bit (relative to a transition bit at 1)?
Components of an embedded system. The question: What are some components/subsystems you'd find in an embedded system?
An embedded system is a small computer hidden inside a product, such as a thermostat or a washing machine.
Its job is to read inputs from the real world, decide what to do, and control outputs.
To do that, a processor needs memory to hold its program, power, a clock, a way to start cleanly, and connections to sensors and outputs.
Think of a small restaurant kitchen. The cook is the processor. The recipe book is the program memory, and the counter is the working space for the dish in progress.
Gas and electricity are the power, and the kitchen timer is the clock. Orders come in (inputs), and plates go out (outputs).
Every shift starts with the same opening routine, like a reset. Without any one of these, the cook can't work.
Power, clock, reset and debug all feed the MCU. Inputs, outputs and communication buses leave from it. When a board is dead, check the four arrows into the MCU first.
Embedded system: a computer built into a product to do one specific job.
Microcontroller (MCU): one chip holding the processor, memory and input/output hardware ("Microcontroller vs microprocessor").
Flash and RAM: flash keeps the program (the firmware) with the power off. RAM is working space that is wiped at power-off.
Clock: a steady tick that paces everything the chip does. Reset: a signal that puts the chip in a known starting state ("Reset signal: what and why").
A battery-powered temperature logger has a temperature sensor, a microcontroller that stores each reading, a coin cell for power, and a slow clock that wakes the chip every 10 seconds.
The chip is awake for 20 milliseconds (thousandths of a second) and draws 5 milliamps (thousandths of an amp). Over 10 seconds, that averages 10 microamps (millionths of an amp).
Sleep adds about 1. 5 microamps. A coin cell rated 220 milliamp hours can supply 1 milliamps for 220 hours, so this lasts about two years, an upper estimate.
That is the whole idea.
"An embedded system is a processor, usually an MCU, with its memory, plus the supporting blocks that make it run: power and decoupling, a clock, reset, and a debug port.
Around that are inputs, like sensors and buttons, and outputs like LEDs, motors and displays, plus communication buses such as I2C, SPI, UART, CAN and USB.
Protection like ESD, a watchdog and brown-out detection makes it robust, and the firmware, including drivers, a bootloader and maybe an RTOS, is the last component."
Quick check. Which of these is NOT normally part of the support circuitry needed for an MCU to run?
Examples of embedded systems. The question: What are some examples of embedded systems?
The question asks you to name products with a small dedicated computer inside and say what makes each tricky to build.
Examples are everywhere: microwaves, thermostats, TV remotes, car brake controllers, pacemakers, drones and routers.
Each runs one fixed job, reads the world through sensors, and controls something.
The useful way to tell them apart is by their main limit: tight cost, tiny battery, strict timing, or safety.
Picture keeping a bath at the right temperature. You touch the water, decide it is too cold, open the hot tap a bit, and check again.
That repeating cycle of sense, decide, act is what most embedded systems do. The difference is the stakes. In a bath, being a few seconds late doesn't matter.
In an airbag, a few milliseconds late is a failure.
A typical embedded control loop: read the sensor, run the control law, drive the actuator; the physical process closes the loop back to the sensor.
Sensor: a part that measures something real, such as temperature or wheel speed. Actuator: a part that does something physical, such as a motor, heater, valve or lamp.
Control loop: the repeating cycle of reading sensors, deciding, and driving actuators. Real-time: the answer has to arrive by a deadline to count as correct.
Hard real-time: missing a deadline is a failure, not just a slowdown. Constraint: a limit on cost, battery life, size or timing.
A thermostat reads a temperature sensor, turns the heater on at 20 degrees Celsius and off at 21 degrees Celsius, and repeats. Nothing is urgent, so a cheap chip is enough.
Now take a car engine at 6000 rpm (turns per minute).
That is 100 turns per second, so one turn takes 10 milliseconds (thousandths of a second), and one degree of rotation lasts 10 milliseconds over 360 about 28 microseconds (millionths of a second).
The spark must be timed to about that precision, so dedicated timer circuits on the chip handle it. Same loop, very different constraints. That is the whole idea.

"An embedded system is a computer dedicated to one job inside a product: a microwave, a thermostat, a TV remote, a car's engine and ABS controllers, a pacemaker, a drone's flight controller, a router, a 3D printer.
They differ by what constrains them: pacemakers are ultra-low power and safety-critical, ABS and engine control are hard real-time, remotes are cost-driven, routers are throughput-driven.
For example, an engine controller must time ignition to within a fraction of a crank degree, about 28 microseconds at 6000 rpm."
Quick check. Which is the best example of a hard real-time embedded system?
Common microcontrollers and microprocessors. The question: What are some common microcontrollers/microprocessors?
A microcontroller (MCU) is a complete tiny computer on one chip: a processor, program storage, working memory and input/output hardware. It runs one fixed program and sips power.
A microprocessor (MPU) is mainly the processor.
It needs separate memory chips and storage, and it typically runs a full operating system (software such as Linux that juggles many programs).
Picture a studio apartment next to a house. In the studio, the bed, kitchen and bathroom all fit in one room. It is small, cheap to run, and ready at once. That is the MCU.
A house has a separate kitchen, bedrooms and utility connections. It is far roomier, but you must supply and connect each part. That is the MPU.
The line is blurry, since some big studios are roomier than small houses.
Each point is a representative part (values are typical headline numbers; the Pi 4's 4 GB is external DRAM; H743 is STM32H743, RT1062 is i.
MX RT1062, whose point is nudged up for legibility).

The microcontrollers cluster at low clock and kilobyte-scale on-chip RAM; crossover MCUs reach hundreds of MHz with about 1 MB; application processors jump to GHz clocks and gigabytes of external memory.
Microcontroller (MCU): processor, memory and input/output on one chip ("Microcontroller vs microprocessor").
Microprocessor (MPU): a processor that needs external memory and an operating system. Core: the processor part of a chip, such as Arm Cortex-M for MCUs or Cortex-A for MPUs.
Bit width: how many bits (single 0 seconds and 1 seconds) the processor handles at once. 8-bit parts are simple; 32-bit parts are the workhorse.
Clock speed: ticks per second that pace the chip, in MHz (millions) or GHz (billions). DRAM: bulk working memory in a separate chip, used by MPUs.
The ATmega328P in the Arduino Uno is an 8-bit MCU running at 16 megahertz.
It has 32 KB (kilobytes, thousands of bytes; a byte is 8 bits) of program storage and 2 KB of working memory, and it finishes most instructions in one tick, so about 16 million per second.
A Raspberry Pi 4 uses four Cortex-A72 cores at 1. 5 gigahertz with gigabytes of separate DRAM, running Linux.
Both are computers, but the Pi has millions of times more working memory. That is the whole idea.

"Microcontrollers integrate CPU, flash, RAM and peripherals: AVR like the ATmega328P in Arduino, PIC, the low-power TI MSP430, and above all 32-bit ARM Cortex-M parts like STMicro's STM32, Nordic's nRF52, the RP2040, plus the Wi-Fi/Bluetooth ESP32.
Microprocessors are CPUs needing external DRAM and an OS: Cortex-A chips such as the Raspberry Pi's Broadcom SoC, NXP i. MX, TI Sitara, and x86.
The boundary is blurry, since fast Cortex-M7 MCUs and chips with both A and M cores exist."
Quick check. Which of these is a microprocessor board that normally runs Linux with external DRAM?
Microcontroller vs microprocessor. The question: What is the difference between a microcontroller and a microprocessor?
A microcontroller (MCU) is a whole small computer on one chip: processor, program storage, working memory and input/output hardware.
A microprocessor (MPU) is mostly the processor. It needs separate memory and storage chips and usually runs a full operating system. The trade is simple.
The MCU is cheap, frugal and predictable. The MPU is far more powerful but costs more, uses more power and is harder to design with.
An MCU is like a pocket calculator. Switch it on and it works at once, and it takes the same time to do the same job every time. An MPU is like a laptop.
It has much more power, but it needs memory and storage installed, takes a while to start, and how fast it answers depends on whatever else is running.
The MCU system is a chip, a regulator and a crystal.
The MPU system is the processor surrounded by DRAM, boot storage and a power-management IC, each of which needs its own routing and layout.
Microcontroller (MCU): processor, memory and input/output blocks together on one chip ("Common microcontrollers and microprocessors").
Microprocessor (MPU): a processor that relies on external memory and storage.
Operating system (OS): the software layer, such as Linux, that runs and shares the hardware among many programs. Deterministic: the same job takes the same time on every run.
Interrupt: a hardware signal that makes the processor drop its work and handle an event right now. Boot time: how long the chip takes to start doing useful work after power-on.
A typical small MCU (an Arm Cortex-M) starts handling an interrupt in about 12 clock ticks.
At 48 megahertz (48 million ticks per second) that is 12 / 48 million = 250 nanoseconds (billionths of a second), every time.
A Linux MPU might handle the same event in microseconds on one run and milliseconds on the next. The MCU also wakes in milliseconds and can sleep on millionths of an amp.
So a battery door lock uses an MCU, while a video doorbell uses an MPU. That is the whole idea.
"A microcontroller integrates the CPU, flash, SRAM and peripherals on one chip, so it runs on its own: low cost, microamp sleep, millisecond boot, deterministic timing, bare-metal or an RTOS.

A microprocessor is mainly the CPU and relies on external DRAM, storage and a PMIC; it's faster and runs Linux with an MMU, but costs more, draws watts, needs a complex board, and has non-deterministic timing.
Use an MCU for control and low power, an MPU for rich software, and often both together."
Quick check. Which item is typically NOT on the MCU die but is needed for a microprocessor to run Linux?
Blocks of an MCU and an MPU. The question: What are the blocks of a microcontroller and microprocessor?
Inside a microcontroller, a processor core is joined by wires, called a bus, to the memory and to hardware blocks that do specific jobs, such as timers and serial ports.
Support blocks handle the clock, reset, interrupts and bulk data copying.
A microprocessor chip has the processor, a small fast memory called a cache, and controllers that reach outside memory chips. The main memory and storage sit off the chip.
Picture a small office. The manager (the processor core) works at a desk.
A filing cabinet holds procedures (program memory), and a whiteboard holds today's notes (working memory).
A receptionist taps the manager's shoulder when something urgent arrives.
Departments do specialist jobs (the peripherals), and a courier carries parcels between them so the manager doesn't have to.
Hallways connect every room, and the wall clock sets the pace.
Masters (CPU and DMA) reach slaves (flash, SRAM, peripherals) through the bus matrix. Peripherals raise events into the NVIC, which interrupts the CPU.
Clock and reset blocks feed everything.
Core: the part of the chip that runs instructions. Bus: the shared wires that carry addresses and data between blocks.
Peripheral: a hardware block that does one job, such as a timer, a serial port or an analog-to-digital converter ("How an MCU talks to peripherals").
Interrupt: a signal from a block that makes the core pause and handle an event. DMA: a helper block that copies data between memory and peripherals without the core.
Register: a small storage slot that controls a block. Software writes to it like writing to a memory address.
An analog-to-digital converter (a block that turns a voltage into a number) produces 1 million numbers, or samples, per second.
If each sample interrupted the core, and each interrupt cost 100 clock ticks, the core would need 100 million ticks per second.
A 72 megahertz core has only 72 million, an impossible 139% load.
With DMA, the samples are copied into memory automatically, and the core is interrupted only when a whole block of memory (a buffer) is full. That is the whole idea.

"An MCU is a CPU core connected through a bus matrix to on-chip flash and SRAM, plus clock and reset logic, an interrupt controller, DMA, and peripherals: GPIO, timers, serial ports, ADC/DAC, a watchdog and a debug port, all memory-mapped.
A microprocessor has the CPU cores with caches and an MMU, a DRAM controller, an interrupt controller and I/O blocks, but the DRAM, boot storage and power management are separate chips on the board."
Quick check. Which block lets data move between a peripheral and memory without CPU involvement for each transfer?
How an MCU talks to peripherals. The question: How does a microcontroller interact with external peripherals?
A microcontroller doesn't wiggle its pins one by one from software. Each hardware block on the chip, called a peripheral, has a set of control registers at fixed addresses.
Firmware (the chip's program) writes settings into those registers, tells the block to go, and reads status back. The block then drives the pins with the right timing.
Which block you use depends on what is attached.
Picture a control panel on a machine in the next room. You flip switches to choose the settings, press "go", and read the indicator lights to see progress.
To know when the job is done, you can stare at the light (polling), wait for a bell (an interrupt), or hand the job to an assistant who carries the results to your desk (DMA).
The registers are the panel, and the peripheral is the machine.
Left: a pushbutton with a pull-up resistor gives a defined high when open and low when pressed (an input, ideally debounced).
Top right: an LED with a series resistor on an output pin. Bottom right: an I2C sensor on SDA and SCL, each pulled up to VDD because the bus is open-drain.
Each of the three uses a different MCU mechanism: GPIO input, GPIO output, serial peripheral.
Register: a control slot at a fixed address. Writing to it sets up a peripheral or sends data.
GPIO pin: a general-purpose pin the firmware can drive high or low, or read as an input.
Serial bus: a few wires that send bits one after another, such as I2C, SPI and UART ("I2C, SPI and UART: how each works").
Polling: the processor repeatedly checks a status flag until the job is done. Interrupt: the peripheral signals the processor when it needs attention.
DMA: a helper block that moves data to and from memory without the processor.
To light an LED (a light-emitting diode), firmware makes three register writes: switch on the clock for the pin's group, set the pin as an output, then write a 1.
The LED uses up about 2. 0 volts and should get 5 milliamps, so from 3. 3 volts it needs a resistor of (3. 3-2. 0) over 5 milliamps equals 260 ohms.
A standard 270 ohms gives about 4. 8 milliamps. That is the whole idea.
"The firmware talks to hardware through memory-mapped registers: configure a peripheral, then read and write its data and status registers.
Depending on the device, the pins are GPIO for on/off signals, ADC for analog in, timers and PWM for waveforms, or a serial bus like I2C, SPI, UART or CAN for smart peripherals.
Data moves by polling, interrupts or DMA, depending on rate and latency.
And electrically I make sure the levels match, open-drain buses have pull-ups, and pins are protected and current-limited."
Quick check. What is the most common reason that writes to a peripheral's registers appear to do nothing on a freshly reset MCU?
MCU vs ASIC vs FPGA. The question: When do use MCU vs ASIC vs FPGA?
A microcontroller (MCU) runs a program one step at a time on a fixed chip.
An FPGA is a chip whose internal wiring you configure after it is made, so it becomes custom hardware that does many things at once.
An ASIC is a chip designed and manufactured for one job and cannot be changed.
The usual rule is to start with the cheapest option that works, an MCU, and move up only when a requirement forces you to.
Think of printing a book. An MCU is a person copying pages by hand: cheap to start and very flexible, but slow. An FPGA is a print shop with rearrangeable type blocks.
You set it up once for your job, then it prints many pages at the same time. An ASIC is a press built for that exact book.
Each copy is the cheapest of all, but building the press costs a fortune, and if you find a typo the press must be rebuilt.
Total cost against volume on log axes. The FPGA is cheaper than the ASIC below about 73,000 units and more expensive above it, because its unit cost is 13 times higher.
The MCU line stays cheapest if the MCU can meet the requirements at all, which is why the first question is feasibility, not cost.
(The MCU and ASIC lines cross at the far right only because I gave both similar placeholder unit costs; it is an artefact, not a design rule.)
MCU: a small chip that runs a stored program, one instruction at a time ("Microcontroller vs microprocessor").
FPGA: a chip you configure after manufacture to form your own digital circuit. ASIC: a chip custom-made for one job, with wiring fixed at the factory.
NRE: the one-time cost to design the chip and set up manufacturing. Parallelism: doing many operations at the same moment.
Break-even: the volume at which two options cost the same in total.
A filter (math that cleans up a signal) must do 64 multiplications for each of 100 million measurements, or samples, per second. That is 6. 4 billion multiplications per second.
A 100 megahertz MCU does one per tick, 100 million per second, which is 64 times too slow. An FPGA with 64 multiplier blocks at 200 megahertz does 12.
8 billion per second, so it fits. That is the whole idea.
"Default to an MCU: it's cheapest, quickest to develop and the most flexible, but it executes sequentially.
Use an FPGA when you need massive parallelism, nanosecond deterministic latency or custom interfaces, with low NRE and reprogrammability but higher unit cost and power.
Use an ASIC only at very high volume with a stable design, since NRE is in the millions and a bug means a respin.
The break-even is NRE plus unit cost times volume, and hybrids like SoC FPGAs are common."
Quick check. Which platform has the highest non-recurring engineering (NRE) cost?
How to spec an MCU. The question: How do you spec an MCU? What specs do you look for?
Specifying an MCU means turning what your product must do into numbers, and then choosing the smallest chip that meets them with room to spare.
Start from the requirements, not a datasheet (the maker's spec sheet). Work out how much processing, memory, input/output and battery life you need.
Then check candidate chips against those totals. Too small a chip hits a wall late in the project. Too big a chip wastes cost and power.
Picture choosing a moving truck. You first measure what you must move: the volume of boxes, the heaviest item, and how far you are going.
Then you add some extra room, because you will always find more stuff. A truck that is too small means a second trip halfway through.
A truck that is far too big costs more to rent and burns more fuel.
For frequent tasks (left) the part with lower energy per task (B: 6 µC against 10 µC) wins; for rare tasks (right) sleep current dominates and part A wins.
The crossover is where 4 micro C over T equals 14 micro A . The lesson is to model your own duty cycle before choosing on a single datasheet figure.
Cycle budget: how many clock ticks the processor has for each pass of its main task. Headroom: spare capacity left over for new features and surprises.
Peripheral: a built-in hardware block such as a timer, converter or serial port ("How an MCU talks to peripherals").
Pin multiplexing: one physical pin can serve several functions, but only one at a time. Sleep current: the tiny current the chip draws while idle, which drives battery life.
Errata: the maker's list of known bugs in the chip.
A motor control loop runs 20,000 times per second on a 72 megahertz chip. The cycle budget is 72 000 000 over 20 000 equals 3 600 ticks per pass.
If the algorithm needs 1,800 ticks, it uses half, which leaves good headroom. For memory, say the program (firmware) is 64 KB (kilobytes).
Safe updates need room for a second copy, plus a 16 KB starter program (a bootloader) that picks which copy runs.
That is 2 times 64 plus 16 equals 144 KB, so you pick the next size up, 256 KB. That is the whole idea.
"I derive the spec from the requirements. CPU: cycles per loop, such as 3,600 cycles per 20 kilohertz iteration at 72 megahertz, with at most about half used.
Memory: flash for code, bootloader and update image, RAM for buffers, plus 30–50% margin.
Peripherals: enough timers, ADC channels and rate, buses and DMA, checked against pin muxing. Power: supply range, µA/MHz and sleep current.
Then temperature grade, package, ecosystem, errata, cost and availability, ideally within a pin-compatible family."
Quick check. What should the first step in specifying an MCU be?
Reset signal: what and why. The question: What is a reset signal? What does it do? Why is it useful?
A reset signal forces a chip into a known starting state and then lets it begin running from a fixed place.
It exists because a chip's internal memory cells power up in random states, and the supply voltage takes time to rise. The chip must wait until power and clock are good.
Reset also gives a way to recover if the program hangs or the supply dips too low.
Think of a race. The runners are held behind the starting line until everyone is ready and the track is clear.
Then the starting gun fires, and all of them start from the same line. A reset holds the processor still while the supply and clock settle, then fires the gun.
The same signal can also recall the runners mid-race if something goes wrong.
VDD rises first. The oscillator starts a little later.
Reset is held low until both are good, plus a delay margin, and only then does the CPU fetch the reset vector and run startup code. Reset must outlast the slowest of these.
Reset: forcing the chip's settings and built-in hardware blocks to their defaults, then restarting the processor. Active-low: "on" when the pin is pulled to 0 volts.
The reset pin, often called NRST, is usually active-low. Power-on reset: circuitry inside the chip that holds it in reset until the supply has risen high enough.
Brown-out: the supply sagging below a safe level while the chip runs, which can corrupt its work. Watchdog: a timer that resets the chip if the program stops checking in.
Reset vector: the stored address where the processor starts running after a reset.
Suppose the supply ramps from 0 to 3. 3 volts over 10 milliseconds.
A bare resistor and capacitor on the reset pin (10 kilohms and 100 nanofarads) would release reset after about 3 milliseconds. At that moment the supply is only about 1.
1 volts, too low for reliable running. A supervisor (a small chip that watches the supply), or the MCU's built-in power-on reset, waits until the supply is high enough.
That is the whole idea.
"A reset signal forces the chip into a known state: registers go to defaults, peripherals are disabled, and the CPU restarts from the reset vector.
It comes from power-on reset, brown-out detection, an external active-low pin, the watchdog, or software.
It matters because flip-flops power up randomly, supplies ramp slowly, and firmware can hang: reset gives a deterministic start and a way to recover, and keeps the chip from running on a bad supply."
Quick check. Why is a reset needed when power is first applied to a microcontroller?
I2C, SPI and UART: how each works. The question: What are the three common communication protocols? How do they (I2C, SPI, UART) work?
I2C, SPI and UART are three ways for chips on a board to pass bytes (groups of 8 bits) to each other. All three send one bit at a time, which saves wires.
They differ in how the receiver knows when to read each bit, and that choice sets their wire count, speed and how many devices they can serve.
UART links two devices with no shared clock. SPI is fast but needs a select wire per device. I2C shares two wires among many devices.
Picture three ways of passing notes in a classroom. In UART, two friends agree beforehand on how fast to talk, and each keeps their own watch.
In SPI, a teacher claps a steady beat that everyone follows, and each student has a private line to the teacher.
In I2C, the whole class shares one party line, and each student answers to their own name.
Each direction has its own wire, so both sides can talk at once.
The signal names swap (MCU TX goes to module RX) and the grounds must be common, because logic levels are voltages measured against ground.
Serial: sending bits one after another on a single wire. Clock: a steady tick on its own wire that tells the receiver when to read each bit.
Baud rate: how many bits per second both sides agreed to use. UART needs it because it has no clock wire. Chip select: a wire that wakes up one SPI device.
Address: a number that picks one device on a shared I2C bus.
Send one byte. UART adds a start bit and a stop bit, so it is 10 bits. At 115,200 baud, that is 10 over 115 200 about 86. 8 microseconds.
SPI at 8 megahertz sends the 8 bits in 8 clock ticks, which is 1 microseconds.
I2C at 100 kilohertz takes 9 ticks per byte, 8 data bits plus an acknowledge bit (the receiver's "got it"), so 90 microseconds, plus another byte for the address.
SPI is fast; I2C is slower but uses only two wires. That is the whole idea.
"UART is two wires and no clock: start bit, data LSB first, stop bit, and both sides just agree on a baud rate.
SPI is synchronous: the controller drives a clock, data goes out on MOSI and comes back on MISO at the same time, and each device gets its own chip-select, so it's fast but uses more pins.
I2C is two shared open-drain wires, SCL and SDA, where each device has a 7-bit address and acknowledges every byte, so it scales to many devices but runs slower, typically 100 to 400 kilohertz."
Quick check. Which of the three protocols has no clock wire between the devices?
I2C versus SPI differences. The question: What is the difference between I2C and SPI?
I2C and SPI both move bytes between a main chip (the controller) and helper chips, using a shared clock. They differ in how a device is picked and how wires are driven.
SPI gives each device its own select wire and drives every wire hard, so it is fast but uses more pins.
I2C puts the device's address on the data wire and lets a resistor pull the wires high, so it uses two wires but is slower.
In a room of people, SPI is tapping one person on the shoulder and then speaking quickly. It is fast, but each person needs their own tap, and an empty chair never answers.
I2C is calling out a name to the whole room and waiting for that person to say "yes." It is slower, but needs no private line, and silence means the person is missing.
SPI's pin count grows linearly with the number of targets while I2C stays flat.
Daisy-chaining (for parts that support it) flattens SPI too, but the whole chain is read or written as one long shift register. See "SPI daisy-chaining explained".
Chip select: a dedicated wire that wakes up one SPI device. Address: a number sent on the shared wires that picks one I2C device ("I2C, SPI and UART: how each works").
ACK: the receiver's reply bit meaning "I got that." SPI has none. Pull-up resistor: a resistor that lifts an I2C wire to high when no device pulls it low.
It makes the climb from low to high slow. Full duplex: data flowing both ways at once, as in SPI.
Read 14 bytes from a sensor.
On I2C at 400 kilohertz, it is 14 data bytes plus 3 overhead bytes (the address, the register number, the address again; a register is a numbered slot), at 9 clock ticks each.
So 17 times 9 = 153 ticks, about 382 microseconds. On SPI at 10 megahertz, it is 1 command byte plus 14 data bytes at 8 ticks each, 120 ticks, or 12 microseconds.
That is about 30 times faster, at the cost of a select wire per device. That is the whole idea.
"SPI is four-plus wires, push-pull, full duplex and fast, but every extra device costs a chip-select pin.
I2C is two shared open-drain wires with pull-ups, devices selected by address, half duplex and slower, but it adds ACK, multi-master and clock stretching.
So I2C scales better in pins, SPI scales better in speed. I'd use I2C for many slow sensors and SPI for flash, displays, or high-rate ADCs."
Quick check. How are devices selected on an I2C bus compared with SPI?
Why SPI is faster than I2C. The question: Which is faster? Why?
SPI is faster than I2C for two reasons.
First, SPI drives its wires hard in both directions, while I2C drives a wire down firmly but lets a resistor pull it back up, and that climb is slow.
Second, I2C carries more extra bits around each byte: an address and a confirmation bit. Together these let SPI run at tens of MHz, while I2C tops out near 1 megahertz.
Picture a bucket whose water level is the wire's voltage. A big drain empties it fast, which is a device pulling the wire low.
I2C refills it through a thin hose, the pull-up resistor, so the level creeps up slowly. SPI has both a big drain and a big hose, so it fills and empties fast.
A thicker hose helps, but it wastes more water whenever the drain is open.
When the device's switch is closed it pulls the line low quickly (a transistor, ohms).
When it opens, only R p is left to charge C b , so the rise is an exponential with time constant R pC b .
The fall is fast, the rise is slow, which is why I2C waveforms look asymmetric.
Push-pull: an output that actively drives the wire both high and low. SPI uses it. Open-drain: an output that can only pull the wire low.
I2C uses it ("Advantages of open-drain outputs"). Pull-up resistor: the resistor that lifts an I2C wire to high ("I2C pull-ups: why and how to size").
Bus capacitance: the electrical "bucket size" of the wires, pins and traces that must be charged ("What is I2C bus capacitance").
Rise time: how long a signal takes to climb from low to high. Overhead: bits on the wire that are not data, such as the address and confirmation bits.
A good estimate is that the rise time is about 0. 85 times R times C . An I2C bus with a 4. 7 kilohms pull-up and 100 picofarads of capacitance gives 0.
85 times 4700 times 100 picofarads about 400 nanoseconds (billionths of a second). The limit for 400 kilohertz mode is 300 nanoseconds, so this is too slow.
An SPI output with about 30 ohms on the same capacitance gives roughly 2. 5 nanoseconds. That is the whole idea.
"SPI is faster for two reasons. First, its push-pull outputs drive both edges hard, so you can clock at tens of MHz. I2C's rising edge is an RC charge through a pull-up, about 0.
85 R pC b , which caps it around 100 kilohertz to 1 megahertz. Second, I2C has more overhead: 9 clocks per byte plus an address and often a register byte.
So a 14-byte read is roughly 380 microseconds on 400 kilohertz I2C versus 12 microseconds on 10 megahertz SPI."
