How chips talk to each other. The question: How do different chips talk to each other?
For two chips to exchange data, they must agree on four things. First, what voltages mean 1 and 0, so each chip can read the other. Second, when to read each bit.
Third, who a message is for, and where it starts. Fourth, what the bytes mean. I2C, SPI and UART are just different ways of settling the middle two.
The meaning part is usually a table of numbered registers.
Think of a phone call between two people. First they must hear each other clearly. Then they must talk at a pace both can follow.
They must also know who is calling whom, especially on a party line. Finally, they must speak a language both understand.
A bus fault is debugged the same way, one layer at a time.
Each box translates between layers.
Firmware sees a function call; the peripheral sees register writes and a state machine; the wire sees voltages; the sensor sees bits that select a register.
A failure in any box looks like "the sensor does not work", so debugging means checking each layer in turn.
Logic level: the voltage range that counts as a 1 or a 0 ("What logic levels are"). Common ground: both chips share the same 0 volts reference.
Clock: a tick that tells the receiver when each bit is valid, or the agreed bit speed if there is no clock wire.
Address: a number that picks which device on a shared bus should answer. Register: a numbered storage slot in a chip that holds a setting or a result.
Interrupt line: an extra wire a chip uses to say "something happened." A bus alone can't do that.
A microcontroller reads a temperature sensor at I2C address 0x48 ("0x" marks a number written in base 16, hexadecimal).
It sends that address, then the register number 0, then reads back two bytes: 0x0C and 0x80. Together they make 0x0C80, which is 12 times 256 plus 128 equals 3200 .
The datasheet (the maker's spec sheet) says each count is 1/128 degrees Celsius, so the temperature is 3200 over 128 equals 25. 0 degrees Celsius.
The wires carried only bytes; the datasheet gave them meaning. That is the whole idea.
"Chips talk by agreeing on four layers. Electrical: compatible logic levels and a shared ground.
Timing: either a shared clock like SPI and I2C, or an agreed baud rate with start bits like UART. Framing: a chip-select or an address to say who a message is for.
And meaning: usually a register map, so reading a sensor means writing a register address then reading bytes back.
I pick the bus by data rate, pin count, device count and distance."
Quick check. Which of the following must two chips share for logic levels to be meaningful?
Asynchronous versus synchronous communication. The question: What is the difference between asynchronous vs synchronous communication? What are the tradeoffs?
Every receiver must decide when to read each bit. Synchronous links, like SPI and I2C, send a clock along with the data, and the receiver reads on the clock's tick.
Asynchronous links, like UART, have no clock wire.
Both sides agree on a speed beforehand, a start bit marks the beginning of each byte, and the receiver counts time with its own clock.
Picture two rowers. In the synchronous case, a coach beats a drum and both follow it, so they stay together at any speed. In the asynchronous case, there is no drum.
Each wears a watch, they start on the same signal, and each counts strokes by their own watch.
If the watches differ a little, they stay together briefly and drift apart over a long stretch. That is why asynchronous bytes are short, and each starts with a fresh signal.
Synchronous. Data changes at falling clock edges and is sampled at the rising edges (vertical lines).
Setup and hold are naturally half a clock period each, and if the clock slows down the data slows down with it. The sampling point is tied to the data by construction.
Synchronous: sender and receiver share a clock, and bits are read on its ticks ("I2C, SPI and UART: how each works"). Asynchronous: no shared clock.
The receiver times each bit with its own oscillator. Baud rate: the agreed number of bits per second on an asynchronous line.
Start and stop bit: extra bits framing each asynchronous byte, a 0 at the start and a 1 at the end. Oscillator: the circuit that makes a chip's clock tick.
Quartz-crystal ones are accurate; cheap built-in ones drift.
A common UART byte (8N1) is 1 start bit, 8 data bits and 1 stop bit, 10 bits in all, so only 80% are data. The receiver reads the last bit 9. 5 bit lengths after the byte begins.
If its clock runs 5% fast, it reads 9. 5 times 0. 05 = 0. 475 of a bit early, almost half a bit, so it is near failing. The limit is 0. 5 over 9. 5 about 5. 3 % .
That is the whole idea.
"Synchronous means the sender and receiver share a clock, so the receiver samples on that clock's edge. SPI and I2C work this way.
It's fast and low overhead but costs a clock wire and has setup and hold timing to meet.
Asynchronous, like UART, has no clock wire: both sides agree on a baud rate, a start bit resynchronizes the receiver, and it samples each bit with its own clock.
That saves a wire but adds about 20% overhead and needs both clocks within a few percent."
Quick check. What is the defining difference between synchronous and asynchronous serial communication?
What logic levels are. The question: What are logic levels?
In real hardware, 0 and 1 are voltage ranges, not exact voltages. A sending chip promises to keep its 1 above one voltage and its 0 below another.
A receiver accepts anything above a threshold as a 1 and anything below a lower threshold as a 0.
The receiver's rules are looser than the sender's promises, which leaves room for noise (small unwanted wiggles).
Imagine judging a room cold or warm by a thermometer. You call it cold below 15 degrees Celsius and warm above 25 degrees Celsius, and between them you are unsure.
A heating company promises its warm rooms are at least 28 degrees Celsius and its cold ones at most 12 degrees Celsius.
Their promises beat your rules by 3 degrees, so small thermometer errors can't fool you.
What a 3. 3 volts LVTTL-style driver guarantees (left) against what a receiver demands (right). The driver promises at least 2. 4 volts for a 1 and at most 0.
4 volts for a 0; the receiver only needs 2. 0 volts and 0. 8 volts. The red arrows are the noise margins, 0. 4 volts each.
The orange band is the undefined region, where nothing is guaranteed.
Logic level: the voltage range that counts as a 1 or a 0. V OH and V OL : the lowest voltage a sender guarantees for a 1, and the highest it guarantees for a 0.
V IH and V IL : the lowest voltage a receiver requires to read a 1, and the highest it accepts as a 0. Noise margin: the gap between the sender's promise and the receiver's need.
Undefined region: input voltages between V IL and V IH , where the reading is not guaranteed. Floating input: a pin connected to nothing, so its voltage drifts.
In a common 3. 3 volts chip family (chips built to the same rules), a sender guarantees at least 2. 4 volts for a 1 and at most 0. 4 volts for a 0. The receiver needs at least 2.
0 volts for a 1 and at most 0. 8 volts for a 0. That is 0. 4 volts of noise margin on each side. Now connect a 1. 8 volts sensor to it. Its high of 1. 8 volts is below 2.
0 volts, so it may not read as a 1. That is the whole idea.
"Logic levels are the voltage ranges treated as 0 and 1.
A driver guarantees V OL at most and V OH at least; a receiver requires V IL at most for a 0 and V IH at least for a 1, with an undefined gap in between.
The link works if V OH is above V IH and V OL is below V IL ; the leftover is noise margin.
CMOS thresholds scale with the supply, roughly 30% and 70% of V DD , so mixed-voltage systems need level checks."
Quick check. Which statement correctly describes V OH and V IH ?
Common logic levels and standards. The question: What are some common logic levels?
Logic chips come in standard voltage families: 5 volts, 3. 3 volts, 2. 5 volts, 1. 8 volts and 1. 2 volts. Each defines what voltage counts as a 1 and a 0.
Two chips can be wired together only if the sender's high is high enough for the receiver, and the receiver's pin can survive the sender's voltage.
The first makes a link unreliable; the second can destroy a pin. A level shifter translates.
Think of traveling with electrical appliances. A 230 volts appliance in a 120 volts socket gets too little voltage and doesn't work properly.
A 120 volts appliance in a 230 volts socket burns out. Logic voltages behave the same way. One quirk: a 3.
3 volts output can still drive some 5 volts inputs, since they need only 2. 0 volts.
Input threshold bands for the common single-ended families. Green is "reads as 1", blue is "reads as 0", orange is the undefined band. Note that 5 volts TTL and 3.
3 volts LVTTL share the same thresholds (0. 8 volts and 2. 0 volts), while the CMOS families scale with their supply. The numbers beside each bar are V IL and V IH .
TTL levels: fixed thresholds of 0. 8 volts for a 0 and 2. 0 volts for a 1, whatever the supply. Many 3. 3 volts parts use the same numbers.
CMOS levels: thresholds set as fractions of the supply, about 30% and 70%. Absolute maximum rating: the highest voltage a pin can take without damage, often about 0.
3 volts above its supply. 5 volts-tolerant: a pin on a lower-voltage chip that is rated to accept 5 volts.
Level shifter: a part that translates signals between two voltage families. Supply voltage: the voltage that powers a chip. A family's name, such as 3. 3 volts, is its supply.
A 3. 3 volts output reaches about 3. 1 volts under load. Feed it to a 5 volts CMOS input that needs 70% of 5 volts, which is 3. 5 volts. It falls 0. 4 volts short: the link fails.
Feed it to a 5 volts TTL-compatible input that needs only 2. 0 volts, and it passes with 1. 1 volts to spare. A 5 volts output into a 3.
3 volts pin that is not 5 volts-tolerant can damage it. That is the whole idea.
"The main single-ended ones are 5 volts TTL and CMOS, 3. 3 volts LVTTL/LVCMOS, 2. 5 volts, 1. 8 volts and 1. 2 volts. TTL thresholds are fixed, 0. 8 volts and 2.
0 volts; CMOS thresholds are roughly 30% and 70% of the supply. So 3.
3 volts can drive 5 volts TTL-compatible inputs but not 5 volts CMOS inputs, and anything lower than the receiver's supply needs a translator.
Then there are non-logic-supply standards: RS-232 at plus and minus several volts, and differential RS-485, CAN and LVDS."
Quick check. What input thresholds do 5 volts TTL and 3. 3 volts LVTTL share?
What I2C is and what it stands for. The question: What is I2C? What does it stand for?
I2C stands for Inter-Integrated Circuit. It is a bus (a shared set of wires), just two wires, that lets many chips on one board talk to a controller.
One wire carries a clock, SCL, and one carries data, SDA. Every chip has its own address, so the controller says whom it wants and only that chip answers.
It is slow, from 100 kilohertz up to about 1 megahertz, so it suits sensors, memories and clocks that need few bytes.
Picture a single street with numbered houses. A delivery truck uses two lanes: one for the beat, one for packages.
The truck calls out a house number, and only that resident answers "got it". Each lane has a gate that anyone can pull down but nobody can push up.
A spring lifts it again when everyone lets go, so no two houses can ever fight over it. The spring is the pull-up resistor.
Every device taps into the same two lines. There is one pull-up per line for the whole bus (not per device), and the addresses (for example 0x48, 0x50, 0x68) tell targets apart.
The controller is simply the device that starts the transaction.
SCL and SDA: the clock wire and the data wire of the bus. Open-drain: an output that can only pull the wire low. A resistor makes it high ("Advantages of open-drain outputs").
Pull-up resistor: the resistor that lifts the wires to high when nobody pulls them low ("I2C pull-ups: why and how to size").
Controller and target: the chip that starts a transfer, and the chip that answers. Older documents say master and slave. Address: a 7-bit number that picks one target.
ACK: a reply bit from the receiver meaning "got it."
A controller writes the value 0x3 amps to a chip at address 0x48 ("0x" marks a hexadecimal, base-16, number).
It sends a START signal, then the address 0x48 plus a "write" bit, and the chip replies with an ACK.
Then it sends the byte 0x3 amps, gets another ACK, and finishes with a STOP signal. The two bytes take 18 clock ticks, about 180 microseconds at 100 kilohertz.
That is the whole idea.
"I2C stands for Inter-Integrated Circuit.
It's a two-wire serial bus, SCL for the clock and SDA for data, both open-drain with pull-up resistors, invented by Philips for connecting chips on one board.
Each device has an address, the controller sends START, address and read/write bit, the target ACKs, then bytes follow, each ACKed, until STOP.
It's slow, 100 to 400 kilohertz typically, but lets many devices share two pins."
Quick check. What does I2C stand for?
How I2C transactions work step by step. The question: How does it work? Explain its operation.
An I2C transaction is a fixed script on the two wires. The controller signals START, sends the address of the chip it wants plus a read-or-write bit, and waits for an acknowledge.
Then bytes flow, each followed by an acknowledge bit, and the controller signals STOP. Both wires sit high when idle. Data may change only while the clock is low.
START and STOP are the only exceptions.
Picture a drive-through window. You pull up, which is START. You name the window you want (the address) and hear "OK" (the acknowledge).
You say your order, one item at a time, and each gets an "OK". On your last item you say "that's all", which is a NACK. Then you drive off, which is STOP.
On a real bus, "OK" is the receiver pulling the data wire low for one clock tick.
A read-direction frame.

The address byte (0x48, 1001000) with R = 1 is driven by the controller; on the ninth clock the target ACKs; then the target drives the first data byte (0x0C here) and the controller's ACK would follow.
Look for the rule: every SDA transition sits in an SCL-low window.
START and STOP: special moves of the data wire while the clock is high. START begins a transaction and STOP ends it.
Address byte: the 7-bit address of the chip, plus one bit saying read or write ("I2C address and data frames").
Read/write bit: 0 means the controller will write, and 1 means it will read. ACK and NACK: the receiver's reply on the ninth clock.
ACK is the data wire pulled low, and NACK is left high ("I2C ACK and NACK"). Repeated START: a new START without a STOP before it, which keeps the bus claimed.

To read two bytes from register 0 of the chip at address 0x48, the controller sends START, 0x90 (hexadecimal for the address with the write bit), register number 0x00, a repeated START, and 0x91 (the address with the read bit).
Then it clocks in two bytes. That is 5 bytes at 9 clock ticks each, 45 ticks, about 112 microseconds at 400 kilohertz.
The controller ACKs the first byte, NACKs the last, then sends STOP. That is the whole idea.
"Both lines idle high.
The controller pulls SDA low while SCL is high, that's START, then clocks out a 7-bit address and a read/write bit, MSB first, changing SDA only while SCL is low.
On the ninth clock the addressed device pulls SDA low to ACK. Data bytes follow, each with its own ACK; on a read the controller NACKs the last byte.
A STOP, SDA rising while SCL is high, ends it. Register reads use a repeated START between the pointer write and the read."
Quick check. Which event on the lines is a START condition?
Interfacing an MCU with I2C targets. The question: How interface with slaves?
To use an I2C chip, you connect its two wires to the microcontroller's I2C pins, add pull-up resistors, and set the speed.
Each chip is like a small set of numbered registers that hold its settings and readings. You address the chip, tell it which register you want, then read or write bytes.
The chip's datasheet is the manual. The first thing to do when a new board first powers up is read a fixed identification register, which proves the wiring works.
Picture a filing cabinet with numbered drawers. To read a drawer, you first tell the cabinet "open drawer 3", and then you ask for its contents.
Reading several neighboring drawers in one go is faster than opening each one separately. The note on the cabinet saying what is in each drawer is the datasheet.
Targets are told apart only by address; the controller needs no extra pins as devices are added.
The addresses shown (0x48, 0x50, 0x68) are common defaults for LM75-style temperature sensors, 24-series EEPROMs and DS3231-style RTCs; always confirm in the datasheet.
Target address: the 7-bit number that picks one chip on the bus. Datasheets sometimes quote it with the read/write bit attached ("I2C address and data frames").
Register: a numbered slot in the chip holding a setting or a measurement.
Pull-up resistor: the resistor that lifts each wire to high when nobody pulls it low ("I2C pull-ups: why and how to size").
Burst read: reading several consecutive registers in a single transaction. ID register: a register with a fixed value, often called WHO AM I, used to check the connection.
Bus scan: trying every address and noting which ones answer with an ACK.
You want six consecutive registers from a chip. Reading them one at a time costs 4 bytes each: the address, the register number, the address again, and one data byte.
That is 24 bytes at 9 clock ticks, 216 ticks. One burst read is 3 overhead bytes plus 6 data bytes, 9 bytes, or 81 ticks. That is 2.
7 times faster, and all six values come from the same sample. That is the whole idea.
"All targets share SDA and SCL with one pull-up per line, and each is addressed by its 7-bit address.
In firmware I configure the MCU's I2C peripheral for 100 or 400 kilohertz, then for a sensor I write the register pointer, do a repeated START with the read bit, and read the data bytes.
I read an ID register first to prove the wiring and address, check for NACKs and timeouts, and use burst reads for efficiency."
Quick check. How does an I2C controller choose which target to talk to?
How many targets fit on an I2C bus. The question: How many slaves can there be?
There are two limits on how many chips an I2C bus can hold. The address limit: a 7-bit address gives 128 codes, but 16 are reserved, so 112 chips at most.
The electrical limit is tighter.
Every chip pin and centimeter of wiring adds a little capacitance (stored charge), and the pull-up resistor must fill all of it each time a wire rises.
Too much makes the rise too slow, and that usually stops you first.
Picture a bridge with 112 numbered parking spots and a weight limit. Each parked car adds weight, and so does every meter of road.
You hit the weight limit long before the last spot fills. The spots are the addresses, and the weight is the capacitance.
The 7-bit space has 128 codes. The lowest 8 (0x00 to 0x07) and the highest 8 (0x78 to 0x7 farads) are reserved for special functions, leaving the green 112 for ordinary targets.
In 10-bit addressing the 0x78 to 0x7B block is the prefix that announces a two-byte address.
Usable addresses: the 112 of the 128 possible 7-bit codes that ordinary chips may use.
Bus capacitance: the total load on a wire from pins, traces and connectors, in picofarads (pF). The spec caps it at 400 picofarads ("What is I2C bus capacitance").
Pull-up resistor: the resistor that lifts a wire to high, whose value is limited on both sides ("I2C pull-ups: why and how to size").
Rise time: how long a wire takes to climb from low to high. It must stay under 300 nanoseconds at 400 kilohertz.
Multiplexer: a chip that connects one of several side-branches to the main bus, so each branch carries only its own load.
Suppose each chip pin adds 10 picofarads, and traces and connectors add 60 picofarads. At the 400 picofarads limit, that is (400-60) over 10 equals 34 chips.
With a 25% margin, 300 picofarads, it is (300-60) over 10 equals 24 chips. At 400 kilohertz and 3.
3 volts, no pull-up value works above about 366 picofarads: one strong enough to rise in time draws more current than the chips can pull low.
So 300 picofarads is the sensible limit. Shared default addresses can limit you sooner. That is the whole idea.
"Addressing-wise, 7 bits give 128 codes, 16 reserved, so 112 targets; 10-bit addressing gives about a thousand.
But the real limit is electrical: total bus capacitance is capped at 400 picofarads, and each device and each centimetre of trace adds capacitance, which slows the rise time.
In practice that's around 20 to 40 devices. Beyond that, or when addresses collide, you use address pins, an I2C multiplexer or a bus buffer."
Quick check. What is the bus-capacitance limit for Standard and Fast mode I2C?
When an I2C bus needs multiple controllers. The question: When would you need more masters?
Most I2C buses have one controller, the chip that starts every transfer. But I2C is designed so that two or more controllers can share a bus.
That helps when two processors both need the same sensors.
If two start at the same moment, the bus settles who goes first by itself, with no damage and no lost data for the winner.
Imagine two people starting to talk at once in a meeting. Each speaks one word at a time and listens while doing so.
If you meant to stay silent for a word but hear someone else speaking, you know they are saying something different. You stop and wait, and the other person is never disturbed.
In I2C, speaking is pulling the wire low, and staying silent is letting it go. Speaking always wins.
Two controllers start together and send the first address bits 1, 0, 1, .. (A) and 1, 0, 0, .. (B). The first two bits match, so neither notices anything.
In the third bit A releases SDA (1) while B pulls it low (0). The bus follows B, so at the rising SCL edge A reads 0 where it sent 1: arbitration lost.
From then on A stays off the bus (dashed) while B continues with the bit it was sending, completely undisturbed.
Controller: the chip that starts a transfer and runs the clock. Older documents call it the master.
Arbitration: how two controllers that start together decide who goes on, by comparing what each sends with what the wire shows.
Wired-AND: the wire is low if any chip pulls it low, and high only if all let go. Bus free: the quiet period after a transfer ends with a STOP, when any controller may start.
Sensor hub: a small low-power chip that reads sensors on behalf of a main processor.
Controller A sends the address 0x48 (hexadecimal), which is 1001000 in binary. Controller B sends 0x44, which is 1000100. The first three bits match, so neither notices anything.
On the fourth bit, A releases the wire to send a 1, while B pulls it low to send a 0. The wire reads 0. A sees it sent a 1 but read a 0, so it stops and waits.
B carries on with no damage. The lower address wins. That is the whole idea.
"You need multiple controllers when two devices both need to start transactions on the same bus: a main processor plus a sensor hub, a host and a charger sharing a fuel gauge, redundant controllers.
I2C handles it with arbitration: both drive open-drain lines; whoever releases a 1 but reads back a 0 has lost, stops, and waits for a STOP, while the winner continues uncorrupted.
SCL is wired-AND too, so clocks synchronize. But it adds complexity, so I'd prefer an interrupt line or separate buses when possible."
Quick check. Two I2C controllers start simultaneously. How does a controller detect that it lost arbitration?
I2C address and data frames. The question: Explain address/data frames.
Everything on an I2C bus is built from 9-clock units: 8 bits plus one acknowledge bit. The first byte after START is the address frame.
It holds the 7-bit address of the chip and one bit saying read or write, and the chip that matches answers with an ACK. Every later byte is a data frame. Bytes go on until STOP.
Think of a delivery handed over in stages. The first item is the label: which house it is for, and whether you are delivering or collecting.
Every item after that is parcel contents. At each handoff, the receiver says "thanks" with one extra beat, the acknowledge. The bus fixes the label's meaning.
The contents are private between sender and house, and nothing says how many items remain.
A write to address 0x50 with data 0xA5. Read the SDA row left to right: the bits after START are 1010000 (0x50), then 0 for write, then the target pulls SDA low for the ACK.
The next eight bits, 10100101, are the data byte 0xA5, and the target ACKs again. SDA changes only while SCL is low.
Address frame: the first byte after START, with the 7-bit address and the read/write bit. Data frame: any later byte, 8 data bits followed by an acknowledge bit.
MSB first: the most significant bit (the leftmost, worth the most) goes out first. Read/write bit: the lowest bit of the address byte.
0 means the controller writes and 1 means it reads.
7-bit vs 8-bit notation: a datasheet may quote the address byte as sent on the wire, such as 0x90, instead of the 7-bit address, 0x48.
Register pointer: by habit, the first data byte after a write address picks a register inside the chip.
A chip has 7-bit address 0x48 (hexadecimal), which is 1001000 in binary.
The byte on the wire is the address shifted left one place (which doubles it), with the read/write bit added at the end. That gives 0x90 for a write and 0x91 for a read.
A datasheet that says "0x90" is quoting the wire byte. Give a software library 0x48. One address frame plus three data frames is 4 frames of 9 clocks, 36 clock ticks.
That is the whole idea.
"Each frame is nine clocks.
The address frame is 7 address bits MSB first plus a read/write bit, with the target pulling SDA low on the ninth clock to ACK; address 0x48 becomes 0x90 for a write and 0x91 for a read.
Data frames are 8 bits MSB first plus an ACK, driven by the controller on a write and by the target on a read. There's no length field: bytes continue until STOP.
What the bytes mean, such as a register pointer, is defined by the target."
Quick check. In the address frame, which bit is sent last (just before the ACK clock)?
Changing or resolving an I2C target address. The question: How can you change a slave's address?
Two I2C chips must not answer to the same address, or both respond at once and corrupt each other. Sometimes you can pick different addresses with pins on the chip.
Some chips let software write a new address. If a chip's address is fixed, you can keep the two apart with a multiplexer or a second bus instead.
Imagine two houses on a street with the same number. The mail carrier can't tell them apart. You have several fixes. Choose different numbers when building, which is the pins.
Repaint one number later, which is a programmable register. Or put the houses on different streets, which is a multiplexer or a second bus.
Repainting has a catch: if the paint washes off whenever the power goes off, you must repaint each time.
The same part number twice. ADC #1 has ADDR tied to ground (0x48); ADC #2 has ADDR tied to VDD (0x49).
For a part like TI's ADS1115, tying ADDR to SDA or SCL gives 0x4 amps and 0x4B, so four copies can share a bus.
(Values quoted from the commonly used device family; confirm in the datasheet.)
Address-select pin: a pin you tie to ground, supply or another level to choose one of a few addresses for the chip ("I2C address and data frames").
Default address: the address a chip answers to right after power-up. Programmable address: a register where firmware can write a new address.
Volatile: lost when power is removed, so it must be set again at every start. Enable pin: a pin that keeps a chip switched off until you release it.
Multiplexer: a chip that connects one of several side-branches to the main bus ("How many targets fit on an I2C bus").
Four identical sensors all answer at 0x29 when powered. Each has an enable pin. Hold three disabled and release the first. Write its new address, 0x30.
Release the second and write 0x31, and so on. Now all four have unique addresses, though you must repeat the routine at every power-up.
A fixed-address chip needs a multiplexer instead. With three address pins, each tied high or low, a chip has 2 to the 3 equals 8 addresses.
Behind an 8-channel multiplexer, you can reach 8 times 8 equals 64 such chips. That is the whole idea.
"Usually you don't change it in firmware; you set it in hardware. Many parts have address pins strapped to ground, supply, SDA or SCL to pick among two to eight addresses.
Some parts have a programmable address register, so with identical parts you use their enable pins to bring them up one at a time and give each a new address.
If neither is possible, isolate them with an I2C multiplexer or a second bus. SMBus ARP and I3C also assign addresses dynamically."
Quick check. Which is the most common way to give two identical I2C sensors different addresses on the same bus?
I2C ACK and NACK. The question: Explain NACK/ACK.
After every byte on an I2C bus, there is one extra clock tick, the ninth. On it, the receiver of the byte answers. If it accepted the byte, it pulls the data wire low.
That is an ACK. If it does nothing, the wire stays high, which is a NACK. A NACK is not a message anyone sends. It is silence, and it is not always an error.
Think of a teacher taking roll. The teacher calls a name, and a raised hand means "here". No hand means nothing happened, but you can't tell why.
The student might be absent, might not have heard, or might be busy. I2C works the same way.
A raised hand is the receiver pulling the wire low, and silence is the wire's pull-up resistor (which lifts it whenever nobody pulls down) leaving it high.
Two bytes on the bus.

In the first byte (bits 1, 0, 1 shown), the target pulls SDA low on the ninth clock: the SDA-bus row dips low while the controller row shows it released (dashed) and the target row shows it driving low: ACK.
In the second byte nobody drives on the ninth clock, so the bus rises to the pull-up level: NACK. Then the controller issues STOP.
ACK: the receiver pulls the data wire low on the ninth clock, meaning "got it." NACK: the wire stays high on the ninth clock, meaning nobody confirmed.
Receiver: whichever chip just received the byte. It makes the reply. On a read, that is the controller.
Bus scan: sending each address and noting which chips ACK, to find what is on the bus.
ACK polling: repeatedly addressing a memory chip until it ACKs, which shows its internal write has finished.
A NACK after the address means no chip answered: wrong address, no power, or missing pull-ups. A NACK after a byte the controller wrote means the chip rejected it.
At the end of a read, the controller NACKs the last byte on purpose, so the chip lets go of the wire and a STOP can follow. A memory chip busy writing NACKs its address.
One poll takes about 11 clock ticks, 110 microseconds at 100 kilohertz, so a 5 milliseconds write is polled about 45 times. That is the whole idea.
"The ninth clock after every byte is the acknowledge. The receiver of the byte pulls SDA low for an ACK; if nobody pulls it, the pull-up leaves it high, which is a NACK.

A NACK after the address means no device answered; after a written data byte it means the target rejected it; and on a read the controller deliberately NACKs the last byte so the target lets go of SDA for the STOP.
EEPROMs use NACK on their address while busy, so you poll until it ACKs."

I2C clock stretching. The question: Explain clock stretching.
Clock stretching is when an I2C target holds the clock wire low to tell the controller "wait, I'm not ready."
It works because the clock wire is shared by all chips, and any chip can pull it low. The wire goes high only when everyone lets go.
The controller must therefore release the clock, then check that it really went high before going on. It suits slow targets but costs speed.
Imagine a teacher dictating a sentence one word at a time to a student who writes. The teacher says each word and moves on at a steady pace.
If the student needs more time, they hold up a hand, and the teacher waits until it goes down. The teacher must look up to see whether the hand is still raised.
The hand is the target pulling the clock low.
The orange row is the target. It begins holding SCL low just after a falling edge (period 2).
The controller (blue) releases SCL at period 3 (dashed means "released"), but the bus row (bottom) stays low until the target releases at period 5: the stretch.
SDA does not change during it. Only at period 5 does the bus clock rise and the controller can continue; its measured high time starts then.
Clock stretching: a target holding the clock wire low to make the controller wait.
Wired-AND clock: the clock wire is low if any chip pulls it low, and high only if all release it ("Advantages of open-drain outputs").
Release and check: the controller lets go of the clock, then reads it back to see whether it is really high.
Timeout: a limit on how long the controller will wait, so a stuck target can't hang everything.
Controller and target: the chip that runs the clock and starts transfers, and the chip that answers.
At 400 kilohertz, one byte takes 9 clock ticks, which is 22. 5 microseconds. Suppose the target stretches the clock 50 microseconds on every byte. Each byte now takes 72.
5 microseconds, so the effective speed is 9 bits per 72. 5 microseconds, about 124 kilohertz. A target that never lets go hangs the bus, so timeouts exist. That is the whole idea.
"Clock stretching is a target holding SCL low to make the controller wait. Because SCL is open-drain, the bus only goes high when both release it.
After releasing SCL, the controller must read it back and wait for it to actually go high before continuing.
It's used by slow targets like MCUs running an ISR or sensors mid-conversion.
The downside is lower throughput and, if a target never lets go, a hung bus, which is why SMBus has a roughly 25 to 35 milliseconds timeout."

I2C wire count and adding slaves. The question: How many pins/wires are needed? What if I have more slaves?
An I2C bus needs two signal wires, SDA for data and SCL for the clock, plus a shared ground and pull-up resistors. Adding another chip costs no extra wires.
It taps onto the same two lines, and the controller picks it by its address. So six sensors still cost two microcontroller pins. But it is not unlimited.
Addresses must not collide, and each chip adds capacitance (stored charge the pull-ups must fill), which slows every rise from low to high.
Think of a single bus route with many stops. Adding a stop needs no new road. Each stop has a number, and the driver calls the one they want. Two limits remain.
There are only 112 usable numbers, and two stops with the same number cause confusion. And every stop adds load, which slows the bus down.
Three slaves and the MCU share the same two signal wires. Adding a fourth sensor means tapping the same lines again, with no new MCU pin.
(The full drawing with pull-ups and ground is in "Drawing an I2C bus connection".)

There are 112 usable values. Address collision: two chips with the same address, so both answer at once.
Bus capacitance: the load from all pins, connectors and traces, measured in picofarads (pF) ("What is I2C bus capacitance").
Multiplexer: a chip that connects one of several side-branches to the main bus ("How many targets fit on an I2C bus").

That is the whole idea.

More slaves go on the same two wires and are picked by their 7-bit address, so there are no extra pins.
The limits are address collisions, which you fix with address straps or an I2C mux, and the 400 picofarads bus capacitance limit, which you fix with smaller pull-ups, a slower clock, or a buffer."

Drawing an I2C bus connection. The question: How do I make the connections? Draw it out.
To draw an I2C bus, put the controller on one side with two pins, SCL and SDA.
Run two straight lines from those pins to every other chip, connecting SCL to SCL and SDA to SDA, straight through (unlike UART, where one chip's send pin goes to the other's receive pin).
At one point, add one resistor from each line up to the supply, called a pull-up. Tie all grounds together, and strap address pins so no two chips share an address.

A pipe is full only when every valve is closed, and the thin tap refills it. That is a pull-up resistor and open-drain outputs.
Nobody pushes water in, so no two devices can fight. The taps appear once for the whole bus.

At one point on the bus I add one pull-up resistor from each line to the supply, around 2. 2 to 4. 7 kilohms at 3. 3 volts.

I2C pull-ups: why and how to size. The question: Why are pullups needed? How do you spec them?
I2C devices can only pull a wire down to ground or let go. Nothing on the bus pushes the wire up.
A pull-up resistor from the wire to the supply does that, giving the high level and lifting the wire after a device lets go. Its value is a balance.
Too small, and a device cannot pull the wire low enough. Too large, and the wire rises too slowly.
Picture a heavy door with a return spring. Anyone can push the door shut, and the spring swings it open when they let go.
A stronger spring opens the door quickly but makes it hard to hold shut.
A weaker spring is easy to push against, but the door drifts open slowly, and a heavier door is slower still.
The spring is the pull-up resistor, and the door's weight is the bus capacitance.

What is I2C bus capacitance. The question: What is bus capacitance?
Bus capacitance is the total capacitance between an I2C wire and ground. Every chip pin, centimeter of trace, connector and length of cable adds a little.
Capacitance is a wire's reluctance to change voltage, since charge must be moved on or off it.
The pull-up must supply that charge each time the wire rises, so more capacitance means a slower rising edge.
The I2C spec caps it at 400 picofarads (picofarads) per line for Standard and Fast mode.
Think of heating a room with a small heater. The more furniture and wall to warm, the longer it takes.
The heater is the pull-up resistor, and the stuff to warm is the capacitance. Cooling is different. Opening a big window cools the room almost at once.
That is a chip pulling the wire low: falling edges are fast, rising edges slow.

Each of SDA and SCL has its own. Pin capacitance: the small capacitance each chip pin adds, typically 2 to 10 picofarads.

What changes I2C bus capacitance. The question: How would bus capacitance change? What impacts it?
Bus capacitance is a sum, so anything you add to the line or change about its geometry moves it. Each device pin adds a few picofarads (pF, tiny units of capacitance).
The circuit-board trace adds about 1 picofarads per centimeter. Connectors and cables add more, tens of picofarads per meter for cable.
It also shifts while the system runs, such as when you plug in a module.
Think of a backpack. Everything you put in adds weight: each device, each centimeter of trace, each connector, a long cable.
Leaving some bags at the door means they don't count, which is what a multiplexer does for unused branches. The load also changes at run time as bags come and go.
For the bus, the weight is capacitance, and rise time grows with it.
Five buckets cover almost everything.
Devices and layout are fixed at design time, interconnect is fixed by the product architecture, run-time configuration varies in use, and operating conditions give the small second-order effects.
Bus capacitance ( C b ): the total capacitance from one bus wire to ground ("What is I2C bus capacitance").
Trace capacitance: the trace and the ground layer below act like the two plates of a capacitor. A longer or wider trace, or a thinner layer between them, holds more.
Dielectric: the insulating board layer between the trace and the ground layer ("Dielectrics and permittivity").
Multiplexer: a chip that connects one side-branch at a time, hiding the capacitance of the others.
Hot-plug: connecting a module while the bus is powered, which adds its capacitance suddenly.

"Bus capacitance goes up with everything you hang on the line.
Each device pin is a few pF, the trace adds about 1 picofarads per centimetre and grows with width and shrinks with dielectric thickness, and connectors and cables add tens of pF.
It also changes at run time: hot-plugging a module or selecting a mux channel adds or removes branches, and junction capacitance depends on voltage.
I'd control it by keeping traces short, picking low-capacitance parts, isolating branches with a switch, and measuring the rise time."

Changing I2C rise time. The question: How do you increase rise time on I2C?
I2C is a two-wire connection that lets chips talk. When no chip is pulling a wire low, a resistor pulls it back up to the supply voltage.
The "rise time" is how long that climb takes. Careful: "increase the rise time", taken literally, means make the climb slower.
People almost always mean the opposite: the climb is too slow, and they want a shorter rise time. Say which one you mean, answer that usual case first, then cover the other.
Think of a bucket filled from a tap through a hose. The bucket is the wire's stored charge. A narrow hose (a big resistor) fills it slowly.
A wide hose (a small resistor) fills it fast. A bigger bucket (more wire and more chips attached) takes longer.
The analogy misses one limit: with a wider hose, a chip must swallow more current to pull the wire low.

Why I2C rise time is too slow. The question: Why would rise time be too slow on I2C?
I2C is a two-wire connection that lets chips talk. After a chip stops pulling a wire low, a resistor pulls it back up. The "rise time" is how long that climb takes.
If it is too slow, the data goes wrong, usually at higher speeds.
This page is about finding out why it is slow: either the resistor is too big, the wire holds too much charge, or an extra part on the bus adds charge or resistance.

I2C logic low not low enough. The question: If the logic low state of signal doesn't reach logic-low threshold of device, what could be happening?
On an I2C wire, a chip signals "low" by switching the wire down to ground. That switch is not perfect, so the wire sits a little above 0 volts.
The pull-up resistor keeps pushing current into the switch, and that current raises the level further.
If the wire's "low" ends up too high, the receiving chip no longer counts it as low. This page is about why that happens and how to find the cause.
Picture a tap pouring water into a sink with a partly clogged drain.
The tap is the pull-up resistor, the drain is the chip's switch, and the water level in the sink is the "low" voltage. A stronger tap pushes the level up.

Advantages of open-drain outputs. The question: What are advantages of the open-drain output drivers?
An open-drain output can only pull a wire down to ground or let go of it. It can never push the wire up.
A resistor to the supply, called a pull-up, brings the wire back up when everyone lets go. This sounds like a limit, but it is what lets many chips share one wire safely.
If two chips disagree, "low" simply wins and nothing is harmed.
Picture a cord held up by a spring, with several people each holding a handle. Anyone can pull the cord down. Nobody ever pushes it up.
When all of them let go, the spring lifts it. Two people pulling down never fight each other. The analogy shows the cost too: a spring lifts slowly, while pulling down is quick.
That is why this kind of wire is slow to go high.
Dashed segments mean "released" (the pull-up is providing the level). Whenever either device pulls low the bus is 0; it's 1 only when both release.
No time slot exists where two outputs fight.
Open-drain: an output with only a pull-down switch. It pulls low or lets go. Push-pull: an output with two switches, one that drives high and one that drives low.
Pull-up resistor: the resistor that lifts the wire high when nobody pulls it low. Contention: two outputs driving opposite levels at once, so current flows straight through both.
Wired-AND: a shared wire that is high only if every chip lets go.
Two chips share a wire on a 3. 3 volts supply. Suppose both were push-pull, and one drives high while the other drives low.
Current flows from supply to ground through both switches. If those switches have about 25 ohms and 20 ohms, that is 3. 3 over 45 about 73 milliamps. That can damage the chips.
Now make both open-drain with a 2. 2 kilohms pull-up. The worst case is the pull-up current through a chip pulling low: 3. 3 over 2200 equals 1. 5 milliamps.
That is the whole idea.
"Open-drain outputs can only pull low; a pull-up makes the high.
That gives a wired-AND, so devices can share a wire without contention: if two disagree, low simply wins, instead of a shoot-through current between a PMOS and an NMOS.
It's what enables I2C's arbitration, clock stretching and ACK. It also makes level mixing easy and tolerates hot-plug.
The cost is a slow rising edge set by R pC b and static current when the line is low."

Typical I2C logic levels. The question: What are typical logic levels?
I2C does not use fixed voltages for "0" and "1". It defines them as fractions of the supply voltage.
A chip reads a wire as low below 30% of its supply and as high above 70% of its supply. The high level itself is not driven by any chip.
It is simply the voltage of the supply the pull-up resistor is connected to.
Picture a water tank with two marks painted on its side: one at 30% of the height and one at 70%. Below the lower mark means "low". Above the upper mark means "high".
The tank's full height is the supply voltage. The pull-up decides how high the water can rise, and a chip pulling down empties it.
The blue and orange lines are the thresholds; the red line is the guaranteed output low. The vertical gap between red and orange is the low-side noise margin (0. 59 volts at 3.
3 volts, 0. 18 volts at 1. 8 volts). The gap between the dashed line and blue is the high-side margin.
Supply voltage: the voltage a chip is powered from, such as 1. 8 volts, 3. 3 volts or 5 volts. Input low and high thresholds: the limits a receiver uses to decide "low" ( 0.
3 times supply) or "high" ( 0. 7 times supply). Output low: how low a chip's pull-down gets, at most 0. 4 volts at 3 milliamps.
Pull-up rail: the supply the pull-up resistor connects to. It sets the high level. Level translator: a small circuit that lets two parts on different supply voltages share a bus.
At 3. 3 volts, the low limit is 0. 3 times 3. 3 equals 0. 99 volts and the high limit is 0. 7 times 3. 3 equals 2. 31 volts. At 5 volts the limits become 1. 5 volts and 3.
5 volts. So a 5 volts chip needs 3. 5 volts to see a high, and a 3. 3 volts pull-up cannot provide it. That is the whole idea.
"I2C levels are ratiometric: a low is below 0. 3 times the device's supply, a high is above 0. 7 times, and outputs pull low to at most 0. 4 volts at 3 milliamps.
The high level is just the pull-up rail. Common bus voltages are 3. 3 volts, 1. 8 volts and 5 volts, so at 3. 3 volts the thresholds are about 1 volts and 2. 3 volts.
The gotcha is mixing supplies, such as a 5 volts device needing 3. 5 volts to see a high, which is where level translators come in."

Typical I2C clock speeds. The question: What are typical clock speeds?
I2C runs at a few standard speeds. The common ones are 100 kilohertz ("Standard"), 400 kilohertz ("Fast") and 1 megahertz ("Fast-mode Plus").
The number is how many clock ticks per second the bus runs, and one bit moves per tick. It is a ceiling, not a promise.
The wire's slow rise, the slowest chip, and the extra bits for addressing and acknowledgments all hold the real data rate lower.
Think of a road with a posted speed limit. The limit is the clock rate. A convoy can only go as fast as its slowest car, so one slow chip slows the whole bus.
Toll booths along the way, such as the address byte and the acknowledgment after each byte, eat time too. So your real average speed ends up below the posted limit.
At 2. 2 kilohms, Standard mode tolerates 536 picofarads (so the 400 picofarads spec ceiling dominates), Fast mode 161 picofarads, and Fm+ about 64 picofarads.
So a 150 picofarads bus is a Fast-mode bus with 2.
2 kilohms; to use 1 megahertz you would need smaller resistors (which the 20 milliamps Fm+ drivers allow) or much less capacitance.
Clock frequency (SCL): ticks per second on the clock wire. One data bit moves each tick. Rise time limit: the longest allowed time for the wire to climb to high.
It is 1000 nanoseconds, 300 nanoseconds and 120 nanoseconds for the three modes above. Bus capacitance: charge the wire and parts soak up, which slows the rise.
ACK: a one-bit "got it" reply that follows every byte. Overhead: bits that carry no data, such as the address, the ACKs, and the start and stop markers.
At 100 kilohertz each tick lasts 10 microseconds. A byte takes 8 data bits plus 1 ACK bit, so 9 ticks, which is 90 microseconds. That is at most about 11,000 bytes per second.
At 400 kilohertz a byte takes 22. 5 microseconds, about 44,000 bytes per second. That is the whole idea.
"The standard speeds are 100 kilohertz Standard, 400 kilohertz Fast, 1 megahertz Fast-mode Plus, and 3. 4 megahertz High-speed, plus a 5 megahertz write-only Ultra-fast mode.
Most sensors run at 100 or 400 kilohertz.
Those are ceilings set by rise time, since the pull-up has to charge the bus capacitance within 1 microseconds, 300 nanoseconds or 120 nanoseconds, and by the slowest device.
Each byte costs nine clocks, so 400 kilohertz is at most about 44 kilobytes per second."

What SPI is and stands for. The question: What is SPI? What does it stand for?
SPI stands for Serial Peripheral Interface. It is a way for one chip, the master, to exchange data with another chip, the slave, over four wires.
A shared clock wire sets the pace, so each bit has a clear moment when it counts. The master also uses one wire to pick which slave should listen.
SPI is simple and fast, so flash memory, displays and sensors use it a lot.
Imagine two people sitting across a table, each holding a row of eight cards. A drummer beats a steady rhythm. On every beat, each person slides one card across to the other.
After eight beats, they have traded entire rows. That is SPI: sending and receiving happen on the same beats. The drummer is the clock.
To "read" from the slave, the master hands over throwaway cards and keeps whatever comes back.
MOSI carries the master's register out into the slave's; MISO carries the slave's register back into the master's. SCLK shifts both at the same instant.
CS (active low) selects this slave and frames the transfer.
Master and slave: the master controls the clock and starts every exchange. The slave answers. Newer documents say controller and peripheral.
SCLK: the clock wire, driven by the master. Every tick moves one bit. MOSI and MISO: the data wires. MOSI carries bits from master to slave. MISO carries bits back.
Chip select (CS): a wire the master pulls low to pick one slave and mark the start and end of a transfer. Synchronous: using a shared clock to time each bit.
The master holds one byte, 0xA5, and the slave holds another, 0x3C. ("0x" marks hexadecimal, a short way to write bytes.) The master pulls chip select low.
Then it sends eight clock ticks. On each tick, one bit leaves the master on MOSI while one bit leaves the slave on MISO.
After eight ticks, the master holds 0x3C and the slave holds 0xA5. Then chip select goes high. That is the whole idea.
"SPI is Serial Peripheral Interface: a synchronous, full-duplex bus with one master and one or more slaves, using SCLK, MOSI, MISO and a chip select.
It works as two shift registers in a ring: on each clock the master and slave swap one bit, so after eight clocks they've exchanged a byte.
Push-pull drivers make it fast, but there's no addressing, ACK or formal standard. The master picks the slave with CS and sets the mode (CPOL and CPHA)."
Quick check. What does SPI stand for?
How many SPI slaves. The question: How many slaves can there be?
SPI has no limit on the number of slaves. The real limits are practical. The master needs one way to pick each slave, and every added chip loads the shared wires a bit more.
So "how many" depends on how many chip selects you can make and whether the bus still works.
Think of a teacher speaking to a classroom. Everyone hears the same voice, which stands for the shared clock and data wires.
But the teacher points at one student, and only that student answers. Pointing is the chip select. The teacher is limited by how many fingers (pins) are free, not by any rule.
The analogy shows one extra rule: students who were not picked must stay silent, or their answers collide.
Independent chip-selects grow linearly; a decoder grows logarithmically (a 3-to-8 gives 8 slaves for 3 select pins); a daisy chain is flat at four wires.
At sixteen slaves it's 19, 7 and 4 pins respectively.
Chip select (CS): the per-slave wire that picks it. GPIO pin: a general-purpose pin on the microcontroller that software can switch.
Decoder: a chip that turns a binary number on a few wires into one active line out of many.
Daisy chain: slaves connected in a line, each passing data to the next, all sharing one chip select.
Tri-state: an output that can disconnect from the wire, so unselected slaves do not fight on the shared data-return wire, MISO.
The basic setup shares three wires (clock, MOSI, MISO) and gives each slave its own chip select. Eight slaves need 3 plus 8 equals 11 pins. A 3-to-8 decoder chip cuts that.
Three pins choose a number from 0 to 7, and the decoder pulls exactly one of its eight outputs low. That needs 3 plus 3 equals 6 pins, plus an enable wire.
A daisy chain needs just four wires in total. That is the whole idea.
"SPI has no addresses, so the slave count is limited by how many chip-selects I can make and how loaded the bus gets. The simple scheme is one CS per slave, costing 3 plus N pins.
If I'm short on pins I can use a decoder on the CS lines, three GPIOs for eight slaves, or daisy-chain slaves that support it so they share one CS.
The electrical limits are bus loading and making sure unselected slaves tri-state MISO."

Interfacing with SPI slaves. The question: How to interface with slaves?
Talking to an SPI slave means following a short routine that the chip's datasheet describes. SPI itself only moves bits, so each chip defines its own commands.
You set up the master to match the chip's clock mode and speed. Then you pick the chip, send a command, send or collect the data, and let go of the chip.
Picture asking a librarian for a book. You walk up (chip select goes low). You say the shelf code (the command).
Then you hold out your hands (dummy bytes), and the librarian places the book in them (the reply). You walk away (chip select goes high).
The key detail is that the librarian can only answer after hearing the code. So whatever came back while you were still speaking is meaningless. The real answer arrives afterward.
First byte on MOSI is 0x8 farads (read, address 0x0 farads); MISO is don't-care during this byte. The slave drives MISO only during the second byte, here 0x33.
CS stays low for both bytes; the master sends dummy data (don't-care) on MOSI in the second byte.
Datasheet: the chip maker's document that lists the mode, maximum speed and commands. SPI mode: which clock edge samples each bit. The master must match the chip.
Register: a numbered storage cell inside the chip that holds a setting or a reading.
Dummy byte: throwaway data the master sends just to generate clock ticks, so the slave's reply can shift back.
Chip select (CS): the wire that picks the slave and keeps the transfer together.
Say you want to read a chip's ID register at address 0x0 farads. (Numbers starting with "0x" are hexadecimal, a short way to write a byte.)
The datasheet says to set the top bit of the address to mean "read", so the command byte is 0x8 farads. Pull CS low. Send 0x8 farads.
The byte that comes back during this step means nothing. Next, send one dummy byte, 0x00. The byte that comes back now is the register's value, say 0x33. Raise CS.
That is the whole idea.
"I read the datasheet for mode, max clock, bit order and word size, and configure the master.
A transaction is: pull CS low, clock out a command, then for a write clock out data, and for a read clock out dummy bytes while capturing the reply on MISO, then raise CS.
I watch the mode matching, that the reply usually arrives a byte after the command, and that CS stays low for the whole transaction with proper timing.
With several slaves only one CS is low at a time."

Wiring an SPI bus. The question: How do I make the connections?
Wiring SPI means connecting four signal wires between the master and the slave (clock, two data wires, and chip select), plus ground and power.
The rule is simple: every wire runs from one chip's output pin to the other chip's input pin. The usual mistake is with names.
Slave pins are often labeled SDI and SDO, from the slave's own point of view, so it is easy to cross the data wires.
Think of two people talking. Each has a mouth (an output) and an ear (an input). The wiring rule is mouth to ear, never mouth to mouth.
The master's data-out wire goes to the slave's data-in pin. The slave's data-out wire comes back to the master's data-in pin.

Four signal wires: SCLK and MOSI leave the master through 33 ohms source resistors, MISO returns from the slave's SDO, and CS goes to the slave's CS with a 10 kilohms pull-up so the slave stays deselected while the master's GPIO is floating at reset.
Each chip also needs VDD and a 100 nanofarads capacitor (not drawn).
MOSI and MISO: master-out-slave-in and master-in-slave-out. These names are from the master's point of view.
SDI and SDO: data in and data out, named from the slave's own point of view. Master MOSI goes to slave SDI. Chip select (CS): the wire that picks the slave. It is active when low.
Pull-up resistor: a resistor from a wire to the supply, holding it high when nothing else drives it.
Decoupling capacitor: a small capacitor next to a chip's power pin that supplies quick bursts of current.
Connect master SCLK to slave SCLK. Connect master MOSI to slave SDI. Connect slave SDO to master MISO. Connect a spare master pin to slave CS.
Join the two grounds, and place a 100 nanofarads capacitor at each chip's power pin. Add a 10 kilohms pull-up on CS.
While the microcontroller is still starting up, its pin floats (nothing drives it high or low), and the pull-up keeps the slave from mistaking noise for a command.
Data lines need no pull-ups. That is the whole idea.

"Four wires, function to function: SCLK to SCLK, MOSI from the master's output to the slave's data input, MISO from the slave's data output to the master's input, and CS from a master GPIO to the slave's active-low select.
Common ground and a decoupling cap on each chip.
No pull-ups on the data lines since the drivers are push-pull, but a pull-up on CS keeps the slave deselected at boot, and series resistors help at high clock rates.
More slaves share the three lines and each gets its own CS."

SPI daisy-chaining explained. The question: How does daisy-chaining work?
A daisy chain connects SPI slaves one after another, like links in a chain. The master's data goes into the first chip.
Each chip passes its data on to the next, and the last chip sends it back to the master. All the chips share one clock and one chip select.
The whole chain acts like one long row of storage cells.
Imagine a line of people, each holding a card. On every beat of a drum, each person hands their card to the next person down the line.
To end up with a chosen card in every hand, you feed in the card for the farthest person first. Cards for nearer people go in later.
When a whistle blows, everyone keeps the card they hold. In SPI, that whistle is chip select going high.
SCLK and CS (top) are shared by all three devices; the data path is a single series loop: MOSI to Dev 1 to Dev 2 to Dev 3 to MISO.
Four wires from the master regardless of chain length.
Daisy chain: devices connected in series, so data passes through each one in turn. Shift register: a row of storage cells that moves every bit one place along on each clock tick.
Frame: one period with chip select low. Here it spans the whole chain. Latch: copying the collected bits into the part that drives the outputs.
It happens when chip select goes high. Chip select (CS): the shared wire that marks the frame.
Chain three chips, each holding 8 bits. You want them to end up with bytes A, B and C, in order from nearest the master to farthest. Pull CS low. Send C first, then B, then A.
That is 24 clock ticks, or 2. 4 microseconds at 10 megahertz. The first byte travels through two chips and settles in the last one.
Raise CS, and all three chips latch their bytes at the same moment. That is the whole idea.
"Daisy-chaining connects SPI slaves in series: MOSI goes into the first device, each device's output feeds the next input, and the last output returns on MISO, with SCLK and CS shared.
The chain behaves as one long shift register, so a frame is N words of clocks with CS low, the first word ends up in the last device, and the CS rising edge latches everything at once.
It saves pins and updates simultaneously, but every frame has to cover the whole chain and the parts must support it."

Typical SPI logic levels. The question: What are typical logic levels?
SPI does not define any voltage levels. The voltages are whatever the chips on the bus use. Each output drives its own supply voltage for a high and ground for a low.
When they differ, you must check each wire in its own direction, and you may need a level translator.
Imagine two people talking, each at their own volume. The supply voltage is how loud a person speaks.
A listener has a quietest sound they will still hear as a "yes", and a loudest sound they can take without being hurt.
If a loud speaker talks to a listener who can only handle quiet sounds, the listener is damaged.
If a quiet speaker talks to a listener who needs loud sounds, the message is missed.
A level translator is a go-between who repeats each message at the right volume, in both directions.
Three lines run master to slave (SCLK, MOSI, CS) and one runs the other way (MISO). The translator must be directional or auto-direction, and fast enough for the clock.
Each side's supply sets the logic levels on that side.
I/O supply: the voltage a chip's input and output pins run from. It sets that chip's high level. Input high threshold: the lowest voltage a receiver reliably reads as high.
It is often about 70% of its supply. Absolute maximum rating: the highest voltage a pin can see without damage. For many pins it is the supply plus about 0. 3 volts.
Level translator: a chip that converts signals between two supply voltages.
A 3. 3 volts microcontroller talks to a 1. 8 volts flash chip. The microcontroller's 3. 3 volts high goes into a flash pin that tolerates only about 2. 1 volts.
Going the other way, the flash's 1. 8 volts high must be read by the microcontroller, which needs 0. 7 times 3. 3 equals 2. 31 volts. So the flash's high may not be recognized.
Both directions fail, so you add a fast level translator. That is the whole idea.
"SPI defines no logic levels. It's push-pull CMOS at whatever the devices' I/O rails are, commonly 3. 3 volts, 1.
8 volts or 5 volts, with thresholds around 30% and 70% of the supply from each datasheet. Each output drives its own rail, unlike I2C where the pull-up sets the high.
If the two sides differ, check both directions against V IH and absolute maximum, and use a push-pull level translator fast enough for the clock, with MISO going the other way."

Typical SPI clock speeds. The question: What are typical clock speeds?
SPI has no official speed grades. Each chip has its own maximum clock speed, and the board and the master chip can lower it further.
Typical clocks are a few MHz for simple sensors, 10 to 50 megahertz for displays, SD cards and flash, and 100 megahertz or more for fast flash.
The usual limit is the time budget for data coming back.
Imagine two people playing catch to a drum beat. One throws on each beat, and the other must catch before the next beat.
The gap between the throw and the catch has to cover three things: the thrower's reaction time, the ball's flight, and the catcher getting set.
Beat faster and that gap shrinks until the catch fails.
With a 12 nanoseconds slave ( t V ) and 5 nanoseconds of setup, the 4 nanoseconds board delay allows 23.
8 megahertz; adding two 5 nanoseconds translators (14 nanoseconds total) drops it to 16. 1 megahertz.
A slow slave ( t V = 25 nanoseconds) cannot exceed about 17 megahertz even with no delay at all.
Clock frequency: ticks per second. 10 megahertz means 10 million ticks per second. Datasheet maximum: the highest clock the maker guarantees.
Reads are sometimes limited lower than writes. Clock-to-output delay: how long a slave takes, after a clock edge, to put its next bit on the wire.
Setup time: how long the master needs the bit to be steady before it samples it. Level translator: a chip that links two supply voltages. It adds a few nanoseconds of delay.
In the common clock mode, the slave sends a new bit on one clock edge, and the master reads it on the next edge, half a period later.
Say the slave takes 12 nanoseconds to respond, the board adds 4 nanoseconds for the round trip, and the master needs 5 nanoseconds of setup.
That is 21 nanoseconds, so half a period must be at least 21 nanoseconds. The period is then 42 nanoseconds, or about 24 megahertz.
Two level translators adding 10 nanoseconds push it to about 16 megahertz. That is the whole idea.
"SPI has no standard speed grades.
Sensors and ADCs typically run 1 to 10 megahertz, SD cards, displays and flash 10 to 50 megahertz, and fast flash 100+ MHz, with dual and quad modes multiplying throughput.

The limits are the slave's datasheet max, the MCU's clock divider, signal integrity, and the MISO timing: the slave's clock-to-output delay plus round-trip propagation plus setup has to fit in half a period.
At 10 megahertz you get 1. 25 MB/s, roughly ten times I2C at 1 megahertz."

What UART is and stands for. The question: What is UART? What does it stand for?
UART stands for Universal Asynchronous Receiver/Transmitter.
It is a small block of hardware that sends a byte out one bit at a time on a wire, and rebuilds bytes from the bits arriving on another wire.
"Asynchronous" means the two chips share no clock wire. They agree on a speed, and marker bits wrap each byte.
Imagine two people who agree to tap a message to each other at a set tempo. To keep in step, the sender gives a distinct first tap that means "a byte starts now".
The receiver starts counting beats from that tap. Then the sender taps out eight data beats, and ends with a closing tap that returns to the resting state.
The character "A" in 8N1 at one column per bit time.
The line idles high, falls for the start bit, sends 1,0,0,0,0,0,1,0 (LSB first, so 0x41 reads backwards), and ends with a high stop bit.
The first falling edge is the only thing the receiver gets to lock onto.
Asynchronous: no shared clock wire. Each side keeps its own time. Baud rate: the agreed speed. For UART it is the number of bits per second on the wire, such as 115200.
Start bit and stop bit: the low bit that begins a byte and the high bit that ends it. The line rests high between bytes. Frame: one byte plus its start and stop bits.
TX and RX: the transmit pin and receive pin. They cross between the two chips.
Send the letter "A", which a computer stores as the byte 01000001. The line rests high. First comes a low start bit.
Then the eight data bits go out starting from the rightmost bit: 1, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 0. Last comes a high stop bit. That is 10 bits for one byte.
At 115200 baud each bit lasts about 8. 68 microseconds, so a byte takes about 86. 8 microseconds. That is roughly 11,520 bytes per second. That is the whole idea.
"UART is Universal Asynchronous Receiver/Transmitter. It's a peripheral that serialises a byte onto a TX pin and rebuilds bytes from an RX pin.
Asynchronous means there's no shared clock wire.
Both ends just agree on a baud rate, like 115200, and each byte is framed with a start bit, the data bits LSB first, and a stop bit so the receiver can lock on.
You wire it TX to RX, RX to TX, plus ground. It's slow but simple, and it's what you use for debug consoles, GPS and Bluetooth modules."
Quick check. What does the "A" in UART stand for, and what does it mean?
How UART transmits and receives. The question: How does it work?
A UART has a sending half and a receiving half.
To send, it loads a byte into a shift register and pushes out a frame (the byte wrapped in a low start bit and a high stop bit) one bit at a time, each lasting one agreed bit time.
To receive, it watches for the falling edge (the drop from high to low) of a start bit.
Then it waits half a bit, and reads the line once per bit time, near the middle of each bit.
Imagine a starter's pistol and a flashing lamp. The pistol is the start bit. The lamp then shows one bit per beat, and you have a watch that counts beats.
You do not look at the lamp when it changes, because that is when it is blurry.
You wait half a beat after the pistol, then look at the middle of each beat, when the lamp is steadiest.
Software writes the byte (TXE drops), and TXE goes high again as soon as the byte moves into the shift register, long before the frame is finished.
The line is only done when the stop bit completes, which is what the separate transmission-complete (TC) flag reports.
Shift register: a row of storage cells that moves bits along one place per tick, turning a byte into a stream or back.
Baud-rate generator: a timer that divides the chip's clock down to the bit rate. Framing error: the stop bit was read low, which usually means the two speeds do not match.
Send the letter "H", stored as the byte 01001000, at 9600 baud. Each bit lasts about 104 microseconds.
The line goes low for the start bit, then sends the data bits rightmost first: 0, 0, 0, 1, 0, 0, 1, 0. Then it goes high for the stop bit.
The receiver sees the falling edge and waits 52 microseconds, half a bit. It confirms the line is still low, then reads once every 104 microseconds.
It collects the same eight bits and checks the stop bit. That is the whole idea.
"Transmit: the UART loads a byte into a shift register and sends a frame, a low start bit, the data bits LSB first, optional parity, then a high stop bit, each lasting one baud period.
Receive: it watches for the falling start edge, waits half a bit to confirm it and to centre itself, then samples every bit time in the middle of each bit and shifts the bits into a register.
It checks parity and that the stop bit is high, then flags the byte for the CPU. A bad stop bit means a framing error, usually a baud mismatch."
Quick check. In which order are the data bits of a standard UART frame sent?
How many wires UART needs. The question: How many wires does it have?
A basic two-way UART link needs three wires: transmit (TX), receive (RX), and ground. Each direction of data gets its own wire.
Ground is the shared reference that gives "high" and "low" their meaning. If data only flows one way, two wires are enough. Some links add two more wires for flow control.
Picture two towns joined by two one-way roads, one in each direction. Both roads can carry traffic at the same time, so neither side waits its turn.
Now picture a map that shows how high each road climbs. Both towns must measure height from the same sea level, or "uphill" means different things to each.
Ground is that shared sea level.
Three wires, the minimum for two-way UART. The moving dots show the direction each data wire carries.
The ground wire carries no data but defines what "high" and "low" mean for both receivers.
TX and RX: a device's transmit and receive pins. One device's TX goes to the other's RX. Ground (GND): the shared 0 volts reference both devices measure voltages from.
Full duplex: data moving in both directions at the same time. Separate wires make that possible. RTS and CTS: two optional wires that let a receiver tell the sender to pause.
This is called hardware flow control. Point-to-point: a link between exactly two devices, with no sharing.
Connect board A's TX to board B's RX. Connect B's TX to A's RX. Join the two grounds. That is three wires, and both boards can talk at once.
A GPS module that only streams data needs just its TX to the microcontroller's RX, plus ground, so two wires. Adding RTS and CTS makes five.
For comparison, SPI needs four wires plus one chip select for each extra device. That is the whole idea.
"The minimum for full duplex is three wires: TX, RX and a common ground. TX and RX are separate so each direction has its own wire.
Ground is the reference for the logic levels, so I always count it. If you only need data one way you can use two. Add RTS and CTS for hardware flow control and you're at five.
RS-485 variants use differential pairs instead, but it's the same framing.
Compared with SPI, which needs four plus a chip select per device, UART is very cheap in pins, but it's point-to-point."
Quick check. What is the minimum set of wires for a two-way UART link between two boards?
Wiring a UART connection. The question: How do I make the connections?
To wire two UART devices, you cross the data wires: one device's TX goes to the other's RX, and the other's TX goes back to the first's RX. You also join the grounds.
Before powering up, you check that both devices use the same logic voltage. If they do not, you add a level shifter.
Picture two houses joined by water pipes. Each house has an outlet (TX) and an inlet (RX). You connect each outlet to the other house's inlet.
Both houses must also measure pressure from the same drain level, which is ground. The pressure is the voltage.
If a high-pressure house feeds a weak inlet, the inlet bursts, so you add a pressure reducer first.
The canonical connection. Both labels are written from each chip's own perspective, so the data lines cross: MCU TX lands on the bridge's receive pin (RXD).
Some boards silkscreen the other device's name, so read the datasheet before you trust a pin label.
Crossover: connecting TX to RX and RX to TX. Pin names are from each device's own point of view. Ground (GND): the shared 0 volts reference. It must be joined between devices.
Logic level: the voltage that means "1", such as 3. 3 volts or 5 volts. Level shifter: a small circuit or chip that converts between two logic voltages.
USB-UART bridge: an adapter that gives a PC a TX and RX pin at logic level. RS-232: an older standard that uses much larger voltages, both positive and negative.
It needs a converter chip, such as a MAX3232, and can destroy a logic pin if wired directly.
Wire a 3. 3 volts microcontroller's TX to a USB-UART bridge's RXD, the bridge's TXD to its RX, and ground to ground. Now suppose a 5 volts sensor's TX must feed the 3.
3 volts microcontroller's RX. Put a 1 kilohms resistor in the wire, then a 2 kilohms resistor to ground. The midpoint sits at 5 times 2 over 3 equals 3. 33 volts, which is safe.
That is the whole idea.
"Cross the data lines, so each TX goes to the other device's RX, and tie the grounds. Before powering up I check logic levels match: 3. 3 volts to 3.
3 volts is direct; a 5 volts TX into a 3. 3 volts MCU needs a level shifter or at least a divider like 1 k and 2 k. To a PC I use a USB-UART bridge at the right voltage.
To a real RS-232 port I'd use a MAX3232-type transceiver, and for long noisy runs RS-485. And I double-check baud and framing."

Standard UART baud rates. The question: What are some standard communication rates?
The standard UART speeds are 9600, 19200, 38400, 57600 and 115200 baud. Baud is bits per second on the wire.
The two you meet most are 9600, common on GPS modules and old sensors, and 115200, the usual default for debug consoles.
Because each byte needs 10 bits on the wire, the bytes per second are one tenth of the baud rate.
Imagine a master wheel spinning fast, with a chain of gears that slow it down. Each gear divides the speed by a whole number.
The standard UART speeds are exactly what you get from one special master wheel, 1. 8432 megahertz, divided by 16 and then by small whole numbers.
If your master wheel is a different speed, you can only choose whole-number gears, so you land slightly off the target.
Time scales as 1/baud, so every doubling of baud halves the transfer time. A 100 kB firmware image takes about 8.
9 seconds at 115200 baud but 107 seconds at 9600, which is why bootloaders ask for the higher rate when the link allows it.
Baud: symbols per second. For UART each symbol is one bit, so 115200 baud is 115200 bits per second. 8N1: the usual frame: 8 data bits, no parity, 1 stop bit, with a start bit.
That is 10 bits per byte. Baud-rate divisor: the number the chip divides its clock by to make the bit timing.
Divider error: how far the achieved rate lands from the target, because the divisor must be a whole number. Crystal: the part that sets the chip's clock frequency.
At 115200 baud one bit lasts 1 over 115200 about 8. 68 microseconds. A 10-bit frame takes about 86. 8 microseconds, so you move about 11,520 bytes per second.
Now take a 16 megahertz clock whose receiver counts 16 ticks per bit. The divisor should be 16 000 000 over (16 times 115200) about 8. 68 , but it must round to 9.
That gives 111,111 baud, about 3. 5% too slow. Using a 14. 7456 megahertz crystal instead gives a whole divisor and zero error. That is the whole idea.
"The classic ones are 9600, 19200, 38400, 57600 and 115200, then 230400, 460800, 921600 and a megabaud or more on modern parts.
9600 is the old default for GPS and sensors, 115200 for debug consoles. Baud is bits per second, and at 8N1 each byte takes ten bits, so 115200 gives about 11.

UART device count and direction. The question: How many devices can talk to each other? What is the direction of communication?
A basic UART link joins exactly two devices. Each wire has one sender and one receiver.
Because TX and RX are separate wires, both devices can talk at the same moment, which is called full duplex.
If you want a third device, you cannot just join its TX onto an existing wire.
To reach more devices you add more UARTs, use a shared bus standard such as RS-485 with addresses, or pick a different bus like I2C.
Picture a phone call where each person has their own line, one for speaking and one for listening. Both can talk at once, and nothing collides.
Now a third person wants to join by speaking into the same line as someone else. Two voices on one line become a muddle.
A group needs a meeting with a chair, where only one person speaks at a time and each is called by name.
Two wires, each with exactly one driver and one receiver. The two directions are independent, so A and B can transmit simultaneously (full duplex).
Point-to-point: a link between exactly two endpoints. Full duplex: both directions at the same time, because each direction has its own wire.
Contention: two outputs driving opposite levels onto one wire at once. RS-485: a shared two-wire bus standard whose drivers can switch off, so many devices can take turns.
Addressing: a rule in the message, such as a device number, that says who should answer.

You can't just wire more TX pins together because push-pull drivers would fight.
To reach more devices, use one UART each, or RS-485 with tri-state drivers and an addressing protocol like Modbus, which is half duplex, or the 9-bit address mode.
