UART: synchronous or asynchronous. The question: Is it synchronous or asynchronous?
UART is asynchronous. That means there is no clock wire between the two devices. Each chip runs its own clock, and they only agree in advance on a speed.
Every byte is wrapped in a start bit and a stop bit, so the receiver can lock on to the timing again at the start of each byte.
Imagine two people with separate watches, set to count at the same speed. No two watches run exactly alike, so over an hour they drift apart.
But if you reset your timing at every whistle and only need to stay in step for about ten counts, the small drift never matters. The start bit is the whistle.
The watches only have to agree well enough for one frame.
The synchronous signal needs two wires (clock plus data) and the receiver just samples on the rising clock edge in the middle of each bit.
The asynchronous signal is a single wire; the receiver must make up its own sample times. The UART trace shows the alternating 'U' (0x55) pattern.
Asynchronous: no clock wire is shared. Timing comes from an agreed speed and the start bit.
Synchronous: a clock wire travels with the data, and the receiver reads data when the clock ticks. SPI is an example.
Baud rate: the agreed bits-per-second speed both ends count to.
Re-synchronization: the receiver restarts its timing at each start bit, so timing errors never build up past one frame.
Clock mismatch: how much faster or slower one chip's clock runs than the other's, as a percentage.
Two chips agree on 115200 baud, so each bit lasts about 8. 68 microseconds. The receiver reads the stop bit 9. 5 bit times after the start edge. Suppose its clock is 3% slow.
By then its reading point has drifted 9. 5 times 0. 03 equals 0. 285 of a bit. That is still inside the half-bit window, so the data is read correctly. At about 5.
3% the drift reaches half a bit, and the last bit is misread. In practice, designers budget only 3 to 4%. That is the whole idea.
"Asynchronous. There's no clock wire. Both sides pick the same baud rate and each uses its own oscillator.
To make that work, each byte is framed by a start bit and a stop bit, so the receiver can lock onto the falling start edge and then sample each bit in the middle using its own clock.
Compare that with SPI or I2C, where the clock is on a wire and the receiver samples on its edges.
Async saves a wire and tolerates unrelated clocks but costs about 20% overhead and needs the rates to match within a few percent."

A UART receiver has no clock wire, but it knows how long one bit should last because both sides agreed on the speed.
The line rests high, so a falling edge (a drop from high to low) can only mean "a byte starts now". From that edge the receiver counts time with its own clock.
It reads the line once per bit time, near the middle of each bit.
Picture stepping stones across a stream. You spot the edge of the first stone. You step half a stone in, so you stand in the middle of it.
Then you take strides exactly one stone long, and each lands in the middle of the next stone. The middle is the safest spot, because it is far from both edges.
If your stride is slightly off, the error adds up over ten stones. But once you cross, you restart at the next bank.
One column is half a bit.
The falling edge at the start of the start bit is detected; each rising edge of the "sample" row lands in the middle of a bit cell, so the receiver reads start = 0, D0 = 1, D1.
D5 = 0, D6 = 1, D7 = 0 (that is 0x41, 'A', LSB first) and a high stop bit. The samples are half a bit from every transition.
Start edge: the falling edge that begins a byte. It is the receiver's only timing reference. Bit time: the length of one bit, which is 1 divided by the baud rate.
Mid-bit sampling: reading the line at the middle of each bit, where the signal is steadiest.
Framing error: the stop bit was read low, which usually means the two speeds do not match.
Take 115200 baud, so one bit lasts about 8. 68 microseconds. The receiver sees the line fall at time zero. It waits half a bit, about 4.
34 microseconds, and checks the line is still low. If so, it is a real start bit. Then it reads the line every 8. 68 microseconds: at about 13. 0 microseconds, 21.
7 microseconds, and so on for the eight data bits. The stop bit is read at 9. 5 bit times, about 82. 5 microseconds, and should be high. That is the whole idea.
"The line idles high, so the receiver waits for the falling start edge. From that edge it counts its own bit times using the agreed baud rate.
It waits half a bit to land in the middle of the start bit and confirms it's still low, then samples once per bit time, so every sample lands in the middle of a bit, where the signal is steadiest.
After the data it checks the stop bit is high. Because it re-syncs on every start edge, clock error only builds up over one frame, so up to a few percent mismatch is tolerable."

UART oversampling and common rates. The question: What is oversampling? How is it implemented? Why is it needed? What are some common oversample rates for UART?
Oversampling means the UART receiver looks at the incoming line many times during each bit, not just once. The usual choice is 16 looks per bit.
The receiver counts these looks, called ticks, to find the middle of each bit. It also uses several looks near the middle to outvote a brief noise spike.
The cost is that the receiver's counting clock must run 16 times faster than the baud rate, the number of bits per second.
Imagine watching a traffic light by glancing at it. If you glance only once per light cycle, you cannot tell when it changed.
If you glance 16 times per cycle, you can say roughly when it flipped, within one glance. Count 8 glances after the flip and you are at the middle of the phase.
Take three glances around that point and go with the majority.
The receive-side flow. The tick counter is the whole mechanism: count to N over 2 for the centre of the start bit, then count N for each bit.
In real chips this is a small counter plus a shift register.
Oversampling factor: how many ticks the receiver counts per bit. 16 is the classic. 8 is common on modern chips.
Tick: one step of the receiver's fast counting clock, 1/16 of a bit at 16x.
Majority vote: taking three samples near the bit's middle and using the value that at least two agree on.
At 115200 baud with 16x oversampling, a tick is about 0. 54 microseconds. The receiver sees the line fall and starts counting. After 8 ticks, about 4.
3 microseconds, it checks the line is still low. Then it looks every 16 ticks, about 8. 7 microseconds, so each look lands near the middle of a bit.
It may use ticks 7, 8 and 9 and take the majority.
With a 48 megahertz clock, 16x allows at most 3 Mbaud, and 8x allows 6 Mbaud, since the maximum is the clock divided by the factor. That is the whole idea.
"Oversampling means the receiver samples the line at a multiple of the baud rate, typically 16x. A counter runs at 16 times the baud.
When it sees the falling start edge it counts 8 ticks to reach the middle of the start bit, confirms it's low, then samples every 16 ticks, so each sample lands mid-bit.
It often takes three samples around the centre and majority-votes.
It's needed because there's no clock: finding the bit centre and rejecting noise needs finer resolution than one sample per bit.
16x is classic; 8x is common on modern MCUs to reach higher baud rates."

What a GPIO is and does. The question: What is a GPIO? What does it stand for and what are its use cases?
GPIO stands for General-Purpose Input/Output. It is a pin on a microcontroller whose job you choose in software.
As an output, the pin drives itself high or low, for example to light an LED. As an input, the pin reads whether the voltage on it is high or low, for example from a button.
Picture a hose fitting on a control panel that you can set to one of two modes. In output mode it is a small pump outlet, which pushes water out.
In input mode it is a pressure gauge, which only reads. The small pump can fill a small cup but cannot run a big machine.
For the machine you use the pump to flip a valve, and the valve controls the large flow.
A GPIO pin works the same way: it signals a transistor, and the transistor switches the big load.
The two classic GPIO uses on one MCU. Top: an output pin drives an LED through a 270 ohms resistor (about 4. 8 milliamps).
Bottom: an input pin reads a pushbutton with a 10 kilohms pull-up; the pin reads high when the button is open and low when pressed.
Notice that nothing about the pin itself tells you which role it has; software picks.
Direction: whether the pin is set as an input (read) or an output (drive). Current limit: how much current a pin can supply or absorb, typically a few to a few tens of milliamps.
Pull-up resistor: a resistor that holds an unused input high, so it never drifts between high and low.
Transistor: an electrically controlled switch that lets a small pin current control a bigger one.
To light a green LED from a 3. 3 volts output, you need a series resistor. The LED drops about 2. 0 volts, so the resistor must drop the other 1. 3 volts.
For 5 milliamps, R equals 1. 3 over 0. 005 equals 260 ohms. A standard 270 ohms resistor gives about 4. 8 milliamps.
For a button, you set a pin as an input with a pull-up and wire the button to ground. The pin reads high when the button is open and low when it is pressed.
That is the whole idea.
"GPIO is General-Purpose Input/Output: a microcontroller pin whose direction and function you choose in software.
As an output it drives high or low; as an input it reads the level, optionally with a pull-up or pull-down and edge interrupts.
Typical uses: LEDs, buttons, chip selects, enables and resets, interrupt lines, driving transistors for bigger loads, and bit-banging simple protocols.
The thing to remember is the electrical limit, usually a few to a few tens of milliamps per pin, so for relays and motors I drive a transistor rather than the pin directly."

Meaning of "general purpose" in GPIO. The question: What does "GP" refer to?
"General purpose" means a pin is not tied to one fixed job. A general-purpose pin has no assigned job until software gives it one.
Software picks whether it is an input or an output, and what level it drives. In practice these pins are shared with other functions, and they are not all identical.
Picture a hotel with a few fixed-use rooms, such as the ice machine room and the lobby, which can never be anything else.
The rest are general rooms that can be booked as a bedroom or a meeting room. A booking board decides each room's use at any moment.
But the rooms differ: some have a window, some are wheelchair-accessible. The booking board is the pin multiplexer, and the room features are things like 5 volts tolerance.
One physical pad, several possible owners. The mux selects exactly one at a time.
Plain "GPIO" is just one of the choices, which is why the pin is called general-purpose: its default owner is the software-visible port.
Dedicated pin: a pin with one fixed job, such as power, ground, reset or the clock crystal. General-purpose pin: a pin whose role is chosen in software.
Pin multiplexing (alternate function): a selector in front of the pin that connects it to the plain GPIO block or to a built-in hardware block (a peripheral), such as a serial port's transmit line.
High-impedance input: the usual state right after reset. The pin neither drives nor loads the wire. 5 volts tolerant: able to accept 5 volts on a 3. 3 volts chip.
Say a 48-pin microcontroller uses 9 pins for power, ground, reset, crystal and dedicated USB. That leaves at most 48 minus 9 equals 39 general-purpose pins.
If your design needs a UART (2 pins), SPI (4 pins) and I2C (2 pins), those peripherals take 8 of them, and 31 remain for plain GPIO.
Also, after reset those pins float as inputs, so any external part wired to them must be safe in that state. That is the whole idea.
"GP means general-purpose: the pin has no fixed job, so software decides whether it's an input or an output and what level it drives.
That contrasts with dedicated pins like power, ground, reset or the crystal, which always do one thing.
In practice GPIO pins are multiplexed with peripherals, so the same pad can be a GPIO, a UART TX, a PWM output or an ADC input depending on configuration.
And general doesn't mean identical: some pins are 5 volts tolerant, analog capable or boot straps, so I check the datasheet's pin table when assigning."

When you run out of GPIOs. The question: What can I do if I don't have enough GPIOs?
When a microcontroller runs out of GPIO pins, you can often get more without changing it. The first question is whether you can free up pins, or pick a chip with a bigger package.
If not, you add a small chip that turns a few pins into many. Each trick trades pins for time, extra parts, or more complex software.
Imagine one loading door feeding eight shelves through a conveyor belt. You slide items onto the belt one at a time.
When all eight are in place, you press a single button, and every shelf locks at once. But it takes eight steps instead of one. That is the trade: fewer pins, more time.
A decision path for choosing a technique. Notice the first question is not "which chip?" but whether the constraint can be removed.
Shift register: a chip with a row of storage cells that you fill one bit at a time. It turns a few pins into 8 or more outputs, such as the 74HC595.
Latch: a pulse that copies all the bits to the outputs at once, so they do not flicker while you load.
I/O expander: a chip that adds 8 or 16 extra GPIO pins, controlled over a two-wire (I2C) or four-wire (SPI) bus.
Key matrix: wiring buttons in rows and columns, so a few pins read many buttons.
A 74HC595 needs three microcontroller pins: data, clock and latch. It gives 8 outputs. Chain four of them on the same three pins, and you have 32 outputs.
Sending 32 bits at a 1 megahertz clock takes 32 microseconds. For buttons, a 4 by 4 matrix reads 16 keys with only 8 pins.
An I2C expander can add 16 pins on two wires, but each update takes roughly 100 microseconds, so it is too slow for fast signals. That is the whole idea.
"First I'd see if I can free pins or step up to a bigger package.

Otherwise: for outputs a 74HC595 shift register turns three pins into eight outputs and chains for more; for inputs a 74HC165; for both, an I2C or SPI I/O expander like the MCP23017 gives 16 pins on two wires.
For buttons and LEDs I'd use a matrix, so 8 pins read 16 keys, Charlieplexing for LEDs, or a resistor ladder on one ADC pin. A decoder gives chip selects.
The cost is speed, CPU time and firmware complexity."

Inside a GPIO pin, two switches connect to its metal contact, the pad. One switch joins it to the supply voltage. The other joins it to ground.
Close the top switch and the pin is high. Close the bottom one and the pin is low. Open both and the pin is an input, because it is no longer driven.
A small sensing circuit, the input buffer, reads the pad's voltage. Protective diodes complete the circuit.
Picture a pipe junction with two taps. The top tap connects to a tank of water at supply level. The bottom tap connects to a drain.
Open the top tap and the pipe fills, which is high. Open the bottom tap and it drains, which is low. Close both and the pipe is free, so you can read its water level from outside.
Relief valves on the pipe vent any dangerous overpressure.
The gating that creates three output states from two bits. When OE is 0, NAND gives 1 (PMOS off) and NOR gives 0 (NMOS off): high impedance.
When OE is 1, both gates see the inverse of D.
PMOS and NMOS: two kinds of transistor, used as electrically controlled switches. The PMOS joins the pad to the supply. The NMOS joins it to ground.
High impedance (high-Z): both switches off. The pin neither drives nor loads the wire. This is input mode. Clamp diode: a diode that conducts when the pad goes about 0.
7 volts beyond the supply or ground, steering the extra current away.
Say each switch has about 25 ohms of resistance when on. With data 1, the top switch conducts and the pad sits near 3. 3 volts.
With data 0, the bottom one conducts and the pad sits near 0 volts. Now suppose two such pins on one wire disagree. Current flows through both switches: 3.
3 over (25 plus 25) equals 66 milliamps, far too much. Likewise, 5 volts on a 3. 3 volts pin not rated for it turns on the upper diode and pushes current into the supply.
That is the whole idea.
"The pad connects to a CMOS pair: a PMOS to VDD and an NMOS to ground, driven by the output data and an enable.
Data 1 turns on the PMOS and pulls high, data 0 turns on the NMOS and pulls low, and with the enable off both are off, so the pin is high impedance, which is input mode.
The input goes through a Schmitt-trigger buffer into the input register.
There are optional pull-up and pull-down resistors with switches, and two ESD diodes, one to VDD and one to ground, to clamp overvoltage. Configuration registers choose the mode."

Push-pull vs open-drain trade-offs. The question: What are the two most common types of GPIO implementations? What are their tradeoffs?
A GPIO output can be push-pull or open-drain. A push-pull pin actively drives both high and low, so its edges are fast and it needs no extra parts.
An open-drain pin can only pull low or let go. A resistor, called a pull-up, brings it high when released. Push-pull is faster.
Open-drain lets several devices safely share one wire.
Picture a bathtub. A push-pull pin is a tub with a big filling tap and a big drain. It fills and empties quickly.
But if two people share the tub, one with the tap open and one with the drain open, water just pours straight through, wasted.
An open-drain pin is a tub with only drain plugs and a trickle tap. Anyone can pull a plug without a fight. The price is slow refilling.

Right: open-drain, one transistor and an external pull-up: the NMOS pulls the line down when its gate is high, and the resistor pulls it up when the NMOS is off.
(The "in" drive polarity is inverted in the right figure; a real pin hides this in its logic.)
Push-pull: an output with two switches, one driving high and one driving low. Open-drain: an output with only a pull-down switch. It pulls low or lets go.
Pull-up resistor: the resistor that brings an open-drain line high when nobody pulls it low. Wired-AND: a shared open-drain line that is low if any device pulls it low.
Rise time: how long the wire takes to climb from low to high. Capacitance: the charge a wire stores. It must be filled before the voltage can rise, like a bucket.
Take a 3. 3 volts line with 100 picofarads of capacitance. A push-pull pin with a 25 ohms switch charges it in a few nanoseconds ( 25 ohms times 100 picofarads equals 2.
5 nanoseconds). An open-drain pin with a 4. 7 kilohms pull-up takes about 400 nanoseconds to climb from 30% to 70%. Whenever it holds the line low, that pull-up draws 3.

7 kilohms and 100 picofarads, and it burns current when low.
But devices can share the line safely as a wired-AND, and the pull-up can be at a different voltage for level translation.
So push-pull for point-to-point speed, open-drain for shared buses like I2C and interrupt lines."

Open-drain and push-pull meaning. The question: What does open-drain/push-pull mean?
Push-pull and open-drain describe how an output pin is built from transistors, which are electrically controlled switches. A push-pull output has two switches.
One pushes the pin up to the supply and the other pulls it down to ground, so the pin is always firmly driven. An open-drain output has only the pull-down switch.
For a high level it simply lets go, and an outside resistor pulls the pin up.
Think of a window blind. A push-pull blind has a motor that rolls it up and rolls it down. An open-drain blind has only a cord that pulls it down.
When you let go, a spring in the roller lifts it, but that spring is something you supply, not part of the cord. The spring is the pull-up resistor.

Push-pull: an output with two switches, one driving high and one driving low. Open-drain: an output with only a pull-down switch.
The transistor's output end, called the drain, is left unconnected ("open") inside the chip.
Pull-up resistor: the outside resistor that supplies the high level for an open-drain pin. Released state: the pull-down switch is off, so the pin is not driven at all.
Wired-AND: several open-drain outputs on one line. The line is low if any one of them pulls low.

As open-drain with a 4. 7 kilohms pull-up, writing 0 turns the bottom switch on. If that switch has 25 ohms, the pin sits at 3. 3 times 25 over 4725 about 0. 02 volts.
Writing 1 releases the pin, and the resistor lifts it to 3. 3 volts. With no pull-up, writing 1 leaves the pin floating. That is the whole idea.
"Push-pull means the output has two transistors: a PMOS that pushes the pin up to VDD and an NMOS that pulls it to ground, so it actively drives both high and low.
Open-drain means there's only the NMOS, and its drain is left open: it can pull the pin low, or release it. To get a high you need an external pull-up resistor.
So push-pull is fast and needs nothing else, while open-drain needs a resistor but lets several outputs share a line, with the line low if any one pulls low."

When and how to size pull-ups. The question: When are pullup/pulldown resistors necessary? How do you size them?
A pull-up or pull-down resistor gives a wire a default level when nothing else is driving it.
You need one on undriven inputs, open-drain outputs, and control lines that must be safe at boot. Sizing is a balance.
A large resistor is weak, slow, and easy for noise and leakage to upset.
A small one is strong and fast, but wastes current and may be more than the chip pulling the line low can handle.
Think of a self-closing door with a door closer. The closed position is the default level. A strong closer snaps the door shut quickly and ignores drafts.
But holding it open takes effort, which is the current you waste whenever something pulls the opposite way.
A weak closer is easy to hold open, but the door drifts in the wind and closes slowly. The right closer is the strongest one you can afford to fight against.
Rise time is proportional to R. For a 100 picofarads I2C-like bus, staying under 1 microseconds means R below about 4. 5 kilohms (10-90%).
For a slow button node at 20 picofarads, even 1 megohms gives 44 microseconds, irrelevant for human timescales but too slow for a UART RX or an SPI line.
Floating input: an input with nothing driving it. It picks up noise and can read randomly.

Typical configurable GPIO settings. The question: What are some typical configurable GPIO settings?
A GPIO pin has a small set of settings, and every microcontroller family has the same set under different names. They fall into groups.
What the pin is: input, output, analog, or handed to a peripheral. How it drives: output type, starting value, edge speed and strength.
How it senses: pull resistors, input filtering, and interrupts.
Picture a faucet with several dials. One dial chooses which appliance the pipe feeds. Another sets how hard the water can flow. A third sets how quickly you open the valve.
If you slam a valve open, the pipes bang and shake the whole house. The same happens on a chip: a very fast edge on one pin creates noise on the supply and in the air.
The settings fall into four groups. Whenever you meet an unfamiliar MCU, find where each group's registers live; the details differ but the groups do not.
Mode: whether the pin is a digital input, a digital output, an analog input, or handed to a peripheral (a built-in hardware block).
Alternate function: routing a peripheral's signal, such as UART TX or SPI clock, to the pin instead of the GPIO block. Output type: push-pull or open-drain.
Slew rate (speed): how fast the output switches between low and high (each switch is an edge). Slower edges cause less noise.
Drive strength: how much current the pin is allowed to deliver. Stronger drive makes sharper current spikes.
Interrupt: a pin-change event that makes the processor stop and respond, chosen as rising edge, falling edge or both.
Set up three pins. An SPI clock running at 40 megahertz is an alternate function, push-pull, with high speed so its edges stay clean.
An LED enable is a plain output, push-pull, at the lowest speed. An I2C data line is an alternate function, open-drain, with an external pull-up.
A 2 nanoseconds edge makes noise up to roughly 160 megahertz, while a 10 nanoseconds edge reaches only about 32 megahertz. That is the whole idea.
"I think of three groups. What the pin is: mode (input, output, alternate function, analog) and which alternate function.
How it drives: output type, push-pull or open-drain, initial value, drive strength and slew rate, which trade edge speed against EMI and ground bounce.
How it senses: pull-up, pull-down or none, Schmitt trigger or filter, and interrupt edge, enable and wake-up.
Plus housekeeping: atomic set/reset registers, a lock bit, and remember most pins reset to floating inputs."

Bus contention causes and cures. The question: What is bus contention?
Bus contention means two or more outputs are driving the same wire at the same time, to different levels.
One is pushing the wire up to the supply while another pulls it down to ground. That makes a direct path from supply to ground through both outputs.
The result is a wire stuck at a mid-level that reads as garbage, a large wasted current, and hot or damaged output circuits.

If the teams are equally strong, the marker stays in the middle and neither team wins. But both teams strain hard the whole time, which is wasted effort that tires them out.
Here the strain is current, and the tiring is heat.

What a microcontroller timer is. The question: What are timers in a microcontroller?
A microcontroller timer is a hardware counter that adds one on every tick of a clock. It runs on its own, without the processor doing anything.
When the count reaches a number you chose, or wraps around to zero, the hardware can set a flag (a status bit), signal the processor, flip a pin, or restart itself.
That gives you exact timing while the processor does other work.
Picture a tap dripping steadily into a measuring cup. Each drip is one clock tick, and the water level is the count. You paint a fill line on the cup.
When the water reaches it, a bell rings, and a siphon empties the cup so it can start again. While the cup fills, you are free to do other jobs.
Every timer is this pipeline.

The clock goes through a divider into a counter; comparators watch for the match value and the reload value, and each can produce a pin change, a flag, an interrupt or a trigger to another peripheral.
Counter: the storage that holds the current count and goes up by one each tick. Tick: one step of the counter. It is the smallest time the timer can resolve.
Prescaler: a divider before the counter that slows the clock, so longer times fit in the counter. Compare or reload value: the number the counter is checked against.
A match sets a flag or restarts the counter. Interrupt: a signal that makes the processor pause its work and respond to the timer.
A chip runs at 16 megahertz. A prescaler that divides by 16 gives a 1 megahertz tick, which is one tick per microsecond. Let the counter run from 0 to 999 and then restart.
That is 1000 counts, so the timer produces an event every 1 milliseconds, a 1 kilohertz rate.
Note the off-by-one: the counter includes 0, so a reload value of 999 gives 1000 counts, not 999. The timing stays exact however busy the main program is. That is the whole idea.
"A timer is a hardware counter that counts clock ticks independently of the CPU.
A prescaler slows the clock, and a compare or reload register tells it when to raise a flag, fire an interrupt, or toggle a pin.
So with 16 megahertz and a prescaler of 16 I get a 1 megahertz tick, and counting to 1000 gives me an exact 1 milliseconds event regardless of what the code is doing.
The same hardware is used for PWM, measuring pulse widths with input capture, and scheduler ticks."

What you can do with timers. The question: What can you do with timers?
A timer can do four kinds of jobs, all in hardware. It can make things happen on a schedule, such as a regular signal to the processor or a PWM signal.
It can measure time, such as how long a pulse lasts. It can count pulses from outside. And it can trigger other parts, such as starting a measurement.
Picture a kitchen timer that has been upgraded. As an alarm, it rings every minute on schedule.
As a lap timer, you press a button when a runner crosses a line, and it records the exact time, even if you were busy. As a tally clicker, it counts how many people walk past.
As a switch, it turns a lamp on for part of each second.
One counter, four families of use.
Notice that the same counter register serves all of them; what differs is which event (overflow, compare match or edge) you hook to a pin, flag or trigger.
PWM (pulse-width modulation): switching a pin on and off repeatedly, so the average power depends on how long it stays on.
Duty cycle: the fraction of each period that the pin is on. 25% means on for a quarter of the time.
Input capture: saving the counter value at the instant an input signal switches level, to timestamp it exactly.
A hobby servo wants a pulse every 20 milliseconds, which is 50 hertz, and the pulse width sets its angle.
With the counter ticking once per microsecond (1 megahertz), set the period to 20,000 counts. Switching the pin off at count 1500 makes the pulse 1.
5 milliseconds wide, the centered position. The duty cycle is 1500 over 20000 equals 7. 5 % . Now the other direction: an ultrasonic sensor sends back an echo pulse.
Input capture records when the pulse starts and ends, to one tick, 1 microseconds. A 10 milliseconds echo means the target is 343 times 0. 010 over 2 about 1. 7 m away.
That is the whole idea.
"Timers let you generate, measure and count in hardware.
Generate: periodic interrupts for a system tick or ADC sampling, and output compare for PWM, servo pulses or one-shot strobes.
Measure: input capture timestamps an edge with one-tick resolution, so I can time an echo or tach pulse.
Count: clock the timer from a pin to count pulses or run a quadrature encoder. Plus watchdog and RTC variants.
It's all deterministic and runs without the CPU, which is why I prefer it over software delays."

Keeping accurate time in a microcontroller. The question: How do keep track of time accurately in a microcontroller?
A timer counts clock ticks exactly. But the time it reports is only as accurate as the oscillator producing those ticks.
So accurate timekeeping depends on two things: choosing a good clock, and writing software that does not add error. Clock accuracy is measured in parts per million, or ppm.
A common crystal is accurate to a few tens of ppm. The internal oscillator on a chip is accurate to only about a percent.
Imagine measuring with a ruler. The counter is like counting the marks on it, which you do perfectly.
But if the ruler is stretched by 1%, every length you measure is 1% off, no matter how carefully you count.
A better ruler, such as a crystal, has marks that are almost exactly the right spacing. Re-aligning the ruler by hand on every reading adds error too.
The error is linear in ppm, so on log axes it is a straight line.
Notice the three clock classes: a TCXO (fractions of a second per day), a plain crystal (a couple of seconds) and an internal RC (minutes).
Choose the clock from the error you can tolerate.
Oscillator: the circuit that makes the steady clock the timer counts. It sets the time scale. ppm (parts per million): a tiny fractional error. 1 ppm is about 0.
086 seconds per day. Crystal: a quartz part that gives a stable frequency, typically within 10 to 50 ppm.
Drift: an error that builds up over time because the clock is steadily fast or slow. Wrap-around: a counter reaching its maximum and starting again from zero.
Multiply the error by the seconds in a day, which is 86,400. A 20 ppm crystal is off by 86400 times 20 times 10 to the -6 about 1. 7 seconds per day.
A 1% internal oscillator is off by 0. 01 times 86400 equals 864 seconds, or 14. 4 minutes.
On the software side, let the timer free-run, because restarting it from software every period loses a few microseconds each time, and those add up.
Compute elapsed time as "now minus start" with whole-number math that rolls over the same way the counter does, so it stays correct across a wrap-around. That is the whole idea.
"The counter is exact; the clock isn't. So I pick the clock for the accuracy I need: the internal RC is about 1% (14 minutes a day), a crystal is around 20 ppm (1.
7 seconds a day), and a 32 kilohertz watch crystal into the RTC gives low-power timekeeping.
In software I let the timer free-run, use auto-reload so no error accumulates, and use unsigned subtraction for elapsed times so counter wrap doesn't matter.
For better than crystal accuracy, add a TCXO or calibrate against a reference like GPS."

How timers work and are implemented. The question: How do they work? How are they implemented?
Inside the chip, a timer is a row of flip-flops that counts in binary, plus a small circuit that checks whether the count equals a stored number.
A flip-flop is a one-bit memory that updates on each clock tick. When the count matches, the hardware sets a flag (a status bit).
That flag can signal the processor, flip a pin, or send the counter back to zero.
Think of a car's odometer. Each digit wheel advances one step when the wheel to its right rolls past 9.
A binary timer works the same way, but each wheel has only two positions, 0 and 1. Now add an alarm that rings when the odometer shows a chosen number, and resets it to zero.
That is a timer.
Feeding Q̄ back to D makes Q flip at every rising clock edge, so Q is a square wave at half the clock frequency.
Chain n of these (each clocked from the previous Q) and you divide by 2 to the n .
Flip-flop: a one-bit memory that copies its input when the clock ticks. Counter: flip-flops that each flip when all the lower bits are 1, so together they count up in binary.
Comparator: logic that checks whether two numbers are equal, bit by bit. Prescaler: a small counter that lets the main counter advance only once every N clock ticks.
Take a 3-bit counter. Bit 0 toggles on every tick, bit 1 on every second tick, and bit 2 on every fourth. Together they count 0, 1, 2, up to 7, then wrap. That is 8 states, not 7.
Now a real timer: a 16 megahertz clock and a prescaler that emits a pulse every 16th tick make the counter advance at 1 megahertz. A reload value of 999 is stored.
When the count equals 999, the next tick loads 0 instead of adding 1. That makes 1000 states per period, so 1 kilohertz. That is the whole idea.

"A timer is a synchronous binary counter made of flip-flops with an incrementer, a prescaler that is itself a small counter giving an enable pulse every N clocks, and comparators that check the count against a value in a register.
A match sets a flag that can interrupt, toggle a pin, or reload the counter.
For input capture, an external edge goes through a synchroniser and loads the count into a capture register.
The CPU just accesses all of it as memory-mapped registers, often with shadow registers so changes apply cleanly at the next period."

Timer applications in embedded systems. The question: What are some applications?
Nearly every embedded product, meaning a device with a small built-in computer, uses timers.
The most common use is a steady tick, once per millisecond, that slower jobs hang off: blinking an LED, debouncing a button, timing out a reply.
Timers also make PWM, which is rapid on-off switching used for dimming lights and controlling motors. They also measure pulses and reset a frozen chip.
Picture an orchestra with a conductor who gives one steady beat.
Each section keeps its own count of beats, and plays when its turn comes: strings every two beats, brass every eight.
The conductor is the one hardware timer, and each section is a software timer that is just a number compared against the beat count.
But a section cannot play between beats, so the beat limits how fine the timing can be.
One hardware timer fans out into many software timers.
Each software timer is just a variable and a comparison, so you can have dozens at almost no cost; the only limit is the tick resolution.
System tick: a regular timer interrupt, a signal that briefly pauses the main program (see "What interrupts are"), often every 1 milliseconds, used as the software's time base.
Software timer: a stored deadline compared with the tick count. Debounce: ignoring a switch's rapid flicker by requiring a steady state for a set time.
PWM (pulse-width modulation): switching a pin on and off fast, so the average power follows the fraction of time it is on.
Watchdog: a timer that resets the chip if software forgets to restart it, which catches a hang.
Set a hardware timer to a 1 kilohertz tick. Its interrupt routine only adds 1 to a millisecond counter. If it takes 5 microseconds, it uses 5 micro s times 1000 equals 0.
5 % of the processor. For a button: sample it every millisecond, and accept a change only after 20 samples in a row agree, so 20 milliseconds of stable signal.
The rule of thumb is to use hardware timers for tight timing and software timers for slow jobs. That is the whole idea.

"The big ones are the system tick, which drives scheduling, debounce and timeouts; PWM for LEDs, motors, servos and converters; and input capture for measuring things like an ultrasonic echo or a tachometer to a microsecond.
Timers can also trigger the ADC at an exact rate so sampling has no software jitter. And the special timers, the watchdog for fault recovery and the RTC for low-power wake-ups.
In every case I choose a hardware timer when timing is tight and a software timer on the tick when it's slow."

Reacting right when an external event occurs. The question: If you want to do something right when an external event occurs, what can you do?
To react to an outside event, you have three choices. You can check for it again and again in software, which is polling.
You can let the event interrupt the processor so it runs a short routine right away. Or you can wire the response in hardware so no code runs at all.
A button can wait tens of milliseconds, while a safety shutoff may need a microsecond or less.
Imagine waiting for a visitor. Polling is walking to the door every few minutes and looking, so you may miss them by a whole trip.
An interrupt is a doorbell: it makes you stop what you are doing and answer, and you can nap until it rings.
A hardware path is an automatic door that opens by itself, with nobody needed. The doorbell is not instant: if you are busy, the answer waits.
The CPU is diverted at an instruction boundary. Latency is the time from "Pin" to the first ISR instruction; resume latency adds the unstack on exit.
Each arrow is a few clock cycles, so the whole round trip on a Cortex-M is roughly 25-35 cycles for a trivial handler.
Polling: the processor repeatedly checks a pin or status bit in its main loop. Interrupt: a signal that makes the processor pause its work and run a short handler.
Latency: the time from the event until the first useful action. Jitter: how much that latency varies from one event to the next. A hard deadline cares about the worst case.
A motor driver must shut off if it draws too much current. A processor at 72 megahertz takes about 12 clock cycles (ticks of its clock) to enter an interrupt.
That is 12 over 72 about 0. 17 microseconds. Add about 10 cycles of handler code and the shutoff happens in about 0. 3 microseconds.
If the main loop takes 100 microseconds, polling can take up to 100 microseconds. So a 20 microseconds deadline rules out polling but allows an interrupt.
A deadline of 1 microseconds or less is safest in hardware, with the sensor's output wired straight to the shutdown input. That is the whole idea.
"It depends on how fast 'right when' has to be. Polling the pin in the main loop is simplest but the latency is a full loop time and the CPU stays busy.
The standard answer is an interrupt on the pin: the hardware jumps to an ISR in about a dozen cycles, around 170 nanoseconds on a 72 megahertz Cortex-M, and the CPU can sleep in between.
For hard deadlines I'd skip the CPU entirely: use timer input capture, a comparator tied to a PWM break input, or DMA, which react in nanoseconds with no jitter."

What interrupts are. The question: What are interrupts in a microcontroller?
An interrupt is a hardware signal that tells the processor "something needs attention now".
The processor finishes its current instruction, saves where it was, and runs a short function to deal with the event. Then it returns and carries on exactly where it left off.
Interrupts exist so the processor does not have to keep checking for events. It can do other work, or even sleep, until something happens.
Picture a cook following a recipe when the phone rings. The cook puts a bookmark in the recipe, answers briefly, then returns to the exact step and carries on.
The analogy breaks in one place: a real program does not know it was interrupted. To it, only some time passed, which is why saving and restoring its state exactly matters.
The main code is paused at an instruction boundary, then continues exactly where it was. From its point of view only time passed.
Interrupt: a hardware signal that makes the processor pause its main work. ISR (interrupt service routine): the short function that runs in response.
Context: the processor's working state, such as its position in the code and the values it is working on. It is saved and then restored around the ISR.
Polling: repeatedly checking for an event in software instead of being notified. Enable (mask): a bit that decides whether a given interrupt is allowed to reach the processor.
A serial port (UART) at 115,200 bits per second delivers a byte every 86. 8 microseconds. Suppose the main program runs a loop that takes 500 microseconds.
If it only checks for a byte once per loop, the byte is overwritten before it is read, and data is lost. With an interrupt, the UART signals when each byte arrives.
A 2 microseconds handler reads the byte and stores it. That uses only 2 over 86. 8 about 2. 3 % of the processor. That is the whole idea.
"An interrupt is a hardware signal that makes the CPU pause what it's doing, save its state, run a short handler called an ISR for the event, and then resume exactly where it left off.
It exists so the processor doesn't have to poll for things like a button, a UART byte or a timer tick, and it can even sleep until something happens.
A controller handles enables and priorities, and the main rule is to keep ISRs short."

How interrupts work and are implemented. The question: How do they work? How are they implemented?
An interrupt travels along a chain. A hardware block such as a timer sets a flag when its event happens. If its enable bit is on, it sends a request to the interrupt controller.
When the processor is free, it saves its state, looks up where the handler's code sits in a table, and jumps there. At the end, it restores its state and carries on.
Think of a hospital call system. A patient presses a call button, which sets the flag. The switchboard holds the waiting calls and sorts them by urgency.
The nurse finishes the step she is on, writes down where she was, and looks up the patient's room on a directory. She goes, does the job, then returns to her note and resumes.
The switchboard can be told "do not disturb", which is the mask.
Every diamond is a gate that can stop an interrupt. When "my interrupt never fires", walk down the diagram testing each gate in turn (flag set? peripheral enabled? line enabled?
priority? global mask?)
Interrupt flag: a bit that records "this event happened".
Interrupt controller: the part that holds each interrupt's pending, enable and priority bits, and picks the next one to run. Priority: how urgent an interrupt is.
A more urgent one can interrupt a less urgent handler. Vector table: a table in memory holding the address of each interrupt's handler.
Stack: a memory area where the processor saves its state, so it can resume afterward.
On an Arm Cortex-M chip, a timer overflow (the count wrapping past its maximum) sets its flag. The timer's enable bit is on, so the request goes to the controller.
The controller checks it is enabled, urgent enough, and not masked. After the current instruction, the chip saves 8 values, 32 bytes, onto the stack.
Interrupt 28's table entry sits at offset 4 times (16 plus 28) equals 176 bytes, so the chip fetches the handler address there and jumps.
Entry takes about 170 nanoseconds at 72 megahertz. That is the whole idea.
"The peripheral sets a flag, and if its enable bit is on, signals the interrupt controller, which tracks enable, pending and priority per line and picks the winner.
At the next instruction boundary the core pushes its state onto the stack, reads the handler address from the vector table, and jumps to my ISR.
When it returns, hardware pops the state and resumes.
In firmware I enable the peripheral interrupt, the controller line and global interrupts, name the handler to match the vector, and clear the flag inside it."

ISRs at the hardware and software level. The question: Describe how ISRs work at the hardware and software levels.
When an interrupt fires, hardware and software share the work. On an Arm Cortex-M chip, the hardware automatically saves eight registers onto the stack.
It then fetches the handler's address and jumps there. Because of this, the handler can be an ordinary function written in C, a common programming language.
The handler's job is short: read the data, clear the event's flag bit, and update shared variables. Returning triggers the hardware to restore everything and resume.
Picture hot-desking. Before a colleague borrows your desk, a porter automatically boxes up the papers you use most and notes the page you were on.
If the colleague needs any other drawer, he tidies it back himself before leaving. Then the porter unpacks the box, and you carry on as if nothing happened.
The porter is the hardware. The colleague's own tidying is extra code the compiler adds.
The 8-word frame is pushed by hardware, growing the stack by 32 bytes before the first ISR instruction runs.
Anything the compiler adds (R4-R11 and local variables) goes below it, so a nest of k ISRs costs at least 32k bytes.
Register: a tiny, fast storage cell inside the processor that holds values being worked on.
Stack frame: the saved state the hardware pushes onto the stack, a memory area used as scratch space. On Cortex-M that is 8 values, 32 bytes.
Compiler: the program that turns C code into the processor's instructions.
Magic return value: a special value, EXC RETURN, that tells the hardware "this is an interrupt return, so restore the saved state".
At 72 megahertz, entry takes about 12 cycles, so 12 over 72 megahertz about 167 nanoseconds. The handler reads a received serial byte, which also clears the flag.
The return takes about 12 more cycles. That is 24 cycles, or about 0. 33 microseconds of overhead per interrupt.
At 50,000 interrupts per second, the overhead alone is 24 over 72 megahertz times 50 000 about 1. 7 % of the processor.
On a small 8-bit AVR chip, the compiler's code does most of the saving, so the same job costs about 34 cycles. That is the whole idea.

"In hardware, the NVIC picks the interrupt, the core finishes its instruction, pushes eight registers onto the stack, reads the handler address from the vector table and switches to handler mode, about 12 cycles on a Cortex-M.
Because the caller-saved registers are already saved, the ISR is a plain C function: it reads the data, clears the flag and touches volatile shared variables.
Returning with the special EXC RETURN value makes the hardware pop the frame and resume. On AVR the software prologue does more of this."

Interrupt applications in embedded systems. The question: What are some applications?
Interrupts are how a microcontroller deals with the outside world without wasting time. They handle incoming serial bytes, regular timer ticks, button presses, and fault alarms.
Between events the processor can do other work or sleep, which is what makes battery products last for years. The limit is event rate.
Very fast events overwhelm the processor, so hardware takes over.
Picture a night watchman who sleeps until a bell rings. Different bells mean different things. The fire bell outranks the doorbell, so if both ring, he handles the fire first.
Each time he wakes, he does only the quick, necessary action and writes a note for the day staff. But if bells rang a thousand times a second, he would never finish anything.
Load is (t body plus t entry over exit) times r .
The lines show where each ISR hits the wall: a 2 microseconds ISR reaches 100% at about 430 kilohertz, a 10 microseconds ISR at about 97 kilohertz.

ISR (interrupt service routine): the short function the interrupt runs. Ring buffer: a fixed-size queue.
The handler writes bytes in and the main program reads them out, so no byte is lost while the main program is busy.
Sleep and wake-up: a low-power mode where the chip does nothing until an interrupt wakes it.
DMA: hardware that moves data into memory without the processor, and interrupts only when a whole block is done.
A serial port at 115,200 baud delivers a byte every 86. 8 microseconds. A 2 microseconds handler that stores the byte in a ring buffer uses about 2. 3% of the processor.
Now a battery sensor. It sleeps at 2 microamps and wakes once a minute for 20 milliseconds at 10 milliamps. Average current is 2 plus 10 000 times (0. 02 over 60) about 5.
3 microamps, so a coin cell lasts years. But a 1 MB/s data stream would mean a million interrupts per second, so that needs DMA instead. That is the whole idea.

"Interrupts handle communication (UART/SPI/I2C bytes into ring buffers), timing (periodic ticks and fixed-rate control or ADC sampling), inputs (button or sensor data-ready pins, and waking from sleep), and faults (overcurrent, brown-out, watchdog warnings).
They keep the CPU free or asleep until something happens.
The limit is event rate: very fast streams or encoders go to DMA or timer hardware, and interrupts are used for block-level events."

What can trigger an ISR. The question: What can trigger ISRs?
Almost any event inside or outside a microcontroller can trigger an interrupt.

Sources include a pin changing state, a timer reaching its count, a serial port receiving a byte, an analog-to-digital converter finishing a measurement, a clock failing, and the processor itself reporting a fault.
Often several sources share one handler, which must read a status register (a set of flag bits) to find out which one fired.
Imagine a building alarm panel with one shared bell. When the bell rings, the guard looks at the panel to see which light is on, deals with it, and resets that light.
Some alarms latch: the light stays on after the door closes until the guard resets it. Others follow the sensor: the light is on only while the door is open.
If the guard forgets to fix a following alarm, the bell keeps ringing.
Three families: pins, peripherals, and the core and system blocks.
All end up as a request line into the same controller ("How interrupts work and are implemented"), which is why the handling is uniform even though the origins differ.
Status flag: a bit that records which event happened. Edge-triggered: the request comes from a change, such as low to high, and is latched until cleared.
Level-triggered: the request stays active as long as the condition holds. The handler must remove the cause. Shared vector: several sources using one handler.
A serial port can interrupt for a received byte, an empty transmit buffer, or an overrun error (a new byte arrived before the last was read).
One handler reads the status register once. It handles each flag that is set and enabled: read the byte, send the next one, count the error. It clears only the flags it handled.
Now three sensors share one interrupt wire. The wire goes low if any sensor pulls it low.
With an edge trigger, a second sensor that pulls it low while the wire is already low creates no new edge, so its event is lost.
A level trigger keeps requesting until every sensor is serviced. That is the whole idea.

"Almost any event: an external pin edge or level, timer overflow, compare or input capture, UART or SPI or I2C events like byte received and transfer complete, ADC conversion complete or out-of-range, comparator output, DMA complete, RTC alarm, watchdog early warning, brown-out, plus software-triggered interrupts like PendSV and CPU faults.
Sources can be edge or level triggered, and many flags share one vector, so the ISR reads the status register to see which one fired and clears it."

Limitations of interrupts. The question: What are some limitations of interrupts?
An interrupt lets a peripheral (a hardware block such as a timer or serial port) make the CPU (the processor) pause its work and run a short handler right away.
That is very useful, but it is not free. Interrupts add delay, can be lost, use CPU time, and can corrupt data the main code is using.
Knowing these limits is how you use interrupts safely.
Picture a cook who also answers the doorbell. Every ring stops the cooking.
If a second ring comes before the cook reaches the door, the cook remembers only "someone rang", not how many times. If the bell rings every few seconds, no cooking gets done.
A real CPU resumes exactly where it stopped, but data shared with the handler can still be left half updated.
Two events (A and a second event B) arrive close together.
Event B arrives while ISR A is still running, but the flag is already set, so it adds nothing; when ISR A clears the flag with a blanket clear, B's record disappears and B is lost.
The practical consequences are missed counts, dropped bytes and wrong timestamps unless hardware buffers the events.
Interrupt: ("What interrupts are"): a hardware signal that makes the CPU pause the main code and run a handler.
ISR: ("What an ISR is"): the short handler function that runs in response. Latency: the delay between the event and the first handler instruction.
Jitter: how much that latency changes from one event to the next. Pending flag: one bit that records "an event happened". It cannot count events.
Race condition: a bug where the result depends on whether the interrupt lands before or after a step of the main code.
A sensor sends events at least 100 microseconds apart. The handler takes 8 microseconds. The main code sometimes switches interrupts off for 12 microseconds.
Worst case, an event waits 12 microseconds and then the handler runs 8 microseconds: 20 microseconds in total, well under 100 microseconds, so nothing is lost.
Now switch interrupts off for 150 microseconds instead. A second event arrives while the first is still pending, and the two merge into one. That is the whole idea.

Events can be lost because there's only one pending bit and a long ISR misses the next event.
Entry and exit overhead makes very high rates infeasible, so those need DMA or timer hardware.
Shared data between ISR and main creates race conditions, nesting uses stack, and ISRs can't block or do heavy work.
I mitigate with short ISRs, deferred processing, careful priorities and hardware offload."

What an ISR is. The question: What is an interrupt service routine (ISR)?
An ISR (interrupt service routine) is a function that the hardware runs for you when an interrupt happens.
It lets the CPU react at once to an event, such as a received byte, and then go straight back to its work. You never call it yourself, so it takes no inputs and returns nothing.
It passes results to the main code through shared variables.
You are reading a book when the phone rings. You use a bookmark, answer, write the message on a sticky note, hang up, and carry on. Later you read the sticky note.
The ISR is the quick call, and the sticky note is the shared variable. You do not choose when the phone rings. A long chat would make every other caller wait.
The ISR and main code never call each other; they exchange information through shared state. One side writes, the other reads.
That pattern, with exactly one writer per variable, keeps the shared-data problem manageable.
Interrupt: ("What interrupts are"): a hardware signal that makes the CPU pause and run a handler.
Vector table: ("How interrupts work and are implemented"): a list in memory holding the handler's address for each interrupt.
Flag: a bit in the peripheral (the hardware block, here the serial port) that says "I need service". The ISR must clear it, or the interrupt fires again at once.
volatile: a C keyword telling the compiler a variable can change behind its back, such as inside an ISR.
A UART (a serial port) receives a byte and sets a flag. The CPU pauses the main code and looks up the ISR's address in the vector table.
The ISR reads the byte, which also clears the flag, stores it in a buffer, and sets byte arrived to 1. Later the main code sees byte arrived and processes the byte.
At 115,200 bits per second a byte arrives about every 87 microseconds, so a 2 microseconds ISR uses only about 2. 3% of the CPU's time. That is the whole idea.

"An ISR is the function that the hardware calls when an interrupt happens: its address is in the vector table, it takes no arguments and returns nothing, and it interrupts the main code asynchronously.
A good one identifies the source, clears the flag, does the minimum work, like storing a received byte, and signals the main code through a volatile flag or buffer.
It must be short, can't block, and any data it shares with main must be volatile and accessed safely."
Quick check. What is an ISR?
Rules of thumb for writing ISRs. The question: What are some rules of thumb when implementing ISRs?
An ISR is the short function the hardware runs when an interrupt happens. While it runs, it holds up other work, so a few habits keep it harmless.
Keep it very short, clear the interrupt flag, never wait for anything, and hand the real work to the main code. Each rule prevents one specific failure.
Think of a receptionist. When a visitor arrives, the receptionist notes the name, presses the buzzer, and passes the visitor on.
A long conversation at the desk would leave everyone else standing in the lobby.
The picture breaks down in one place: the receptionist can write down many visitors, but a peripheral's flag only records that something happened, so a slow ISR can lose arrivals.
Load grows linearly with the control ISR time, reaching 100% when the ISR fills the whole 50 microseconds period.
A 12 microseconds ISR gives about 28% total, which is comfortable; lengthening it to 25 microseconds already hits 50% total.
ISR: ("What an ISR is"): the handler function that the hardware runs for an interrupt.
Flag: a bit in the peripheral (the hardware block, such as the serial port) that says "I need service". Clear it, or the ISR runs again at once.
Blocking: waiting for something else to happen, such as a delay or a lock. Deferred work: the ISR leaves a note (a flag or a queue) and the main code does the heavy part later.
A UART (a serial port) at 115,200 bits per second delivers a byte about every 87 microseconds. A good ISR reads the byte, puts it in a buffer, and sets a flag.
That takes about 2 microseconds, roughly 2. 3% of the processor's time. A bad ISR parses a whole command and prints a reply, taking 500 microseconds.
About five more bytes arrive meanwhile (500 / 87 is about 5. 7), and without a hardware buffer they are lost. That is the whole idea.
"Keep ISRs short, a few microseconds, since they delay everything else. Clear the flag correctly and only what you handled.
Never block or call printf, malloc or anything slow or non-reentrant. Make shared variables volatile and update them atomically, ideally one writer per variable or a ring buffer.
Defer the real work to main or a task by setting a flag or posting to a queue.
Assign priorities by deadline, budget stack for nesting, and measure the worst-case ISR time on a scope."
Quick check. Which of these should NOT normally be done in an ISR?
Interrupt inside an ISR: nesting. The question: What happens if an ISR gets called while in an ISR? How can this be avoided?
Nesting means one interrupt handler gets interrupted by a more urgent one. The urgent handler runs inside the first, then control goes back to the first.
On ARM Cortex-M chips, the interrupt controller compares priorities: a higher priority preempts, and an equal or lower one waits.
Nesting serves urgent events quickly, but it costs memory and creates new hazards.
A doctor is treating a patient when an emergency call comes in. She pauses, handles the emergency, and returns to the patient. A less urgent call waits until she is free.
Each paused patient needs a note saying where she stopped, so the more she is interrupted, the taller the pile of notes.
One difference: the same patient calling again does not interrupt her. It is noted once for later.
On Cortex-M the NVIC walks exactly this decision. A masked or lower-priority source never interrupts the running handler; it queues.
Only a strictly higher-priority, unmasked source nests.
Priority: a number saying how urgent an interrupt is. On Cortex-M a lower number is more urgent. Preempt: to interrupt a running handler so a more urgent one runs first.
Pending: recorded by the hardware and waiting for its turn. Stack: memory where the CPU saves what it was doing. Each nested level uses some.
Handler A (priority 3) is running. Event B (priority 1) arrives. Since 1 is more urgent than 3, the hardware saves A's state (at least 32 bytes of stack) and runs B.
When B finishes, A resumes. Now event C (priority 3) arrives during A. It has the same priority, so it waits as pending until A returns.
On an AVR chip the hardware blocks all interrupts on entry, so nothing nests unless the code turns them back on. That is the whole idea.
"On a Cortex-M it depends on priority. A higher-priority interrupt preempts: the hardware stacks another frame, runs it, and returns into the first ISR, which is nesting.
Equal or lower priority waits as pending and runs after, and the same interrupt can't preempt itself, so a repeat just pends.
On AVR the global interrupt flag is cleared on entry, so no nesting unless you re-enable.
To avoid problems, set priorities deliberately, keep ISRs short, protect shared data, and budget stack."
Quick check. On a Cortex-M, an ISR is running and a request of equal priority arrives. What happens?
Connecting a sensor to a microcontroller. The question: Draw a circuit to connect a sensor to a microcontroller.
How you connect a sensor depends on what kind it is. An analog sensor gives a voltage that the microcontroller measures with an ADC (a circuit that turns a voltage into a number).
A digital sensor sends numbers over wires using a bus, a shared set of signal lines.
Either way, the sensor needs power, a common ground, and signal levels the microcontroller can safely accept.
Compare reading a thermometer yourself with getting a text from a friend who reads it for you. With the thermometer, glare or a shaky hand changes what you read.
With the text, the number arrives intact, but both sides must follow the same rules. Analog needs care with noise. Digital needs care with the bus rules.
The thermistor and 10 kilohms resistor form a divider whose midpoint is 1. 65 volts at 25 C. The 1 kilohms and 100 nanofarads RC (corner about 1.
6 kilohertz) filters noise and supplies charge for the ADC's sampling capacitor. The ADC reference is the same rail as the divider, so supply variation cancels.
ADC: ("How an ADC works"): a circuit that measures a voltage and reports it as a number. Thermistor: a resistor whose resistance changes with temperature.
The common NTC type drops as it warms. Voltage divider: ("Voltage divider: draw, equation, derivation"): two resistors in series that turn a voltage into a fraction of itself.
Pull-up resistor: ("When and how to size pull-ups"): a resistor to the supply that holds a line high when no chip pulls it low.
Analog case: run 3. 3 volts through a 10 kilohms resistor and then a 10 kilohms thermistor to ground. The point between them is at 3. 3 times 10/(10 + 10) = 1.
65 volts, and that goes to the ADC pin. If the thermistor warms and falls to 5 kilohms, the point drops to 3. 3 times 5/15 = 1. 1 volts.
Digital case: a two-wire bus called I2C needs four wires (power, ground, data, clock). Chips can only pull its two signal lines low, so each gets a 4. 7 kilohms pull-up to 3.
3 volts. That is the whole idea.
"It depends on the sensor type, so I'd ask. For an analog sensor like an NTC thermistor, a divider from 3.
3 volts with the midpoint into an ADC pin through a small RC filter, ratiometric so supply error cancels. For an I2C sensor, SDA and SCL with 4. 7 kilohms pull-ups to 3.
3 volts, a 100 nanofarads decoupling cap at the sensor's VDD, and a common ground. If the sensor is 5 volts, I'd divide or level-shift so I don't exceed the MCU's 3.
3 volts input limit."
Quick check. Why do I2C lines need pull-up resistors?
Connecting a button to a microcontroller. The question: Draw a circuit to connect a button to a microcontroller.
A pushbutton connects a microcontroller pin to ground when you press it.
A pin left unconnected reads random values, so a resistor pulls it up to the supply voltage when the button is open. The pin reads high when released and low when pressed.
The only other trick is that real buttons chatter for a few milliseconds when pressed.
A rubber band holds a flag up. That is the pull-up: with nobody touching it, the flag is up (high). Pressing the button yanks the flag to the floor (low).
The band is weak, so the button easily wins. The chatter is like dropping a ball: it bounces several times before it settles, and each bounce looks like a new press.
Open switch: no current flows and the pull-up holds the pin at 3. 3 volts (logic 1). Pressed: the pin is connected to ground (logic 0) and 0.
33 milliamps flows through the pull-up. The pin itself draws only leakage, so the resistor sets the level.
Pull-up resistor: ("When and how to size pull-ups"): a resistor from the pin to the supply that holds it high when nothing else drives it.
Floating input: a pin connected to nothing, so it reads unpredictable values. Active-low: "pressed" is shown by a logic 0 (low), not a 1.
Contact bounce: the rapid on-off chatter of switch contacts when pressed. Debounce: filtering out the bounce so one press counts once.
Wire the button from the pin to ground, with a 10 kilohms pull-up to 3. 3 volts. Released: the pin sits at 3. 3 volts and reads 1, with no current flowing.
Pressed: the pin is shorted to ground and reads 0, and 3. 3 volts / 10 kilohms = 0. 33 milliamps flows through the resistor.
The bounce may produce ten edges in a few milliseconds. A simple software fix is to accept a new state only after it has stayed the same for a short time, such as 20 milliseconds.
That is the whole idea.
"The standard way is a pushbutton from the GPIO pin to ground with a pull-up resistor, 10 kilohms, to 3. 3 volts, or the MCU's internal pull-up.
Open, the pull-up holds the pin high; pressed, it reads low, so it's active-low. The pull-up is needed so the pin doesn't float.
Because contacts bounce for a few milliseconds, I debounce either with an RC and a Schmitt trigger input, or in software by requiring about 20 milliseconds of stable readings.
For a front-panel button I'd add a series resistor for ESD."
Quick check. Why does a pushbutton input normally need a pull-up or pull-down resistor?
Driving LEDs, high-power and dimming. The question: Draw a circuit to drive a LED from a microcontroller. What about a high-power LED? What if I want to change the brightness?
An LED is controlled by the current through it, not the voltage across it. You set that current with a resistor in series with the LED.
A microcontroller pin can supply only a few milliamps, so a bright LED needs a transistor to switch the larger current.
To dim it, you switch it on and off very quickly and let your eye average the result.
Think of an LED as a step that always drops you about 2 volts, like a fixed 2-meter drop on a staircase. If the supply offers 3. 3 volts, the other 1.
3 volts of drop has to happen somewhere, and the resistor takes it. A bigger resistor means less current flows. With no resistor, nothing limits the current and the LED burns out.
Flicking a light on and off fast makes it look dimmer.
A GPIO output high (3. 3 volts) pushes current through R and the LED to ground. With 3. 3 volts minus 2. 0 volts = 1. 3 volts across 270 ohms the current is 4. 8 milliamps.
Reversing the connection (LED to 3. 3 volts, pin sinks) works equally well and is often the stronger direction on MCUs.
Forward voltage ( V f ): the voltage an LED drops across itself when lit. Series resistor: the resistor in line with the LED that sets the current, I equals (V S-V f) over R .
MOSFET: a transistor used as a switch. A small voltage on its gate pin switches a large current.
PWM: ("What you can do with timers"): pulse-width modulation, switching on and off quickly at a fixed rate. Duty cycle: the fraction of each cycle the output is on.
A red LED drops 2 volts and should carry 5 milliamps from a 3. 3 volts pin. The resistor must drop 3. 3 minus 2 = 1. 3 volts at 5 milliamps, so R = 1. 3 / 0. 005 = 260 ohms.
The nearest standard value is 270 ohms, which gives 1. 3 / 270 = 4. 8 milliamps.
For dimming, switch the pin at 1 kilohertz with a 50% duty cycle: the LED is on half the time, so the average current is about half, and it looks dimmer. That is the whole idea.
"For a small LED I'd use a series resistor from a GPIO: R equals (V DD-V f) over I , so for a 2 volts red LED at 5 milliamps on 3. 3 volts that's 260 ohms, so a 270 ohms resistor.

For a high-power LED the pin can't supply the current, so I'd drive a logic-level N-MOSFET low-side switch from the pin, and regulate current with a constant-current driver rather than a lossy resistor.
To change brightness I'd use PWM from a timer at around 1 kilohertz with a gamma correction, or lower the driver's reference current for analog dimming."
Quick check. Why is a series resistor needed with an LED on a voltage source?
Driving a motor, isolation and speed control. The question: Draw a circuit to drive a motor from a microcontroller. What if isolation is required?
What if I want to change the speed?
A motor draws far more current than a microcontroller pin can give, especially when starting or stalled.
Its coils of wire also resist any sudden change in current, so when you switch it off it pushes back with a voltage spike.
So the pin only controls a transistor switch, a diode absorbs the spike, and extra parts handle direction, speed and sometimes electrical isolation.
Picture water rushing through a long pipe, with momentum. If you slam the valve shut, the water hammers against it and pressure spikes.
A bypass pipe beside the valve lets the flow keep circulating, and the spike goes away. In the motor, the current is the flow, and the diode is that bypass pipe.
The MOSFET switches the motor's ground return.
The Schottky diode D₁ sits across the motor with its cathode on the supply side: when Q₁ turns off, the motor current continues through D₁ instead of forcing the drain voltage up.
Without D₁ the drain would spike far above 12 volts.
MOSFET: a transistor used as a switch. A small voltage on its gate pin switches a large current.
Flyback diode: a diode across the motor that gives the current a path when the switch opens.
H-bridge: four switches arranged around the motor so you can reverse the voltage across it, and so its direction.
PWM: ("What you can do with timers"): switching on and off quickly, where the on-time fraction (duty cycle) sets the average power.
Stall current: the current when the motor is held still, which is the supply voltage divided by the winding resistance.
Say a 12 volts motor has 2 ohms of winding resistance. Held stalled, it draws 12 / 2 = 6 amps, hundreds of times what a pin can supply.
So the pin drives a MOSFET that switches the motor to ground, with a flyback diode across the motor.
Switching it with PWM at 50% duty gives an average of about 6 volts, so it spins at a little under half its full speed. That is the whole idea.

"For one direction I'd use a logic-level N-MOSFET as a low-side switch, gate through about 100 ohms with a pull-down, and a flyback diode across the motor to catch the inductive kick, plus a bulk capacitor.
For direction, an H-bridge with dead time to avoid shoot-through. For speed, PWM at around 20 kilohertz so the average voltage is duty times supply, ideally with encoder feedback.
If isolation is needed, optocouplers or digital isolators on the control signals, with an isolated gate driver and isolated supply on the power side."
Quick check. What is the purpose of the flyback diode across a motor driven by a MOSFET?
How an ADC works. The question: How does an ADC work?
An ADC (analog-to-digital converter) turns a voltage into a number that a microcontroller can use. It does this in three steps.
It samples, meaning it grabs the voltage at one instant. It quantizes, meaning it decides which of a fixed set of equal steps the voltage falls in.
Then it outputs that step's number as a binary code.
Imagine a ruler with 4,096 tick marks spread over 3. 3 volts. You hold a voltage up to the ruler and report the nearest tick below it.
You can never report a value between two ticks, so there is always a small rounding error.
If the voltage wiggles while you read it, your reading blurs, so the ADC freezes the voltage first and measures the frozen copy.
The conversion chain. Two inputs control it: the sample clock decides when the voltage is measured, and the reference decides what a code is worth .
Everything to the left of the quantizer is analog and sets noise and aliasing; everything to the right is digital and exact.
Resolution (bits): how many binary digits the code has. N bits gives 2 to the N possible steps. Reference voltage: the voltage that marks the top of the ruler.
The ADC measures the input as a fraction of it. LSB: the size of one step, the reference divided by 2 to the N .
Quantization error: the rounding error from snapping to a step: up to one step if you report the tick below, half a step if you report the middle of the step.
Sample-and-hold: ("What is sample and hold?") : the circuit that freezes the voltage while it is measured.
Take a 12-bit ADC with a 3. 3 volts reference. It has 2 to the 12 equals 4096 steps, so each step is 3. 3 / 4096, about 0. 8 millivolts. An input of 1.
65 volts is exactly half of the reference, so the code is 2048, half of 4096. A 1. 6504 volts input would give the same code, because it is less than one step higher.
That is the whole idea.
"An ADC samples the input, holds it steady, then compares it to a reference to pick one of 2 to the N levels and outputs that level as a binary code.
Resolution is the reference divided by 2 to the N , so a 12-bit ADC on 3. 3 volts has about 0. 8 millivolts per step.

How it finds the level depends on architecture: flash uses one comparator per level for speed, SAR does a binary search in N steps and is what most microcontrollers use, and delta-sigma oversamples to get very high resolution at low speed.
I'd always add an anti-alias filter and a clean reference."
Quick check. Which step of an ADC conversion throws information away irreversibly?
How a flash ADC works. The question: How does a flash ADC work?
A flash ADC measures a voltage in one step by checking every possible level at the same time.
One comparator (a circuit that says whether one voltage is higher than another) sits at each level. Counting how many say "yes" gives the answer.
It is the fastest kind of ADC, but the number of comparators doubles with every extra bit.
Picture a tank with a row of float switches at evenly spaced heights. When the water rises, every switch below the water line trips, and every switch above it stays off.
To know the level, you just count the tripped switches. The input voltage is the water, and the comparators are the switches.
The weakness is the cost: a finer reading needs many more switches.
A 2-bit flash ADC. Three comparators (C3, C2, C1) compare V in with taps at 3/4, 1/2, 1/4 of V ref ; each tap goes to the inverting (minus ) input.
The input bus runs to all the non-inverting (+) inputs, and wires that cross without a dot are not connected. A priority encoder turns the thermometer code T3 T2 T1 into D1 D0.
ADC: ("How an ADC works"): a circuit that turns a voltage into a number. Comparator: a circuit whose output says whether its input is above a threshold voltage.
Resistor ladder: ("Voltage divider: draw, equation, derivation"): equal resistors in series that make evenly spaced voltages, one at each tap.
Thermometer code: the pattern of comparator outputs, a run of ones with zeros above, like mercury in a thermometer.
Encoder: logic that turns the thermometer code into an ordinary binary number.
A 3-bit flash ADC with a 3. 3 volts reference uses 8 equal resistors, which make 7 thresholds spaced 3. 3 / 8, about 0. 41 volts apart: 0. 41, 0. 83, 1. 24, 1. 65, 2. 06, 2.
48, 2. 89 volts. An input of 1. 9 volts is above the first four, so those four comparators output 1 and the other three output 0.
The encoder turns four ones into binary 100, which is 4. An 8-bit version would need 255 comparators. That is the whole idea.
"A flash ADC compares the input against every possible threshold at once. A resistor ladder makes 2 to the N-1 evenly spaced reference voltages, one comparator per threshold.
The comparators output a thermometer code, ones up to the input level, and an encoder turns that into binary.
It's the fastest ADC architecture, one comparator delay, but the comparator count, area and power double with each bit and offsets must be below an LSB, so it's limited to around 8 bits."
Quick check. What is the main advantage of a flash ADC?
How a SAR ADC works. The question: How does a SAR ADC work?
A SAR ADC finds the number for a voltage by asking yes-or-no questions, one bit at a time, each question cutting the remaining range in half.
SAR stands for successive approximation register, the memory that holds the guess.
Most microcontrollers have one inside because it needs only one comparator and is cheap and low power.
Think of a balance scale and a set of weights worth 1/2, 1/4, 1/8 and 1/16 of a kilogram. To weigh something, you try the biggest weight first.
If the scale tips, that weight is too heavy and you take it off. If not, you keep it. Then you try the next one.
After four tries you know the weight to within the smallest weight. A SAR ADC does exactly this with voltages.
The SAR loop. The conversion costs N trips around the B, C, D/E, F cycle.
The time per trip is set by the DAC settling, the comparator's decision time and the logic, so the ADC clock sets the speed.
Comparator: a circuit that says whether one voltage is higher than another. It plays the role of the scale.
DAC: ("How a DAC works"): a circuit that turns a binary number into a voltage. It plays the role of the weights. MSB: the most significant bit, the one worth the most.
It is tested first. Sample-and-hold: ("What is sample and hold?") : a circuit that freezes the input so it cannot move during the search.
