How a flip-flop or latch works. The question: How does a flip flop/latch work?
A flip-flop or latch remembers one bit by feeding a circuit's output back into its own input. Two cross-coupled gates settle into one of two stable states, 0 or 1, and stay there.
Add an enable and you get a D latch. Put two latches in series with opposite enables and you get a flip-flop that changes only at a clock edge.
Think of a rocker light switch. Push it up and it stays up; push it down and it stays down. It remembers which way it was last pushed.
Balanced exactly in the middle, it is unstable, and the slightest nudge tips it one way or the other. A gate loop does the same: feedback reinforces whichever state it is in.
The solid curve is one inverter's transfer function; the dashed curve is the other inverter's, drawn with axes swapped.

They intersect at three points: two full-rail states that are stable (the slope product is less than one there, so errors shrink) and one at the switching threshold, which is unstable (slope product greater than one, so errors grow).
Positive feedback: feeding an output back so that it reinforces its own state, giving two stable states (bistable).
NOR gate: a logic gate whose output is 1 only when both inputs are 0. Cross-coupled means each gate's output feeds the other's input.
SR latch: two cross-coupled NOR gates with set (S) and reset (R) inputs. D latch: a gated latch whose output follows input D while its enable is active.
Master-slave: two latches with opposite enables, forming a flip-flop.
Take an SR latch made of two cross-coupled NOR gates. Say it stores Q = 1. With S and R both 0, it just holds. Pulse R to 1. The top NOR now outputs 0, so Q = 0.
That makes the other output 1, and the loop locks in the new state. Return R to 0 and Q stays 0. Pulsing S to 1 does the reverse.
Setting S and R both to 1 is forbidden, because both outputs go to 0 and releasing them together is unpredictable.
"Feedback is the key. Two cross-coupled NOR gates form an SR latch with two stable states, so it stores a bit: set, reset, or hold, with both inputs high forbidden.
Gate the inputs with an enable and tie them to D and its complement and you get a D latch, which is transparent while enabled.

Put two D latches in series with opposite enables and you get a flip-flop: the master captures D while the clock is low, and at the rising edge the slave takes it to Q, so the output only changes on the edge."
Quick check. What makes cross-coupled gates able to store a bit?
Design a memory cell. The question: Design a memory cell.
First ask what you need: speed, density and standby power. For fast memory inside a processor chip, the answer is the SRAM cell.
A loop of two inverters holds the bit, and two access transistors connect it to the bit lines for reading and writing.
For dense main memory, the answer is a DRAM cell, one transistor and one capacitor.
A rocker switch stays where you leave it, as long as it has power, which is SRAM.
A bucket with a tiny leak holds water for a while, but you must top it up regularly, which is DRAM. The bucket is smaller, so you fit billions.
The bucket picture misses that reading a DRAM cell drains it, so the value must be written back.
Net labels with the same name are connected.
Node Q (between MP1 and MN1) is wired straight to the gates of MP2/MN2, and node Q̄ (between MP2 and MN2) returns to the gates of MP1/MN1 through the matching Q̄ labels: that is the bistable loop.
MA1 and MA2 connect Q and Q̄ to BL and BLB, and share the word line WL.
SRAM: static RAM. Each bit sits in a loop of two inverters (gates whose output is the opposite of their input), each feeding the other. It needs no refresh. DRAM: dynamic RAM.
Each bit is charge on a tiny capacitor, which leaks. Word line and bit line: the word line selects a row of cells. Bit lines carry the data to and from them.
Access transistor: a switch that connects a storage node to a bit line when the word line is on.
Refresh: periodically reading and rewriting DRAM cells before their charge leaks away.
An SRAM cell has 4 transistors in the inverter loop plus 2 access transistors, 6 in all. To write, drive the bit lines and turn on the word line; they overpower the loop.
Now a DRAM read. Say the supply is 1. 2 volts, the cell capacitor is 25 fF (femtofarads, a tiny capacitance), and the bit line is 100 fF, precharged to 0. 6 volts.
A stored 1 shares charge and moves the bit line by 0. 12 volts, or 120 millivolts, which a sensitive amplifier (the sense amplifier) detects.
"I'd first ask volatile or not, and speed versus density.
For fast on-chip storage I'd use a 6T SRAM cell: two cross-coupled CMOS inverters hold the bit, and two NMOS access transistors on a word line connect the storage nodes to the bit lines.
Write by driving the bit lines and overpowering the cell; read by precharging and sensing which line droops.
Sizing is the trade-off: the pull-downs must beat the access devices for read stability, and the access devices must beat the pull-ups for write.
For density I'd use a 1T1C DRAM cell, which needs refresh."

Why digital systems need clocks. The question: Why are clocks needed?
A clock is a signal that ticks at a steady rate, and digital circuits use the ticks to decide when to update.
Logic gates need a little time to settle on the right answer, and they can show wrong values on the way.
The clock says "capture now", so every memory element grabs its input at the same instant, after things have settled.
Picture a classroom where every student does scratch work and a bell rings at regular intervals. At each bell, everyone copies their current answer onto the board.
Between bells the scratch work can be as messy as it likes, because nobody reads it. Only what is on the board at the bell counts.
The catch: the time between bells must be long enough for the slowest student to finish.
When A falls, the AND term A·B falls at once but the other term rises one inverter delay later, so F glitches low (red) for one slot between two clock edges.
Q only samples F at the edges: just before the glitch and again after F has settled back to 1 (the setup margin is what guarantees it has settled).
The glitch itself is never captured. The clock decides when you look.
Clock period: the time between ticks. The frequency is 1 divided by the period.
Flip-flop: a one-bit memory that copies its input only at a clock tick ("How a flip-flop or latch works").
Combinational logic: gates whose output depends only on their current inputs, with no memory. Glitch: a brief wrong output while gates are still settling.
A block of logic needs 4 nanoseconds to settle, and the flip-flop adds about 0. 5 nanoseconds of its own delay. Choose a period of 5 nanoseconds, which is a 200 megahertz clock.
The output may glitch for the first 4 nanoseconds, but the flip-flop only looks at the 5 nanoseconds tick, when the answer is clean.
A 2 nanoseconds period would capture an unfinished answer. That is the whole idea: the clock turns messy, continuous change into clean steps.
"Logic takes time to settle and glitches on the way, so we need a point at which values are guaranteed valid.
The clock provides it: flip-flops capture on the edge, and between edges the logic can glitch freely.
That makes the design a simple state-to-next-state machine, lets us pipeline for speed, orders operations, and gives timers and protocols a time base.
The costs are clock power, skew and jitter, and EMI; the alternative is asynchronous design, which is harder."
Quick check. What is the main reason digital systems use a clock?
What happens when a clock is too fast. The question: What happens if a clock is too fast?
Every clock tick gives the logic a fixed amount of time to finish its work.
If you speed the clock up so the next tick arrives before the slowest logic is done, the circuit captures an unfinished answer.
You get wrong results, often only for certain inputs.
A baker pulls a tray out of the oven on a fixed timer. Most items bake in 10 minutes, but the thick loaf needs 20.
Set the timer to 15 minutes and the rolls come out fine while the loaf comes out raw. A chip behaves the same way: the slowest path fails first.
Heat or a lower supply voltage slows every path, so a clock that works on a cool day can fail on a hot one.
As the available time shrinks (clock gets faster), the fraction of failing paths climbs from essentially zero to nearly all.
A design that is marginal fails some paths first, which is why failures start sporadically and then become systematic.
(A logistic curve is used here as a smooth stand-in for a Gaussian delay distribution.)
Clock period: the time between ticks, which is 1 divided by the clock frequency. Critical path: the slowest chain of logic between two flip-flops (one-bit memories).
It sets the fastest safe clock. Slack: spare time on a path, equal to the period minus the time the path needs. Negative slack means failure.
Metastability: when data changes right at the capture instant, the output can hover in between before settling ("What is metastability").
An 8-bit adder passes its carry (the "1" carried to the next column) through 8 stages of 0. 25 nanoseconds each, plus 0. 5 nanoseconds of flip-flop overhead.
The slowest case needs 8 times 0. 25 plus 0. 5 equals 2. 5 nanoseconds, so the safe maximum clock is 400 megahertz. At 2. 0 nanoseconds (500 megahertz) the slack is -0.
5 nanoseconds. Adding 1 + 1 still works, since its carry moves only one stage.
Adding 255 + 1 sends the carry through all 8 bits, so the top bit gets a stale carry and the answer is wrong. That is the whole idea.
"If the clock period is shorter than clock-to-Q plus the longest logic delay plus setup, flip-flops sample before data has settled: setup violations.
The longest paths fail first, so you get pattern-dependent wrong results, worse when hot or at low voltage, and possibly metastability.
Power and heat rise with frequency too, and interfaces like memory or SPI slaves have their own limits. Hold violations aren't affected by frequency.
The fix is to pipeline or optimize the critical path, raise the voltage, or lower the clock."
Quick check. What is the most direct result of clocking a design faster than its critical path allows?
What is a register. The question: What is a register?
A register is a small group of one-bit memories that share one clock and hold a multi-bit number together.
It keeps its value steady, then loads a new one at a clock tick when told to. Chips use registers between calculation steps, inside CPUs, and as control knobs for software.
Picture a row of eight light switches, each set to on (1) or off (0), plus a row of eight dials in front of them. A single lever, the clock, is wired to all eight switches.
When someone pulls the lever, every switch copies its dial at the same moment. Between pulls the switches hold still.
A lock on the lever, the load enable, decides whether a pull does anything.
Four flip-flops sit side by side.
Each D input takes one bit of the data bus, every clock pin (the small triangle input) is on the same CLK net, and the Q outputs together form the stored word.
All four bits update at the same clock edge.
Flip-flop: the one-bit memory that copies its input at a clock tick ("How a flip-flop or latch works"). A register is a row of them.
Clock tick: the repeating signal that says "capture now" ("Why digital systems need clocks"). Load enable: a control input.
The register only takes new data on ticks when it is on. Memory-mapped register: a register at an address that software can read or write to control a peripheral such as a timer.
Take an 8-bit register that starts at 0. The data input shows 0000 0101, which is 5. With load enable on, the next tick copies it, so the register holds 5.
Now the data input changes to 0000 1001, which is 9, but load enable is off. The next tick changes nothing, and the register still holds 5.
Turn load enable on, and the following tick loads 9. That is the whole idea.
"A register is a group of flip-flops sharing a clock that stores a multi-bit value: on the active edge, when enabled, all bits load together, and in between it holds.
An 8-bit register is eight D flip-flops.

In logic design it's the state between combinational stages; in a CPU it's the fast register file; a shift register moves bits along each clock; and in firmware, peripheral registers are memory-mapped addresses you read and write to configure and monitor hardware."

What is metastability. The question: What is metastability?
Metastability happens when a flip-flop's input changes at the very instant it is supposed to capture it.
The flip-flop cannot decide between 0 and 1, so its output hovers somewhere in between for a short, random time before falling to one side.
The danger is that different gates read the muddy in-between voltage differently and disagree.
Picture a ball balanced on the top of a hill with a valley on each side. A clear push sends it rolling into one valley right away.
A tiny nudge leaves it wobbling on the peak, and nobody can say how long before it tips. The closer to perfect balance, the longer it takes.
The ball always tips eventually, but there is no upper limit on the wait.
The closer the initial state is to the exact midpoint, the longer resolution takes, growing logarithmically without bound. Starting 1 millivolts off takes about 6.
4 time constants (192 picoseconds); starting 1 nV off takes about 20 time constants (0. 6 nanoseconds).
Because the offset is a continuous random variable, there is always some chance of a very long resolution.
Flip-flop: a one-bit memory that grabs its input at each clock tick ("How a flip-flop or latch works").
Setup/hold window: the tiny interval around a clock tick when the input must hold still ("Setup and hold times").
Asynchronous input: a signal with no timing relationship to your clock, such as a button press. Resolution time: how long the output takes to settle to a clean 0 or 1.
Synchronizer: two flip-flops in a row on the same clock. The first may go muddy, but it gets a full clock period to settle before the second one reads it.
A signal from elsewhere, changing about 100 million times a second, feeds a flip-flop clocked at 1 gigahertz.
Now and then a change lands inside the window, and the flip-flop goes metastable. With the page's sample numbers, if the next stage reads it only 0.
7 nanoseconds later, the average time between failures is about 7,000 seconds, under two hours.
Add a second flip-flop, which gives about 1 nanoseconds more time to settle, and the average gap grows to about 65 billion years. That is the whole idea.
"Metastability is when a flip-flop samples a data change inside its setup/hold window and its internal bistable loop is left near the unstable midpoint.
Positive feedback then amplifies the tiny difference exponentially, so the output eventually settles to 0 or 1, but after a random and unbounded time, during which it may sit at an in-between level.
You can't prevent it for asynchronous inputs, so you use synchronizers: two flip-flops in series give the first one a full cycle to resolve, making the MTBF astronomically long.
Multi-bit buses need FIFOs or handshakes."
Quick check. What causes a flip-flop to go metastable?
What is a mux. The question: What is a mux?
A mux, short for multiplexer, is a switch controlled by digital signals. It has several data inputs, a few select inputs, and one output.
The select inputs, read as a binary number, choose which data input gets passed to the output.
Think of the input selector knob on an old stereo, with positions for CD, tape and radio. Whatever position the knob points to is what you hear, and the other sources are ignored.
A mux is that knob, except the knob position is a number written in 0 seconds and 1 seconds instead of an angle.
A 2:1 mux from gates. The inverter makes the S' signal that enables A, and S itself enables B; the OR merges the two (only one AND output can be 1 at a time).
Notice that S' is made by an extra gate, so S' arrives one inverter delay later than S. That delay is the origin of the glitch discussed below.
Data inputs: the signals you choose between. Select lines: the control inputs that pick which data input reaches the output.
Binary number: a number written with only 0 seconds and 1 seconds. Two select lines give 4 combinations, so they can choose among 4 inputs ("Converting between number bases").
Start with the smallest mux: 2 inputs, A and B, and one select line S. If S is 0, the output Y copies A. If S is 1, Y copies B. Suppose A is 1 and B is 0.
With S = 0 the output is 1, and with S = 1 the output is 0. Now make it a 4-input mux. It needs two select lines, because two lines give 4 combinations.
Select 10 (binary for 2) and the output copies the input numbered 2, counting from 0. That is the whole idea: select lines pick one input and the output copies it.
"A mux is a digitally controlled switch: N data inputs, log-two-of-N select lines, one output that follows whichever input the select picks.
A 2-to-1 is Y equals not-S times A plus S times B, so an inverter, two ANDs and an OR, or just two transmission gates in CMOS. You can tree them to make bigger ones.
They're used for register source selection, ALU result select, and every if-else in RTL.
They're also universal: tie the data inputs to constants and you've got a look-up table, which is what an FPGA is built from."
Quick check. How many select lines does a 16:1 multiplexer need?
Draw logic gate symbols. The question: Draw a NOT/AND/etc gate symbol.
A logic gate is a tiny circuit with one or two inputs, each 0 or 1, and one output that follows a fixed rule.
Each rule has its own drawn symbol, so an engineer can read a circuit diagram at a glance.
This question asks you to sketch the standard ones: NOT, AND, OR, NAND, NOR, XOR and XNOR.
Think of road signs. You don't read a sign, you recognize its shape. Gate symbols work the same way. A small circle on a symbol, called a bubble, means "flip the answer".
So the family is a few base shapes plus an optional bubble.
The one-input gates. The buffer is the bare triangle. Adding the bubble at the tip turns it into the inverter. Everything that follows reuses that same bubble.
NOT: the output is the opposite of the input. It is a triangle with a bubble. AND: the output is 1 only if all inputs are 1. It is a flat-backed "D" shape.
OR: the output is 1 if at least one input is 1. It has a curved back and a pointed front. Bubble: the small circle that inverts a signal.
A bubble on the output of AND makes NAND, on OR makes NOR, and on XOR makes XNOR. XOR: the output is 1 when the two inputs differ.
It is an OR with one extra curved line behind it.
Draw an AND gate: a flat back, a round front, two input wires on the left, one output on the right. With A = 1 and B = 1, the output is 1. With A = 1 and B = 0, the output is 0.
Add a bubble on the output tip and you have a NAND, which gives the opposite answers: 0 and 1. That is the whole idea: a few shapes plus a bubble cover the family.
"I draw inputs on the left, output on the right. A triangle is a buffer, and a triangle with a bubble is NOT. AND is a D shape, OR is the curved-back shield shape.
Add a bubble on the output of those and you get NAND and NOR. XOR is OR with an extra curved line at the back, XNOR adds a bubble. The bubble always means inversion.
I'd write the expression next to each one: A·B, A+B, A⊕B. And the symbol only tells you the function, not how it's built."
Quick check. Which symbol is a NOR gate?
Logic gates from CMOS transistors. The question: Draw a NOT/AND/etc gate from transistors.
Inside a chip, logic gates are built from transistors, which act as tiny switches controlled by a voltage. A CMOS gate uses two teams of switches.
One team can connect the output to the supply voltage (a 1). The other can connect it to ground (a 0).
For any input, exactly one team is on, so the gate wastes almost no power when nothing is changing.
Imagine a bucket that holds the output level. A valve on a pipe from a high tank can fill it (a 1), and a valve on a drain can empty it (a 0).
The design rule is that the two are never both open and never both closed.
The CMOS inverter. The PMOS (top) connects Y to V DD when A is low; the NMOS (bottom) connects Y to ground when A is high.
Both gates share the input A and both drains share the output Y.
NMOS: a transistor switch that closes when its input is 1. It connects the output to ground. PMOS: a transistor switch that closes when its input is 0.
It connects the output to the supply. Supply and ground: the supply voltage is the "1" level, and ground (0 volts) is the "0" level.
In series / in parallel: switches in a line, where all must close to conduct, versus side by side, where any one is enough.
Inverter: one PMOS to the supply and one NMOS to ground, sharing the input. Input 0: the PMOS closes, the NMOS opens, so the output is 1. Input 1 reverses it, and the output is 0.
NAND: two NMOS in series to ground, two PMOS in parallel to the supply. With A = B = 1, both NMOS close, so the output is 0.
With A = 0 and B = 1, A's PMOS closes and the NMOS chain is broken, so the output is 1. That is the whole idea.
"The base cell is the CMOS inverter: a PMOS from VDD to the output, an NMOS from the output to ground, gates tied together.
Input low pulls the output up, input high pulls it down, and one is always off so there's no static current.
A NAND has two NMOS in series on the bottom and two PMOS in parallel on top; a NOR is the dual.
The rule is: pull-down implements the complement of the function, AND as series, OR as parallel, and the pull-up is the dual.
AND and OR are those gates plus an inverter, six transistors."
Quick check. In a CMOS inverter, which transistor connects the output to ground?
Truth tables for logic gates. The question: Draw the truth table for NOT/AND/etc gate.
A truth table lists every possible combination of inputs to a gate and the output the gate gives for each one. With 2 inputs there are 4 combinations, so the table has 4 rows.
This question asks you to fill in the table for each standard gate. Once the table is written, nothing about the gate is left to guess.
Think of a multiplication table on a poster. Every possible question is on the edges, and the answer is in the grid. You never calculate, you just look up.
A truth table is the same poster for a gate, small enough to be complete. It is simpler than a times table, because every answer is just 0 or 1.
The same truth table as a waveform. A and B step through 00, 01, 10, 11 (one column each).
Compare AND with NAND, OR with NOR, and XOR with XNOR: in every pair, each bit is flipped.
Notice that XOR is high exactly when A and B differ (columns 2 and 3), and that NOR is high only in the first column.
Row: one input combination and its output, such as A = 1, B = 0 giving Y = 0. Binary counting order: listing rows as 00, 01, 10, 11. It makes a missing row easy to spot.
AND / OR: AND gives 1 only if all inputs are 1. OR gives 1 if at least one input is 1. XOR: gives 1 when the inputs differ. For two inputs that means exactly one is 1.
Complement: swap every 0 and 1. NAND is the complement of AND.
List the four rows 00, 01, 10, 11 for inputs A and B. AND gives 0, 0, 0, 1, because only the last row has both inputs at 1.
XOR gives 0, 1, 1, 0, because the middle two rows differ. NAND is the complement of AND, so it gives 1, 1, 1, 0.
That is the whole idea: list the rows in order, then fill one column per gate.
"With two inputs there are four rows: 00, 01, 10, 11. AND is 0, 0, 0, 1. OR is 0, 1, 1, 1. NAND and NOR are those inverted: 1, 1, 1, 0 and 1, 0, 0, 0.
XOR is 0, 1, 1, 0, high when the inputs differ, and XNOR is 1, 0, 0, 1. NOT just flips its one input.
I remember the rule rather than the columns: AND needs all ones, OR needs any one, XOR needs an odd number of ones. For n inputs the table has 2 to the n rows."

The universal logic gate. The question: What is the universal logic gate?
A universal gate is one type of gate from which you can build every other logic gate, and therefore any digital circuit. NAND is universal, and so is NOR.
This matters because everything can be built from one simple gate repeated many times.
Imagine a toy set with only one kind of brick. With enough bricks you can still build a house, a car or a bridge, though some builds take more bricks than a mixed set would.
A universal gate is that one kind of brick. The catch is the same: a design built from a single gate type is often bigger than one using a mix.
NOT, AND and OR built only from NAND2 gates. Counting: NOT uses 1 gate, AND uses 2 (the second one is the inverter), OR uses 3 (two inverters feeding a NAND).
With these three, any function can be built.
NAND: AND followed by a flip. Its output is 0 only when all inputs are 1 ("Truth tables for logic gates"). NOT (inverter): a gate that flips 0 to 1 and 1 to 0.
AND / OR: gates described on "Draw logic gate symbols". Any circuit can be written using AND, OR and NOT. Tied inputs: wiring both inputs of a gate to the same signal.
Make a NOT from a NAND by tying both inputs together. If A = 0, NAND(0, 0) = 1. If A = 1, NAND(1, 1) = 0. That is a NOT. Make an AND by following a NAND with that NOT.
With A = B = 1, the NAND gives 0 and the NOT turns it into 1. Any other input gives NAND = 1 and AND = 0, which is right.
So NAND can make NOT and AND, and an OR is built from NANDs too. With those three, anything can be built. That is the whole idea.
"NAND, and also NOR, is universal: any logic function can be built from that single gate.
For NAND: tie both inputs together for a NOT, add a NOT after a NAND for AND, and NAND the two inverted inputs for OR by De Morgan.
Since AND, OR and NOT can build anything, NAND can. NOR is the dual. AND and OR alone aren't universal because they can't invert.
NAND is preferred in CMOS because its series stack is NMOS, so it's faster and smaller than NOR."

Converting between number bases. The question: Convert some binary/hex/oct/decimal number to a different base.
A number base is how many different digits a counting system uses. Decimal uses 10 digits, binary uses 2 (0 and 1), and hexadecimal (hex) uses 16 (0 to 9, then A to F).
Converting between bases changes how a number is written, not how big it is. Hardware stores everything in binary, but people find hex shorter to read.
Suppose you must pay 13 cents. With coins worth 1, 10 and 100 you pay one 10 and three 1 seconds, which is the decimal "13".
With coins worth 1, 2, 4 and 8 you pay one 8, one 4 and one 1, which is binary 1101. The amount is the same, and only the coin set changes.
The same 16 bits grouped two ways.
Hex groups of four from the right give B, E, E, F; octal groups of three from the right give 1, 3, 7, 3, 5, 7 (the leftmost group has just one bit, padded with zeros).
Because both groupings start at the right-hand end (the LSB), the number needs no arithmetic to convert: 0xBEEF = 0o137357.
Base (radix): how many different digits the system has, such as 2, 10 or 16. Place value: the worth of a digit's position. In binary the places are 1, 2, 4, 8, and so on.
Bit and nibble: a bit is one binary digit. A nibble is 4 bits, which is exactly one hex digit. Hex digits A to F: stand for 10 to 15, so a single character holds a value up to 15.
Convert 175 to binary. Pick the largest place values that fit: 128 + 32 + 8 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 175. That puts a 1 in those places and a 0 in the others, which gives 1010 1111.
For hex, split the bits into groups of four from the right. 1010 is 10, written A, and 1111 is 15, written F. So 175 is 0xAF, and as a check, 10 times 16 plus 15 equals 175 .
That is the whole idea.
"Every base is positional, so to get to decimal I add digit times power of the base: 0xAF is 10 times 16 plus 15, which is 175.
Going from decimal, I divide repeatedly by the target base and read the remainders bottom to top.
For binary to hex or octal I just group the bits, 4 per hex digit and 3 per octal digit, starting from the right: 1010 1111 is AF, and 10 101 111 is 257 in octal.
Then I check by converting back."

What is a truth table?. The question: What is a truth table?
A truth table is a complete list of what a circuit does. Each row is one combination of inputs, with the output the circuit gives for it. With n inputs there are 2 to the n rows.
It only works for circuits with no memory, where the output depends only on the inputs right now.
Picture three light switches in a hallway, wired so the light comes on when at least two are up.
You could describe the wiring in words, but it is clearer to list all 8 switch settings and write "on" or "off" beside each.
Nobody can argue with that list, and it leaves nothing out. A truth table is that list. It does not say how the wires are connected, only what the result is.
Rows (orange) grow exponentially, but the number of possible functions (blue) grows exponentially in the number of rows , a double exponential.
Four inputs already have 65,536 possible functions; five have about 4. 3 billion. This is why synthesis tools and K-maps exploit structure rather than enumerating.
Row: one input combination and its output. Combinational logic: a circuit whose output depends only on its present inputs, with no stored history.
Sum of products: an OR of AND terms. You read it off the table from the rows where the output is 1.
Don't-care: an input combination that never happens, so its output can be left open.
Use the three switches A, B, C and the rule "light on if at least two are on".
List the rows in counting order: 000 gives 0, 001 gives 0, 010 gives 0, 011 gives 1, 100 gives 0, 101 gives 1, 110 gives 1, and 111 gives 1. Four rows are 1.
Read the AND terms for those rows and simplify them, and the circuit becomes AB + AC + BC (AB means A AND B, and + means OR).
That is the whole idea: list every row, then read the circuit from the table.
"A truth table lists every possible combination of a circuit's inputs and the output for each one. With n inputs there are 2 to the n rows.
It fully specifies a combinational function, and I can get the Boolean expression straight from it by ORing the minterms of the rows where the output is 1.
Then I'd simplify with a K-map. It doesn't work for circuits with memory, because there the output also depends on state, so you'd need a state table."
Quick check. How many rows does the truth table of a 5-input combinational function have?
Do the K-map for a truth table. The question: Do the K-map for a given truth table.
A K-map (Karnaugh map) redraws a truth table as a grid so you can spot, by eye, groups of 1 seconds.
Each group lets you write a shorter expression, which means fewer gates in the circuit. It is a hand method for simplifying small logic functions.
Imagine a wall of lamps in a grid, with some lit. A big rectangle of lit lamps can be described with a short rule, like "the whole top row".
A single lit lamp needs its full address.
The K-map is arranged so that lamps next to each other differ in only one input, so a rectangle of lit lamps means those inputs do not matter.
One difference from a normal wall: the edges wrap around, so the left edge touches the right edge.
The K-map for f = Σm(0,1,2,5,8,9,10). Small grey numbers are minterm indices; note how they are not in counting order.
The blue corner circles (wrapping around both edges) are B'D', the dashed red top-and-bottom pair of blocks is B'C', and the green pair is A'C'D.
Truth table: a list of every input combination and its output ("What is a truth table?") Gray order: the label order 00, 01, 11, 10, in which each step changes only one bit.
Group: a rectangle of 1 seconds whose size is 1, 2, 4 or 8 cells. Bigger groups give simpler terms.
Product term: an AND of some of the inputs, such as A times B' (the apostrophe means "not").
Take two inputs, A and B, with output 1 for A B = 10 and A B = 11, and 0 otherwise. On the map, those two 1 seconds sit side by side, in the row where A = 1.
They differ only in B, so B does not matter: the output is 1 whenever A = 1. The group of two removed one input, so f equals A .
That is the whole idea: neighbors that differ in one input merge into a shorter term.

"I lay out the K-map with the variables in Gray code so neighbouring cells differ in one bit, fill in the 1 seconds from the truth table, and circle the biggest rectangles of 1 seconds in powers of two, wrapping around the edges.
Each group becomes one product term containing just the variables that don't change within it. OR the terms together and I have a minimal sum of products.
Don't-cares can be used to enlarge groups, and I always check that every 1 is covered."

What is an FSM?. The question: What is an FSM?
A finite state machine (FSM) is a circuit that is always in exactly one of a small, fixed set of situations, called states.
On every clock tick it moves to a next state that depends on its current state and its inputs. This is how hardware remembers what has happened so far.
FSMs run things like traffic lights, protocol controllers and pattern detectors.
Think of a subway turnstile. It has two states: locked and unlocked. Put in a coin, and it goes from locked to unlocked. Push through, and it goes back to locked.
Pushing while locked changes nothing, and neither does another coin while unlocked.
You can predict what happens next from just two things: which state it is in now, and what you do to it.
Every synchronous FSM has the same skeleton. The loop through the state register is what stores history. The dashed arrow (input to output logic) exists only in a Mealy machine.
Clock and reset go only to the flip-flops.
State: one of the machine's situations, a summary of what it needs to remember. Transition: a move from one state to another on a clock tick.
State register: the flip-flops (one-bit memories) that hold the current state ("What is a register"). Moore / Mealy: two styles. In Moore, outputs depend only on the state.
In Mealy, they also depend on the current inputs ("Mealy vs Moore FSM"). Reset state: the known starting state the machine enters on reset.
The turnstile has 2 states, so the state register needs just one flip-flop: 0 for locked, 1 for unlocked. The rules are: coin when locked goes to unlocked.
Push when unlocked goes to locked. The other two combinations keep the state. Reset puts it in locked. That is the whole idea: a stored state plus rules for the next state.
"An FSM is a clocked circuit that is in one of a finite number of states and moves between them based on its inputs.
Hardware-wise it's a state register of flip-flops, next-state logic that depends on state and inputs, and output logic.
If outputs depend only on state it's Moore; if they also depend on inputs it's Mealy.
I'd use one for anything with history: protocol handlers, sequence detectors, arbiters, controllers.
Key design points are state encoding, a reset to a known state, and synchronizing asynchronous inputs."

Mealy vs Moore FSM. The question: What is the difference between a Mealy and Moore FSM?
Both are finite state machines, circuits that remember a state and step through states on a clock ("What is an FSM?") The difference is what the output depends on.
In a Moore machine, the output depends only on the current state. In a Mealy machine, it depends on the current state and the current inputs.
That leads to trade-offs in speed of reaction, state count and cleanliness.
A vending machine has a "PAID" lamp. The lamp shows which state the machine is in, so it only changes when the state changes. That is Moore.
Now add a bell that rings at the very moment the last coin drops. It reacts to an input right now, without waiting for a state change. That is Mealy.
The bell is quicker but can also ring by mistake if the coin sensor flickers.
In both machines the state register feeds back through the next-state logic. Mealy adds one extra arrow, from the inputs straight to the output logic.
That arrow is the origin of everything different: earlier response, fewer states, and an input-to-output combinational path.
State: the machine's stored situation. Moore output: depends on the state alone. Mealy output: depends on the state and the inputs right now.
Latency: the number of clock cycles between an input and its visible effect. Glitch: a brief wrong pulse on an output while logic settles.
Take a detector that raises its output when the input bits are 1, 0, 1 in order. Feed it 1 in cycle 1, 0 in cycle 2 and 1 in cycle 3.
The Mealy version raises its output in cycle 3, as soon as it sees the last 1, and needs 3 states.
The Moore version must first move to a "just matched 101" state, so its output rises in cycle 4. It needs 4 states.
That is the whole idea: Mealy is quicker and smaller, Moore is slower and cleaner.
"In a Moore machine the outputs depend only on the current state; in a Mealy machine they depend on the current state and the current inputs.

So a Moore output changes only on clock edges and is clean, while a Mealy output can respond within the same cycle, which is one cycle faster and usually needs fewer states, but it can glitch if the inputs do.
For an overlapping 101 detector, Moore needs four states and Mealy three.
I'd use Moore for clean registered outputs and Mealy when I need the fast response, and register the output if it feeds anything sensitive."

Name some computer architectures. The question: Name some computer architectures.
A computer architecture is the overall design of a processor: how it organizes memory, which instructions it understands, and how it carries them out.
Many designs exist because jobs differ. A coin-cell sensor and a data-center server both run instructions, but they need very different trade-offs in speed, power and cost.
Think of vehicles: a bicycle, a car, a bus and a freight train. None is best. Each trades cost, speed, capacity and fuel for a different job. Processor designs work the same way.
A small, simple core sips power, a big complex one is fast, and a graphics chip moves huge amounts of data at once but is slow at any single task.
In a von Neumann machine, instructions and data share one memory port, so an instruction fetch and a data access cannot happen in the same cycle. Harvard separates them.
Real CPUs mimic Harvard at the L1-cache level (split I-cache and D-cache) while presenting one unified memory above that.
Instruction set (ISA): the list of basic commands a processor understands, such as add ("What is an ISA?") Von Neumann: instructions and data share one memory and one path.
Harvard: separate memories and paths for instructions and data. RISC / CISC: a small set of simple instructions versus a large set of complex ones ("RISC vs CISC advantages").
SIMD: one instruction working on many data items at once.
Compare von Neumann and Harvard. Suppose 30% of instructions also read or write data. In a von Neumann machine, each instruction needs 1 memory access to be fetched, plus 0.
3 on average for data. That is 1. 3 accesses per instruction through one door, so it can never do better than 1. 3 cycles per instruction.
A Harvard machine has two doors and does both in the same cycle.
Real CPUs get this benefit by keeping two small, fast memories (caches) next to the core, one for instructions and one for data.
That is the whole idea: each name is a different trade-off.
"I'd split them up. By memory: von Neumann, with one shared memory for code and data, and Harvard, with separate ones; real CPUs are modified Harvard with split L1 caches.
By instruction set: CISC like x86 and RISC like ARM, RISC-V and MIPS.
By execution style: in-order pipelined, superscalar out-of-order, VLIW, SIMD/vector, GPU-style SIMT, and multicore. Then special-purpose ones like DSPs and neural accelerators.
Each one targets a bottleneck: memory bandwidth, instruction throughput, or energy per operation."
Quick check. Which statement best describes a Harvard architecture?
Architectures in phones and consumer electronics. The question: What type of computer architectures are often used in smartphones/consumer electronics?
Phone processors are almost all built around Arm cores.
The bigger idea is that a phone chip is a system on a chip (SoC): CPU cores plus dedicated blocks for graphics, the camera, AI and the radio, all on one piece of silicon.
Everything is designed around one limit, which is battery life and heat.
Picture a restaurant kitchen. A star chef (a fast, power-hungry core) handles the rush. Line cooks (small, efficient cores) handle routine orders all day.
Specialist machines, like a bread slicer, each do one job using far less effort than a chef would.
Phones assign work the same way, choosing the cheapest worker that can do the job in time.
Slowing from 2. 5 gigahertz to 1 gigahertz cuts performance to 40% but power to about 20% and energy per operation to 49%, because both frequency and V^2 fall.
The V(f) model is made up for illustration; real silicon curves come from the vendor's characterization.
SoC (system on a chip): the CPU, graphics, camera, AI and other blocks integrated in one chip.
Arm: the instruction set used by nearly all phone CPUs, licensed to many chip makers. big. LITTLE: pairing fast cores for bursts with small efficient cores for background work.
Accelerator: a block built for one job, such as video or AI, that uses less energy than a CPU would.
DVFS: lowering the clock speed and voltage together when full speed is not needed.
Dynamic power, the power spent switching transistors, depends on frequency and on voltage squared. With the page's illustrative numbers, 2. 5 gigahertz needs 1. 0 volts, but 1.
0 gigahertz needs only 0. 7 volts. At 1. 0 gigahertz the speed is 40% of before. Power drops to about 20%, and energy per operation to about 49%.
So a modest task run slowly at low voltage costs about half the energy. That is the whole idea: a phone saves energy by matching each task to the cheapest hardware.
"Phones and most consumer electronics use Arm-based RISC cores, because they're very efficient per watt and the licensing model lets each vendor build its own SoC.
A phone chip is heterogeneous: big out-of-order cores for bursts, small efficient cores for background work, plus a GPU, image processor, DSP, neural engine and modem on the same die.
Small devices like earbuds use Cortex-M style microcontrollers, and RISC-V is growing. It's all driven by battery life and heat."

What is a CPU?. The question: What is a CPU?
A CPU (central processing unit) is the part of a computer that runs programs. A program is a list of simple instructions stored in memory, such as "add these two numbers".
The CPU repeats three steps over and over: fetch the next instruction, decode what it means, and execute it.
Imagine a cook following a recipe, one card at a time, with a finger on the current step.
The cook reads the step (fetch), works out what it asks for (decode), and does it (execute). Then the finger moves to the next card. A CPU does this billions of times per second.
Unlike a cook, it can also jump to a different card when a step says to.
One instruction's trip through a simple CPU.
The program counter addresses memory, the control unit decodes, the register file supplies operands, the ALU computes, and the result returns to the register file.
The control unit updates the PC at the end. Real CPUs overlap many of these steps using a pipeline.
Instruction: one basic command, such as add, load a value or jump.
Program counter: the register holding the address of the next instruction, like the finger on the recipe ("What is the program counter?")
ALU: the block that does the arithmetic and logic ("What is an ALU?") Register: a tiny, very fast storage spot inside the CPU.
Clock cycle: one tick of the clock that paces the CPU.
How long does a program take? Suppose it has 3 billion instructions, each needing 1. 5 clock cycles on average, on a 2 gigahertz clock. That is 4. 5 billion cycles.
At 2 billion cycles per second, the time is 4. 5 / 2 = 2. 25 seconds. Fewer instructions, fewer cycles each, or a faster clock would all make it quicker.
That is the whole idea: a CPU steps through instructions, and its speed comes from three factors.
"A CPU is the circuit that executes a program.
It repeatedly fetches an instruction from memory using the program counter, decodes it, and executes it using an ALU and a register file.
Internally it's a datapath controlled by a finite state machine, all synchronized by a clock.
Its speed is instruction count times CPI times clock period, and modern ones use pipelining, caches and branch prediction to execute many instructions in parallel."
Quick check. Which pair of components makes up the two main parts of a simple CPU?
Blocks inside a CPU. The question: What are some blocks in a CPU?
A CPU is a set of small blocks that each do one job, wired together. One block remembers which instruction comes next.
Others fetch it, work out what it means, supply the numbers, do the math, and talk to memory. Following a single instruction through these blocks shows how they fit.
Picture a small office. A bookmark marks the next order on the list (the program counter). A manager reads the order and tells everyone what to do (the decoder and control unit).
The desk holds the numbers in use right now (the registers). A calculator does the arithmetic (the ALU).
A runner fetches things from the filing cabinet down the hall (the load/store unit and memory).
The main blocks of a simple in-order CPU. Solid arrows are data; the control unit (decoded from the instruction) steers the register file, ALU and memory.
The dotted line is the branch outcome that redirects the PC. Real chips add pipeline registers between stages and forwarding paths from ALU output back to its inputs.
Program counter: holds the address of the next instruction ("What is the program counter?") Control unit: turns the instruction into signals that steer the other blocks.
Register file: a small, very fast set of storage spots for the numbers in use. ALU: the block that does arithmetic and logic ("What is an ALU?")
Cache: a small fast memory next to the CPU that holds recently used instructions and data. Load/store unit: the block that reads data from memory and writes it back.
Take the instruction "add x1 and x2, put the result in x3", with x1 = 4 and x2 = 6.
The program counter gives the instruction's address, and the instruction comes from the instruction cache.
The control unit sees "add" and tells the register file to read x1 and x2. The ALU adds them to get 10, and 10 is written into x3.
That is the whole idea: each block has one job, and the instruction flows through them in order.

"Following an instruction: the program counter addresses the instruction cache, the decoder and control unit turn the opcode into control signals, the register file supplies operands, the ALU computes, the load/store unit talks to the data cache and memory, and the result is written back to the register file.
Real CPUs add a branch predictor, MMU and TLB, a floating-point unit, an interrupt controller, and in high-end cores register renaming and a reorder buffer."
Quick check. Which block holds the address of the next instruction to fetch?
What is an ALU?. The question: What is an ALU?
The ALU (arithmetic logic unit) is the part of the CPU that does the math and logic.
It takes two numbers and a few control bits that choose the operation, such as add, subtract, AND, OR or shift.
It outputs the result plus some flags, which are one-bit notes about the result.
Think of a calculator with a dial. Two numbers go in, you turn the dial to an operation, and one answer comes out.
Next to the display are small indicator lights: one for "result is zero", one for "result is negative".
A one-bit full adder from gates. The first XOR makes p = A xor B and the first AND makes g = A and B. The second XOR gives S = p xor Cin.
The second AND and the OR give Cout = g + p·Cin. Chain n of these and you have an n-bit ripple-carry adder.
Full adder: a one-bit circuit that adds two bits plus a carry-in, giving a sum bit and a carry-out. An ALU chains these.
Carry: the "1" passed to the next column, as in 9 + 1 in decimal. Flag: a one-bit status from the result, such as zero, negative, carry or overflow.
Two's complement: a way to write negative numbers so that subtracting is adding the flipped bits plus 1.
Add 5 and 3 in 4 bits: 0101 + 0011. The lowest column is 1 + 1 = 0 with a carry.
The next is 0 + 1 + 1 = 0 with a carry, then 1 + 0 + 1 = 0 with a carry, and the top is 0 + 0 + 1 = 1. The answer is 1000, which is 8, and the zero flag is 0.
Subtract 5 - 3 with the same adder. Flip 0011 to 1100, add 1 as carry-in, and add: 0101 + 1100 + 1 = 10010. Drop the extra top bit and you get 0010, which is 2.
That is the whole idea.
"The ALU is the combinational block in a CPU that does arithmetic and logic.
It takes two operands and control bits selecting the operation, like add, subtract, AND, OR, shift or compare, and outputs a result plus flags like zero, negative, carry and overflow.
It's built from a full-adder chain, with subtraction done by inverting the second operand and adding one, plus logic gates and a mux.
Carry propagation is the critical path, so real ALUs use carry-lookahead or prefix adders."

What is the program counter?. The question: What is the program counter?
The program counter (PC) is a register inside the CPU that holds the address of the next instruction to run.
Each step, the CPU fetches the instruction at that address and updates the PC. Normally the PC just moves to the following instruction.
Branches, function calls, interrupts and reset can load a different address instead.
Picture a bookmark in a long book of instructions. Normally you finish a page and move the bookmark to the next one.
Sometimes the text says "go to page 64", so you move the bookmark there. Page numbers are the memory addresses. The PC is the CPU's "you are here" marker.
If a device gets stuck, you can pause it and read the marker to see where it is.
The PC datapath. The register feeds the instruction memory and two adders (the +4 incrementer and the branch-target adder).
A mux, controlled by the decoder and the branch-condition result, selects what gets loaded on the next clock edge. Reset and exceptions come in through the same mux.
Address: the numbered location of something in memory. Register: a tiny, fast storage spot inside the CPU ("What is a register").
Branch / jump: an instruction that sends the PC somewhere other than the next instruction. Return address: where a function call should come back to, saved before the jump.
Interrupt: an outside event that makes the CPU jump to a handler routine ("Interrupts in computers vs embedded systems").
Suppose each instruction takes 4 bytes. The PC starts at 0. The CPU fetches the instruction at 0, and the PC becomes 4. It fetches at 4, and the PC becomes 8.
Now the instruction at 8 says "jump to 64". The PC becomes 64, not 12, so the next fetch comes from address 64.
That is the whole idea: add the instruction size, unless something says go elsewhere.
"The program counter is a register that holds the address of the next instruction to fetch.
Normally it increments by the instruction size each cycle; branches, jumps, calls, returns, interrupts and exceptions load a new value into it instead.
In hardware it's a clocked register, an incrementer and a mux selecting between PC+4, a branch target, a register jump target and an exception vector.
On reset it's loaded with the reset vector, where boot code starts."
Quick check. In a 32-bit fixed-width byte-addressed RISC machine, how does the PC normally change after each sequential instruction?
How the PC changes over time. The question: How does the contents of the program counter change over time?
The program counter mostly counts up. After each instruction it advances by that instruction's size, which is 4 bytes for a 32-bit instruction.
Sometimes it jumps instead: a loop sends it backward, a function call sends it to the function, a return sends it back, and an interrupt sends it to a handler.
Imagine walking down a street of numbered houses, visiting every fourth address in order. Now and then a note on a door says "go to house 64, then come back here".
Or it says "go back to house 4 until the counter hits zero". Loops make you revisit the same few houses many times.
The PC against instruction count.
The staircase of +4 steps is sequential code; the spikes to 64 are calls to the function; the drops back from 12 to 4 are the loop's backward branch.
Notice the repeating pattern: the same five PC values per iteration, which is why caches and branch predictors do so well on loops.
Sequential flow: the PC moving to the next instruction in address order. Taken / not-taken branch: a branch is taken when its condition is true and the PC jumps.
When not taken, the PC just goes on to the next instruction. Return address: the spot a call saves so the PC can come back after the function.
Interrupt handler: the routine the PC jumps to when an outside event needs attention ("Interrupts in computers vs embedded systems").
Use the page's small program, with addresses in plain numbers. The PC goes 0, 4, 8. At 8 a call jumps to 64, saving return address 12.
It runs 64, then 68, where a return sends the PC back to 12. At 12 a loop branch is taken and the PC jumps back to 4. The page's program repeats that cycle three times in total.
The final time the branch is not taken, so the PC moves on to 16. That is the whole idea: the PC steps by 4 and is occasionally overwritten.
"The PC normally steps forward by the instruction size, so by 4 for 32-bit instructions.

A taken branch or jump loads a new address, so loops jump backward and repeat; a call loads the function's address and saves the return address, and the return restores it; an interrupt saves the PC and loads a handler address, then returns; and reset loads the reset vector.
Plotted over time it's a staircase with occasional jumps. In a pipeline the fetch PC runs ahead speculatively and is redirected on mispredictions."
Quick check. Which event makes the PC jump backward during a loop?
Fetch/execute cycle. The question: What is the fetch/execute cycle?
The fetch-execute cycle is the loop a CPU repeats forever.
It fetches the instruction at the address in the program counter, decodes what it asks for, executes it, and writes the result back.
Then it starts again with the next instruction. Everything a CPU does is built from this loop.
Think of a clerk with a stack of request slips.
The clerk takes the top slip (fetch), reads it to see what is wanted (decode), does the task (execute), and files the answer (writeback). Then the clerk takes the next slip.
One real difference: some slips, like "go back to slip 4", change which slip is taken next.
Control FSM of a simple multi-cycle CPU. Every instruction starts with FETCH and DECODE, then branches into an instruction-specific path, and finally returns to FETCH.
Loads go through FETCH, DECODE, MEMADR, MEMRD, WB (5 states = 5 cycles); R-type goes FETCH, DECODE, EXEC, WB (4); a branch goes FETCH, DECODE, BRANCH (3).
Fetch: reading the instruction from memory at the address in the program counter ("What is the program counter?")
Decode: working out which operation the instruction asks for and which registers it uses.
Execute: doing the operation, usually in the ALU (for a memory instruction, working out the address). Writeback: storing the result into a register.
Instruction register: holds the instruction while it is being worked on.
Take "load word": lw x5, 8(x2) , meaning "read the memory at x2 plus 8 into x5".
Say x2 = 0x2000 and the memory at 0x2008 holds 0xCAFE (numbers starting with 0x are written in hex, base 16).
Fetch: read the instruction at the PC, and the PC moves to the next one. Decode: read register x2. Execute: the ALU adds 0x2000 + 8 to get address 0x2008.
Memory: read that address and get 0xCAFE. Writeback: put 0xCAFE into x5. A simple design spends one clock cycle on each step, so 5 cycles. That is the whole idea.
"It's the loop every CPU runs. Fetch: read the instruction at the address in the PC into the instruction register and increment the PC.
Decode: work out what the instruction is and read its source registers. Execute: the ALU computes the result, a memory address, or a branch condition.
Memory: loads and stores access memory. Writeback: write the result to a register. Then repeat.
A simple CPU does this in 3 to 5 cycles per instruction; a pipeline overlaps the phases to finish about one per cycle."

The five-stage pipeline. The question: Describe the five-stage pipeline.
The five-stage pipeline splits the work of each instruction into five steps: fetch, decode, execute, memory and writeback.
Each step has its own hardware, so five instructions can be in progress at once, each at a different step. Once the pipeline is full, one instruction finishes every clock cycle.
Think of laundry with a washer, a dryer and a folding table. You don't wait for load 1 to be folded before washing load 2. While load 1 is in the dryer, load 2 is in the washer.
Every step stays busy, and loads come out at a steady pace. The catch is when one load needs something the previous load has not finished yet, and you have to wait.
Short bursts don't benefit much because filling the pipeline costs 4 cycles. Long streams approach the ideal factor of 5 but never reach it.
Real speedup is lower still because of hazards, stage imbalance, and register overhead.
Stage: one step of the instruction's work, with its own hardware ("What is pipelining?")
Pipeline register: storage between stages that carries each instruction's partial results to the next stage.
Throughput vs latency: how many instructions finish per second, versus how long one instruction takes.
Hazard: a situation where the next instruction can't safely go ahead yet, such as needing a result not ready. Stall: a cycle where a stage waits and does no useful work.
Run 5 instructions through 5 stages. Without a pipeline, each takes 5 cycles, so 25 cycles in total.
With a pipeline, the first one finishes after 5 cycles and one more finishes every cycle after that. So the total is 5 + 4 = 9 cycles. That is a speedup of 25 / 9, about 2. 8.
For 100 instructions it is 500 / 104, about 4. 8, closing in on 5. That is the whole idea.
"Five stages: instruction fetch, decode and register read, execute in the ALU, memory access, and writeback.

Pipeline registers between them let five instructions be in flight, so once it's full one instruction completes per cycle, a throughput of up to five times, though latency per instruction stays five cycles.
Hazards break the ideal: data hazards are fixed with forwarding plus a one-cycle stall for load-use, and control hazards with branch prediction and flushing."

Offloading work from the CPU. The question: How can you offload tasks from the CPU? What are things you can do in parallel and what are the tradeoffs?
Offloading means handing a job to dedicated hardware so the CPU doesn't have to do it.
A timer can generate a pulse pattern, a DMA engine can copy data, and an accelerator can crunch numbers. The CPU is then free to do other work or go to sleep.
It only pays off when the job is big enough to be worth the handoff.
Think of a manager with assistants. The manager takes a minute to explain a task, the assistant works alone, and then taps the manager's shoulder when finished.
For a big job, that is a great trade. For a ten-second job, the explaining takes longer than doing it. Assistants also share the same hallway, and too many of them can jam it.
Each step costs more silicon and design effort but removes more work from the main CPU. Most embedded designs should start at the top; a phone SoC uses all of them.
Polling: the CPU repeatedly checking whether something has happened.
Interrupt: hardware tapping the CPU only when something happens ("Interrupts in computers vs embedded systems").
DMA (direct memory access): an engine that moves data between memory and devices without the CPU.
Accelerator: dedicated hardware for one kind of work, such as encryption or video. Overhead: the setup and wake-up cost of making the handoff.
A UART (serial port) sending 115,200 bits per second, at 10 bits per byte, delivers 11,520 bytes per second.
If each byte raises an interrupt costing 200 clock cycles on a 48 megahertz CPU, the CPU spends 11520 times 200 over 48 000 000 equals 4. 8 % of its time on it.
Let DMA collect the bytes instead, with one interrupt per 256-byte block. That is 45 interrupts per second at about 500 cycles each, which is about 0. 047%.
The load drops about 100 times. That is the whole idea: a handoff frees the CPU.

"I'd push repetitive or time-critical work to hardware: peripherals like timers, PWM and serial FIFOs, interrupts rather than polling, DMA to move blocks without the CPU, and accelerators or extra cores for heavy compute.
In parallel you can run DMA and peripherals while the CPU computes, using double buffering.
The trade-offs are area and power for the hardware, less flexibility, shared-bus contention, setup and synchronization overhead, cache coherence and software complexity.
Offload only pays when the task is big enough to beat that overhead, and Amdahl's law caps the gain."

Increasing CPU throughput. The question: What can you do to increase the throughput of a CPU?
Program run time equals the number of instructions, times the average clock cycles per instruction (CPI), times the length of one clock cycle.
Every way of making a CPU faster attacks one of those three.
You can shorten the cycle, keep the hardware busy so each instruction needs fewer cycles, or make each instruction do more work.
Picture a bakery making 1,000 rolls. Total time is rolls times minutes per roll. A bigger tray lets one action handle several rolls, which is fewer instructions.
Keeping every oven and worker busy is a lower CPI. A hotter oven is a faster clock, but it burns much more fuel.
The slowest part is often waiting for flour to arrive, like a CPU waiting on memory.
Every percentage point of miss rate costs 0. 3 CPI in this model.
Going from a 5% to 2% miss rate (bigger or better-organized cache, prefetching, blocking in the code) speeds the program up by 2. 5/1. 6 = 1.
56x, far more than any ALU improvement could, because the core was idle waiting on memory 60% of the time at 5%.
Instruction count: how many instructions the program needs. CPI: average clock cycles per instruction.
Its inverse is IPC, instructions per cycle ("Characterizing CPU performance"). Clock period: the time of one cycle, which is 1 divided by the clock frequency.
Cache miss: the data wanted isn't in the small fast memory, so the CPU waits for slow main memory.
Say the ideal CPI is 1, but 30% of instructions access memory, 5% of those accesses miss the cache, and each miss costs 100 cycles. Then CPI = 1 plus 0. 3 times 0.
05 times 100 equals 2. 5 . The CPU is idle more than half the time, waiting on memory. Cut the miss rate to 2% and CPI becomes 1 plus 0. 3 times 0. 02 times 100 equals 1. 6 .
That is 2. 5 / 1. 6, about 1. 56 times faster, with no change to the clock. That is the whole idea: find which factor is the bottleneck.
"I'd use the iron law: time is instruction count times CPI times clock period. To cut the clock period, make stages shorter, with a power cost.
To cut CPI, use pipelining, superscalar and out-of-order execution, branch prediction and caches so the CPU is never waiting.
To cut instruction count, use better compilers and SIMD. Beyond that, add parallelism with multithreading, multiple cores and accelerators.
The limits are power, memory bandwidth and Amdahl's law."

What is pipelining?. The question: What is pipelining?
Pipelining means starting the next instruction before the previous one has finished. The work of an instruction is split into stages, with a register between each pair of stages.
Each stage then works on a different instruction at the same time. A single instruction takes no less time, but instructions finish at a much higher rate.
Picture a car assembly line. One station fits the engine, the next the doors, the next the wheels. At any moment, several cars are being built, each at a different station.
A finished car rolls off each time the slowest station finishes its job.
Building one car from start to end takes no less time, and a bit more, but the factory produces far more cars per day.
The solid curve flattens at 3. 33, well under the dashed ideal limit of 5.
The gap is stage imbalance (MEM 250 picoseconds vs 180 picoseconds average) and the 20 picoseconds register overhead.
Even the ideal curve only approaches 5 slowly because of the fill time.
Stage: one slice of the instruction's work that fits in one clock cycle. Pipeline register: storage between stages that holds each instruction's in-progress data.
Throughput: how many instructions finish per second. Latency: how long one instruction takes from start to finish.
Hazard: a dependency that stops the next instruction from going ahead on schedule ("The five-stage pipeline").
Use the page's five stages, which take 200, 150, 200, 250 and 100 picoseconds, plus 20 picoseconds of register overhead.
Without pipelining, one instruction takes 900 picoseconds, so one finishes every 900 picoseconds.
With pipelining, the clock must fit the slowest stage plus overhead: 250 + 20 = 270 picoseconds. Now one instruction finishes every 270 picoseconds, about 3.
3 times the throughput. But one instruction's own trip is 5 times 270 = 1350 picoseconds, which is longer than 900 picoseconds.
That is the whole idea: higher throughput, same or worse latency.
"Pipelining splits an instruction's work into stages separated by registers so several instructions are in flight at once, each in a different stage.
The clock only has to cover the slowest stage instead of the whole path, so you get a much higher clock and, once full, roughly one instruction per cycle.
Latency for a single instruction doesn't improve, it gets slightly worse, so it's a throughput win.
The speedup is less than the number of stages because of register overhead, unbalanced stages and hazards like data dependencies and branches."

Branch prediction and its algorithms. The question: What is branch prediction? Describe some branch prediction algorithms.
A branch is an instruction that may jump somewhere else instead of continuing.

A modern CPU works on several instructions at once, like an assembly line (a pipeline), so it must keep fetching new ones before the branch's outcome is known, so the CPU makes a guess based on past behavior.
A right guess costs nothing. A wrong guess throws away the work done on the wrong path.
Imagine a driver who has turned left at the same fork every morning. Today the driver keeps going left without checking the map. Usually that saves time.
On the rare day the road goes right, the driver must turn around and loses time. A predictor works like that driver, learning from history.
At the same 5% miss rate a 2-cycle penalty costs 2% in CPI, while a 15-cycle penalty costs 15% and a 25-cycle penalty 25%.
Deeper pipelines make accuracy far more valuable, which is why predictors got so elaborate.
Taken / not taken: a branch is taken when it jumps and not taken when execution continues to the next instruction.
Misprediction penalty: cycles lost when the guess is wrong, roughly how many stages deep the branch is resolved ("The five-stage pipeline").
History: a record of how a branch behaved before, kept in a small table. 2-bit counter: a counter from 0 to 3 that predicts "taken" when 2 or 3.
It takes two wrong outcomes in a row to change the prediction.
A loop runs 10 times. Its branch at the end is taken 9 times, then not taken once, and then the loop starts again.
A predictor that just repeats the last outcome is wrong at the exit and wrong again at the next visit's first pass. That is 2 misses in 10, or 80% accurate.
A 2-bit counter stays on "taken" after the single not-taken exit, so it misses only once. That is 90% accurate.
That is the whole idea: guess from history, and a bit of memory beats none.
"Branch prediction is the CPU guessing a branch's direction and target before it resolves, so a pipeline can keep fetching instead of stalling.
A wrong guess flushes the speculative instructions and costs the pipeline depth in cycles. Static schemes are always-not-taken or backward-taken.
The standard dynamic one is a table of 2-bit saturating counters indexed by the PC, which mispredicts a loop only once at the exit instead of twice like a 1-bit predictor.
Better ones like gshare also use global branch history, and a BTB supplies the target address."

Interrupts in computers vs embedded systems. The question: What are interrupts? When can they be used and why are they important?
How does their usage often differ from that of embedded systems?
An interrupt is a hardware signal that tells the CPU "something needs attention now".
The CPU finishes its current instruction, saves where it was, runs a short handler routine for that event, and then returns to exactly where it left off.
It is the alternative to polling, where the CPU keeps checking. On a PC the operating system handles it, while on a small embedded chip you often write the handler yourself.
Picture waiting for a package. You could walk to the door every minute to look (polling), which wastes your day. Or you can work on something else and let the doorbell ring.
When it rings, you put a bookmark in your work, answer the door, and return to your page. The catch: the bell must be answered quickly, and your place must be saved exactly.
The CPU only accepts the interrupt at an instruction boundary, when it is enabled and not masked.
The ISR must clear the device's pending flag, or the request stays asserted and fires again as soon as the ISR returns.
Interrupt handler (ISR): the short routine that runs in response to an interrupt. Polling: the CPU repeatedly checking whether an event has happened.
Vector table: a list of handler addresses, indexed by interrupt number. Latency: the delay from the event to the first instruction of the handler.
Mask: a control bit that temporarily blocks an interrupt from being taken.
A serial port at 115,200 bits per second sends 10 bits per byte, so a byte arrives every 86. 8 microseconds.
A 48 megahertz CPU that does nothing but poll uses 100% of its time just waiting. With an interrupt, the handler costs about 64 cycles (40 for its work, 12 to enter, 12 to exit).
That is 64 over 48 000 000 seconds about 1. 33 microseconds per byte, so the CPU is busy only about 1. 5% of the time.
That is the whole idea: the CPU does other things until an event arrives.
"An interrupt is a signal that makes the CPU pause its current program, jump through a vector table to a handler, and then resume where it left off.
It lets hardware events like timers, incoming data or faults get attention without the CPU polling, which saves cycles and gives fast response.
They're also how an OS regains control for multitasking.
On a PC the OS kernel owns the interrupts and defers heavy work to threads; in embedded systems you often write the ISR yourself, keep it very short, and use interrupts to wake the chip from sleep."

What is microarchitecture?. The question: What is microarchitecture?
The instruction set (ISA) is the contract that says which instructions exist and what each one does.
Microarchitecture is the internal hardware design that carries them out: how many pipeline stages, what caches, how many instructions at once.
Many different microarchitectures can implement the same ISA. That is why the same software can run on a small slow chip and a large fast one.
Think of cars. The steering wheel, pedals and gearshift are the contract: any driver can use any car.
Under the hood, one car has a small economy engine and another a big turbo engine. Both obey the same controls, but they differ in speed, fuel use and cost.
Software sees only the controls. It can tell the difference only by how fast it runs.
Everything above the ISA line sees only the contract. Everything below it can change without breaking software.
Microarchitecture is the first layer under the contract and the one that sets CPI, clock, area and power.
ISA: the instructions and registers visible to software ("What is an ISA?") Pipeline: overlapping the steps of several instructions ("What is pipelining?")
In-order / out-of-order: running instructions strictly in program order, versus as soon as their inputs are ready.
Cache: a small fast memory that holds recently used data to cut waiting. CPI: average clock cycles per instruction. Fewer is better.
Run the same program of 10 to the 9 instructions on two cores that share one ISA. Core A is simple: CPI 1. 0 at 2 gigahertz, so the time is 10 to the 9 times 1.
0 over (2 times 10 to the 9) equals 0. 50 seconds. Core B has a deeper pipeline and bigger caches: CPI 1. 3 at 3 gigahertz, so the time is 10 to the 9 times 1.
3 over (3 times 10 to the 9) equals 0. 433 seconds. B is about 15% faster, but it is bigger and uses more power. Both are valid implementations.
That is the whole idea: same contract, different insides.
"Microarchitecture is how a specific processor implements its ISA: the pipeline, issue width, in-order or out-of-order execution, execution units, caches, branch predictors and buses.
The ISA is the contract software sees; the microarchitecture is the implementation and it can differ wildly while running identical programs, like an Arm Cortex-A53 versus an A76.
It's what determines CPI and clock speed, so performance, area and power, and it's chosen for the target, from tiny low-power MCUs to server cores."

What is an ISA?. The question: What is an instruction set architecture (ISA)?
The ISA (instruction set architecture) is the rulebook a processor offers to software.
It lists the instructions, how each is written in bits, the registers, how memory addresses work, and how interrupts and errors behave.
It is a contract: software depends only on the ISA, so the hardware inside can change.
Think of a restaurant menu. Customers order from the menu, and each dish has a fixed description.
The kitchen can change its stoves, staff and layout, as long as the dishes that arrive match the menu.
Likewise, a program written for an ISA runs on any chip that follows it, whether the chip is tiny or huge.
The ISA is the narrowest point in the stack.
Everything above it targets the contract; everything below can be rebuilt (pipelined, out-of-order, different cache sizes) as long as it honours the same behaviour.
Instruction: one basic command the processor understands, such as add. Register: a small fast storage spot named in the instruction.
Opcode: the part of an instruction's bits that says which operation it is. RISC / CISC: simple, regular instructions versus larger, more complex ones ("RISC vs CISC advantages").
Microarchitecture: the hardware design that carries out the ISA ("What is microarchitecture?")
In the RISC-V ISA, add x3, x1, x2 means "put x1 plus x2 into x3". It is stored as one 32-bit word, 0x002081B3 (the 0x means hexadecimal).
The word is made of fields: an opcode saying "register arithmetic", the destination register 3, the source registers 1 and 2, and a field that selects "add".
Change only that last field and the same word becomes sub , 0x402081B3.
The assembler (the tool that turns written instructions into bits) and every compliant chip agree on this layout. That is the whole idea: an ISA fixes meaning and bit layout.

"An ISA, or instruction set architecture, is the contract between software and a processor: the instructions and their encodings, the registers, data types, addressing modes, memory model and exception behaviour.
Software only depends on the ISA, so different microarchitectures can implement the same ISA and run the same binaries.
RISC ISAs like Arm and RISC-V use simple fixed-length load/store instructions, while CISC like x86 has variable-length, more complex ones. Examples are x86-64, Arm and RISC-V."
Quick check. Which of the following is part of the ISA?
Microarchitecture vs ISA. The question: What is the difference between microarchitecture and ISA?
The ISA is what software can see and rely on: the instructions, the registers, how memory behaves.
Microarchitecture is how one particular chip delivers that: how deep its pipeline is, how big its caches are, how many instructions it handles at once.
The ISA stays stable, so old programs keep working. The microarchitecture is where speed and power are won.
Picture a wall outlet. The plug shape and voltage are the standard, so any appliance works in any outlet.
Behind the wall, the power can come from a small local generator or a huge grid. Appliances can't tell which, except that the supply may be stronger.
The outlet standard is the ISA, and what lies behind it is the microarchitecture.
The ISA is the narrow waist. Everything above it is portable across implementations and everything below it is free to change.
Performance, power and area are mostly decided below the line, while compatibility is decided at it.
ISA: the contract between software and hardware ("What is an ISA?") Microarchitecture: one chip's internal design that implements the ISA ("What is microarchitecture?")
Binary compatibility: the same compiled program runs on every chip that implements the ISA.
Architectural state: the registers, program counter (the address of the next instruction) and memory that the ISA defines and software can see.
Out-of-order execution: running instructions as soon as their inputs are ready, while results still appear in program order.
Run 10 to the 9 instructions on two chips that share one ISA. Old core A runs at 2 gigahertz with CPI 1. 6 (cycles per instruction), so the time is 10 to the 9 times 1.
6 over (2 times 10 to the 9) equals 0. 8 seconds. New core B runs at 3 gigahertz with CPI 1. 1, so the time is 10 to the 9 times 1. 1 over (3 times 10 to the 9) about 0.
367 seconds. That is about 2. 2 times faster, and the same compiled program was used with no changes.
That is the whole idea: a stable ISA lets hardware improve under the software.
"The ISA is the contract software sees: instructions, registers, memory model, exceptions.
The microarchitecture is how one chip implements that contract: pipeline, issue width, caches, branch predictor.
One ISA, like x86 or Arm, has many microarchitectures, from tiny in-order cores to wide out-of-order ones, and they all run the same binaries.
That split lets hardware improve every generation without breaking software."
