What is RISC-V. The question: What is RISC-V?
RISC-V (said "risk five") is an open instruction set, a public rulebook for how a processor's instructions work.
Anyone can read it and build a chip that follows it without paying a license fee. It is a specification, not a chip.
It is also modular: a small base set of instructions, plus optional add-ons.
Imagine an open cookbook that anyone may cook from without paying.
The recipes are free, but ingredients, kitchens and chefs still cost money, and some kitchens turn out better dishes than others. RISC-V works the same way.
The rulebook is free, but designing, testing and manufacturing a chip are not, and chip quality varies a lot.
Fields are at fixed positions in R-type. In I-type the rs2 and funct7 fields merge into a 12-bit immediate, but rs1, rd and opcode stay put.
Fixed positions let hardware read the register file in parallel with decode.
ISA: the programmer-visible rulebook of instructions and registers ("What is an ISA?") Open: free to read and implement, with no fee to the ISA's owner.
Base ISA: the small required core, such as RV32I (32-bit integers). Extension: an optional add-on, such as M (multiply and divide) or C (shorter 16-bit instructions).
Core: one specific processor design that implements the ISA.
A name like rv32imc tells you what a core supports.
The 32 is the register width, the I means the base integer instructions, M means multiply and divide, and C means compressed instructions.
Software built for rv32imc will not necessarily run on a core that lacks M or C. Meanwhile, add x3, x1, x2 is the same 32-bit word, 0x002081B3, on every RISC-V core, tiny or huge.
That is the whole idea: one open rulebook with a base and optional parts.
"RISC-V is an open, royalty-free instruction set architecture, started at Berkeley and now run by RISC-V International.
It's a clean load/store RISC with fixed 32-bit instructions and 32 registers, built modularly: a small base like RV32I plus optional extensions such as M, F, C and V.
It's only the spec, not a chip, so anyone can build their own core."
Quick check. What is RISC-V?
RISC-V: ISA or microarchitecture. The question: Does RISC-V specify the ISA or microarchitecture?
RISC-V is an ISA, which means it is a specification. It defines the instructions, registers and rules that software can see.
It does not say how many pipeline stages a chip has, whether it runs instructions out of order, or how big its caches are.
Those choices are the microarchitecture, and each RISC-V chip makes its own.
Think of a piece of sheet music. The score fixes which notes are played and in what order. A school band and a full orchestra can both play it.
They differ in speed, size and cost. RISC-V is the score, and each chip design is a different orchestra. The score does set some rules every performer must respect.
Everything above the Microarchitecture box constrains behavior software can see. Everything below is the implementer's freedom.
Profiles exist to stop the top of the stack from fragmenting into incompatible extension combinations.
ISA: the contract between software and hardware ("What is an ISA?") Microarchitecture: a chip's internal design that carries out the ISA ("What is microarchitecture?")
Core: one specific processor design that implements the ISA. Pipeline, out-of-order, cache: internal speed tricks.
They overlap the steps of several instructions, run instructions as soon as their inputs are ready, and keep recent data in a small fast memory.
Extension: an optional standard addition to the ISA. Software only runs on cores that have the extensions it needs.
Take one loop of 8 instructions per pass, with one hard-to-predict branch and one load that sometimes misses the cache.
Run the identical RISC-V binary (compiled program) on three cores. The page's illustrative model gives 8. 8 cycles per pass on simple core A, 8. 9 on core B, and 4.
5 on a wide out-of-order core C. At 1 gigahertz for A and B, and 2 gigahertz for C, the times are 8. 8 nanoseconds, 8. 9 nanoseconds and 2. 25 nanoseconds.
That is roughly a 4 times gap with the same software. That is the whole idea: "RISC-V" says nothing about speed.
"It specifies the ISA. RISC-V defines the instructions, registers, privilege modes, traps, virtual memory and memory model, but not the pipeline, caches or branch predictor.
Those are microarchitecture, chosen by whoever builds the core.
That's why in-order cores like Rocket and out-of-order cores like BOOM can both be RISC-V and run the same software at very different speeds and power."

RISC vs CISC advantages. The question: What are some advantages of RISC vs CISC?
RISC and CISC are two styles of instruction set. RISC uses a small set of simple instructions that are all the same size, and only loads and stores touch memory.
CISC has richer instructions of varying size, and one can do several things, like adding a number straight from memory.
RISC's advantages are mostly in hardware: simpler decoding, cleaner pipelines and smaller control logic.
Think of giving directions. RISC says: "walk one block, turn left, walk one block". Each step is simple and quick to understand.
CISC says: "go to the library", which is one short instruction, but the listener must work out many steps. Short directions save paper.
Simple steps are easier for a pipeline to handle in an assembly-line way.
The two top rows show why CISC is paid for in the front end. After decode, both styles feed a similar out-of-order engine.
The x86 path needs extra stages (and often a micro-op cache so the expensive decode can be skipped on hot loops), which costs power.
Load/store architecture: only load and store instructions access memory. Everything else works on registers. Decode: working out what an instruction asks for.
Same-size instructions make this easy. Micro-op: a simple internal step. Modern x86 chips split complex instructions into these. Code density: how compactly a program is encoded.
CPI: average cycles per instruction ("Characterizing CPU performance").
Take "add register R2 to the value in memory at A". CISC does it in 1 instruction. RISC takes 3: load, add, store.
With the page's teaching numbers, a CISC program has 10 to the 9 instructions at CPI 2. 2, and a RISC program has 1. 4 times 10 to the 9 at CPI 1. 1, both on a 2 gigahertz clock.
CISC takes 1. 10 seconds and RISC takes 0. 77 seconds. RISC has 40% more instructions but half the CPI. That is the whole idea: RISC trades more instructions for simpler hardware.
"RISC uses simple, fixed-length, load/store instructions with lots of registers.
That makes decode cheap and pipelining clean, so you get low CPI, a fast clock and less area and power.
CISC packs more work into each instruction and has better code density, which lowers instruction count. By the Iron Law it's a trade between IC and CPI.
Today x86 translates to micro-ops internally, so the difference is mostly the cost of the front end."

Characterizing CPU performance. The question: How do you characterize CPU performance?
The most honest measure of CPU performance is how long it takes to finish real work.
That time splits into three factors: the number of instructions, the average clock cycles each needs (CPI), and the length of one clock cycle.
Clock frequency alone tells you very little, because two chips at the same GHz can differ a lot in CPI.
Picture comparing two restaurants. You could ask how fast the chef chops, but that is only one piece.
What you care about is how long one diner waits (latency) and how many dinners go out per hour (throughput).
The fair test is a real busy evening of orders, not a single fast demo. Benchmarks do the same for CPUs, running a standard set of real programs.
Each extra 1% of memory accesses that go to DRAM adds 0. 45 to CPI. Beyond about 0. 85% the DRAM term is bigger than the branch and L2 stalls combined (0. 384).
This is why memory behavior, not core width, is often the first thing to examine.
Instruction count: how many instructions the program needs. CPI: average clock cycles per instruction. Its inverse is IPC, instructions per cycle.
Clock period: the time of one cycle, 1 divided by the frequency. Latency vs throughput: how long one task takes, versus how many tasks finish per second.
Benchmark: a standard set of programs run to compare machines.
Run a program of 10 to the 9 instructions on two chips. Chip A runs at 3 gigahertz with CPI 2, so the time is 10 to the 9 times 2 over (3 times 10 to the 9) about 0. 67 seconds.
Chip B runs at only 2 gigahertz with CPI 1, so the time is 10 to the 9 times 1 over (2 times 10 to the 9) equals 0. 50 seconds. The slower clock wins.
In the page's own example, halving a cache miss rate cuts CPI from 2. 5 to 1. 75, which is more than a 40% faster clock would give.
That is the whole idea: judge by time on real work.
"Performance is execution time. The Iron Law says time is instruction count times CPI times clock period, so clock speed alone is meaningless.
I'd measure with representative benchmarks like SPEC, summarize with a geometric mean, and separate latency from throughput.
Then look at what limits it: memory stalls, branch mispredicts, Amdahl's law, and finally performance per watt and thermal throttling."

What is a GPU. The question: What is a GPU?
A GPU (graphics processing unit) is a processor built to do a huge number of simple, similar calculations at the same time.
A CPU has a few powerful cores that each run one task fast. A GPU has thousands of small, simple arithmetic units, called lanes.
It was made to color the millions of pixels on a screen, and the same design now also speeds up science and AI.
Imagine painting a giant mural made of 8 million tiny squares. One master painter works fast but still does one square at a time.
A crowd of 10,000 helpers, each painting one square at a time from the same simple instructions, finishes far sooner, even though each helper is slower. A GPU is that crowd.
Not to scale and schematic. The CPU spends most of its area on cache and control logic to make one thread fast.
The GPU spends area on arithmetic lanes and register files and on a wide memory interface, accepting that each thread is slower.
Throughput: total work finished per second, as opposed to how fast one task finishes. Thread: one independent stream of work, such as the program for one pixel.
Shader: the small program run for each pixel, each triangle corner (vertex) or each compute thread. SIMT: single instruction, multiple threads.
Groups of threads run the same instruction together. Memory bandwidth: how many bytes per second can move between memory and the chip.
A 4K frame is 3840 times 2160 equals 8 294 400 pixels, about 8. 3 million. At 60 frames per second that is about 498 million pixels per second.
Assume 300 arithmetic operations per pixel, counting extra drawing and effects. That is roughly 150 billion operations per second.
Each pixel can be shaded without waiting for its neighbors. A modern GPU delivers tens of trillions of operations per second, so this is a modest share.
That is the whole idea: independent work spread across many lanes.

"A GPU is a throughput-oriented parallel processor with thousands of small lanes that run the same program on many threads at once, backed by very high memory bandwidth and fixed-function graphics units.
Graphics is perfect for it because millions of pixels are independent. It hides memory latency with massive multithreading instead of big caches.
Today the same hardware also runs compute and machine learning."

How a GPU works. The question: How does a GPU work?
You write a small program called a kernel for one thread, then launch it across thousands or millions of threads. The hardware bundles threads into groups of 32 called warps.
A warp runs one instruction on all 32 of its lanes (small arithmetic units) at once.
When a warp must wait for memory, the GPU switches to another ready warp, so the waiting is hidden by having many threads.
Picture one chef tending many pots. While one pot simmers, which is like waiting for memory, the chef stirs another, so no time is wasted.
The more pots there are, the less the chef ever stands idle. One difference: the 32 lanes in a warp must all do the same step together, like 32 burners controlled by one knob.
The block scheduler decouples the program from the machine size. Blocks are independent, so any number of SMs can work on them.
Within an SM, the warp scheduler (not the program) chooses which warp issues each cycle.
Kernel: the function launched on the GPU and run by many threads. Warp: a group of 32 threads that execute the same instruction together.
Latency hiding: switching to another warp while one waits, so the processor stays busy. Divergence: lanes in one warp wanting different branches. The warp runs each path in turn.
Coalescing: merging neighboring threads' memory reads into one wide read.
Say a memory load takes 400 cycles, and a warp does about 10 independent instructions between loads.
To keep the processor busy, it needs roughly 400 / 10 = 40 other warps ready to run. That is why a GPU keeps thousands of threads resident. Memory pattern matters too.
If 32 threads read 32 consecutive 4-byte numbers, that is 128 bytes in one transaction. If they read scattered addresses, it takes up to 32 transactions, and bandwidth collapses.
That is the whole idea: hide waiting with parallelism, and keep threads in step.
"You write a kernel for one thread and launch it over a huge grid. The hardware groups threads into warps of 32 that run the same instruction in lockstep on an SM.
Each SM holds many warps, and when one stalls on memory the scheduler instantly issues another, so latency is hidden by parallelism.
Divergent branches and uncoalesced memory accesses are what cost performance."

The GPU graphics pipeline. The question: What does the GPU pipeline look like?
The graphics pipeline turns a 3D scene made of triangles into the pixels on your screen.

Data flows through stages: first the corner points of the triangles are positioned, then the hardware works out which screen pixels each triangle covers, then each pixel is colored, and finally the nearest surface wins and the result is written to the image.
Some stages run programs, and others are fixed hardware.
Imagine a shadow-puppet stage. A stagehand places cardboard cutouts in the scene (positioning the corners).
A grid of tiny squares on a screen then records which squares each cutout covers (finding the pixels). A painter colors each covered square (coloring).
Finally, if two cutouts overlap on a square, the nearer one hides the farther one. Many cutouts and squares are in progress at the same moment.
One frame as a data flow. The programmable boxes (vertex and fragment shader) run on the same cores. The rest are fixed-function units tuned for throughput.
Each arrow carries a stream, and every box can be busy on a different triangle at the same time.
Vertex: a corner point of a triangle. Rasterization: working out which pixels a triangle covers. Fragment: a candidate pixel produced by a triangle. It may still be hidden.
Shader: a small program run on every vertex or fragment. Depth test: dropping a fragment if something nearer already covers that pixel.
Take one triangle with corners at (0,0), (8,0) and (0,8) on a pixel grid. The vertex stage moves those 3 corners to their screen positions.
The rasterizer then finds that the triangle covers 28 pixel centers (the triangle's area is 32, and the diagonal edge cuts partial pixels).
The fragment shader colors each of the 28 fragments. The depth test then keeps each one only if nothing nearer has already been drawn there.
That is the whole idea: vertices, then pixels, then color, then depth.
"Vertices go through a vertex shader that transforms them to screen space, then primitive assembly builds and clips triangles.

The fixed-function rasterizer finds the pixels each triangle covers, the fragment shader colors them using textures and lighting, and the ROP stage does depth test and blending and writes the framebuffer.
The shaders are programmable and share the same cores, while raster, texture and ROP hardware are fixed-function. Mobile GPUs render by tile to save bandwidth."

GPU vs CPU. The question: What is the difference between a GPU and CPU?
A CPU is designed to make one task finish as fast as possible. A GPU is designed to finish as much total work per second as possible.
Almost every other difference follows from that one choice. CPUs are best at code that must run step by step and makes many decisions.
GPUs are best at regular work that splits into many independent pieces, such as graphics and matrix math.
Think of a motorbike courier versus a freight train. The courier gets one parcel across town in minutes.
The train is slow to start and heads in one direction, but it moves tons of cargo per hour. The right choice depends on the load.
A GPU is the train: huge throughput, poor at urgent one-off jobs.
Left of each ridge the machine is bandwidth-bound and performance rises linearly with intensity, so the GPU leads by its bandwidth ratio (18x).
Right of the ridge it is compute-bound at its peak, 35x apart. Low-intensity kernels (vector add at 0. 083 FLOP/B) gain only the bandwidth ratio, not the 35x headline.
Latency vs throughput: how fast one task finishes, versus how many finish per second. Data-parallel: the same operation applied to many independent pieces of data.
Memory bandwidth: how many bytes per second can move between memory and the chip. Arithmetic intensity: operations performed per byte moved from memory.
PCIe: the bus linking a separate GPU card to the CPU. Copies across it cost time.
Compare peak arithmetic on the page's example chips: about 1 TFLOP/s for a CPU (one trillion arithmetic operations on decimal numbers per second) and 35 TFLOP/s for a GPU, roughly 35 times.
But adding two long lists moves 12 bytes of memory for each addition (two reads, one write), which is low arithmetic intensity. Such a job is limited by memory, not arithmetic.
With 50 GB/s for the CPU and 900 GB/s for the GPU, the speedup is the bandwidth ratio, about 18 times, not 35. That is the whole idea: the winner depends on the workload.
"A CPU is latency-optimized: a few big out-of-order cores with big caches and branch prediction to run one thread fast.
A GPU is throughput-optimized: thousands of simple lanes running in lockstep, hiding memory latency by switching among tens of thousands of threads, with very high memory bandwidth.
CPUs win on branchy serial code, and GPUs win on regular data-parallel work like graphics and matrix math.
In practice the CPU orchestrates and the GPU does the heavy parallel part."
Quick check. Which statement best captures the CPU vs GPU design difference?
GPU optimizations and trade-offs. The question: What optimizations does a GPU have so it vastly outperforms CPUs in graphics tasks? What are the tradeoffs?
GPU designers assume the work is millions of independent, similar pieces, and every optimization uses that.
Each instruction is fetched once and run on 32 small arithmetic units (lanes) at once, many threads take turns to hide memory delays, and the memory is very wide and fast.
Dedicated hardware handles common jobs. Each of these gives up flexibility for efficiency, so a GPU is poor at single tasks, branchy code and small jobs.
Think of a bottling plant. It is superbly efficient at filling millions of identical bottles: one control system runs a hundred filling heads, and the conveyor never stops.
But ask it to make one custom jar, or to handle bottles that each need different treatment, and it wastes most of its machinery. The speed comes from giving up flexibility.
The dashed line is the arithmetic floor E a = 4 pJ. With overhead 10x the arithmetic cost, widening the group from 1 to 32 lanes cuts energy per operation by 8. 4x.
Beyond about 16 lanes the gains flatten near the arithmetic floor, which is why going wider than 32 to 64 buys little but costs divergence.
Amortization: spreading a fixed overhead, such as fetching and decoding an instruction, across many operations.
Fixed-function unit: dedicated hardware for one job, such as texture filtering, that beats general code.
Divergence: lanes in the same group of 32 wanting to take different branches, which leaves some lanes idle ("How a GPU works").
Memory bandwidth: bytes per second between memory and the chip.
Use the page's illustrative energy numbers. Fetching and scheduling one instruction costs 40 pJ (picojoules, tiny units of energy), and the arithmetic itself costs 4 pJ.
A scalar machine, which does one operation per instruction, pays both for every operation: 44 pJ. A GPU sharing one instruction across 32 lanes pays 40 over 32 plus 4 equals 5.
25 pJ per operation. That is about 8. 4 times less energy. The trade-off: if branches leave lanes only 60% useful, the cost per useful operation is 5. 25 over 0. 6 equals 8.
75 pJ. That is still about 5 times better. That is the whole idea: each trick trades generality for efficiency.

"GPUs exploit massive independent parallelism: SIMT amortizes fetch and decode over 32 lanes, thousands of threads hide latency instead of caches, very wide memory like GDDR or HBM feeds them, and fixed-function raster, texture and blend units do common work very efficiently.
Compression and on-chip tiles cut bandwidth.
The costs are weak single-thread speed, divergence and memory-pattern sensitivity, huge register files and power, limited memory, and harder programming."
Quick check. Why is the energy per operation lower on a GPU than on a typical CPU core?
Characterizing GPU performance. The question: How do you characterize GPU performance?
To characterize GPU performance, you measure three things: compute (how many operations per second it can do), memory (how many bytes per second it can move), and efficiency (work per watt).
Then you check which limit your workload actually hits. For graphics, you also look at frame time. Peak numbers say what the chip could do, not what your program gets.
Picture a factory with fast workers inside and one narrow loading door for materials. If each product needs little material, the workers are the limit.
If each product needs a lot, the door is the limit, and hiring more workers changes nothing. A GPU is like that.
Kernels that do little arithmetic per byte are limited by the memory "door".
Left of the orange ridge, performance rises linearly with intensity because bytes are the bottleneck; adding cores does nothing there.
Right of it, the flat roof is the compute peak. SAXPY sits far down the slope at 0. 24% of peak, a large tiled matrix multiply sits on the roof.
FLOPS: floating-point operations per second. A fused multiply-add (a multiply and an add done in one step) counts as 2.
Memory bandwidth: bytes per second between the GPU and its memory. Arithmetic intensity: operations done per byte of memory traffic.
Roofline model: attainable speed is the smaller of peak compute and bandwidth times intensity. Frame time: time to draw one frame.
Worst-case frames show stutter that average FPS (frames per second) hides.
Take 80 clusters of 128 lanes (small arithmetic units) at 1. 7 gigahertz. Peak is 80 times 128 times 2 times 1. 7 gigahertz about 34. 8 TFLOPS.
A 256-bit memory bus at 16 Gb/s per pin gives 256 times 16 over 8 equals 512 GB/s.
Now run y equals ax plus y : it does 2 operations per 12 bytes moved, which is 1/6 operation per byte.
The memory limit gives 512 times 10 to the 9 over 6 about 85 GFLOPS, about 0. 24% of peak. That is the whole idea: find which limit binds.
"I'd look at compute, memory and efficiency. Peak FLOPS is SMs times lanes times two times clock, about 35 TFLOPS for a typical card.
Memory bandwidth is bus width times data rate over eight, say 512 GB/s. The ratio, the ridge point of the roofline, tells me whether a kernel is compute- or memory-bound.
For graphics I add fill rate and frame-time percentiles. Then performance per watt and achieved versus peak, measured on my real workload including transfers."

GPU compute beyond graphics. The question: What are other tasks that GPUs may excel at besides graphics processing? Why?
A GPU helps with any job that applies the same operation to a huge amount of independent data.
The headline example is machine learning, which is mostly multiplying big grids of numbers, called matrices.
Others are scientific simulation, image and video processing, and Monte Carlo methods (averaging many random trials).
A GPU does not help with branchy code, tiny problems, or jobs where copying the data takes longer than the math.
A combine harvester is fantastic on a huge, uniform wheat field. It does the same simple action over and over across a wide area.
It is useless for picking fruit from a few winding orchard trees, where each tree needs a different decision. GPU work is the wheat field.
The harvester also has to be driven to the field first, and that trip counts.
Small matrices are slower on the GPU because launch and transfer dominate.
Past N of about 300 the cubic compute outgrows the quadratic transfer and the speed-up climbs toward the compute ratio (the gray line).
Even at N = 4096 the PCIe copy keeps it near 13x instead of 35x.
Data parallelism: the same operation on many independent data elements. GPGPU: general-purpose computing on a GPU, outside of graphics.
Tensor core: hardware that does a small matrix multiply-add in one operation. Arithmetic intensity: operations done per byte of memory traffic.
Offload: sending a job to the GPU, which adds copying costs ("Offloading work from the CPU").
Multiplying two N times N matrices takes about 2N to the 3 operations on about 12N squared bytes of data (three matrices of 4-byte numbers).
Double N , and the arithmetic grows 8 times, but the data grows only 4 times. So for small N , the copy and launch overhead make the GPU slower.
Past some size the arithmetic outgrows the copying, and the GPU wins. The page's example hardware has a break-even near N equals 300 .
That is the whole idea: the GPU wins when the job is wide, regular and arithmetic-heavy compared with its data.

"GPUs excel at anything that's the same operation over lots of independent data: machine learning, which is mostly matrix multiplies, scientific simulation, image and video processing, FFTs, Monte Carlo and hashing.
The reasons are thousands of parallel threads, regular memory access that uses the wide high-bandwidth memory, and high arithmetic intensity.
They struggle with branchy, serial or pointer-chasing code, small problems, and jobs dominated by PCIe transfers."

What is a system on chip. The question: What is a SoC?
A system on chip (SoC) is one piece of silicon that holds most of a small computer: a processor, memory, and the circuits that talk to the outside world.
Putting it all on one chip makes a product smaller and often cheaper at large volumes, and it can save power.
A few parts, such as the big main memory and the power supply, usually stay outside.
Picture an old town where each shop sits in its own village, joined by long, slow highways. A SoC is one compact city where the same shops sit a few blocks apart on short streets.
Every building has a street number, so anyone can reach it by number. The picture breaks down in one place: a chip has a fixed size and cannot hold everything.
Masters (blocks that start transactions) and slaves (blocks that respond) meet at the interconnect.
Because everything shares one address map, software talks to hardware by loads and stores. Clocking, power, reset and debug (not drawn) touch every block.
Die: the single small square of silicon that the circuits are built on. Processor core: the part that runs program instructions.
Peripheral: a block that talks to the outside world, such as a serial port (a link that sends data one bit at a time) or USB.
Interconnect: the on-chip wiring and switching that lets blocks send data to each other.
Address map: the list of numbers that says where each block lives, so software reaches a block by its number.
Microcontroller: a small SoC with a processor, built-in memory and peripherals.
The old way uses three chips: a processor, a memory chip and a serial-port chip, wired together on a board. A SoC puts all three blocks on one die.
To send a byte, the program writes it to the serial block's address. The interconnect routes that write to the serial block, which sends the byte out.
You still add a crystal (a part that sets the clock beat) outside. That is the whole idea.

"A SoC integrates a whole system, CPU cores, memory controllers, often a GPU and accelerators, peripherals like UART, SPI, USB and PCIe, plus clocks, power management and security, onto a single die, tied together by an on-chip interconnect and a shared address map.
It cuts size, power and board cost at volume, though you still need DRAM, regulators and a crystal outside, and the design effort is large. A microcontroller is a small SoC."
Quick check. Which best describes a system on chip?
SoC applications. The question: What are its applications?

A system on chip ("What is a system on chip") is a whole small computer on one piece of silicon, and you find one inside nearly every electronic product: phones, watches, cars, routers, cameras and tiny sensors.
The idea is the same everywhere. What changes is the main limit of each product, such as battery, heat, safety or speed, and that limit decides which blocks go on the chip.
Think of packing a backpack. For a day hike you take little and travel light. For a month-long expedition you take much more, but you have to carry it.
The weight you can carry is the limit, and it decides what you pack. A chip works the same way. The power it may use decides which blocks it gets.
The picture is incomplete in one way: chips also have a heat limit, and a backpack has no such limit.
Each line is life = energy / power. To get years from a coin cell the average power has to be in tens of microwatts, which is why IoT SoCs spend over 99% of time in deep sleep.
A phone has about 13x more energy than a watch but its SoC draws 100x more power on average, so it lasts hours rather than days.
Average power: total energy used divided by time, counting the idle moments too. Battery life: stored energy divided by average power.
Sleep current: the small current a chip draws while it waits and does nothing.
Accelerator: a block built for one job, like decoding video, that uses far less energy than a general processor doing the same job.
Throttling: slowing the chip down so it does not get too hot. Functional safety: designing so that faults are caught before they can hurt people, which matters in cars.
A coin cell battery stores about 0. 675 watt-hours (Wh) of energy. A sensor chip that averages 30 microwatts lasts 0. 675 over 0. 00003 equals 22 500 hours, about 2.
6 years in an ideal case. A phone battery stores 15. 4 watt hours. At an average of 1. 5 watts it lasts about 10 hours.
The formula is the same, but the power is 50,000 times different, so the chips look very different. That is the whole idea.
"SoCs power phones and tablets, wearables, IoT sensor nodes, laptops and consoles, cars, networking gear, smart TVs, cameras, drones and industrial controllers.

The architecture is the same, but the mix of blocks and the constraint differ: phones are limited by battery and heat, sensor nodes by microamps of sleep current, cars by safety and temperature range, routers by throughput.
Integration is what makes the small, low-power, low-cost versions possible."
Quick check. Which constraint most strongly shapes a coin-cell-powered wireless sensor SoC?
Components on a SoC. The question: What are some components on a SoC?
A system on chip ("What is a system on chip") is built from separate blocks, and each block has one job.

It is easiest to remember them in five groups: blocks that compute, blocks that remember, the wiring that links them, blocks that talk to the outside world, and housekeeping blocks for clock, power, security and debugging.
Think of a restaurant. The kitchen does the real work (compute). The pantry and fridge hold supplies (memory). Corridors and waiters carry things between rooms (the wiring).
The front door and the delivery entrance connect to the outside (inputs and outputs).
The manager, the electricity supply and the wall clock keep everything running (housekeeping). Every room has a numbered door, which is how software finds each block on a chip.
Compute blocks (top) are masters; memory and I/O (bottom) are slaves reached through the fabric.
Around this core sit blocks that touch everything: PLLs and clock gating, reset, the power-management unit, security and debug.
CPU core: the general-purpose part that runs program instructions.
Accelerator: a block built for one heavy job, such as graphics, camera images or neural networks, that does it with less energy than the CPU.
SRAM: fast memory built right into the chip. DMA: an engine that copies data between blocks without bothering the CPU.
Peripheral: a block that connects to the outside world, such as a UART (serial port) or USB. PLL: a circuit that turns a slow, steady clock into a much faster one.
Take a small sensor chip. It has one CPU core, memory (SRAM) for working data, a block that measures voltage, and a UART to send results out.
A DMA engine moves the readings into memory so the CPU can do other work. A PLL takes a 24 megahertz crystal and multiplies it by 100 to get 2. 4 gigahertz.
Dividing that by 2 gives a 1. 2 gigahertz clock for the CPU. Everything sits behind numbered addresses, so software controls each block by writing to its address.
That is the whole idea.
"I group them by function. Compute: CPU cores with caches, a GPU, and accelerators like NPU, DSP, ISP and video codec.
Memory: on-chip SRAM, boot ROM, a DRAM controller and PHY, flash in MCUs. A bus matrix or network-on-chip with DMA and an interrupt controller ties them together.
Peripherals: GPIO, UART, SPI, I2C, ADC, USB, PCIe, Ethernet, camera and display. Infrastructure: PLLs, resets, power management, security and debug. All in one address map."
Quick check. What is the main purpose of a DMA engine on a SoC?
SoC versus separate components. The question: What are some tradeoffs between going for a SoC vs all separate components?
You can build a product's electronics as one integrated chip (a SoC, "What is a system on chip") or as several separate chips on a board.
One chip is smaller, uses less energy to move data, and is cheaper per unit when you make many. The price is a big one-time design cost and less freedom to change parts later.
So the right choice depends mostly on how many units you will make.
Think of moving boxes inside one house versus between buildings across town. Inside the house, you carry a box a few steps.
Across town, you load a truck, drive, and unload, which takes more time and fuel. A SoC is the house: data moves short distances. Separate chips are the buildings.
The picture misses one thing: designing a custom house costs a lot up front, while renting existing buildings costs almost nothing to start.
Below about 180,000 units the discrete board has the lower average cost because the SoC's NRE is spread over too few chips.
Above it the SoC wins and approaches its 18 USD floor, while the discrete design flattens near 45 USD.
Change the NRE or unit costs and the crossover moves, which is the real content of the answer.
Energy per bit: the energy needed to send one 0 or 1 across a link. Shorter wires cost less.
NRE (non-recurring engineering): the one-time cost of designing, verifying and making the chip. Unit cost: what it costs to make each extra chip once the design exists.
Break-even volume: the number of units where two options cost the same in total. Respin: a new version of the chip made to fix a bug, which costs time and money.
Compare a custom SoC with a board of separate chips. The SoC has an NRE of 5,000,000 USD and costs 18 USD per unit. The board has an NRE of 150,000 USD and costs 45 USD per unit.
The SoC saves 27 USD per unit but costs 4,850,000 USD more up front. Break-even is 4 850 000 over 27 about 180 000 units. Below that, the board is cheaper. Above it, the SoC wins.
That is the whole idea.
"Integration wins on size, power, speed and unit cost at volume: on-die wires are shorter and cheaper to drive than package pins and traces, and you cut packages, passives and board area.
It loses on upfront NRE, schedule, flexibility and process compromises, and heat is concentrated.
So integrate when volume and size or power limits justify the NRE, and use discrete parts or a module for low volume or uncertain requirements."
Quick check. Why does integrating blocks on one die usually lower power compared with connecting them with separate chips?
Components needed around a SoC. The question: When designing a system, what other components are needed in addition to a SoC?
A SoC ("What is a system on chip") cannot run alone.
It needs power at the right voltages, a clock to set its pace, a reset to start cleanly, and, for bigger chips, outside memory and storage.
It also needs connectors, interface chips and protection to reach the real world. The job is to list what the chip cannot make for itself, and why.
Think of a car engine sitting on a workbench. It is the heart of the car, but it goes nowhere without a fuel tank, a battery, a key to start it, and wheels. The SoC is the engine.
The supporting parts are the tank, key and wheels. A board with the chip but missing power or a clock does nothing.
The SoC is the hub. Arrows from the top row are things it cannot start without (power, clock, reset); double arrows below are interfaces to external devices.
Missing a top-row item means the board will not boot; missing a bottom-row item means the product lacks a feature.
Rail: a power line held at one fixed voltage, such as 0. 9 volts or 1. 8 volts. PMIC: one chip that makes several rails and switches them on in order.
Decoupling capacitor: a small capacitor beside a power pin that supplies quick bursts of current.
Crystal: a tiny part that vibrates at a precise frequency and gives the chip its clock beat. Reset: a signal that holds the chip in a known starting state until power is stable.
PHY: a chip that turns digital data into the signals a cable carries, such as Ethernet.
An application chip needs a 0. 9 volts core rail at 3 amps, fed from a 5 volts input. The core uses 0. 9 times 3 equals 2. 7 watts.
A regulator (a circuit that turns 5 volts into 0. 9 volts) that is 88% efficient draws 2. 7 over 0. 88 about 3. 07 watts from the input. That is about 3. 07 over 5 about 0.
61 amps at 5 volts. The board also needs more rails, a crystal, a reset circuit, memory, boot storage, and a PHY for Ethernet. That is the whole idea.
"Beyond the SoC you need power: a PMIC or regulators with the right rails, sequencing and decoupling, plus a charger if it's a battery product.
Clocks and reset: a crystal or oscillator, a 32 kilohertz RTC crystal and a reset supervisor. Memory: DRAM and boot flash or eMMC unless they're on-chip.
I/O parts: PHYs, connectors, ESD protection, level shifters and radios. Then sensors, display and user I/O, plus debug access, boot straps, test points and a thermal solution."

System on module versus SoC. The question: What is a system on module (SoM)? What is the difference/tradeoffs vs a SoC?
A SoC ("What is a system on chip") is a chip.
A system on module (SoM) is a small circuit board that carries a SoC plus memory, storage and power parts, and plugs into your own board. It is a ready-made mini computer.
Using one saves design time and risk. Designing around the bare chip costs more up front but is cheaper per unit when you make many.
Think of a restaurant choosing between a ready-made sauce and cooking it from scratch.
The ready-made sauce lets you open tomorrow and avoids kitchen mistakes, but you pay more per serving.
Cooking from scratch takes time to get right, but costs less per serving once you serve thousands. The module is the ready-made sauce.
One difference: a module is a board, so it adds height and a connector to your product.
The module hides the hardest board-level design (DDR, power sequencing) behind a connector.
The carrier board then needs only the interfaces, which is why it can be a simpler, lower-layer-count PCB.
SoM (system on module): a small board with a SoC, memory, storage and power parts, sold as one unit.
Carrier board: your product's own board, with connectors and sensors, that the module plugs into. Chip-down: placing the bare SoC and its parts directly on your product board.
Board-support package (BSP): the ready-made startup software and drivers (code that runs each part) for one board.
NRE (non-recurring engineering): the one-time cost of designing and getting a design working. Break-even volume: the number of units where two options cost the same in total.
A module design has an NRE of 60,000 USD and costs 38 USD per unit. A chip-down design has an NRE of 250,000 USD and costs 24 USD per unit.
Chip-down costs 190,000 USD more up front but saves 14 USD per unit, so break-even is 190 000 over 14 about 13 600 units.
At 1,000 units, the module averages 98 USD per unit and chip-down 274 USD. That is the whole idea.
"A SoM is a small board containing a SoC plus DRAM, flash and power management, plugged into your carrier board.
The SoC is the silicon; the SoM is a ready-made mini-system around it.
A SoM cuts time to market and layout risk, since DDR routing, sequencing and the software support are done, but costs more per unit and locks you into its form factor.
Chip-down with the bare SoC wins at high volume."

Trade-offs of integration. The question: What are some tradeoffs of integration?
Putting more functions on one chip brings them close together. That saves energy, speeds things up and shrinks the product. But it has costs.
Big chips are far more likely to be ruined by a tiny flaw, so the cost of each working chip climbs fast.
Different functions also want different manufacturing recipes, noisy circuits disturb sensitive ones, and heat gathers in one spot.
The modern fix is to split a big design into smaller chips in one package.
Imagine cutting shirts from a cloth that has random stains. A small shirt panel is often clean. A huge panel almost always catches a stain, and you throw away the whole piece.
A wafer, the round slice of silicon that chips are cut from, works the same way: every flaw ruins the chip it lands on.
The cloth picture does not cover noise or heat, which are separate costs of putting things together.
Cost per good die is convex in area. Going from 100 to 600 mm² multiplies area by 6 but cost by about 12 at D0 = 0.
1, and by far more at the higher defect density of a young process (red).
This is the economic pressure behind chiplets and the reason that early in a node's life only small dies are built.
Die: one chip's piece of silicon, cut from a wafer. Defect: a tiny flaw that ruins any die it lands on. Yield: the fraction of dies that come out good.
Cost per good die: the wafer's cost divided by the number of good dies. Chiplet: a small die made to share one package (the protective case around chips) with others.
Respin: a new version of the chip made to fix a bug.
A wafer costs 10,000 USD, and flaws average 0. 1 per square centimeter. A 100 mm² die gets 640 dies per wafer, and about 90. 5% are good in a standard simple model.
That is roughly 579 good dies, or about 17 USD each. A 600 mm² die gets only 91 dies, and about 54. 9% are good. That is roughly 50 good dies, or about 200 USD each.
Six times the area costs about 12 times as much. That is the whole idea.
"Integration gives lower energy, higher bandwidth, lower latency and smaller, cheaper systems.

The costs: yield drops with die area so cost per good die rises faster than linearly; one process can't suit logic, analog, RF and memory; digital noise couples into sensitive blocks; heat concentrates; and verification, NRE and respin risk grow.

Which SoC blocks use the most power. The question: Which blocks of the SoC consume the most power?
It depends on what the chip is doing. Under heavy work, the biggest users are the compute blocks: the CPU cores, the graphics block (GPU) and, for AI work, the neural engine.
Moving data to and from main memory comes close behind. When the chip sits idle, a small leftover current called leakage matters most.
Designers save power by keeping unused blocks off.
Picture a workshop. The big machines use the most electricity while they run. Trips to a distant warehouse for materials also burn real fuel, often more than the work itself.
At night, nothing runs, but a few lights stay on, and that trickle adds up. Compute is the machines, memory trips are the warehouse runs, and leakage is the lights.
The best savings come from switching off whatever you are not using.
At 3 gigahertz both strategies use 0. 9 volts and 2. 9 watts. Dropping to 1 gigahertz with fixed voltage gives only a linear saving (0.
97 watts) but with DVFS the voltage also falls and power drops to 0. 59 watts. Energy per operation tells the same story: at 1 gigahertz the DVFS point uses (0. 7 over 0.
9) squared equals 60 % of the energy per cycle. Voltage cannot fall below a minimum where logic still meets timing, which is why DVFS curves flatten at low frequencies.
Dynamic power: power spent while circuits switch, because each switch fills or empties wires with charge.
It is about C V squared f : capacitance (how much charge the wiring holds per volt), voltage squared, and clock frequency.
Leakage: a small current that flows through transistors (the chip's tiny switches) even when nothing switches.
DVFS: lowering voltage and frequency together when less speed is needed. Clock gating: stopping the clock to an idle block so it does not switch.
Power gating: cutting the supply to an idle block, which also removes its leakage. Workload: the job the chip is doing right now.
Take a CPU cluster with an effective switched capacitance (the total capacitance that flips each cycle) of 1. 2 nanofarads. At 0. 9 volts and 2. 5 gigahertz, P equals 1.

Frequency fell to 60%, but power fell to 36%, because voltage counts squared. That is the whole idea.
"Under load it's the compute blocks, the CPU cluster and GPU, and NPU if it's running, followed closely by the memory subsystem, because moving data from DRAM costs far more than computing on it.
Dynamic power goes as alpha C V squared f, so high-voltage, high-frequency blocks dominate; at idle, leakage in SRAM and powered domains does.
Designers manage it with clock and power gating, DVFS, heterogeneous cores and fixed-function engines."

Where data and program live. The question: Where can data and program be stored in memory?
A program and its data are both just patterns of bits, so they can sit in any memory in the system.
Memories differ in speed, size, and whether they keep their contents with the power off. The program is usually stored in memory that survives power loss.
Values that change while it runs live in fast memory that forgets.
Think of an office. The filing cabinet holds everything permanently, but digging through it is slow.
Your desk holds what you are working on, and it is cleared when you leave for the night. Your hands hold the one or two things you are using this second.
The cabinet is flash or disk, the desk is RAM (such as SRAM), and your hands are the CPU's registers.
The same flat address space routes to different physical blocks.
Flash (green) holds code, constants and the initial values of globals; SRAM (blue) holds everything that changes; peripheral registers (orange) look like memory but are hardware control points.
The curved arrow is the startup copy of . data .
Non-volatile: keeps its contents with the power off. Volatile memory forgets them. Flash: non-volatile memory that holds the program and constants.
It reads fast but is slow to rewrite. SRAM: fast, volatile memory for variables that change.
Register: a tiny storage slot inside the CPU that holds the value being worked on right now. Startup code: the first code to run after reset, which prepares memory.
A small chip has 64 KB of flash and 20 KB of SRAM. The program code is 38 KB, constants such as lookup tables are 6 KB, and the starting values of variables are 1 KB.
Flash holds 38 plus 6 plus 1 equals 45 KB. At power-up, the startup code copies those 1 KB of starting values into SRAM.
SRAM also holds 3 KB of variables that start at zero, so 4 KB in all.
That leaves 16 KB for the stack (scratch space for function calls) and the heap (memory a program asks for while running). That is the whole idea.
"Program and data are both just bits, so they can live in registers, caches, SRAM, DRAM, flash and disk. At rest the program sits in non-volatile memory like flash or an SSD.
When it runs, instructions and data are brought into RAM and then into caches and registers.
On a microcontroller, code and constants stay in flash, variables and the stack live in SRAM, and the startup code copies initialized globals from flash into RAM.
Von Neumann machines share one memory for both, Harvard machines keep them separate."

Data memory vs program memory. The question: What is the difference between data and program memory?
Program memory holds the instructions a CPU follows. Data memory holds the values those instructions work on, such as variables and buffers.
The difference is mostly about role: instructions are read in order, while data is read and written all the time.
Some chips keep the two in separate memories, and others share one memory for both.
Picture trucks crossing a river. Instruction trucks bring the next step to the CPU. Data trucks bring or take away the numbers it works on.
With one shared bridge, the trucks take turns, so a data truck makes an instruction truck wait. With two bridges, both cross at the same time.
The shared bridge has one advantage the picture hides: you can use its space for whatever you need, with no fixed split.
Left, one bus carries both instruction fetches and data traffic, so they must take turns.
Right, two buses let the CPU fetch the next instruction while the current one reads or writes data.
Program counter (PC): the CPU's bookmark, holding the address of the next instruction to read. Load/store: instructions that read data from memory or write data to it.
Harvard architecture: separate memories and paths for instructions and data. Von Neumann architecture: one memory and one path shared by both.
CPI: the average number of clock cycles (ticks of the chip's timing beat) each instruction takes.
An ATmega328P microcontroller is a Harvard chip. It has 32 KB of flash (memory that keeps data without power) for the program and 2 KB of SRAM (fast memory that forgets) for data.
Now take a simple processor that reads one instruction per cycle, where 30% of instructions are loads or stores.
With one shared memory, each load or store blocks the next instruction fetch for one extra cycle. So CPI equals 1 plus 0. 30 equals 1. 30 . With separate memories, CPI stays at 1.
0. The Harvard design is 1. 3 times faster at the same clock. That is the whole idea.
"Program memory holds the instructions the CPU fetches with the program counter; data memory holds the variables and buffers the instructions load and store.
Program memory is mostly read-only at run time and often non-volatile flash, while data memory is read/write, usually SRAM.

In a Harvard architecture they're physically separate so you can fetch and access data in the same cycle; in von Neumann they share one memory and bus, which is more flexible but creates a bottleneck.
Modern CPUs use split L1 caches over a unified main memory."

The memory hierarchy and its trade-offs. The question: Explain the memory hierarchy. What are the tradeoffs of each? What type of data is stored in each?
The memory hierarchy is a stack of storage types. At the top, storage is tiny and very fast. At the bottom, it is huge but slow.
No single technology is fast, big and cheap at once, so computers combine several. The stack works because programs reuse recent data and touch nearby data.
A small fast memory can therefore answer most requests.
Think of cooking. Salt sits on the counter, within reach. Milk is in the fridge, a few steps away. Flour is in the pantry down the hall.
Anything else means a trip to the supermarket. You keep what you use most close by, so most of the time you never leave the kitchen.
One difference: the fast levels in a computer hold copies of what the slower levels hold.
Each step to the right adds about a decade or two of capacity and one to three decades of latency.
Notice the large gaps: DRAM to SSD is roughly 1000x and SSD to disk about 100x, which is why paging to disk is catastrophic compared with a cache miss.
Latency: the time you wait for memory to answer. Locality: programs tend to reuse recent data and use data stored next to it.
Cache: ("What a cache is and how it works"): a small, fast memory that keeps copies of recently used data. Hit / miss: a hit finds the data in the fast level.
A miss must go to a slower level. DRAM: ("What RAM is (SRAM vs DRAM)"): the large main memory, slower than a cache.
AMAT: average memory access time, equal to hit time plus miss rate times the extra time a miss costs.
A fast cache answers in 1 nanoseconds, and the main memory (DRAM) answers in 80 nanoseconds. Say 95% of accesses hit the cache and 5% miss and go to DRAM.
Then the average time is 1 plus 0. 05 times 80 equals 5 nanoseconds. Without the cache, every access takes 80 nanoseconds, so the cache makes the average 16 times faster.
That is the whole idea.
"The memory hierarchy stacks storage levels, each bigger, slower and cheaper than the last: registers, L1/L2/L3 SRAM caches, DRAM main memory, then SSD or disk.
No one technology is fast, large and cheap, so we exploit locality: keep the working set in small fast levels and most accesses never reach the slow ones.
Registers hold live operands, caches hold copies of hot code and data, DRAM holds running programs, storage holds everything persistently.
With a 95 percent L1 hit rate and 80 nanoseconds DRAM, average access time drops from 80 nanoseconds to a few ns."
Quick check. Why does a memory hierarchy improve performance?
What a cache is and how it works. The question: What is a cache?
A cache is a small, very fast memory between the processor and the slow main memory. It keeps copies of data the processor used recently, plus the data stored next to it.
The processor is far faster than main memory, so without a cache it would mostly wait. Programs reuse recent data and read neighbors, so a small cache answers most requests.
Think of the speed-dial list on a phone. It holds a few numbers, while the full phone book holds thousands.
Most calls go to people you called recently, so the short list usually has the number.
When it does not, you search the big book, add the number, and drop the one you used longest ago. The list is a copy of part of the book.
The index addresses one set, the tag is compared against every way in that set simultaneously, and the offset selects bytes within the matching 64-byte line.
The three field widths sum to the address width: 20 + 6 + 6 = 32.
Cache line: the chunk of memory, usually 64 bytes, that the cache copies in one go. Hit / miss: a hit finds the data in the cache.
A miss does not, so the line must come from main memory. Locality: programs tend to reuse recent data and read data next to it.
Tag: a label stored with each line, saying which memory address it copies. Eviction: throwing out an old line to make room for a new one.
A program adds up an array of 4-byte numbers in order. A 64-byte line holds 16 numbers. The first read misses, and the cache copies the whole line. The next 15 reads hit.
So the miss rate is 1 over 16 equals 6. 25 % . Say a hit takes 1 nanoseconds and each miss costs 80 nanoseconds extra. The average is 1 plus 0.
0625 times 80 equals 6 nanoseconds per read, instead of 80 nanoseconds with no cache. That is the whole idea.
"A cache is a small, fast SRAM between the CPU and main memory that holds copies of recently used data and instructions.
It works because of locality: programs reuse data and use neighboring data.

The address is split into tag, index and offset; the index selects a set, tags are compared, and a match is a hit in a cycle or few; otherwise it's a miss and a 64-byte line is fetched from the next level.
With a 95 percent hit rate and 80 nanoseconds DRAM, average access time falls from 80 nanoseconds to about 5 nanoseconds."
Quick check. Why do caches improve performance?
What registers are. The question: What are registers?
A register is a small piece of storage inside the processor that holds one value, such as a 32-bit number. Registers are the fastest storage in the whole system.
The processor takes the numbers for each operation from registers and puts the answer back into a register. A processor has only a few of them, and each has a purpose or a name.
Picture a mechanic's workbench with 32 numbered trays within arm's reach. An instruction says "add tray 5 and tray 6, put the answer in tray 7".
No searching is needed, because the tray number tells you exactly where to go. Only a few trays fit, since a longer bench means a longer reach for every tool.
The warehouse across the yard is main memory: far bigger, but much slower.
The register only changes on a clock edge when write-enable is high: the edge with WE = 1 captures 0x1 farads, while the later value 0xA0 on D in is ignored because WE has dropped.
Between edges the value is stable, which is exactly what makes registers the "memory" of synchronous logic.
Flip-flop: a circuit that stores one bit and updates it on a clock tick. Register: a group of flip-flops that holds one multi-bit value. A 32-bit register is 32 flip-flops.
Register file: the whole set of registers, plus the wiring to read two and write one at a time. Program counter: a register holding the address of the next instruction.
Spilling: parking a value in memory when the registers are full. Peripheral register: a control or status register for a hardware block, at a fixed address.
A simple RISC-V processor (RV32I) has 32 registers of 32 bits each. That is 32 times 32 equals 1024 bits, or 128 bytes of storage.
The instruction "add register 5 and register 6, put the result in register 7" names three registers.
Each name needs 5 bits to pick one of 32, so the instruction spends 3 times 5 equals 15 bits on them. The processor reads two registers and writes one. That is the whole idea.
"A register is a small, very fast storage element inside the CPU made of flip-flops: an n-bit register is n D flip-flops sharing a clock and write enable.
Registers are the top of the memory hierarchy: the ALU reads operands from them and writes results back in about a cycle.
There are general-purpose registers, plus special ones like the program counter, stack pointer and status flags, and pipeline registers between stages.
They're named in the instruction rather than addressed, so there are only a few.
Peripheral control registers in a microcontroller work the same way but sit at memory-mapped addresses."

What RAM is (SRAM vs DRAM). The question: What is RAM?
RAM is working memory that you can both read and write, where any location takes about the same time to reach. There are two main kinds.
SRAM stores each bit in a small circuit that holds its value while power is on.
It is fast but takes a lot of space, so it is used for caches (small, fast memories next to the processor). DRAM stores each bit as a tiny electric charge.
It is smaller and cheaper, so it is used for main memory, but the charge leaks away and must be topped up.
SRAM is a light switch. Once you set it on or off, it stays there. DRAM is a bucket with a slow leak: a full bucket means 1 and an empty one means 0.
You must refill the full buckets every so often, before they run dry. Checking a DRAM bucket means pouring it out to see what was in it, so it is refilled after each read.

Two cross-coupled inverters (the outputs Q and QB feed each other's input) hold one bit; the word line WL turns on both access NMOS transistors so the bit-line pair BL/BLB can read or overwrite the latch.
Volatile: loses its contents when power is removed. Transistor: a tiny electrically controlled switch.
Capacitor: a tiny part that stores electric charge, like a very small bucket.
Refresh: reading and rewriting every DRAM row (one line of cells) regularly, before its charge leaks away.
Sense amplifier: a circuit that detects a tiny voltage change and boosts it to a clear 0 or 1.
Compare 1 MB of each. 1 MB is 8,388,608 bits. An SRAM cell uses 6 transistors, so the array needs about 50 million transistors.
A DRAM cell uses 1 transistor and 1 capacitor, so it needs about 8. 4 million of each. That is why DRAM packs far more bits into the same area.
The price is refresh, which happens every 64 milliseconds or so, and slower access. That is the whole idea.
"RAM is random-access, read/write, normally volatile working memory. There are two main types.
SRAM stores a bit in a six-transistor latch, so it's fast and needs no refresh but takes a lot of area; it's used for caches and on-chip RAM.

DRAM stores a bit as charge on a capacitor with one access transistor, so it's dense and cheap but slower, reads are destructive, and the charge leaks, so rows must be refreshed every tens of milliseconds.
Hence SRAM for small fast levels and DRAM for large main memory."
Quick check. How many transistors are in a standard SRAM cell?
What "random access" means. The question: What does "random access" refer to?
"Random access" means you can reach any location in memory directly, and it takes about the same time whichever one you pick or whichever one you used last.
"Random" does not mean the data is random. It means the order of access can be anything.
The opposite is sequential access, where you must pass through everything stored before the item you want.
Compare a music CD with a cassette tape. On a CD, you jump straight to track 12. On a cassette, you wind past tracks 1 to 11, and the wait depends on how far away the track is.
RAM works like the CD: the hardware picks the exact spot from its number. The comparison is not perfect: in real memory, some nearby accesses are a bit faster than others.
Horizontal lines (RAM, SSD) are what "random access" means: distance does not matter.

The HDD curve rises roughly with the square root of distance (seek) on top of a 4 milliseconds rotational term, and tape rises linearly with distance (it looks compressed only because the y-axis is logarithmic).
Values are illustrative orders of magnitude, not specs.
Address: the number that names one memory location. Access time (latency): the wait between asking for data and getting it.
Sequential access: reaching data only by passing through everything stored before it, as on tape.
Address decoder: a circuit that turns an address into a signal that selects exactly one row of memory. Row buffer: the open row inside a DRAM chip.
Reading from an open row is faster than opening a new one.
A hard disk is in between the two. On a disk spinning 7200 times a minute, a random 4 KB read waits about 8 milliseconds for the reading arm to move, then 4.
17 milliseconds on average for the disk to spin the data under it. That is about 12 milliseconds, or about 82 reads per second, which is only 0. 34 MB/s.
Reading the same disk in order streams about 150 MB/s, over 400 times faster. In RAM, the position hardly matters, and each read takes tens of nanoseconds. That is the whole idea.
"Random access means any address can be read or written in about the same time, independent of where you accessed last, because an address decoder selects the cell directly.
It doesn't mean the data is random.
It's contrasted with sequential access like tape, where reaching a location means winding past everything before it, and semi-random media like hard disks, where seek and rotation depend on position.
Real DRAM isn't perfectly uniform because of row buffers and caches, but the hardware still gives direct access to any byte."

What is stack overflow?. The question: What is stack overflow?
The stack is a region of memory where the computer keeps track of the functions (named pieces of a program) running right now.
Every call adds one block, and every return removes one. A stack overflow happens when the blocks pile up past the memory reserved for the stack.
Common causes are a function that keeps calling itself, or a very large list of values declared inside a function. A big computer stops the program with an error.
A small chip often keeps going and silently damages other data.
Picture a plate dispenser in a cafeteria, a well of fixed depth. Each call puts a plate on top, and each return takes the top plate off. Pile on too many and they overflow.
On a PC, a solid wall sits at the bottom of the well, so you notice at once.
On a small chip, the well sits right next to your other belongings, and extra plates silently knock them over.
Each recursive call adds one frame below the previous one. The stack pointer (SP) walks toward low addresses.
When it crosses the end of the allocated region, a system with a guard page faults immediately; a system without one lets it silently overwrite whatever is next.
Stack frame: the block for one call. It holds the return address (where to go back to) and that function's local variables.
Stack pointer: a register (a tiny storage slot in the processor) that marks the current top of the stack. Recursion: a function that calls itself.
Guard page: a protected piece of memory just past the stack that triggers an error if touched.
A recursive function uses 48 bytes per call. A PC with an 8 MB stack fits about 8 388 608 over 48 about 175 000 nested calls.
The next call touches the guard page, and the program stops with an error. A small chip with a 2 KB stack and 24 bytes per call fits only about 2048 over 24 about 85 calls.
With no guard, call 86 silently overwrites whatever sits next to the stack. That is the whole idea.
"A stack overflow is when the call stack outgrows the region of memory reserved for it.
Each function call pushes a frame with the return address and locals, so very deep or infinite recursion, or big local arrays, can push the stack pointer past the limit.
On a PC the OS has a guard page, so you get a segfault. On a microcontroller with no MMU it silently overwrites globals or the heap.
You prevent it by avoiding unbounded recursion, keeping big buffers off the stack, and measuring the stack high-water mark."

Stack versus heap. The question: What is the difference between the stack and the heap?
The stack and the heap are two parts of RAM that hold data created while a program runs. The stack is for function calls. It is automatic, very fast, small and fixed in size.
The heap is for data that must outlive a call or whose size is unknown until the program runs. You ask for a piece and give it back yourself.
The heap is flexible but slower, and it can leak or fragment. Small chips in gadgets therefore use the stack and fixed buffers wherever they can.
The stack is a pile of papers on your desk. You add each new one on top, and you always remove the top one first. The heap is a parking lot.
Cars stay as long as their owners want, and they leave in any order. After many cars come and go, empty spaces are scattered.
A bus may not fit even when plenty of spaces are empty in total.
Code and globals are fixed at link time. The stack and heap are the two regions that change size at runtime, growing toward each other from opposite ends of the free RAM.
On a desktop, virtual memory makes the gap huge; on a microcontroller it may be a few hundred bytes.
Stack: memory for function calls. It is freed automatically, newest first. Heap: memory you request and release yourself, in any order.
malloc / free: the C calls that request a heap block and give it back. Memory leak: a heap block you never freed and can no longer use.
Fragmentation: free memory split into pieces too small to use. Memory pool: a set of equal-size blocks reused with no fragmentation.
Allocating on the stack is one subtraction from the stack pointer (the number marking the top of the stack), and returning undoes it. A heap block needs a search for free space.
Picture a 1,000-byte heap holding ten 100-byte blocks, all in use. Free the five odd-numbered blocks.
Now 500 bytes are free, but the biggest hole is only 100 bytes, so malloc(200) fails. That is the whole idea.
"The stack holds function-call frames: locals and return addresses.
It's allocated by moving the stack pointer, freed automatically on return, fast and cache friendly, but small and strictly LIFO.
The heap holds data that has to outlive a call or has a runtime-determined size.
It's allocated with malloc and freed explicitly, so it's flexible but slower and can leak or fragment.
In embedded I prefer stack and static allocation because the heap can fail unpredictably in the field."
Quick check. Which statement correctly contrasts stack and heap allocation?
Memory management unit (MMU). The question: What is a memory management unit (MMU)? What does it do and why is it needed?
A memory management unit (MMU) is a hardware block that sits between the processor and memory. Programs use made-up "virtual" addresses.
The MMU translates each one into the real address in RAM, and it checks that the program is allowed to touch that spot.
This keeps programs from damaging each other or the operating system. It also lets every program believe it has its own large, tidy block of memory.
Think of a hotel. Each guest is told "your room is number 12", but guest A's room 12 and guest B's room 12 are different real rooms.
The front desk looks up the real room and refuses to let guests into rooms that are not theirs. The MMU is the front desk.
It keeps a cheat sheet of recent lookups, so most guests are answered in an instant.
Each 9-bit index picks one of 512 entries in a 4 KB table; that entry points to the next table, and the last level yields the physical frame.
The 12-bit offset bypasses translation. A full walk costs up to four dependent memory reads, which is exactly what the TLB exists to avoid.
Virtual address: the address a program uses. Physical address: the real location in RAM. Page: a fixed-size block of memory, usually 4 KB, translated as one unit.
Page table: the operating system's lookup table from virtual pages to real locations. TLB: a small, fast memory of recent translations.
Page fault: the error signal when an address has no translation or the access is not allowed.
Pages are 4,096 bytes. A program uses virtual address 5,000. That is page 1 (bytes 4,096 to 8,191), at offset 5000-4096 equals 904 inside the page.
The page table says virtual page 1 sits in real frame 7 (a page-sized slot in RAM). The real address is 7 times 4096 plus 904 equals 29 576 .
The offset passes through unchanged, and only the page number is swapped. Another program's page 1 can map to a different frame, so neither sees the other's data.
That is the whole idea.
"The MMU sits between the CPU and memory and translates the virtual addresses programs use into physical addresses, using page tables, with a TLB caching recent translations.
It also checks read, write and execute permissions on every access.

We need it for isolation between processes and the kernel, for giving every program a clean contiguous address space on top of fragmented RAM, and for features like demand paging and shared libraries.
Small microcontrollers skip it and use a simpler MPU."

Radiation-induced memory errors in space.
The question: If I'm operating my computer in space where there can be lots of radiation that can corrupt my memory, what issues can arise?
What can I do to be resilient against these effects?
Space is full of fast charged particles. When one hits a memory chip, it can flip a stored 0 into a 1, or the other way round. This is called a single-event upset.
The chip is not damaged, but the data is now wrong. A flipped bit in a program or setting can crash a spacecraft. Worse events can burn out a chip, or slowly wear it down.
Designers add error correction, repeat checking, spare copies and recovery tricks.
Picture a ball resting in one of two valleys. Which valley holds it is the stored bit. A strong enough kick sends the ball over the hill into the other valley.
The landscape is unharmed, and putting the ball back fixes it. A cosmic particle is such a kick. A weak one does nothing. A strong one flips the bit.
A few rare ones damage the landscape itself.
The same particle can cause very different results depending on where it lands.
SEU and SET are soft errors; latch-up can be destructive, and TID (not shown) accumulates over time.
Single-event upset (SEU): a bit flipped by one particle strike. Soft error: wrong data with undamaged hardware. Rewriting the bit fixes it.
Latch-up: a particle triggers a short circuit inside the chip, which can burn it out. ECC: extra check bits that let hardware find and fix a flipped bit.
Scrubbing: regularly reading memory, correcting errors and rewriting the data. TMR: triple modular redundancy, meaning three copies with a majority vote.
Protect each 64-bit word with 8 extra check bits. That adds 8 over 64 equals 12. 5 % storage.
The code can fix any one flipped bit and can detect two flipped bits, but not fix them. A word left alone for months might collect two flips.
Scrubbing prevents that by correcting each word often. For circuits that compute rather than store, TMR runs three copies. If they output 1, 1 and 0, the vote returns 1.
That is the whole idea.
"Radiation particles can deposit charge in silicon and flip a stored bit, a single-event upset, which silently corrupts data or instructions.
Worse events include latch-up, which can burn the chip, and accumulated dose that degrades transistors.

To be resilient I'd use ECC on all memories with scrubbing so errors don't accumulate, triple modular redundancy or lockstep for critical logic, radiation-tolerant parts with latch-up protection, and system-level watchdogs and recovery.
Shielding helps but isn't enough on its own."
Quick check. What is a single-event upset (SEU)?
Clock frequency, power and thermals. The question: How does clock frequency impact power, performance, and thermals?
Clock frequency is how many steps per second a chip takes. A faster clock gets more work done per second, but it uses more power, and that power turns into heat.
Faster clocks also need a higher supply voltage, so power grows faster than speed does.
Heat then limits how fast the chip can run for long, so chips slow themselves down when they get too hot.
Picture an assembly line. A faster belt makes more items per minute at the same energy each, so power rises in step with speed.
But past a certain speed, workers need overtime pay to keep up, and that makes every item cost more. Doubling the speed then costs more than double the power.
The factory also warms up, and a hot factory wastes more energy, which warms it further.
A purely compute-bound workload (m = 0) gets the full 2x; a workload that is half memory-bound gets only 1. 33x.
This is why raising the clock alone is a poor way to speed up memory-bound code, and why caches and memory bandwidth matter.
Clock frequency: the number of ticks per second, in hertz. The chip takes one step per tick.
Dynamic power: power spent on switching, equal to alpha C V squared f : the charge the flipping wires hold per volt ( alpha C ), times voltage squared, times frequency.
Leakage: power that flows even when nothing switches. It rises as the chip heats up. Thermal resistance ( theta ): how many degrees the chip warms per watt.
Throttling: lowering the clock so the chip stays cool. DVFS: changing voltage and frequency together to match the load.
Take a chip with alpha C = 20 nanofarads. At 2 gigahertz and 0. 9 volts, power is 20 times 10 to the -9 times 0. 9 squared times 2 times 10 to the 9 equals 32. 4 watts.
At 4 gigahertz it needs 1. 1 volts, so power is 20 times 10 to the -9 times 1. 1 squared times 4 times 10 to the 9 equals 96. 8 watts.
Twice the frequency costs about 3 times the power. With theta equals 0. 5 K/W (0.
5 degrees Celsius per watt) and a 45 degrees Celsius surrounding, the chip runs at about 61 degrees Celsius and then about 93 degrees Celsius. That is the whole idea.
"Dynamic power is alpha C V squared f , so at fixed voltage it's linear in frequency.
Performance also rises with frequency, but only for the part of the workload not waiting on memory.
The catch is that higher frequency needs higher voltage to meet timing, so along a DVFS curve power grows much faster than linearly, about 3x for 2x frequency in a typical example.
All that power becomes heat, T j equals T a plus P theta , and leakage rises with temperature, which can feed back into throttling.
That's why frequency is the main knob for managing power and thermals."

Why multiple clock domains. The question: Why are multiple clock domains needed?
A chip is not one block ticking to one clock. A processor wants a very fast clock, and a serial port (a slow one-bit-at-a-time link) needs only a slow one.
Interfaces like USB have clocks set by standards. Separate clock domains let each part run only as fast as it needs, which saves power.
The price is that passing signals between unrelated clocks is risky and needs special circuits.
Picture a baton relay between two runners who each step to their own drumbeat.
If the first hands over the baton at a random moment, the second may fumble it, and for a moment neither holds it nor has dropped it.
A safe design hands the baton to a waiting shelf first. The second runner picks it up one full beat later, once it has settled.
Both flops are clocked by the destination clock (CLK B). FF1 samples the asynchronous input and may become metastable; the full cycle before FF2 samples gives it time to resolve.
Never put logic between FF1 and FF2.
Clock domain: a group of circuits driven by one clock, or by clocks with a fixed relationship. Flip-flop: a circuit that stores one bit, capturing its input on each clock tick.
Metastability: a flip-flop stuck between 0 and 1 for a short while, because its input changed just as it captured.
Synchronizer: two flip-flops (flops, for short) in a row that give the first one time to settle. Gray code: a counting code where each step changes only one bit.
For a single-bit signal, a synchronizer on the receiving side gives the first flop a full tick to settle before the second reads it. A multi-bit counter is trickier.
Binary 0111 (7) goes to 1000 (8), and all four bits change. If the other side samples mid-change, it may read 1111 (15), a value that never existed.
In Gray code, 7 is 0100 and 8 is 1100, so only one bit differs, and a sample is either 7 or 8. That is the whole idea.
"Different blocks need different clock rates: CPUs run at GHz, peripherals at a few MHz, an always-on timer at 32 kilohertz, and interfaces like USB or DDR have clocks set by their standards.
Separate domains let me save dynamic power, apply DVFS and clock gating per block, and keep clock trees manageable.
The price is clock domain crossing: signals between unrelated clocks can go metastable, so I use synchronizers for single bits and Gray-coded async FIFOs or handshakes for buses."
